While Lincoln and Davis are bleeding each other white in the Potomac mud, there will not be a federal garrison left standing between the Rio Grande and the Fraser River. Ready the Third and Fourth Lancers for desert service. We are staying out of their war so that when they are both on their knees, there will be no one left to dispute the peace."

***

Three thousand miles to the east, under a blazing July sun that turned the red clay of northern Virginia into a choking haze of brick-dust, General Marcus Vance sat his lathered chestnut gelding on the crest of Matthews Hill and watched the nineteenth century tear itself to ribbons through a pair of Carl Zeiss field-glasses.

He was thirty-three now, though the severe lines carved from his nostrils to the corners of his mouth made him look ten years older. He wore no uniform—only a plain civilian riding-coat of gray-blue linen covered in fine red dust, with the brass badge of an accredited foreign military observer pinned to his lapel alongside the Prussian and French attachés. In his saddle-bags lay an official diplomatic passport signed by Elias Thorne, accrediting him to the War Department in Washington as an "Inspector of Sanitary and Logistics Commissions from the Neutral Territory of California"—a thin polite fiction that Secretary Seward had swallowed only because Washington dared not provoke a second war on the Pacific while rebel campfires were visible from the dome of the Capitol.

Below him, across the shallow, muddy ditch of Bull Run and up the long, trampled slope of Henry House Hill, fifty thousand men who six weeks ago had been dry-goods clerks in Boston, plough-boys in Ohio, and law-students in Carolina were butchering one another in a chaos so amateurish it made Marcus’s teeth ache.

"Look at their intervals, Colonel," muttered Major von Wrangel, the Prussian observer, reining his horse beside Marcus and spitting a mouthful of Virginia dust into the trampled clover. Through the swirling gray fog of unrefined black-powder smoke, a regiment of New York Zouaves in ridiculous baggy scarlet trousers was advancing straight into a pine copse without skirmishers, their ranks bunched like sheep at a gate. "No flank-guards. No unified artillery reserve. Their generals ride about waving their hats like country squires at a fox-hunt, and half their muskets are smoothbore conversions from the Mexican war!"

Marcus did not lower his glasses. The smell of the battlefield drifted up the slope—not the clean, sharp ozone and coal-smoke of the Pacifica proving grounds, where Krupp breech-loaders fired by the stopwatch, but the sour, stomach-turning stench of badly corned black powder, burning wool, scorched horse-hair, and the open latrines of undisciplined volunteer camps.

"Watch the batteries on the crest, Major," Marcus said, his voice flat and clinical, his left hand resting on the leather case where he kept his pocket chronometer and his topographical sketchbook. "Ricketts and Griffin have pushed twelve rifled pieces within three hundred yards of that rebel brigade by the pine-belt without infantry support on their right flank. They think they are still shooting at Mexican peons at Buena Vista."

Even as he spoke, a long, ragged line of men in dirty gray homespun and faded militia wool rose out of the scrub-pines behind the Henry house. A single, crashing volley of musketry tore through the afternoon heat. Through his lenses, Marcus saw the Federal artillery horses go down in a kicking, screaming tangle of severed traces; he saw the red-legged Zouaves break into a stumbling run toward the rear, throwing away their haversacks and blanket-rolls as a wild, high-pitched yipping cry—like a pack of prairie coyotes—rose from the Southern line.

Within twenty minutes, the Federal right wing was not retreating; it was dissolving.

Marcus slipped his field-glasses back into their leather case, buckled the strap with neat, unhurried fingers, and pulled out his notebook. While the French attaché beside him cursed in excitement and the civilian congressmen who had driven out from Washington in barouches with picnic hampers of cold chicken and champagne began whipping their carriage-horses in blind panic toward the Stone Bridge, Marcus calmly penciled three lines of figures under the heading: *Deficiencies of Atlantic Ordnance and Command.*

A stray twelve-pound solid shot from a rebel smoothbore bounced across the turnpike fifty yards below them, smashing the rear axle of a Congressman’s phaeton and sending a shower of splintered hickory and wickerwork into the air. A fat gentleman in a white beaver hat tumbled out into the ditch, screaming that the Black Horse Cavalry was upon them, while hundreds of grime-streaked Union soldiers pushed past his overturned wheels, their eyes wide and blank, their rifles dropped in the weeds.

"My God, Vance, we must ride for Centreville before the bridge is choked!" shouted a young clerk from the British Legation, his mare rearing as a riderless artillery caisson thundered down the grade behind four maddened horses, its iron tires striking sparks from the limestone macadam.

Marcus did not touch his spurs. He sat motionless in the midst of the rout, watching the proud Republic that had burned Elias’s cabin—the Republic that had threatened to hang them all as traitors in ’fifty-three—choking on its own hubris in a dusty Virginia lane. These men had no staff college. They had no rolling mills capable of casting a single steel breech-block. They would fight here in the mud and the briars for four years, perhaps five, grinding their youth and their gold into bloody mulch until their cities were bankrupt and their fields were graves.

And on the other side of the continent, behind the granite wall of the Sierra, four hundred thousand tons of Pacifica iron were cooling in the molds.

A wild-eyed colonel of Ohio volunteers, his coat-tail shot away and blood trickling from a powder-burn on his cheek, stumbled out of the choking dust-cloud and grabbed wildly at Marcus’s stirrup-leather.

"Give me that horse!" the officer rasped, his hand fumbling at the empty holster on his belt as a second shell burst high in the hot air above the turnpike, raining iron fragments into the roadside oaks. "In the name of the United States Government, I requisition this mount to rally the brigade at Cub Run! Get out of the saddle, damn you!"

Marcus looked down at the sweating, panicked face of the citizen-soldier. With a slow, deliberate movement of his right hand, he drew the hidden five-shot Colt revolver from his saddle-holster and laid the cold octagonal barrel directly across the bridge of the colonel’s nose.

"Take your hand off my leather," Marcus said, his voice cutting through the roar of the stampede like a surgical saw through bone. "The United States Government has no jurisdiction under this saddle, Colonel. Keep walking toward the river."

The Ohioan froze, staring into the dark bore of the San Francisco pistol and the colder, deadlier gray eyes behind it. He let go of the stirrup and stumbled backward into the ditch as Marcus turned his chestnut’s head neatly toward the south—not toward Washington, where the beaten rabble was streaming, but toward the telegraph relay at Alexandria, to wire the Protector via the Havana cable that the bleeding had begun.

***

Two thousand miles southwest of that Virginia ditch, where the Santa Cruz River shrank to a warm, alkaline trickle between banks of blistered caliche and giant saguaro cacti, Elias did not wait for Marcus’s cipher. The desert air at noon was a brass furnace, thick with the dry, resinous tang of creosote bush, hot iron, and the rank lather of six hundred garrison-fed cavalry mounts.

Before him lay the adobe ramparts of the Tucson Federal Arsenal—the central ordnance depot for the New Mexico Territory, where the War Department had stockpiled twelve thousand Springfield rifle-muskets, four hundred barrels of DuPont cannon powder, and sixteen bronze mountain howitzers to keep the Apaches and the Texans in check. Above the flat mud roof, the thirty-four-star bunting of the Union hung limp and faded against a sky the color of bleached bone.

"Major Crittenden says he has orders from Santa Fe to burn the magazine rather than surrender the keys to irregulars, sir," said Colonel Caleb Vance. The old man was past fifty now, his beard white as gypsum dust against his dark navy tunic, sitting his mule beside a low breastwork of mesquite logs where two of Elias’s new steam-tractors had dragged a pair of rifled twelve-pounder Krupp breech-loaders into battery. The portable donkey-boilers behind the caissons hissed softly, leaking small plumes of oily vapor that reeked of scorched mineral lubricant and sulfur.

Elias lowered his binoculars. He wore no gold lace in the field—only a dust-caked linen duster over his blue wool coat and a broad-brimmed campaign hat pulled low against the glare. Since crossing the Colorado at Yuma ten days prior, he had not fired a shot. The outlying federal dragoon posts along the Gila had simply looked at the flanking columns of Pacifica Lancers, counted the repeating carbines and the iron-plated supply wagons rolling on wide traction wheels, and stacked their arms in exchange for silver transit-vouchers to the Missouri border.

Why Crittenden—a stubborn Kentuckian whose father had once sat on the bench in Lexington—chose to bar the heavy mesquite gates of the Tucson compound with seventy fever-riddled regulars was a question of pride, not tactics. And pride, as Elias had learned on the Platte, was poor cover against steel.

"He won’t burn it," Elias said, his rough, low voice scarcely louder than the pant of the traction-engine’s steam-valve. "His wife and three daughters are inside the adobe commandant’s quarters right behind the powder-house. A man who talks about blowing himself up before breakfast is just asking for a receipt to show his court-martial."

He turned in the saddle toward the young Japanese artillery lieutenant—one of twenty Bakufu samurai sent from Nagasaki to study Western siege-craft under the Treaty of Edo—who stood beside the right-hand Krupp piece with a brass quadrant in his gloved hand.

"Lieutenant Takashima," Elias said. "Do not touch the magazine. Put one solid conical bolt through the second-story adobe two feet beneath the flagstaff. Cut the timber beam that holds the garrison bell."

"*Hai*, Protector," Takashima replied in clipped, precise English. He stepped back, raised a small red signal pennon, and dropped it.

The breech-loader did not roar with the dull, booming thud of an Eastern smoothbore; it cracked like a giant whip, spitting a flat, vicious tongue of orange flame and a cloud of sharp blue smoke. A heartbeat later, four hundred yards down the glare-white plain, the top of the arsenal’s watchtower dissolved into a geyser of red dust and pulverized sun-dried brick. The heavy bronze mission bell, hung there by Spanish friars a century before, tore loose from its shattered crossbeam and plunged through the roof of the guardhouse with a brazen, discordant clang that echoed off the Santa Catalina mountains.

Before the brick-dust had settled back onto the prickly-pear, Elias touched his rowels to his horse’s flanks. He did not order the Lancers forward; he rode alone up the baked wagon-trace toward the gate, his hands resting loosely on his pommel, the hot wind lifting the skirts of his linen duster.

From the loopholed parapet above the gate, three rifle barrels poked out through the mud bricks, wavering in the heat-shimmer.

"Halt there!" bawled Major Crittenden’s voice from behind the timber parapet. The top of his foraging cap appeared over the adobe crest, white with powdered clay. "Halt, or I’ll give you a volley! You are on property of the United States War Department, Mr. Thorne! There is no truce between Washington and Sacramento for armed brigandage!"

Elias reined in thirty paces from the gate, right in the open beaten zone where a recruit could not miss a barn door. He looked up at the sweating face under the blue cap.

"There is no War Department within fifteen hundred miles of this ditch, Major," Elias called back, his voice carrying clearly across the dead quiet of the desert noon. "General Twiggs has already surrendered the Texas garrisons to the Southern secessionists. Colonel Loring resigned his commission in Santa Fe forty-eight hours ago to ride for Richmond. The pay-wagons from Fort Leavenworth were captured by Missouri bushwhackers on the Arkansas River last Tuesday. Whom are you holding these rifles for?"

Crittenden’s jaw worked behind his graying whiskers. "For the Union, damn your eyes! My oath is to the Constitution!"

"Your oath is to a government that has left seventy men in this oven with four days of salt pork and dry wells outside the wall," Elias said. He drew a folded sheet of heavy vellum from his breast pocket. "If I fire a second shell, Major, it will not be solid shot, and it will not be aimed at the bell-tower. It will be a percussion canister filled with rock-oil from the Santa Paula wells, dropped straight into your hay-corral. In twenty minutes your horses will be roast meat and your family will be choking in the cellar."

He paused, letting the dry rattle of a locust in the mesquite fill the silence between them.

"Or you can march your command out with colors flying and sidearms belted," Elias continued evenly. "I will buy your twelve thousand Springfields and your sixteen howitzers for thirty thousand dollars in stamped San Francisco gold coin, paid over the drumhead right now. Every enlisted man who wishes to go East gets a mule, ten days’ rations, and safe-conduct to the Rio Grande. Every man who wishes to trade that sweaty wool coat for Pacifica blue gets double pay and a bounty warrant in the Gila copper mines. You have three minutes before Lieutenant Takashima reloads."

Elias pulled his silver pocket-watch from his vest and clicked open the lid. He did not look up at the rifles again. He watched the blued-steel second hand sweep around the dial—ten seconds, twenty, forty—while from behind the mud wall came the low, fierce murmur of the regular sergeants arguing with their officers, followed by the sudden, sharp weeping of a woman in the courtyard.

At ninety seconds, the heavy iron crossbar behind the mesquite double-gates groaned and slid back. The timber leaves swung inward on dry, screaming hinges.

Major Crittenden walked out into the glare, his sword sheathed at his hip, his face gray beneath its sunburn. Behind him, four corporals dragged the first of the green-painted ordnance wagons by its tongue-chains.

"You are a thief with a ledger, Thorne," Crittenden said bitterly, stopping five paces from the nose of Elias’s horse and throwing the heavy iron ring of magazine keys into the alkali dust.

"No, Major," Elias replied, snapping his watch shut and nodding to Caleb Vance to bring up the bullion chests. "A thief takes what belongs to another man. I am merely picking up the tools that a bankrupt carpenter dropped in the road."

***

By the third night after the fall of Tucson, the captured Springfields were already rattling southward in forty mule-drawn wagons toward the dry, jagged hills of the Sonora line, while Elias rode ahead with a single troop of Lancers into the walled courtyard of the Hacienda San Bernadino—two leagues south of the international boundary stones.

Here the desert night was cool and fragrant with crushed lime-leaves, woodsmoke from mesquite braziers, and the pungent aroma of roasting goat-flesh and dark Veracruz cigars. Under the whitewashed colonnade of the patio, where twenty clay *ollas* sweated cold well-water in the lantern-light, Governor Ignacio Pesqueira of Sonora sat in a carved leather campaign chair, his crippled left leg propped upon an ammunition box that still bore the stenciled eagle of the United States Ordnance Department. Across the table from him, fanning away the moths with a silk handkerchief scented with sandalwood, sat Lady Kaiulani—having come up from the Pacifica gunboat *Hilo* at the port of Guaymas by fast mule-litter that very morning.

"Don Ignacio was just reminding me, Protector," Kaiulani said smoothly in Spanish as Elias strode up the tiled steps, stripping the desert gauntlets from his scarred hands, "that President Juárez in Mexico City still recognizes Mr. Lincoln’s minister, and that the French bondholders in Paris are threatening to send warships to Veracruz if Mexico displeases the Atlantic powers."

Pesqueira did not rise, though his dark, intelligent eyes flicked with undisguised respect toward the tall American whose boots were still white with the dust of the captured federal forts. Beside the Governor stood two French-trained Mexican artillery colonels and a pair of silk-hatted British copper-factors from Hermosillo.

"It is a matter of geography, *Señor* Protector," Pesqueira said, gesturing with his cigar toward the dark bulk of the Sierra Madre rising beyond the courtyard walls. "President Juárez is fighting the clerical reactionaries in the south; he has no pesos, and Mr. Seward in Washington has promised us a loan of ten million dollars if we allow Union troops to land at Guaymas and march up through Sonora to retake Arizona from your militia. A scrap of paper from Washington is worth little today, perhaps—but if the French Emperor lands troops at Veracruz this autumn, Mexico cannot afford to have the Yankees as enemies on our northern flank."

Elias did not take the cushioned chair the servants offered. He walked to the end of the long cedar table, where two of his Cantonese sappers had just set down one of the captured Tucson rifle-crates and pried off the lid with a bayonet. He lifted out a brand-new 1861-pattern Springfield, the bright steel barrel gleaming with cosmopolitan armory grease under the hanging lamps, and laid it directly across Pesqueira’s maps.

"Mr. Seward promised you ten million dollars in Treasury notes that are already discounted twelve percent in London," Elias said, his border-Spanish blunt, hard, and stripped of diplomatic ornament. "And as for the Union troops landing at Guaymas—there is not a single United States transport between Panama and Puget Sound that does not belong to my registry, and my ironclad *Monterey* is anchored across the mouth of Guaymas harbor right now with eight-inch rifled guns trained on the channel. The Yankees could not row a jolly-boat ashore in Sonora without my permission."

Pesqueira’s thick eyebrows rose, a slow smile creasing his leathery cheeks. "And the French, *Señor* Thorne? Can your ironclads swim across the mountains to Puebla if Louis Napoleon sends his Zouaves to collect his bonds?"

"No," Elias said. "That is why I brought you three thousand of these rifles tonight, and why three thousand more will cross the line at Nogales before the new moon, along with two hundred thousand percussion caps and four batteries of bronze mountain guns."

He leaned both fists on the table, looking straight into the Mexican governor’s eyes.

"Keep Juárez in his saddle with my iron," Elias said. "In return, Sonora and Chihuahua sign a twenty-year commercial concordat with the Confederation of Pacifica—not with Mexico City, with *you*. Your cattle, your mule-herds, and every pound of copper and saltpeter mined between Hermosillo and Durango flow north through my customs-houses, duty-free, paid for in silver thalers from the Carson mint. You close the border to every agent from Washington or Richmond, and you lease the port of Guaymas to Lady Kaiulani’s maritime commission for ninety-nine years as a coaling station. If the French come, they will find your regiments armed with repeating carbines from Sacramento. If you wait for Mr. Seward’s paper dollars, you will be hanging from a French gallows before Mr. Lincoln gets his volunteers across the Potomac."

Lady Kaiulani opened her inlaid leather portfolio and slid a parchment scroll—written in parallel columns of Spanish, English, and Hawaiian—across the table beside the greased rifle, dipping a gold-nibbed pen into the horn inkwell.

"The first quarterly subsidy of two hundred thousand silver pesos is already unloaded on the mole at Guaymas, Excellency," she murmured, her dark eyes catching the lantern-glow as she held out the pen. "My launch returns to the *Hilo* at dawn. Shall I instruct our paymaster to release the chests to your cavalry escort, or shall we steam back to San Diego with the rifles?"

Pesqueira looked down at the cold steel of the Springfield, then at the quiet, immovable face of the frontier Caesar who had just swept the United States Army out of half a continent in ten days without losing a wagon. With a soft grunt, the Governor stubbed out his cigar on the heel of his boot and reached for the gold pen.

***

To understand how a single stroke of a pen in a Sonoran courtyard—and the simultaneous closing of the Golden Gate—struck the great commercial heart of the Atlantic Republic, the historian of the Confederation need not examine the casualty lists of the Virginia campaigns; he need only open the ledgers of the New York Clearing House for the third week of August, 1861.

For twelve years, though Elias Thorne had carefully strangled the export of raw Sierra bullion, the vast maritime engine of the Pacific had still lubricated the counting-houses of Manhattan and Threadneedle Street through secondary veins: the forty million dollars in annual bills of exchange drawn upon the China clippers, the silver invoices from the Mexican mule-trains via Santa Fe, and the quarterly interest payments on the municipal bonds that New York banks had underwritten before the Sacramento Coup. Upon that thin, glittering thread of Western credit hung three hundred million dollars of watered railway stock, half the textile mills of Massachusetts, and the entire war-loan floated by Secretary Chase to feed and clothe the defeated mobs retreating upon Washington.

On the morning of Friday, the sixteenth of August, the thread snapped.

A steady, drenching summer rain was falling through the soot-stained canyon of Wall Street, turning the horse-droppings on the cobblestones into a foul, steaming porridge and soaking the black silk umbrellas of the five thousand depositors who had been crushed together from the steps of the Sub-Treasury to the corner of Broad Street since daybreak. The air tasted of wet wool, cigar-ash, and the sour sweat of terrified men.

High above the wet sea of top-hats, on the marble portico of the Bank of the Republic, Cornelius Schuyler—chairman of the Associated Banks’ Loan Committee—stood with his hand braced against a Doric pillar while a liveried clerk nailed a freshly painted pine board over the bronze doors.

*BY ORDER OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS: SPECIE PAYMENTS SUSPENDED UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE.*

Down in the street, a roar went up that drowned the clatter of the Broadway omnibuses—a sound half-groan, half-snarl, as three hundred brokers burst out of the side doors of the Merchant’s Exchange, their white linen collars torn open, waving worthless pink slips of the August War Loan and screaming quotes that dropped ten points between one curbstone and the next.

"Look at them, Mr. Schuyler!" gasped Arthur Tappan, the third assistant secretary of the Treasury, who had come up from Washington on the midnight mail-train and now stood shivering inside the tall glass vestibule behind the bolted bronze doors, his damp broadcloth trousers clinging to his thin shins. "If the New York banks refuse to redeem the seventy-three-percent Treasury notes in gold coin this afternoon, the contractors in Cincinnati will stop shipping beef to the Army of the Potomac on Monday! The government’s credit will sink lower than a Mississippi wildcat bank!"

Schuyler turned from the glass pane, his heavy Dutch jowls gray as dough above his satin cravat. In his fist he held the wet yellow flimsy that had just arrived from the Aspinwall steamer *Northern Light*, docked an hour ago at the foot of Cortlandt Street without a single iron strongbox in her hold.

"Redeem them with what, Mr. Tappan?" the banker demanded, his voice cracking as a cobble thrown from the crowd outside shattered the upper transom window, showering the tessellated marble floor with jagged glass and cold rain. "Read the manifest from Panama! Not an ounce of California dust! Not a bar of Mexican silver from the Chihuahua mint! Thorne’s lancers seized the Santa Fe trail at Mesilla two weeks ago, and his Port Admiral in San Francisco has confiscated every cargo of bullion consigned to an Atlantic port under his damned Neutrality Act! He is paying off his own eastern bond-holders in salt pork and timber-warrants, and shipping forty tons of pure bullion straight to Rothschild’s agents in Hong Kong and Yokohama to buy Krupp steel!"

"We have sixty millions in the Sub-Treasury vaults across the street—" Tappan began, his pale fingers twitching at his watch-chain as the crowd outside surged against the iron railings, their umbrellas snapping like dry twigs under the boots of a platoon of Metropolitan Police who were laying about with locust-wood clubs.

"You had sixty millions on the first of July!" Schuyler shouted back, stepping over the broken glass and seizing the young Treasury official by the lapel of his wet coat, dragging him toward the inner mahogany doors of the counting-room where forty clerks stood idle beside their closed brass-bound ledgers. "Forty-two millions of it has gone out to Liverpool on the Cunard steamers in the last three weeks because the British cotton-factors won't touch Mr. Chase’s paper! Without the California gold-ships coming up from the Isthmus every fortnight to refill the cistern, there is not enough hard coin left between Boston and Philadelphia to pay the interest on the national debt until October, let alone buy half a million rifles in Europe!"

Outside, the iron gate at the top of the cellar stairs gave way with a shrieking rend of wrought-iron bolts. Two dozen muddy boot-heels drummed against the lower oak panels as a dry-goods jobber in a torn frock-coat climbed onto the base of the portico pillar, pressing his bleeding face right against the thick plate-glass window six inches from Schuyler’s shoulder.

"Open the vaults, you thieves!" the man screamed, his breath fogging the rain-streaked glass as he hammered on the pane with the heavy brass handle of his walking-stick until the web of cracks spider-webbed across the banker’s reflection. "My notes are signed by the Treasurer of the United States! Give me my coin!"

Schuyler did not flinch as the glass bowed inward; he merely signaled the chief clerk to drop the iron storm-shutters over the tall embrasures, plunging the vestibule into a sepulchral gloom lit only by a single flickering gas-jet.

"Go back to the telegraph office, Mr. Tappan," the old financier said into the dark, while the heavy oak panels shuddered under the battering of paving-stones outside. "Tell Mr. Lincoln that the vaults of Manhattan are dry. If he wishes to buy gunpowder after Tuesday, he will have to print green ink on rag-paper and pray at the point of a bayonet that the farmers take it."

***

While the merchants of Wall Street tore their linen over empty iron boxes, the autumn rains of 1861 began to chill the high granite passes of the Rocky Mountains—and it was there, along the timbered spine of the South Pass, that the polite fiction of Pacifica’s bloodless neutrality finally met the cold lead of Federal authority.

Before riding north from the Arizona border to meet the territorial delegates assembling at Cherry Creek, Elias had paused for six days at Monterey to review the new municipal ordinances with Lady Kaiulani. Even there, beside the quiet curve of the bay where the bells of the old Spanish mission now rang out the quarter-hours alongside the bronze gongs of a newly erected Shinto shrine for the Edo shipwrights, the friction of his great design had begun to show through the varnish. 

They had walked together along the high timber seawall above the customs wharf, where Cantonese masons were laying courses of gray Sierra granite beneath a curved, copper-sheathed roof modeled after the audience halls of Honolulu and Osaka. Down on the slips, three hundred Bakufu iron-workers in dark indigo tunics were marching to their barracks with wooden practice-swords thrust through their sashes, while a company of discharged Missouri dragoons—now wearing the high-collared navy wool of the Pacific Legion—lounged against a pile of Krupp gun-crates, spitting tobacco juice onto the freshly swept flagstones and muttering curses at the "heathen idol-house" rising above the anchorage.

"Your Americans have strong backs for the pickaxe, Protector," Kaiulani had remarked, drawing her sea-otter mantle closer against the salt wind as a sergeant of the Legion Deliberately jostled a Japanese master-carpenter off the dry plankwalk into the ankle-deep mud. "And they die well enough when you point them at a Mexican battery. But they still carry the parish vestry in their skulls. Yesterday, two of Colonel Mulligan’s veterans broke the porcelain lanterns outside the Cantonese guild-hall because the laborers worked through the Christian Sabbath. And in Honolulu last month, your provost marshal tried to billet horse-artillery in the sacred taro terraces of Nu’uanu without asking the *Ali’i* council."

Elias had stopped by the parapet, watching the Japanese carpenter rise from the mire, his hand frozen on the lacquered hilt of his short-sword while two Legion corporals Fingered the butts of their Colt revolvers.

"Sergeant Croker," Elias had called down from the wall. His voice was neither loud nor hurried, yet every man on the wharf went rigid as a pine mast. "Take off your belt."

The Missouri veteran looked up, his ruddy face blanching beneath his beard. "Protector? The yellow devil wouldn't yield the crown of the walk to a white soldier—"

"That man is a third-class artificer of the Naval Foundry, drawing the pay of a lieutenant," Elias said, descending the stone steps two at a time. "He cast the trunnions on the cannon that kept you alive at Tucson. Take off your belt, or I will have the provost strip your hide and put you in the chain-gang on the Benicia breakwater before the dinner-bell rings."

When the disgraced sergeant had been marched away to the guardhouse under the custody of his own squad, Elias had turned back to Kaiulani, his gray eyes hard as river-ice. "They will learn," he told her.

"By the lash?" she asked softly, her dark gaze steady and unblinking beneath the brim of her feathered bonnet. "You can bolt iron plates together with hot rivets, Elias, because iron has no memory. Men are not ore. My cousins in the islands gave you Pearl Lagoon because I promised them the Kamehameha line would sit as kings beside an emperor, not as clerks beneath a board of San Francisco syndicate directors. If your frontier captains treat the princes of Oahu and the sword-gentry of Satsuma like conquered peons, your Confederation will fracture along the tide-line the morning after your heart stops beating."

"Then I had better not die until the new generation is out of the schoolhouse," Elias had answered, looking out toward the fog-bank rolling through the Gate. "I am not asking them to love each other, Kaiulani. The Roman legionary from Gaul did not love the Greek ship-master from Alexandria. They obeyed the same standard because the road was paved, the pirate was hung, and the coin had the same face stamped on both sides. You write the code for the courts; I will break the teeth of the first man who spits on it."

Now, three weeks later, that same ruthless necessity had brought him seven thousand feet above the sea, where the wind off the Wind River Range carried the sharp, bitter scent of juniper smoke, frozen horse-dung, and wet gunpowder.

Along the narrow defile of Willow Creek, where the stage-road from Fort Laramie dipped down toward the headwaters of the Colorado, Colonel Philip St. George Cooke—a Virginian who had refused to follow his state into the Southern rebellion and still commanded four squadrons of the United States Second Dragoons in the Utah Territory—had thrown a line of dismounted skirmishers across the frozen gravel bar. In his pocket Cooke carried an unsealed warrant from Secretary of War Cameron, commanding him to arrest "Elias Thorne, calling himself Protector of California, and sundry other traitors in arms," and to escort them in irons to Fort Leavenworth.

Elias sat his claybank stallion behind a granite outcrop four hundred yards down the gorge. Around him, two battalions of the Pacific Legion—four hundred Missourians and Texans on the right flank, and three hundred riflemen of the First Hawaiian Royal Guard on the left, their dark Polynesian faces calm beneath fleece-lined shakos—lay flat in the snow-crusted sagebrush, the blued steel barrels of their seven-shot Spencer repeating carbines resting across the stones.

Down in the creek-bottom, a Federal trumpeter blew a single, brassy parley call that echoed weirdly off the red sandstone cliffs. Cooke himself rode fifty paces out in front of his blue-coated line, his gray mustache stiff with frost, waving a folded parchment above his gauntleted fist.

"Disperse to your homes, you deluded rascals!" the old regular colonel roared, his voice cracking in the thin mountain air. "You are firing upon the colors of the United States! Deliver up the usurper Thorne, and every enlisted man who lays down his weapon shall have the President’s amnesty!"

Beside Elias’s stirrup, Caleb Vance spat into the crusted snow, his thumb rubbing the brass elevation screw of a mountain howitzer that two mules had packed up the timber trail. "That’s old Cooke, Elias. I served under him at Fort Riley in ’thirty-four. He’s got three hundred regulars behind those cottonwoods with Sharps single-shot carbines. If we open with canister at this range, there won't be enough left of the Second Dragoons to fill an ambulance."

Elias looked down at the faded stars and stripes fluttering above the creek. Until this morning, every fort he had taken had surrendered to silver or the threat of hunger. Not one drop of regular army blood had stained his ledger. Once the lead flew in this canyon, there would be no treaty of recognition signed by a tired Congress in Washington; there would only be conquest.

"He has his orders, Caleb," Elias said, his voice flat and low against the whistle of the gorge wind. "And we have the pass. Tell the Hawaiians on the left bench to aim for the horse-holders behind the grove. When their mounts break, give the skirmish line two volleys from the Spencers and drop a shell into the road-cut."

"God forgive us," Caleb muttered, though his hand did not tremble as he pulled the friction-primer lanyard.

The bronze howitzer barked once, the sharp crash rolling down the granite walls like a rockslide. Three seconds later, the case-shot burst ten feet above the Federal horse-lines in the cottonwoods, a dirty puff of white smoke and shrieking lead balls that sent eighty riderless cavalry mounts plunging and screaming through the frozen brush. Before the echo died, the left ridge erupted in a continuous, rattling roar—not the slow, measured *boom-pause-boom* of muzzle-loading muskets, but the terrifying mechanical clatter of three hundred lever-action Spencers firing fourteen rounds a minute.

Through his field-glasses, Elias watched the blue skirmish line along the gravel bar simply melt into the snow. Men who had fought the Sioux and the Cheyenne with single-shot locks stood up in bewilderment to ram cartridges, only to be struck three times before their ramrods touched the bore. Colonel Cooke’s charger reared straight up, blood spouting from its nostrils, and crashed backward onto the ice, pinning the old Virginian beneath his saddle-bags while his surviving troopers scrambled wildly up the opposite talus in a panic-stricken rout.

"Cease fire!" Elias barked, raising his gloved hand. 

The rattling carbines stopped on the instant, leaving only the shrill whinnying of gutted horses and the groans of forty wounded regulars staining the white drift crimson. Elias rode slowly down the shale slope onto the creek-ice, the iron shoes of his claybank ringing against the blood-splashed stones, and looked down at Colonel Cooke, who was struggling to draw his heavy dragoon revolver from beneath his dead horse’s flank.

"Leave it in the leather, Colonel," Elias said quietly. "My surgeons will set your leg. You may keep your sword, and when the roads clear in the spring, you may take your wounded back to the Missouri. Tell Mr. Cameron that the warrants of the United States no longer run west of the Continental Divide."

***

Five days after the snow reddened at Willow Creek, the cold November rain was sluicing down the muddy clay ruts of Alexandria, Virginia, where the grand cantonments of the Army of the Potomac stretched for twelve miles in a sodden misery of leaking Sibley tents, typhoid hospitals, and overflowing mule-corrals. 

Inside a commandeered brick tavern near the wharf, General Marcus Vance stood before a smoky pine-knot fire, methodically feeding his preliminary rough drafts into the flames with the brass poker. He no longer wore the civilian linen of the summer’s battle; he was dressed in a heavy rubberized poncho over a plain traveling suit, his saddle-bags packed and strapped beside the door. Across the deal table sat three men in the dark blue frock-coats of the United States Corps of Topographical Engineers and the Ordnance Bureau—men whose names had stood near the top of the West Point register ten years before, and who now looked out at the mud of McClellan’s camp with the hollow, disgusted eyes of craftsmen forced to work for an asylum.

"You have the cipher key for the Cincinnati foundry agents, Major Sterling?" Marcus asked, not turning from the grate as a curl of tracing-paper blackened and rose up the chimney.

"Sewn into the lining of my valise, General," replied Sterling, a lean, spectacles-wearing Pennsylvanian who had spent the last four months trying in vain to convince Secretary Cameron’s political brother-in-law not to buy five thousand condemned Belgian muskets at twenty dollars a stand. "And Captain Mordecai has the complete blueprint folios for the Parrott rifled cannon and the Rodman coastal columbiads, along with the roster of every master machinist at the Watervliet Arsenal who has not been paid since the August bank suspension."

"What of the cavalry patrols along the Leesburg pike?" asked the third officer, a hard-bitten regular dragoon captain named Custer whose yellow hair hung damply over his collar. "General McClellan’s provost-guard arrested two Maryland legislators at the ferry this morning. If Baker’s detectives suspect four regular officers are boarding the Baltimore packet without leave-papers from the War Department, we’ll be in the Old Capitol Prison before midnight."

Marcus turned from the hearth. His face was as bloodless and composed as an iron casting. During the four months since Bull Run, while he had dined with Northern senators and inspected the chaotic supply depots along the Chesapeake, he had executed the true mission for which Elias had sent him East: he had not merely observed the Union’s paralysis; he had harvested its brains. While Lincoln appointed Tammany Hall ward-heelers and abolitionist newspaper editors to command brigades, Marcus had quietly approached thirty-six of the finest young engineers, artillerists, and quartermasters in the regular establishment—men sickened by the corruption of the Washington contractors and terrified that the Republic was bleeding itself into anarchy.

"Baker’s detectives are looking for Southern sympathizers crossing the river into Virginia," Marcus said, picking up his heavy pocket chronometer and checking the hour against the muffled tolling of the Alexandria church bell. "We are not going south, gentlemen. My launch from the British mail-tender is waiting at the coal-wharf two hundred yards below the arsenal wall. By dawn we will be aboard a Clyde-built screw steamer clearing the Capes under the flag of the Kingdom of Hawaii. Once we pass the three-mile limit, there is not a blockading cruiser in the Atlantic Squadron fast enough to catch our smoke."

He walked to the table, where a leather dispatch-case stamped with the eagle of the War Department lay open, and drew out a single sheet of tissue-paper that had come through the Havana cable two hours before.

"Protector Thorne engaged the Second Dragoons at South Pass on the nineteenth," Marcus said evenly, watching their faces in the tallow-light. "Cooke’s command was broken in twelve minutes. The mountain passes are closed, and the delegates from Colorado, Utah, Nevada, and the Oregon country are assembling at Denver this week to sign the Act of Confederation. When you step into that boat tonight, you leave your commissions in the United States Army on this table. There is no returning to the East. In San Francisco, a major of engineers draws three hundred dollars a month in gold coin, commands a regiment of three thousand disciplined laborers, and answers to one man instead of a committee of country pettifoggers. If any one of you prefers to stay here and rot in the Virginia mud while Mr. McClellan polishes his boots, speak now."

Major Sterling stood up and unpinned the tarnished gilt shoulder-straps from his blue coat, dropping them with a soft thud onto the scarred pine table beside the empty ink-bottle. One by one, the others did the same.

"The tide is at the flood, General," Sterling said. "Let us go to the wharf."

***

By the first week of December, the raw pine-log shanties and canvas saloons of Denver City were buried to the eaves in crisp, blinding snow, while sixty miles to the west the great jagged wall of the Front Range stood against the sky like a line of white-hot iron teeth. 

Inside the Broadwell House—the largest brick hotel between St. Joseph and Salt Lake—the long dining room had been stripped of its gaming tables and billiard cloths to accommodate the fifty-two men who claimed to speak for two million square miles of mountain, desert, and canyon. The air was stifling, thick with the reek of wet buffalo-skin coats, cheap cherry-wood tobacco, coal-oil lamps, and the sour tallow of mountain boots drying beside four roaring cast-iron stoves.

They were a harder, rougher breed than the silk-stockinged planters of Charleston or the maritime grandees of Sacramento: there were Mormon bishops from the Salt Lake valley with square, shovel-trimmed beards and eyes like flint; silver-prospectors from the Washoe lodes wearing velveteen waistcoats covered in gold watch-chains; rugged wheat-factors from the Willamette; and half-wild territorial judges from the Santa Fe ring whose pockets bulged with hidden derringers.

At the center of the floor, William Gilpin—whom President Lincoln had sent out in the spring as Territorial Governor of Colorado with an empty treasury and a bundle of unsigned promissory notes—stood beside a pine table, his tall frame shaking with fury as he shook a handful of green-tinted Federal demand notes in the face of the delegation from the Pike’s Peak mining districts.

"I tell you that to sign articles of confederation with San Francisco is to put a rope around every neck in this room!" Gilpin shouted, his voice hoarse from three days of losing debate. "The Congress in Washington has appropriated five hundred thousand dollars for the defense of this territory! My drafts upon the Treasury—"

"Your drafts aren't worth the grease it takes to fry a side of bacon, Governor!" roared old Judge Slaughter from the Auraria bench, slamming his hickory cane down on the floorboards while a dozen miners in the gallery jeered. "The stage from Omaha hasn't brought a sack of hard mail in three weeks because the Cheyenne have burned the relay stations along the Platte, and your friends in Washington pulled every regular soldier out of Fort Wise to go fight Beauregard in Virginia! Who’s going to buy our quartz-crushers when the New York banks won't pay gold? Who’s going to keep the Arapaho out of the gulches this winter—Abe Lincoln’s postmaster?"

The heavy double doors at the rear of the dining hall did not bang open; they were swung back with quiet, oiled precision by four troopers of the Pacific Legion wearing wolf-skin pelisses over their navy tunics, their Spencer carbines held at the carry.

Elias walked down the narrow aisle between the benches. He had ridden down from the Cheyenne pass three hours before at the head of eight hundred cavalry and two batteries of rifled Krupp field-pieces, whose brass muzzles were even now trained down Larimer Street from the high bank of Cherry Creek. He had not changed his campaign clothes; his heavy cavalry boots were crusted with frozen alkali and red mountain mud, and his short-cropped hair was silvered with frost at the temples. Behind him walked Caleb Vance and Elder Kimball of the Salt Lake delegation, with whom Elias had concluded a private concordat at Fort Bridger four days prior.

The clamor in the room died until nothing could be heard but the hissing of the snow melting off the troopers’ boots against the stove-plates.

Elias stepped up onto the low pine platform beside Governor Gilpin. He did not look at the federal appointee; he turned and faced the fifty-two delegates, unbuttoning his heavy wool greatcoat so they could see the plain, unadorned tunic beneath.

"Three weeks ago," Elias began, his rough, low voice filling the timbered room without effort, "Colonel Cooke of the United States Army tried to close the South Pass with four squadrons of regular dragoons. His men are now in my field-hospitals at Green River, and his rifles are in my wagons outside."

Gilpin took a step forward, his hand dropping toward the breast of his frock-coat. "Mr. Thorne, by virtue of the commission I hold from the President of the United States, I command you to lay down your—"

Elias turned his head half an inch. His pale, wintry gaze fixed upon Gilpin’s face with such crushing weight that the Governor’s jaw clicked shut in the middle of the syllable.

"You hold a piece of paper from a town that cannot pay its own clerks in silver, Mr. Gilpin," Elias said evenly. "Look out that window. On the tracks beside the creek sit forty freight-wagons drawn by steam-traction engines from the Sacramento works. In those wagons are ten thousand repeating rifles, four hundred tons of flour from the San Joaquin, and two hundred thousand silver thalers minted at Carson City. Tomorrow morning, my surveyors begin laying the grade for a broad-gauge iron railway from the Salt Lake through the Wasatch canyons to the Golden Gate."

He turned back to the benches, where the Mormon elders and the mining captains were leaning forward over their knees, their eyes gleaming in the yellow lamp-light.

"The East is dead to you," Elias said, each short sentence falling like a hammer-stroke on an anvil. "Between this creek and the Missouri River lie six hundred miles of burned grass, hostile tribes, and bankrupt wildcat banks. If you look toward Washington, you will starve in the snow while two factions of Eastern lawyers butcher half a million farm-boys over the corpse of a Constitution they tore up themselves. If you look west, you look toward the sea. Sign the Act of Union with the Confederation today, and by noon my paymasters will redeem every dollar of Governor Gilpin’s worthless paper in hard Pacifica silver at par. Every territory represented in this hall will keep its own local courts, its own church laws, and its own militia captains, under one article: that your bullion flows west to the San Francisco mint, your railroads run to the Pacific tidewater, and your outer frontier is guarded by the iron of my Legion."

From the center bench, Elder Kimball rose slowly to his feet, his broad-brimmed black hat held across his chest. "And the federal judges that Washington sent to Utah to jail our elders, Captain Thorne? What becomes of them under your Protectorate?"

"They are riding in the same eastbound stagecoach that leaves with Governor Gilpin in twenty minutes," Elias replied, drawing the heavy vellum roll of the Western Compact from his belt and slapping it down across the pine table so hard the ink-horn jumped. He reached out, lifted the brass-handled dip-pen from Gilpin’s motionless fingers, and held it out toward Judge Slaughter at the head of the Colorado bench. "Come forward and put your names to the iron, gentlemen, before the horses freeze in the traces."

***

By the break of spring in 1862, the ink on the Denver parchment had dried into a line of fire that stretched from the Black Hills of Dakota to the red-dirt crossings of the Red River. If the mountain territories were to remain an impregnable citadel while the great railways were bolted to the granite of the Sierra and the Rockies, the vast oceanic glacis of the Great Plains had to be swept clean of anything that could feed a marching regiment or draw an ordinance wagon.

On the nineteenth of May, Elias stood on the high cedar gallery of the burned stage-station at Fort Kearny, where the Platte spread out into a mile of braided, muddy channels through the newly sprouted buffalo-grass. Twenty-four years had passed since he had crawled out of the frozen mule’s ribs sixty miles upriver; now, as he looked eastward down the valley toward the Missouri border, the horizon was darkened by seven distinct columns of greasy black smoke rising straight into the windless spring sky.

"The telegraph relay at Plum Creek is down, Protector," reported General Marcus Vance, coming up the charred timber stairs with a sheaf of wet dispatch-flimsies in his gauntlet. He had returned from the Atlantic coast in February via the Panama steamer, bringing with him forty-two former regular officers who now wore the plain navy wool of the Pacifica General Staff. "Major Custer’s lancers took the last four federal supply trains three miles east of the Little Blue at dawn. Two hundred wagons of salt pork and hardbread bound for Fort Riley. We shot the draft-oxen in the yokes, poured rock-oil over the spokes, and fired the canvas. Not a wheel turns between here and Topeka."

Elias did not lower his brass spyglass. Down on the river-flat below the ruined fort, three hundred Cantonese sappers and two companies of Hawaiian pioneers were methodically sledging the iron tires off a captured park of Union commissary wagons, loading the scrap metal onto flat-bedded steam-lorries while their traction boilers hissed and panted in the damp grass, reeking of sulfur and hot cylinder-oil. Beside the road-bed, four thousand head of requisitioned Missouri beef-cattle were being driven westward at the point of the lance by a band of Kotsoteka Comanches and Cheyenne auxiliaries—men whose war-chiefs now wore heavy silver peace-medals stamped with Elias’s profile and carried breech-loading carbines supplied from the Benicia arsenals.

"What of the wells along the Smoky Hill route?" Elias asked.

"Poisoned with arsenic and dead mules from Fort Wallace to Salina," Marcus answered, his voice as dry and methodical as if he were reading a quartermaster’s receipt for winter forage. "And the grass will be dry enough by July to burn the whole prairie from the Republican Fork to the Arkansas. General Halleck in St. Louis wired the War Department yesterday that it would require forty thousand cavalry and ten million dollars in wagon-forage just to reach the hundredth meridian. He has neither."

From the courtyard below came a sudden, shrill clatter of tongues. A detail of Missouri Legionnaires had dragged a captured federal quartermaster—a stout, red-faced captain of Illinois volunteers—out of the sod cellar where he had been hiding among the broken pickle-barrels. As the prisoner stumbled into the sunlight, he spat at the boots of a Japanese artillery surveyor who was measuring the brick foundations of the magazine with a brass theodolite.

"You Christian turncoats!" the Illinois captain bawled, wrenching against the hemp cord on his wrists as he glared up at the gallery where Elias stood. "You’re burning the bread of your own countrymen and turning painted savages loose on the frontier while white men fight for the flag in Tennessee! Is this your Western law, Thorne—handing American soil over to heathens and Kanakas?"

Beside Elias at the rail, Lady Kaiulani—who had ridden up from the Denver rail-head in an armored stagecoach to oversee the settlement of the Indian boundary treaties—rested her gloved fingertips on the scorched cedar balustrade. She wore a traveling habit of dark green broadcloth cut in the European fashion, though her throat was clasped with a collar of braided human hair and whale-ivory, the ancient *lei niho palaoa* of the island chiefs.

"The gentleman from Illinois seems distressed by the company you keep, Protector," she murmured, her dark eyes cool and clinical as she watched the prisoner forced to his knees in the mud.

"He is distressed because his dinner is burning," Elias said. He walked to the head of the stairs and looked down into the yard. "Captain."

The Illinois officer jerked his chin up, his face purple. "I demand the rights of a prisoner of war under the Geneva usage! You have no right to destroy private homesteads and public wells!"

"A well in the desert is not a homestead," Elias said, his rough, low voice dropping into the silent yard like lead into water. "It is a stepping-stone for an invader. You came out here with six hundred wagons to feed regiments that Mr. Lincoln intended to march through South Pass when he finished with Virginia. Take a long look at this river, Captain. For three hundred miles east of this post, there will not be a blade of green grass, a standing telegraph pole, or a cup of sweet water left by August. Any man who crosses the ninety-eighth parallel carrying a United States musket will not be fought; he will die of thirst before he sees the smoke of my camps. Marcus—put his boots in his saddle-bags and turn him loose on foot toward Omaha. Let him walk back and show General Halleck what the road to California looks like."

As the provosts cut the captain’s bonds and stripped off his riding-boots, Kaiulani turned slightly from the rail, the wind off the burned prairie lifting the black veil at her hat-brim. "A moat of ash seven hundred miles wide," she said quietly, so that even Marcus, standing three paces behind them, could not catch her words. "It is effective, Elias. No army will cross this waste in our lifetime. Yet when we rode through the camps at Cheyenne last week, I heard your Texas lancers singing around the grease-fires. Do you know what they sang? That when they had finished burning the Yankees off the plains, they would ride back to San Francisco and throw the bronze Buddha out of the Monterey temple into the bay."

Elias turned his head, his eyes meeting hers without a flicker of surprise. "Men who live by the saddle talk big when their bellies are full of salt beef."

"Men who burn churches on the Platte today will burn shrines on the Sacramento tomorrow unless they know the shrine belongs to the crown," she replied, her voice sharpening like a steel blade drawn from silk. "You use the Cheyenne to strip the plains; you use my islanders to hold your mountain passes; you use the Shogun’s samurai to cast your cannon. To your Missourians, they are merely tools—like those steam-tractors down in the mud—to be scrapped when the fort is built. If this empire is to be more than a military camp that dies with its general, the law must sit higher than the camp-fire. Give my council the provost-courts in the coast cities this summer, or by autumn you will be fighting a mutiny in your own shipyards."

Elias looked down at the Japanese surveyor, who had calmly resumed sighting his brass level across the smoking ruins of the federal bakery while two sullen Missouri troopers watched him with folded arms.

"Draw the commission tonight," Elias said. "Three judges on every maritime bench—one American, one Hawaiian, one Edo magistrate. And tell the *Ali'i* that any soldier of the Legion who lays a finger on an imperial shrine or a guild-house gets twenty lashes at the cart’s tail and five years in the quicksilver mines at New Almaden. Order is not a bargain, Kaiulani. It is a hammer. It hits both ways."

***

To the chronicler who studies the diplomatic archives of the short-lived Southern Confederacy, the summer of 1862 presents a spectacle of tragic delusion unmatched since the ambassadors of Athens begged the Persian satraps for gold while Spartan spears already ringed the Long Walls. In Richmond, where the church bells rang for the seven days’ slaughter before the Chickahominy and the hospitals stank of gangrene and turpentine, President Jefferson Davis and Secretary of State Judah Benjamin clung with the desperation of drowning men to a single strategic chimera: that the iron tyrant of San Francisco, having broken the Union’s western flank and ruined the banks of New York, was their natural brother-in-arms.

They had forgotten—or chose in their extremity not to remember—that the man who now ruled from Sitka to the Rio Grande had begun his march not in the parlors of Charleston, but beside the smoking ashes of a Kentucky squatter’s cabin.

In the first week of August, while the heat lay thick and wet as a poultice over the brick tobacco-warehouses of the Virginia capital, Major Julian St. Clair—now wearing the buff-and-gray frock coat of a Confederate State Department commissioner—sat in the high, shuttered library of the Brockenbrough mansion with his dispatch-case open upon his knees. Fifteen years had passed since that foggy midnight on Clark’s Point when he had tossed the gold medal of the Golden Circle onto a redwood table and offered a twenty-one-year-old frontier captain fifty thousand British sovereigns to guard the Southern flank. Now St. Clair’s hair was white, his left sleeve was pinned empty to his breast from a federal shell-fragment at Shiloh, and his hand shook with tertian fever as he held out the cipher telegram that had just arrived from Matamoros via the Havana blockade-runner.

"Read it yourself, Mr. Benjamin," St. Clair said, his voice a dry rattle in the dim room where the flies buzzed lazily against the Venetian blinds. "I rode three hundred miles by mule from San Antonio to the Pecos crossing in June to meet Thorne’s outposts. His provosts would not even let my escort cross the river into New Mexico. They made me wait four days in an adobe sheep-pen at Presidio del Norte like a Mexican horse-thief until General Vance arrived on an armored railway flatcar from El Paso."

Judah Benjamin took the tissue slip, his plump, olive-skinned face losing its habitual courtly smile as his dark eyes scanned the decoded lines. Across the mahogany table, President Davis leaned back in his horsehair armchair, a cold compress pressed to his neuralgic eye.

"What does he say to the Treaty of Mutual Guaranty, Judah?" Davis asked impatiently. "We offered him permanent recognition of the Rocky Mountain line and a twenty-percent reduction on all cotton shipped through Guaymas to the Cantonese looms, provided his ironclad squadron steams around the Horn to break Farragut’s blockade at the mouth of the Mississippi and his cavalry marches from the Red River into Missouri."

Benjamin did not read the dispatch aloud at first. He laid it softly beside the brass inkstand, as if the paper itself were hot enough to blister his fingers.

"Mr. Thorne sends no treaty, Mr. President," the Secretary of State said quietly. "He sends an invoice."

Davis pulled the damp cloth from his temple, his gaunt cheek flushing dark red. "An invoice?"

"From Marshal Vance at El Paso," Benjamin read, his voice dropping into a flat, funereal monotone. *"'The Protector of the Grand Confederation acknowledges receipt of the memorandum from the belligerent authorities at Richmond. The Confederation of Pacifica recognizes no government east of the hundredth meridian save that of force in being. The fifty thousand sovereigns advanced by the Charleston syndicate in the year 1847, together with six percent compound interest, were discharged in full by the shipment of salt pork and lead to Matamoros in January last. Should the Richmond authorities desire the passage of cotton through the port of Guaymas, the tariff is forty percent ad valorem, payable exclusively in pig-iron, locomotive boilers, or skilled negro mechanics who shall upon crossing the Rio Grande become free indentured artificers of the Pacifica Crown. As for the Mississippi River, the Protector bids Major St. Clair inform Mr. Davis that when the guns of Pacifica appear upon the father of waters, they will not come to open a port for cotton-planters; they will come to collect the mortgage on the continent.'"*

A dead, suffocating silence fell over the library, broken only by the clatter of an ambulance-wagon passing over the cobblestones of Clay Street outside.

"Free indentured artificers," Davis whispered, his thin hands clenching the arms of his chair until the knuckles shone like bone. "He asks us to sell him our own slaves to build his railroads across Texas—and calls us *belligerent authorities*, as if we were a band of Nicaraguan filibusters! Does the man imagine that because he has stolen a few empty deserts and bribed a Polynesian princess, he can dictate terms to the sovereign states of the South?"

"He does not imagine it, Mr. President; he is executing it," St. Clair said bitterly, rising from his chair and walking to the tall wall-map where the vast western half of North America had been shaded by the War Department clerks in heavy blue pencil. "You have not seen his camps, sir. I saw them at the Pecos. We are fighting this war with flintlocks converted to percussion and locomotives held together with baling-wire. Vance’s troopers ride behind steam-wagons that lay their own iron track across the sandhills at four miles a day. Their artillery is cast steel from Essen and Nagasaki; their infantry carries seven-shot repeaters that can empty a saddle at six hundred yards. When I reminded General Vance of the oath Thorne gave me in forty-seven, do you know what he did? He pulled out a pocket-watch made in Geneva, told me my pass expired in twenty minutes, and said that if General Sibley’s Texas brigade ever set foot west of the Brazos again, they would hang every officer from the telegraph poles."

Benjamin folded the telegram into a neat square, his dark eyes fixed on the ceiling. "He waited until McClellan’s cannon were within five miles of this house, and until Grant had split our line in Tennessee. He wants neither a restored Union nor a victorious Confederacy. He intends that we shall strangle each other in the ditch, and when the last dollar is spent and the last regiment is buried, he will walk down the eastern slope of the mountains and buy the ruins for the price of a meal."

***

He did not wait for the last regiment to be buried. A master carpenter does not wait for the rotting timber of an old barn to fall upon his head; when the dry-rot has eaten two-thirds through the main beam, he takes an axe to the king-post.

Throughout the winter of 1862 and the bloody, inconclusive spring of 1863—while Lee and Hooker mauled each other in the Virginia wilderness and Grant’s battered army rotted in the mud canals before Vicksburg—fourteen thousand laborers had been working behind a triple cordon of cavalry in the dry bed of the Tehuantepec Isthmus and the ship-slips of Guaymas. No newspaper in New York or London knew what was being bolted together in the modular iron sections that came down the coast from the Clark’s Point rolling mills. They were not deep-sea frigates. They were broad-beamed, turret-mounted river monitors of shallow draft, their hulls constructed in twenty-four numbered steel compartments that could be carried across the Mexican divide on double-track railway cradles, reassembled by pneumatic riveters in the lagoons of the Gulf Coast within twelve days, and driven by twin high-pressure screw propellers burning crude rock-oil from the southern California wells.

On the fourth of July, 1863, while the gunboats of Rear Admiral Porter and the starving garrison of General Pemberton stared at each other through the heat-haze of the Mississippi bends, the river suddenly darkened three miles below Natchez.

Elias stood on the armored bridge-house of the flagship *Sacramento*—a twin-turreted monitor whose sloped six-inch casemates of rolled nickel-steel rose scarcely four feet above the turbid brown flood. Twenty-six years had passed since he had stood barefoot on the pine planks of Red Higgins’s broadhorn flatboat, his heels split by frost and his palm clutching a clipped Mexican quarter-real while the *General Jackson* thrashed past him in a cloud of scorched grease. Now, behind his wake, steamed twelve iron sisters in line ahead, their telescopic funnels trailing thin, colorless plumes of superheated petroleum vapor, while forty armor-plated troop-barges towed alongside carried twenty thousand veterans of the Pacific Legion—Missouri riflemen, Hawaiian guards, and three regiments of Bakufu marine infantry under the rising-sun pennon of the Confederation.

"Federal tin-clad picket boat rounding the point at six hundred yards, Protector," reported Captain Takashima from the conning-slit below, his voice echoing hollowly through the brass speaking-tube as the monitor’s twin screws churned the muddy current into yellow yeast. "It is the *Baron DeKalb*. She is hoisting the United States signal for identification and running out her bow Dahlgrens."

Beside Elias on the narrow iron grating, General Marcus Vance checked his pocket chronometer against the mileage chart of the lower river. The humid air of the Mississippi bottomlands was a steaming cauldron after the clean dry winds of the Sierra; it carried the reek of rotted cypress knees, mud-flats, and the rank, sweetish stench of dead mules floating down from Grant’s siege-lines above.

"Both belligerents are exhausted, sir," Marcus said, not looking up from his map-board. "Pemberton’s men inside Vicksburg have been eating pea-meal and mule-meat for forty days. Grant’s regiments in the trenches have forty percent on the sick-list with malaria, and their only supply line is the single river channel north to Memphis. If we sink the picket boat and steam straight between the batteries before dusk, neither side has a gun heavy enough to dent our turret-glacis."

Elias looked across the mile-wide expanse of brown water toward the eastern bluffs, where the white columns of a burned Louisiana sugar-plantation stood like broken teeth among the live-oaks. In his pocket lay the silver twenty-five-cent piece Red Higgins had thrown at him on the St. Louis levee a quarter-century ago—worn smooth now by his thumb, the eagle almost rubbed away.

"Do not sink the picket boat with shell," Elias said, his low voice vibrating with the deep, steady thrum of the oil-burners beneath the deckplates. "We did not bring these guns two thousand miles to waste powder on river-scows. Takashima—give the *Sacramento* full steam ahead. Put our ram-bow straight through her midships, and let the current carry the wreck down to New Orleans so Admiral Farragut can see what kind of iron cuts wood. Marcus, hoist the blue-and-gold standard at the main-truck and tell the buglers on the barges to sound the general assembly."

On the Federal gunboat ahead, a flash of orange flame and a dirty cloud of white smoke burst from the bow-ports. Two nine-inch round-shot struck the sloped steel prow of the *Sacramento* with the deafening *clang* of a sledgehammer on an anvil, flattened into ragged lead-colored saucers, and skipped harmlessly fifty feet into the air before splashing into the muddy wake.

Elias did not flinch as the iron splinters whined overhead; he braced his gauntleted hands against the armored coaming of the bridge while the massive steel ram beneath his boots surged forward at twelve knots, the water boiling white over her submerged snout as the wooden side-paddles of the Union vessel frantically beat astern to escape the oncoming mountain of steel.

"Two hundred yards!" Takashima called through the tube as the terrified faces of the Federal gun-crews became visible behind their thin boiler-iron bulwarks, men dropping their rammers and scrambling toward the stern-rail. "One hundred! Brace for collision on the main deck—"

"Hold your course," Elias commanded, his eyes fixed beyond the doomed vessel toward the smoke-shrouded bluffs of Vicksburg rising in the northern haze, "and signal the second division to drop their anchor-chains across the Yazoo mouth the moment we pass the bend; before the moon rises tonight, not a skiff crosses this ditch from Minnesota to the Gulf without a pass signed by my Provost-General."

The steel beak of the *Sacramento* struck the *Baron DeKalb* just abaft the port paddle-box with a sound like a dry pine forest snapping in a hurricane. Twelve feet of solid, forged San Francisco iron sheared straight through oak frames, iron boiler-plate, and coal-bunkers, lifting the Union gunboat’s bow six feet out of the yellow flood before rolling her over on her beam-ends in a roaring geyser of escaping steam and boiling river-mud.

When the steam cleared from the Mississippi that evening, both Grant’s starving besiegers and Pemberton’s hollow-eyed garrison looked down from their rifle-pits to see twelve silent steel monsters moored bow-to-stern across the channel, their twin eight-inch rifled turrets trained equally upon the stars-and-stripes on the right bank and the stars-and-bars on the left.

***

The seizure of the Mississippi spine did not bring immediate peace to the continent; it merely transferred the burden of history from the battlefield to the council-chamber. Before the final eastward march to the Atlantic could be undertaken, Elias was forced to return to Monterey in the winter of 1863 to weld together the disparate halves of the colossus he had conjured from the sea.

The capital of the Confederation had outgrown its Spanish adobe bones. Along the curving granite esplanade above the bay, a new imperial architecture had risen from the coastal fog: vast administrative ministries built with the heavy, pillared porticoes of Virginia, yet crowned with the sweeping, upturned cedar eaves of Kyoto and flanked by the basalt *ahu* altars of the Hawaiian islands. On the morning of the Winter Solstice, a cold drizzle blew in off the Pacific surf, carrying the sharp tang of kelp, wet coal-ash from the naval foundries, and the heavy aromatic smoke of aloeswood drifting from the great syncretic cathedral of St. Michael and the Sun Goddess on the hill.

Inside the Hall of the Council, where forty-foot columns of polished redwood met a ceiling coffered in beaten copper, Elias sat at the head of the semicircular table. He wore no crown—he had refused the title of King when the Diet offered it in October—but his high-collared tunic of dark navy wool was fastened with clasps of raw California quartz-gold. Before him stood three men and one woman: Lady Kaiulani, Lord Shimazu of the Satsuma naval mission, and Judge Jeremiah Black, spokesman for the newly annexed Mississippi Valley territories.

"The settlers in Missouri and Iowa will not endure it, Protector!" Judge Black was saying, his broad red face slick with sweat as he struck a vellum scroll against the table. "Your Marshal Vance has quartered two regiments of Japanese infantry in the courthouse at St. Louis, and yesterday a magistrate sent from Honolulu fined a Christian minister fifty silver thalers for preaching against the Shinto shrine erected at the Arsenal! We joined the Confederation to escape the abolitionist fanatics of New England and save our farms from ruin, not to have our Anglo-Saxon common law subordinated to the decrees of Polynesian royalty and pagan sword-men!"

On the opposite side of the table, Lord Shimazu did not move a muscle of his narrow, bronze-cast face, though his left thumb rested lightly upon the gold-lacquered guard of the long sword thrust through his silk sash. Behind him, through the tall arched windows, the cranes of the naval yard swung sixteen-inch steel gun-barrels into the holds of the transport fleet.

Lady Kaiulani did not raise her voice. She wore a gown of deep forest-green velvet cut in the severe Victorian fashion, yet across her shoulders lay the royal feather cape of Kamehameha—ten thousand tiny crimson and yellow *mamo* feathers that caught the gray winter light like living fire.

"Judge Black forgets whose rifles cleared the Cheyenne from the Platte so that his Missouri wagons might reach the river," Kaiulani said, her diction crystal-clear and cold as mountain snow-melt. "And he forgets that three thousand subjects of the Hawaiian Crown and four thousand samurai of the Western Clans lie buried in the passes of the Rockies and the mud of Vicksburg to purchase the safety of his cornfields. When you signed the Compact of Denver, sir, you did not join a white republic. You entered an oceanic empire."

"An empire must have a foundation in nature!" Black retorted, turning his desperate gaze back toward Elias. "In the old states, a white man knew his station! Here, my own nephew—a captain in the Missouri militia—was ordered yesterday to salute a Cantonese commissary officer at the Sacramento rail-depot! If you force this unnatural mingling upon the Valley, Protector, you will have fifty thousand rifles in rebellion from Dubuque to Memphis before the snow melts!"

Elias leaned forward, placing both rough, weather-beaten hands flat upon the polished redwood. For a long moment he said nothing, listening to the deep, booming roar of the Pacific swells breaking against the granite sea-wall below the cliff.

"When I was fourteen years old, Judge," Elias said, his low, rasping voice silencing the whisperings of the clerks along the wall, "a gentleman of pure Anglo-Saxon blood rode out from Philadelphia with a parchment writ and burned my mother’s roof over her head for sixty-two dollars. When I was fifteen, I would have frozen to death in a mule’s belly on the Platte if a Delaware Indian with cropped ears had not shown me how to shoot a buffalo bull in the drift. I care nothing for the color of a man’s skin, and less for what name he gives to the Almighty on Sunday morning."

He rose slowly to his feet. Though he was not the tallest man in the room, the sheer, immovable weight of his presence seemed to press the air out of the chamber.

"Look out that window, Mr. Black," Elias commanded, pointing a blunt finger toward the gray expanse of the harbor. "Fifty leagues west of that fog-bank, the ocean runs clear to Asia. There are four hundred million souls on the far side of this basin, and less than thirty million on this side. The Atlantic states tried to build a nation on the notion that one race of shopkeepers could sit in a parlor and argue about human rights while their country rotted. They are dying in the Virginia ditches tonight because of it."

He walked around the curve of the table until he stood directly between the Missouri judge and the Japanese lord.

"In Pacifica, there is only one race: those who serve the state," Elias said, his pale eyes locking onto Black’s until the older man shrank back into his chair. "And there is only one blasphemy: mutiny. Your nephew will salute the Cantonese commissary because that commissary holds my commission, and if your nephew refuses, Marshal Vance will shoot him against the depot wall. On the other hand—" Elias turned his head toward Kaiulani and Lord Shimazu "—no Shinto priest and no Hawaiian provost will interfere with a Christian congregation west of the Mississippi so long as the taxes are paid in silver and the conscripts report to the muster-rolls on time. Lady Kaiulani, you will amend the Maritime Code before tonight’s sitting: local parish courts in the Valley retain jurisdiction over marriage, church property, and Sabbath observance. Imperial Provost Courts retain absolute jurisdiction over treason, commerce, and military discipline."

Kaiulani inclined her head half an inch, the yellow feathers of her cloak rustling softly against the velvet. "It is a wise distinction, Protector. Render unto Caesar the iron, and leave the villagers their prayer-books—so long as the prayer-books are printed on imperial presses."

"Wait outside, Judge Black, and sign the proclamation with the Chancellor," Elias said, dismissing the Missourian with a flick of his wrist. 

When the heavy bronze doors had closed behind the judge and the Japanese envoys, leaving only Kaiulani standing beside the great globe in the center of the floor, the mask of iron slipped for a breath from Elias’s face. He walked to the tall window and rested his forehead against the cold glass, watching a column of Hawaiian recruits in dark blue greatcoats marching through the rain toward the troop-trains bound for the East.

"You yield to the Missourians today so that your railways will not be torn up behind you while you march on Washington," Kaiulani said quietly, coming to stand beside his shoulder. She did not look at the soldiers; she looked at the silver threads multiplying at his temples. "But you know as well as I do, Elias, that a patchwork quilt holds together only while the tailor’s needle is in the cloth. What happens when we have swallowed the Atlantic coast? A hundred million people who hate our laws, bankrupt and starving, chained to an ocean they have never seen."

"We will not govern them as states," Elias answered, his breath fogging the pane. "We will govern them as provinces. We will take their young men and put them in garrisons on the Amur River and the islands of the South Sea, and we will put Lord Shimazu’s samurai on the ramparts of Fort Monroe. By the time their grandchildren come home, they will not remember whether their fathers wore blue or gray. They will only remember the eagle and the sun."

***

Ten months later, in the bleak, freezing twilight of November 1864, that eagle stood above the muddy bluffs of the Potomac.

The campaign that had begun at Vicksburg had not been a war in any sense that Napoleon or Washington would have understood; it had been an engineering foreclosure. Moving eastward along the parallel lines of the Baltimore & Ohio and the Pennsylvania Central behind armored rail-cruisers that swept the countryside with rifled Krupp shell at four miles’ range, the hundred thousand veterans of the Pacific Legion had simply rolled up the exhausted, ragged remnants of the Union and Confederate armies like wet carpet. Richmond had fallen in September without a siege after its last rail-line to the Carolinas was severed by Marcus Vance’s flying columns; Lee’s starving regiments had stacked their rusted muskets at Appomattox Court House in exchange for three hundredwagon-loads of California flour.
