Now, only the Federal District remained—a ten-mile ring of red mud, felled abatis, and fifty-eight earthen forts manned by invalid home-guards, treasury clerks, and the stubborn skeleton of the Sixth Corps.

Elias sat his aging claybank stallion on the heights of Arlington, directly in front of the Doric columns of Robert Lee’s abandoned mansion. The air was bitter with the smell of wet woodsmoke, rotted horse-carcasses in the canal below, and the sulfurous coal-fumes of the twenty siege-locomotives parked on the Alexandria siding. Across the half-mile width of the leaden river, the city of Washington lay beneath a low, dirty blanket of sleet-cloud.

Since his boyhood by the burning logs in Kentucky, Elias had imagined the seat of Eastern power as a place of marble and towering arrogance. Through his field-glasses, he saw a sprawling, half-built village drowning in yellow mire. The great white dome of the Capitol stood finished at last above the leafless trees, yet around its base lay acres of rotting slaughter-pens, muddy teamsters’ camps, and boarded-up brick boarding-houses. Halfway between the Capitol and the river rose the pathetic, flat-topped stump of the Washington Monument, abandoned at a hundred and fifty feet, its wooden derrick rotting against the gray sky like a broken gallows.

"General Meigs refuses the summons to surrender the river bridges, Protector," said Marcus Vance, riding up the muddy carriage-drive through the dripping oaks. His dark blue greatcoat was splattered to the waist with Virginia clay, and a fresh white bandage was wrapped around his left hand where a sniper’s Minié ball had grazed his knuckles at the Chain Bridge that morning. "He sent the flag of truce back from the Long Bridge five minutes ago. He says President Lincoln and a quorum of the rump Congress are still sitting in the Capitol basement, and that they will blow the aqueduct and fight from street to street until the spring thaw."

Elias lowered his glasses. Beside his stirrup stood his old comrade Caleb Vance—now a brigadier of the reserve, his white beard tucked into the collar of his wolf-skin pelisse—and Colonel Takashima of the First Edo Artillery.

"A man who has eaten salted horse-meat for six weeks does not fight from street to street, Marcus," Elias said, his voice flat and unhurried against the whistle of the sleet through the oak boughs. "He sits behind a pile of cobblestones until someone gives him an excuse to drop his rifle without being shot by his own provost. How many shells do we have in the armored cars at the bridge-head?"

"Four thousand rounds of eight-inch percussion, sir, and twelve hundred incendiary canisters," Marcus replied promptly, opening his damp leather field-book. "The wind is from the northwest. If we drop forty canisters into the timber yards along the Seventh Street wharf, the whole lower town from the canal to Pennsylvania Avenue will be afire in an hour."

"No fire," Elias said. "I am not burning a house I have already bought. Those departments are full of tax rolls, land surveys, and coast-charts that took seventy years to draw. We will need the clerks on Monday morning to audit the Eastern debt."

He turned his horse slightly, looking down the steep mud bank where two of the giant steam-traction rams—iron-plated behemoths forty feet long, driven by four-cylinder oil engines and armed with revolving Gatling batteries in their prows—were hissing and clanking on the planking of the Long Bridge.

"Break the barricade at the southern end of the bridge with the rams," Elias ordered, pulling on his heavy leather gauntlets. "Do not fire a single large shell into the residential squares. Put the First Hawaiian Guard and the Missouri Lancers straight up Maryland Avenue at the double-quick, and sweep the Mall to the foot of Capitol Hill. Use the Gatlings on any earthwork that shows a flag, and throw a cordon around the Executive Mansion before their cabinet can burn the cipher-books. Marcus—you have the vanguard. I want the doors of the Capitol open in forty minutes."

***

Twenty minutes later, General Marcus Vance stood in the armored conning-cupola of the lead traction-ram *Tahoe* as its eight-foot iron cleaver-wheels ground over the splintered remains of the Federal toll-gate on the Washington side of the river. 

The transition from the quiet geometry of the Arlington heights to the streets of the dying capital was a descent into a slaughterhouse. The broad expanse of Maryland Avenue—laid out seventy years before by French engineers to be a boulevard of republics—was a knee-deep quagmire of frozen mud and sewage, choked with overturned omnibus-bodies, barrels of frozen dirt, and breastworks of cordwood torn from the government fuel-yards. 

From the second-story windows of a brick row-house on Seventh Street, a ragged volley of musketry cracked out; a dozen lead balls flattened with sharp, ringing *spangs* against the *Tahoe*'s half-inch boiler-plate skirt. Behind the ram, a corporal of the Hawaiian Guard pitched face-down into the slush, his dark blood pooling bright crimson against the gray sleet.

"Battery left—second story brick!" Marcus barked down the hatchway, his face devoid of anger or haste, his pocket watch held open in his bandaged left palm.

The twin six-barrel Gatling guns mounted in the forward casemate swung forty degrees on their greased bronze trunnions. The gunner cranked the handle. A tearing, mechanical roar—like a giant ripping sheets of corrugated iron—filled the narrow street as four hundred .58-caliber bullets a minute chewed straight through the brick mullions, shattering the window-sashes, collapsing the interior lath-and-plaster walls, and shredding the blue-coated marksmen inside into bloody rags before they could draw a second ramrod.

"Forward!" Marcus ordered, snapping his watch shut as the column debouched out of the avenue onto the open, sleet-swept pastures of the Mall.

Ahead of them, looming vast and spectral through the driving snow-squalls and the drifting clouds of black powder smoke, rose the white marble tiers of the United States Capitol. Across the gravel plaza at the western base of the hill, behind a formidable redoubt built of granite blocks hauled from the unfinished Treasury extension and reinforced with overturned army baggage-wagons, stood the last line of the Atlantic Republic: two thousand veterans of the Iron Brigade and the regular artillery, their coats in tatters, their gaunt faces blackened with powder, standing shoulder-to-shoulder behind six brass Napoleon twelve-pounders. Above them, nailed to a splintered lance-staff driven into a pile of paving-stones, a torn silk regimental flag flapped wildly in the freezing gale.

"Halt the infantry at the canal bridge!" Marcus shouted through his brass speaking-trumpet as the four Napoleon guns on the slope flashed simultaneously in a long sheet of red flame. 

Four solid twelve-pound shot came howling across the dead grass of the Mall. One struck the cast-steel glacis of the *Tahoe* with a tremendous, ear-splitting *boom* that filled the conning-tower with hot iron-scale; a second tore through the wheel-house of the flanking traction-engine, severing a steam-pipe in a shrieking cloud of scalding white vapor and hurling two Cantonese engineers broken into the mud.

Marcus did not duck as the shrapnel screamed past the vision-slit. His gray eyes measured the three hundred yards of frozen turf between the Botanical Garden fence and the granite barricade. If he sent the Missouri infantry up that icy slope with bayonets, those starving regulars behind the stones would kill four hundred of his men before the breastwork was carried—and dead soldiers were an unpardonable waste of rolling-stock capacity.

"Bring up the two railway-mortars on the B&O spur!" Marcus commanded, turning to Major Sterling, who was crouching behind the ram’s rear fender with a portable field-telegraph key clicking furiously in an oilskin box. "Do not shell the building—the Protector wants the marble whole. Elevation twelve degrees, fuse cut to one and one-half seconds. Drop six hundred-pound Krupp air-bursts directly over the gun-emplacements behind the granite wall, then advance the three rams abreast at full throttle and crush the wagons!"

Back by the river-tracks, two monstrous short-barreled steel mortars mounted on eight-wheeled iron flatcars elevated their snouts toward the gray heavens. When they fired, the concussion shattered every unbroken pane of glass along Pennsylvania Avenue for half a mile.

Six seconds later, the sky fifty feet above the Capitol barricade turned into a furnace of screaming, jagged steel. The Krupp high-explosive shells did not burst with the lazy white puff of black powder; they detonated with the blinding, yellow-white flash of picric acid, scything downward like an invisible iron flail. When the smoke-cloud tore apart in the wind, four of the six brass Napoleons lay dismounted on broken axles amidst a writhing heap of disemboweled artillery horses and mangled gunners.

Before the dazed survivors behind the granite blocks could stagger to their feet, Marcus dropped his gloved hand. 

"Sound the charge!" he said.

With their steam-whistles shrieking in a discordant, terrifying chorus that drowned the pitiful cheers of the dying defenders, the three forty-ton traction rams surged up the slope of Capitol Hill, their wide iron cleats chewing the frozen turf into red mire, while two thousand Pacifica riflemen came behind them at a dead run, firing their seven-shot Spencers from the hip as the steel prows of the machines crashed straight through the granite-and-wagon barricade with a rending roar of splintered oak.

***

While Marcus Vance’s iron rams were grinding the last barricade below the Capitol dome into kindling, Elias rode at a walk up the deserted width of Pennsylvania Avenue toward the Executive Mansion, accompanied only by Caleb Vance, Lady Kaiulani in an armored carriage, and fifty troopers of the Life Guard.

The street was a graveyard of paper. From the broken windows of the Treasury Building on the corner of Fifteenth Street, thousands of unissued greenback dollar bills, quartermaster vouchers, and pension ledgers had been tossed into the wind by fleeing clerks; they blew across the frozen cobbles like dirty snow, sticking to the wet fetlocks of the horses and swirling around the abandoned boots of deserters. The great iron gates of the White House stood wide open—one leaf hanging crookedly from a broken hinge where a six-mule baggage wagon had struck it during the midnight flight of the Cabinet toward the Baltimore turnpike.

Elias reined in beneath the tall white columns of the north portico. There were no sentries. Only a dead artillery mule lay frozen in the circular driveway, its belly bloated under a dusting of sleet, while a half-starved hound dog licked at a spilled sack of oats on the marble steps.

He swung down from his saddle, his stiff knees popping in the cold, and handed the reins to Caleb. 

"Keep the troopers in the yard, Caleb," Elias said, looking up at the tall, soot-streaked windows of the mansion, where a single torn lace curtain fluttered through a broken pane. "No looting. If a soldier pockets so much as a silver spoon from the pantry, shoot him on the lawn."

He walked up the steps alone, his heavy cavalry boots ringing hollowly against the stone, and pushed open the tall oak front doors.

The entrance hall was cold as a vault and smelled of stale tobacco smoke, wet dog, and the sour tallow of extinguished chandeliers. Across the black-and-white marble tiles, someone had dragged a heavy iron safe, leaving two deep, jagged gouges in the stone before abandoning it beside the foot of the grand staircase. Down the corridor, in the East Room where the velvet draperies had been cut down by soldiers for blankets, a squad of invalid Union veterans from the Veteran Reserve Corps sat around a dying fire built directly on the parquet floor out of broken gilded chairs, boiling coffee in tin cups. When they saw the tall figure in the navy wool greatcoat and the four-pointed gold star at the collar step across the threshold, they did not reach for the muskets leaning against the wallpaper; they simply stared up with dull, sunken eyes, took off their forage caps, and went back to warming their blue fingers.

Elias did not speak to them. He climbed the wide mahogany staircase to the second floor, his hand sliding up the banister that Jackson and Polk and Lincoln had gripped. The upstairs hallway was ankle-deep in charred telegraph flimsies and torn maps of Virginia.

At the southeast corner of the passage, the white-painted door to the President’s office stood ajar. Elias pushed it open with the toe of his boot.

The oval-ended library was empty, though the coal fire in the marble grate was still warm, radiating a faint, dry heat that smelled of burned sealing-wax and old leather. On the long oak cabinet table in the center of the carpet lay an unfinished meal—a plate of hardtack biscuits, a half-empty glass of buttermilk with a skin of ice forming at the rim, and a pair of steel-rimmed spectacles resting beside an unsigned proclamation calling for three hundred thousand more men to save the Union. Through the tall south windows, beyond the sleet-whitened expanse of the lawn and the stinking mud-flats of the Tiber canal, the gray waters of the Potomac rolled down toward the sea.

Twenty-seven years ago, a bailiff from Philadelphia had stood in the smoke of a Kentucky cabin and told a fourteen-year-old boy that blood was not legal tender in the District of Columbia. 

Elias walked slowly across the worn Brussels carpet, his spurs clinking softly in the quiet room. He stood behind the high-backed leather armchair at the head of the table, where the green baize was stained with ink and scarred by the pen-knives of twenty-five presidents. He reached out with one rough, weather-chapped hand, touched the cold leather of the backrest, and sat down.

For a full minute he did not move. He looked at the brass inkwell, at the spectacles left behind by a tired lawyer from Illinois, and then up at the tarnished gilt eagle painted on the plaster ceiling above the chandelier.

Heavy footsteps echoed in the corridor outside, accompanied by the rustle of silk. Lady Kaiulani stepped through the doorway, her dark sea-otter pelisse sparkling with melted sleet, followed closely by General Marcus Vance, whose right hand still held his drawn saber while his left carried a wet sheaf of telegraphic dispatches.

"The Capitol has surrendered, Protector," Marcus said, coming to attention before the oak table, his boots leaving tracks of red Maryland clay across the presidential carpet. "General Meigs delivered his sword at the foot of the eastern steps ten minutes ago. Mr. Lincoln and Secretary Stanton escaped northward toward Philadelphia on a hand-car before the B&O tracks were severed at Bladensburg, but eighty-four members of the Senate and House are under guard in the old Supreme Court chamber awaiting your pleasure."

Elias picked up the steel-rimmed spectacles from the green baize, folded their thin wire temples with a gentle *click*, and laid them inside the open drawer of the desk.

"Let Mr. Lincoln run to Boston if he likes," Elias said, his low, rough voice sounding strangely loud in the small, low-ceilinged room that had once governed half a continent. "A president without a treasury or an army is just a country lawyer on a hand-car. We will not make a martyr of him."

Kaiulani walked to the south window, her dark fur mantle gleaming with melted sleet as she looked out through the falling snow toward the broken stump of the Washington Monument, then turned her luminous eyes back toward Elias as he sat framed between the velvet curtains.

"And the eighty-four gentlemen in the basement across the avenue, Elias?" she asked softly. "They still believe they are the Roman Senate waiting in their curule chairs for the Gauls. If you march them out in irons, every newspaper in London and Paris will call it the murder of liberty."

"I am not going to put them in irons," Elias said, leaning back into the deep leather of the chair and resting his elbows on the arms as he looked up at his general. "Marcus, take two wagons of hard silver coin from the pay-train—minted with the sun and anchor—and drive them up to the Capitol steps. Pay every senator and every representative his back mileage from the day the banks suspended in sixty-one, provided he signs a receipt acknowledging the Articles of Dissolution and the transfer of the Atlantic Debt to the Imperial Receivership at San Francisco. Any man who signs goes home on the evening train with his pockets full. Any man who refuses stays in the cellar without coal until he changes his mind."

Marcus’s thin lips twitched in the ghost of a grim smile as he reached into his breast pocket and drew out a fresh, urgent dispatch printed on the blue paper of the trans-continental wire. "It will cost less than a regiment’s rations for a week, sir. But before I go back to the hill—this just came through the Fort Churchill relay from Nagasaki, forwarded by Admiral Farragut at New Orleans. The British China Squadron and four French ironclads have anchored off Shimonoseki, demanding that the Shogunate repudiate the exclusive coaling monopoly with Pacifica or face bombardment before the new moon."

Elias’s fingers tightened on the mahogany arms of Lincoln’s chair. The gray eyes that had looked out over the Sierra pass twenty years before seemed to look right through the brick walls of the White House, back across three thousand miles of conquered prairie and mountain toward the great, roaring arena of the western ocean.

"So London thinks our hands are full in this mud-hole," Elias said, rising from the chair and reaching for his wet campaign hat on the table while Marcus stepped forward to unroll the Pacific chart across the unsigned Union proclamation. "They think because we marched twenty thousand men to the Potomac, the slips at Yerba Buena are empty. Let us finish the funeral of this Republic before sundown, Marcus. I have no time to waste on eastern bailiffs when the British fleet is knocking at the gates of Edo."

***

To the Chronicler who has examined the original parchment of the Articles of Dissolution—preserved today under thick crystal in the Rotunda of the Diet at Monterey—nothing is more instructive of the fall of the first American Republic than the sheer, ledger-bound banality of its final hour. Great empires are supposed to expire in the glare of burning palaces or beneath the shields of dying legions; the Union of Washington and Jefferson ended at four o’clock in the afternoon in the damp, gas-lit basement of the old Supreme Court chamber, amidst the scratching of steel nibs and the heavy clinking of Mexican-milled silver.

The semicircular cellar, with its low masonry vaults designed by Latrobe to resemble the tombs of Etruria, was choked with the vapor of eighty steaming wool overcoats and the sour reek of unwashed bandages from the temporary hospital in the crypt next door. At the center of the floor, directly beneath the plaster figure of Justice whose scales had been chipped by a stray rifle ball during the morning’s assault, Marshal Marcus Vance had ordered two green-painted commissary chests placed upon the clerk’s mahogany table. Behind him stood twelve troopers of the First Hawaiian Guard, the rainwater dripping from their dark blue capes onto the worn carpet, their repeating carbines held at rest.

"The terms of the Receivership are non-negotiable, gentlemen," Marcus said, his weary, pragmatic voice echoing off the low stone arches as he turned a page of his roster. "By signing the instrument before you, you attest that the compact of 1787 is void by reason of insolvency and civil war; that the federal custom-houses upon the Atlantic seaboard are mortgaged in perpetuity to the Treasury of Pacifica to satisfy eighty-two million thalers in war claims; and that the sovereign states east of the Mississippi are hereby reconstituted as autonomous protectorates. As the Clerk calls your state, step to the baize, sign the parchment, and Captain Takashima will weigh out your back allowances in silver coin."

From the rear bench, where a cluster of New England radicals sat huddled in their shawls like wet crows, Senator Charles Sumner of Massachusetts rose to his full, imposing height. His face was ghostly pale above his black cravat, and a bruise from a fallen plaster cornice discolored his temple.

"This is not a treaty, sir!" Sumner’s rich, oratorical baritone boomed through the vault, though it trembled at the edge with exhaustion. "This is the ransom of Brennus! You bring armed Polynesians and Japanese mercenaries into the sanctuary of the Constitution, you throw a butcher’s ledger upon the altar of the law, and you ask the representatives of a free people to sell their birthright for thirty pieces of silver!"

Marcus did not look up from his list. "Thirty-four hundred pieces of silver in your case, Mr. Sumner, calculating mileage to Boston at forty cents the league since the August suspension. And I must remind you that the furnace boilers in the cellar were extinguished at noon to conserve coal for our locomotives. Those gentlemen who decline to sign the Articles will remain in this chamber until the Provost-General convenes the military commission for the trial of belligerent debtors on Monday."

He nodded to the clerk. "Call the roll. State of Maine."

For twenty seconds no man moved. Only the drip of melting sleet from the broken basement casements and the distant, terrifying hiss of the traction-rams parked on the plaza outside disturbed the silence. Then a representative from the Portland shipping district—a man whose three merchant brigs were currently rotting at the wharf for want of clearance papers—slowly unbuttoned his coat, walked down the narrow steps with his eyes fixed upon the toes of his boots, and took the pen from Captain Takashima’s gloved fingers.

The scratch of the steel nib across the vellum sounded loud as a saw in the quiet room. Immediately afterward came the bright, musical cascade of hard Pacifica thalers pouring from a brass scoop into a canvas sack.

At the sound of the silver, a visible shudder ran through the benches. Men who had lived for three years on depreciated green paper that would hardly buy a pair of boots in a Washington tavern craned their necks toward the chests. When New Hampshire was called, two congressmen jostled each other in the aisle; by the time the clerk reached Pennsylvania and Ohio, forty politicians were lined up three deep before the mahogany table, blowing on their chilled fingers and signing away the Continental Congress’s inheritance with the frantic haste of country passengers scrambling for the last stagecoach before a flood. Inevitable providence had reduced the rhetoric of eighty years to its true denominator: the weight of metal in a scale.

Only nineteen men remained seated in the darkening alcove behind Sumner when the last canvas bag was tied.

"Clear the hall of the signatories, Captain," Marcus ordered, snapping his roster shut and looking toward the silent nineteen in the shadows. "Give them passes for the six o’clock train to Baltimore. As for Senator Sumner and his companions—lock the iron grilles on the corridor and post four sentries with bayonets. The Protector will deal with the irreconcilables after the ceremony on the portico."

***

Outside, the sleet had ceased, leaving the sky above the Potomac torn into long, ragged bands of amber light that caught the wet marble of the Capitol’s eastern front and turned the puddles in the gravel plaza into pools of liquid brass. 

Elias stood alone on the central platform of the grand steps, where nine presidents had taken their oaths beneath the Corinthian columns. Below him, filling the broad expanse between the portico and the iron fences of the green, stood no cheering crowd of citizens in beaver hats, but twelve thousand soldiers drawn up in hollow squares: the Missouri Lancers on the right with their red pennons drooping in the damp wind; the dark-skinned battalions of the Hawaiian Royal Guard in the center; and on the left, four regiments of liberated negro railway-pioneers and Bakufu artillerymen standing beside the smoking boilers of the forty-ton traction-rams.

Directly at the foot of the stairs, on a temporary pine dais covered in wet bunting, sat sixty men in civilian broadcloth—not the ragged congressmen who had just crept out the back basement doors with their sacks of silver, but the Peace Commissioners from New York, Philadelphia, and Richmond whom Marcus’s provosts had brought up by special train that morning: mayors of bankrupt port cities, railway presidents whose tracks were held by Pacifica garrisons, and the surviving Peace Democrats of the midwestern legislatures.

"In the name of the Provisional Diet of the Atlantic Municipalities," read Horatio Seymour of New York, his voice thin and trembling as the cold wind off the river whipped the parchment in his red-knuckled hands, "and to prevent the utter desolation of industry, commerce, and Christian society between the Alleghenies and the sea, we do hereby constitute these sovereign commonwealths as the American Free States, under the perpetual protection, customs-union, and military suzerainty of Elias Thorne, Protector of the Grand Confederation of Pacifica and Providentor of the Atlantic Realm."

Elias did not take the scroll when Seymour held it up the steps. He let Lady Kaiulani—who stood one step below him in her green velvet gown, the crimson-and-yellow feather cape of the island kings blazing against the white marble—receive the vellum and pass it to the Chancellor.

Elias stepped to the stone balustrade. As his rough hands gripped the cold marble, the brass bands of the Legion did not strike up *Hail, Columbia*; instead, eighty cornets and great bronze siege-horns sounded the three slow, crashing chords of the Imperial Fanfare, a sound so vast and metallic that it shook the loose glass in the Capitol dome overhead.

"You have called these territories the Free States," Elias said when the echoes had died away down the muddy valley of the Tiber. He did not shout; he spoke in the short, blunt sentences of the frontier, yet the silence in the plaza was so absolute that every word carried to the gun-crews sitting on the caissons by the gate. "Understand what you are free from. You are free from the speculators who turned your treasuries into paper rags. You are free from the lawyers who sent six hundred thousand of your sons into the ditches for a tariff bill and an abolition tract. From this evening, no state between Maine and Florida will coin money, build a warship, or raise a regiment of militia beyond its municipal police."

He looked out over the heads of the shivering mayors toward the eastern horizon, where the night was already rising out of the Chesapeake—and where, ten thousand miles across the curve of the earth, the British guns were trained on the straits of Japan.

"Your coastal forts will be garrisoned by my troops," Elias continued. "Your customs houses will pay thirty percent of their gross receipts into the railway and naval chests at Monterey. In return, my granaries in the San Joaquin and the Mississippi will feed your cities through the winter, and the iron of the Pacific will guard your harbors. Go back to your counting-houses. Beat your muskets into plowshares and boiler-plate. The war on this continent is finished; the work of the ocean has begun."

He turned his back on the newly christened Free States before the commissioners could even raise their hats in a ragged cheer, walking straight back toward the bronze doors of the Rotunda, where Marcus Vance was already waiting in the shadow of the portico with a lantern in his hand.

"How many refused the silver, Marcus?" Elias asked, not breaking his stride as he crossed the threshold into the vast, echoing gloom of the Capitol.

"Nineteen in the cellar, sir," Marcus answered, falling into step beside him while their boot-heels rang across the sandstone flags beneath Trumbull’s paintings of the Revolution. "Sumner of Massachusetts, Thaddeus Stevens of Pennsylvania, Wade of Ohio, and sixteen others. And we took Secretary Stanton’s chief provost-marshal, Colonel Baker, trying to burn the War Department cipher-archive on Seventeenth Street with a squad of six partisan rangers. They killed two of our Cantonese sappers with pistol-shot before we took them."

Elias stopped beneath the great dome. High overhead, in the freezing twilight filtering through the oculus, Brumidi’s fresco of Washington sitting in the clouds looked down like a faded ghost from another world. Behind Elias, Lady Kaiulani paused by the marble pillar, her dark eyes watching the lines of fatigue around his mouth.

"We cannot leave eighty thousand troops on the Potomac through the spring, Marcus," Elias said quietly, his voice dropping so that only his general and Kaiulani could hear. "If the British and the French bombard Shimonoseki before our cruisers arrive, the Satsuma clans will think our alliance is a paper shield, and the whole western basin will slip from our grasp while we police bread-riots in Baltimore. I need four divisions of the Legion on the troop-trains for San Francisco before Wednesday noon."

"If we pull four divisions out of the eastern provinces this week, Protector," Marcus said, his tone hardening, "Sumner and Stevens will have a rebel congress sitting in Boston before Christmas, and every bushwhacker from Virginia to Pennsylvania will be shooting our tax-collectors from the woodlots."

"Not if we pack the governing machinery into boxcars and take it with us," Elias said.

Kaiulani took half a step forward, the feathers of her cloak rustling in the cold draft of the rotunda. "Elias. A senator in a cellar is an old man with a dry tongue. A senator on a scaffold is an immortal spirit. My ancestors knew when to break a chief’s bones with a club, and when to bring his household gods into the king’s own compound. Leave no martyrs in this swamp, and leave no seat of authority for a mob to rally around."

Elias looked up at the great dome overhead, and then down toward the dark doorway leading to the crypt. "She is right, Marcus. We will not hang Mr. Stevens on the monument. A gallows only makes a shrine for Boston preachers. Hang Colonel Baker and his six bushwhackers from the burnt rafters of the Seventeenth Street archive where they killed our sappers—quietly, as common arsonists, before the street-lamps are lit. As for Stevens, Sumner, and the seventeen irreconcilables—put them in a locked Pullman car behind my own engine tonight."

Marcus paused, his pencil hovering over his leather field-book. "You are bringing them to the Coast, sir?"

"I am bringing the entire carcass of their government to the Coast," Elias replied, turning back toward the eastern portico where the cold rain was beginning to turn to sleet again. "Strip the Treasury of its plates and dies. Empty the Patent Office, the Coast Survey, and the War Department vaults. Unbolt the printing presses, pack the original parchments of their laws into zinc-lined crates, and take down the bronze doors of this building. By Saturday night, I want Washington to be nothing more than a country turnpike junction between the tobacco fields. When a man in New York or Richmond wants a land-patent, a customs-clearance, or a pension-warrant, he will not look toward the Potomac. He will face west."

***

The physical translation of an empire’s center of gravity is no clean feat of draftsmanship; it is an exhausting, mud-choked migration of iron and paper across two thousand miles of winter mountain and alkali flat. For six weeks in the opening months of 1865, the single completed broad-gauge track of the Central Pacific groaned beneath the weight of forty-two special convoys creeping westward through the snow-sheds of the Sierra Nevada. While the Provisional Diet sat in Monterey to adjudicate the ancient ceremonial privileges of the Polynesian and Bakufu missions, Elias decreed that the executive engines of the realm—its mints, its archives, and its high courts of receivership—should sit directly upon the granite jaws of the Golden Gate.

On the nineteenth of February, Elias stood beneath the dripping redwood scaffolding of the new Citadel on Rincon Hill, watching a double-team of steam-winches haul a twelve-ton crate of cast-iron Treasury plates up the mud-slick plankway from the Embarcadero. The morning fog off the bay was thick with coal-soot from the donkey-engines, the rank brine of the mud-flats at low tide, and the sweet, heavy smoke of camphor-wood burning in the braziers of the Cantonese stone-masons.

Yet the grand design was already creaking at the joints. Half a mile down the hill, where the wooden shanties of the newly arrived Baltimore and Philadelphia treasury clerks pressed against the brick walls of the Edo naval barracks, a dull, angry murmur rose through the mist. Four hundred Eastern copyists—men who had been uprooted from their Maryland brick row-houses at the point of a bayonet and shipped across the continent in unheated passenger coaches—had gathered in the ankle-deep mire outside the commissary depot, waving their soggy ration-tickets at a line of Hawaiian provost-guards.

"The axle-boxes on the third archive train gave out at Truckee yesterday, Protector," said Major Sterling, limping up the wet timber ramp with a manifest clipped to a cedar board. The former Union engineer looked ten years older than he had that night in Alexandria; his eyes were bloodshot from seventy hours without sleep, and his navy tunic was stained with locomotive grease. "We have six hundred boxes of Eastern land-deeds and the entire registry of the Philadelphia Mint sitting on a siding in twelve feet of snow because the Sacramento rolling-mills diverted our spare wheel-castings to the naval yard. And these Washington clerks down on First Street are refusing to open the customs ledgers unless they are given brick quarters with coal-grates and paid in silver instead of quartermaster vouchers."

Elias did not look down at the shouting clerks. He rested his rough palm against a freshly dressed block of Sierra granite—cold, wet, and cut with the combined mason-marks of a Cornish quarryman and an Osaka castle-builder.

"Why were the wheel-castings diverted without my counter-signature?" Elias asked, his voice low and rasping against the wheeze of the winch-boilers.

"Marshal Vance’s requisition, sir," Sterling answered, lowering his voice as Lady Kaiulani stepped out from the arched doorway of the temporary Chancery behind them, a dark wool shawl drawn over her high-collared silk dress. "And Lord Shimazu’s naval board. They claim the British China Squadron at Hong Kong has taken on four thousand tons of Welsh steam-coal and twelve hundred Royal Marines. If the drydocks at Hunters Point are not finished before the spring typhoons clear, Shimonoseki will stand alone."

"If the customs ledgers are not opened by Monday, Major," Kaiulani said, her musical voice cool and sharp as she looked down the muddy slope toward the simmering riot at the commissary, "neither Marshal Vance nor Lord Shimazu will have the silver to pay the rivet-gangs by April. You have swallowed a whale, Elias, and it is kicking in your belly. Those clerks down there are small men, soft-handed and full of Eastern spite, yet they are the only men on this continent who can read the cipher-codes of the Boston and New York tariff-houses. If you put them on the breakwater with a pickaxe, the Atlantic revenues stop tomorrow."

Elias watched a corporal of the Hawaiian Guard drop the butt of his carbine onto the toes of a grey-haired clerk from the Sixth Auditor’s Office who had tried to push past the rope. Immediately, twenty Japanese sword-gentry off duty from the foundry strolled out of a neighboring tea-house, their hands resting on their hilts, watching the loud-mouthed Americans with undisguised contempt.

Here was no clean skirmish line in the desert where a volley of repeaters could settle the arithmetic. This was the slow, grinding friction of three worlds crushed into a single narrow peninsula of rock and mud.

"Take twenty wagons of seasoned oak cordwood from the military reserve at the Presidio, Sterling," Elias said, turning from the parapet. "Issue every married clerk from the Washington departments two cords of wood, a sack of white San Joaquin flour, and ten silver thalers against his March salary. Tell them that at noon tomorrow, the Providentor will inspect the counting-rooms in person. Every ledger that is balanced and open on the desk by twelve o’clock carries a warrant for a freehold house-lot on the Mission slopes. Every desk that is empty at five minutes past twelve will have its occupant shipped to the Sitka timber-camps on the evening packet. As for the wheel-castings—come with me to the boat-slip. It is time Marshal Vance remembered that a fleet without a treasury is only scrap-iron floating on salt water."

***

Three miles south of the muddy chaos on Rincon Hill, where the volcanic serpentine rock of Potrero Point jutted out into the deep-water channel of the bay, General Marcus Vance stood upon a vibrating catwalk of bolted iron grating fifty feet above the floor of Graving Dock Number Two.

To the Chronicler, the Imperial Shipyards of San Francisco in that winter of 1865 resembled nothing so much as the forge of Hephaestus roofed over with corrugated Birmingham iron and timbered with the primeval forests of Oregon. Beneath Marcus’s mud-caked boots lay the cavernous stone trough of the basin, pumped dry by four giant Cornish beam-engines whose walking-beams rose and fell through the roof-steam like the elbows of titans. In the pit sat the skeleton of the *Kamehameha*—a five-thousand-ton ocean-going ironclad frigate, her massive cellular double-bottom forged from Sacramento pig-iron and plated with six-inch compound armor rolled at the Nagasaki and Clark’s Point works.

The din inside the shed was physical, pressing against the eardrums until a man had to shout to hear his own thoughts: the deafening, staccato thunder of four hundred pneumatic and hand-swung riveting hammers beating simultaneously against red-hot boiler plate; the shriek of circular steel saws biting through teak backing-timbers; the hiss of leaking steam-pipes; and the hoarse chants of six hundred Cantonese coolies hauling a forty-ton Krupp stern-post along greased iron skids to the strike of a bronze gong.

Yet for all the terrifying grandeur of the spectacle, Marcus Vance’s gray eyes saw only the flaws in the iron.

"Look at that starboard strake below the water-line, Takashima," Marcus said, pointing with his brass-tipped walking-stick toward a chalk-marked plate near the bilge-keel where a gang of Scottish boilermakers and Satsuma shipwrights were arguing fiercely through an interpreter, their hammers lowered while the red-hot rivets cooled to a dull purple in the tongs. "The edges have blistered three-eighths of an inch on the bend. That is the third plate from the Benicia furnaces we have had to condemn since Tuesday."

Colonel—now Rear-Admiral of Ordnance—Takashima wiped a smear of black coal-grease from his cheek with a white cotton handkerchief, his narrow eyes dark with fatigue. "The pig-iron from the new Oregon mines carries too much phosphorus, Marshal. And the rolling-mill crews have been working eighteen-hour shifts since the Protector telegraphed from Washington. Yesterday, two of my master-smiths from Kagoshima drew their blades on an Irish foreman from Pittsburgh because he spat tobacco into the quenching-trough after the Shinto priest had purified the new steam-hammer. We lost four hours on the main shaft while the provosts separated the guilds."

Marcus opened his damp leather ledger, resting it against the iron railing of the catwalk while a traveling overhead gantry-crane rumbled past three feet above their heads, showering them with fine black flakes of soot and hot lubricating oil. The numbers on the page were merciless. 

In the field, an army lived on momentum; you took the enemy’s corn, you burned his bridges, and if a hundred horses died in the traces, you requisitioned mules from the next county. Here, at the edge of the great water, geography refused to be bullied. To steam six thousand miles across the western ocean and meet the Royal Navy in the Straits of Shimonoseki required three tons of anthracitic coal for every mile of steaming, drydocks at Honolulu and Midway that were still half-dredged coral lagoons, and armor plate that did not crack when an Armstrong three-hundred-pounder struck it at point-blank range.

"We cannot wait for the Benicia chemists to sweeten the Oregon ore," Marcus said, his pencil scratching a rapid calculation in the margin of his book. "If Lord Palmerston’s cabinet in London learns that we have stripped our Eastern garrisons before the *Kamehameha* and the *Satsuma* are ready for sea, the British squadron at Esquimalt will steam down from Vancouver Island and blockade the Puget Sound coal-colliers inside a week. Strip the four river-monitors we left at Cairo and Memphis. Have their six-inch turret-plates unbolted, loaded onto flatcars, and rushed through the South Pass before the March blizzards close the grade."

"Unbolt the river-monitors?" Takashima repeated, a rare note of alarm breaking through his samurai reserve. "Marshal, if you disarm the Mississippi flotilla now, the Illinois and Tennessee partisans will cross the river in flatboats before the month is out! General Caleb Vance wired from St. Louis this morning that he has barely enough riflemen to guard the railway bridges against disbanded Confederate bushwhackers!"

"Let them burn a bridge in Illinois," Marcus replied coldly, snapping his ledger shut as the shrill whistle of the Protector’s steam-launch sounded from the fitting-out basin outside the shed. "We can hang bushwhackers at our leisure next autumn. If the British and French burn the Shogun’s forts at Shimonoseki in May, we lose the Western Ocean forever. Come down the ladder, Admiral; the Protector has just rounded the mole, and by the look of Major Sterling behind him, the civilian departments are already crying for our iron."

***

By the third week of March, the struggle between the demands of the dockyard and the collapse of the Eastern counting-houses had reached a pitch that no provost’s bayonet could quiet. 

In the cities of the Atlantic protectorates—from the silent textile towns of Massachusetts to the weed-choked wharves of Charleston—three different kinds of worthless paper swirled through the gutters: the bloated greenbacks of Mr. Lincoln’s fugitive congress, the dead grey notes of Richmond, and the temporary grain-vouchers of the Pacifica military governors. Farmers in Ohio refused to bring their winter wheat to the rail-depots for paper; bakers in New York shuttered their ovens while ten thousand unemployed dock-wallopers marched down Broadway behind black flags, smashing the windows of the municipal customs-receivers.

On the twenty-fourth of March, Elias summoned the Joint Council of the Realm and the captive commissioners of the Eastern banks to the great vault-hall of the new Imperial Mint on Market Street.

The building was a fortress of rusticated blue basalt and brick, its tall chimney-stacks pouring continuous heat into the damp spring sky from twenty assaying furnaces in the cellar. Inside the central weighing-room, the air was scorching and sharp with the nitric-acid fumes of the parting-vats, the smell of hot beeswax, and the heavy, greasy odor of six steam-powered coining presses that stood in a row along the north wall like iron guillotines. 

At the center of the granite floor, stacked upon low oak pallets until they formed a solid breastwork four feet high and thirty feet long, lay four thousand unstamped bars of pure Sierra quartz-gold and Washoe silver—the accumulated hoard that Elias had locked behind the mountain passes while the East bled itself white.

Around this gleaming rampart stood a strange, uneasy congregation: Lord Shimazu and two Tokugawa treasury officials in dark silk *hakama*; Lady Kaiulani flanked by the merchant-princes of Oahu; Cornelius Schuyler of the New York Clearing House, who had been brought overland under military escort; and rising from a wooden bench near the iron doors, his wrists free of chains though two Hawaiian guards stood behind his shoulders, Senator Charles Sumner of Massachusetts.

Elias walked out from the assaying office in his plain dark wool tunic, holding a single newly struck coin between his thumb and forefinger. He did not mount a platform; he stepped directly onto the lowest tier of the bullion-pallets, his heavy military boot resting upon five hundredweight of dull yellow metal.

"Mr. Schuyler," Elias said, his rough voice carrying over the low hiss of the steam-presses. "You told my Treasury Secretary yesterday that the merchants of New York and Boston cannot collect the thirty-percent customs tribute because no man between Maine and the Mississippi knows what a dollar is worth."

Schuyler swallowed hard, wiping the acid-sweat from his bald crown with a crumpled silk handkerchief as his eyes stared with hypnotic terror at the mountain of gold beneath the Protector’s boots. "It is a matter of commercial faith, sir! There are nine hundred millions of Federal greenbacks and national bank-notes in the hands of the eastern public! If you repudiate them entirely, every savings-bank, every widow’s annuity, and every insurance company from Portland to Baltimore will crash before noon! Yet if you leave them in circulation without specie redemption, no cargo will move on the Erie Canal this spring!"

"And by what right," thundered Charles Sumner, rising from his bench despite the hand of the Hawaiian sergeant pressing down on his broadcloth shoulder, "does a military usurper in a frontier mint presume to annul the public faith of the United States? Those notes bear the sacred pledge of a free Congress, issued to preserve the Union and strike the shackles from four million bondsmen! If you turn them into ashes to build your pagan ironclads, history will curse your name alongside Alaric and Attila!"

Elias looked across the yellow bars at the tall Massachusetts senator. There was no anger in Elias’s face—only the flat, weathered patience of a man who had watched a prairie fire burn itself out against a river.

"Your Congress printed nine hundred million dollars of promises on rag-paper because you did not have the stomach to tax your own shopkeepers for the blood you were spilling," Elias said evenly. "A piece of paper is not faith, Mr. Sumner. It is a lie signed by a clerk who hopes he will be out of office before the note comes due."

He tossed the heavy gold coin across the width of the bullion-pile. Schuyler caught it clumsily against his waistcoat. It was broader and thicker than the old American double-eagle, stamped on the obverse with the rising sun over an anchor and the legend *IMPERIUM PACIFICUM*, and on the reverse with its weight in pure grains across three languages—English, Japanese *kanji*, and Hawaiian.

"At six o’clock this morning," Elias declared, looking from the New York banker to the foreign envoys along the wall, "I signed the Currency Decree. From the first of April, there is only one legal tender between the Atlantic Ocean and the China Sea: the Pacifica gold thaler and its silver tenth. Every furnace in this cellar and every press in Carson City and Osaka is running day and night to coin eighty million thalers before the summer solstice."

Schuyler’s fingers trembled as he turned the heavy disk in the gas-light. "And the nine hundred millions in Federal greenbacks, Protector? At what discount will your customs-houses receive them?"

"At one hundred cents on the dollar—for ashes," Elias said, stepping down from the bullion pallet and walking toward the nearest of the great brick assaying-furnaces, where a Cantonese stoker stood with his long iron slice-bar before the roaring white-hot grate. "Bring up the first crate from the Washington train, Marcus."

Four sappers wheeled an iron hand-truck across the granite flags and tipped a zinc-lined box of unissued hundred-dollar Treasury notes beside the furnace door.

"Hear the law," Elias said, his hand resting on the warm brickwork of the flue while the orange glare of the coals lit the deep lines around his jaw. "For ninety days, every holder of a Federal greenback or an Atlantic bank-note may bring his paper to the provost-marshals in New York, Chicago, or New Orleans. We will redeem the old Union paper at twenty cents on the dollar—not in coin, which would flee to London on the next packet, but in twenty-year Pacifica Railway and Dockyard bonds bearing four percent interest in gold, redeemable only upon the completion of the Shimonoseki and Honolulu fortifications. As for the paper of the Southern rebellion, it is waste-rag. And every Federal note handed in across the counter will come here."

He nodded to the stoker. The Cantonese laborer swung open the heavy cast-iron furnace door; a blast of dry, roaring heat swept across the room, making Sumner and Schuyler flinch backward.

"You are chaining every bank in New York to the wheels of your war-chariot in Asia!" Schuyler cried out, taking a half-step forward as the first bundle of green-tinted Washington bank-notes was pitched onto the white-hot coals, flaring up instantly into a blinding sheet of yellow-green flame from the copper-oxide ink.

"I am giving your banks a foundation of rock instead of swamp-mud," Elias replied over the roar of the draft, watching the engraved portraits of Hamilton and Lincoln curl into black cinders and vanish up the chimney while Marcus Vance stepped quickly through the side door from the telegraph room, a wet blue cipher-strip held tight in his bandaged hand.

"Protector," Marcus said, not waiting for the banker to answer as he came straight to Elias’s elbow, the heat of the burning millions beating against their faces, "a fast dispatch-steamer from Hakodate just made the Cape Flattery wire-station. Admiral Kuper has rejected the Shogun’s mediation and cleared his gun-decks in the Inland Sea—and our lead cruiser off Midway has just blown her starboard high-pressure cylinder."

Elias did not move a muscle of his face as the green flames of the dying Republic danced across his buttons. If Schuyler or the Japanese envoys saw him flinch now, the twenty-year dockyard bonds would be worth no more than the cinders going up the flue.

"Keep your voice down, Marshal," Elias murmured under the roar of the furnace blower. "Let the stokers finish the crate. Tonight we dance with their wives and daughters on Nob Hill. If the patricians of Manhattan and Boston are to pay for a second fleet across the Pacific, they must first believe the first one has already won."

***

By nine o’clock that evening, the nitric fumes of the Market Street Mint had been exchanged for the warm beeswax and bruised tuberose of the Protectorate Palace on the crest of Mason Street. Where the wind-scoured chaparral had stood fifteen years before, a vast quadrangle of pale Sierra granite and gilded cast-iron conservatory domes rose above the fog-line, its architecture a deliberate, overwhelming marriage of West and East: Corinthian pilasters carved from white marble met sweeping, copper-tiled roofs modeled after the shogunal audience halls of Nijo, while the ballroom floor was laid in alternating strips of dark Hawaiian koa and California redwood polished with pumice until it reflected the three hundred gas-chandeliers like black water.

Elias stood near the raised dais beneath the great silk banner of the rising sun, wearing a plain dress coat of dark navy wool without a single medal upon his breast. Around him moved five hundred prisoners disguised as guests. They were the cream of the old Atlantic oligarchy—the Schuylers and Livingstons of New York, the Cabots of Boston, the Biddles of Philadelphia, and the surviving rice-grandees of the Carolina low-country—whom Marcus Vance’s railway commissioners had politely invited to winter in San Francisco while their eastern estates were assessed for the Imperial Receivership.

In the center of the floor, a string orchestra from the Vienna Conservatory was playing a Strauss waltz, though the music was punctuated every thirty seconds by the deep, subterranean thud of the fifty-ton drop-forges down at the Potrero Point armor-works, a vibration that made the Venetian crystal prisms on the candelabra shiver and chime.

"You see how quickly the thoroughbred takes to the new harness, Elias," Lady Kaiulani said softly beside his elbow. She wore a gown of amber Lyons silk draped with the royal crimson feather-work of Oahu across the bodice, a tiara of raw Washoe diamonds and black pearls binding her dark hair. She tilted her ivory fan toward the refreshment tables, where Cornelius Schuyler’s nineteen-year-old daughter was laughing behind her gloved hand at a compliment from young Captain Takashima, whose Satsuma clan crest was embroidered in gold thread upon the high collar of his naval tunic, while three paces away, Judge Biddle of Chestnut Street was earnestly inquiring of Lord Shimazu’s factor regarding the dividend yields on the Nagasaki coal-mines.

"A horse takes the harness when the whip is in the driver’s boot," Elias replied, his low voice rough as unplaned timber beneath the swell of the violins. "Judge Biddle is asking about Nagasaki coal because we burned his Pennsylvania railway bonds at noon. He wants to know which way the trough is tilting before he puts his snout back in."

"Do not despise their greed, Protector; it is the mortar that will save you ten regiments of garrison troops east of the mountains," Kaiulani murmured, smiling graciously as Mrs. Livingston—a matriarch whose grandfather had signed the Declaration of Independence—swept past them and dropped a stiff, reluctant curtsy to the Polynesian envoy. "If you leave these families sitting in their cold parlors on Beacon Hill and Gramercy Park, nursing their humiliation like old wine, they will finance every partisan bushwhacker from Maine to Georgia. Marry their daughters to your frontier colonels and your samurai admirals. Give their younger sons clerkships in the Amur fur-monopoly and seats on the Honolulu Sugar Board. Within twenty years, a Cabot will draw a sword against Boston to protect his wharf-shares in Yokohama."

Cornelius Schuyler detached himself from a knot of Baltimore shipping merchants and approached the dais, his bald head gleaming with perspiration under the gas-jets, a glass of Sonoma champagne held unsteady in his plump fingers. The terror of the morning had faded into the calculating deference of a broker who has examined the bailiff’s books and decided to join the syndicate.

"A magnificent house, Protector," the New York financier said, bowing low enough that his white cravat brushed his watch-seal. "My wife was just remarking to Lady Kaiulani’s chamberlain that the Tuileries itself has no finer glass-work than your winter garden. Though—if an man of business may speak plainly among friends—the news from the Western Ocean has caused some tightness among our underwriters tonight. A rumor reached the Exchange Room at the Palace Hotel an hour ago that the *Midway* has put back into Honolulu with a cracked cylinder-head, and that the British fleet at Hong Kong outnumbers Lord Shimazu’s steam-sloops two to one."

Elias looked down at the banker. His gray eyes were completely still, giving back nothing but the twin pinpoints of the chandelier overhead.

"The *Midway* is a scout-corvette of twelve hundred tons, Mr. Schuyler," Elias said, his voice loud enough that six neighboring gentlemen from Philadelphia and Charleston stopped their conversation and turned their ears toward the dais. "When a wheel breaks on one of your Broadway omnibuses, do you close the clearing-house?"

"No, sir, certainly not, only—"

"The *Kamehameha* and the *Monterey* carry twelve inches of rolled compound iron on their water-lines, Mr. Schuyler, and they do not steam alone," Elias continued, stepping down from the dais so that the old-money patricians were forced to give way before his broad shoulders. "Since you gentlemen are now the principal bond-holders of the Imperial Dockyards, it is right that you should see how your four-percent interest is secured. Tomorrow morning at eight, my launch will take you across the bay to the Marin magazines. And as for the union of our two coasts—I have decided tonight to establish the Order of the Golden Gate. Fifty hereditary baronies of the Pacific Realm, carrying ten thousand acres apiece of prime timber and coal land on Vancouver Island and the Amur estuary, free of the Eastern war-tax."

A sharp, collective intake of breath rustled through the silk gowns and black tailcoats around the floor. Even Judge Biddle’s austere Quaker jaw dropped half an inch.

"The first twelve patents," Elias said, his gaze passing slowly over Schuyler’s daughter and resting upon the pale, handsome young scions of the Boston and Carolina houses standing by the pillars, "will be conferred on the first of June upon those eastern houses whose sons accept commissions in the Pacific Marine Corps for the Asian station, or whose daughters wed officers of the General Staff roster. Enjoy the music, gentlemen. The lists open in the Chancellor’s office at ten."

***

It is the custom of the beaten provinces along the Atlantic to portray the great migration of the late eighteen-sixties as a Babylonian captivity—a forced transplanting of mechanics, farmers, and gentlefolk driven at the point of Marshal Vance’s lances to build the pyramids of a Western Pharaoh. Yet the Chronicler, who has stood upon the stone viaducts of the Humboldt River and examined the parish registers from the Willamette to the Straits of Juan de Fuca, must record a far stranger and more majestic truth. Once the tumor of parliamentary faction had been excised by the sword of Sacramento, the pent-up energies of the continent burst westward not like a chain-gang, but like a mountain river when the ice-jam is dynamited in the spring.

History provides few spectacles to match what the court philosophers of Monterey termed *The Salutary Effects of Order*. For thirty years prior to the Coup, the settlement of the interior had been paralyzed by the endless wrangling of Washington lawyers: whether a territory should be slave or free, whether a railroad should run through Chicago or New Orleans, whether a squatter’s pre-emption took precedence over a speculator’s scrip. Under the iron hand of the Providentor, these questions vanished overnight.

Where four months of creaking ox-wagon misery had once separated the Missouri from the Pacific tidewater, double-tracked broad-gauge railways now spanned the alkali sinks and pierced the granite heart of the Sierra through tunnels illuminated by coal-gas and ventilated by giant steam-fans. Every week through the summers of 1865 and 1866, thirty-six immigrant trains—each drawn by twin ten-wheeled Baldwin-Nagasaki locomotives whose brass cow-catchers bore the rising sun—rolled down the western slopes into the valleys of the Sacramento, the San Joaquin, and the Columbia. They carried no ballot-boxes, no party newspapers, and no land-lawyers. They carried disbanded soldiers from the armies of Grant and Lee who had found their eastern homesteads mortgaged to the chimney-tops; they carried Lancashire cotton-spinners starved out by the blockade, Cornish tin-miners, Bavarian iron-founders, and ten thousand emancipated negroes from the Mississippi delta, each holding a brass-stamped Imperial Freehold Warrant that guaranteed forty acres of irrigated ditch-land or three silver thalers a day in the timber-mills in exchange for seven years’ liability in the Territorial Reserve.

To travel the Great Trunk Road from Salt Lake to Monterey in those years was to witness the birth of a new race under an older, sterner sky. The chaotic, mud-walling individualism of the old frontier was gone, replaced by the geometric grandeur of Imperial engineering. At every fifty-mile division point rose the standardized stone depot, the grain-elevator sheathed in galvanized iron, and the syncretic garrison-chapel where the bronze cross of the Christians and the polished mirror of the Sun Goddess stood side by side beneath a roof of red redwood shingles. In the mining towns of the Washoe and the Idaho gulches, where six years earlier drunken prospectors had shot one another over disputed claim-stakes in the mud, the great quartz-stamps now thundered day and night with the regularity of cathedral clocks, their waste-waters channeled through masonry aqueducts built by Cantonese sappers to turn five hundred thousand acres of sagebrush desert into orchards of peach and olive.

Nor was the transformation merely one of iron and wheat. In the new port cities springing up around the deep waters of Puget Sound—at New Osaka on the Elliott Bay and Port Vance below the snow-dome of Mount Rainier—the narrow, puritanical horizon of the old American republic dissolved into the salt-scented immensity of the Great Arena. Here, the grandson of a Connecticut ship-carpenter worked at the same drafting-table with a naval architect from Edo; here, the ordinances of the harbor were cried in three tongues from the steps of basalt customs-houses; and the children of Illinois ploughmen grew up watching the great four-masted iron tea-clippers and armored depot-ships coming home from Canton, Manila, and the Kuriles with the weeds of the western ocean trailing from their copper hulls.

Men forgot very quickly how to vote for a county sheriff when the granaries were full, the silver coin never varied by the tenth of a grain, and a woman could walk from the Rio Grande to the Fraser River without seeing a highwayman who was not hanging in chains from an iron telegraph pole. If this was servitude, as Senator Sumner continued to write from his walled villa above the Santa Cruz redwoods, it was a servitude that paved the wilderness with gold and taught a fractured nation to march to the beat of a single drum. Yet, as the great historians of antiquity have ever reminded us, an engine that cannot stop must continually find new fuel to burn, lest its own steam tear the boiler apart.

***

On a bitter, sleet-driven afternoon in November of 1866—eighteen months after the British demonstration at Shimonoseki had ended in a tense, armed truce along the thirty-second parallel—Elias stood at the northern rail of the headland battery above Cape Flattery, where the black basalt cliffs of the Washington Territory met the full, unbroken fury of the winter Pacific.

Below the gun-parapet, two hundred feet straight down, the gray swells came charging out of the northwest fog-bank like ranks of white-maned horses, smashing themselves against the jagged sea-stacks with a boom that shook the wet turf beneath Elias’s boots and sent plumes of freezing spindrift flying high over the muzzles of the ten-inch Rodman columbiads. Behind him, along the timbered shore of the Strait, four colliers from the Nanaimo mines were battling the head-wind, their screw-propellers thrashing out of the troughs as they crept toward the coaling-hulks at Port Angeles.

Elias was forty now. The hard, tireless campaigning that had carried him from the Kentucky ashes to the steps of the Capitol in Washington had left its mark not in fat, as it does with hereditary kings, but in a dry, weathered tightening of the sinew; the wind off the North Pacific whipped his iron-gray hair flat against his skull, and a deep vertical furrow was permanently chiseled between his eyebrows.

Beside him stood General Marcus Vance, his oilskin cape streaming water as he held open a weighted zinc map-cylinder to shield a Russian Admiralty chart from the freezing drizzle.

"Admiral Takashima’s squadron cannot hold the Kurile passage through another winter without a windward base, Protector," Marcus shouted over the thunder of the surf below the cliff. He looked gaunt and hollow-cheeked; the logistics of keeping twelve ocean-going ironclads supplied with coal and boiler-tubes four thousand miles across the northern steamer-lane via Midway had aged him five years in eighteen months. "We lost two coal-barques in the October gales south of the Aleutians, and the *Satsuma* had to burn her own teak cabin-bulkheads to make Hakodate with her bunkers empty. If the British reinforce Esquimalt in the spring and the Royal Navy closes the southern belt from Singapore to Hong Kong, our ships in the Sea of Japan will be trapped in a bottle."

Elias did not look at the chart. His gaze was fixed northward across the twenty miles of white-capped grey water where the mountainous, pine-blackened spine of Vancouver Island loomed through the squall—under the Union Jack—and beyond that, toward the vast, fog-shrouded curve of the globe where the continent bent westward like a drawn bow toward Asia.

"A man does not cross a canyon on a single rope when there is a stone bridge three miles upstream, Marcus," Elias said, his low, rough voice cutting through the hiss of the sleet against their oilskins. "How many miles is it from Honolulu to Yokohama against the winter westerlies?"

"Thirty-four hundred marine leagues, sir," Marcus answered instantly, his cold-stiffened finger tracing the long, empty southern curve across the chart. "And two thousand miles of it without a single sheltered anchorage or a seam of coal between Midway and the Bonins."

"And by the Great Circle?" Elias asked, raising his gloved hand and pointing straight into the teeth of the freezing northwest gale, up the coast past the British forts at Victoria, toward the fifty-fourth parallel. "Up the inside passage to Sitka, along the stepping-stones of the Aleutian chain, and straight down to the Kuriles and the mouth of the Amur?"

Marcus’s eyes dropped to the top of the zinc cylinder, where the Russian characters of the Imperial Fur Company marked the indented, island-choked coastline of Russian America. "Twenty-five hundred miles from Puget Sound to the Japanese straits, Protector. With land-locked harbors every hundred leagues, timber to spar ten fleets at Sitka, and outcrop coal at Cook Inlet and Unalaska. You could steam torpedo-rams and shallow-draft monitors all the way from Seattle to Kamchatka without ever being more than forty hours from a drydock or a telegraph cable."

"Baron Stoeckl is at New Osaka this week," Elias said, turning from the stone parapet so that the wind caught his heavy wool greatcoat and flattened it against his boots. "He came over from St. Petersburg via the Siberian post-road and the Nikolayevsk packet. The Tsar’s treasury is empty from the Polish rebellion and the emancipated serf-loans, and the Grand Duke Constantine knows that if war breaks out between Russia and England this winter, the British squadron at Esquimalt will sail up and seize Novo-Arkhangelsk before a single Russian frigate can clear Kronstadt."

"Stoeckl has been hinting at a sale of the fur-posts since fifty-nine," Marcus said, a sudden, sharp light coming into his weary eyes as he let the zinc map-cover snap shut. "Before the war, he offered the territory to Buchanan’s cabinet for five million dollars, and the eastern senators laughed him out of the room because they said it was nothing but icebergs and walrus-blubber."

"The eastern senators never looked at a globe," Elias said, walking down the wet granite steps of the battery toward the timber guard-house where their horses stood steaming under a cedar shed, while three Hawaiian signalmen worked the semaphore arms on the cliff-edge above them. "They looked at flat maps on a parlor wall and thought the top of the world was an edge you fell off. Look at the curve of that coast, Marcus. With the Aleutians under our thumb, the North Pacific is not an ocean; it is a roofed lake, and the British station at Vancouver is caught in the nutcracker between Puget Sound and Sitka."

Marcus fell into step beside him on the muddy corduroy road, his hand dropping to the hilt of his saber to keep it from banging against his wet boot. "If we buy Russian America, Lord Stanley in London will read it as an act of encirclement against British Columbia. The Hudson’s Bay factors are already arming the steamer-crews at Victoria, and our ironworks at Clark’s Point are six months behind on the heavy turret-castings for the third division."

"Let London read it how they please," Elias said, stopping beside the stirrup of his big bay gelding and taking the wet leather reins from the orderly’s hand. "We are not buying it with gold that the Tsar can spend in London, Marcus. Tell Lady Kaiulani to have the Chancellor meet me at the telegraph car at four. We will offer Baron Stoeckl seven million two hundred thousand thalers—half in silver bullion delivered at Vladivostok, and half in four armored coastal monitors built on the slips at San Francisco to guard the mouth of the Amur for the Tsar. If the British want to stop the deed, they will have to fight the Russian bear and the Pacific eagle in the same pass."

He swung his boot into the iron stirrup and pulled himself up into the wet saddle, the leather creaking beneath his weight as a fresh squall of hail came howling off the gray rollers below, stinging the cheeks of the horses and rattling like buckshot against the corrugated roof of the telegraph shed.

"And Marcus," Elias added, leaning down from the saddle as his general reached for the bridle of the second mount, the hail whitening the shoulders of his navy cloak while the semaphore paddles above them suddenly began to clack wildly in the mist with an incoming priority cipher from the south—

The heavy cedar door of the telegraph shanty burst open before Elias could finish the sentence. Major Sterling stumbled out into the sleet without his cap, the blue paper ribbon of the Port Townsend submarine cable trailing wetly from his fingers.

"Protector!" Sterling shouted over the roar of the breakers below the cliff. "From the harbour-master at Port Angeles—relayed from our picket-corvette off the San Juan channel! Rear-Admiral Denman has just warped the British ironclad *Zealous* and two screw-frigates out of Esquimalt harbour under full steam! They are heading north through the Georgia Strait with two battalions of Royal Marines aboard, and the British Governor at Victoria has issued a proclamation placing the Russian American Company’s coal-seams at Cook Inlet under the temporary protection of Her Majesty’s fleet to prevent foreign piracy!"

Marcus Vance’s boot froze in his stirrup. He looked northward across the twenty miles of churning gray water, where the dark smudge of coal-smoke from the British dockyards was swallowed by the low-hanging cloud-wrack. "Denman knows Stoeckl is with us. Someone in the St. Petersburg Foreign Ministry sold the draft treaty to the British ambassador. If the *Zealous* drops anchor in Sitka sound before the cession is signed and our garrison is ashore, Denman will raise the Union Jack over the Russian governor’s house and call it a preventative occupation. We have nothing in the Strait tonight heavier than two wooden torpedo-launches and the monitor *Shasta*."

Elias did not dismount. Instead, he reined his bay gelding hard around on the wet logs of the road, forcing the animal’s iron shoes to bite into the bark right beside the doorway of the telegraph hut. His face was stone.

"How many knots can the *Zealous* make against a northern gale, Marcus?" Elias asked, his low voice dropping beneath the shriek of the wind.

"Eight, perhaps nine if she burns her prime Welsh coal," Marcus answered instantly, his mind already sorting the tide-tables and bunker-capacities. "It is seven hundred miles up the outside passage to Sitka. With the winter rollers running off Queen Charlotte Sound, Denman will take the inside channel behind Vancouver Island. That gives us ninety hours before his marines can row ashore at Baronov Castle."

"And the Russian overland wire through Nikolayevsk and Irkutsk?" Elias looked down at Sterling.

"Open all the way to the Winter Palace, sir!" Sterling cried, wiping the sleet from his spectacles. "We laid the last splice across the Amur mouth three weeks ago, and Baron Stoeckl is waiting in your railway car at the Port Angeles siding right now with the St. Petersburg cipher-clerks!"

"Good," Elias said. He did not touch the spurs to his horse; he dismounted in a single heavy drop, handing the reins back to the orderly, and strode straight into the cramped, kerosene-heated belly of the telegraph shed. "Marcus, wire the naval yard at New Osaka. Put the First and Second Regiments of the Atlantic Free States Volunteer Rifles—the old Pennsylvania and Virginia veterans—aboard the fast paddle-transports *Oregon* and *Constitution* tonight. Tow the monitor *Shasta* behind them with double hawsers. You will leave the Strait before midnight, steam outside Vancouver Island through the open sea regardless of the gale, and beat Denman to Sitka desk by six hours."

"The *Shasta* has only eighteen inches of freeboard, Protector," Marcus said, stepping into the doorway as the brass sounder on the pine table chattered like an angry squirrel. "If we tow a flat-bottomed river monitor into the open North Pacific in November, the swells will bury her turret before we clear Nootka Sound."

"Batten her hatches with tarred canvas and lash two coal-barges alongside her beam to break the wave-slap," Elias said, stripping off his wet leather gauntlets and throwing them onto the operator’s table beside the humming galvanic batteries. "If the sea takes her, she sinks. If she reaches Sitka, her fifteen-inch Dahlgren will punch through the *Zealous*'s four-inch armor like wet pasteboard. Get to the boats, Marshal. By the time your transports clear Cape Flattery, that coast will belong to Pacifica—or the Tsar will have no empire left on the Pacific to sell."

***

Four hours later, in the mahogany-paneled saloon of the armored command-car parked beside the Port Angeles coaling-pier, the air was thick with the pungent smoke of Turkish cigarettes, hot sealing-wax, and the damp wool of six men who had ridden twenty miles through a coastal hurricane. Outside the double-paned windows, the locomotive’s boiler panted with a low, rhythmic throb to keep the steam-radiators hot against the freezing rain, while two hundred yards down the jetty, the red torches of the dock-gangs flared through the sleet as three thousand veterans of the old Army of the Potomac and the Army of Northern Virginia—now wearing the slate-gray greatcoats of the Atlantic Auxiliary Corps with the rising sun brassard on their sleeves—marched up the gangplanks of the troop-steamers.

At the center of the saloon table sat Baron Eduard de Stoeckl. He was sixty, bald-headed, with deeply pouched, cynical eyes that had watched the courts of Europe and America for thirty years. Before him lay two strips of blue telegraph tape that had just come off the trans-Siberian wire from the Ministry of Finance in St. Petersburg—six thousand miles of copper cable strung across the frozen birch-forests of the Amur, the steppes of Irkutsk, and the snows of the Urals, humming with the dying breath of European diplomacy.

Beside Stoeckl stood Lady Kaiulani, her dark hair still damp from the ride down the mountain trail, her fingers resting lightly on the back of the Chancellor’s chair as she translated the French cipher-groups aloud.

"Prince Gorchakov is hesitant, Protector," Stoeckl said in his heavily accented English, tapping his gold snuff-box nervously against the green baize. "He wires from the Winter Palace that the British Ambassador, Sir Andrew Buchanan, called upon him at midnight Petersburg time. London warns that if His Imperial Majesty transfers the ports of Russian America to a belligerent maritime power that holds the American Atlantic states in receivership, Great Britain will consider the Treaty of Paris void and will move her Baltic squadron to Revel in the spring. The Grand Duke Constantine urges caution. He asks for a thirty-day armistice in the negotiations while a joint commission meets in Berlin."

Elias did not sit. He stood at the head of the narrow car in his mud-spattered boots, his broad shoulders nearly filling the space between the polished redwood bulkheads. He picked up the brass telegraph key connected to the repeater-line and looked down at the Russian envoy.

"In thirty days, Baron," Elias said, his rough voice slow and deliberate, "Rear-Admiral Denman’s marines will be drinking rum in your governor’s cellar at Sitka, and the Union Jack will be flying from Mount Edgecumbe. Do you think Lord Stanley will pay the Tsar seven million thalers for a house he has already taken with a squad of sailors?"

"The British claim they are merely policing the waters against filibusters," Stoeckl protested weakly, though a bead of sweat rolled down his powdered cheek. "And Prince Gorchakov objects to the medium of payment. St. Petersburg requires gold coin in London to meet the Rothschild railway coupons in January. Your offer of four monitors and silver bars at Vladivostok does not satisfy the Tsar’s bankers."

"The Tsar’s bankers in London are Englishmen," Elias replied, leaning both calloused palms flat upon the table until the brass lamp-brackets rattled. "If I send seven million in gold sovereigns to Threadneedle Street tomorrow, the Bank of England will attach every penny of it before noon to satisfy the defaulted cotton-bonds of the old Southern states, or lend it to their own Admiralty to build ironclads for the Baltic. Tell Prince Gorchakov to wipe the sleep out of his eyes and look at the map."

He turned to the telegraph operator hunched in the corner cubicle. "Clear the Siberian line to the Winter Palace. Tell the relay clerks at Irkutsk and Omsk that if a single key drops out of circuit before I finish speaking, I will cut the subsidy to the Amur Telegraph Company at midnight. Take this down in plain English—let the Russian clerks translate it for the Tsar’s cabinet as it comes off the wire."

The operator’s fingers closed on the vulcanite knob. The sharp, metallic clatter of the armature filled the quiet railway car.

"From Thorne, Protector of Pacifica, to Alexander Imperator and Prince Gorchakov at St. Petersburg," Elias dictated, his eyes never leaving Stoeckl’s face. "The British ironclad *Zealous* cleared Esquimalt four hours ago to seize Russian America by force of arms. My fleet is already at sea to intercept her. If His Imperial Majesty signs the Act of Cession before four o’clock this morning Pacific time, back-dated to the first of November, the soil of Sitka is Pacifica territory, and I will blow Admiral Denman out of the water as a trespasser upon my realm.
