If the treaty is not signed within the hour, I will recall my troop-ships to Puget Sound, open the Straits of Juan de Fuca to the Royal Navy, and inform London that Pacifica has no objection to a British annexation of both Sitka and the mouth of the Amur River."

Baron Stoeckl half-rose from his velvet seat, the snuff-box spilling brown powder across his white waistcoat. "Monsieur le Protecteur! That is an ultimatum to the Autocrat of All the Russias! You cannot speak to the Winter Palace as if you were dealing with a Mexican customs-collector!"

"A bankrupt is a bankrupt, whether he wears a sheepskin coat or a diamond crown," Elias said coldly. "And I will sweeten the iron for him, Baron. Tell Gorchakov that in addition to the seven million two hundred thousand in silver and monitors, I will hand over the complete working drawings of the Clark’s Point compound marine engines and send fifty Edo and Scottish master-machinists to the shipyards at Kronstadt before the spring thaw. Russia does not need London’s gold; she needs steam and steel to keep the British out of the Black Sea. Send the wire."

For twenty-two minutes, while the rain lashed the glass and the deep whistle of the transport *Oregon* sounded three long blasts from the harbor mouth as Marcus Vance’s flotilla cast off into the dark, no one spoke inside the car. Lady Kaiulani poured a small porcelain cup of hot green tea and set it beside Elias’s elbow; he did not touch it. He watched the brass pendulum of the bulkhead clock swing right, left, right, measuring the seconds it took for an electric spark to leap across the frozen roof of the world—through the log stations of Kamchatka, under the ice of the Okhotsk sea-margins, past the convict-mines of Nerchinsk, and into the gilded telegraph room where the Tsar’s ministers stood in their embroidered coats.

At eighteen minutes to four, the receiving magnet clicked once, twice, and then broke into a furious, steady stream of dots and dashes.

The operator tore the blue slip from the brass spool with trembling hands and laid it before Baron Stoeckl.

Stoeckl adjusted his gold-rimmed pince-nez. As he read the French groups, the bluster drained out of his shoulders, leaving him an old diplomat staring at the birth of a colossus he could neither comprehend nor arrest.

"His Imperial Majesty accepts the terms of the Port Angeles convention in full," Stoeckl whispered, looking up at Elias with a mixture of dread and reluctant awe. "I am instructed to affix my seal to the parchment immediately, and to wire Captain Pestchouroff at Sitka that the territory, forts, timber, and ice of Russian America are transferred to the sovereign crown of Pacifica from the stroke of noon yesterday."

"Give the Baron the pen, Kaiulani," Elias said, reaching for his wet cavalry cloak on the brass hook behind the door. "And have the operator forward the Tsar’s order to the Sitka semaphore station ahead of the fleet. Marcus will need the paper dry before his guns clear the headland."

***

Five days later, at the gray, cheerless dawn of November twenty-fourth, General Marcus Vance stood upon the ice-sheathed hurricane deck of the paddle-transport *Oregon* as she rolled heavily through the mountainous, lead-colored swells off Sitka Sound. 

The voyage up the outside passage had been a logistical nightmare that only a commander schooled in the winter blizzards of the Platte could have survived. For ninety hours, a sixty-knot sub-arctic gale had screamed down from the Gulf of Alaska, coating the walking-beams and wire rigging of the steamers in six inches of solid blue ice and snapping the port towing-hawser of the monitor *Shasta* off Queen Charlotte Island. Three times the flat-bottomed ironclad had disappeared entirely beneath forty-foot green rollers, her single smoke-pipe belching black brine and steam as her Cantonese stokers worked knee-deep in freezing bilge-water to keep the oil-burners lit; only the two timber-laden coal-barges lashed tight against her armored sponsons had kept her from turning turtle in the trough.

Now, as the snow-squall parted ahead, the jagged, volcanic cone of Mount Edgecumbe rose out of the black water like a shrouded ghost, and beyond the spray-lashed granite reefs of the channel lay the Russian settlement of Novo-Arkhangelsk—a cluster of heavy spruce-log blockhouses, red-painted shingled roofs, and the green-copper onion dome of the Cathedral of St. Michael, huddled beneath the sheer timber ramparts of Baronov’s rock.

"Look to starboard, General!" shouted Captain Takashima from the ice-crusted wheelhouse, pointing his brass glass toward the southern entrance of the sound, where the timbered islets met the open sea.

Through the driving veil of snow, three miles off the Biorka channel, a massive, three-masted black hull with twin yellow funnels was thrashing through the kelp-beds under both steam and reefed topsails, her bow throwing up twin curtains of white foam as she raced for the inner anchorage. It was Her Britannic Majesty’s armored frigate *Zealous*, having come up the inside passage four hours behind them.

Marcus did not waste a breath on theatrical orders. His face was blue-white with frostbite around the cheekbones, and his eyelashes were crusted with frozen rime as he leaned over the bridge-rail.

"Cast off the towing-cables on the *Shasta*!" Marcus roared through his speaking-trumpet to the deck-crews below, where forty former Virginia infantrymen were hacking at the frozen hemp hawsers with boarding-axes. "Signal Lieutenant Mordecai in the turret to clear his fifteen-inch guns and lay his hull directly across the four-fathom channel between Japonski Island and the town! If the Englishman attempts to force the inner harbor, put a solid cored shot through his rudder-post!"

He turned to Colonel Mulligan, the one-armed veteran of San Pasqual who now commanded the First Atlantic Free States Regiment—twelve hundred lean, battle-hardened survivors of Gettysburg and Chancellorsville who stood packed in the waist of the steamer, their slate-gray coats buttoned over thick buffalo-wool vests, the breath smoking from their beards as they greased the breech-blocks of their Spencer repeaters.

"Get the whaleboats into the water, Colonel," Marcus ordered, checking the time on his silver watch before tucking it back beneath his heavy wool scarf. "Do not wait for the ships to anchor. Row the first four companies straight to the Russian timber-wharf, march up the steps to the Governor’s castle at the double-quick, and put twenty riflemen in each of the log blockhouses overlooking the beach. I want the sun-and-anchor flying above that flagpole before Admiral Denman’s gig touches the kelp."

Twenty minutes later, Marcus’s boots crunched onto the frozen gravel of the Sitka parade-ground at the summit of the rock. The air smelled of wet spruce-bark, rancid seal-oil from the native Tlingit canoes drawn up along the stockade wall, and the sour tallow of the Russian garrison’s tallow candles. 

Before the tall spruce flagstaff stood two hundred soldiers of the Siberian Line Battalion in their long, ankle-length drab overcoats and flat forage caps, their faces hollow with scurvy and homesickness, while Captain Pestchouroff and Prince Maksutov, the last Governor of the Russian American Company, waited in full gold-laced uniform beside the halyards. Down in the harbor below the log parapet, the low, flat iron turtle-back of the *Shasta* had just swung broadside across the narrow channel, her twin fifteen-inch muzzles gaping black and sinister in the gray light at less than four hundred yards’ range as the towering black bow of the British *Zealous* came shuddering to a halt against her backed screw-propellers, her anchor-chains roaring down into the mud to avoid running onto the monitor’s ram.

"You have the dispatch from Baron Stoeckl, General Vance?" Prince Maksutov asked in stiff French, his breath puffing white in the freezing drizzle as his Princess wept quietly into her sable muff on the timber gallery behind him.

"I have the Tsar’s own cipher, Excellency, and two hundred thousand silver thalers in the purser’s strongbox below to pay the arrears of your garrison," Marcus replied, drawing the oilskin packet from his breast and handing it over as four hundred of Mulligan’s veterans came clattering up the wooden stairs from the wharf, their bayonets glinting dull gray through the snow, filing rapidly into the casemates behind the rusted Russian thirty-two-pounders.

Maksutov glanced once down at the harbor, where a British twelve-oared cutter had just been dropped from the davits of the *Zealous*, a red-faced Royal Navy post-captain standing in the stern-sheets waving a white boat-cloak toward the wharf. A dry, bitter smile touched the Russian prince’s lips.

"It appears our English friends have arrived too late for the christening," Maksutov said, turning to his sergeant at the flagstaff. "Lower the eagles."

As the Russian drums beat a slow, mournful ruffle, the double-headed imperial eagle came jerking down the spruce mast. Halfway down, the wet hemp fouled on a resinous knot in the wood, leaving the yellow silk flapping damply against the bark. At a nod from Maksutov, a Russian sailor climbed the icy shrouds, freed the line, and dropped the standard into the waiting arms of the Siberian guard.

Marcus did not wait for the British boat to reach the landing-stage. He stepped forward, hooked the brass grommets of the Pacifica ensign—heavy blue wool embroidered with the golden rising sun and the iron anchor—onto the halyard, and nodded to Colonel Mulligan.

"Haul away, Sergeant," Mulligan barked.

As the blue-and-gold banner rose straight up into the arctic snow-squall, snapping taut in the gale from the Gulf, the fifteen-inch gun in the turret of the *Shasta* below roared out the first gun of a twenty-one-gun salute—a blank charge of fifty pounds of mammoth powder whose concussion shook the icicles from the eaves of St. Michael’s Cathedral and stopped the British cutter dead in the water fifty yards off the piles.

When the British post-captain finally climbed the slippery timber steps to the castle gate ten minutes later, his cocked hat white with snow and two armed Royal Marines behind him, he found no Russian governor to receive his proclamation. He found only General Marcus Vance standing beneath the dripping spruce arch, flanked by a rank of former Pennsylvanian and Virginian riflemen whose repeating carbines were held at the ready across their chests.

"I am Captain Hewett of Her Majesty’s Ship *Zealous*!" the Englishman snapped, his hand on his sword-hilt as he glared up at the unfamiliar blue-and-gold banner whipping overhead. "Rear-Admiral Denman demands to know by what authority an armed force of American irregulars has occupied the fortification of a friendly European power in time of peace!"

"You are standing on the soil of the Northern Province of the Grand Confederation of Pacifica, Captain," Marcus said, his weary, flat voice carrying not a trace of triumph, only the cold finality of an engineer who has driven the last spike into a bridge. "Purchased by treaty from His Imperial Majesty Alexander the Second on the nineteenth of November. Admiral Denman may water his ships at the outer anchorage for twenty-four hours if his boilers are dry; after noon tomorrow, any British warship entering these waters without a clearance-pass from the Port Admiral at New Osaka will be treated as an enemy vessel. Good morning, sir."

***

To purchase half a million square miles of frozen wilderness with a telegraph key is the work of an afternoon; to digest it requires a stomach of cast iron. 

While the diplomatic salons of London and Paris rang with angry denunciations of the "Port Angeles Fraud" and Lord Stanley rushed two regiments of Canadian militia overland toward the Red River, Elias did not remain in the warm marble council-rooms of Monterey. He knew that a treaty is merely ink until a road is cut through the timber. On the twelfth of January, 1867—in the dead, black heart of the sub-arctic winter, when the sun rose scarcely four hours above the southern horizon—Elias stood inside the great log trading-hall of Baronov Castle at Sitka, surrounded by steam-radiators that his engineers had bolted into the old Russian porcelain stoves.

The long spruce table was covered with geological surveys, coal-samples from the Kenai Peninsula, and rough birch-bark maps drawn by Russian creole fur-traders. Outside the frost-feathered panes, where a hundred Tlingit laborers and Cantonese railway-graders were clearing the snow from the foundation-trenches of the new naval foundry by the glare of pine-tar cressets, the temperature stood at twelve degrees below zero. The air inside the hall was heavy with the smell of wet dog-sled harnesses, seal-blubber, hot machine-oil, and the strong black brick-tea that Baronov’s old clerks brewed in brass samovars.

"The coal at Cook Inlet is lignite, Protector," Marcus Vance was saying, his finger tapping a chunk of dull, flaky black stone on the edge of the chart. "It will serve for the stationary donkey-engines at the timber-mills and the domestic stoves, but it clinkers the grates of the high-pressure cruisers. Until we sink deep shafts into the Matanuska valley behind the mountains, our northern squadron will still have to haul thirty thousand tons of Nanaimo or Welsh steam-coal a month up the inside passage—right past the muzzles of the British batteries at Victoria."

Beside the stove, Lady Kaiulani sat wrapped in a heavy mantle of silver fox-fur that Prince Maksutov had presented to her before sailing for Vladivostok. Despite the stifling heat of the iron pipes, her slender fingers were stiff with the northern chill as she turned the pages of the native census ledger.

"And your Tlingit chiefs along the Lynn Canal are not the plains Comanches, Elias," she said, her voice clear and low against the howling of the williwaw wind coming down off the glaciers behind the town. "The Russians stayed inside their log stockades for sixty years because four thousand Sitka and Chilkat warriors hold the mountain passes to the interior. They have British Hudson’s Bay muskets, they trade with Victoria by canoe, and their shamans told my interpreter this morning that if your Cantonese pioneers cut a single cedar tree on their burial islands for your drydock pilings, they will burn every fishing-station from here to Wrangell."

"Give the Chilkat chiefs fifty repeating carbines apiece, ten barrels of Sacramento valley flour for every village, and commission their headmen as Imperial Wardens of the Passes with the pay of cavalry captains," Elias said, pacing slowly down the length of the spruce table, his hands clasped behind the small of his back. "Let them tax the British Hudson’s Bay trappers fifty percent on every beaver-pelt that comes down the Stikine River, and keep half the silver for their own lodges. When a chief draws a government salary to rob his old friends, he forgets his shaman very quickly."

Before Marcus could enter the order in his ledger, a heavy commotion broke out in the timber guard-room at the foot of the stairs. The guttural Russian challenge of a creole sentry was answered by a hoarse, frost-cracked American oath, followed by the heavy thud of snow-shoes being kicked off against the log wall.

The double spruce doors swung open. Major Sterling stepped inside, holding a lantern above the head of a man who looked as if he had been dug out of a glacier.

It was Luke Harmon, a former Washoe silver-prospector and scout of the Pacific Legion whom Elias had sent north across the Chilkat divide with two Russian half-breeds in October, three weeks before the treaty was even signed, to trace the rumors of yellow gravel that old Hudson’s Bay factors had whispered about at Fort Yukon.

Harmon could scarcely stand. His wolf-skin parka was charred down the left sleeve from sleeping too close to a spruce-fire; the tip of his nose and two fingers of his left hand were wrapped in greasy rags black with dry gangrene from frostbite; and his beard was a solid mass of yellow icicles and dried caribou blood. Yet as two Hawaiian orderlies caught him by the elbows to keep him from pitching face-first onto the floor, he wrenched his right arm free and clutched a heavy, greasy moose-hide poke against his breastbone.

"Clear the door, Sterling," Elias said, stepping around the table and pulling a heavy wooden armchair up to the stove with one hand. "Sit down, Harmon. Give him a mug of rye."

Harmon did not touch the whiskey when Sterling held the tin rim to his split, purple lips. He sank into the oak chair, his snow-blinded, bloodshot eyes squinting fiercely against the lamp-glare until they found Elias’s face.

"Is the paper signed, Captain Thorne?" the scout rasped, his voice like two pieces of dry sandstone rubbed together. "Did you buy the ice from the Rooshians?"

"Every foot of it from the Portland Canal to the Frozen Ocean," Elias said, standing over him as the rime in the scout’s wolf-fur began to melt and drip onto the spruce planks with a rapid *pat-pat-pat*. "Where are the two creoles I sent with you?"

"Left the young one under a pile of stones at the White Horse rapids when our canoe stove in the November freeze," Harmon wheezed, his good hand fumbling with the stiff rawhide strings of the moose-skin bag. "The old one’s down on the sled with his feet froze black to the ankles. We came four hundred miles down the ice of the big river—the Kwikpak, the Indians call it—and back over the Chilkat pass in the dark with the thermometer forty below and the mercury froze solid in the bulb. The Hudson’s Bay men at Fort Selkirk tried to bushwhack us on the Pelly when they seen where we was panning. I put a Spencer ball through their factor’s brisket and took his dogs."

With his teeth and his remaining thumb, Harmon tore the rawhide knot loose and upended the moose-hide poke directly over the geological charts of Cook Inlet.

A cascade of dull, heavy, butter-yellow metal rattled across the paper, rolling over the ink lines of the Russian forts and knocking Baronov’s brass inkwell onto its side. These were not the sharp, white-quartz crystals of the Sierra mother-lode that Elias had pulled from the American River nineteen years before; they were smooth, water-worn nuggets the size of horse-beans and pigeon-eggs, mixed with two pounds of coarse, greasy flakes that shone in the kerosene light like the scales of a golden carp.

Marcus Vance’s breath caught in his throat. Even Lady Kaiulani rose slowly from her chair by the stove, the silver fox-furs slipping from her shoulders as she looked down at the table.

"We didn't even have a pickaxe to reach bed-rock, Protector," Harmon whispered, leaning forward over his knees, his frost-blackened fingers trembling as he pushed a three-ounce slug of pure gold across the map toward Elias’s thumb. "The ground up on those feeder-creeks by the Klondike and the Sixty-Mile is froze harder than cast iron twenty feet down. We had to build spruce-fires on the gravel at night to thaw six inches of muck, and scoop it out with a frying-pan in the dark. Every pan we washed carried ten thalers to the dirt! There’s three hundred miles of creeks up behind that mountain wall where the gold’s laying in the frozen gravel thicker than cheese in a sandwich—hundreds of millions of it, Elias, laying right across the British line!"

Elias picked up the largest of the nuggets. It was still bitter cold from the scout’s coat, heavy and greasy between his calloused fingers, bearing the dark red stain of the Hudson’s Bay factor’s blood in its crevices. He did not look at the metal for long; he looked at the faint dotted line on Stoeckl’s map where the hundred and forty-first meridian ran straight up through the blank white paper toward the polar sea.

"The creek where you shot the Englishman," Elias said, his voice dropping low and flat in the overheated log hall. "Which side of the Russian line does it lie on?"

Harmon spat a string of bloody saliva onto the floorplates. "Ten leagues east of the stake, Captain, up the Pelly fork. In Queen Victoria’s pasture. Though there ain't a white man within five hundred miles of it now that the factor’s under the ice."

"There is no line where there are no surveyors," Elias said. He walked to the window and looked down through the black sub-arctic noon toward the harbor, where the twin funnels of the *Oregon* were already raising steam for the return run to San Francisco. "Marcus. Have the surgeon take Harmon’s fingers off in the cellar and lock him and the creole in the inner ward of the castle with two Hawaiian sentries at the door. If a single sailor on the transports hears the word *Klondike* before my clerks in San Francisco have drawn the boundary statutes, we will have fifty thousand deserters streaming over the passes in canoes, and the British cabinet will send the Channel Fleet to Vancouver before the ice breaks."

***

Three weeks later, on the fourteenth of February, 1867, the fog off the Golden Gate pressed cold and salt-heavy against the tall arched windows of the Old Custom House on Battery Street, though inside the newly partitioned third floor the air was dry and smelled sharply of fresh pine shelving, hot red sealing-wax, and the iron-gall ink of sixty steel pens scratching in unison.

Elias walked slowly down the central aisle between the double rows of high mahogany standing-desks. Here sat no bearded veterans in buckskin, no Texas rangers cleaning revolver cylinders on their knees. The sixty men perched upon the tall iron stools wore identical coats of plain slate-colored wool with black linen sleeve-protectors tied at the elbows; half of them were former auditors of the United States Treasury from Philadelphia and Baltimore, and the other half were clerks of the Tokugawa rice-magistracies from Osaka, their hair cropped in the Western fashion, working side by side over massive leather-bound folios stamped in gold leaf with the cipher of the *Department of the North*.

Behind Elias walked Lady Kaiulani, her dark green velvet skirts whispering against the oiled redwood floorboards, and Cornelius Schuyler, whom Elias had appointed three days prior as Chief Comptroller of the Northern Bullion Reserve.

"You see the beauty of the double-entry system when applied to wilderness, Protector," Schuyler murmured, his plump hand gesturing proudly toward a long wall of pigeon-holes where thousands of brass-tagged zinc cylinders were racked according to latitude and stream-bed. The New York banker had lost his hunted look; given a monopoly to administer, he glowed with the quiet zeal of an archbishop inspecting a cathedral. "Unlike the chaos of forty-nine—where every roughneck who stumbled into a creek in the foothills claimed freehold over the mineral—no private foot touches the Yukon basin. Under the Organic Statute you signed on Monday, the entire watershed north of the fifty-eighth parallel is declared Crown Ordnance Domain."

Elias stopped beside the drafting table of a young Japanese topographer who was laying down red ink contour lines across a blank chart of the Chilkat and White Pass trails, translating Harmon’s rough grease-paper sketches into the rigid geometry of military engineering.

"How many tons of provisions are staged at the Lynn Canal depot, Mr. Schuyler?" Elias asked, his rough voice low enough not to break the rhythm of the scratching pens around them.

"Fourteen thousand barrels of salt pork, six thousand sacks of dried beans, and two hundred miles of portable narrow-gauge iron rail," Schuyler replied promptly, consulting an ivory memorandum tablet. "Every laborer who embarks from Puget Sound or Canton signs a five-year indenture with the Department before he steps onto the gangplank. He receives a brass neck-tag stamped with his battalion and creek-number, four pounds of bacon a week, and two silver thalers a day credited to his book in this room—payable only upon his return to San Francisco. The gold itself never enters a miner’s pocket. It goes straight from the sluice-box into locked iron amalgam-retorts under the eye of a departmental assay-clerk and two Hawaiian guards."

"And the boundary with the British possessions?" Kaiulani asked, pausing before the great wall-map where the fresh crimson paint of the Pacifica border bulged two hundred miles eastward of the old Russian meridian, swallowing the entire headwaters of the Yukon and the Pelly down to the Cassiar range. "Lord Stanley’s minister in Washington sent a formal protest through the Montreal wire yesterday. The Hudson’s Bay Company claims their factor at Fort Selkirk has been missing since November, and that our surveyors have moved the Russian boundary-cairns five degrees east into Rupert’s Land."

Elias looked up at the wet red paint on the wall. The boy who had watched the Philadelphia bailiff condemn his father’s cabin with a ribbon of parchment was gone; in his place stood a sovereign who understood that a clerk’s ruler, backed by ten-inch cannon, was deadlier than a brigade of cavalry.

"The treaty of St. Petersburg states that the boundary follows the summit of the mountains parallel to the coast," Elias said evenly. "If the mountains happen to lie two hundred miles inland around the headwaters of the Pelly, that is an error of the Almighty’s geography, not of my surveyors. Write to the British Commissioner at Victoria, Kaiulani. Tell him that the Department of the North has established six meteorological and police posts along the upper river to protect the native tribes from unlicensed whiskey-peddlers, and that we will be happy to appoint a joint boundary commission to examine the cairns—in the summer of eighteen-seventy. By the time their surveyors walk up those canyons with a transit, we will have washed the gravel clean to the bedrock."

***

To the Chronicler who has traveled the great iron road of the Northern Department in later, gentler decades—when heated Pullman cars carry imperial magistrates from the wharves of Skagway to the electric-lit boulevards of Dawson in fourteen hours—the records of that first terrible spring of 1867 read like a descent into the circles of Dante’s ice. History, in its grand balance-sheet, concerns itself only with the two hundred and forty million thalers of hyperborean bullion that flowed into the vaults of Market Street between the signing of the Sitka treaty and the outbreak of the British war; yet providence demands that we do not avert our eyes from the furnace in which that key was forged.

There was no feverish stampede of singing prospectors, no dance-halls or gaming-tents along the Klondike. Instead, as the March gales howled down the funnel of the Lynn Canal, thirty thousand men were landed on the boulders of Dyea beach from the holds of blackened iron troop-transports. They were the sweepings of two continents and an ocean: disbanded Confederate infantrymen from the prisoner-of-war Stockades at Rock Island who had traded their shackles for a five-year northern pickaxe; starving Irish navvies from the bankrupt Erie railway towns; Cantonese coolies from the Pearl River delta; and four battalions of stony-faced Satsuma pioneers who marched up the ice-steps with wooden numbering-tallies hanging from their belts.

Above the beach rose the Chilkoot—not a pass, as men understand the word in the Alps or the Sierra, but a thirty-five-degree chute of blue glacier-ice and granite talus rising three thousand feet straight into a sky the color of wet slate. 

At the foot of the ice-wall stood the stone blockhouse of the Department of the North. Here, beneath a giant painted board bearing the words *ORDER IS PROVIDENCE*, twelve clerks in wolf-skin coats sat behind pine trestles heated by sheet-iron charcoal braziers, weighing every man’s pack upon brass steelyards before the provost-guards unlocked the timber turnstile. No man climbed with less than seventy pounds of Departmental pig-iron, boiler-plate, or salt-pork upon his spine; no man broke his place in the human chain that stretched like a black, wriggling ant-column up the blinding white face of the mountain.

When a blizzard swept down from the summit, burying the notched ice-steps in four feet of dry, suffocating powder that froze the eyelashes together and turned a man’s breath into a mask of blue rime across his throat, the whistle of the steam-winch at the Crater Lake station above did not stop. If a Virginia veteran or a Cantonese bearer slipped from the hemp guide-rope—his lungs bursting in the thin, razor-edged air, his knees buckling beneath the weight of a cast-iron sluice-gate—the file behind him did not halt to lift him. A halt of ten minutes on the upper chute meant that two hundred men would freeze solid in their tracks before the line could move again. The provost-corporals, wearing iron crampons on their boots and carrying stout hickory alpenstocks, simply rolled the fallen man and his pack out of the trough into the soft drift beside the trail, chalked the four-digit number from his brass neck-tag onto a slate, and waved the next bearer up the step.

And beyond the summit, down on the flat, timberless marshes of the Klondike and the Bonanza creeks where the sun in April merely rolled like a cold brass disk along the southern hills before plunging back into twenty hours of violet darkness, the earth itself fought the pickaxe. 

For ten thousand years the auriferous gravel had lain locked in permafrost forty feet deep—a cement of black muck, ancient mammoth bones, and blue ice that turned the steel point of a Cornish pick as if it had struck an anvil. To reach the yellow scales lying upon the rotten slate bedrock, the legions of the Department turned the sub-arctic valleys into a smoky, sulfurous inferno. For twenty miles along the winding trenches of the Eldorado, every dwarfish spruce and stunted birch was stripped from the hillsides to feed ten thousand night-fires at the bottom of narrow, timber-shored shafts. 

All through the arctic night, the canyon was choked with a low, poisonous roof of yellow woodsmoke, the stench of thawing Pleistocene carrion, and the acrid tang of tallow-dip candles flickering in the frozen mud. Half-naked men, their wool shirts stiff with frozen sweat at the shoulders while their boots stood ankle-deep in boiling black slush, worked in twelve-hour relays beneath the earth, scooping the thawed six inches of fiery gravel into iron buckets before the frost could bite the dirt hard again. Above them, on the lip of the drifts, the high-pressure donkey-boilers brought over the pass in numbered pieces panted and wheezed in the forty-below air, shooting jets of scalding steam through iron pipes to thaw the dump-heaps before the summer sun could even melt the snow.

Scurvy blackened the gums of the Irishmen; pneumonia carried off the Cantonese by platoons when they came dripping out of the steam-drifts into the arctic wind; and the graveyard on the frozen bench above the river grew faster than the log barracks. Yet every morning at six, when the bronze gong sounded from the Assay Stockade, the armed mule-sleds drove down the creek-bed to collect the iron amalgam-cans. Every man’s tally was entered in the great ledgers in duplicate; every ounce of coarse yellow metal was weighed, sealed with the red wax of the Protectorate, and stacked like cordwood in the log magazine to await the breaking of the river-ice. It was not gold-mining as the old world had known it; it was the industrial gutting of a continent’s cellar, conducted by stopwatch and bugle-call so that a fleet six thousand miles away might have the sinews of empire.

***

On the nineteenth of June, 1867, the northern harvest came home to the Golden Gate.

A stiff afternoon wind was blowing in from the Farallones, driving whitecaps across the deep blue expanse of the bay and whipping the smoke from the seventy foundry chimneys of Potrero Point and Clark’s Point into a long, gray canopy that reached all the way to the Oakland mud-flats. Down on the private granite mole of the Naval Citadel, the air was sharp with the brine of low tide, hot valve-oil from the dockside hydraulic cranes, and the damp, tarry smell of hemp hawsers drying in the sun.

Elias stood near the edge of the stone quay, his hands thrust deep into the pockets of his navy wool greatcoat. Beside him stood General Marcus Vance, Cornelius Schuyler, and Rear-Admiral Takashima, while twenty paces behind them a double rank of the Life Guard held the dock-gates against four hundred curious foreign consuls, shipping underwriters, and reporters from the London *Times* and the Paris *Débats* whom Elias had deliberately permitted to stand upon the upper timber gallery overlooking the slip.

Out in the main channel, her black iron hull streaked with white salt-crust to the tops of her paddle-boxes and her bow-plates dented by the pack-ice of the Bering Sea, the armed treasure-steamer *Sitka* was warping slowly against the stone pilings behind two wheezing harbor tugs.

"Seven hundred and forty days since we closed the eastern banks, Protector," Cornelius Schuyler said, his voice trembling slightly with an emotion that was almost religious as he watched the steamer’s heavy iron gangway swing out from her bulwarks under the chains of the dock-crane. "Lord Rothschild’s agent in San Francisco told me at breakfast that the Bank of England has raised its discount rate to nine percent on the rumor that your northern mines were nothing but iron pyrites and frozen mud. Look at the British Consul up there on the gallery—he has his spyglass trained right on the main hatch."

"Let him look," Elias said. His rough, low voice was quiet against the screaming of the gulls and the deep hiss of the *Sitka*’s waste-steam pipe roaring off pressure. "A man with a spyglass saves me the cost of a telegram to Downing Street. Marcus, how many chests are in this first run?"

"Two hundred andforty iron-bound boxes, sir," Marcus answered, consulting the manifest that the harbour-master’s launch had brought ashore twenty minutes earlier. "Eleven tons of retorted Klondike bar-gold and coarse nuggets from the April washings. Enough to plate four first-rate battleships and buy every ton of saltpeter in Chile for three years."

On the deck of the *Sitka*, the boatswain’s pipe trilled. The heavy steam-winch by the mainmast clattered into gear, its wire cable singing taut as it hoisted the first load out of the hold—not a canvas sack, and not a rough wooden crate, but a rectangular chest of polished oak bound with thick straps of blued San Francisco steel, suspended in a rope net four feet above the deck.

As the crane-boom swung the chest out over the granite quay and lowered it onto a flat-bedded iron hand-truck, four burly Cornishmen strained at the handle-bars; the solid cast-iron wheels groaned and shrieked against the stone flags under the dead, concentrated weight of five hundred pounds of pure metal.

Elias stepped forward and raised one gloved hand. The Cornishmen halted the truck three paces from the foot of the gallery stairs, where the foreign consuls were leaning so far over the redwood railing that their top-hats threatened to tumble into the slip.

"Open the first box, Mr. Schuyler," Elias said, pitching his tone so it carried up to the timber gallery. "The damp air of the northern sea sometimes rusts the locks. Let us see if the metal has spoiled on the voyage."

Schuyler stepped forward with a heavy brass key, unlocked the double padlocks on the steel hasps, and threw back the oak lid.

The late afternoon sun, dropping toward the Marin headlands in a blaze of clear sunset gold, struck directly into the open chest. Inside, packed without sawdust or shavings, lay twenty-four rough, unstamped bricks of dull, buttery yellow bullion, each the size of a mason’s hod-stone, covered to the brim with ten-pound drifts of coarse, water-worn Klondike nuggets that spilled over the oak lip and rattled down onto the granite flagstones at Elias’s boots.

Up on the gallery, the British Consul’s spyglass clicked shut. A dead, suffocating silence fell over the forty European observers above, broken only by the steady clank-hiss of the *Sitka*’s winch bringing the second chest—and behind it the third, the fourth, the tenth—up out of the dark hold in an endless, measured procession of yellow iron.

Elias did not look up at the gallery. He bent down, picked up a single jagged nugget the size of a walnut from the stone by his toe, and rolled it once across his palm before tossing it back into the chest with a dull, heavy thud.

"Admiral Takashima," Elias said, turning his head slightly toward the Japanese officer while the second iron truck came rumbling down the granite pier behind them.

"Protector," Takashima answered, his hand tightening on the hilt of his naval dirk.

"The British Ambassador in St. Petersburg warned Baron Stoeckl in November that Her Majesty’s Government would never permit a single power to hold both sides of the North Pacific," Elias said, his pale eyes lifting toward the western sky where the hulls of the First Armored Squadron rode at anchor off Alcatraz. "You will take the *Kamehameha*, the *Satsuma*, and the four new turret-ships out with the morning tide. Do not steam by the northern circle yet. Before we force the gates of Yedo, we must bolt down our own threshold in the mid-ocean."

Down at the end of the mole, the door of the dockyard signal-tower flew open, and Major Sterling came running down the granite steps with his coat-tails flying in the salt wind, waving a wet yellow cable-dispatch from the Honolulu-Midway relay before he had even reached the guard-line.

"Protector!" Sterling shouted, his boots skidding on the wet kelp by the crane-base as Marcus Vance stepped sharply forward to intercept him. "From the Consulate at Honolulu—relayed via the French packet! King Lot Kamehameha the Fifth has refused to renew the Pearl Lagoon dockyard lease without a vote of his Privy Council, the British frigate *Curaçoa* has dropped anchor inside the reef with four hundred Royal Marines, and the native royalists have seized the water-batteries at Punchbowl Hill to bar our colliers from the harbor!"

Elias took the damp slip from Sterling’s fingers without haste. For fourteen years, the Treaty of 1853 had left the Hawaiian monarchy an ornamental crown—a polite fiction of dual sovereignty designed to flatter the island chiefs while Pacifica’s engineers dredged their lagoons and conscripted their youth. Now, with the British China Squadron probing the western approaches, a half-tamed vassal sitting astride the coal-bunkers of the central ocean was a luxury the Empire could no longer afford.

"Marshal Vance," Elias said, folding the cablegram into a neat square. "Divert the *Kamehameha* and the First Atlantic Auxiliary Division from the northern run. Embark four batteries of street-artillery tonight. Since King Lot has forgotten whose iron keeps the French and the English out of his palace, you will sail to Oahu and remind him."

***

Twelve days later, the morning trade wind coming down off the emerald ridges of the Ko’olau range carried the sweet, heavy fragrance of crushed ginger-blossom, drying copra, and the warm coral brine of the reef, only to have it fouled before noon by a greasy, low-hanging pall of Nanaimo coal-smoke that stained the turquoise waters of Mamala Bay.

Lady Kaiulani stood alone upon the high stone *lanai* of the old harbour-customs house, her hands resting motionless upon the sun-bleached teak rail. She had come home five days ahead of the main battle-squadron aboard the fast dispatch-steamer *Hilo*, hoping against the cold arithmetic in her own breast that she might persuade her royal cousin at Iolani Palace to open the lagoon gates before Marcus Vance’s turret-ships cleared Molokai channel. She had failed. Behind her, in the dusty palm-shaded streets of Honolulu, three thousand native retainers from the outer islands—men armed with old whaling-muskets, rusted Spanish pikes, and wooden shark-tooth clubs—were piling coral blocks across the intersections of King and Nu’uanu streets, singing the ancient war-chants of Kamehameha the Great.

And out beyond the white line of the surf, where the deep-water channel had been blasted thirty feet through the living coral by Cantonese divers ten years before, the true masters of the ocean were coming in.

They did not sail in with the tall, graceful canvas of the old Boston missionaries or the white-painted wooden hulls of the British sloops. They crept through the boiling foam of the reef-gap like seven iron sea-turtles, painted a dull, leaden imperial blue from waterline to funnel-top, their decks stripped clear of bulwarks so that nothing showed above the Pacific swell save the massive, sloped cylinders of their twin gun-turrets and the armored conning-towers spitting jets of white waste-steam.

At the head of the column steamed the *Kamehameha*—five thousand tons of California steel bearing the stolen name of her own dynasty upon its stern in letters of cast brass. And behind the ironclads came four immense, black-hulled screw-transports, their upper decks dark with the slate-gray uniforms of the Atlantic Free States Regiments: men who had learned war in the slaughter-pens of Fredericksburg and Vicksburg, and who looked up at the green volcanic cliffs of Oahu not as an island paradise, but as another redoubt to be carried by the bayonet.

"The British frigate is slipping her cable, Your Highness," murmured Keoni, her aged chamberlain, stepping out onto the gallery with a brass telescope trembling in his spotted hands. "Captain Bowden-Smith signaled the Palace twenty minutes ago that he has no instructions from London to engage six-inch armor inside a closed reef. He is standing out to sea and leaving the King’s batteries to face the Marshal alone."

Kaiulani did not reach for the glass. Her dark eyes, shadowed by the broad brim of her woven *lauhala* hat, watched the British warship scurry past Diamond Head under full steam and topsails like a gull fleeing a squall. For fourteen years she had walked the marble halls of Monterey and Sacramento; she had written the syncretic codes, she had dined with Elias’s generals, and she had told herself that by bending like the reed before the mainland gale, she was preserving the blood and the sceptre of her people inside the belly of the whale.

Now, as the lead monitor swung its twin fifteen-inch guns directly toward the coral parapet of Fort Kekuanohu at three hundred yards’ range, the reed was being ground beneath the iron wheel.

"They call it protection in the dispatches, Keoni," she said softly, the trade wind lifting the black silk scarf at her throat as the first longboat dropped from the davits of the transport *Constitution*, packed gunwale-to-gunwale with Missouri and Pennsylvania riflemen whose bayonets flashed like needles in the tropical sun. "When we signed the first alliance in fifty-three, Elias promised my uncle that our flag would fly beside the rising sun on every masthead. Look at the main-truck of the *Kamehameha*."

The chamberlain raised his glass, then lowered it slowly, his leathery brown cheek sagging. The eight stripes of the Hawaiian kingdom were gone from the yardarm; in their place flew only the solitary blue-and-gold standard of the Protectorate, and beneath it, the blood-red battle-pennant of the Provost-General.

"Go to the Palace by the back taro-paths, Keoni," Kaiulani commanded, turning from the rail as the deep, brazen roar of the *Kamehameha*’s steam-siren echoed off the walls of Punchbowl crater, drowning the drums of the royalist militia in the square below. "Tell King Lot that if his gunners on the hill pull a single lanyard when those boats touch the wharf, there will not be a stone of his throne-room left standing by sunset. I am going down to the quay to meet General Vance before his Virginians set the thatch on fire."

***

Two thousand miles northeast of that smoking reef, in the high, cedar-vaulted cabinet room of the Citadel on Rincon Hill, the afternoon fog off the Golden Gate was shut out by heavy crimson curtains and the dry, steady crackle of anthracite coal burning in a grate of polished Sierra black marble.

Elias stood before the great table of inlaid Hawaiian koa-wood, his broad back turned to the four men sitting in the leather armchairs behind him: Chancellor Gwin, Cornelius Schuyler, and the two frightened envoys of the Honolulu Privy Council who had been detained at the Palace Hotel since the arrival of the first cipher. On the wall above the mantelpiece hung a newly finished hydrostatic chart of the Pacific Basin, ten feet square, upon which the draftsmen of the Naval Bureau had drawn thick crimson lines radiating outward from San Francisco like the web of an iron spider—north to Sitka and the Kuriles, south to Guaymas and the Galapagos, and dead center through the Sandwich Islands to the gates of Canton and Yedo.

"The treaty of fifty-three was a solemn compact between two sovereign crowns, Protector!" protested Judge Varigny, the French-born minister to King Lot, his pale forehead gleaming with sweat as he half-rose from his chair. "His Majesty merely asserted his ancient royal prerogative to audit the harbour-dues of Honolulu and regulate the quartering of foreign sailors! To declare the Kingdom an Imperial Prefecture by unilateral decree is an act of naked annexation that will outrage every court in Europe!"

Elias did not turn around. He was looking up at the small, ink-blackened cluster of dots in the center of the chart where the Hawaiian chain sat alone in two thousand leagues of blue paper.

"What is a sovereign crown, Monsieur Varigny?" Elias asked, his rough, low voice filling the quiet room without rising half a tone. "Can King Lot cast a twelve-inch gun? Can he roll a single plate of two-inch iron, or mine a ton of steam-coal to fill the bunkers of the ships that keep the French and the British from dividing his beaches like a melon?"

"He has the law of nations—" Varigny began.

"The law of nations is written by the men who hold the coaling-stations," Elias said, turning from the hearth and walking slowly to the head of the koa table. Before him lay a single sheet of heavy vellum, engrossed in the three imperial scripts and bearing at its foot a broad cake of unpressed scarlet wax. "For fourteen years I have allowed Honolulu to play at being a court because Lady Kaiulani kept the lagoon open and the native regiments full. Last week, while my northern fleet was preparing to sail for Japan, your King listened to the British consul over a glass of port and closed my drydocks."

He placed both wide, weather-roughened palms flat upon the table, leaning slightly forward until the Frenchman sank back into the leather cushions.

"A bridge across a chasm cannot have a toll-gate in the middle of the span where a drunken gatekeeper can drop the bar whenever London whistles," Elias said. "From this noon, the Polynesian Protectorate Act is the supreme statute of the sea. Every island, reef, and anchorage between the Tropic of Cancer and the Marquesas—from Kauai to Tutuila and the mid-ocean shoals—is incorporated forever into the Maritime Domain of Pacifica. The King at Honolulu will retain his palace, his feather-cloaks, and an annuity of one hundred thousand silver thalers from the sugar-tax, provided he signs the abdication of his military and customs prerogatives before Marshal Vance’s forty-eight hours expire. If he does not sign, there will be no king in Oahu on Thursday—only a provost-marshal in a stone fort."

Chancellor Gwin dipped the heavy gold pen into the inkwell and held it out. "And Lady Kaiulani, Protector? Her signature is not upon the draft, and her cousins sit in the house of nobles that you are abolishing."

Elias took the pen. For the space of a single heartbeat, his thumb paused over the engraved gold shaft; he saw her dark, unblinking eyes beneath the wet spruce boughs at Sitka, warning him that men were not iron ore to be bolted together with hot rivets. Yet when a ship is clearing for action in a typhoon, the captain does not ask the figurehead whether it wishes to take the wave.

"Lady Kaiulani is a Princess of the Realm and High Commissioner of the Insular Courts," Elias said, driving the steel nib across the vellum with a firm, scratching stroke that left a broad black track of ink, and then pressing his heavy signet ring deep into the hot red wax. "She knows better than any man in this room that an empire has only one head. Wire the text to the Midway relay, Mr. Gwin. Tell Marshal Vance the Act is law; he has my leave to clear the streets."

***

In Honolulu, the forty-eight hours had shrunk to twenty minutes, and the air along Queen Street no longer carried the scent of ginger-blossoms; it was thick with the choking dust of pulverized coral, the stink of hot whale-oil lubricant from the traction-engines, and the sour sweat of terrified men trapped between the mountain and the sea.

General Marcus Vance sat his tall bay charger at the junction of the harbour road and Fort Street, fifty paces behind a barricade of overturned sugar-carts and coral blocks that the royalist retainers had thrown up across the entrance to the Palace square. He wore his high-collared navy wool tunic buttoned to the chin despite the ninety-degree tropical glare, a white linen havelock hanging from his peaked cap to shield his neck. Around him, in double files that stretched all the way back to the stone wharves, stood sixteen hundred veterans of the First Atlantic Auxiliary—lean, sun-blackened men from the Shenandoah and the Susquehanna, their gray tunics dark with sweat at the armpits, holding their seven-shot Spencer carbines at the hip while two six-barrel Gatling batteries were trundled forward by Cantonese artillerymen on wide-tired iron carriages.

Down from the banyan trees by the custom-house rode Lady Kaiulani on a lathered white mare, her green riding-habit white with coral-powder to the knees. She reined in sharply beside Marcus’s stirrup, her hand seizing the brass bit-rein of his bridle before his orderly could interpose.

"General Vance!" she cried, her musical voice tight and breathless over the deep, rhythmic thumping of the *Kamehameha*’s steam-pumps down at the pier and the ominous clashing of shark-tooth clubs against sheet-iron shields from the three thousand islanders massed behind the coral wall ahead. "Hold your artillery for one hour! I have just come from the Palace basement—King Lot is weeping over his father’s bones, and the British consul has fled to the hills! The *Ali’i* will sign the customs lease if you will only march your white regiments back to the wharf and let my own Royal Guard police the square!"

Marcus looked at her with eyes that were gray, weary, and utterly empty of malice or pity. In his left gauntlet he held the decoded slip that had arrived off the *Hilo*’s wire-boat ten minutes before, bearing Elias’s signature to the Pacific Island Act. "It is no longer a question of a customs lease, Your Highness," Marcus said, his flat, logistical cadence cutting right across the howling of the conch-shells from the native barricade. "The Protector signed the Insular Incorporation statute at San Francisco yesterday. There is no Kingdom of Hawaii. And I cannot wait an hour; the tide turns at four, and I have three colliers waiting outside the reef to coal the *Satsuma* for the Yokohama run. Every hour these streets are blocked costs the fleet forty tons of steam-coal." "Those men behind the carts are my blood!" Kaiulani said, her fingers digging into his sleeve as Colonel Mulligan stepped out in front of the lead Gatling piece, his single arm raising a brass speaking-trumpet toward the barricade. "They have old flintlocks and wooden spears, Marcus! If you open on them with machine-guns in this narrow lane, you will butcher five hundred men in three minutes and turn every island from here to Hawaii into a charnel-house of hate!" "If I spend three minutes now, Your Highness, I save six months of bushwhacking in the sugar-canes later," Marcus replied, gently but inexorably lifting her gloved hand from his forearm and turning in his saddle toward the battery commander. "A surgical amputation requires speed, not parley. Sergeant—take Her Highness’s bridle and lead her mount behind the custom-house wall." Before the two Missouri troopers could close on her mare’s head, a tall warrior in a yellow feather helmet leaped onto the crest of the coral barricade eighty yards away, brandishing a brass-bound whaling lance and screaming a curse in the old tongue. Beside him, twenty rusty muskets poked through the sugar-cart wheels and belched a ragged cloud of dirty white smoke. A lead ball hummed like an angry hornet past Marcus’s ear and smashed a clay flowerpot on the veranda behind him; a second struck a Pennsylvania corporal in the throat, pitching him backward onto the crushed coral with a bright spray of arterial crimson. Marcus did not draw his saber. He raised two fingers of his right hand and dropped them toward the barricade. "Battery," Marcus said. "Clear the street. Two hundred rounds per piece, traverse from flank to flank, then advance the first battalion with the bayonet." "Marcus, no—!" Kaiulani screamed, spurring her rearing mare straight against the chests of the provost-guards as Colonel Mulligan dropped his arm and the two gun-captains threw their weight onto the iron cranks of the Gatlings. The twin bronze clusters began to revolve, and as the first terrible, clattering roar of twelve hundred .58-caliber lead slugs tore down the palm-lined tunnel of Fort Street—splintering the wooden carts into flying toothpicks, bursting the coral blocks into blinding white dust, and scything the feathered line of islanders down like dry cane before a brush-hook—Marcus Vance consulted his timepiece by its gold chain, his thumb pressing the stem to measure the advance while Colonel Mulligan’s veterans leveled their bayonets and stepped into the drifting smoke. Three minutes. In the ledger of the General Staff, it was merely a tick of the escapement wheel, the time required for two bronze barrels to heat until the whale-oil boiled on their trunnions. To Kaiulani, held fast behind the coral masonry of the custom-house while two Missouri privates hung onto her mare’s foaming bit, those three minutes were the death-rattle of a thousand years. When the mechanical clatter ceased, replaced by the single, ragged cheers of the Shenandoah and Susquehanna veterans going over the splintered carts with eighteen inches of cold steel, the silence under the banyan trees was wetter and heavier than the tropical noon. Then came the cries—not the defiant war-chants of the *Ali’i*, but the high, bubbling shrieks of boys from the Kona fishing-villages whose bellies had been opened by half-inch lead, and the sharp *pop-pop* of Spencer carbines settling the wounded in the hibiscus ditches. Twenty minutes later, they led her between two files of bayonets across the trampled grass of the Palace yard. Her green riding-skirt was stiff to the hem with the red mud of Fort Street—mud that was not rain, for no rain had fallen since dawn. On the wide stone steps of Iolani Palace, a young chief from Maui whom she had danced with at the autumn *luau* lay doubled over an overturned brass spittoon, his yellow *mamo* feather cape soaked black between the shoulder-blades, a Virginia corporal calmly stripping the gold signet ring from his stiffening finger. Inside the throne room, the tall Venetian shutters had been smashed open by rifle-butts to let out the powder-reek. King Lot sat slumped in the carved koa-wood chair upon the dais, his broad Polynesian face gray as pumice, his hands trembling upon his knees while four American engineers in muddy boots hammered a portable telegraph repeater directly into the mahogany wainscoting beside the royal coat of arms. On the center table, where the kahili standards of crimson bird-plumes had been thrown down like dirty brooms to clear the wood, lay the vellum sheet of the Insular Incorporation Act. Marcus Vance stood at the foot of the dais. He had taken off his peaked cap; a dark line of sweat stained the band of his forehead, and his right cuff was spotted with dried white coral-lime. "The King’s hand is too unsteady for the pen, Your Highness," Marcus said as Kaiulani walked across the blood-tracked matting. He did not offer her a chair; he held out a steel-nibbed dip-pen whose brass barrel was still warm from the clerk’s fingers. "And since His Majesty’s signature alone might be contested by the outer island chiefs as given under duress, the Protector’s instructions from San Francisco are explicit. Your name goes beneath the royal seal as Regent-Guarantor of the Insular Courts. When the people of Kauai and Hawaii see the daughter of the Oahu line upon the proclamation, they will lay down their muskets." Kaiulani stopped two paces from the table. Through the shattered louver of the eastern window, she could hear the rhythmic *chug-hiss* of the steam-excavators down at the reef-channel—they had not even stopped dredging the coral during the three minutes of the slaughter—and closer at hand, the heavy thud of corpses being pitched onto the beds of the military bullock-carts in the square. "And if I break that pen across your face, Marshal Vance?" she asked. Her voice was not loud; it was dry and brittle as burned palm-thatch. "Then Colonel Mulligan hangs the forty royalist nobles we took in the cellar from the breadfruit trees along King Street before the four o’clock tide," Marcus answered without a blink, his gray eyes meeting hers with the terrible, impersonal steadiness of a balance-scale. "And tomorrow morning I send two regiments of the Atlantic Auxiliary over the Pali to burn every taro-patch and every fishing-canoe on the windward coast until the survivors come into the stockades to beg for salt pork. Do not mistake me for a cruel man, Your Highness. I have four thousand tons of coal to load before dark, and Rear-Admiral Takashima’s squadron clears for the Western Ocean in ten days. I have neither the time nor the rifle-cartridges to leave an unpacified island behind my rudder." On the dais, King Lot raised his heavy, tear-streaked face. "Sign it, cousin," the King whispered in the native tongue, his chin sinking onto his gold-braided chest. "The gods of the volcano are dead. Their iron is too heavy for our bones." Kaiulani looked down at the parchment. For fourteen years she had believed she was sitting at the bridle of the beast, guiding itsiron hooves away from her garden. Now she smelled the hot tallow on its hide and saw her own blood between its teeth. Slowly, with fingers that felt as though they had been dipped in the arctic slush of Sitka, she took the brass pen from Marcus’s gauntlet. She did not read the Latin or the English clauses. She drove the steel point into the horn inkwell and wrote *Kaiulani* across the vellum in letters so sharp they tore the fibers of the sheepskin, scattering black droplets like buckshot across the seal of the rising sun. "There is your coal, butcher," she said, dropping the pen onto the table so that it rolled off the edge and stuck point-first into the matting at Marcus’s boot. "May it choke your furnaces when you meet the English guns." *** Nine days later, the fast paddle-frigate *Hilo*—paint-blistered and reeking of scorched cylinder-tallow from a forced run against the northeast trades—backed her paddles inside the Golden Gate and ran out her gangplank at the private stairs of the Citadel wharf. Elias was waiting for her alone in the high, glass-domed conservatory of the Palace on Mason Street. Outside, the late June afternoon was drowning in a cold, salt-heavy summer fog that poured over the Marin hills like dirty wool, blotting out the sun and leaving only the distant, booming groan of the steam-foghorns on Alcatraz and the endless, iron *clink-clank* of the dockyard hammers down at Potrero Point. Inside the glass dome, however, four furnace-flues kept the air at the wet, stifling heat of the tropics; giant tree-ferns brought from the valleys of Hilo and orchids from the Mindanao jungles dripped condensation onto the tessellated marble pavement, filling the vault with the heavy smell of warm loam and wet leaves. When the bronze doors at the end of the palm-walk opened and Kaiulani stepped across the threshold, she did not wear the green velvet of the Monterey court or the diamonds of the Washoe mines. She wore a plain, high-necked mourning gown of dull black bombazine, salt-stained at the hem from the deck of the steamer, and around her shoulders the crimson-and-yellow feather cape of the Kamehamehas—except that down the left breast of the priceless plumage ran a six-inch crust of dried, blackened blood where she had knelt beside the dying Maui boy on the palace steps. Elias stood beside a granite basin where gold-spotted carp from the Shogun’s gardens swam in dark water. He wore his severe blue naval coat, his hands clasped behind his back, his short-cropped hair showing more iron than brown in the gray light filtering through the glass roof. "You made the crossing in two hundred and ten hours," Elias said as the guards closed the doors behind her, leaving them alone among the dripping ferns. "Captain Sterling tells me the *Hilo* burned her spare main-topmast to keep the steam-gauge at forty pounds. I am glad you are here, Kaiulani. The Diet convenes at noon tomorrow to ratify the Insular Prefectures, and your chair beside the rostrum has been empty too long." She walked down the marble flagway until only the stone rim of the carp-basin separated them. Her dark eyes were sunken in hollow rings of violet shadow, yet her spine was stiffer than the bayonet on a sentry’s rifle. "Do you know whose blood this is upon the *mamo* feathers, Elias?" she asked, her voice low, clear, and trembling like a taut wire. "It is Kalanimoku’s son. He was seventeen years old. He had an old whaling-lance with a wooden shaft in his hand, and your Virginians blew his chest open with a machine-gun on Fort Street while General Vance held his timepiece in his palm to see how long it took the carts to splinter." Elias looked down at the dark stain on the yellow feathers. Not a muscle twitched in his weathered cheek; his gray eyes remained as flat and bottomless as the winter water of the Platte. "He had a lance in his hand against my colors while a British frigate lay inside the reef waiting to seize my coal-bunkers," Elias said, his tone low and rough as quarry-stone. "If a boy of seventeen points a weapon at the column when the fleet is clearing for action, he dies like a man of forty. I told you on the Platte five years ago, Kaiulani: order is not a bargain. When King Lot closed the gates of Pearl Lagoon to please an English post-captain, he ceased to be a king and became a mutineer." "He was a king before your grandfather built a log hut in Kentucky!" she cried, her control breaking for a single, blazing instant as she struck the granite rim of the basin with her bare palm. "We gave you the islands when you had nothing but four leaky steamers and a wooden fort on the mud-flats! I wrote your laws! I stood beside you in Sacramento and Sitka and lied to my own blood—I told them that if we gave the American Caesar our harbors and our young men, he would shield our crown beneath his eagle! And the moment your vaults were full of Klondike gold and the Eastern states were in chains, you sent a pack of pardoned Rebel convicts to butcher my cousins in the dust and turn my homeland into a coal-bin!" "Look at me, Kaiulani," Elias commanded. He stepped around the stone basin, closing the distance between them until his broad naval shoulders blotted out the light from the conservatory dome. He did not touch her, yet the sheer, cold weight of his will seemed to press the humid air from her lungs. "Do you think I brought you back from Oahu in nine days to hear a woman weep over a barricade?" he said, each short sentence falling hard and clean. "In three weeks, Admiral Takashima and I meet the combined squadrons of Great Britain and France in the Straits of Shimonoseki. If we lose that battle, Lord Palmerston’s cruisers will be anchored off Honolulu before September, and they will not leave you a feather-cloak or a court-house. They will turn your islands into a sugar-plantation worked by coolies under an English factor’s whip, just as they did in Jamaica and Mauritius." He reached into the breast of his tunic and drew out a heavy gold collar set with the Imperial seal of the Grand Council, holding it between his rough, square-nailed hands. "There can be no little kingdoms inside the hull of an ironclad," Elias said. "The Kingdom of Hawaii is dead because the world is too small for canoes. In its place stands the First Naval Prefecture of the Empire, and you are its High Imperial Advisor and Chancellor of the Insular Diet—second only to myself from the California coast to the China Sea. Four hundred royalist prisoners are sitting in the coral quarry at Oahu tonight under sentence of treason. Put this collar around your neck, walk into the Diet with me tomorrow noon to proclaim the Incorporation, and those four hundred men go back to their valleys with free pardons. Refuse me—and I will send instructions by the midnight cable for Colonel Mulligan to clear the quarry with the Gatlings at sunrise." Kaiulani stared up into the pitiless, iron-cast geometry of his face. Behind him, through the misted glass of the dome, she could hear the deep, unending roar of the Pacific surf beating against the Mile Rocks and the brassy blare of a bugle calling the evening watch at the Presidio. This was the providence the court chroniclers wrote of in their leather books: a steam-hammer that gave you the choice of being the face of the die or the iron crushed beneath it. Her chin lifted half an inch. Her dark eyes went as cold and dead as the volcanic glass of Mauna Loa. "Give me the collar, Protector," she said, her voice stripped of every note of music, leaving only the sharp, hollow ring of steel. "And wire your butcher in Honolulu to unlock the quarry gates tonight. I will sit beside your throne tomorrow—and I will live long enough to see what happens when your boiler bursts." *** To the Chronicler who sails into the great land-locked basin of Pu’uloa—which the Americans call Pearl Lagoon—in the summers following the Act of Incorporation, the ancient pastoral paradise described by Captain Cook and the early Boston missionaries seems as remote as the gardens of the Hesperides. Where the outrigger canoes of the *Ali’i* once glided over clear coral shallows in pursuit of the mullet, and the green taro-terraces stepped gently down from the mist-veiled clefts of the Waianae mountains, the eye now beholds the smoking, terrifying hub of the Great Arena. Geography, when wedded to the relentless steam-engine of Imperial necessity, permits no sentiment. Because the islands of Oahu and Maui sit at the exact mathematical focus of the northern ocean—two thousand miles from the Golden Gate, three thousand from the mouth of the Amur, and four thousand from the gates of Canton—it was inevitable that the garden should be paved with iron. By the autumn of the Incorporation year, the coral reef that had barred the entrance to the inner lagoons for ten millennia had been shattered by forty-ton charges of nitro-glycerine lowered into the surf by Cantonese helmet-divers. Through a straight, vertical-walled canal forty feet deep and three hundred yards wide, lined on either side with casemated batteries of fifteen-inch Rodman and Krupp guns cast at the San Francisco works, the largest armored battleships of the Pacifica Navy could now steam at full speed in any weather to lie secure behind the volcanic ramparts of the island. To stand upon the red-earth heights of Punchbowl Hill at noon is to witness the syncretic machinery of Elias Thorne’s dominion operating at full pressure. Below, along six miles of newly dredged stone quays where the coco-palms have been felled to make room for traveling hydraulic gantry-cranes, thirty colliers from Vancouver and the Kenai mines unload mountains of gleaming black anthracite into iron hopper-cars drawn by small, whistling geared locomotives. The air no longer carries the lazy fragrance of plumeria and woodsmoke; it stings the nostrils with the sharp tang of salt spray, hot cylinder-tallow, wet coal-dust, and the biting sulfur of the vulcanizing sheds. Down in the three vast graving-docks hewn out of the living basalt at Waipio Peninsula, four thousand laborers work in three eight-hour relays under the glare of calcium lime-lights that turn the tropical night into a ghastly, shadowless noon: Hawaiian royal guardsmen in navy-blue tunics stand sentry on the catwalks above gangs of former Confederate prisoners of war from Georgia and Alabama, who swing twenty-pound sledges alongside bare-chested Cantonese riveters and taciturn Satsuma master-machinists. Even the hills above the harbor have been recast in the image of the

new order. Upon the upper slopes of Nu’uanu, where the wind roars down through the Pali gap, the thatched grass houses of the native villagers have been replaced by geometric rows of corrugated-iron barracks and brick ordnance magazines, presided over by the great four-story bulk of the Insular Admiralty—a building whose lower colonnades are hewn from grey Honolulu coral block in the severe American style, while its upper stories rise in the sweeping, red-lacquered timber galleries of a Japanese castle, surmounted by the tall semaphore-masts and humming copper telegraph wires that carry the Protector’s will from the submarine cable-house at Waikiki to the uttermost shoals of Midway and the Bonins. Here, in the mid-ocean clearing-house of empire, a regiment of Missouri cavalrymen disembarks from a San Francisco paddle-steamer to stretch their horses’ legs on the parade-ground beside a battalion of Bakufu samurai infantry drilling with seven-shot Spencer rifles; here, the silver thaler with the sun and anchor buys rice from Saigon, salt beef from the Illinois protectorate, and whale-oil from the Okhotsk sea. The island has ceased to be a country; it has become a stationary ironclad five hundred square miles in beam, anchored forever in the center of the globe to coal the squadrons that rule the water.

Yet before the British and French admirals off Shimonoseki could even test that northern lock, they looked at the mathematical certainty of thirty-six thousand tons of Pacifica armor steaming westward from Pearl Lagoon, weighed the cost of an ocean war six thousand leagues from Portsmouth, and quietly hauled down their battle-pennants to sign the Convention of Nagasaki. The Royal Navy had yielded the northern passage without firing a broadside; yet a master builder knows that an arch is unstable while its southern buttress rests in foreign hands.

On the twelfth of October, inside the high press-room of the *Imperial Gazette* on Montgomery Street in San Francisco, the air was hot and thick with the reek of boiled linseed-oil ink, damp rag-paper, and the sour tallow of the four-cylinder Hoe rotary presses thumping beneath the floorboards. 

Elias stood beside the composing-stone in his plain dark wool tunic, his hands clasped behind his spine while the chief typesetter—a hunchbacked former printer from the *New York Tribune* named Horace—waited with a pair of brass tweezers poised above the lead formes. Across the zinc-topped table stood Lady Kaiulani, still wearing the severe black bombazine mourning-dress she had sworn never to put off while a single Virginia soldier walked the streets of Honolulu, and Cornelius Schuyler, who held a wet, freshly pulled proof-sheet between his plump fingers.

"Read the headline again, Mr. Schuyler," Elias said. His tone was quiet, flat, and hard as iron plate.

Schuyler cleared his throat, his eyes darting nervously toward the tall ink-stained windows where three thousand dock-workers and discharged soldiers were already gathering in the afternoon drizzle along Market Street, drawn by the chalked bulletin-boards outside. "*'SPANISH TREACHERY IN THE MARIANAS! The Pacifica Survey-Corvette* San Joaquin *Blown Up at Anchor in Apra Harbor! Two Hundred American and Hawaiian Seamen Murdered by a Submarine Mine Laid by Order of the Captain-General at Manila!'*"

Schuyler lowered the damp paper, wiping a smear of black printer’s ink from his thumb with his cambric handkerchief. "Protector, the cable from Captain Takashima on the *Hilo* reached my marine insurance desk in cipher two hours ago. The *San Joaquin* was a thirty-year-old wooden collier that we condemned for dry-rot in August. Her forward boiler burst because her chief engineer had been instructed to tie down the safety-valve after the crew was rowed ashore in the dark. There were no two hundred men aboard her—only four Cantonese stokers who failed to reach the jolly-boat in time and a cargo of condemned mule-harness. The Spanish Governor at Guam did not even have a pound of blasting-powder in his magazine; he sent his own launch out to pick our swimmers off the reef!"

"A boiler explosion in an old wooden tub is an insurance claim, Mr. Schuyler," Elias said, walking to the edge of the composing-stone and picking up a heavy three-inch lead woodcut that showed a lurid, fictional engraving of Spanish priests and musketeers firing from a stone fort upon drowning sailors in the surf. "A submarine mine is an act of war."

From the shadow of the tall type-racks, Lady Kaiulani spoke. Since the day she had put on the gold collar of the Insular Diet, she had followed Elias like a dark, merciless conscience—administering his maritime courts with icy perfection while watching every rivet of his hubris tighten around his throat.

"And why must we have an act of war against Madrid this week, Elias?" she asked, her clear, musical voice carrying a winter chill that made the typesetter step back from the stone. "The Queen of Spain is a bankrupt woman sitting in a palace of dusty velvet. Her garrison at Guam consists of sixty half-caste militiamen whose muskets have no flints, and her frigates at Cavite have not been careened since the year fifty-eight. If you want the Philippines and the Ladrones for coaling-stations to flank the British at Hong Kong, why not send Marshal Vance to take them as you took Honolulu? Why play the theater-manager for the San Francisco rabble with four dead Chinamen and a lie printed in two-inch type?"

Elias turned his head and looked at her. The gas-jet above the stone caught the deep, weathered lines around his mouth and the heavy iron-gray at his temples.

"Because the fifty thousand men I am shipping across the ocean on Monday are not your islanders, Kaiulani, and they are not my old Texas rangers," Elias said evenly. "They are the sweepings of the Atlantic Free States—men from Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, and Georgia who spent four years trying to bayonet each other across a stone wall, and who still spit in the street when my Hawaiian provosts walk past. If I order them to board a transport to conquer a coal-harbor for the Crown of Pacifica, half of them will mutiny at the gangplank. Give them a Christian atrocity committed by a Catholic king—tell them that Spanish dons have blown up the flag in the night—and those same Yankees and Rebels will fight each other for the privilege of carrying the first scaling-ladder up the walls of Manila. Hatred is cheaper than silver, and it binds faster."

He set the woodcut down squarely in the center of the lead page-frame with a sharp *clack*.

"Lock the forme, Horace," Elias ordered the printer. "Run off a hundred thousand extras on yellow paper so the ink shows through the rain, and give them to the boys to cry through the Irish wards and the military barracks free of charge. At eight o’clock tonight, when the bonfires are lit in Portsmouth Square, I will go down to the balcony of the Customs House and sign the Declaration of Maritime Reprisal against the Crown of Spain."

***

Eighteen days after the yellow sheets went flying through the wet streets of San Francisco, the sun rose out of the Philippine Sea like a cannonball heated white in a forge, turning the long, oily swells outside the coral barrier of Apra Harbor into blinding sheets of molten brass.

General Marcus Vance stood in the armored conning-tower of the fast fleet-ram *Monterey*, his field-glasses braced against the salted iron rim of the vision-slit. The heat inside the turret-house was suffocating—ninety-eight degrees by the brass thermometer bolted to the bulkhead, thick with the stench of hot mineral oil from the hydraulic turret-gears, bilge-water, and the sour sweat of six signalmen crammed around the speaking-tubes. 

Ahead of the squadron’s bows, across half a mile of emerald-green lagoon where the charred, half-submerged ribs of the scuttled *San Joaquin* still poked above the coral heads like the backbone of a dead whale, lay the Spanish citadel of Santa Cruz and the low, whitewashed stone ramparts of Piti landing. Above the coconut palms, the red-and-gold banner of Castile hung motionless in the steam-bath of the tropical dawn.

"The Spanish battery at Point Orote is not even manned, Marshal," said Rear-Admiral Takashima, lowering his glass as the *Monterey*'s twin screws slowed to dead-slow, her wake washing in milky foam over the sunken coral shelf. "Through the telescope I can see four artillerymen in straw hats leading a yoke of water-buffalo down to the beach with water-casks, and an officer in white linen sitting under an umbrella on the quay. Their submarine cable from Manila was cut by our scouts on Tuesday; they do not even know that Madrid and San Francisco are at war."

"They will know it in four minutes," Marcus replied, his weary, pragmatic voice devoid of the slightest sporting hesitation as he opened his waterproofed leather notebook and checked the tide-tables for the inner lagoon. "We are not here to fight a duel with sixty sleep-walking Spaniards, Admiral. We are here to test whether three regiments of the Atlantic Auxiliary Corps can be put ashore from self-propelled iron landing-barges under covering fire in less than twenty-two minutes. If the timetable fails here, it will fail before the Krupp batteries that the British have secretly sold to the Captain-General at Cavite. Signal the *Oregon* to drop her bow-ramps."

Behind the *Monterey*, two immense, flat-bottomed iron troop-ships—vessels built on the slips of New Osaka specifically for Elias’s new insular doctrine—swung their square, box-like bows directly toward the coral shoals. They did not lower wooden whaleboats to be rowed ashore at two knots by blistered sailors. Instead, as their stern-wheels churned the turquoise water into boiling froth, four forty-foot steel lighters slid out of flooded well-decks in their bellies, each barge driven by a high-pressure donkey-engine burning rock-oil and shielded in front by a sloped, half-inch steel breastwork Loopholed for twin Gatling guns.
