Inside the first two barges stood the Second Virginia Regiment of the Atlantic Auxiliary; in the third and fourth stood the Fourteenth Massachusetts—men who thirty months ago had torn each other’s throats out in the Bloody Angle at Spotsylvania, and who now wore the identical blue-and-slate canvas fatigue jackets of the Pacifica Marine Line, their faces greased against the tropical sun, their thumbs hooked over the hammers of seven-shot Spencer repeaters.

Down on the stone mole at Piti, the Spanish captain under the umbrella suddenly stood up, shading his eyes with his hand as the four smoking iron boxes came chugging across the reef-flat at eight knots. A brass bugle warbled a frantic, cracked alarm from the courtyard of the fort. Ten barefoot native *artilleros* came running out of the guardhouse, struggling to pry the wooden tompions out of the muzzles of two ancient bronze twenty-four-pounders cast in Seville in the reign of Charles the Third.

"Range seven hundred yards to the masonry parapet," Marcus said into the brass tube by his chin. "One round of picric-acid shell from the forward eight-inch rifles. Do not waste a second volley; let the barges take the wharf on the smoke."

The twin rifles in the *Monterey*'s bow-turret slammed back on their hydraulic recoil-slides with a double thunderclap that flattened the sea into white rings for fifty yards around the hull and sent ten thousand white sea-birds screaming up from the mangroves of the Orote cliffs. 

Three seconds later, the center of the Spanish water-battery simply vanished in a towering, dirty-yellow pillar of pulverized coral limestone, shattered coconut logs, and spinning bronze gun-barrels. Before the chunks of blasted stone had finished splashing back into the lagoon, the iron prows of the four self-propelled barges grounded with a harsh, grinding screech upon the gravel beach twenty yards below the smoking breach. 

Steam-winches hissed; the armored bow-ramps dropped flat into the three-foot surf like drawbridges; and six hundred Virginians and New Englanders poured out into the warm, waist-deep water in a single disciplined wave, not firing a shot, their eighteen-inch trowel-bayonets leveled at the hip as they raced up the shattered masonry slope side by side.

Marcus watched the blue-and-slate line crest the ruined parapet and haul down the red-and-gold rag of Spain while the black smoke of the picric shell still hung in the palm-tops.

"Seventeen minutes and forty seconds from the drop of the well-gates," Marcus said, closing his ledger and handing his field-glasses to his orderly. "The Virginia battalion was thirty seconds slow clearing the starboard ramp because their colonel stopped to form company fronts on the wet sand. Have Colonel Armistead report to my cabin when we re-embark at noon; tell him that in the Pacifica service, a man who halts on a beach to dress his ranks will be reduced to the commissary wagons. Admiral—leave two companies of Hawaiian garrison police to hold the coal-hulks, and set course for the Bernardino Strait at four. The timetable for Luzon begins on the first of November."

***

By the twenty-second of November, the winter rains had come early to the coast of northern California, wrapping the high granite towers of the Citadel on Rincon Hill in a weeping, unbroken curtain of cold gray mist that smelled of wet redwood bark, drowned kelp, and the bitter coal-smoke beaten downward from the foundry stacks of the Mission.

Inside the high-arched Map Room on the fourth floor of the Chancery, however, there was neither mist nor cold. Across the entire thirty-foot length of the western wall stretched a newly completed relief-chart of the Great Arena, cast in solid plates of bronze and inlaid with silver wire to mark the submarine cables that now pulsed beneath the dark belly of the sea—from Monterey to Honolulu, from Honolulu to Midway and Guam, and from Sitka down the volcanic chain of the Kuriles to the locked gates of Edo and the mouth of the Pearl River.

Elias stood on the narrow iron gallery before the bronze wall, a brass-mounted magnifying glass in his left hand. He looked older tonight than his forty-one years; the relentless drive that had carried him from the ashes of his father’s cabin in Kentucky to the presidency of half the world had hollowed out the flesh beneath his cheekbones, leaving his jaw looking like an axe-head wedged into the high collar of his dark wool coat. 

Below him, around the green baize council-table, sat the men who kept the books of his providence: Cornelius Schuyler with his portfolio of Eastern customs receipts; Lord Shimazu of the Satsuma mission; Major Sterling, now Director of the Imperial Telegraphs; and at the far end of the mahogany, sitting upright and motionless in her black bombazine mourning-gown beneath the gas-chandelier, Lady Kaiulani.

The side door from the wire-room clicked open. A young Japanese signal-lieutenant in the dark blue uniform of the Cable Corps marched across the parquet floor, bowed twice from the waist before the gallery stairs, and handed a decoded blue tissue slip up to Major Sterling.

Sterling adjusted his spectacles, his lean Pennsylvanian face flushing with sudden, fierce pride as he read the lines aloud into the hush of the vaulted room.

"From Marshal Vance, headquarters aboard the flagship *Kamehameha*, anchored off the Pasig River mouth, Manila Bay—relayed via the Guam cable and Honolulu at six o’clock this evening!" Sterling’s voice rang against the bronze plates of the map. "*'The Spanish squadron of Rear-Admiral Montojo—seven wooden screw-frigates and two iron gunboats—was destroyed at anchor behind the Cavite arsenal at daybreak on the twentieth by our armored division without the loss of a single life aboard the Protectorate fleet. Our ten-inch rifles opened at four thousand yards, firing over the sand-spit; within ninety minutes the Spanish flagship* Reina Cristina *was burned to the water-line and the shore batteries silenced. At noon yesterday, the First and Second Divisions of the Atlantic Auxiliary Corps, supported by the Satsuma Marine Brigade, carried the southern walls of the Intramuros by storm after the railway-mortars breached the Real Gate. Captain-General Jaudenes signed the unconditional capitulation of the Philippine Archipelago at four this afternoon. The sun-and-anchor flies over Fort Santiago, and four thousand Spanish regulars are marching into the stockades.'*"

Around the long table, the American and Japanese councillors rose to their feet with a spontaneous, deep-throated murmur of triumph. Even Cornelius Schuyler slapped his fat palm down upon his leather ledger, his eyes shining with the vision of hemp, sugar, and tobacco monopolies stretching from Luzon to the Sulu Sea.

"God be praised, Protector!" Schuyler cried, looking up at the iron gallery. "Six hundred miles from the coast of China, and ten million new subjects added to the poll-tax rolls in a single morning! With Manila in our fist and Sitka on the north, the British at Hong Kong are caught between the jaws of a vise! There is not an ocean on this planet that can show a sail to match us!"

Elias did not smile. He walked slowly along the iron grating of the gallery until he stood before the lower left quadrant of the bronze map, where the sculpted brass islands of Luzon and Mindanao jutted down toward Borneo and the Malay Strait—the extreme outer rim of the seven-thousand-mile basin he had looked out upon from the snowy crest of the Sierra Nevada twenty-three years before. 

With a slow, deliberate movement, he took a small magnetic marker of gilded iron—shaped like the rising sun over an anchor—from the tray beside the rail and clapped it down upon the bronze indentation of Manila Bay. The magnet bit against the metal wall with a sharp, final *clink*.

Down at the end of the table, Lady Kaiulani had not risen with the others. Her dark, luminous eyes watched the small gold token gleaming on the bronze coast of Asia, and when the murmur of the councillors subsided, her voice rose clear and low through the room.

"The wheel is full circle, Elias," she said, not calling him by his title as she rested her slender, ivory-ringed fingers upon the edge of the mahogany. "Twenty-three years ago you rode over the mountains with two mules and a rusty rifle because the men in Washington tried to rule a country three thousand miles away with a piece of parchment and a bailiff’s horse. Look at your wall tonight. From the customs-house in Boston to the gates of Manila is ten thousand miles of salt water and iron rail. You have three hundred regiments standing guard over sixty million souls who speak twelve tongues and pray to six different gods, and every one of them waits for a wire from this room before he dares to bake a loaf of bread."

Elias looked down from the gallery rail. The yellow light of the gas-globes gleamed off the silver threads in his short-cropped hair and the deep, permanent crease between his brows.

"The men in Washington ruled with lawyers’ ink and fifty-page speeches, Kaiulani," Elias said, his words dropping into the quiet room like blocks of dressed granite falling into place. "I rule with six-inch compound armor and a silver coin that weighs the same in Manila as it does in Baltimore. An empire does not break because it is wide. It breaks when the men at the center grow soft and let the provinces argue with the axle."

He turned from the bronze map and began to descend the narrow spiral of the iron gallery stairs, his heavy cavalry boots ringing *clang, clang, clang* against the cast-iron treads while the councillors below bowed their heads.

"Mr. Schuyler," Elias said as his boot touched the parquet floor, not pausing in his stride as he walked toward the head of the table where the blank vellum sheets of the winter decrees lay waiting beside the red wax taper, "you will draft the Organic Act for the Prefecture of Luzon before you sleep tonight. The Spanish friars’ lands are confiscated to the Crown Naval Reserve; the customs tariff at Manila is fixed at twenty percent in silver thalers, with a complete drawback for goods carried in Pacifica bottoms; and you will notify the British governor at Hong Kong through our consul at Canton that from the first of January, all foreign warships entering the South China Sea north of the tenth parallel will register their coal-manifests with Admiral Takashima’s flag-captain at Cavite—"

He had just reached out his square, weather-beaten hand to lift the heavy gold dip-pen from its stand when the double mahogany doors at the rear of the Map Room were thrown open without a knock, and Colonel Caleb Vance—his white beard wet with November rain and his dark blue reserve uniform mud-splashed to the belt from a hard gallop up the hill from the Oakland ferry-slip—strode straight past the startled Hawaiian sentries with a drawn Colt revolver still gripped in his left fist and a blood-stained leather dispatch-bag in his right.

"Clear the room of the clerks, Elias!" the old frontier veteran barked, his hoarse cry cracking across the Protector’s unfinished sentence as he slammed the bloody leather pouch down directly on top of the wet Manila cablegram. "The Spanish minister from Washington didn't wait for the winter packet. He came over the Sierra on the mail-car with two French priests and a trunk full of royal seals, and some bushwhacking son of a bitch from the Sacramento Irish wards tried to put a knife in his ribs on the ferry-apron!"

Elias did not reach for his pistol. He looked down at the dark crimson smear drying on the salted calfskin of the pouch, and then up at Caleb’s heaving chest.

"Did the Spaniard live?" Elias asked.

"Live? He’s sitting in your anteroom downstairs drinking brandy out of a tin dipper and shaking like a wet dog," Caleb grunted, holstering his revolver and wiping the rain from his forehead with the back of his sleeve. "He says the Queen in Madrid has dismissed her cabinet, the mob is tearing up the cobbles in the Puerta del Sol, and he has full powers from the Escorial to buy back the friars’ estates before Marshal Vance hangs the Archbishop of Manila."

***

To the Chronicler who contemplates the demise of the older maritime thrones of Europe, there is a melancholy grandeur in the spectacle of Madrid during that black December of 1867. Three centuries had elapsed since the galleons of Philip the Second had turned the Pacific into a Castilian lake, carrying the silver of Potosí to the counting-houses of Acapulco and Manila under the shadow of the True Cross. Yet an empire built upon bullion-fleets and papal bulls is merely a crustacean shell; when the living meat inside has shriveled away through two hundred years of sloth, it requires only a single tap from an iron boot to crush the carapace into powder.

The news of Cavite did not arrive in the Spanish capital by the stately courier-ships of the old Indies Council. It leaped out of the brass telegraph instruments at the Ministry of Marine like an electric viper, relayed from Hong Kong through the British wires at Suez and Malta in twelve hours. 

Outside the gray granite facade of the Royal Palace, a bitter Guadarrama wind swept down across the treeless plateau of New Castile, rattling the bare chestnuts of the Prado and driving sleet into the faces of ten thousand citizens who stood packed around the iron railings of the Plaza de Oriente. There were no drums beating for a crusade. There were no volunteers marching to the railway stations as they had when Napoleon’s marshals crossed the Pyrenees. Instead, a vast, suffocating stupor hung over the crowd—the numbness of an ancient gentleman who wakes at midnight to find that a creditor he had considered a barbarian herdsman has kicked down his garden gate and seized his ancestral tapestries.

Inside the Hall of Mirrors, where the portraits of Charles the Fifth and Velázquez’s captains looked down through a blue haze of brazier-smoke and damp wool, Queen Isabella the Second wept loudly into a lace handkerchief while the aged Duke of Valencia, Marshal Narváez, stood beside the gilded console table with the British Ambassador’s cold note of refusal open in his crippled fingers.

"Lord Stanley will not move a single gunboat from Singapore, Your Majesty," Narváez said, his voice a dry, asthmatic wheeze beneath the weight of his gold-embroidered fleece. "And the Emperor Napoleon in Paris sends his regrets through the wire. He says that with the Prussian armies massed upon the Rhine and four hundred thousand American veterans drilling under the rising-sun standard from Boston to New Orleans, France cannot risk a war in the Pacific to save the Augustinian monasteries of Luzon."

"They are pirates!" the Queen sobbed, her fat, jeweled hands striking the velvet arms of the throne. "Heretics and savages who have armed the heathens of Japan with rifled cannon! We have forty thousand troops in Cuba! We have the *Numancia* at Cádiz! Let Admiral Méndez Núñez steam around the Horn and burn this San Francisco to the water!"

The Minister of Marine, an old sailor who had seen the compound-engine monitors of the Protectorate during his embassy to Vera Cruz, bowed his silver head until his chin touched his stock.

"Majesty," the Admiral murmured, "if the *Numancia* steamed around Cape Horn tomorrow, there is not a Spanish port between Valparaiso and Manila where she could buy a basket of coal that is not guarded by Thorne’s lancers or leased to his Honolulu syndicate. Her boilers would be cold before she reached the equator, and the ironclads that Marshal Vance has anchored off the Pasig carry fifteen-inch steel rifles that would pierce our wrought-iron plates at two miles’ distance. The ocean is closed to us. The eighteenth century ended on the twentieth of November; if we do not instruct the Marquis de la Habana at San Francisco to sign whatever parchment the Providentor lays before him this week, Vance’s cruisers will be off Havana before Easter, and we shall lose the Antilles as well."

***

Seven thousand miles from the gilded mirrors of Madrid, the twentieth of November had given way to the steaming, rot-heavy December of the Luzon lowlands, and General Marcus Vance had already discovered that it was a simpler matter to sink seven wooden frigates than to govern a jungle.

He rode at the head of a column of the Second Virginia Auxiliary along the flooded dike-road five miles south of Cavite, where the deep green wall of the bamboo brakes and nipa palms pressed in upon the narrow causeway like a suffocating blanket. The rain had stopped an hour after dawn, leaving the air at ninety-five degrees—a wet, blinding greenhouse mist that reeked of stagnant paddy-mud, rotting water-buffalo hides, crushed betel-nut, and the pungent woodsmoke of burning thatch.

Two hundred yards ahead, at the stone bridge crossing the Imus River, a company of Satsuma Marine pioneers was dragging the bloated corpses of four Missouri telegraph-linemen out of the ditch where they had been ambushed the night before. They had not been shot by Spanish regulars. The Spaniards were sitting quietly behind the barbed-wire stockades on the Luneta, eating Pacifica hardtack and playing cards. These four men had been hacked to pieces with heavy *bolo* knives by the native Tagalog *insurrectos* of Emilio Aguinaldo’s grandfather—men who had risen against the Spanish friars the moment the *Kamehameha*’s guns broke the walls of Intramuros, and who had naively imagined that the dark-blue soldiers from California had come across the sea to hand them a republic.

"They cut down two miles of copper wire between the convent and the river-landing, Marshal," reported Colonel Armistead, reining his sweating Philippine pony beside Marcus’s stirrup. The old Virginian’s slate-gray tunic was dark with mud and green slime to the pockets, and a fresh bolo-slash had taken the tip off his left ear during the night’s skirmish in the cane-fields. "And when my patrols went into the *barrio* behind the church to look for the wire-spools, the village headman swore by the Virgin that every man in the huts was a peaceful fisherman—while our boots were standing in fresh cartridge-paper and three of my corporals took buckshot from a bamboo thicket fifty yards away. You can’t tell a soldier from a farmer in this brush, sir. They don't wear uniforms; they throw their knives in the mud-puddle and pick up a hoe the minute our bugles sound."

Marcus looked down at the four mutilated linemen laid out on the wet stone parapet of the bridge, and then across the emerald expanse of the rice-paddies toward the tin roof of the village church half a mile away, where a hundred native women and barefoot men in white cotton shirts were watching the column from the shade of the mango trees.

There was no anger in Marcus’s gaunt, malaria-yellowed face. Anger belonged to amateurs who believed war was a passion play. To Marcus, guerrilla warfare in the tropics was merely an algebraic equation in which an enemy attempted to hide a small fraction of rifles inside a large denominator of population. To solve the equation, one simply reduced the denominator.

"How many yards of wire are missing, Colonel?" Marcus asked, pulling his damp leather field-ledger from his saddle-holster and resting it on his pommel.

"Eight hundred yards of number-nine galvanized, sir," Armistead answered.

"That is sixteen hundred minutes of interrupted communication between the fleet anchorage and the southern outposts," Marcus said, his pencil moving neatly across the page. "We will not chase men with big knives through bamboo swamps in ninety-degree heat, Colonel. A Virginian or a Pennsylvanian costs the Treasury four hundred thalers to train and transport six thousand miles; a Tagalog bushwhacker costs nothing. Unlimber the two twelve-pounder mountain howitzers on the bridge, and bring up the rock-oil wagons from the rear guard."

Armistead’s weathered jaw tightened slightly as he glanced toward the mango grove. "The women and young ones are still in the *barrio*, General."

"They have legs," Marcus replied, not looking up from his ledger. "Give the church bell three strokes with a rifle-butt. Every soul who walks out onto the stone road between here and the bridge within ten minutes with empty hands will be marched down to the Cavite drydocks and indentured to the coaling-gangs for five years to pay for the wire. At the eleventh minute, put four rounds of canister through the bamboo huts, pump two hundred gallons of Santa Paula rock-oil over the thatch, and burn every structure, fishing-proa, and rice-granary within one league of the broken poles. Then take ten men from the village roster—one for every eighty yards of stolen copper—and hang them from the cross-arms of the new telegraph posts before noon."

He closed the ledger with a dry *slap* and tucked the pencil into its loop.

"Publish the order in Spanish and Tagalog on every church door between Manila and Batangas tonight," Marcus continued, turning his horse’s head back toward the smoking funnels of the fleet visible above the palms of the bay. "For every imperial soldier killed from the brush, the nearest village within two miles of the body ceases to exist, its rice-lands are forfeited to the Satsuma military colonists, and its adult males go to the Mindanao sulfur-mines for life. We are not the Spaniards, Colonel; we do not take three hundred years to convert a parish. I have orders from the Protector to release four regiments from this island by February for the Canton demonstration, and by the first of January a child will be able to carry a sack of silver from Cavite to Aparri without losing a thaler."

***

On the twenty-ninth of December, the great oval Council Chamber on the second floor of the Citadel in San Francisco was lit not by the winter sun—which hung invisible behind a solid, roaring wall of Pacific rain beating against the western casements—but by four massive chandeliers of polished brass that burned refined whale-oil and shed a hard, shadowless yellow radiance over the green baize table.

At the center of the table, flanked by two trembling secretaries from the Madrid Foreign Office and a pair of black-robed Dominican procurators who had come up from Manila under parole, sat Don José Gutiérrez de la Concha, Marquis of Havana and Plenipotentiary of Her Catholic Majesty. His court uniform of dark blue cloth and scarlet cuffs was wrinkled from six days on the trans-continental snow-trains, and the bandage where the Irish assassin’s knife had grazed his ribs beneath his shoulder-blade made him sit stiffly upright, like a wooden saint carried in a Good Friday procession.

Opposite him, Elias did not sit. He stood before the roaring redwood fire on the hearth, his broad shoulders framed against the carved stone mantel where the fasces of the Confederation were chiseled into the gray Sierra granite. To his right sat Lady Kaiulani in her black mourning silk, a stack of Pacific hydrographic charts open before her; to his left sat Cornelius Schuyler, his gold-rimmed spectacles perched upon his nose as he totaled a column of figures on a sheet of blue foolscap.

"Two million silver thalers in cash, Señor Protector?" the Marquis of Havana repeated, his thin, aristocratic nostrils flaring with a mixture of incredulity and Castilian revulsion as he looked down at the draft treaty that Schuyler had just pushed across the baize. "You ask the Crown of Spain to cede the entire Philippine Archipelago, the Carolines, the Pelew Islands, and the Marianas—the patrimony of Magellan and Legazpi, containing nine million Christian souls and the richest tobacco and hemp lands in the Orient—for the price of a single sugar-plantation in Matanzas? Why, the stone forts of Cavite and the cathedral plate of Manila alone are worth twenty millions!"

"The forts of Cavite are piles of rubble, Marquis," Elias said. He did not raise his tone; the quiet, level authority in his chest filled the room as effortlessly as the heat from the hearth. "And the nine million souls were cutting the throats of your priests before my marines landed on the beach. I am not buying the islands from Her Catholic Majesty. My soldiers have already taken them with blood and iron. The two million thalers is merely a charitable contribution to pay the passage of your four thousand captive soldiers back to Cádiz so they do not starve in my stockades."

The older of the two Dominican friars leaned forward, his tonsured skull gleaming wetly under the lamps, his rosary rattling against the edge of the table. "And the endowments of the Religious Orders, Excellency! For three hundred years the Augustinians and the Dominicans have held the titles to the estates of Cavite and Laguna under the royal seal! By the law of Christendom, private property cannot be confiscated by a conqueror!"

"Your orders held those lands on the condition that you kept the peace for Madrid," Elias replied, stepping away from the fire and walking to the edge of the table. "You failed. A landlord who cannot keep his tenants from shooting my telegraph-linemen has forfeited his deed. Every acre of church land in the islands goes into the Imperial Naval Reserve to pay for the dredging of Subic Bay and the settlement of my veterans. Your friars may remain in their parish churches and say their Latin masses so long as they preach obedience to the Provost-General at Manila. The first priest who reads a pastoral letter from Rome or Madrid without my censor’s stamp on the margin will be put aboard a timber-brig for Sitka in his cassock."

The Marquis of Havana’s pale hand shook as he picked up the last page of the protocol. "There is an error in the sixth clause, sir. Your clerks have included the harbor of Pago Pago and the eastern islands of the Samoan group—what your whalers call the Navigators’ Islands—together with the German and British copra-stations at Apia. Spain has no garrison in Samoa, and our seventeenth-century claim to those reefs has been dormant for two hundred years! If I sign a quit-claim ceding the Samoan littoral to Pacifica, Lord Stanley in London and Count Bismarck in Berlin will protest that Madrid is giving away what she does not own!"

Beside the charts, Lady Kaiulani raised her dark eyes. For the first time in three months, a faint, chilling smile touched the corners of her mouth as she tapped the southern triangle of the map with her ivory pencil.

"Spain discovered the islands under Queirós in the year sixteen hundred and six, Excellency," Kaiulani said, her musical voice smooth as oiled steel. "The fact that your navigators were too lazy to build a lighthouse at Pago Pago does not extinguish the prior right of the Iberian Crown when transferred to a successor who has the ironclads to enforce it. With Honolulu in the north, Manila in the west, and the land-locked crater of Tutuila in the south, the triangle of the ocean is closed. The British packets from Sydney to Panama will steam through a Pacifica canal, or they will not steam at all."

Elias reached down, picked up the heavy gold pen from beside Schuyler’s inkwell, and held it out across the green baize toward the Spanish ambassador’s bandaged chest.

"Let Count Bismarck send his protest to my harbour-master at Apia when the *Satsuma* drops anchor there next month," Elias said, his gaze locking onto the Spaniard’s watering eyes while the rain hammered against the tall glass behind them. "You have until the clock on that mantel strikes five, Marquis. Sign the parchment, and Mr. Schuyler will hand you a draft on the Bank of Amsterdam for two million thalers before you leave this room. Refuse, and I will wire Admiral Takashima at Cavite to embark ten thousand Satsuma infantry for the Canary Islands, and by March you will be negotiating for the suburbs of Cádiz."

The Marquis’s fingers closed around the warm gold barrel of the pen. As the small mahogany door behind the Chancellor’s desk clicked open and Major Sterling stepped silently onto the carpet with a fresh ribbon of blue telegraph paper, Elias raised two fingers without turning his head, halting the officer in the shadow of the bookcase. There would be no more breathless interruptions; the machinery of the world could wait upon the stroke of a pen.

The steel nib scratched across the vellum, tearing slightly on the rough parchment before leaving a blot of black ink beside the scarlet wax. The Marquis dropped the pen, sank back into his chair, and covered his eyes with a trembling palm as Schuyler slid the Amsterdam bank-draft across the baize.

When the Spaniards and the weeping Dominicans had been ushered out into the rain-darkened corridor, Elias finally looked at Sterling. "What is it, Major?"

"Routine acknowledgment from the Nagasaki relay, Protector," Sterling said quietly, laying the paper on the corner of the desk. "The Tokugawa regency council has died of its own divisions. The young Boy-Emperor at Kyoto has declared the restoration of direct imperial rule, and the French military mission at Yokohama is arming the northern daimyos to contest the decree. Lord Shimazu asks when your flag will appear off Uraga."

Elias looked down at the wet ink of the Spanish cession. He had bought and battered every rim of the basin—from the ice of the Yukon to the swamps of Luzon—yet as he pressed his thumb against his left ribs, where a dull, persistent ache had lived beneath his breastbone since the winter crossing of the Rockies, he felt the terrifying weight of the roof he had raised. He had no son. If his heart stopped before the western anchor of the arch was mortared into place, Marcus Vance would rule by the camp-kettle, Schuyler by the counting-house, and Kaiulani would watch the whole iron edifice rust into rival kingdoms within a decade.

"Tell Lord Shimazu to have his pilots waiting off Cape Sagami on the first of March," Elias said, walking slowly toward the tall, rain-lashed window. "I am not sending a squadron this time. I am bringing the line of battle myself."

***

On the fourth of March, 1868, the morning mist over the Uraga Channel did not part before a gentle spring breeze; it was beaten flat against the dark green waters of Edo Bay by the concussion of twenty-four compound marine engines turning twin screws at eighty revolutions to the minute. 

Elias stood alone upon the open flying-bridge of the *Prometheus*—no longer the three-thousand-ton frigate of the fifties, which had been broken up for scrap to feed the furnaces of Clark’s Point, but a nine-thousand-ton casemate battleship whose hull was painted the deep, somber imperial blue that the Japanese coast-watchers still called coal-black in their dispatches. Fifteen years earlier, Commodore Matthew Perry had been turned back at the Cape of Good Hope for want of Welsh coal, leaving the treaties of Shimoda to be negotiated by Elias’s merchant-captains and four light corvettes. Those early conventions had been the polite bargains of equals who needed iron and shipwrights. Today, the Sovereign of the Eastern Shore came to audit the books of the West.

Behind the *Prometheus*, stretching in two parallel columns four miles down the strait toward the smoking volcanic cone of Oshima, steamed sixteen ocean-going ironclads and eight monstrous troop-liners: the *Leviathan*, the *Kamehameha*, the *Monterey*, the *Sitka*, and their sisters, their armored sides rising like sheer cliffs of riveted Pittsburgh and Sacramento steel above the frail cedar hulls of the local fishing-junks. From every masthead snapped the sunset-gold sun over the iron anchor, while twenty-eight telescopic funnels poured a continuous, thunderous canopy of black Nanaimo coal-smoke across the snowy peak of Mount Fuji in the western sky.

"The Tokugawa fort on Sarushima Island is manning its barbette batteries, Protector," said Rear-Admiral Takashima, mounting the iron ladder to the bridge with his binoculars slung across his gold-laced breast. Though the Satsuma officer had served Pacifica for seven years, his bronze cheeks were tight as drum-skin as he looked upon the pine-clad headlands of his native realm. "And the French dispatch-corvette *Dupleix* is anchored off the Yokohama bund with her boarding-nets triced up. The Shogun’s harbor-commissioner has just put off from the Shinagawa mole in a twelve-oared barge waving the red banner of parley—they are signaling us to drop anchor below the treaty-line at Kanagawa."

Elias rested his gloved hands upon the cold brass rail of the bridge. The salt spray kicking up from the battleship’s submerged ram-bow tasted of kelp and the pine-smoke drifting from the shore villages, mixing with the hot tallow and scorched mineral oil rising through the engine-room gratings beneath his boots. In his chest, that small, tight knot beneath the breastbone pulsed once against his wool waistcoat, reminding him that a man of forty-one who had lived on hardtack and telegraph tape could not afford three years of oriental ceremony.

"The treaty-line of fifty-four was drawn for wooden ships that feared the shoals, Admiral," Elias said. His voice was quiet, rough, and pitched to carry no farther than the wheelhouse behind him. "How much water do we have under the keel off the Shinagawa batteries?"

"Six fathoms at the flood, sir," Takashima answered. "Within two thousand yards of the Shogun’s own castle ditches."

"Hold your speed at ten knots," Elias ordered. "Do not slow for the commissioner’s barge; let our wake roll him back to the beach. If the French corvette off Yokohama does not dip her tricolor before our beam passes her anchorage, clear the port sixteen-inch turret and train the muzzles on her water-line until she finds her halyards. We will drop anchor where the people on the castle walls can smell our fires."

***

To the Chronicler who has conversed in later years with the aged councillors of the Bakufu—men who watched that terrible armada round the headland of Kanonzaki on the third day of the third moon—no words in the courtly vocabulary of Kyoto or Edo could compass the vertigo that seized the realm. For a decade, the Japanese had seen the merchant-steamers of San Francisco and the isolated cruisers that brought machinery to Nagasaki; they had flattered themselves that by sending five hundred samurai youth to work in the foundries of Clark’s Point and Monterey, they were learning the barbarian’s trick of fire and iron so that they might one day close the gates again.

They had mistaken a bucket of water for the sea.

When the sixteen steel leviathans steamed straight past the treaty-buoys of Kanagawa without furling a yard or answering the frantic gongs of the guard-boats, the very tide of the bay seemed to rise against the sea-walls of the capital. Along the five miles of timber wharves and stone bastions at Shinagawa, two hundred thousand citizens, two-sworded retainers of the northern clans, and shaven-pated priests stood frozen in the cold spring wind. They did not see ships; they saw floating mountains of black and blue iron that moved against a head-tide without a rag of canvas, propelled by a subterranean thunder that made the paper sliding-doors in the tea-houses along the Tokaido road rattle in their grooves three miles inland.

Inside the pentagonal earthworks of the First Daiba—the island battery that the Shogun’s Dutch engineers had built to bar the inner harbor—the gun-captains stood beside their bronze eighty-pounder smoothbores with smoking match-ropes in their hands, staring through the embrasures as the towering armored flank of the *Prometheus* glided past at four hundred yards’ distance.

"Look at the thickness of the casemate around the gun-ports," whispered Matsudaira, the Commander of the River Guard, his lacquered war-fan dropping forgotten into the wet sand at his sandals. "A thirty-two-pound round-shot would shatter against that curve like a clay teacup thrown at a temple bell. And look upon the aft deck of the second vessel—those are not sailors at the rail. Those are the red-lacquered helmets of the Satsuma and Choshu clans standing beside the giant hairy artillerymen from the American river!"

It was true, and in that sight lay the supreme, paralyzing terror of Elias Thorne’s syncretism. The Protector had not come merely with foreign monsters of iron; he had returned with Japan’s own children re-forged in the furnace of California. As the fleet dropped its thirty-ton bower anchors in unison off the mouth of the Sumida River—a sound like a hundred iron bridges collapsing into the sea at a single whistle-blast—there was no smoke of clumsy black powder from the gun-ports. Instead, from the fighting-tops of the *Leviathan* and the *Kamehameha*, great parabolic mirrors of polished silver caught the blinding rays of electric carbon-arc lamps powered by the ships’ dynamos, sweeping long, unnatural beams of white noon-light across the gray battlements of Edo Castle through the afternoon haze. 

And when the brass bands upon the twelve quarterdecks struck up the Imperial Anthem, the heavy European tubas and cornets were answered by the deep, bone-shaking boom of giant *taiko* war-drums and the shrill, mournful wail of Polynesian conch-horns. Feudalism, with its silk banners, its hereditary stipends of rice, and its exquisite sword-play learned in cedar halls, looked out across four hundred yards of oily water at the standardized, pitiless geometry of the nineteenth-century machine—and knew, before a single shell was chambered, that its world was already dead.

***

Three days later, the scene shifted from the salt-stung parapets of the harbor to the inner sanctuary of the Nijo audience-halls—for by Elias’s express demand, the young Emperor Mutsuhito and his regency council had been brought down from the ancient, land-locked seclusion of Kyoto by forced litter-march to meet the Lord of the Pacific within sight of the fleet’s guns.

The afternoon rain fell softly through the twisted black pines of the inner garden, dripping from the green bronze gargoyles of the upturned eaves onto beds of raked white river-gravel. Inside the Great Hall of the Pine, the air was cold and smelled of aged hinoki cypress, damp straw *tatami* mats, and the heavy, resinous smoke of aloeswood burning in bronze tortoises at the four corners of the chamber.

At the northern end of the room, upon a raised dais hung with split bamboo curtains through which the outlines of silk-robed courtiers glimmered like ghosts in a pond, sat the sixteen-year-old Son of Heaven. Two paces below the curtain knelt Prince Sanjo and the leaders of the Western Clans—Lord Shimazu among them—their foreheads touching the matting.

Elias did not kneel, nor had he removed his heavy cavalry boots at the lacquer threshold. As he walked down the center of the priceless cypress floor, flanked by General Marcus Vance in full blue-and-gold staff uniform and Lady Kaiulani wearing the royal feather mantle of the islands over her black silk, the steel rowels of his spurs left tiny, regular crescent-scars in the soft straw matting that had never before felt the leather of a foreign shoe. Behind them marched twelve troopers of the Life Guard—six six-foot Missourians and six giant Hawaiians—carrying seven-shot repeating rifles with bayonets fixed.

Ten paces from the bamboo screen, where a low table of red lacquer had been set to mark the limit of approach, Elias halted.

"Tell the Regent," Elias said to Rear-Admiral Takashima, who stood half a pace to his right as interpreter, "that I cannot speak to a sovereign through a basket. Raise the screen."

A horrified hiss, like wind through dry reeds, ran along the ranks of the kneeling *kuge* nobles in their tall black gauze hats. Prince Sanjo raised his shaved head from the mat, his face white as rice-paper.

"The person of the Heavenly Sovereign has not been looked upon by unanointed eyes since the age of the gods, Excellency!" Sanjo said through Takashima, his voice trembling with outrage. "Even the Shogun spoke to the throne from the lower floor!"

Elias did not raise his voice. He looked past the kneeling prince toward the shadow behind the bamboo slats, while outside in the bay, three miles away, the sixteen-inch gun of the *Prometheus* fired its noon time-signal—a single, dull *thump* that made the paper screens along the garden veranda shiver in their frames.

"The age of the gods ended when my ships dropped anchor off Shinagawa, Prince Sanjo," Elias said. "I am not a Dutch merchant come to crawl on my belly for a cargo of copper, and I am not a Tokugawa clerk. I rule from the Atlantic Ocean to the China Sea. If the Emperor of Japan wishes to sit beside me as a brother-monarch when we divide the western coast of this ocean, he will look me in the face. If he prefers to hide behind split cane like a woman in a harem, I will go back to my flagship, recognize the Tokugawa rebels in the north, and turn Edo into another Manila before the cherry-trees bloom."

For ten seconds no man breathed in the hall. Only the rain pattered on the gravel outside, and from the rear of the chamber came the dry, metallic click of Marcus Vance opening the lid of his pocket watch. 

Then, from behind the bamboo blind, a young, high-pitched voice spoke three sharp words in the court dialect of Kyoto.

Two chamberlains in white silk crept forward on their knees, grasped the braided crimson tassels, and drew the bamboo screen up to the cedar lintel.

The boy sitting upon the lacquer throne chair was slight, narrow-shouldered, and dressed in stiff, voluminous robes of white and purple brocade that seemed too heavy for his frame; yet as the light from the garden fell across his painted eyebrows and dark, almond-shaped eyes, he did not look down at the floor. He looked straight past his trembling ministers at the tall, broad-chested American in the plain navy wool coat whose hair was the color of forged iron.

Elias inclined his head two inches—the exact salute he gave to his own fleet admirals—and stepped forward until his boot touched the red lacquer table.

"Your Majesty," Elias said, his deep, rough voice filling the cypress vault as Takashima translated sentence by sentence. "Three hundred years ago, the Spaniards and the Portuguese came to your islands with wooden ships and iron crosses to turn your people into subjects of Madrid. Twenty years ago, the English came to Canton with opium and smoothbore cannon to turn the Emperor of China into a tax-collector for London cotton-mills. Today, the British sit at Hong Kong and Singapore, the French are landing soldiers in Cochin-China, and the Russians are building forts at Vladivostok. If Japan stands alone with her wooden junks and her clan-swords, within ten years your ports will be British treaty-ports and your samurai will be pulling rickshaws for Liverpool clerks."

The boy on the dais did not blink. His small, pale hand tightened on the ivory sceptre across his knee. "And the Protector of the Eastern Ocean?" the Emperor asked, his voice thin but steady as Takashima rendered the words. "You come with sixteen ships of iron and ten thousand foreign soldiers into my inner sea. How is the eagle of San Francisco different from the lion of London?"

"Because London wants a market of beggars, and I want an ally of iron," Elias answered, stepping around the low lacquer table while Prince Sanjo gasped and half-reached for a ceremonial dirk, only to freeze as Lady Kaiulani took a single step forward and laid a heavy parchment scroll bound in blue velvet directly upon the steps of the dais.

"I have eighty million people on my side of the water, and too many miles of prairie to police with American farmers alone," Elias continued, his pale gaze holding the boy-emperor’s eyes as he pointed toward the scroll. "You have thirty million subjects who know how to obey an order and die without asking a parliament why, sitting on barren rocks without iron ore, without rock-oil, and without wheat. Sign the Grand Pacific Alliance today, and I will give your throne the monopoly of the Asian mainland from the Yalu River to the gates of Canton. My rolling-mills at Sacramento and Nagasaki will plate your ships; my granaries in California will feed your armies; and for every regiment of Japanese infantry that serves under my Marshal in the Atlantic provinces to keep the Eastern cities quiet, my fleet will put two regiments of your samurai ashore in Korea and Manchuria under the joint standard of the Sun and the Anchor."

Mutsuhito looked down at the velvet-bound treaty lying upon the black lacquer steps, then out through the open screen toward the wet pines, beyond which the grey smoke of the Pacifica battleships stained the afternoon sky. With a slow, deliberate grace that belonged to ten centuries of unbroken blood, the boy extended his hand and touched the blue velvet.

***

By the third week of April, the cherry blossoms along the bluff above Yokohama had been beaten into the red mud by the boots of twelve thousand recruits, and the spring wind coming off the bay smelled no longer of wet cedar and tidal flats, but of cosmoline grease, scorched wool, and the pungent sulfur of forty thousand brass cartridges expended every morning on the Kanagawa rifle-butts.

General Marcus Vance stood upon a raw pine reviewing-stand erected over the ruins of the old Dutch factor’s warehouse, his binoculars raised to his eyes while the cold drizzle ran down the collar of his oilskin cape. Below him, across two miles of drained rice-paddy that his Cantonese engineers had graded and rolled with crushed volcanic cinders into a level parade-plain, the first four brigades of the New Imperial Japanese Army were executing a wheel by battalion at the double-quick.

They were a strange, terrifying hybrid to look upon. The two-handed swords, the lacquered bamboo breastplates, and the flowing silk *hakama* of the Tokugawa wars lay stacked in huge, rusting heaps behind the quartermaster sheds, waiting to be melted down for scrap-ballast in the Nagasaki cupolas. In their place, every man from the proudest Satsuma lance-corporal to the humblest Choshu peasant-conscript wore the standardized, high-collared tunic of dark imperial blue wool woven in the conquered mills of Lowell, Massachusetts, topped by avisored cap bearing the brass chrysanthemum above the Pacifica anchor. In their hands they carried the new model 1867 Sacramento needle-rifle—a breech-loading steel weapon firing a paper-patched metallic cartridge at nine rounds to the minute.

"The third battalion of the Sendai regiment is still bunching at the pivot, Colonel Armistead," Marcus said, not lowering his glasses as he spoke to the scarred Virginian standing beside him. Armistead, along with two hundred former officers of the Army of Northern Virginia and the Union Sixth Corps, had been brought up from Manila on the March transports to serve as drill-masters for the new levies.

"It’s the clan-pride in ’em, General," Armistead replied, shifting a plug of damp Virginia leaf in his cheek and pointing with his hickory rattan stick toward the left flank, where a young samurai captain was furiously beating a slow pivot-man across the shoulders with the flat of a steel saber. "The Satsuma boys on the right wing march like clockwork because Admiral Takashima’s cousins command the companies, but those northern men from Aizu and Sendai still think it’s a dishonor to take their dressing from a peasant corporal who carried night-soil buckets last winter. Yesterday evening in the barracks, one of the Aizu lieutenants cut his own belly open with a sharpened bayonet because my sergeant major from Pennsylvania dressed him down in front of the privates for having rust on his firing-pin."

Marcus lowered his binoculars and drew his damp memorandum book from his breast pocket. The malaria he had contracted in the Luzon swamps still lived in his marrow, giving his gaunt cheeks the tint of old tallow and leaving a persistent, ringing hum behind his temples that no dose of quinine could entirely silence. 

"A soldier who kills himself over a rusty firing-pin wastes twenty-four hundred grains of government powder and six months of rations," Marcus said, his pencil noting the regiment’s number on the wet page. "Issue a general order to the division commanders before evening mess: the ancient custom of *seppuku* is hereby classified as self-mutilation to avoid duty in time of war. Any officer who takes his own life without the written warrant of a Provost Court will have his corpse hung in chains over the regimental latrine, his family’s rice-pension forfeited to the Crown, and his clan-name erased from the rolls. If they wish to die for their Emperor, Colonel, let them do it in front of a British battery at Hong Kong where their bodies will at least soak up lead meant for my artillery horses."

Down on the cinder-plain, a bugler of the First Maryland Auxiliary blew a long, brassy blast. Instantly, the twelve thousand blue-coated figures dropped to one knee in the wet gravel; twelve thousand steel breech-blocks clicked open with the sound of a locust-swarm descending on a cornfield; and at the drop of Rear-Admiral Takashima’s saber, a single, continuous sheet of orange flame and grey smoke tore across the front as four brigades poured three volleys in twenty seconds into the plank targets eight hundred yards away against the sea-wall.

Through the drifting smoke-bank, six four-gun batteries of light Krupp mountain pieces—drawn not by horses, which were scarce and small in the islands, but by teams of twenty bare-legged Japanese artillery-coolies trotting in rope harnesses—came bounding through the intervals of the infantry line, unlimbering their steel trails in the mud in forty seconds flat.

Marcus watched the wooden targets down by the beach dissolve into flying splinters under the impact of the high-explosive shell. There was no need here for the lash that kept the Irish and Confederate conscripts moving on the Chilkoot ice, nor for the silver bribes that bought the politicians of Washington. These men were iron that had been tempered for eight hundred years in a closed furnace; all they had lacked was the die-stamp of modern logistics.

Yet as Marcus turned his head toward the foreign settlement on the bluff behind them—where the Union Jack still drooped over the brick compound of the British Legation, and four hundred Royal Marines of the 9th Foot watched the drill through the iron palings with sullen, pale faces—a sudden spasm of coughing shook his narrow chest, leaving a fleck of bright pink foam upon his gray wool gauntlet.

He wiped the glove clean against his hip before Armistead could see it. The machine was nearly complete, stretching from the Potomac to the Sumida, yet the men who had built the boiler were burning out their own grates to keep the pressure up.

***

Two months later, on the sixteenth of June, 1868, the summer sun hung high and blinding above the cold gray fog-banks rolling through the Golden Gate, turning the gilded copper roofs of the Citadel on Rincon Hill into beacons that could be seen from twenty miles out at sea.

Elias did not receive the Imperial Japanese Embassy in the small oval cabinet room where he had dictated the humiliation of Madrid. For the ratification of the Treaty of Edo—the instrument that closed the Western Ocean forever to the merchant flags of Europe—he had ordered the great Rotunda of the Chancery thrown open to three hundred delegates of the Diet, the marshals of the Atlantic Protectorates, and the captive diplomatic corps.

The chamber was a monument to the terrifying speed of Elias’s dominion: eighty feet in diameter, its lower walls faced with green serpentine marble from the coast ranges and hung with the captured regimental battle-flags of the old Union, Confederate, and Spanish armies, while from the coffered dome overhead hung the massive bronze chandelier cast from the melted cannon of Fort Sumter and Cavite. The air smelled of beeswax, damp broadcloth, the sharp brine blowing up from the naval slips below the cliff, and the faint, bitter camphor of the ceremonial robes worn by Prince Sanjo’s retinue.

Elias sat upon the raised chair of state—not a throne of velvet and gilt, which he despised as the furniture of bankrupt Bourbons, but a severe curule seat cast from solid, dull-gray Washoe silver and upholstered in plain navy leather. He wore his unadorned blue wool tunic, buttoned to the throat. Though his shoulders were still broad as an ox-yoke, the skin around his temples had grown tight and dry as drum-parchment over the bone, and while his right hand rested open upon his knee, his left thumb was tucked inside his breast-button, pressing steadily against the dull, hot iron weight that had settled behind his ribs since the voyage home from Yokohama.

At the center of the porphyry table below the dais, Prince Sanjo—now wearing the gold-braided court coat of a Pacifica Privy Councillor over his silk trousers—affixed the great vermilion seal of the Chrysanthemum Throne to the vellum scroll, while Chancellor Gwin and Cornelius Schuyler countersigned on behalf of the Maritime Board.

"By the seventh and eighth articles of this perpetual concordat," Chancellor Gwin read aloud, his voice booming proudly toward the diplomatic gallery where Sir Edward Thornton, the British Minister, stood rigid as a poker beside the French envoy, "His Imperial Majesty the Tenno of Japan and the Providentor of the Grand Confederation of Pacifica declare the waters of the Western Sea, from the Kurile Straits to the Formosa Channel, to be an exclusive customs-preserve of the Two Crowns. From the first day of August next, all extra-territorial concessions heretofore granted to European powers at Yokohama, Kobe, and Nagasaki are annulled. No foreign vessel not registered upon the rolls of San Francisco, Honolulu, or Edo shall discharge cargo within the Empire of Japan save upon payment of a sixty-percent differential duty in gold thalers; and the policing of the treaty-ports is hereby transferred in perpetuity to the Joint Imperial Admiralty."

Up in the gallery, Sir Edward Thornton did not wait for the reading to conclude. His face purple beneath his gray side-whiskers, the British Minister clapped his tall beaver hat onto his head inside the chamber, turned on his heel, and strode toward the gallery doors, his secretary hurrying behind him with his portfolio.

Elias watched the Englishman’s back vanish through the mahogany arch. Around the floor below, the syndics of San Francisco and the railway barons of Sacramento broke into a deep, rumbling cheer, striking their canes against the marble tiles; Schuyler was beaming like a man who had just been handed the keys to the Bank of England. 

Only Lady Kaiulani, sitting in her high-backed chair to the left of the silver seat with the heavy gold collar of the Insular Diet resting upon her black mourning silk, did not applaud. As Elias rose slowly to take the gold pen and add the final *E. Thorne, Providentor* beneath the red wax, she leaned slightly toward him under cover of the cheering.

"You have locked the shop door in the lion’s face, Elias," she murmured, her dark eyes fixed not upon the Japanese prince, but upon the slight, involuntary beads of cold sweat that had sprung out along Elias’s hairline as he bent over the porphyry table to write. "And your hand is shaking on the nib."

Elias did not look up. He drove the steel point through the last letter of his title with deliberate, crushing force, laid the pen down upon the silver tray without a click, and straightened his spine against the cold ache in his chest.

"My hand is steady enough to sign the sailing-orders for the China Squadron, Kaiulani," he said, his voice low and rough as river-gravel, pitched for her ear alone as Prince Sanjo bowed three times before the dais. "Let Sir Edward run to his telegraph wire. We have forty-two ironclads in commission between Sitka and Cavite, and sixty million thalers of Klondike bullion in the Mint cellar. If London wants to open the gates of Edo again, they will have to send their fleet sixteen thousand miles around the world without a coaling-station between the Falklands and Hong Kong."

"It is not London’s fleet I am looking at, Protector," she replied softly, her gaze dropping for an instant to the left breast of his tunic, where his thumb had slipped back between the brass buttons. "A roof that rests upon a single pillar does not need a cannonball to bring it down. It only needs the winter rot inside the oak. Look at your floor below: Schuyler is already whispering with the Boston railway factors about who shall control the Treasury when you are gone, and Admiral Takashima’s samurai do not even look at General Vance’s officers when they pass in the corridor. Who holds the hammer when your arm grows cold?"

Elias looked out over the sea of upturned faces—the greedy, florid jowls of the American syndicate directors, the stony, inscrutable masks of the Satsuma lords, the scarred, bitter veterans of the conquered East standing guard beneath the captured banners. For forty years he had never looked backward, and he had never imagined a morning when the sun would rise over the Pacific without his boot on the deck. Now, for the space of a single breath, the marble hall seemed to tilt beneath his heels, as if the granite of Rincon Hill were only the plank of a flatboat riding a brown, bottomless flood.

"The hammer does not leave my hand while I draw breath," Elias said, turning from her to face the cheering Diet and raising his right arm for silence.

***

To the Chronicler who seeks the true origin of the First Contest with Great Britain, it is not to be found in the naval estimates of Whitehall nor in the proud traditions of Trafalgar; it lies in the ledger-books of the Manchester Cotton Exchange and the smoking chimneys of Sheffield during that black summer of 1868.

For a hundred years, since the sails of Lord Clive and Captain Cook had first whitened the eastern seas, the island kingdom of the North Atlantic had rested upon a single, unchallenged axiom of providence: that the oceans of the earth were a single continuous highway paved by the Royal Navy so that the raw cotton, tea, and bullion of the outer continents might flow into the looms of Lancashire and the vaults of Threadneedle Street, returning outward as Birmingham hardware and six-percent loans. That a backwoods surveyor from the American wilderness—a man whose name had not even appeared in the *Almanach de Gotha* fifteen years prior—should first tear the United States in half, reduce New York and Boston to tax-farms, swallow the Russian ice and the Spanish islands in a single winter, and finally bolt the doors of Japan and the northern China coast with a stroke of a pen, struck the Victorian mind not merely as a political injury, but as a blasphemy against the order of nature.

On the night of the twenty-eighth of June, twelve days after Sir Edward Thornton’s cipher had passed beneath the Atlantic cable from Halifax to Ireland, a thick, yellow coal-fog mixed with summer drizzle hung over the wet cobblestones of Whitehall. Inside the high, oak-paneled Cabinet Room at Number Ten Downing Street, the gaselier hissed softly above the long green cloth where Prime Minister Benjamin Disraeli sat with his chin sunk into his black satin cravat, his dark, hooded eyes fixed upon the First Lord of the Admiralty and the Governor of the Bank of England.

"Fourteen textile mills in Oldham and Blackburn shut their gates on Saturday, Prime Minister," said Lord Stanley, the Foreign Secretary, laying a sheaf of consular dispatches beside the silver inkstand. "Since Thorne’s Customs Decree went into force at Manila and Yokohama, sixteen British tea-clippers and eight P&O steam-packets have been turned back from the Japanese straits with their cargoes of Manchester shirting unbroken in their holds. And worse—the Bank of Rotterdam notified us this morning that the San Francisco Mint is dumping thirty million thalers of pure Yukon gold onto the Frankfurt market exclusively to buy up the Krupp ordnance patents and the entire nitrate output of Peru. If we permit this Pacifica monopoly to stand through the autumn, the pound sterling will be driven out of every counting-house east of Singapore before Christmas."

At the foot of the table, Admiral Sir Sydney Dacres, First Sea Lord of the Admiralty, struck the edge of his brass-bound Pacific chart with a heavy, sun-freckled fist. He was sixty-four, a veteran of the Crimea who had grown grey in a world where a single British gunboat could bring an oriental kingdom to its knees before breakfast.

"The fellow is a blown-up land-pirate playing at Bonaparte with river-scows!" Dacres growled, his bushy white whiskers bristling as he leaned over the map. "Give the word to the telegraph office tonight, Mr. Disraeli. We have seven first-rate ironclads of the Channel Fleet lying with banked fires at Spithead—the *Warrior*, the *Black Prince*, the *Hercules*, and the *Monarch*. Order them to Gibraltar and around the Cape to join Admiral Kuper’s squadron at Hong Kong, while we send four armored rams through the Straits of Magellan to reinforce Esquimalt. We will catch this San Francisco upstart between Vancouver Island and the China Sea, burn his wooden docks at Puget Sound, and blow his Japanese allies back into their rice-swamps before the November gales!"

Disraeli did not move his head. Only his long, sallow fingers, flashing with a single emerald ring, rose an inch from the green baize to check the old sailor’s outburst.

"And how much Welsh coal does the *Hercules* burn in twenty-four hours at ten knots, Sir Sydney?" the Prime Minister asked, his voice smooth, theatrical, and heavy with an ancient, weary irony that belonged to an older sea than the Atlantic.

"Eighty tons a day, sir, when the grates are clean," Dacres answered bluntly.

"Eighty tons," Disraeli murmured, turning his dark gaze toward the Governor of the Bank, who sat wiping his spectacles with a trembling hand. "And from the Cape of Good Hope to Hong Kong is six thousand miles; from the Falkland Islands to Vancouver is seven thousand. Since this 'land-pirate' seized Honolulu, Guam, Manila, and the Samoan craters in December, while leasing every coaling-mole in Chile and Sonora with his Yukon silver, pray tell the Cabinet, Admiral: in what harbor between Valparaiso and Puget Sound will your four iron rams fill their bunkers when their coal-sacks are empty off the equator?"

Dacres opened his mouth, his ruddy face darkening to the color of old port, then hesitated as his stubby finger traced the vast, terrifying blankness of the eastern Pacific chart—five thousand miles of blue paper where every red dot marking a deep-water anchorage now bore the penciled cross of a Pacifica battery.

"We will send colliers under convoy from Cardiff and Sydney—" the Admiral began.

"Slow sailing-barques towed behind steam-battleships across the roaring forties," Disraeli interrupted softly, rising from his chair and walking with his slightly stooped, dandyish gait toward the tall window, where he pulled back an inch of the heavy crimson drapery to look out at the wet gas-lamps shining on the policemen’s capes in Whitehall. "While Mr. Thorne sits at the center of the circle, moving his squadrons along interior lines from Sitka to Yedo with coal dug at the water’s edge, and holding four million Irish and American riflemen at the border of Canada ready to march into Montreal the morning our first shot is fired at Esquimalt."

He let the curtain fall back into place and turned to face the room, his thumbs hooked into the armholes of his embroidered waistcoat.

"Do not deceive yourselves, my lords," Disraeli said, his voice dropping until every minister at the board had to lean forward to catch the words. "We are not dealing with the Tsar at Sebastopol, nor with the Emperor of China at the Peiho forts. Those were medieval states rotting from the inside. What has risen on the far side of the American mountains is Rome with a steam-engine in its belly—an empire that has strangled its own senate, married its iron to the thirty million sword-men of Japan, and turned the greatest ocean on the globe into a private mill-pond. We cannot fight Mr. Thorne across twelve thousand miles of empty water with colliers this autumn. Before the lion springs, we must first cut the tendons behind his knees—in Canada, in the discontented cities of New England, and among the proud island princes whom his Marshal Vance has just trampled in the mud of Honolulu."

He walked back to his seat and rested his slender hand upon a locked red morocco dispatch-box stamped with the royal cipher of the Secret Service.

"Lord Stanley," Disraeli said, his dark eyes glinting in the gas-light as he turned the small gold key in the brass lock of the box and lifted the lid an inch, "you will instruct Sir Rutherford Alcock at Peking to release fifty thousand sovereigns from the Hong Kong secret service fund to the anti-foreign secret societies in Shantung and Chihli—the Militia of Righteous and Harmonious Fists, as the mandarins call them. Let them burn the railway sleepers that Mr. Thorne’s engineers are laying from Tientsin, and let them besiege the foreign legations. If the American Caesar wishes to own the Asian littoral, let him try to digest four hundred million starving peasants while his own heart-valves are failing in the fog of San Francisco."

***

Three months later, the autumn equinox of 1868 turned the shallow, silt-choked expanse of the Yellow Sea into a boiling cauldron of ochre foam. 

Fifty miles off the low mud-flats of the Peiho River mouth, where the turbid discharge of the northern Chinese plains stained the salt water the color of rusted iron for twenty leagues out to sea, the First Armored Battle Squadron of Pacifica rode the long, greasy ground-swell in double column. At the head of the windward line steamed the flagship *Prometheus*, her massive nine-thousand-ton hull rolling ten degrees to port and starboard as the north wind whipped the coal-black smoke from her twin telescopic funnels flat across the yellow wave-tops.

Inside the armored chart-house beneath the flying bridge, the air was stifling with the heat of the steam-radiators and the sharp tang of camphor-spirits. Elias sat upon a bolted oak locker beside the brass binnacle, his navy wool tunic unbuttoned at the throat to ease the constriction around his windpipe. On the mahogany chart-table before him, weighted down by lead bars against the roll of the ship, lay the hydrographic survey of the Taku forts—and beside the chart stood a small blue glass phial of digitalis that his chief surgeon had discreetly left by the water-carafe that morning.

Elias did not touch the medicine. His broad, square-nailed thumb rested upon the inked soundings of the river bar, though every fourth beat of his pulse sent a dull, irregular thud up into the base of his carotid artery, like an engine-piston knocking against a worn cylinder-head.

"The water on the Taku bar is scarce eleven feet at low tide, Protector," said Rear-Admiral Takashima, bracing his sea-boots against the pitch of the deck as he leaned over the chart with a pair of brass dividers. "The *Prometheus* and the *Leviathan* draw twenty-four. Even at the spring flood tonight, our heavy battleships cannot cross the mud-spit to reach the inner anchorage. And the smoke from the shore shows that the Boxers have already fired the Russian and French timber-concessions at Tientsin."

Across the narrow cabin, Lady Kaiulani sat wrapped in her dark sea-otter mantle, her back straight against the iron bulkhead. She had accompanied the flagship from Nagasaki as High Commissioner of the Maritime Courts to adjudicate the seized customs-houses of the northern treaty ports, yet her dark eyes were fixed not upon the Chinese coast, but upon the gray, ashen ring around Elias’s lips.

"They are not merely burning timber, Admiral," Kaiulani said, her clear voice rising over the groaning of the iron rudder-chains beneath the deck. "The British consul at Chefoo wired before the lines were cut that the Empress Dowager’s guard regiments have joined the Righteous Fists. They have torn up forty miles of the new Pacifica railway grade between Taku and Peking, crucified eight of our Cantonese survey-clerks upon the telegraph poles, and surrounded the legation quarter. It is remarkably convenient for Mr. Disraeli that a peasant uprising in Shantung should strike exclusively at the wharves and rail-depots mortgaged to San Francisco."

Elias lifted his head. Through the thick, salt-crusted bull's-eye glass of the forward port, the low horizon toward the west was smudged with a dirty, copper-colored pall—the smoke of burning coal-yards and missionary compounds drifting out over the Bohai Gulf. 

"Convenient for London in September," Elias said, his rough voice steady despite the tightness in his chest as he closed his fist over the blue glass phial and slipped it unseen into his coat pocket. "Fatal for London by Christmas. For twenty years the European ministers at Peking have kept us out of the northern provinces by claiming that their treaties with the Manchu court guaranteed the peace of the coast. Now the Manchus have broken the lock themselves, and the British have only four wooden sloops in the river."

He rose from the oak locker, bracing his wide shoulders against the brass stanchion as a heavy yellow sea broke over the *Prometheus*'s turtle-back bow, sending a sheet of muddy spray rattling like gravel against the armor-plate.

"A merchant who cannot protect his warehouse forfeits his lease to the man who brings the fire-engine," Elias said. "We do not need the battleships inside the bar, Takashima. Transfer my pennant to the shallow-draft monitor *Sacramento* and bring up the twelve armored river-barges we towed from Nagasaki. When the tide makes at four o'clock, cross the mud-flats and lay our fifteen-inch turrets three hundred yards off the South Fort. Do not summon the Mandarin to parley. Open with high-explosive picric shell upon the water-gates until the mud walls slide into the ditch, and put Marshal Vance’s vanguard ashore on the wet silt before the smoke clears. We are going to rescue the European ambassadors whether they wish to be rescued or not—and when the fire is out, the keys to the river stay in my pocket."

***

Nine days after the fifteen-inch guns of the *Sacramento* reduced the mud-brick casemates of Taku to a smoking vitrified slag-heap, the autumn wind coming down from the Mongolian steppe struck the high, serrated ridges of the Yan Mountains like a blade of polished ice.

Here, forty miles north of the burning plains around Peking, the ancient stone rampart of the Great Wall twisted across the granite hogbacks like the petrified spine of a dragon that had died before Rome was pupped. The air at two thousand feet was bone-dry and tasted of pulverized yellow loess-dust, wild wormwood, and the rank, ammoniac reek of two thousand Manchurian pack-mules straining up the paved military road toward the Nankou Pass.

General Marcus Vance sat his gaunt, raw-boned California mare in the shadow of a crumbling Ming watchtower whose crenelated brickwork had been chipped three centuries ago by the iron arrows of the Tartars, and three hours ago by the four-inch rifled shells of the Pacifica Mountain Artillery. 

Despite the biting chill of the northern gale sweeping down the gorge, Marcus’s sunken cheeks were flushed with the dry, consuming fire of the Luzon malaria that recurred every third afternoon, and beneath his heavy navy-blue greatcoat his ribs ached with the pleurisy that had settled in his lungs during the crossing of the Yellow Sea. He did not unbutton his coat, nor did he look at the hospital ambulance waiting down by the mule-lines. He held his Carl Zeiss binoculars braced against the stone parapet of the wall, watching the spectacle unfolding down the long, boulder-strewn defile toward the south.

In the entire history of warfare since Alexander marched his Macedonians and Persians across the Hindu Kush, the sun had never looked down upon such an army as the column now winding through the broken gates of the Chinese Empire.

At the head of the pass marched the First and Third Regiments of the Atlantic Free States Auxiliary—three thousand sun-blackened veterans who five years earlier had worn the faded blue of the Army of the Potomac or the ragged butternut of Lee’s Virginians, and who now stepped in four-deep cadence beneath the Sunset Gold and Imperial Blue standard of the Protectorate. Their bearded Anglo-Saxon faces were coated grey with the ancient dust of Cathay; across their shoulders they carried seven-shot Sacramento repeating carbines; and behind their company guidons rumbled six armored steam-traction engines from the Clark’s Point works, their wide iron cleaver-wheels crushing the two-thousand-year-old granite flagstones of the Chin Dynasty into white powder as they dragged heavy steel siege-mortars up the grade.

And marching flank-to-flank with the Americans, occupying the left half of the stone road in silent, lock-stepped battalions, came the Second Imperial Division of Satsuma and Choshu infantry.

The old veterans of Gettysburg and Shiloh no longer spat tobacco at the smaller, bronze-skinned men beside them. During the bloody night-assault through the burning sorghum-fields of Tientsin four days prior—when thirty thousand screaming Boxers in red turbans and Prince Tuan’s Manchu Bannermen had charged the railway embankment through a blinding dust-storm—a Virginia regiment whose ammunition-mules had stampeded would have been hacked to ribbons had not two battalions of Choshu riflemen wheeled into the gap without a bugle-call, pouring nine aimed rounds a minute into the massed lances before going in with eighteen-inch steel bayonets in dead, terrifying silence.

"The Boxers have thrown up a barricade of carts and stone blocks across the southern mouth of the pass, Marshal," reported Colonel Armistead, riding up the rubble slope where a squad of Cantonese sappers was already bolting a porcelain telegraph-insulator directly into the masonry of the Great Wall. "And their flankers are rolling powder-barrels down the cliffs from that Buddhist monastery on the left spur. If we send the infantry down the gut in column, we’ll lose two hundred men before we reach the plain."

Marcus lowered his glasses, suppressing a tight, dry cough into his wool gauntlet so that the staff officers behind him would not see the red fleck on the cloth. His eyes were dull with fever, yet his brain worked with the cold, unhurried precision of an adding-machine.

"We will not send the infantry down the gut, Colonel," Marcus said, his voice scraping like dry sand against his windpipe as he turned in the saddle to look back down the northern slope, where four thousand Manchu cavalry from the Kalgan garrison had just been driven into a box-canyon by the flanking fire of his Japanese mountain-guns. "How many prisoners did General Saigo’s brigade take at the upper gate this morning?"

"Twelve hundred, sir," Armistead answered, squinting through the yellow dust. "Mostly Red Fist militia and Shantung sword-men."

"Have the Satsuma provosts wire their wrists together in ranks of twenty and drive them down the stone road three hundred yards ahead of our lead traction-engine," Marcus ordered, drawing his field-book from his coat and resting it on his saddle-horn. "If the monks on the cliff roll their powder-barrels, they will blow up their own brethren. Meanwhile, put two batteries of the four-inch Krupp rifles onto this watchtower parapet. Elevation four degrees. Do not shell the barricade—put forty rounds of white-phosphorus incendiary shell straight through the tiled roofs of that monastery on the spur. When the timber catches, the draft from the gorge will roast every marksman on the cliff inside ten minutes."

Armistead’s weathered hand rose to his cap-brim. "And when we clear the pass, General? The road to Peking is open across the flat for thirty miles. The British and Russian commanders down at Tientsin sent a courier this morning asking that we halt outside the Tartar Wall so that the European detachments can come up and enter the Forbidden City at the head of the column."

A grim, skeletal shadow of a smile touched Marcus’s fever-cracked lips. He looked out past the ancient grey battlements of the Ming emperors toward the southern haze, where the yellow roofs of the northern capital waited like ripe grain for the sickle.

"The European detachments are still sitting in the mud at Yangtsun waiting for their bullock-carts," Marcus said, closing his book. "We have steam-traction and they have mules. March the Virginia and Satsuma brigades through the night in two-hour relays. By dawn tomorrow, I want our mortars unlimbered before the Chienmen Gate and the Sun-and-Anchor flying over the Temple of Heaven before the first British marine sees the smoke of the city. If Sir Rutherford Alcock wishes to enter Peking, he will present his pass to a Pacifica corporal at the gate."

***

While Marcus Vance’s iron wheels were grinding the flagstones before the Forbidden City into dust, Elias did not go up to the dry, medieval furnace of Peking. A carpenter who knows where the main rafters of a house are joined does not waste his strength climbing into the garret; he sits down at the front threshold where all the grain and silver of the household must pass in and out.

Three hundred miles south of the Yellow Sea, where the Whangpoo River joins the vast, chocolate-colored deluge of the Yangtze Kiang—the arterial highway that drains the wealth of two hundred million souls from the tea-hills of Hankow to the silk-looms of Soochow—lay the mud-flat port of Shanghai.

On the twelfth of November, 1868, a cold autumn rain fell vertically into the river, pitting the brown current and wrapping the stone banking-houses of the British and French Bund in a sodden, coal-stained twilight. Yet along the two miles of river-front north of the Soochow Creek—where the old American missionary settlement of Hongkew had stood six weeks earlier—the twilight was banished by the glare of two hundred electric arc-lamps mounted on tall iron lattice-poles.

Here, the birth of the Pacifica Concession was proceeding not by treaty with the Taotai of Shanghai, whose yamen was currently occupied by two companies of the First Hawaiian Guard, but by the pile-driver and the steam-dredge. Down in the liquid mud of the foreshore, three thousand Cantonese coolies and twelve hundred conscripted Shantung prisoners worked knee-deep in the cold slime beneath the hissed steam of twenty floating donkey-engines, driving sixty-foot trunks of Oregon Douglas fir into the silt to support a continuous quay of Sierra granite blocks brought over as ballast in the holds of the San Francisco grain-fleet.
