The air was a thick, suffocating soup of river-sewage, wet coal-soot, the sharp nitric tang of blasting-gelatine, and the sweet, heavy smoke of opium and sandalwood drifting from the crowded native sampans that had been corralled behind a boom of chained timber spars across the creek.

Inside the upper gallery of the newly erected Admiralty House—a gaunt, three-story fortress of red brick and cast-iron columns bolted together from prefabricated Sacramento sections in twenty-eight days—Elias stood before the open casement window, his heavy wool boat-cloak draped loosely over his shoulders. 

He had not slept in forty hours. Below his left collarbone, the dull iron weight had sharpened since the morning into a slow, rhythmic vice that squeezed his ribs with every third breath, sending a cold, tingling numbness down the inside of his left arm all the way to the ring-finger. He kept his left hand buried deep in his coat pocket so that neither Cornelius Schuyler nor Sir Harry Parkes—Her Britannic Majesty’s Minister Plenipotentiary, who had steamed up from Hong Kong in a furious haste the night before—could see that his fingers were the color of tallow.

"This is no mere violation of the Treaty of Tientsin, Mr. Thorne!" Sir Harry Parkes was saying, his small, wiry frame trembling with indignation as he struck his wet umbrella against the parquet floor beside the mahogany table where Lady Kaiulani sat calmly sorting the stamped customs-manifests of forty detained British tea-clippers. "Marshal Vance has occupied the Imperial Ministry of Revenue in Peking with Japanese infantry! He has forced Prince Kung at the point of a bayonet to sign a decree transferring the entire Maritime Customs Service of the Yangtze Valley to a board of San Francisco syndics—and now your harbor-master informs the captain of the P&O steamer *Ganges* that he may not warp into the British Bund without paying tonnage dues to a Hawaiian port-warden!"

Elias did not turn from the window immediately. Down on the wet granite apron of the new pier, a traveling steam-crane was swinging a forty-ton locomotive boiler bearing the brass plate of the *Central China & Pacifica Railway* out of the hold of the transport *Oregon*, lowering it directly onto the broad-gauge iron rails that already stretched five miles inland across the leveled graves of the suburban rice-fields.

"Mr. Robert Hart and your British inspectors collected the customs for the Manchu court on the condition that you kept the river open and the rebels down, Sir Harry," Elias said, turning slowly from the casement. His rough, low voice carried the same flat, immovable weight it had held in the snows of the Platte thirty years before, though he had to pause for a fraction of a second between his phrases to let the spasm under his breastbone subside. "Last month, while your gunboats were anchored right out there off the Bund, the Boxers burned the silk-filatures at Soochow and murdered thirty foreign factors within ten miles of your consulate flagstaff. Your roof leaked. I have put a new one on."

"You have erected a fortified colony in the throat of the Yangtze!" Parkes shot back, his Whiskers bristling as he pointed through the rain-streaked glass toward the mouth of the Woosung river, where the twin sixteen-inch turrets of the *Leviathan* lay moored in mid-channel, blocking the fairway to every merchantman in the East China Sea. "Look at the boundary stones your engineers have driven into the mud along the Defense Creek! You have annexed twelve square miles of the richest alluvial delta in Asia, declared it sovereign territory of the Sacramento Diet under the laws of the Insular Code, and placed a twenty-percent transit tax on every chest of tea and bale of raw silk that

passes down the river from the interior to the British godowns!"

"Twenty-five percent, Sir Harry, if the cargo is insured in London rather than at Mr. Schuyler’s desk on Montgomery Street," corrected Lady Kaiulani smoothly, not looking up from her register as she dipped her steel pen into the inkwell and affixed the red stamp of the Insular Court to a clearance warrant. "Though any British merchant house in the old settlement is free to remove its offices three hundred yards north across the Soochow Creek into the Pacifica Concession, where it may enjoy the protection of our provost-courts, our electric telegraph, and our five-percent preferential tariff—provided fifty-one percent of its stock is registered in San Francisco gold thalers."

Parkes stared from the dark-eyed Polynesian princess in her black mourning silk to the plump, smiling face of Cornelius Schuyler, who stood warming his coattails before the coal-grate like a cat in a dairy. The Englishman’s ruddy face went pale with the sudden realization of the trap.

"You do not intend to fight us at Hong Kong at all," Parkes whispered, his grip tightening on the ivory handle of his umbrella. "You intend to starve Hong Kong to death without firing a gun. By holding the mouth of the Yangtze here and the railway at Peking, you drain the whole trade of the Chinese Empire into your own paved compound and leave our concessions downriver as empty mud-banks!"

"A man does not batter down a stone fort when he can turn the river into a new channel upstream, Sir Harry," Elias said, walking slowly from the window toward the head of the table, his right hand sliding casually along the back of a leather armchair to steady his knees against a sudden, blinding wave of vertigo that turned the gas-lamps into spinning yellow rings. "The Concession of Shanghai is open to all nations that acknowledge the Maritime Code. Your merchants may come across the bridge and trade in my silver, or they may sit behind your consular palings and watch the grass grow between the cobbles."

He reached the head of the mahogany table and stood looking down at the great map of the Yangtze basin, where the fresh red ink of the new Imperial Concession sat like a steel padlock upon the commercial heart of Asia. From Sitka to Tutuila, from the ruined Capitol on the Potomac to the mud of the Whangpoo, the circle was welded shut. There was no more west left upon the earth to conquer.

Yet as Sir Harry Parkes bowed stiffly and stalked toward the double doors, and Cornelius Schuyler stepped eagerly forward with a bundle of newly printed Shanghai Municipal Bonds in his hand, the iron band around Elias’s chest gave a sudden, savage twist—like a cold bayonet turned between the ribs—and as he reached out with his right hand to take the gold pen from Kaiulani’s fingers, the dark room tilted forty degrees to starboard, the inkwell slid into blackness, and the great frame of the Protector struck the parquet floor with the heavy, dead thud of a felled redwood.

***

For eleven days during that rain-swept November of 1868, while Elias Thorne lay behind the triple-bolted oak doors of the Shanghai Admiralty’s upper bedchamber with mustard plasters upon his chest and the smell of camphor and digitalis thick in the curtains, the world did not learn that the heart of the colossus had missed its stroke. Lady Kaiulani herself took the keys to the submarine cable-room before the surgeon had even risen from his knees. Not a cipher went out under the sea to Monterey or London that did not pass beneath her black sleeve; to the guards below, and to the restless captains of the Satsuma and American divisions, it was given out that the Providentor was secluded with the Ch’ing variance rolls, drafting the new provincial tax-codes in his own hand.

Yet to the Chronicler who walked the muddy alleys of Chihli and the stone quays of the Yangtze during that suspended fortnight, an extraordinary phenomenon manifested itself among the conquered populations—a religious and political contagion that neither Cornelius Schuyler’s clerks nor Rear-Admiral Takashima’s provosts had foreseen, and which history has since termed *The Thornean Mandate*.

For twenty years the peasantry of the Middle Kingdom had endured the slow, agonizing death-throes of the Manchu dynasty: the twenty million corpses of the Taiping rebellion, the burning of the Summer Palace by the Anglo-French armies, the flooding of the Yellow River, and the final, suicidal madness of the Righteous Fists. In the mind of the Chinese tiller of the soil and the scholar-gentry of the river towns alike, the *T’ien-ming*—the Mandate of Heaven— did not belong to a line of blood by divine right; it was a cosmic lease held only so long as the sovereign kept the dikes repaired, the bandits hung, and the grain-barges moving on the Grand Canal. When the dynasty grew corrupt and failed to command the elements, Heaven sent a scourge from beyond the mountains to sweep the threshold clean.

And what scourge had ever arrived with such terrifying, unmistakable providence as the iron fleets of the Eastern Sea?

Unlike the British and the French, who had merely nibbled at the treaty-ports like wharf-rats to sell Indian opium and Lancaster calico before sailing away, this new Lord of the Ocean had come with the geometry of an ancient founder of dynasties. Within three weeks of the fall of Taku, while Elias still lay gray-faced against his pillows listening to the rain beat on the Whangpoo, sixty thousand conscripted coolies under the supervision of Satsuma engineers and Virginia quartermasters were already dredging the silted bends of the Peiho with giant steam-shovels that did the work of ten thousand baskets. Along the ruined post-roads where the Boxers had burned the granaries, the standardized stone depots of the Pacifica Commissariat rose at twenty-li intervals, distributing white San Joaquin wheat and stamped silver coins whose weight never varied by a barleycorn.

In the tea-houses of Soochow and the ruined temples of Tientsin, where the Taoist fortune-tellers and wandering Buddhist mendicants gathered around the charcoal-pans, the whispered myth took shape with the speed of a prairie fire. The foreign Protector, they said, was no Western merchant-barbarian like the red-haired English; had he not brought the warriors of the Eastern Dwarfs and the dark kings of the Southern Isles kneeling at his stirrup? Had he not broken the White Tribes of the Atlantic first, and bound the Dragon of the Ocean in chains of black iron? 

Before November was out, the woodblock printers along the Bund were secretly striking off thousands of cheap vermilion broadsheets that found their way into the ancestral shrines of five provinces. Upon them, Elias was depicted in the stiff, terrifying iconography of the Ming martial gods: seated upon a throne of riveted boiler-plate beneath the Rising Sun and the Iron Anchor, his brow furrowed with the celestial thunderbolt, holding in his left hand a scroll of the Universal Land-Tax and in his right a seven-shot repeating carbine. The Confucian magistrates who had fled Peking before Marcus Vance’s railway-mortars began returning quietly to the yamen gates in their mule-litters, brushing the dust from their ceremonial robes to petition the Hawaiian and American provost-courts for new seals of office under what the literati gravely styled *The Ta-P’ing-Yang Ch’ao*—the Dynasty of the Great Peace of the Ocean. They did not ask whether the new Emperor in the brick house by the river could stand without his surgeon’s arm; to four hundred million souls weary of chaos, the steam-engine was the voice of Heaven, and the man who held the throttle was the Son of Sky.

***

Two months later, the winter fog of January 1869 rolled through the Golden Gate so thick and yellow with the smoke of a hundred foundry chimneys that the gas-lamps along the Embarcadero had to be kept burning at high noon. 

Lady Kaiulani stood upon the high, covered timber bridge that connected the second story of the Imperial Custom House with the great brick Immigration Barracoons on the Pacific Mail wharf. Below her, through the tall, salt-rimmed casements, the deck of the five-thousand-ton paddle-transport *Canton* was discharging its human cargo down four broad gangways into the sleet-chilled drizzle, while the heavy donkey-winches aft swung crate after crate of raw Kiangsu silk, Hankow brick-tea, and pigs of Yunnan tin onto the waiting flatcars of the Trans-Continental Railway.

Inside the glass-walled gallery where Kaiulani stood, the air was warm from the steam-pipes, yet it smelled heavily of wet wool, carbolic disinfectant from the quarantine pens below, and the pungent garlic and tobacco of the four thousand Shantung and Kwangtung laborers filing past the registration desks on the concrete floor underneath.

"Fourteen thousand landed at this pier since the first of the month, Your Highness," said Cornelius Schuyler, bustling up the gallery stairs with a thick leather portfolio tucked beneath his velvet-collared overcoat. Since the two weeks in Shanghai when he and Rear-Admiral Takashima had stood outside Elias’s locked bedroom door, eyeing each other like two wolves over a sick stag while Kaiulani held the cipher-key in her palm, the New York financier had grown markedly deferential toward the dark-robed woman beside him. "Three thousand are assigned to the Washoe silver drifts, four thousand to the Puget Sound timber-gangs, and the remainder go directly into the boxcars at Oakland to double-track the Pennsylvania Central through the Alleghenies. Yet the Municipal Board in Philadelphia wired my desk again this morning—they protest that our bringing Chinese coolies and Japanese garrison regiments into the eastern towns is driving the native mechanics into the woods to join the Fenian bushwhackers."

Kaiulani did not turn her head from the window. She wore her habitual black bombazine, the gold collar of the Insular Diet gleaming dully against her collarbone in the yellow fog-light. Her hands, encased in tight gloves of black kidskin, rested motionless upon the redwood rail as she watched a squad of Hawaiian provosts below stamping the brass neck-tags of a newly arrived company of northern Chinese stone-masons.

"Let the Philadelphia mechanics go into the woods if they prefer acorns to silver, Mr. Schuyler," Kaiulani said, her musical voice low and devoid of warmth. "For every Irish bricklayer in Pennsylvania who throws down his trowel to listen to a rebel preacher, I have ten men from the Yellow River down on that wharf who will lay twice the brick for half the rice, and who do not care whether Mr. Lincoln is hiding in Montreal or in hell."

"It is the cost of the garrison transports that troubles the syndicate directors, Your Highness," Schuyler murmured, lowering his tone and glancing toward the end of the gallery where two Satsuma staff-captains from Admiral Takashima’s naval board stood watching the unloading of the tin-ingots with cold, proprietary eyes. "While the Protector remains in Peking with Marshal Vance, the Admirals here are demanding another six million thalers for the Cavite drydocks, and General Caleb Vance insists that we cannot spare a single locomotive from the Missouri military district to haul Boston coal. Every department pulls the blanket toward its own side of the bed. If—God forbid—the Protector’s winter cough should worsen in that northern ice—"

Kaiulani turned her head slowly. Her dark, deep-set eyes fixed upon the plump banker until Schuyler’s tongue clicked dry against his teeth.

"The Protector’s cough is entirely mended, Mr. Schuyler," she said, each syllable cut as cleanly as a diamond scratching glass. "He walked the walls of the Tartar City yesterday for three hours without his cloak. And while he remains across the water, the blanket remains pinned where I have nailed it."

She picked up a stamped parchment schedule from the clerk’s desk beside the pillar and held it out toward him.

"You will inform the Philadelphia and Boston boards that the Pacific Arc is a single cistern," Kaiulani continued, watching the long line of blue-bloused Chinese laborers march out through the iron turnstiles below toward the waiting ferry-boats, their breath rising in a single cloud of white steam under the lamps of the wharf. "The iron of Pennsylvania goes to Nagasaki to plate the fleet; the silver of Nevada goes to Shanghai to buy the silk; and the muscle of Shantung goes to the Potomac and the Hudson to rebuild the roads the Yankees tore up. If any syndicate director on Montgomery Street or Wall Streetwithholds a single carload of rolling-stock from my labor-trains this month, I will not wait for the Protector’s cable. I will sit in the High Court of Receivership at noon, annul his bank’s charter under the Insular Emergency Statute, and divide his wharf-shares among Lord Shimazu’s factors. Do we understand one another, Comptroller?"

Schuyler bowed so low that his gold pince-nez swung free from his waistcoat ribbon. "Perfectly, Your Highness. The locomotives will be at the Oakland mole before the six o’clock tide."

When the banker had retreated down the timber stairs, his silk hat held tightly against his chest, Kaiulani remained alone above the roaring human river of the barracoons. In her pocket lay the private cipher that had come from Peking three hours ago—not from Elias, but from Marcus Vance’s chief surgeon, reporting that the Protector had suffered a second, milder spasm on the steps of the Temple of Heaven and was hiding the digitalis phials in his saddle-holsters. 

She looked out through the dirty glass at the gray water of the bay, where a Hawaiian war-corvette was saluting a Japanese troop-transport with three blasts of her steam-whistle. They had bound the two halves of the earth together with copper wire and iron rail, turning empires into labor-gangs and kings into customs-clerks; yet as the cold fog seeped through the casement joints and touched her cheek, she heard the creaking of the overstrained timbers beneath the paint.

***

In Peking, there was no fog; there was only the blinding, crystalline winter sky of the northern plain—a dome of pale imperial blue so cold and dry that the breath of the sentry-horses froze into white powder on their bits before it could form icicles—and beneath it, the vast, silent sea of yellow glazed tiles that roofed the Forbidden City.

On the afternoon of the nineteenth of January, 1869, Elias walked alone up the central marble ramp of the Hall of Supreme Harmony—the carved dragon-stone pavement over which, for five hundred years, no mortal foot had passed save the bearers of the Son of Heaven’s palanquin. 

Thirty-two years had passed since the autumn twilight when he had pried the hot iron hinge-straps from the threshold of his father’s burning cabin in Kentucky with a green hickory limb. He wore no gold-braided uniform today, nor the heavy silver collar that the Diet in Monterey had sent across the sea for his investiture as Sovereign of the Realm; he wore the same severe, high-collared dark blue wool greatcoat he had worn at Vicksburg and Washington, its skirt whipping around his mud-stained cavalry boots in the razor-edged wind coming down from Mongolia.

Fifty paces below him, at the foot of the triple white marble terrace where the gilded bronze cranes and incense-burners stood cold and smokeless in the sun, General Marcus Vance leaned heavily upon his saber-scabbard beside Rear-Admiral Takashima and a silent, fur-hatted delegation of the Grand Secretariat under Prince Kung. Even from the height of the terrace, Elias could hear Marcus’s dry, rattling cough echoing off the vermilion pillars behind him—the sound of a worn-out bellows pumping air through cracked leather.

Elias did not look back to wait for them. He climbed the last ten marble steps deliberately,measuring his stride so that the treacherous, fluttering monster behind his breastbone would not betray a stumble to the two thousand soldiers of the Virginia Auxiliary and the Satsuma Guard drawn up across the immense flagged courtyard below. When he reached the top platform, he paused with his scarred right palm resting against one of the massive, red-lacquered cedar columns that supported the double-eaved roof, and looked southward.

Before him, gate beyond gate, court beyond court, stretched the geometric heart of the oldest empire on the globe: the Meridian Gate, the bridges of white jade arching over the frozen Golden Water, and beyond the towering outer bastions, the brown, smoke-hazed immensity of the Chinese plain rolling away toward the ocean he had made his own.

A strange, intoxicating lightness—sharper than the thin winter air and sweeter than the strong wine of the Rio Frio—filled his skull as the sun caught the ten thousand yellow tiles below him and turned them into a floor of solid sunset gold. 

When he was twenty, reading the dog-eared Latin histories in the dead priest’s library at Mission Dolores while the rain beat on the adobe roof, he had paused over the pages where Arrian described the Macedonian standing upon the banks of the Hyphasis, weeping because the world had run out of horizons before his sword was dull. Alexander had been a boy with a bronze spear who conquered a strip of desert from Greece to the Indus, and his empire had shattered into four pieces before his corpse was cold in Babylon because he had nothing to bind it with but horse-flesh and parchment.

*I have gone farther than the Greek,* Elias thought, his lips moving soundlessly in the cold wind as he walked out from the shadow of the eaves into the open doorway of the great throne-hall. *He stopped at the edge of the eastern mountains. I have taken the mountains in my stride, I have bridged the great water that he never knew existed, and I have bolted the two ends of the earth together with steel rails and copper wire so tight that not a sparrow falls between Boston and Canton without its weight being entered in my books.*

Inside the cavernous gloom of the Hall of Supreme Harmony, the air was twenty degrees colder than the terrace outside, smelling of ancient dry dust, cedar-rot, and the dead, cold tallow of ceremonial candles extinguished when the Empress Dowager fled westward toward Shensi two months before. Seventy-two giant pillars of *nanmu* timber, each felled in the forests of Szechuan three centuries ago and covered in flaking gold leaf, rose into the dark coffered ceiling where the carved wooden dragons coiled around the pearl of heaven.

Elias’s spurs rang *clink-clank, clink-clank* across the black, polished bricks of the floor—bricks that had been baked in the kilns of Soochow and soaked in boiling tung-oil until they shone like dark ice. He climbed the seven steps of the high lacquer dais at the center of the hall and stood before the Dragon Throne.

Behind him, at the wide threshold of the southern doors, footsteps scraped against the marble sill. Marcus Vance and Rear-Admiral Takashima stepped into the slant of pale winter sunlight, their breath smoking white in the freezing vault, while Prince Kung halted outside on the terrace, refusing to cross the sill where the barbarian’s boots had profaned the sanctuary.

"Protector," Marcus said. His voice was hoarse and thin, echoing weirdly among the seventy-two golden columns as he held out a portfolio that had just come up from the Tientsin wire-head. "The plenipotentiaries of the northern provinces are waiting in the Board of Ceremonies to hear the terms of the salt-gabelle mortgage. And the surgeon asks—"

"Damn the surgeon," Elias said, not turning around as he reached out with his bare, weather-chapped right hand and laid his fingers upon the carved gold dragon-head of the throne’s armrest. The wood was colder than the ice on the Platte. "Come up here to the steps, Marcus. Both of you. Look out through those doors."

Marcus and the Japanese admiral walked slowly across the black bricks and stood at the base of the lacquer platform, looking up at the tall, gray-haired figure framed against the gilded screen of the Ming emperors.

"Twenty-two years ago, Marcus," Elias said, his rough, low voice filling the silent throne-room with a terrifying certainty as he turned to face them, his left hand slipping unconsciously beneath the breast-flap of his coat while his pale gaze burned with a feverish, unblinking brilliance in the half-dark, "your uncle Caleb and I stood on a rock in the Sierra snow and looked down at an empty sea. They told us in Washington that the continent belonged to the lawyers, and they told us in London that the ocean belonged to the Queen’s ships. Look at the map in your hand today. There is no Washington. There is no border. From the ice of the Yukon to the gates of this palace, three hundred million men eat bread from my granaries, coin my silver, and march when my bugle blows."

He took half a step down the lacquer stair, his right hand rising to point straight through the open red doors toward the blinding blue sky above the southern gates.

"Alexander died in a fever-swamp at thirty-two because he thought the world ended at the Indian sea," Elias said, his voice rising until the old dust sifted down from the dragon-beams overhead. "We have no edge to stop at. By the spring thaw, our broad-gauge rails will run from this gate through the Kalgan pass straight across the Gobi to Irkutsk, and when the Russian Tsar cannot pay the interest on the Sitka monitors next winter, we will foreclose on Siberia all the way to the Urals and look down into Europe from the back door! Takashima—tell your Emperor at Edo that the title of Protector belongs to a republic’s nursery. On the first of May, when the fleet assembles at Honolulu, the Diet will proclaim the—"

A sudden, terrible cough from Marcus Vance broke across the words as the Marshal doubled over at the foot of the stairs, pressing his handkerchief to his mouth; and as Elias stepped down the second lacquer tread to catch his general’s shoulder, his own boot-heel slipped on the frozen tung-oil brick, his left hand tore at his collar as if an unseen wire had just been drawn tight around his windpipe, and the seventy-two golden pillars spun into a single blinding whirlpool of dark red lacquer.

He did not let his knees touch the Ming bricks. Even as his vision blackened at the edges and the cold iron vice beneath his sternum squeezed the breath from his lungs in a ragged wheeze, Elias locked his right elbow around the carved wooden tail of the dragon balustrade, holding his two hundred pounds upright by the sheer, stubborn refusal of his wrist-bones to yield in front of a Satsuma admiral. For six weeks they hid that second stumble behind the high walls of the northern capital, feeding the Protector digitalis in porcelain teacups while Takashima and Cornelius Schuyler’s cable-agents circling the sickroom began to measure the breadth of his coffin with their eyes.

Yet by June, when the sub-arctic summer finally broke the pack-ice of the sixty-sixth parallel, Elias Thorne was not in a coffin; he was standing upon the basalt headlands of Cape Prince of Wales, where the uttermost western horn of the American continent thrusts its black volcanic chin out toward the bleak, snow-streaked cliffs of East Cape in Asia.

Between the two worlds ran fifty-three miles of racing, lead-colored water, split dead in the center by the twin granite tables of the Diomede Islands.

The wind here did not smell of the tropics or the southern foundries; it came straight out of the Chukchi Sea, tasting of green glacier-melt, crushed granite, and the sour coal-smoke of six armored ice-breakers that were methodically ramming their reinforced steel prows into the rotting floes two hundred yards offshore. On the gravel beach below the cliff, where the whale-rib huts of the Eskimo had stood the previous autumn, four thousand Cantonese and Irish convicts from the Yukon camps were already dragging massive timber caissons toward the surf behind wheezing steam-winches, while overhead the seagulls screamed around the tall, raw pine derricks of the Imperial Engineering Corps.

Elias sat inside a glass-enclosed wind-shelter bolted directly to the bedrock of the cape, wrapped to the chin in a heavy sea-otter pelisse. He had lost thirty pounds since the winter in Peking; the skin of his cheeks hung slack and gray as wet buckskin around his jaw, and a brazier of glowing Nanaimo anthracite burned between his boots to keep the arctic damp out of his congested lungs. Around the cramped, cedar-planked shelter stood the four pillars of his realm, pressed shoulder to shoulder in a closeness that smelled of wet wool and barely concealed mutiny: Marcus Vance, whose own sunken eyes burned with the dry hectic flush of consumption; Rear-Admiral Takashima; Cornelius Schuyler, shivering miserably in three fur waistcoats; and Lady Kaiulani, who stood behind Elias’s chair like a black-robed regent waiting for the last sand to run through the glass.

"The soundings across the channel never exceed thirty fathoms, Mr. Schuyler," Elias said. His voice was no longer the resonant bugle that had rallied the rangers on the Rio Frio; it was a dry, gravelly rasp that required a pull of breath after every fifth word, yet not a man in the glass box dared look away from his eyes. "Twenty-seven miles from this rock to the Big Diomede. Twenty-six miles from the Little Diomede to the Siberian shore. A mud-bottom overlaid with gravel, and two granite islands placed by providence in the exact middle of the ditch to serve as central piers."

Schuyler adjusted his fogged spectacles, looking down with open horror at the six-foot blueprint roll that Major Sterling had pinned across the drafting-trestle. "Protector, the syndicate boards in San Francisco and New York have examined Major Sterling’s estimates with the utmost care. To sink four hundred pneumatic cast-iron caissons into a tide-race where the winter pack-ice moves at six knots with the weight of ten million tons—to span fifty miles of sub-arctic sea with tubular steel trusses high enough to clear the masts of a whaler—will consume eight hundred thousand tons of Bessemer plate and two hundred million gold thalers! The Market Street Mint is already overdrawn by the Yangtze railway bonds, and the Boston banks are threatening to suspend the quarterly tribute if we float another forced loan this autumn! Why build a bridge at the top of the world where nothing lives but walruses and ice-bears, when our steamers can cross from Puget Sound to Vladivostok in twelve days?"

"Because a steamer can be sunk by a British cruiser in a fog, and a sea-lane can be closed by a typhoon," Elias said, lifting his gaunt right hand from beneath the sea-otter fur and tapping a blunt, bluish fingernail against the inked span of the Bering Bridge. "When my heart missed its beat in Shanghai last November, Mr. Schuyler, how long did it take you and Lord Shimazu’s factors to begin whispering in the telegraph room about dividing the shipping monopolies between Edo and San Francisco?"

Schuyler’s pudgy cheeks went the color of lard. Beside him, Rear-Admiral Takashima’s hand stiffened on the hilt of his dirk.

"You think I did not hear you through the oak door?" Elias asked softly, a terrible, ghost-like smile pulling at the corner of his mouth as he looked from the banker to the samurai. "You think because a man lies on a mattress with mustard on his chest, he is already under the sod? If I leave this empire held together only by wooden ships and copper wires under the salt water, the morning after you bury me at Monterey, Takashima’s admirals will cut the cable at Midway and take Asia for the Tenno, while Schuyler’s friends in New York call back the lawyers from Montreal to sell the Atlantic provinces to London."

Behind his chair, Lady Kaiulani’s dark eyes gleamed with a sharp, cold amusement. "The Providentor knows his heirs well, gentlemen," she murmured, her gloved fingers resting lightly on the high wooden back of Elias’s seat. "Water divides; only iron holds."

"We are going to bolt the two continents together so tight that ten generations of traitors will not have the chisels to pry them apart," Elias rasped, leaning forward over the blueprint until the heat of the charcoal brazier reddened his hollow chin. "Double-track broad-gauge steel from the depot at Oakland, up the Fraser and the Yukon, straight across the Bering piers on tubular trusses eighty feet above the ice-pack, and down through the Stanovoy mountains to the Amur and Peking. When a locomotive can roll from the piers of Manhattan to the gates of the Forbidden City in fourteen days without wetting a wheel in salt water, there will be no East and no West. There will only be the road."

"And the Tsar’s charter for the western abutment, Protector?" Takashima asked, his narrow eyes fixed on the Siberian shore dimly visible through the lifting sea-smoke across the strait. "Baron Stoeckl sold us the American ice in sixty-six because he believed the water between these capes was an eternal moat. Our survey-parties on the Chukotka peninsula report that the Governor-General at Irkutsk has refused to countersign the land-grants for the western bridge-head, and four sotnias of Amur Cossacks are riding north from Anadyrsk to drive our engineers into the sea."

Elias coughed once into his fur collar, his eyes watering with the iron stab in his breast, then looked at Marcus Vance.

"The Tsar owes the San Francisco Treasury four million thalers in unpaid interest on the Kronstadt engine-patents," Elias said. "If Alexander will not sign the right-of-way for the western piers at his desk in St. Petersburg, Marshal Vance will take three regiments across the strait on the ice-breakers this afternoon and sign it on the ground. Put the first caisson into the water, Major Sterling. I intend to ride the pilot-engine across that channel before I die."

***

To the Chronicler who has studied the secret archives of the Winter Palace during the sixty-ninth year of the century, the design of the Bering Bridge marks the precise moment when the great geopolitical pendulum of the modern world swung from the maritime circumference to the continental heartland. For three hundred years, since Yermak the Cossack had crossed the Urals with his matchlock-men, the Empire of the Tsars had expanded eastward through the birch-forests and the tundra like a glacier moving in the dark—secure in the knowledge that at its back lay the impenetrable ice of the pole, and before it an empty ocean across which no European army could ever march.

Now, in the pale, sleepless midsummer nights of St. Petersburg, when the granite embankments of the Neva shone with a spectral, mother-of-pearl twilight at midnight, that ancient security vanished like river-mist. Inside the Malachite Room of the Winter Palace, Emperor Alexander the Second paced beneath the gilded ceiling, the smoke of his papiros drifting across a vast green military map of Eastern Siberia upon which the Minister of War, General Milyutin, had pinned the intercepted lithographs of Major Sterling’s tubular bridge.

To the Russian mind—nurtured on the memory of the Tartar hordes and the Grande Armée marching across the Niemen—a bridge was never an instrument of trade. A bridge was a spear-shaft.

"Baron Stoeckl assured the Imperial Council that we were selling a frozen wilderness to a maritime syndicate that looked southward toward Canton," the Tsar said, his tall, heavy-shouldered frame rigid inside his Chevalier Guard tunic as he stopped beside the malachite pilasters. Through the tall windows, the golden spire of the Peter and Paul Fortress pricked the white night sky like a bayonet. "We took his seven million thalers to build railways to Odessa and Sebastopol, believing the Strait of Behring was fifty miles of pack-ice that no steam-engine could ever cross. Now you tell me this San Francisco dictator is driving four hundred cast-iron piers into the sea-floor at the Diomedes, and that his Japanese vassals are already grading a double-track bed up the valley of the Anadyr!"

General Milyutin did not offer the soothing platitudes of the diplomatic corps. He was a modern soldier who had studied the campaigns of Vicksburg and the Nankou Pass, and he knew what a broad-gauge rail-line meant when Marcus Vance sat at the throttle.

"Sire, it is not commerce that requires eighty-pound steel rails and stone blockhouses every ten versts across the tundra," Milyutin answered, tapping the blank, unmapped expanse between the Stanovoy Range and Lake Baikal. "We have scarce twelve thousand line-infantry and six regiments of irregular Cossacks scattered across four thousand miles of wilderness between Irkutsk and the sea. We have no railroad east of Perm. In winter, it takes a courier eighty days by sleigh to carry an order from this room to the mouth of the Amur. If we permit Thorne’s engineers to link their Yukon track to the Siberian shore, San Francisco will be fourteen days by locomotive from the heart of Asia, while our own reinforcements are still marching on foot through the mud of Tomsk."

Prince Gorchakov, the aged Chancellor, adjusted his spectacles with a dry, papery sigh from his armchair beside the cold porcelain stove. "And yet, Your Majesty, how are we to forbid him? The British Cabinet has washed its hands of the northern sea since the fall of Shanghai, and Mr. Schuyler’s agents in Frankfurt hold forty million rubles of our state railway obligations. When I reminded the Pacifica envoy yesterday that Chukotka is the sovereign soil of the Russian Crown, the woman—this Polynesian princess who signs their maritime decrees in red ink—sent back a note stating that since the Ministry of Finance is six months in arrears on the Vladivostok dockyard bonds, the Confederation is merely exercising the right of a mortgage-holder to improve the bailiwick."

"A mortgage-holder!" Alexander’s fist came down upon the malachite table so hard the bronze inkwells leaped. The Romanov autocracy had survived Charles of Sweden and Bonaparte of France; to be treated like a bankrupt squire by an American border-ruffian and a cohort of Japanese and island ministers was a humiliation that burned through the Tsar’s veins like raw vitriol. "Today he claims the right to lay iron rails across Chukotka to collect four million thalers. Tomorrow, when his tracks reach the Lena and the Amur, he will claim the gold-washings of Nerchinsk and the forests of Baikal to pay for the coal his engines burned on the road!"

The Tsar walked to the map and swept the lithograph of the Bering Bridge onto the parquet floor with the back of his gloved hand.

"Send a priority wire to Governor-General Korsakov at Irkutsk before the sun rises," Alexander commanded, his pale, protuberant eyes fixed upon his War Minister. "Tell him to mobilize the Trans-Baikal Cossack Host and move every battery of bronze field-guns on the Amur northward toward the Anadyr divide. They are not to wait for a formal declaration from St. Petersburg. Tear up the American survey-stakes, burn their timber-trestles, and drive their Chinese digging-gangs back into the sea. If the whale wishes to crawl out upon the land, it will find the bear’s claws waiting in the moss."

***

Four thousand miles east of the Neva’s marble quays, there were no malachite columns, and the summer night did not bring the polite twilight of European courts; it brought twenty-two hours of blinding, brassy sun that hung low along the northern rim of the tundra, breeding swarms of black arctic mosquitoes so thick they turned the air into a humming gray fog and choked the nostrils of the horses through their net-veils.

General Marcus Vance sat upon an upturned barrel of tallow-grease beside the open door of an armored flatcar, three leagues inland from the western shore of the Bering Strait. Beneath the wheels of the construction train, the spongy Siberian sphagnum moss had been stripped away down to the blue permafrost by two thousand Cantonese graders, who were laying a mattress of felled larch-trunks and crushed volcanic basalt to hold the seven-foot cross-ties of the Asian Trunk Line. The air smelled of sour swamp-water, creosote oil, wet horse-blankets, and the pungent smudge-fires of green alder-bark that the Virginia infantrymen kept burning around their rifle-pits to drive off the flies.

Marcus did not wear his coat. Despite the sixty-degree damp of the July afternoon, his linen shirt was soaked dark with night-sweat between his shoulder-blades, and he held a tin cup of boiled willow-bark and quinine in his left hand while his right thumb kept the place in his calfskin calculation-book.

Wait-times were lengthening. That was the first symptom of decay in an over-extended campaign, and Marcus’s clinical mind noted it with the detached displeasure of a watchmaker listening to a rusted mainspring. In the old days along the Platte or the Potomac, when he had signed a requisition for ten thousand kegs of track-spikes or four hundred mules, the iron had arrived on the flatcars within the hour. Now, every bolt and fish-plate had to be pried loose from the jealous fingers of three rival ministries before it ever reached the ships at Puget Sound.

"Look at these priming-tubes from the Market Street arsenal, Marshal," growled Colonel Armistead, limping up the gravel embankment with a handful of corroded brass friction-primers in his scarred palm. The old Virginian’s face was swollen and lumpy with mosquito-bites beneath his smeared axle-grease. "Half of ’em are filled with sweepings and brick-dust instead of fulminate. Mr. Schuyler’s new civilian contractors in Philadelphia are shaving two cents a hundred off the ordnance contracts and splitting the silver with the Treasury clerks, while Admiral Takashima’s quartermasters down at the beach refused to unload our spare repeating-carbine cases this morning until the ice-breakers had finished landing twelve hundred tons of cut granite for the Satsuma war-memorial on the Diomede rock! If the Protector stays in his sick-bed at San Francisco another month, the bankers and the samurai will have stolen the tires off our caissons before we see a single Russian."

Marcus took a slow sip of the bitter quinine, his sunken gray eyes lifting toward the western ridge where the dwarf-willows gave way to barren ridges of shattered slate. Since the eleven days in Shanghai when Elias had lain behind the locked doors of the Admiralty, the seamless iron unity of the Confederation had begun to hair-crack along every joint. Schuyler’s syndicate directors in San Francisco viewed the Bering Bridge as a bottomless sinkhole that starved their Yangtze cotton-mills of capital; Takashima’s admirals viewed any land-road into Asia as a direct threat to the Japanese Navy’s monopoly over the northern sea-lanes. Both factions were quietly starving Marcus’s vanguard of coal and brass, hoping the Siberian winter would freeze the survey-parties in their tracks and force the old man in the Citadel to abandon the work.

"We do not need the Philadelphia primers for the mortars today, Colonel," Marcus said, his voice a dry, rasping whisper that barely carried over the clang of the Chinese spike-mauls behind the car. "And as for Admiral Takashima’s granite—I had Major Sterling’s sappers dump four hundred blocks of it into the soft bog at the second culvert an hour ago to serve as ballast for our trestle. When the Admiral comes ashore to unveil his monument, he can look for it under my locomotive wheels."

He rose stiffly from the tallow-barrel, suppressing the familiar bubbling rattle in his left lung, and unslung his field-glasses as a solitary horseman in the buckskin shirt of the Nez Perce scouts came galloping hard down the shale ridge a mile ahead, his pony’s hooves kicking up splashes of black peat-water from the bogs.

Behind the scout, crowning the skyline where the trail dipped down toward the Anadyr river-basin, a long, glittering bristle of eight-foot steel-tipped lances rose out of the willow-scrub.

"There is your Russian answer to the mortgage-note, Armistead," Marcus said, bracing his elbows against the iron side of the flatcar as he focused the lenses. "Six sotnias of the Amur Cossacks—about seven hundred saddles. And they have dragged two batteries of bronze nine-pounders up the river-bed on sledges. They are forming line for a charge against the Chinese grading-gangs at the end of the track."

Down at the rail-head four hundred yards away, a shrill cry of terror went up from the unarmed Cantonese coolies as the wild, long-coated horsemen in their tall sheepskin caps came trotting down the slope, the flat blades of their curved *shashka* sabers flashing in the low arctic sun while a Russian bugler sounded the gallop. Several hundred laborers dropped their shovels and bolted backward down the wooden sleepers toward the beach, threatening to swamp the two companies of the First Pennsylvania Auxiliary who were kneeling behind a breastwork of stacked iron rails.

"Shall I pull the coolies back behind the flatcars, General?" Armistead asked, his hand dropping to the holster of his Colt as the Cossack line broke into a dead run across the spongy turf, their shrill, wolfish *Hourrah!* echoing off the basalt hills while the two Russian bronze guns on the ridge opened fire with a dirty puff of white black-powder smoke.

A nine-pound round-shot buried itself with a harmless *thuck* in the frozen peat fifty yards short of the embankment.

"If you let two thousand coolies run through the Pennsylvania line, they will carry the riflemen into the ditch with them," Marcus said, his hand reaching into his coat for his pocket chronometer and clicking open the case. "Tell Captain Rafferty to drop the first ten labourers who cross the ditch with the bayonet; that will turn the rest back to their picks. Then run the locomotive forward fifty yards and open with the two steam-Gatlings from the cupola at four hundred yards’ range. Do not fire at the riders—aim low into the chests of the horses. A dismounted Cossack in high boots three hundred miles from his base is merely a corpse that has not yet lain down."

***

Six days after the Amur Cossacks left three hundred dead ponies and two bronze cannon in the black moss of the Anadyr trail, the mid-July fog lay cold and motionless against the glass dome of the Citadel conservatory in San Francisco.

Inside the steaming, fern-choked vault, the air was eighty-five degrees and smelled of decaying orchid-bark, wet marble, and the bitter herbal smoke of the stramonium leaves that the physicians burned in a silver dish beside Elias’s wicker chair to ease the spasms of his breath. 

The Protector had not gone down to the Council Room since the fleet returned from the north in late June. He sat propped upright among cushions of dark blue horsehair beside the carp-basin, a heavy woolen lap-robe tucked tightly around his shrunken thighs to hide the terrible, watery swelling that had crept up from his ankles to his knees over the past fortnight. On a low redwood table at his right elbow lay the bronze-mounted telegraph repeater connected directly to the St. Petersburg and Irkutsk cable; at his left sat Lady Kaiulani, her black mourning-gown rustling softly as she sorted the afternoon dispatches from the four quarters of the basin.

Before the carp-pool stood Cornelius Schuyler and Rear-Admiral Takashima, summoned from a stormy session of the Joint Supply Board downstairs.

"It is sheer madness to push the rail-head another mile into Chukotka, Protector!" Schuyler was saying, his plump face shining with the wet heat of the conservatory as he mopped his neck with a silk handkerchief. Though he spoke to Elias, his eyes flicked constantly toward Kaiulani’s calm, inscrutable profile, as if seeking to gauge how many weeks of life remained in the grey-faced shell in the wicker chair. "The Rothschilds in Paris and Frankfurt have just refused our new issue of Siberian Bridge debentures following the skirmish on the Anadyr! The Tsar has ordered six army corps from Moscow and Poland to begin marching toward the Urals, and the Russian cruisers at Vladivostok have seized three of our timber-brigs off Sakhalin! If we fight a continental war across five thousand miles of frozen desert to build a road nobody wants, the silver reserve on Market Street will fall below the twenty-percent statutory limit before October!"

"And the Imperial Navy cannot spare another ton of compound armor-plate for Major Sterling’s bridge-caissons, Excellency," Takashima added, his voice stiff with the formal courtesy of Edo, yet carrying an edge of iron defiance that had never been heard in that room while Elias stood on two good legs. "Lord Shimazu wires from Nagasaki that the Russian Baltic Squadron has passed Gibraltar heading for the Cape of Good Hope. My board has therefore suspended the shipment of the forty girder-spans from the Sacramento rolling-mills and diverted the steel to complete the two new turret-rams at Yokosuka. The sea is our wall; let General Vance hold the beach at Cape Prince of Wales with his rifles and leave the Siberian marshes to the wolves."

For ten seconds Elias did not move. Only his broad, bluish-nailed hands, resting upon the wicker arms of the chair, closed slowly until the woven rattan cracked under his knuckles. The stramonium smoke curled past his hollow cheek; beneath his navy wool coat, his enlarged heart beat with a heavy, laboring thud—*one, two, pause, three*—like a crippled donkey-engine trying to haul a forty-ton boiler up a wet grade.

"You diverted my bridge-steel, Admiral?" Elias asked. His voice was scarce louder than the drip of the tree-ferns into the pool, a dry, gravelly scrape at the bottom of his throat.

"By vote of the Joint Naval Commission this morning, Protector," Takashima replied, his chin lifting slightly as he exchanged a swift, sidelong glance with Schuyler. "In view of Your Excellency’s... temporary indisposition, the Commission deemed it necessary to prioritize the defense of the Western Sea."

Elias turned his head half an inch toward Kaiulani. "Give me the wire from Irkutsk."

She lifted the blue slip from her lap and placed it between his fingers. As her dark hand brushed his cold knuckle, her eyes met his—deep, pitiless, and clear as volcanic glass. She had promised him in this very room that she would sit beside his throne and watch his boiler burst; yet as she looked at the banker and the samurai standing like impatient buzzards on the marble flags, she hated the jackals more than she hated the lion.

"General Korsakov at Irkutsk wires in the Tsar’s name," Elias rasped, not looking at the paper he already knew by heart, his pale, sunken eyes locked upon Takashima’s throat. "He offers an armistice along the coast if we dismantle the Diomede caissons before August and pay two million thalers indemnity for the Cossacks Marcus shot in the moss."

"A most reasonable basis for negotiation!" Schuyler cried eagerly, taking half a step forward. "With two million thalers we can stabilize the Frankfurt exchange by Monday, and—"

With a sudden, terrifying convulsion of will that seemed to tear the years and the dropsy from his frame, Elias kicked the woolen lap-robe from his swollen knees, seized the heavy iron walking-stick leaning against the basin, and hauled himself upright onto his feet. Schuyler staggered backward, his plump heel catching against a glazed terracotta fern-pot until the muddy water slopped over his patent-leather shoes. Even Takashima’s hand dropped instinctively to the gold-wrapped hilt of his naval dirk as the tall, skeletal figure towered over the carp-pool, swaying slightly on his pillar-like legs while a dark, congested flush of blood surged up into his weathered cheekbones. For three weeks the Comptroller and the Admiral had met in the cedar-paneled smoking room of the Union Club down on Montgomery Street, dividing the post-Thorne world over glasses of dry Madeira: the Eastern banking syndicate would take back the Atlantic customs-houses and sell the Yukon mines to a joint-stock company in London, while the Satsuma Navy would sever the northern bridge-head and keep the Yellow Sea as a private fief of the Tenno. They had calculated the dosage of his digitalis; they had bribed his body-servant to count the wet handkerchiefs in his laundry-basket; they had measured the water in his ankles to the eighth of an inch. Yet they had forgotten that a dying wolf with its spine against the rock still has the jaw-strength to snap a hound’s neck before the light leaves its eyes. "If a single girder-span is missing from the Sitka freight-steamer when the tide turns at six o’clock tonight, Takashima," Elias roared, the old frontier thunder breaking through the fluid in his chest like a twelve-pounder bursting through a plank door, "I will have Marshal Vance march a battalion of Virginia riflemen into the Japanese compound on Rincon Hill and hang every member of your Naval Board from the telegraph poles by their own silk sashes! And if you mention the Frankfurt exchange in my hearing again before the bridge is bolted to the Siberian rock, Mr. Schuyler, I will strip your coat off your back and send you up the Chilkoot chute with seventy pounds of pig-iron chained to your spine!" He struck the tessellated marble floor with the ferrule of his iron stick—a sharp crack that cracked a square of green serpentine in half and sent the golden carp flashing into the dark weeds at the bottom of the pool—and pointed his trembling left hand at the bronze telegraph key on the table. "Sit down at that key, Kaiulani," Elias commanded, his breath whistling through his teeth like wind through a keyhole as he leaned his weight hard upon the stick, refusing to sink back into the cushions while their eyes were upon him. "Clear the line through the Bering cable to Irkutsk and the Winter Palace. Tell the Russian operators to take this down in plain French so every clerk from Lake Baikal to the Neva can read it before supper." Kaiulani slid onto the velvet stool before the repeater. She did not hurry, nor did she look at the two men standing frozen beside the ferns; her black-gloved fingers closed over the vulcanite knob with a sharp, metallic click as the circuit opened. "From Thorne, Providentor of the Grand Confederation, to Alexander Romanov at St. Petersburg," Elias dictated, his gaze sweeping from the blanched, sweating jowls of the New York banker to the rigid brow of the Satsuma admiral as the armature began to chatter in the damp heat of the conservatory. "You sold me the threshold of the North, and no man locks the door in my face after I have paid the silver. My engineers are laying two miles of broad-gauge iron a day toward the valley of the Lena. If the gates of Siberia are not opened to my surveyors from the Strait to Lake Baikal before the first snow falls on the Stanovoy mountains, I will not wait for your six corps to walk across the Urals. I will put two hundred thousand American and Japanese rifles across the Bering piers before the ice breaks, burn Irkutsk to the ground, and water my horses in the Obi. Send that first, Kaiulani—and then keep the circuit open to the northern fleet." *** To the Chronicler who has stood upon the basalt heights of East Cape during that breathless, sun-bleached August of 1869, the mobilization of the Pacifica Armada in the waters of the Bering Strait presented a spectacle that belonged less to the annals of human seamanship than to the nightmare of a mechanized Titan. For ten thousand years, those fifty-three miles of racing green water between the continents had known only the skin-covered kayaks of the Chukchi hunters and the occasional grease-stained topsails of a New Bedford whaling-bark dodging the summer pack-ice. Now, the roof of the world was black with iron and sour with the breath of a hundred furnaces. Because the Providentor knew in the secret arithmetic of his own failing arteries that his empire would fracture into three warring succession-states the morning after his funeral unless the army and the fleet were locked together in the vise of an irreversible foreign campaign, he had emptied every slip from Puget Sound to Nagasaki into the northern funnel. Between the granite tables of the Diomede Islands and the gravel beaches of Chukotka rode forty-six ocean-going vessels of war and eighty-two iron-hulled colliers, cable-layers, and troop-transports, moored in six parallel lines five miles long against the six-knot tide-race. The arctic air, which in August should have carried only the clean, sharp tang of snow-melt and wet lichen, hung low and suffocating over the strait in a greasy yellow-gray canopy of burned Nanaimo coal-soot, boiled whale-oil lubricant, and the sulfurous fumes of the floating foundry-hulks. Day and night, beneath a sun that never dipped more than four degrees below the northern horizon, the sea vibrated with the relentless, sub-aqueous thrum of steam-condensers and pneumatic air-pumps. Along the three-mile line of the eastern bridge-way, twenty-eight cylindrical caissons of bolted San Francisco boiler-plate—each forty feet in diameter and filled with two thousand tons of Sierra granite rubble and Portland cement—already rose like a row of decapitated black towers out of the churning white water. Between them, monster floating sheer-legs mounted on double-hulled iron pontoons groaned and shrieked as their wire cables hoisted three-hundred-foot spans of lattice-steel girder into the freezing mist, while swarms of Cantonese and Irish riveters clung like black beetles to the swinging iron sixty feet above the waves, their red-hot portable forges dropping showers of orange sparks that hissed out in the frigid swells below. And through the narrow channels between the bridge-piers steamed the vanguard of the invasion: twenty-two shallow-draft armored rams and turret-monitors of the *Sacramento* and *Kamehameha* classes, their low steel decks piled high with bags of Welsh and Vancouver anthracite to save bunker-space, their sixteen-inch Krupp and Rodman gun-barrels coated thick with white tallow-lead to keep out the arctic salt-rime. Aboard the eighty troop-liners, sixty thousand men sat packed between the iron bulkheads—veterans of the Potomac and the Shenandoah who had grown grey in the Pacifica blue, flanked by entire divisions of Choshu and Satsuma infantry whose regimental priests burned aloeswood before brass mirrors bolted to the ships’ mainmasts, and regiments of Hawaiian pioneers who sang the sad, rhythmic canoe-chants of Oahu while they sharpened eighteen-inch trowel-bayonets on grindstones turned by steam-belts. It was an engine of such monstrous, unnatural weight that it seemed to press the very crust of the earth downward into the polar sea; yet to the officers who walked the ice-slicked bridge-wings with their collars turned up against the sleet, every rattle of the anchor-chains carried the same unspoken terror: that the old man in the glass house three thousand miles to the south might stop breathing before the first gun was fired, leaving sixty thousand armed men of four races trapped together in an iron cage at the end of the world. *** In San Francisco, Elias had refused to return to his bedchamber. For four days and nights following the scene by the carp-pool, he had lived inside the high-arched Map Room on the fourth floor of the Chancery, having an iron camp-cot—the same narrow frame of bolted gas-pipe he had slept upon before the walls of Vicksburg—set up directly beneath the thirty-foot bronze relief-chart of the Pacific Basin. The room smelled no longer of clean beeswax and salt wind; it was thick and sour with the odors of a dying sickroom: camphor-liniment, burnt stramonium weed, cold mutton-broth, and the sharp ammonia that the surgeons used when the fluid in his pleura threatened to choke him at three in the morning. Yet he wore his dark blue Engineer’s tunic buttoned to the third hook, and his heavy cavalry boots remained laced over his swollen calves—for he knew that once the boots were cut off his feet, he would never get them on again, and a Caesar in bedroom slippers was already half a corpse in the eyes of his marshals. On the afternoon of the twelfth of August, the yellow summer fog pressed blind against the tall western casements. Around the green baize table sat the four heirs of the realm, summoned to watch him move the iron across the board: Kaiulani at the telegraph desk, her black bombazine skirts hiding the small Derringer pistol she now carried in her reticule against the afternoon when Takashima’s marines or Schuyler’s provosts might try to seize the wire-room; Cornelius Schuyler at the foot, his ledger-books open though his pale eyes never left the purple, distended vein pulsing in Elias’s neck; Rear-Admiral Takashima standing rigid beside the Japanese coast-charts; and Major Sterling at the speaking-tube. Elias sat on the edge of the iron camp-cot, his scarred hands resting upon the cross-piece of his iron walking-stick between his knees. Every breath he drew sounded in the quiet room like a dry brush being dragged across sandpaper. "General Korsakov has burned the timber-depots at Anadyrsk and pulled his Cossacks back behind the Kolyma range," Elias said. He spoke slowly, rationing his wind as a desert scout rations water from a canteen, yet his pale gaze was clear and sharp as flint. "He thinks because the tundra is five hundred miles wide and the frost begins in twenty days, he can draw Marshal Vance’s locomotives into the bogs and let January fight his battle for him, the way his grandfather did to Bonaparte at Moscow." "It is the traditional strategy of the Russian War Ministry, Protector," Takashima said cautiously, stepping half a pace toward the bronze wall. "And General Vance’s own medical chief wired from the Strait yesterday that the Marshal is coughing blood twice a day and has to be lifted onto his flatcar by two orderlies. If our columns march inland from the Bering beach into forty-below cold while their commander is dying on a stretcher, the Siberian winter will swallow forty thousand men without Korsakov firing a cannon." "We are not going to march five hundred miles across the moss after Cossack ponies, Admiral," Elias rasped, a grim, grey smile twitching at the corner of his mouth. "You and Mr. Schuyler have been hoping for three weeks that I had gone soft in the head with the dropsy and would bury the Legion in the Chukotka snow so you could divide the treasury at your leisure in December. Stand up to the map, Sterling." Major Sterling stepped onto the low iron stool before the left-hand plates of the bronze wall, holding a long brass pointer tipped with a magnet. "Bonaparte walked into Russia by the front door across the Niemen because he had no ships," Elias said, lifting his iron stick two inches from the parquet floor and pointing it not at the Bering Strait at the top of the chart, but fifteen hundred miles southward down the jagged, fog-bound coast of the Sea of Okhotsk and the Tartar Strait, to the long, narrow horn of rock that curved around the Golden Horn Bay at the forty-third parallel. "The Tsar’s back door has only one hinge. Move the fourth and fifth divisions from the Strait to Hakodate, Sterling. Put the *Prometheus* and the twelve heavy turret-ships through the Tsugaru channel at full steam." Takashima’s bronze cheek twitched. "Vladivostok, Protector? The Russian batteries on Cape Egersheld and Gold Horn Bay mount sixty-four rifled steel Krupp guns that they sledged down the Amur last winter! And if you place a Pacifica garrison at the mouth of the Ussuri, sixty leagues from the Korean border, the Privy Council at Edo will view it as an infringement upon the northern sphere promised to the Tenno in the treaty of March!" "The Tenno will take what I give him after my guns have broken the gate, not before," Elias said, his voice hardening as he leaned forward on his stick, forcing the Satsuma officer to drop his eyes. "And as for Marshal Vance—if Marcus has only thirty days of breath left in his lungs, he will not spend them sitting in a tent on the Anadyr watching Cantonese coolies shovel mud. I have wired him to leave Colonel Armistead with ten thousand men to bolt the bridge-spans together through the winter, and to take the main battle-fleet south himself. If we take Vladivostok and the Amur mouth before September, Korsakov’s army in Siberia is cut off from the sea, and the whole Russian Pacific coast falls into our lap like a rotten plum. Kaiulani—read the Marshal’s acknowledgment from the *Prometheus*." Beside the repeater, Lady Kaiulani lifted a strip of blue paper from the brass basket. As she looked across the green baize at Takashima and Schuyler, she knew that by sending Marcus Vance two thousand miles south into the cannon’s mouth at Vladivostok, Elias was stripping himself of the only loyal sword that could keep these two jackals from his throat if his heart stopped before the equinox; yet she read the words in a voice as clear and cold as a temple bell: "*'From Vance, Commanding Expeditionary Force aboard flagship Prometheus off Kurile Islands, twelfth August: Fleet cleared Tsugaru Strait at four this morning in dense fog. My lungs are sufficient for the tonnage required. We shall be off the Golden Horn at daybreak on the fifteenth, and I will place the keys of the Russian citadel on the Protector’s desk before the first frost.'*" *** Seventy-two hours later, at five o’clock on the morning of the fifteenth of August, a wet, impenetrable sea-fog lay rolled like greasy sheepskin wool across the Peter the Great Gulf, hiding the steep, oak-forested hills of the Muravyov-Amursky Peninsula and the green-painted iron roofs of Vladivostok inside a gray twilight that smelled of rotting sea-kelp and cold mud. Yet four miles southwest of the rocky promontory of Cape Egersheld—outside the waters of the Eastern Bosphorus, in the open sea beyond the stony spine of Russky Island—there was no silence. In a curved, two-mile arc anchored bow-and-stern with heavy kedge-cables to prevent the current from swinging their hulls a single degree off the compass-mark, rode eight monstrous, flat-decked iron vessels that looked less like ships of war than floating brick-kilns. They were the new *Vulcan*-class steam-bombardment monitors, built in secret behind the high board fences of the Mare Island yard during the winter after the Manila campaign, and brought across the northern circle under tow. They carried no masts, no yards, and no broadside casemates. Amidships of each vessel’s four-thousand-ton cellular hull rose a single, fixed oval citadel of fourteen-inch compound steel armor, out of whose slotted roof protruded the stubby, gaping muzzles of twin twenty-inch rifled breech-loading steam-mortars—weapons cast at the Potrero Point works around an inner tube of compressed Essen steel, loaded not by human muscle, which could never have lifted their twelve-hundred-pound conical shells, but by telescopic hydraulic rams driven directly from the ships’ main boilers at three hundred pounds of pressure to the square inch. Inside the armored conning-tower of the flagship *Prometheus*, anchored five hundred yards to the rear of the mortar-line, General Marcus Vance sat propped in a high wooden barber’s chair that the ship’s carpenters had bolted directly to the steel deck-plates around the periscope-slit so that the Marshal could observe the range-buoys without standing on his trembling legs. The narrow iron chamber was ninety degrees from the heat of the engine-room uptakes directly aft, and reeked of carbolic acid, hot cylinder-oil, and the dark, sweetish smell of blood. Marcus wore his navy wool coat buttoned over a flannel chest-protector soaked in turpentine; across his knees lay his waterproofed calculation-book and his Geneva chronometer, while beside his right boot stood a porcelain spittoon half-filled with crimson-streaked sawdust. He had not slept since passing the La Pérouse Strait two nights ago. His face in the yellow light of the binnacle-lamp was the color of bleached bone, the skin stretched so tight over his cheekbones and the bridge of his nose that he looked like a skull wearing a peaked military cap; yet the gray eyes squinting through the brass binocular-tubes bolted to the vision-slit were as steady and pitiless as a surveyor’s transit. "The tethered balloon from the tender *Shasta* has reached twelve hundred feet above the fog-bank, Marshal," reported Major Sterling, standing beside the speaking-tubes with a pair of electric ear-phones strapped over his temples, connected by an insulated copper wire that ran up through the conning-tower roof to the silk observation-gasbag floating in the clear sunlight above the mist. "Lieutenant Mordecai in the basket reports the Russian coastal batteries on Cape Goldobina and the Egersheld point have their gun-crews sleeping beside their pieces under tarpaulins. Admiral Erdmann’s four wooden corvettes are moored bow-to-stern inside the Golden Horn right below the Governor’s magazine. They cannot see a yard through the sea-smoke on the water, and their lookouts are facing the eastern channel—they have no idea

an enemy ship is within twenty leagues of the coast, let alone anchored behind the island with two miles of rock between us and their guns." Marcus lifted a folded white linen handkerchief to his lips, coughed once—a wet, tearing sound deep in his chest that made his lean shoulders jerk against the leather straps of the barber’s chair—and dropped the stained cloth into the spittoon at his feet before his fingers closed upon his pencil. "They fortified the narrows on the assumption that a fleet must see a fort in order to shoot at it, Sterling," Marcus whispered, his voice reduced by the tubercular ulcers in his throat to a harsh, metallic rasp that barely carried to the speaking-tube six inches from his chin. "That is the error of gentlemen who learned their mathematics before the telegraph was married to the mortar. A gun does not need eyes when a man in a silk bag twelve hundred feet in the air has a copper wire and a triangulation table. What is the wind-drift at a thousand feet?" "Four knots from the south-southeast, sir," Sterling answered, reading the needle on the brass dial before him. "And the barometric pressure is thirty point one-two." Marcus’s pencil scratched three rapid logarithms across the damp page of his book, converting the triangle between the invisible target beyond the forested hills of Russky Island, the balloon in the sky, and the anchored monitors into degrees of arc and pounds of nitro-cellulose powder. "Signal the mortar flotilla by the underwater cable," Marcus ordered, his bony thumb pressing the stem of his chronometer as he leaned his forehead against the cold iron brow-pad of the vision-slit. "Ships one through four: azimuth thirty-four degrees twelve minutes east, elevation fifty-two degrees. Ships five through eight: azimuth thirty-six degrees four minutes, elevation fifty-one and one-half. Charge: one hundred and eighty pounds of prismatic cocoa-powder; fuse: delayed percussion with four hundred pounds of wet guncotton bursting-charge in the core. Do not fire at the water-batteries on the cape—let the Russian gunners sit by their cannon and watch the sky fall on their backs. Put the first salvo straight over the mountain ridge into the main powder-magazine and the foundry slips at the head of the Golden Horn, four miles inland." Down on the wet steel decks of the eight *Vulcan* monitors, red electric lamps blinked once inside the armored turrets. Steam-valves hissed violently; the massive bronze hydraulic rams shoved eight six-foot cones of forged steel—each taller than a man and packed with enough high explosive to level a city block—into the rifled chambers of the twenty-inch monsters; the heavy screw-breeches swung shut and locked with the dull, greasy *thud* of a bank-vault closing; and at the drop of the Marshal’s thin white hand in the conning-tower of the *Prometheus*, Major Sterling pressed the brass firing-key on the bulkhead. Eight mortars did not fire in a ragged broadside; fired by a single galvanic spark from the flagship’s battery, they erupted as one volcano.

***

Yet the volcano at the mouth of the Golden Horn was only the southern hammer-stroke; three weeks later, in the bleak, bone-chilling dawn of September, the true testing-ground of Elias Thorne’s providence remained the fifty-three miles of racing green water at the sixty-sixth parallel. He had refused to wait in the warm conservatory on Mason Street while other men bolted his monument together. If the factions in the Diet believed him a dying invalid propped on horsehair pillows, he would give them an answer written in five-inch rivets above the Arctic tide.

Elias stepped down from the platform of the armored inspection-car at the tip of the Cape Prince of Wales masonry abutment, leaning his weight upon the heavy iron walking-stick he had brought from San Francisco. Beneath his wide-soled boots—cut twice down the leather seams by his valet that morning to accommodate the bruised, watery swelling of his ankles—stretched the first completed mile of the Bering Bridge.

It was not a bridge as the engineers of London or New York understood the word. It was a colossal rectangular tunnel of black-painted Bessemer plate and open lattice-girders, thirty feet wide and twenty-four feet high, resting eighty feet above the white-maned rollers of the strait upon twin rows of forty-foot cylindrical piers filled with Sierra granite and Portland cement. Through the four-inch gaps between the creosoted Oregon fir cross-ties, Elias could look straight down into the boiling emerald vortex where the waters of the Pacific met the Polar Sea. The wind coming out of the Chukchi fog did not whistle through the ironwork; it struck the four-thousand-ton steel trusses like a continuous battery of solid shot, making the entire mile-long cantilever hum with a deep, subterranean bass note that vibrated up through the ferrule of his stick and straight into his congested ribs.

Behind him, huddled together on the narrow timber catwalk bolted between the broad-gauge tracks, came the three predators who waited for his boots to empty: Cornelius Schuyler, wrapped in a triple-caped sealskin ulster with a fur muffler tied over his ears; Rear-Admiral Takashima, his Satsuma face pinched blue-gray by the twenty-degree gale; and Lady Kaiulani, her black mourning-cloak snapping behind her shoulders like the wings of a raven against the low, grease-colored sky.

"Fourteen piers set into the bedrock since the July thaw, Protector," Schuyler shouted against the roar of the wind and the ear-splitting *rat-tat-tat-tat* of the pneumatic riveting-guns working inside the smoky iron womb of the fifth span ahead. The banker’s teeth were chattering so violently he could barely form the syllables, and his plump hands clung with white-knuckled terror to the vibrating wire guide-rope as a sheet of freezing salt-spume broke over the lower caisson-skirts fifty feet below and showered the track with sleet. "And every pier has cost the Treasury four hundred thousand thalers and thirty dead coolies! The diver-crews in the pneumatic bells below the mud-line are coming up paralyzed with the caisson-sickness six at a time! If we do not suspend the riveting before the October pack-ice comes down from Wrangell Land, the floes will shear our floating derricks from their anchors and sink two million thalers of machinery in thirty fathoms!"

Elias did not turn his head, nor did he touch the wire guide-rope. He walked slowly forward down the center of the six-foot gauge, planting the iron stick squarely upon every third cross-tie to mask the heavy, dragging numbness in his left leg. The air inside the lattice-truss was thick with the acrid smoke of the portable coke-forges where Irish boys heated the nine-inch steel rivets to cherry-red, mixing with the reek of hot whale-oil lubricant and the sharp, salty breath of the sea below.

"When the floating derricks are crushed by the ice, Mr. Schuyler," Elias said, his rough, low voice cutting through the metallic hum of the girders around them as he paused beside a gang of Cantonese riveters who dropped to their knees on the icy ties as his shadow fell across their forge, "we will lay the rails out to the end of the twelfth span, roll the fifty-ton travelling cranes out upon the completed iron itself, and swing the next girders straight forward into the air from the nose of the track. A bridge that waits for summer weather in this latitude will never reach the Diomedes."

"And who will pay the iron-founders at Sacramento when the spring comes, Excellency?" Takashima asked, stepping abreast of Schuyler on the narrow planking, his dark eyes fixed upon the purple, laboring pulse in the hollow of Elias’s throat. "Marshal Vance has taken Vladivostok, yes—at the cost of six thousand shells and two burned-out mortar tubes. Yet General Korsakov did not surrender when the port fell. He has retreated westward up the valley of the Amur and the Shilka toward Lake Baikal, tearing up the post-roads and burning every village behind him. Now the Marshal demands that we ship twenty locomotives and forty thousand tons of coal up the frozen Tartar Strait to Nikolayevsk so he can chase the Russians into the heart of Asia before December! My naval board has voted this morning that the fleet cannot risk its screws in the Okhotsk ice-pack to feed a winter land-campaign two thousand miles from salt water."

Elias stopped dead at the extreme seaward lip of the fifth span. Ten paces ahead of his boots, the wooden cross-ties ended over sheer, dizzying emptiness; only two naked sixty-foot steel I-beams projected out into the swirling gray mist like the jaws of an open vise, waiting for the floor-plates to be hoisted from the pitching barge below.

He turned slowly around on the wet timber, facing the three of them in the narrow iron cage suspended between the sky and the water. The pain behind his breastbone was a dull, red-hot bar of pig-iron pressed against his spine; every fourth heartbeat missed its stroke, leaving a black hollow in his chest that made the cold sleet on his face feel warm by comparison. Yet as he looked at Takashima and Schuyler, huddled against the wind while he stood unbraced at the edge of the abyss, a fierce, pitiless contempt gave his voice the weight of granite.

"Your naval board voted," Elias said softly.

"In consultation with the Treasury Committee, Protector," Schuyler put in quickly, though he took half a step backward along the catwalk, his heel striking a bucket of cold bolts. "The interest on the Eastern Receivership bonds falls due on the first of November. If we pour another thirty millions into Marshal Vance’s Siberian adventure while the winter closes the rivers, the counting-houses in New York and Osaka will refuse our paper! We must consolidate! We must digest what we have taken—"

"You are not consolidators, Mr. Schuyler. You are buzzards waiting on a fence-rail," Elias said. He did not shout; he let the howling wind off the Diomedes carry his words back down the iron tunnel of the bridge.
