"You think because my legs are swollen with water and Marcus is spitting his lungs into a bucket, you can starve his regiments in the Siberian snow this winter, let the Russians cut his throat at Baikal, and then come home to San Francisco to divide the carcass between the counting-house and the quarterdeck."

Beside the girders, Lady Kaiulani’s dark eyes shifted from Elias’s gray face to the Satsuma admiral’s hand. "Be careful, Admiral," she murmured in her clear, clinical voice, her right hand resting inside the warm fur muff where her fingers touched the cold steel trigger of her Derringer. "A bridge has no bulwarks, and the water below is very deep for a man in heavy boots."

Elias took one step back from the open gulf and struck the eighty-pound steel rail at his feet with his iron cane.

"Hear me, both of you," Elias rasped, his gaze locking them to the planks. "I built this empire out of Kentucky ash and Sierra quartz before Mr. Schuyler ever saw a gold thaler or Admiral Takashima ever looked through the breech of a rifled gun. This iron under your shoes is my bone. The wire running through that lead pipe is my nerve. So long as I sit in the chair—whether I sit with boots on my feet or propped in a coffin with a glass front—every bolt goes into this bridge, and every ton of coal Marcus asks for goes up the Amur before the ice locks the bar. If a single collier is held back at Nagasaki this week, I will not convene a council. I will appoint Lady Kaiulani Sole Regent of the Treasury and the Fleet with power of drumhead execution, and her Hawaiian guards will drop both of you through that tie-gap into the strait before the tide turns. Walk back to the car, gentlemen, and sign the Nikolayevsk coal-warrants while my hand is still warm enough to hold the seal."

***

To the Chronicler who seeks to measure the hubris of mortal princes against the ancient, unyielding hostility of the earth, the winter march of the Pacifica Expeditionary Force from the waters of the Amur to the frozen inland sea of Baikal must ever stand as the supreme tragedy of the mechanical age. When Xerxes whipped the Hellespont with iron chains, or when the Corsican drove his half-million Europeans across the Niemen into the summer dust of Lithuania, they contended against distance with the muscles of horses and the leather soles of marching men. Marshal Marcus Vance attempted a thing more terrible and more unnatural: he endeavored to drag the entire roaring, coal-eating industrial carcass of the nineteenth century across two thousand miles of sub-arctic wilderness at forty degrees below zero.

Through the late autumn months of October and November, before the black frost sealed the rivers to the bedrock, sixty shallow-draft stern-wheelers and iron barges brought over from the Sacramento and the Yangtze had fought their way up the turbid, snag-choked current of the Amur and its tributary the Shilka, landing thirty-five thousand veterans of the Atlantic Auxiliary and the Satsuma Infantry at the old Russian convict-depot of Stretensk. From that point westward across the Yablonoi Mountains to Chita and the shores of Lake Baikal, there was no river and there was no railroad—only the Great Siberian Post-Track, a rutted swath of frozen mud and birch-forest across which the Tsar’s couriers had ridden for two centuries.

Upon that frozen mire, Marcus Vance let loose the iron monsters of Clark’s Point.

History has preserved in the war-museums of Monterey the surviving specimens of the thirty *Mammoth*-class steam-traction locomotives that led the vanguard over the Yablonoi pass: forty-ton behemoths encased in half-inch boiler-plate, running not upon rails, but upon eight-foot wide iron wheels fitted with spiked steel cleats and preceded by revolving steam-plows designed to chew through six-foot snowdrifts. Behind each machine clanked a train of twelve iron-wheeled wagons carrying four-inch Krupp field-guns, portable telegraph dynamos, barrels of Santa Paula rock-oil, and the standardized rations of dried San Joaquin beef and compressed bean-cake.

For the first hundred leagues, while the mercury lingered near zero, the geometry of San Francisco seemed to triumph over the steppe. The great traction-engines ground over the frozen ruts at three miles an hour, their tall smokestacks belching pillars of greasy black petroleum-soot across the virgin snows of the taiga, while Cantonese linemen unreeled bare copper telegraph wire directly onto the ice beside the road—needing neither poles nor glass insulators, for the dry, bone-hard snow of the Siberian winter was itself a non-conductor that carried the Protector’s spark unbroken back to the sea.

And then, in the second week of December, the sky cleared to a dome of dark, pitiless imperial blue, the wind died altogether, and the real cold came down out of the pole.

It was not the blustering, windy snow-gale that Elias and Caleb Vance had survived inside the mule’s ribs on the Platte thirty-two years before. It was a vast, crystalline stillness in which the spirit of the thermometer shrank down into the bulb at fifty-two degrees below zero, and nature itself declared war upon the chemistry of iron. 

Under that terrible, soundless pressure, the molecular structure of forged steel changed as if bewitched. The eighty-pound Krupp gun-barrels and the solid wrought-iron axles of the traction-engines grew brittle as Venetian glass; when an artillery wheel struck a frozen boulder in the road, or a sapper struck a steel crowbar with a sledgehammer to clear a trench, the metal did not bend—it shattered into three pieces with a sharp report like a pistol shot. In the feed-pipes of the traction-locomotives, the hot water froze solid between the tender-tank and the injector-valve within three feet of the roaring firebox; if a stoker stopped the donkey-pump for ninety seconds to clear a clinker from the grate, the cast-iron cylinder-head split from end to end with the boom of a bomb, enveloping the crew in a cloud of scalding vapor that fell back upon their coats ten seconds later as a crust of solid white ice.

The very air became an enemy to the lungs of men bred by the Chesapeake or the warm lagoons of Kyushu. A breath drawn too deeply through the open mouth seared the bronchial tubes like a draft of boiling vinegar; the moisture of the eyeballs froze the lashes together; and any soldier who touched the brass breech-block of his Sacramento needle-rifle with a bare thumb left a square inch of living skin welded instantly to the metal. 

Along three hundred miles of white forest between Chita and the Selenga valley, the relentless mechanical march slowed to a spectral crawl through a frozen hell. When the mineral lubricating-oil in the wheel-hubs congealed into hard tallow that resisted the steam-jets, entire battalions of Virginia and Pennsylvania veterans—men wrapped in four layers of tattered wool blankets, raw sheepskins stripped from dead Russian cattle, and straw bound around their boots with telegraph wire—were harnessed by fifties to drag the stalled artillery-sledges through the drifts by main strength. Behind them, in the two-mile wake of blackened snow and spilled coal-cinders, the road was marked no longer by milestones, but by the rigid, frost-whitened carcasses of draft-mules and the crouching figures of Cantonese coolies and Japanese infantrymen who had sat down beside the track for three minutes to adjust a boot-strap and never risen again, frozen into statues of blue marble before the rear-guard ambulances could reach them.

***

By the afternoon of the twenty-first of December—the winter solstice, when the sun above the fifty-second parallel barely lifted its dull, copper-red rim over the snow-choked pines of the Khamar-Daban range before sinking back into the creeping violet twilight—the head of that bleeding iron snake reached the eastern shore of Lake Baikal.

Here the forest ended against a sheer rampart of black granite cliffs, and before the column stretched the Sacred Sea of the Tartars: four hundred miles of fresh water frozen to a depth of six feet into a single, blinding floor of greenish-black mirror-ice, seamed with jagged pressure-ridges ten feet high that groaned and boomed through the twilight with the sound of subterranean artillery as the deep water shifted beneath the frost.

General Marcus Vance did not ride a horse; the last of his California mounts had died of frozen lungs at Verkhne-Udinsk four days prior. He lay propped at a forty-five-degree angle inside a narrow box-sledge mounted on steel runners and towed directly behind the surviving flagship of his land-fleet, the forty-ton armored traction-engine *Sierra*. The sledge was roofed with bolted boiler-plate and heated by a flexible copper steam-pipe bled off the locomotive’s main dome, filling the cramped three-by-six coffin with a wet, ninety-degree stench of leaking cylinder-tallow, carbolic acid, and the rotting tissue of the Marshal’s own left lung.

Through the three-inch slot in the front iron plate, which Major Sterling kept clear of rime by scraping it every two minutes with a bone-handled knife, Marcus looked out across the vast, twilight-purple plain of the frozen lake toward the western shore forty miles away, where the road to Irkutsk climbed the timbered gorge of the Angara.

Two miles out from the gravel beach, directly astride the sled-track that the Russian tea-caravans had used for a hundred years, General Korsakov had built his wall.

It was not a fortress of brick or earth, which could not be dug in fifty-below frost. The Russians had sawed ten thousand three-foot blocks of solid blue lake-ice from the pressure-cracks, stacked them into a continuous crenellated rampart twelve feet high and a mile long between two rocky ice-bound islets, and poured water over the joints until the whole barrier had frozen into a single seamless monolith of living glacier that turned four-inch rifled shells as if they were snowballs. Behind that crystal breastwork waited eighteen thousand Siberian Riflemen in white sheepskin *tulups* and forty heavy bronze siege-cannon dragged out from the Irkutsk arsenals.

"Colonel Armistead reports the Second Virginia and the Choshu Brigade are deployed behind the first pressure-ridge at eight hundred yards, Marshal," Major Sterling said, crouching on his heels beside the sledge-runner with the field-telegraph box between his frost-blackened mittens. Sterling’s left ear was gone, amputated by the surgeon at Chita after the November gale, and a dirty linen bandage was frozen stiff to the side of his skull. "The ice under the *Sierra*’s wheels is sixty-four inches thick by the auger-borings, sir, and ringing like a bell. If we bring the four remaining traction-rams out onto the lake abreast, the weight may hold—but the firing-pins on thirty percent of the men’s needle-rifles are snapping off at the first pull from the cold, and the glycerine in the recoil-cylinders of the Krupp guns has frozen solid since noon. We have to heat the gun-breeches with kerosene-torches before every shot."

Inside the iron box, Marcus did not turn his head from the vision-slit. His skeletal hands, protruding from the sleeves of a wolf-skin coat that was three sizes too large for his wasted frame, rested upon the waterproofed pages of his ledger, where the columns of figures were spotted with dark brown circles of dried blood. His breath came in shallow, whistling gasps—*forty-two to the minute*, he had timed them himself by the Geneva watch hanging from the bolt before his nose—and he knew with mathematical certainty that before the sun rose again over the Manchurian mountains behind him, the last usable air-sacs in his right lung would fill with fluid.

Yet if he halted here on the eastern beach to wait for spring, the word of his repulse would flash back along the copper wire lying in the snow all the way to the Bering Strait and San Francisco within four hours. By noon tomorrow, Cornelius Schuyler would close the Market Street Mint, Takashima’s cruisers would steam out of the Golden Gate to seize Honolulu for the Tenno, and Elias Thorne would die alone in a partitioned village while the vultures tore his maps in half.

"A gun whose recoil-cylinder is frozen is simply a rigid mortar, Major," Marcus whispered, the words rattling like dry pebbles in a tin cup as he lifted his pencil with two blue-nailed fingers and wrote a single three-digit number on the page. "And a rifle whose firing-pin snaps at eight hundred yards still has eighteen inches of cold San Francisco steel fixed to the muzzle. How many gallons of Santa Paula rock-oil remain in the tank-sledges behind the *Sierra* and the *Shasta*?"

"Twelve hundred gallons, General," Sterling answered, squinting through the stinging ice-fog as a battery of Russian twenty-four-pounders atop the glacier-wall two miles away flashed dull orange in the purple gloom, sending four solid cast-iron balls howling and skipping across the polished black ice like monstrous curling-stones; one of them struck a pressure-hummock fifty yards ahead of the locomotive, exploding the four-foot ice-crest into a blinding geyser of diamond-sharp splinters that rattled against the sledge’s armor-plate.

"Solid ice does not shatter under point-detonation because it yields and freezes again," Marcus rasped, his sunken eyes gleaming in the reflection of the binnacle-lamp as he coughed a mouthful of bright scarlet onto the wolf-skin lap-robe and did not bother to wipe it away. "Therefore we will not shoot at their ice-wall with shells, Sterling. We will melt the floor out from under their boots. Order the four traction-engines to disconnect their supply-trains and couple the oil-tankers directly behind their fireboxes. Turn the high-pressure steam-coils into the oil-vats to heat the petroleum to boiling, and advance the four machines in line abreast at full throttle straight across the open lake against the center of the Russian glacier. Behind each engine, put two battalions of the Virginia and Choshu infantry in column of platoons—unloaded rifles, bayonets fixed, no cheering—using the iron hulls as moving shields against their grape-shot."

Sterling stared through the vision-slit at the two miles of glass-smooth black ice, swept clean of snow by the wind and already crisscrossed by the white tracks of bouncing Russian cannonballs. "Marshal, at three hundred yards their heavy bronze pieces will punch right through half-inch boiler-plate! And if we pump boiling rock-oil onto six-foot lake ice and set it afire with shell—"

"It will burn at two thousand degrees across ten acres of the ditch, crack the ice-sheet under the weight of their own cannon, and drop General Korsakov’s center straight into three hundred fathoms of freezing water," Marcus said, his bony hand reaching up to pull the brass whistle-cord that connected his sledge to the cab of the *Sierra* above him. "And if the ice cracks beneath our own cleats as well, Major, then we shall see whether a Virginian or a Siberian sinks faster in fresh water. Pull the lanyard."

The whistle did not shriek; the fifty-below frost choked the brass throat into a hoarse, strangling roar that was instantly swallowed by the grinding of the eight-foot spiked wheels biting into the dark mirror of the lake. 

Inside the towed iron coffin, the vibration was terrible. Every spike of the *Sierra*’s treads transmitted the deep, booming groan of the stressed lake-ice straight through the steel runners into Marcus’s rotting spine. Behind the four advancing behemoths, four thousand men walked in lock-step through the violet twilight, their faces wrapped in bloody sheepskin rags, their breath rising in four parallel walls of frozen white fog that hid the stars. There was no drum, no bugle, no battle-cry—only the wheezing pant of the steam-cylinders and the continuous, ringing *spang-crunch* of four thousand pairs of iron-cramponed boots striking the black glass.

At six hundred yards, the entire mile-long crest of Korsakov’s glacier-wall erupted in a single, rolling sheet of yellow black-powder flame. 

Forty heavy bronze guns spoke together. To the right of the *Sierra*, a twenty-four-pound solid shot struck the forward boiler-casing of the traction-engine *Tahoe* dead center. In the brittle, sub-arctic cold, the wrought-iron plates did not dent; they burst inward like an eggshell struck with a spoon. A geyser of roaring, superheated steam and white-hot anthracite coals exploded fifty feet into the freezing air, instantly scalding the thirty Choshu infantrymen of the leading platoon into red, screaming meat before the fifty-below gale froze the wet steam on their tunics into solid white armor. 

"Hold the interval!" Colonel Armistead’s voice cracked across the ice as the Virginians behind the wrecked machine stepped straight over the steaming, rigid bodies of their Japanese comrades without breaking stride, closing up behind the remaining three engines while Russian grape-shot hissed across the ice like cast-iron hail, snapping off rifle-barrels and taking men’s legs clean off at the knee-joint.

"Four hundred yards, Marshal!" Sterling shouted, his face black with powder-soot and grease as a conical shell glanced off the sloped roof of the sledge three inches above Marcus’s head, the concussion bursting both drums in the Major’s ears and sending a trickle of dark blood down his jaw. "The *Shasta*’s steering-chains are shot away—she’s yawing into the pressure-ridge!"

"Open the oil-cocks on all three vats," Marcus whispered, though Sterling could only read the movement of his bloody lips in the red glare of the firebox. "Elevate the brass nozzles. Pump."

From the prows of the *Sierra* and the *Sacramento*, twin rotary steam-pumps began to throb at two hundred strokes a minute. Out of the brass-bound fire-hoses burst two thick, arching black rainbows of boiling California petroleum, shooting a hundred yards ahead of the crunching wheels and splashing in smoking, viscous floods across the base of the twelve-foot Russian ice-rampart. The smell of raw kerosene and scorched sulfur drowned the scent of blood and frost. Up on the crystal parapet, the Siberian Riflemen in their white sheepskins paused with their ramrods half-drawn, staring down in bewilderment as the black, steaming grease soaked their boots and pooled around the timber sledges of their bronze cannon.

"One round of white-phosphorus canister from the bow-howitzer," Marcus formed the words with his dying breath, his fingers locking like iron claws onto the edge of his calculation-book as the *Sierra*’s spiked cleats ground within eighty paces of the wall.

The short bronze piece in the locomotive’s nose barked once.

Where the phosphorus stars struck the boiling Santa Paula crude, the violet Siberian night vanished. A wall of blinding, roaring orange-white flame forty feet high leaped from the surface of the lake with the thunder of an exploding gas-works, sucking the freezing air out of the soldiers’ lungs for three hundred yards around. The fire did not merely burn upon the ice; fed by twelve hundred gallons of superheated oil, it ate downward into the blue crystal like nitric acid.

For ninety seconds, while the sheepskin coats of the Russian gunners caught fire like tallow-wicks and men leaped screaming from the melting parapet, the six-foot floor of Lake Baikal held. Then, beneath the combined weight of forty bronze siege-pieces, ten thousand tons of stacked ice-blocks, and the two-thousand-degree furnace blistering its skin, the ancient geological fault-line of the lake gave a single, deafening report that sounded from the Khamar-Daban mountains to the gorges of the Angara.

A jagged black fissure, ten yards wide and steaming like the mouth of hell, zig-zagged straight under the center of Korsakov’s battery and backward beneath the wheels of the *Sacramento*. 

The glacier-wall tilted slowly backward, split into three colossal blue bergs, and plunged downward into the black, bottomless water, dragging twelve Russian cannon and six hundred shrieking riflemen in white sheepskins under the boiling scum of burning oil. At the same instant, the ice beneath the forty-ton *Sacramento* gave way like wet rotten timber; her iron prow reared straight up toward the stars, her boiler exploded as the freezing lake-water rushed into her white-hot flues, and she slid backward into the abyss, taking two full companies of the Fourteenth Pennsylvania with her before they could loose their hands from the guide-ropes.

"The center is gone!" Sterling screamed through his deafened ears, clutching the side of the sledge as the *Sierra*’s brakes locked and slid twenty yards along the tilting lip of the black water, where burning oil-patches floated among the bobbing heads of drowning Russians and Americans alike. "General! The road to the western shore is open around the crack!"

Marcus Vance did not answer. His chin had dropped forward onto his turpentine-soaked chest, his Geneva chronometer still ticking steadily against his thumb, while his gray eyes stared open and unblinking through the three-inch slit at the burning water—having balanced his last column of figures at the edge of the world.

***

Six thousand miles away, where the December rain fell warm and salt-heavy upon the granite paving-stones of San Francisco, the news of the Baikal furnace did not bring the ringing of cathedral bells; it brought ten thousand wet, starving men and women into the mud of Plaza Square with iron cobbles and broken pickaxe-handles in their fists.

For four months, since Elias had ordered the autumn levies and the final sixty-million-thaler Siberian Bridge loan, the machinery of the home provinces had been ground between the upper millstone of the war-tax and the lower millstone of the dockyard conscription. The thirty-percent customs tribute from Boston and New York had dried to a trickle as the eastern ports rotted in commercial paralysis; to feed the locomotives in Chukotka and the foundries at Potrero Point, Cornelius Schuyler’s tax-gatherers had raised the excise on San Joaquin flour to four silver tenths a barrel, while the provost-guards swept the Irish and American mechanics’ wards every Tuesday night to fill the replacement drafts for the northern ice.

Inside the high-arched Map Room of the Citadel on Rincon Hill, the winter dusk smelled of wet wool, coal-gas, and the pungent stramonium-smoke that hung like a permanent burial-shroud beneath the coffered ceiling. 

Elias did not sit in his wicker chair. Propped on both elbows against the windowsill of the tall western casement, his swollen legs wrapped in flannel bandages from ankle to thigh beneath his unlaced cavalry boots, he looked down the steep, rain-swept slope of First Street toward the Embarcadero. Down there, through the yellow smear of the gas-lamps, a mile-long column of torches was surging up the hill from the silent ironworks of the Mission. They were not Chinese coolies or Japanese sailors; they were his own people—white-bearded veterans of the forty-nine mining camps, wives of the Pennsylvania and Virginia auxiliaries whose husbands had just gone down under the Baikal ice, and two thousand discharged dock-masons marching behind a black canvas banner painted with a single white skull and the words: *NO MORE BONES FOR THE STRAIT.*

Even through the double-thick plate glass of the Chancery, the low, rhythmic roar of their chanting vibrated against Elias’s breastbone: *"Bread or blood! Bring home the Legion! Bread or blood!"*

"Marshal Vance is dead, Protector," Cornelius Schuyler said from the head of the baize table behind him. The banker’s voice was no longer deferential; the news that the terrible, bloodless shadow who had held the whip over the army was lying frozen in a Siberian box-sledge had put iron back into Schuyler’s spine. Around him stood six directors of the California Steam Navigation Syndicate and Rear-Admiral Takashima. "And four thousand men of the First and Second Divisions are either drowned in Lake Baikal or dying of gangrene in the burned huts along the Selenga! Look down that street, sir! The First California Reserve Battalion at the Presidio refused to draw ball-cartridge when the Provost-Major ordered them out an hour ago to clear Market Street! Their sergeants said they would not shoot down the mothers of the boys who took Vicksburg for you!"

Elias did not turn from the glass. Down at the corner of Folsom Street, the mob had just overturned two of the Treasury’s armored bread-wagons, setting the soaked wood ablaze with coal-oil and hurling paving-stones through the stained-glass windows of the Syncretic Chapel on the corner.

"They are shouting because their bellies are pinched and they smell a funeral in this house, Mr. Schuyler," Elias rasped, his breath rattling wetly in his throat as his scarred right hand gripped the mahogany window-mullion so hard the varnish cracked. "Who gave the casualty lists from the Selenga wire to the printers on Montgomery Street before they crossed my desk?"

Silence fell over the room, broken only by the hiss of the gas-jets and the distant crash of a shop-front giving way down the hill.

Beside the bronze telegraph repeater, Lady Kaiulani raised her head. Her face was pale and sharp as carved ivory above her black mourning-dress, and her right hand lay motionless inside the folds of her skirt.

"Mr. Schuyler’s chief clerk carried the decode to the *Alta California* office at two o’clock, Elias," Kaiulani said, her clear, musical voice cutting through the gloom like a lancet. "And Rear-Admiral Takashima gave orders at four that the marines aboard the *Kamehameha* are to remain at their moorings and take no part in civil disturbances among the American population. They wished you to see the torches from your window so that you would sign the Regency Act before midnight."

Takashima did not deny it. He stepped forward into the yellow circle of the chandelier, his bronze face hard and expressionless. "The Satsuma Brigade lost twelve hundred men on the ice on Tuesday, Excellency, to buy twenty miles of Russian snow while the British China Squadron is reinforcing Singapore. With Marshal Vance dead, there is no general on the continent whom both the American auxiliaries and the Imperial Japanese divisions will obey. The Joint Board therefore requests that Your Excellency retire to the warm springs at Monterey, constitute a Council of Regency under Comptroller Schuyler and myself, and sign the immediate recall of the Siberian and Yukon armies."

Elias turned slowly around from the window. It took him ten seconds to pivot his water-logged boots across the parquet floor, dragging his iron cane inch by inch; a cold grey sweat coated his hollow cheeks, and his lips were the color of a bruised plum from the lack of oxygen in his blood. Yet as he leaned his broad, skeletal shoulders back against the glass—with the orange glare of the burning bread-wagons down in the street framing his iron-gray head like the flames of that Kentucky cabin thirty-two years ago—there was something so terrible in his sunken eyes that Schuyler involuntarily stepped behind his leather chair.

"Marcus is dead," Elias whispered, the rough gravel of his voice scraping across the silence. "He died eight thousand miles west of the river where we met, with his boots pointing toward the Urals. And you think because my best dog is cold in the snow, the wolves can come into the kitchen and divide the meat?"

"Be reasonable, Mr. Thorne!" Schuyler cried, his fat hands gripping the back of his chair as a fresh roar from the ten thousand rioters outside shook the window-panes. "They are three blocks from the Citadel gates! The California militia will not fire on them, and Takashima’s sailors will not land! With what soldiers do you propose to hold this hill tonight—let alone Siberia?"

"With the soldiers who have no mothers in San Francisco," Elias said.

He lifted his trembling left hand and pointed a thick, blue-nailed finger straight at Kaiulani.

"Open the local wire to the Presidio barracks, Kaiulani," Elias commanded, each short phrase torn out of his failing lungs like a nail pulled from oak. "Not to the California Reserve. To Colonel Kalakaua of the First and Second Hawaiian Royal Guard, and to the three battalions of the Shantung Railway Pioneers quartered at the Mint. Tell them that the rabble on First Street has burned the Polynesian chapel and is marching to loot the Cantonese pay-vaults. Order Kalakaua to bring the four steam-rams up from the Embarcadero with the high-pressure boiler hoses coupled to the salt-pumps, and put two thousand Hawaiian and Chinese bayonets down the hill in column of companies. No parley. No blank powder. Clear the streets to the water’s edge, and hang the first twenty white mechanics taken with a torch in their hands from the iron lamp-posts outside Mr. Schuyler’s bank before the clock strikes eight!"

Schuyler’s jaw dropped open, his face turning grey as putty. "You are setting Asian coolies and Kanakas to bayonet American citizens in the streets of San Francisco?!"

"There are no American citizens in my empire, Mr. Schuyler—there are only subjects who obey the law, and traitors who feed the crows," Elias snarled, taking a single heavy, dragging step toward the table and raising his iron stick until the ferrule pointed straight between Takashima’s eyes. "And when Colonel Kalakaua has washed the cobbles clean outside, he will march two companies of his islanders up these stairs to stand behind your chairs while we draft the spring conscription for Lake Baikal. Sit down at that table, Admiral, before I have you shot on the carpet for desertion in the face of the enemy!"

***

To the Chronicler who writes in the quieter noon of the twentieth century—looking back across two decades from the marble libraries of New Edo upon the convulsions that remade the earth—it is plain that the true victim of that terrible winter upon the ice of Baikal was not the Grand Confederation of Pacifica, though Elias Thorne’s empire bled gold and iron from every pore, nor was it the dying Marshal whose embalmed body was brought back across the sea in a lead-lined cask of spirits. The true corpse laid out upon the Siberian snow was the three-hundred-year-old autocracy of the House of Romanov.

History is a balance of weights, and when an iron ball of ten thousand tons is cast into the eastern scale, the western beam must kick heavenward until the fulcrum snaps. 

In the winter of 1869, Emperor Alexander the Second had imagined that he was fighting a frontier border-war against an over-extended maritime adventurer—a campaign that could be settled, like the Crimea, by sacrificing a few regiments of serfs in the snow and signing a parchment in Paris. Instead, the relentless, mechanical jaws of the Pacifica vise closed upon the valley of the Yenisei and never opened again. For eighteen years after the battle on the lake, while the tubular steel spans of the Bering Bridge were bolted one by one across the Diomede piers and the double-track iron road crept inexorably westward through Chita and Irkutsk like a black gangrene eating up the continent, the Russian Empire was forced to bleed its entire youth and treasure into an open grave four thousand miles from Moscow.

To keep the blue-coated legions of San Francisco and Edo from crossing the Obi, the Ministries of War and Finance in St. Petersburg stripped the European provinces bare. Every silver ruble wrung from the starving peasantry of the Volga and the Ukraine went to buy Krupp cannon and coal for the Siberian stockades; every spring, two hundred thousand ploughboys were torn from the communal *mirs* of Great Russia, packed into unheated boxcars along the single, hastily laid military track from Perm, and shipped eastward into the taiga—never to return, or to return five years later as legless, frost-bitten beggars who sat outside the tavern doors of Tula and Kharkov whispering of the terrible yellow-and-white soldiers who rode behind steam-fortresses that spat liquid fire and fired seven times without a ramrod.

An autocracy can survive poverty, and it can survive tyranny, for those are the familiar weather of the steppe; it cannot survive eighteen years of unavenged, bankrupt humiliation at the hands of a power that treats the Tsar of All the Russias as a defaulting tenant. 

By the winter of 1887, the whole vast edifice of European Russia had been hollowed out from within, like an oak tree whose heartwood has been eaten by white ants while the bark still stands painted with the double-headed eagle. The gold reserve in the Fortress of Peter and Paul had vanished into the vaults of Frankfurt and San Francisco to pay for the fruitless counter-offensives of seventy-four and eighty-one; the paper assignats of the Imperial Bank would no longer buy a loaf of black rye bread in the Viborg quarter; and in the cellars of St. Petersburg and the silent, coal-starved iron-mills along the Fontanka, a new and pitiless breed of men had grown up in the shadow of the eastern disaster.

They were not the dreamy constitutional liberals of the fifties who had read French novels and wept over the serfs. They were men hardened in the same iron furnace that Elias Thorne had lit upon the Pacific—engineers, cashiered artillery officers from the Siberian front, and factory-committees who looked at the rotting gilded carriages of the Grand Dukes and asked why the Russian people should starve in the snow to preserve a German dynasty that had lost half of Asia to an American syndicate.

On the nineteenth of February, 1887—the twenty-sixth anniversary of the Emancipation that had given the peasants stones instead of bread—the boiler finally burst along the freezing quays of the Neva.

A dry, twenty-below gale was blowing across the ice from the Gulf of Finland, driving gritty clouds of snow and coal-dust past the tall red granite columns of St. Isaac’s Cathedral and piling white drifts against the bronze hooves of Peter the Great’s horse on the Senate Square. For six days no flour-trains had reached the Nikolaevsky Station from the south because the railway-brigades had seized the locomotives at Ryazan to haul their own starving battalions home from the Urals; in the workingmen’s barracks of the Putilov ironworks, the grates were dead cold.

At ten o’clock in the morning, the great alarm-bell of the Putilov foundry began to toll—not the measured chime of the shift-change, but a rapid, brazen clangor that echoed across the frozen canals and brought forty thousand iron-molders, dock-laborers, and women in ragged shawls pouring out across the ice of the river toward the Admiralty spire. At their head marched four thousand mutinous soldiers of the Pavlovsky and Volynsky Guard depots—men who had received orders the night before to entrain for the Tomsk trenches, and who had instead shot their colonels in the barracks courtyard and tied strips of red bunting from the regimental target-flags to the muzzles of their Berdan rifles.

Inside the high, crimson-damask salon on the second floor of the Winter Palace, overlooking the immense white expanse of the Palace Square where the Alexander Column rose like a frozen exclamation mark against the gray sky, the aging Tsar stood beside the double-paned window with his hands behind his back, watching a squadron of the Chevalier Guard in their brass cuirasses and white horsehair plumes form a thin, shivering line across the snow between the Arch of the General Staff and the palace gates.

"They are carrying the icons of the Virgin mixed with red flags from the machine-shops, Your Majesty," said Count Tolstoi, the Minister of the Interior, his voice shaking as he looked down from the adjacent casement at the dark, roaring human tide that was already spilling out of the Nevsky Prospekt and filling the square from curb to curb with the stink of wet sheepskin, cheap *makhorka* tobacco, and raw hunger. "And the Prefect of Police telephones that the Cossacks of the Don Guard at the Anichkov Bridge refused to use their *nagaikas* when the women walked under the horses’ necks! Sire, you must take the sledge to Tsarskoye Selo while the river-road to the Warsaw station is still open!"

"And leave St. Petersburg to a mob of blacksmiths and deserters because we lost a railway junction in Siberia?" Alexander asked, turning from the glass. He was sixty-eight now, his shoulders bowed beneath the weight of two decades of unbroken defeat, the deep pouches beneath his eyes purple in the cold northern light, yet the stubborn fatalism of his father Nicholas still held his spine rigid. "General Vannovsky—have the artillery of the Guard unlimber the four bronze pieces at the corner of the Millionnaya. Give them one blank charge over the heads of the crowd to clear the base of the column. If they do not disperse to their workshops within five minutes, open with canister."

Down in the square, the forty thousand did not halt when the Chevalier Guard drew their long straight palashes with a single, singing flash of steel in the frosty air.

At the foot of the red granite monolith in the center of the snow, a young captain of the Siberian Sapper Corps—a man whose left sleeve was pinned empty to his grey greatcoat from a Pacifica shrapnel-burst on the Yenisei, and whose chest still bore the tarnished St. George’s Cross—climbed upon the shoulders of two bearded Putilov hammer-men, holding a battered brass speaking-trumpet to his lips.

"Brothers of the Guard!" the one-armed sapper’s voice rang out across the packed snow, carrying clear and hard to the shivering horsemen sitting their mounts before the palace railings. "Look at the coats on your backs! The cloth was mortgaged to the bankers in Berlin before you put it on! Look at the rifles in your mittens! There are ten cartridges apiece in the pouches because the Grand Dukes stole the powder-money to buy diamonds for their dancers while our brothers froze to death in front of the American ironclads at Baikal! Will you shoot down your own mothers in the snow of Petersburg so that the Romanovs can send you to rot in the Siberian marshes tomorrow?"

On the flank of the cavalry line, a young cornet of the Chevalier Guard—barely nineteen, his cheeks pink with the frost beneath his brass helmet—raised his saber high in his gloved fist and screamed: "Close ranks! For the Tsar! Trot—*march!*"

The heavy bay horses took three steps forward into the snow. Then, from the front rank of the mutinous Volynsky infantrymen standing fifty paces away beside the iron lamp-posts, twenty Berdan rifles came up to the shoulder in a single, level rank—not with the wild, ragged aim of street-rioters, but with the cold, mechanical volley-discipline they had learned over eighteen winters of fighting the Pacifica legions along the eastern rivers.

"Aim at the officers' breastplates," the one-armed sapper called through his trumpet, his arm dropping as the palace windows above them shook with the first dull boom of the Guard artillery wheeling into position by the arch, "and fire!"

The volley tore through the freezing air, emptying twelve gilded saddles in a single heartbeat and staining the trampled snow of the Senate Square with the last blood of the Romanov autocracy. 

***

Yet while the winter of 1887 brought the ancient house of Peter the Great crashing down into the embers of the Neva, the three-thousand-mile iron road that had drained Russia’s veins was itself presided over not by a living warrior, but by a terrifying, mechanized mummy.

For eighteen years since that December night in sixty-nine when Colonel Kalakaua’s Hawaiian bayonets had washed the cobbles of First Street clean of rioters, Elias Thorne had refused to die. History records few stranger or more claustrophobic spectacles than the long twilight of the Providentor upon Rincon Hill. The dropsy that had swollen his limbs during the laying of the Bering piers had never receded; by his fifty-ninth year, it had turned the lower half of his body into two useless pillars of cold stone that had to be hoisted from his iron bedstead to a rubber-tired wheeled chair by a brass chain-pulley bolted into the ceilingbeams. He had outlived Caleb Vance; he had outlived the first Marshal Marcus Vance, whose lead-lined coffin sat in the crypt beneath the Monterey basilica; he had even outlived the original generation of Virginia and Pennsylvania captains who had carried his eagles to the Potomac and the Great Wall.

Instead of fracturing into the civil war that Cornelius Schuyler and Admiral Takashima had plotted over their Madeira in the sixties, the empire had calcified around the invalid’s chair into a vast, bureaucratic oligarchy—a triumvirate of mutual suspicion in which the aged Schuyler’s banking syndicates, Prince Takashima’s Satsuma Admiralty, and Lady Kaiulani’s Insular Provostry balanced one another across the wheels of the old man’s bath-chair, each terrified to pull the linchpin lest the others seize the axle. To satisfy the insatiable hunger of the foundries at New Osaka and Nagasaki now that the Siberian frontier was walled off by permanent concrete casemates along the Yenisei, the Triumvirate required a new treasury to gut.

On the afternoon of the fourth of March, 1887, the high glass dome of the Citadel conservatory was no longer heated by coal-flues; it hummed with the dry, steady warmth of naked Edison carbon-filament bulbs strung like yellow hornets among the giant tree-ferns, and smelled of carbolic soap, nitro-glycerine heart-lozenges, and the oiled brass of the pneumatic message-tubes that rose directly out of the marble floor beside the carp-basin.

Elias sat in his wheeled chair of dark koa-wood and nickeled steel, a heavy blanket of sea-otter fur tucked around his dead knees. His hair, cropped close to a skull that showed every suture of the bone beneath the yellow skin, was white as bleached salt; his left eyelid drooped permanently from a minor apoplexy suffered during the Canton rice-riots of eighty-two; yet the single wide, water-clear eye that remained fixed upon the southern hemisphere of the great bronze globe before him still carried the terrifying, unblinking weight of the Kentucky creek-bed.

Behind his right wheel stood Lady Kaiulani. At fifty, the Princess-Chancellor had grown into a figure of severe, almost sacerdotal majesty; her hair was braided with threads of silver above the unchanging black bombazine of her dress, and she alone held the silver spoon with which the Providentor’s afternoon digitalis was measured. Across the basin, leaning upon ebony canes of their own, stood the seventy-year-old Comptroller Schuyler—his jowls hanging like empty saddle-bags over his stiff collar—and Grand-Admiral Marquis Takashima, whose breast was a solid breastplate of Chrysanthemum and Pacifica stars.

"The Russian Republic that the mutineers proclaimed in St. Petersburg last month has signed the armistice at Tomsk, Protector," Schuyler wheezed, tapping a ticker-tape ribbon that had just dropped from the pneumatic chute. "They cede everything east of the Yenisei in perpetuity in exchange for ten million sacks of California wheat to feed Moscow. The northern ledger is closed at last! The sixty thousand troops we have had sitting in the Siberian blockhouses for eighteen winters can be paid off, and the iron-rolling mills at Potrero Point can reduce their shifts to peacetime maintenance!"

Elias’s crooked, blue-nailed right forefinger did not lift from the bronze curve of the globe. It traced a slow, scratching arc down the meridian from Manila—past the spice-straits of Macassar, across the broad, green-enamelled belly of Dutch Java and Sumatra, and down to the vast, buff-colored continent of New Holland, where the British colonies of Victoria and New South Wales sat like fat, unguarded sheep-runs at the bottom of the world.

"Paid off?" Elias’s voice was no longer the rough thunder of his prime; it was a dry, rustling whisper, like dead corn-shucks blown across a frozen barn floor, amplified only by the absolute hush of the fern-house. "If you turn sixty thousand men who have lived on army beef and bayonet-drill for twenty years loose into the streets of San Francisco and Osaka tomorrow, Mr. Schuyler, whose windows do you think they will break before Saturday?"

"The Treasury cannot carry four hundred thousand men under arms in time of peace, Excellency!" Takashima protested, though the old samurai’s eyes flicked uneasily toward Kaiulani’s impassive face. "Our coal-bunkers at Manila and Cavite are choked to the roofs, and the twenty new *Leviathan*-class steel battleships have nothing to shoot at between the Kuriles and the Equator!"

"Look at the bottom of the ball, Takashima," Elias whispered, his heavy white head tilting half an inch toward the bronze southern ocean. "For forty years we have built a roof over the northern water. Yet every pound of gutta-percha that insulates our submarine cables, every barrel of tin for our canneries, and half the petroleum for our new turbine-cruisers sits in the Dutch islands between Borneo and Batavia. And below them sit Sydney and Melbourne—the last open harbors where a British squadron from the Cape can coal and refit to strike our southern flank."

Schuyler’s watery eyes widened behind his gold pince-nez. "The Dutch East Indies and Australia, Protector? Holland is under the protection of the German Emperor in Berlin, and Australia is flesh and blood of the British Crown! Since the panic of seventy-nine, London has transferred half the wealth of the old island to the banks of Melbourne and the gold-fields of Ballarat!"

"Then Melbourne is where the gold is," Elias rasped, a thread of clear saliva gleaming at the drooping corner of his mouth as his hand closed over the carved bronze boss of Capricorn. "A circle with the bottom broken out is only a horseshoe, Mr. Schuyler. When the water runs out of the northern sluice, you tilt the pan south. We do not disband a single regiment from the Yenisei. Put them on the broad-gauge cars for Port Arthur and Manila this week. Tell young Marcus Vance that his father’s memory requires the Dutch straits cleared before the monsoon turns, and have the first division of the Fleet steam for the Timor Sea. I will not go down into the granite at Monterey while an English governor collects customs-dues on the shores of my ocean."

***

Six weeks later, under the steaming, bruised-violet clouds of the April monsoon, the second General Marcus Vance—son of the man who had died in the iron box on Lake Baikal, and grandson of old Caleb’s blood—stood upon the vibrated steel wing of an armored river-monitor pushing up the turbid brown flood of the Solo River in eastern Java.

He was twenty-nine, born in the year of the Sacramento Coup, and unlike his father, who had carried the weary memory of West Point and the old Republic in his bones, the younger Marcus was a pure creature of the Imperial machine. Educated at the Polytechnic Academy of New Edo and the Staff College of Monterey, he spoke Japanese, Cantonese, and English with the same clipped, metallic cadence; he wore no saber, carrying instead a nickeled nine-shot self-loading pistol holstered over his khaki tropical tunic and a slide-rule in his breast pocket.

Around the monitor’s low freeboard, the jungle of the Dutch residency pressed in like a wet green wall of giant teak, banana-fronds, and weeping *waringin* trees, the ninety-eight-degree air heavy with the stench of rotting river-silt, crushed cloves from the burned colonial godowns along the bank, and the sharp, vinegary smoke of smokeless cordite powder.

"The Dutch Governor-General has concentrated four battalions of the Royal Netherlands East Indies Army and two regiments of British Sikh infantry from Singapore behind the railway embankment at Surakarta, General," reported Major Kuroda, his Satsuma chief of staff, wiping the monsoon rain from the celluloid cover of his map-board. "They have dammed the irrigation canals to flood the rice-paddies in front of the rubber plantations, and their Krupp field-guns are registered on the stone bridge. If we deploy the Filipino and Californian brigades across the wet sawahs, the mud will bog our Maxim-gun carriages to the hubs."

Young Marcus did not raise his binoculars; he looked at the brass pressure-gauge of the pneumatic tube-launcher bolted to the monitor’s foredeck, and then down at his wrist, where a radium-dialed chronometer—strapped to the cuff in the new fashion of the Pacifica staff—ticked off the seconds to the noon barrage.

"My father used to say that mud is merely water that has not yet been boiled, Major," Marcus said, his voice thin, rapid, and wholly devoid of emphasis. "The Dutch and the English are fighting to preserve their rubber-trees and their sugar-mills because their shareholders in Amsterdam and Penang expect a six-percent dividend in October. We do not care about the trees; the Treasury only wants the sap-tappers and the tin-dredges. How many drums of the new Baku-Santa Paula jellied naphtha do we have in the lighter-barges?"

"Four hundred drums, sir," Kuroda answered. "And the two squadrons of shallow-draft hydroplane-launches have already worked up the side-canals behind the British left flank."

"Do not shell the railway embankment with shrapnel," Marcus ordered, sliding the ivory cursor of his rule across the logarithmic scale and snapping it shut with a dry *click*. "Open the sluice-gates of the upper oil-barges and pump two thousand barrels of jellied naphtha directly onto the flooded surface of the irrigation canals. The current sets straight down against the foot of the Dutch breastworks at two knots. Give the slick fifteen minutes to coat the water-weeds around their barbed-wire stakes, then have the mortar-boats drop six thermite-shells into the ditch."

Half a mile ahead, where the red-tiled roofs of the Dutch colonial sugar-factory rose above the feathery tops of the bamboo, the twelve-pounder batteries of the Singapore garrison opened a rapid, barking fire through the rain. Two high-explosive shells burst in the mud-bank fifty yards to starboard, showering the monitor’s steel deck-canopy with black slime and shredded palm-fronds; a splinter hummed through the open bridge-screen and shattered the glass face of the engine-room telegraph.

Marcus did not even turn his head toward the broken glass. He watched the black, iridescent film of jellied petroleum spreading out across the flooded rice-terraces ahead of the bows, smoothing the rain-pitted water into a greasy mirror that crept silently around the knees of the Javanese and Sikh skirmishers crouching in the inundated ditches.

"Range nineteen hundred meters," Marcus said into the telephone-mouthpiece wired to the mortar-barge astern. "Thermite canister. Fire."

The compressed-air mortars did not roar; they gave four deep, coughing *thumps*, like a giant clearing his throat in a cellar, and four dull aluminum cylinders tumbled lazily through the grey monsoon curtain.

Where they struck the flooded paddies in front of the railway embankment, the tropical rain turned instantaneously into a screaming, three-thousand-degree hell of white-hot magnesium and liquid fire. The naphtha floating upon the irrigation water ignited with a single, hollow *whoomp* that shook the monitor’s hull against her anchor-chains; within thirty seconds, a solid sheet of greasy, black-edged flame half a mile wide and fifty feet high was rolling straight over the Dutch trenches, boiling the ditch-water around the legs of the screaming Sikh infantrymen, exploding the caissons of the Krupp batteries in showers of brass cartridges, and turning a hundred acres of prime colonial rubber-trees into torches of blistering black resin.

"Advance the Filipino bicycle-battalions along the stone dike on the right as soon as the masonry cools," Marcus said, dropping the telephone receiver onto its hook and pulling out his requisition pad before the screams from the burning cane-brakes had even reached their pitch. "And wire the Comptroller’s agents at Batavia that the Surakarta district is cleared for receivership. Any Dutch planter who brings his coolie-rolls to my provost tent before sundown keeps ten percent of his crop-value in silver certificates; any plantation whose manager has fled to the hills goes to the Satsuma Veteran Colonization Board at par."

***

To the Chronicler who stood upon the sandstone heights of the South Head at the dawn of the twenty-fourth of May, 1887—the very morning when the loyal municipalities of Sydney had hung out their crimson bunting and gilded pasteboard crowns to celebrate the Golden Jubilee of Her Britannic Majesty’s fifty years upon the throne of England—the sky to the eastward gave no warning of providence save a low, unnatural bank of yellow-black coal-haze that stained the pale winter blue of the Tasman Sea against the rising sun.

For a hundred years since Captain Phillip had landed his first boatloads of chained English pickpockets and Irish rebels among the eucalyptus groves of Port Jackson, the colonies of the southern continent had grown fat in a pastoral dream at the uttermost antipodes of the earth. While the old United States was being ground into iron provinces behind the Sierra, and while the ancient empires of China and Russia were bleeding their lives out against the bayonets of the Pacific Legion, the sheep-barons of New South Wales and the gold-bankers of Melbourne had comforted themselves with two delusions: that six thousand miles of salt water was an impassable moat, and that the Royal Navy’s Australian Squadron—five aging iron-hulled corvettes anchored off Garden Island—represented the invincible trident of Trafalgar.

They had not understood that in the new geometry of steam and steel, the ocean was no longer a wall; it was a paved turnpike, and its proprietor had come to collect the rent.

At six-thirty in the morning, as the Jubilee bells of St. Andrew’s Cathedral began to peal across the quiet, mist-wreathed coves of the harbor and the first holiday ferry-boats loaded with picnickers in white flannel put out from Circular Quay, the semaphore-telegraph atop the Macquarie Lighthouse began to jerk its wooden arms in frantic, spasmodic terror. Two minutes later, the six-inch Armstrong rifle in the casemate at Middle Head fired a single blank alarm-gun that sent ten thousand white cockatoos screaming out of the gum-trees along the North Shore.

The holiday crowds streaming down George Street toward the Domain did not run to the cellars; they ran to the seawalls at Mrs. Macquarie’s Chair and the battlements of Fort Denison, shading their eyes with programmes of the Queen’s Regatta as they peered eastward toward the mile-wide gap between the Heads.

Through the sandstone jaws of the harbor mouth, moving at a stately, dead-slow eight knots against the ebbing tide without a single pilot-jack flying at their fore-trucks, came the First and Third Battle Squadrons of the Grand Confederation.

These were no longer the low, turtle-backed monitors that had rammed the Union gunboats at Vicksburg or shelled the mud-forts of Taku twenty years before. What entered the waters of Port Jackson that May morning were fourteen sixteen-thousand-ton barbette battleships of the *Imperator* and *Mutsuhito* classes—towering, castle-like citadels of Harveyized nickel-steel painted a dark, pitiless imperial blue, their hulls sixty feet high from the submerged ram-snouts to the armored fighting-tops where the brass lenses of electric range-finders glinted in the morning sun. Each ship carried four eighteen-inch rifled breech-loaders mounted in twin pear-shaped turrets fore and aft, weapons whose fifty-foot barrels could hurl a two-thousand-pound shell packed with melinite twelve miles over the Blue Mountains; and from their triple yellow-and-black funnels rose a continuous, oily thundercloud of burned Borneo petroleum that smelled of hot asphalt and sulfur, blotting out the scent of the salt-water and the flowering wattle along the cliffs.

On Garden Island, Rear-Admiral Tryon of the Royal Navy stood upon the quarterdeck of his flagship, the composite screw-corvette *Nelson*, his telescope frozen to his eye as the lead monster—the *Elias Thorne*, flying the combined sun-and-chrysanthemum flag of Grand-Admiral Marquis Takashima—glided past Pinchgut Island at four hundred yards’ distance, her upper batteries of rapid-fire six-pounders manned by bare-armed Japanese and American marine gunners standing motionless beside their brass ammunition-hoists.

"Shall we slip the moorings and clear for action, sir?" whispered the *Nelson*’s flag-captain, his face white as his tropical duck trousers as the colossal blue steel flank of the second battleship, the *Kamehameha II*, swung broadside across the mouth of Woolloomooloo Bay, her shadow falling cold and black across the wooden decks of the British corvette until the sun vanished from the binnacle.

Tryon lowered his glass. He was a brave man who had served in the Mediterranean and the Channel, yet he was also a sailor who knew arithmetic. His five corvettes carried wrought-iron armor belts that would split like pine-shingles before a six-inch shell, and the shore batteries at Bradley’s Head had forty rounds of black powder apiece in their magazines. Behind the fourteen battleships, already rounding the South Head in double column as far as the eye could see toward Bondi, steamed thirty-two twin-screw iron troop-transports, their decks dark with the grey-and-blue ranks of forty thousand veterans from the Java and Vladivostok campaigns.

"If you pull a lanyard on this ship, Captain," Tryon said, his voice breaking in the stillness as the deep, ear-shattering roar of the *Elias Thorne*’s steam-siren echoed off the sandstone cliffs of the harbor, "those floating foundries will blow half of Sydney into the brick-fields before our first round-shot reaches their water-line. Keep the men from the braces. Here comes their launch."

Down at the stone stairs of the Man-o'-War Jetty below the Botanical Gardens, where Lord Carington, the Royal Governor of New South Wales, had arrived ten minutes earlier in his state landau wearing his plumed cocked hat and the riband of St. Michael and St. George for the morning levee, a detachment of two hundred Hawaiian Royal Guards and Satsuma Marines was already leaping ashore from four self-propelled steel motor-barges. They did not ask permission of the water-police; with the silent, oiled precision of men who had executed the same drill at Honolulu, Manila, and Shanghai, they fixed eighteen-inch bayonets to their magazine-rifles, wheeled into a hollow square across the quay, and pushed the silk-hatted Sydney aldermen and their weeping wives back against the iron palings of the garden.

Out of the stern-cabin of the lead barge stepped no frontier roughneck in muddy boots, but Lady Kaiulani’s nephew and Deputy-Commissioner for the Southern Ocean, Prince David Kalakaua—dressed in the immaculate white-and-gold tropical uniform of a Pacifica Privy Councillor—flanked by General Marcus Vance the younger, whose khaki boots were still stained with the red clay of Surakarta.

Lord Carington took two steps forward across the flagstones, his hand resting tremblingly upon his ceremonial court-sword as he confronted the tall dark Polynesian prince and the lean, cold-eyed American general beneath the shadow of a Moreton Bay fig tree.

"By what outrageous piratical license," the British Governor demanded, his voice rising shrill and thin against the rumble of twenty-eight anchor-chains roaring down into the mud of Sydney Cove behind them, "do the warships of San Francisco and Edo violate the neutrality of a British self-governing colony upon Her Majesty’s Jubilee? There is no state of war between Whitehall and the Pacific Confederation!"

Young Marcus Vance did not even look at the plumed representative of Queen Victoria; he was already unstrapping his field-telephone case and handing the copper ground-spike to a Cantonese corporal to drive into the mortar between the quay-stones. It was Prince Kalakaua who drew the heavy, brass-bound vellum scroll from beneath his arm, breaking the scarlet seal of the Insular Diet with a thumb that wore the ancient whale-ivory ring of Oahu.

"There is no neutrality inside the Great Arena, My Lord," Kalakaua said in the polished, musical English of the Monterey court, holding the scroll open before the Governor’s blanched face while four companies of the First Virginia and Second Choshu Regiments marched up the stone ramp behind him with the steel wheels of their Maxim-guns rattling over the cobbles. "By the Decree of the Southern Circle, signed at the Citadel of San Francisco on the first of April by the Providentor Elias Thorne, it is declared that the safety of the Pacific Realm no longer permits the maintenance of European penal settlements, naval bases, or crown customs-houses south of the Equator. From the stroke of eight this morning, the colonies of New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland, and New Zealand are detached from the British Crown and constituted as the Southern Commonwealth of Pacifica."

"You are mad!" shouted Sir Henry Parkes, the white-bearded Premier of the colony, pushing his bulky frame past the Governor’s shoulder and shaking his fist at the blue steel battleships towering above the ferry-slips. "There are three million free-born British subjects on this continent! We have our own parliaments! We will tear up the railway tracks to Bathurst and fight you from every gum-tree in the bush before we pay a penny of tribute to a dying Yankee tyrant in a bath-chair and his yellow mercenaries!"

Young Marcus Vance finally looked up from his telephone-box. He pulled his slide-rule half an inch from his breast pocket, pushed it back with a click of his thumb, and looked at the old white-bearded colonial politician with the same clinical curiosity his father had turned upon the Zouaves at Bull Run twenty-six years ago.

"You have six hundred miles of mixed-gauge railway track that cannot even carry a freight-car from Sydney to Melbourne without unloading the boxes at the border, Mr. Parkes," Marcus said, his clipped voice cutting through the premier’s rhetoric as a squad of Satsuma telegraph-sappers ran past them toward the General Post Office on Martin Place with coils of insulated wire over their shoulders, "and forty percent of your wool-clip is already mortgaged to Mr. Schuyler’s banking-house in Hong Kong. If a single rail is lifted between here and Parramatta tonight, I will not chase your bush-rangers into the gum-trees. I will turn the eighteen-inch guns of the *Elias Thorne* upon the Sydney water-reservoir at Botany Swamps, burn the wool-warehouses at Circular Quay with thermite shell, and land thirty thousand Cantonese and Irish railway-navvies at Port Phillip tomorrow morning to re-lay your tracks to the Imperial six-foot gauge while your parliament sits in the coal-hulks. Corporal—take this gentleman’s watch and keys, and escort Lord Carington to the telegraph office; I require his signature on the railway-transfer order before the eight o’clock gun fires."

***

By the third week of July, the document which the court historians at Monterey gravely recorded as the *Australian Petition for Statehood* had arrived in the high conservatory on Rincon Hill, though the twelve colonial premiers, wool-factors, and Ballarat mine-owners who carried it up the marble stairs under the escort of Hawaiian bayonets looked less like petitioners than debtors walking behind a bailiff’s cart.

Inside the glass dome, the summer heat was thick with the smell of camphor-ice, witch-hazel, and the faint, sour corruption of an aged body kept vertical by steel braces and digitalis. Elias had not spoken a full sentence aloud since the second apoplexy struck him on the morning the Java cable was spliced in June. The right half of his face remained carved from gray Sierra granite, the pale eye staring wide and unblinking from its sunken socket, while the left corner of his mouth sagged into the white stubble of his jaw. Yet no member of the Triumvirate dared remove the seal-ring from his bloated, purple-nailed thumb; for so long as the old man sat in his nickeled bath-chair beside the carp-pool, neither Grand-Admiral Takashima’s fleet-captains nor Comptroller Schuyler’s eastern directors could claim the regency without facing Lady Kaiulani’s provost-guards in the corridors below.

"The Delegates of the Southern Commonwealth have signed the Petition of Incorporation at Melbourne, Protector," Kaiulani said, standing beside his right wheel as the twelve Australians halted three paces beyond the fern-pots, their black broadcloth coats smelling of sea-damp and bilge-water from the fast Honolulu packet. She did not look at the parchment that Schuyler held trembling in his spotted hands; her dark eyes, cold and fathomless beneath her silver-braided hair, watched the slight, spasmodic twitching of Elias’s right forefinger upon the sea-otter lap-robe. "They pray that the Crown of Pacifica will assume the forty-million-pound railway debt heretofore owed to the banking-houses of London, unify the continental gauge from Brisbane to Adelaide, and admit the four provinces to the Imperial Customs Union upon the same footing as Oregon and Luzon."

Across the basin, Marquis Takashima’s hand tightened upon the gold-lacquered hilt of his court sword. "A petition that drags our battleships two thousand leagues south of the Equator while the British Admiralty has stripped the Mediterranean and the Channel to send nineteen first-rate ironclads around the Cape of Good Hope!" the old Satsuma noble snapped, dropping the pretense of lowered voices in the presence of the mute figure in the chair. "My cruisers off Timor intercepted the P&O mail-steamer from Colombo four days ago. Admiral Hornby has united the British Cape, Indian, and China Squadrons at Thursday Island—thirty-two armored ships of the line steaming down the Great Barrier Reef to retake Sydney! And my dockyards at Yokosuka are starved of nickel-steel because Mr. Schuyler’s board has diverted sixty thousand tons of rail-iron to Melbourne!"

"The Ballarat gold-escorts and the Broken Hill silver-mines have already yielded twelve million thalers to the Market Street reserve since June, Marquis!" Schuyler wheezed back, his shaking finger jabbing at the leather portfolio under his arm while the Australian delegates looked from one aging oligarch to the other with the dawning comprehension of captives watching their jailers draw knives over the ransom-chest. "If we abandon the southern ports to Hornby’s fleet now, every bond we floated in Frankfurt and New York on the security of the Australian wool-clip will drop to ten cents before noon! General Vance’s land-batteries can hold Sydney—"

*Clang.*

Neither Schuyler nor Takashima had seen the Providentor’s right arm move. With a sudden,jerking sweep of his good shoulder, Elias had knocked the heavy brass inhaling-kettle from the side-table; it struck the tessellated marble pavement, spilling boiling stramonium-water and glowing charcoal across the polished boots of the Japanese admiral and the silk stockings of the New York banker.

From the sagging, paralyzed cavern of Elias’s throat came a sound—not words, for the clot in his brain had locked the tongue that had once hushed the Diet of Sacramento, but a low, rattling animal growl that raised the short hairs on the necks of the Australians by the door. His right hand, swollen like a bruised turnip, rose two inches from the fur blanket, seized the thick parchment of the Australian Petition from Schuyler’s frozen fingers, and crushed the vellum together with the wax seal directly against the hot, wet brass of the overturned kettle until the sheepskin scorched and smoked.

"The Providentor has ratified the Southern Act," Lady Kaiulani said into the hush, her voice smooth and terrible as she stepped between the smoking parchment and the two men, her black skirt brushing the spilled coals. "And he bids me inform the Joint Board that Grand-Admiral Takashima will remain here in San Francisco to sit beside the Treasury desk where I can see his hands, while young General Vance takes the First and Third Battle Squadrons out of Port Jackson tonight to meet Admiral Hornby in the Coral Sea. Gentlemen of Melbourne—you are subjects of the Empire. Go down to the Comptroller’s office and count your iron."

***

On the ninth of August, four hundred miles east of the Queensland coast where the long, sapphire-blue rollers of the Coral Sea break into white foam over the sunken coral ramparts of the Saumarez Reefs, the nineteenth century met the twentieth across six miles of sunlit water.

There was no land in sight. Under a sky of cloudless, blinding brass, the northeast trade-wind blew warm and steady at fourteen knots, smelling purely of tropical brine until the two greatest armadas since Lepanto fouled the Trade with eighty thousand horsepower of burning coal and Borneo residue.

To the north, steaming in two stately, indented columns painted the traditional black-and-white buff of Nelson’s navy, came the last throw of the British dice: nineteen ocean-going battleships and twelve armored cruisers under Admiral Sir Geoffrey Hornby. They were the pride of Portsmouth, Birkenhead, and the Clyde—the turret-rams *Inflexible*, *Devastation*, *Dreadnought*, *Thunderer*, and the new citadel-ships *Colossus* and *Edinburgh*—vessels with twenty-four-inch wrought-iron belts and eighty-ton muzzle-loading woolwich guns, their white ensigns Whipping from every peak as they bore down with the wind at their backs to sweep the colonial usurpers from the southern ocean.

General Marcus Vance the younger did not watch them from an open bridge, nor did he wear a sword. He sat strapped into a revolving steel seat inside the electric fire-control central deep beneath the four-inch armored deck of the flagship *Elias Thorne*, fifteen feet below the waterline where the roar of the sea was drowned by the high, whining scream of the forced-draft steam-turbines and the constant *tick-clack-tick* of the brass range-calculators.

Before him, illuminated by hooded green incandescent bulbs, stretched a ground-glass plotting-table upon which six Japanese and American midshipmen with vulcanite ear-phones moved small lead markers according to the bearings telephoned down every ten seconds from the thirty-foot coincidence range-finders in the armored mastheads eighty feet above.

"Range to the lead British division—the *Inflexible* and *Colossus*—eleven thousand four hundred meters, General," reported Major Kuroda, his eyes fixed on the spinning dials of the Dumaresq mechanical trig-computer bolted to the bulkhead. "Admiral Hornby has formed his heavy rams in double echelon on our port bow. He is closing at thirteen knots under full coal-draft to bring his eighty-ton muzzle-loaders inside three thousand yards, and his flagship is hoisting the signal for a general charge to ram."

Young Marcus adjusted the throat-microphone strapped over his khaki collar, his pale, unblinking eyes watching the green light reflect off the celluloid cursor of his slide-rule. The air in the steel vault was ninety-two degrees, sterile and dry, smelling of warm gutta-percha insulation and lubricating-grease.

"Admiral Hornby thinks he is fighting the French at Lissa in sixty-six," Marcus said into the vulcanite mouthpiece, his clipped voice carried simultaneously by armoured cable to the conning-towers of all fourteen *Imperator*-class battleships steaming in a single, rigid line-ahead at eighteen knots. "His muzzle-loaders take four minutes to sponge and ram by hydraulic chain, and his gunners are sighting over open iron notches through their own coal-smoke. We will not close within eight thousand meters. Alter course twelve degrees to starboard together by flag-telegraph; keep the sun behind their smoke-stacks and hold the range at nine thousand yards. We will kill them with the math before their iron rams ever see our paint."

He flipped the brass switch on the master firing-board.

"All ships: main batteries load fifty-caliber armor-piercing capped shell with cast picric-acid filler. Elevation eleven degrees forty minutes; deflection left four knots. Fire by director-salvo on the flagship’s bell."

Up in the blinding tropical glare above the armored deck, fifty-six eighteen-inch rifled steel barrels—each fifty feet long, fed from below by electric endless-chain hoists that delivered a two-thousand-pound projectile every thirty-eight seconds—swung in simultaneous, oiled unison toward the northern horizon. 

When the circuit closed in Marcus’s hand, the fourteen battleships did not disappear in the dirty white billow of old black powder; they spat a mile-long, pale yellow flash of smokeless nitrocellulose cordite whose concussion stripped the white paint from their own waterways and flattened the trade-wind swells into dead, foaming milk for two hundred yards to leeward.

For twenty-one seconds the fifty-six one-ton cones of hardened San Francisco steel climbed through the upper stratosphere of the southern sky, whistling with the sound of fifty express-trains plunging into a tunnel, before dropping at a forty-five-degree angle straight onto the flat, two-inch wrought-iron decks of the British vanguard five miles away.

In the plotting-room of the *Elias Thorne*, Marcus did not feel the impacts; he heard them only as the observer in the fore-top shouted numbers into the wire:

*"Splash! Straddle on the lead turret-ship! Two—four—five direct hits abaft the funnel! Her central citadel has opened up—she’s blowing her magazines!"*

Across six miles of sparkling blue water, Her Majesty’s Ship *Inflexible*—ten thousand tons of British iron that had taken seven years to build at Portsmouth—had not been pierced on her thick side-armor; she had been gutted from above like a turtle struck by a falling boulder. Two eighteen-inch picric shells had punched clean through her thin teak-and-iron deck-plating and detonated inside her main boiler-rooms and hydraulic-loading chambers. A column of greasy black-and-orange smoke, mixed with spinning iron deck-beams, life-boats, and human limbs, rose twelve hundred feet into the tropical sky; when the base of the pillar collapsed thirty seconds later, the water where the flagship of the Mediterranean had steamed was empty save for a spreading circle of boiling white foam and oil.

And before the second ship in the British line—the *Dreadnought*—could even haul out of the blinding wreckage of her consort, the electric bells inside the Pacifica turrets rang a second time.

For ninety minutes, under a sun that turned the steel decks into frying-pans, the battle was not a combat; it was a methodical, long-range industrial demolition. Steaming four knots faster than the coal-choked British ironclads, the fourteen blue-hulled sisters of the Pacifica line kept their distance along the outer arc of the circle with the cold, mechanical precision of a traction-engine plowing a furrow, pouring fifty-six tons of high-explosive steel every forty seconds into a fleet whose short-barreled muzzle-loaders could only drop their round-shot harmlessly into the swells two miles short of Marcus’s wake.

By two o’clock in the afternoon, the Coral Sea for ten miles leeward of the Saumarez Reefs was a floating abattoir of burning oil-slicks, shattered teak spars, and listing, gutted iron hulks whose red-hot casemates hissed like laundry-irons as they rolled over into the two-thousand-fathom trough. Nine British battleships had gone to the bottom; six more—the *Colossus*, the *Devastation*, and four armored cruisers—lay dead in the water with their rudders jammed, their funnels shot away to the deck-stubs, and their surviving officers waving white bed-sheets from the stumps of their signal-masts while sharks tore at the hundreds of scorched, oil-blinded sailors clinging to the floating hammocks.

Down in the green-lit vault of the *Elias Thorne*, young Marcus Vance unstrapped his ear-phones, wiped a bead of sweat from his upper lip with a clean linen square, and looked at the red ink tallies on the glass table.

"We have expended thirty-four percent of our eighteen-inch outfit to sink or disable fifteen capital units, Major Kuroda," Marcus said, his voice flat and slightly annoyed as he tapped a column of figures with his pencil. "That is twelve rounds per hull—three rounds higher than the Monterey proving-ground tables allowed for wrought-iron targets at nine thousand meters. Have the gunnery officers of the third division explain the variance in their evening reports. Signal the cruisers to pick up Admiral Hornby’s survivors and put prize-crews aboard the four hulks that can still float; their scrap-plate will pay for the cordite when we tow them into Sydney. And open the wireless-telegraph spark to the Noumea cable-head—tell San Francisco the southern ocean is swept."

***

On the nineteenth of August, the city of San Francisco did not wait for nightfall to light its fires. From the granite quays of the Embarcadero to the high, wind-swept ridges of Twin Peaks, four hundred thousand electric arc-lamps and open barrels of blazing Santa Paula tar turned the afternoon fog into a roaring, brass-colored canopy that smelled of hot copper, scorched grease, and the tons of red Chinese firecrackers exploding continuously along the balconies of Dupont and Market streets.

Down in the deep-water channel off Clark’s Point—where forty years earlier a twenty-one-year-old frontier captain had stood in front of a redwood log storehouse and bought twenty discharged soldiers with a canvas sack of Mexican pesos—the three-mile line of the Home Fleet was firing a hundred-and-one-gun salute from twelve-inch breech-loaders, each blank discharge shaking the soot from the seventy foundry chimneys of Potrero Point and setting the bronze bells of the Syncretic Cathedral on Nob Hill booming in a deafening, discordant peal with the steam-sirens of sixty anchored grain-liners.

Inside the high-arched Map Room on the fourth floor of the Citadel, they had rolled Elias’s wheeled chair out onto the narrow iron gallery directly before the thirty-foot bronze relief-wall of the globe so that he might see the last magnet set into its place.

He was very small now inside the vast, dark wool folds of his old Engineer’s coat. Over the past ten days, the dropsical water that had swollen his legs for twenty years had begun to rise into his pericardium, turning his skin the color of wet wood-ash and forcing his chin upward against the leather head-rest so that he could draw the thin, whistling threads of air through his open mouth. The left side of his body was dead from shoulder to heel; his right arm, thin as a hickory ramrod inside the blue sleeve, was strapped lightly to the koa-wood armrest with a silk scarf so that his trembling fingers would not slip off the brass rail.

Yet his right eye—wide, gray, and terrible in its fixed, lidless stare—watched Major Sterling climb the iron ladder with the gilded sun-and-anchor token in his hand.
