Below the gallery, the floor of the hall was packed with the grandees of the finished world: the white-haired Cornelius Schuyler leaning on the arm of his secretary; Grand-Admiral Marquis Takashima in his ablaze of Satsuma stars; the envoys of the tributary courts of Edo, Peking, and Bangkok; and sixty senators of the Diet in their blue-and-gold robes of state.

"Set it upon the barrier reef at the twentieth parallel, Major," Lady Kaiulani called up from her place beside the right wheel of Elias’s chair. She alone wore no gold braid; in her severe black mourning bombazine, with the heavy collar of the Insular Chancelleries resting upon her breast, she looked like the priestess of an iron idol interpreting the silence of the stone. "And read the final paragraph of General Vance’s dispatch from Noumea so that the Comptroller’s clerks may enter it upon the Grand Ledger."

Sterling clapped the heavy gilded magnet onto the bronze indentation of the Coral Sea with a sharp, ringing *clink* that echoed through the hush of the room as the cannon-salutes outside momentarily paused. Turning on the narrow grating, the one-eared veteran of Lake Baikal held up the white paper ribbon from the southern cable.

"*'Admiral Sir Geoffrey Hornby died of his burns aboard our hospital-ship off Brisbane yesterday morning,'*" Sterling read, his voice cracking with old age and pride against the bronze plates of the map. "*'Before his death, he signed the convention surrendering the remaining British naval stations at Esquimalt, Hong Kong, Singapore, and Auckland to our squadrons to prevent the bombardment of Melbourne. Not a single European warship remains afloat between the Cape of Good Hope and Cape Horn. From the eightieth parallel of the Arctic ice to the borders of the Antarctic pack, the ocean is one.'*"

A deep, ragged roar went up from the sixty senators and syndicate directors below—canes hammering the parquet floor, silk hats tossed toward the chandelier, while Cornelius Schuyler wept openly into his cambric handkerchief at the thought of the Hong Kong and Singapore vaults opening their iron doors to his auditors.

Up on the iron gallery, Elias did not blink. Through the roaring in his ears—a sound that was no longer the cheering of the Diet or the booming of the twelve-inch cannon on the bay, but the vast, rushing thunder of the brown Mississippi flood and the howling of the December gale over the dead mules in the Platte coulee—he looked across the thirty feet of cast bronze.

It was all there. Every river-mouth, every coal-seam, every deep-water harbor he had seen in his mind’s eye when he stood in his torn moccasins on the granite lip of the Sierra Nevada forty-three years ago was now stamped with the little gilded suns of his Mint. There was no Philadelphia bailiff left on the earth who could read a writ against his cabin; he had bought the bailiffs, he had melted their law-books into boiler-plate, and he had fenced the half-world with steel rails.

And yet, as his wide gray eye dropped from the bronze wall to the floor below, he saw what the cheering senators did not see.

Down at the foot of the spiral gallery-stairs, Marquis Takashima had not joined in the applause; the old samurai admiral had stepped quietly to the side of the door, whispering three rapid sentences in the Satsuma dialect to two of his naval aides-de-camp, whose hands rested on their sword-hilts as their narrow eyes measured the twelve Hawaiian guardsmen standing around the telegraph repeater. And ten paces to the left, before the echoes of Sterling’s voice had even died in the dome, Cornelius Schuyler was already pulling two Boston railway directors into the shadow of the serpentine pillars, his plump, trembling fingers sketching percentages on the back of the Noumea dispatch—dividing the spoils of the Hong Kong banks before the corpse above them was cold.

*They are waiting for the last wheeze,* Elias thought inside the locked, silent iron box of his skull, while a cold, dark tide of salt water seemed to rise another inch around his labouring heart. *I bolted the continents together with eighty-pound rail, I washed their streets with canister, I gave them an ocean for a pasture—and the minute my eye shuts, the shopkeeper and the swordsman will tear the coat in half over my knees.*

He tried to lift his right hand to strike the iron railing; the silk scarf held his wrist fast to the koa-wood, and only his bloated thumb twitched once against the sea-otter fur, making a dry, scratching sound that no one below the gallery heard.

Except Kaiulani.

She looked down at his purple fingernail scraping against the pelt, and then followed the direction of his solitary, burning eye down to the floor where Takashima’s aides were edging toward the corridor door and Schuyler’s syndicate-men were huddling by the pillars. For twenty years she had worn the black bombazine of Oahu’s dead independence; for twenty years she had watched him grind the world into a single circular trough during that long, eighteen-year twilight between the winter of the Baikal ice and the fall of the Romanovs. They had built the Bering spans, they had starved St. Petersburg into revolution, and they had boiled the Dutch canals of Java—yet the machine had grown so vast that its own creators now stood like thieves in the engine-room, waiting to strip the copper pipes before the pressure-gauge dropped to zero.

Now, as she looked from the dying Caesar in the chair to the greedy, small-souled heirs waiting below to butcher sixty million people in a war of succession over customs-books and clan-fiefs, her dark face settled into a mask harder and colder than the bronze map behind them.

She leaned down over the back of the wheeled chair until her lips brushed the white, cropped bristles above Elias’s right ear, her black mantle shielding his face from the room below.

"Do not spend your breath on their collars, Elias," she whispered, her voice pitched so low it did not stir a hair on his temple as she reached into the bosom of her black dress and drew out not the phial of digitalis, but the small brass master-key to the Citadel’s palace guard-gates, together with the thick, wax-sealed cylinder of the Final Organic Statute that they had drafted in secret through the sleepless nights of his apoplexy. "If you leave them the old territories—if you leave Takashima an intact Japan and Schuyler a solid New York—they will have cannon firing across the bay before your body is in the Monterey vault. Let us break their fiefs into gravel while your eye is still open to watch them sign."

In the shadow of her black sleeve, Elias’s single gray eye shifted half an inch until it found hers. Inside the calcified cage of his ribs, where the fluid pressed like cold lead against his lungs, the old frontier arithmetic flared up in one final, triumphant blaze. He had spent forty years bolting the plates together; now, to keep any smaller man from wielding his sword after he was gone, he had to shatter the hilt into so many pieces that only the throne itself could hold them.

Down by the mahogany doors, Marquis Takashima suddenly realized that the four Hawaiian sentries outside in the corridor had just swung the heavy bronze leaves shut and dropped the iron bar into its sockets with a dull, final *thud*. The Japanese admiral spun around on his heel, his sword coming six inches out of its scabbard as he looked up toward the gallery rail where Lady Kaiulani was stepping forward to the head of the iron stairs, her left hand raised to the four Maxim-gun detachments of the Insular Guard stepping out from behind the velvet draperies of the upper loggia.

"My lords and gentlemen of the Diet," Kaiulani’s clear, musical voice rang out across the sudden, frozen hush of the rotunda, before the first man on the floor could reach the barred doors. "Do not trouble the sentries. The Providentor has observed your anxiety regarding the administration of our newly completed circumference, and before the Te Deum is sung in the cathedral, he has summoned you into executive session to witness the promulgation of the Statute of the Hundred and Twenty-Four States."

Up on the iron gallery, Elias stared down through the dizzying swimming mist of his failing vision as Major Sterling unrolled a second, smaller chart directly across the central balustrade—a map upon which the old names of history had been erased by the surveyor’s straight-edge. There was no California, no Japan, no China, no New England, and no Australia.

"Look upon the wall, Marquis Takashima," Kaiulani commanded, her voice acting as the living tongue for the paralyzed figure behind her whose crooked, swollen right forefinger slowly tapped the brass rail in a steady, relentless rhythm—*tap, tap, tap*—like the beat of a death-watch beetle in the beams of an old house. "Look upon the wall, Comptroller Schuyler. For thirty years the Confederation has tolerated the ancient borders of conquered kingdoms and rebel republics as temporary conveniences of the march. Now that the southern ocean is swept and the Siberian frontier rests upon the Yenisei, those provincial names have become nests for faction and treason."

Below the stairs, Cornelius Schuyler’s jaw sagged open as he squinted through his pince-nez at the red grid-lines bisecting the continents. "You have cut the State of New York into four separate prefectures! You have detached Manhattan from the Hudson valley and joined it to the maritime district of Nova Scotia—and the Sacramento mines are severed from the bay!"

"And the domains of Satsuma and Choshu are dissolved into numbered insular cantons!" Takashima roared, his bronze face mottling with apoplectic fury as he took two steps up the iron spiral stair, only to halt as the four brass water-jackets of the Maxim guns in the loggia swung downward with a synchronized, oiled *click*, training their muzzles directly upon his starred breast. "This is the work of a woman’s cabal! The Tenno at Kyoto signed an alliance of crowns, not an incorporation into an American census-roll!"

Up in the koa-wood chair, Elias felt the dark tide rise another inch inside his chest, drowning the lower lobes of his lungs until the golden chandelier above the rotunda turned the color of dried blood; yet with a terrifying, last spasm of the muscles in his right neck, he forced his chin off the leather pad. His lips parted, and from the ruined cavern of his throat came two words—thick, slurred, and gravelly as a landslide in the Sierra, yet unmistakably his own:

*"Sign... it."* 

The two syllables dropped into the rotunda like a two-thousand-pound shell from the *Elias Thorne*. Every senator on the floor flinched backward from the gallery rail; even Takashima’s fingers froze upon his lacquered hilt as he stared up into that solitary, lidless gray eye burning down from the shadow of the bronze map.

"You hear the voice of your Sovereign," Kaiulani said, descending three steps of the iron stair with the open parchment roll held out before her like a shield. "One hundred and twenty-four imperial states, drawn by watershed, coal-seam, and tonnage capacity—each containing five million souls, each governed by a civil prefect appointed from Monterey and a military commandant drawn from the opposite shore of the ocean. No Japanese soldier will ever again garrison an Asian island; no American regiment will sit within two thousand miles of its native river; and no bank on Montgomery Street will clear a bill of exchange without the counter-stamp of the Bureau of Integration. Step to the porphyry table, Marquis. The Providentor’s eye is upon you, and the gunners have their thumbs upon the triggers."

***

Three weeks later, the old man’s eye was finally shut—sealed beneath six inches of soldered sheet-lead and five tons of polished Sierra granite in the crypt of the Monterey Basilica—yet the ghost of his iron geometry sat heavier upon the neck of the world than his living hand had ever done.

On an afternoon in middle September, when the dry, scorching *diablo* wind blew down from the inner valleys across the bay, turning the sky above San Francisco into a brass dome dusted with red alkali and the soot of the Potrero smelters, Lady Kaiulani sat at the head of the long teakwood table in the Bureau of Integration.

The chamber occupied the entire third story of the old Mint building on Fifth Street, its tall windows barred with wrought-iron grilles against the street-mobs that still gathered weekly around the bread-depots. There were no silk banners here, no bronze maps of conquered oceans. From floor to eighteen-foot ceiling, the walls were lined with galvanized iron pigeon-holes packed with forty thousand sheepskin-bound digests of local law: the *Code Napoléon* of Quebec and Cochin-China, the *Great Qing Legal Code* of the Yangtze provinces, the Anglo-Saxon common law of Massachusetts and New South Wales, the feudal house-statutes of the Tokugawa clans, the *Adat* customary rolls of Java, and the oral *Kapu* genealogies of the Polynesian reefs.

The air was ninety degrees and smelled of sour flour-paste, scorching blotting-paper, and the bitter sweat of twelve men who had been locked in the room with the Regent-Chancellor since six in the morning, trying to hammer the customs of half the human race into a single volume before the autumn assizes opened.

"It cannot be reconciled without provoking a general rising along the Hwang-ho, Your Highness!" cried Magistrate Shen, the former President of the Peking Board of Punishments, his long fingernails clicking furiously against the ivory beads of his abacus as he glared across the ink-stained teak at Chief Justice Field of the California bench and Judge Hoshino of the Edo Cassation Court. "By the forty-second statute of the new Canton Six-Foot Code, your American clerks have written that a son who strikes his father in a dispute over railway wages shall be fined ten silver thalers or sentenced to thirty days on the county road-gang! In the Middle Kingdom, parricide or filial battery is an abomination that shakes the pillars of the sky! If the village elders of Shantung hear that a boy may strike his sire for the price of a pig and walk free, they will tear down the telegraph poles and burn your district magistrates in their beds! The penalty must remain the *Ling-ch'i*—the slicing of the flesh by a thousand cuts in the market-square!"

"And am I to instruct an Anglo-Saxon jury in Boston or Melbourne," thundered Justice Field, his white whiskers bristling as he slammed his copy of Blackstone’s *Commentaries* down upon the teak, sending a cloud of red pounce-dust into the hot air, "that a twenty-one-year-old mechanic who quarrels with his father over a pint of beer is to be tied to a post on Boston Common and carved into beef-steaks by a Cantonese executioner? And what of this clause inserted by Judge Hoshino from the Satsuma house-laws—that a military officer of the third rank may strike off the head of a civilian merchant who fails to dismount from his buggy when the imperial post-carriage passes? Try that on Broadway or in Sydney, madam, and all the Maxim guns in your arsenal will not keep the stones in the pavement!"

Judge Hoshino did not raise his voice; he sat with his small, dry hands tucked into the sleeves of his black alpaca judicial gown, his spectacles glinting coldly. "In the seventy-ninth prefecture—which your surveyors formerly called Victoria—three Australian teamsters spat upon the sedan-chair of Colonel Kuroda’s wife last Tuesday and refused to yield the crown of the road. Because the local magistrate was an Englishman who applied your 'common law' of assault, the teamsters were released on five thalers' bail. That night, two companies of the Choshu garrison marched out of their barracks and burned the teamsters' suburb to the ground. If the law does not protect the honor of the sword, Your Highness, the sword will write its own docket in fire."

Kaiulani rested her temples against the tips of her ungloved fingers. Beneath the heavy black bombazine of her dress, the whale-bone stays cut into her ribs with every breath, and her eyes burned from reading six-point legal proofs in three languages by the glare of the electric bulbs. 

For twenty years she had watched Elias cut through such knots with a single stroke of cavalry saber or a threat to open the sluice-gates. While the conqueror lived, terror had served for jurisprudence; men obeyed contradictory decrees because they knew the crippled Titan on Rincon Hill would send a monitor up their river if they argued. Now Elias was cold lead in Monterey. She had locked Schuyler and Takashima into the Council of Regency with bayonets at their backs, yet she was discovering the terrible secret that awaits every usurper who inherits a machine built by a giant: that you can conquer an ocean with steam and nitro-glycerine, but you cannot govern eight hundred million souls at breakfast with an eighteen-inch gun.

Every concession she made to Justice Field’s Americans was telegraphed within the hour by Takashima’s spies to Edo as proof that the white syndicate was reducing the samurai to coolies; every sop she threw to Shen’s mandarins was printed on secret hand-presses in the cellars of Philadelphia to prove that a Polynesian witch had sold Christendom to the pagans.

"We will have neither the thousand cuts of Peking nor the twelve shopkeepers in a jury-box of Boston," Kaiulani said, her voice cutting cleanly through the babble of the twelve jurists as she dipped her brush into the red vermilion ink-stone that stood beside her English steel pens. "You are still thinking like parish clerks of dead nations. There is no Shantung, Magistrate Shen; there is only the Forty-Second Agricultural Canton. There is no Massachusetts, Justice Field; there is only the Ninth Atlantic Industrial District."

She drew the master-proof of the *Codex Pacificus* across the teak and struck out three pages of Field’s habeas corpus clauses with a single diagonal slash of wet crimson.

"From the first of October," she dictated to the three stenographers sitting behind her chair, "all trials by civilian jury between the Yenisei and the Atlantic are abolished as relics of parliamentary sedition. In their place, every canton court shall consist of a Tripartite Bench: one magistrate of American birth, one of Asian, and one of Insular blood, none of whom may sit within three thousand miles of the province where he was born. As for filial rebellion and insult to the uniform—since the State is now the universal father of all subjects and the sole bearer of the sword—a son who strikes his parent or a teamster who obstructs an imperial officer commits neither a family sin nor a common misdemeanor. He commits *Sabotage of the Imperial Order*, punishable across all one hundred and twenty-four states by ten years’ penal servitude in the Bering tunnel-gangs. Write it down, gentlemen. If the law is too heavy for their tastes, at least it will crush every neck with the same weight."

***

To the Chronicler who walks the broad, granite-paved esplanades of San Francisco or New Osaka in these closing years of the nineteenth century, nothing marks the final burial of the old American Republic so irrevocably as the silence that falls over the cities during the third week of every October.

In the barbarous decades before the Pivot—as the curious student may still read in the yellowing files of the *New York Herald* or the *Charleston Mercury* preserved in the locked stacks of the Chancery—the autumn season along the North American littoral was a time of drunken Saturnalia which the ancients called an Election. Every four years, the workshops were emptied, the counting-houses were shuttered, and millions of unlettered ploughmen, newly landed European ditch-diggers, and tavern-keepers marched through the mud behind brass bands and pine-tar torches, roaring the names of rival country lawyers and stuffing slips of printed rag-paper into wooden boxes to determine who should command the fleets and rob the post-offices for the next forty-eight months.

Today, the pine-tar torches are gone, and the wooden ballot-boxes have long since been split up to kindled the assay-furnaces of the Mint. In their stead stands the Examination Shed.

It was the supreme stroke of Lady Kaiulani’s Regency—conceived in the winter after the Providentor’s burial, when the old millionaire syndics of Montgomery Street and the clan-admirals of Satsuma believed they could turn their seats on the Joint Boards into hereditary baronies—to borrow the most ancient engine of Oriental despotism and weld it to the steel chassis of Western polytechnics. If the hundred and twenty-four fragmented states were not to fly apart by centrifugal force, they required a priesthood of clerks who owed their bread neither to a New York banker’s purse nor to a Japanese daimyo’s pedigree, but solely to the competitive stamp of the Imperial Seal.

To witness the Grand Triennial Examination at the Berkeley compound across the bay from the Golden Gate is to behold the true furnace in which the citizenry of the twentieth century is cast. Here, upon a leveled plateau above the oak-groves, rise ten thousand identical, windowless cells of corrugated Birmingham iron and poured Portland cement, laid out in numbered rows like the honeycombs of a mechanical hive and surrounded by a double stockade of electrified barbed wire patrolled by the Hawaiian Guard.

On the eighteenth of October, before the morning fog has lifted from the water, ten thousand youths between their eighteenth and twenty-second years—the survivors of the rigorous prefectural eliminations held the previous spring in Melbourne, Hankow, Boston, Irkutsk, and Honolulu—file through the main iron turnstiles at the sound of the steam-siren. They are stripped to the skin in the carbolic disinfecting-sheds to ensure that no logarithmic table or political crib is sewn into a hem; each youth—whether he be the fair-haired grandson of a Virginia planter, the spectacled heir of a Soochow silk-mandarin, or the broad-shouldered son of a Maori chief—is dressed in an identical, coarse gray tunic of unbleached prison-duck stamped across the shoulder-blades with a five-digit cipher. He is given two dip-pens, a cake of India ink, a slide-rule of standardized boxwood, a tin bucket of boiled rice and salt beef, and a wooden board that serves alike for seat, bed, and writing-desk inside his four-by-six iron cubicle.

When the heavy steel drop-bars clang shut across the ends of the hundred alleys at the stroke of noon, sealing the ten thousand inside their iron tombs for seventy-two unbroken hours, the silence beneath the fog is so profound that one can hear the scratching of ten thousand steel nibs upon foolscap half a mile away—a dry, rustling murmur like a million silkworms devouring a mulberry forest.

No question of rhetoric, of natural rights, or of the history of dead parliaments ever sullies the white paper pushed through the food-slots by the silent, soft-shoed proctors. Under the *Curriculum of the Three Harmonies* drafted by the Bureau of Integration, the youth who aspires to wear the silver anchor of an Imperial Prefect must prove his orthodoxy in harder coin: during the first twenty-four hours, he must render an edict of the Monterey Chancery concurrently into classical literary Chinese, court Japanese, and English statute-prose without a single variance of legal meaning; during the second, he must calculate the ballistic trajectory of an eighteen-inch melinite shell allowing for Coriolis drift and barometric pressure, together with the coal-tonnage and axle-grease required to move an army corps of thirty thousand men six hundred leagues by broad-gauge rail at thirty below zero; and during the final night, by the glare of the single naked electric bulb suspended above his head, he must compose a five-thousand-word dissertation upon the *Moral Necessity of the Pacific Pivot*, demonstrating from the commentaries of Thucydides, Confucius, and the dispatches of Elias Thorne that parliamentary liberty is merely the infancy of anarchy.

Every morning at six, the iron doors of those cubicles where the scratching has ceased are unlocked by the Cantonese orderlies, and the casualties of the meritocracy are carried out on canvas stretchers: boys from the Ohio valleys who have gone raving mad from seventy hours of logarithmic tables under a sixty-watt glare and tried to dash their brains out against the corrugated iron; consumptive scholars from Kyoto who have coughed their lungs onto the wet ink of their railway-schedules; and third-generation scions of the old Boston and Charleston patriciate who, realizing by the third afternoon that their family names carry no weight behind a five-digit number and that failure means seven years as a private conscript in the Sumatra rubber-swamps, have opened their own femoral arteries with the sharpened steel nibs of their government pens.

Down along the central elevated catwalk that bisects the ten thousand iron roofs, Chief Examiner Shen and General Marcus Vance the younger walked slowly through the drizzling October dusk, their rubberized capes gleaming under the arc-lamps as they looked down through the wire-mesh ventilators into the rows of lighted cells below.

"Candidate Four-Four-Zero-Nine in the third Canton row has stopped writing, General," Shen remarked, pausing beside a ventilator stack and peering down through his thick horn-rimmed spectacles at the top of a cropped yellow head bowed motionless over a blotting-pad fifty feet below their boots. "That is the youngest grandson of Comptroller Schuyler. He has been staring at the third problem of the Siberian coal-modulus for four hours without moving his slide-rule, and his candle-ration is burned to the socket."

Young Marcus Vance did not look down through the wire grate; he pulled his radium-dialed chronometer from his wet cuff, noted the remaining forty-one minutes before the final siren, and turned his pale, unblinking gaze toward the eastern gate of the compound, where a closed black carriage bearing the private crest of the New York Banking Syndicate was waiting in the mud behind two steaming horses.

"The old Comptroller asked me at the Council table yesterday if the mathematics paper might be waived for a boy whose grandfather financed the Market Street Mint," Marcus said, his clipped tone carrying no more inflection than the hum of the electric dynamos at the end of the yard as he rested his gloved hand upon the master bell-switch bolted to the iron post beside them. "He reminded me that when the Providentor was still alive—during the autumn before the stroke in the conservatory, when the old man spent his last walking afternoon inside the State Archives—even Elias Thorne had allowed the syndicate directors to buy exemptions for their eldest sons."

Shen adjusted his spectacles against the cold mist drifting off the bay, his narrow shoulders stiffening beneath his oiled silk cape. "And how did you answer him, General?"

"I told him that when the Providentor walked through the State Archives in the autumn of eighty-five to review the Great Triennial Census, I was the aide who carried his portfolio," Marcus replied, his eyes fixed on the carriage lamps flickering through the rain. "We stood for three hours in the subterranean vaults beneath the Mint, where the Hollerith punch-card tabulators were sorting the tallies from the Yangtze, the Mississippi, and the Yukon. Three hundred million subjects, Magistrate. I watched the old man run his scarred thumb down the summary folios—eighty million in the American provinces, thirty-eight million in the Japanese archipelago, a hundred and seventy million in the Chinese prefectures, twelve million across the southern islands and the Siberian rail-corridors. Do you know what he said to me when the Chief Statistician showed him that the old white families of the Atlantic and California made up less than one-fifth of the military muster-rolls?"

Down in the cubicle beneath their boots, young Schuyler suddenly pushed his wooden board away with a scrape that was audible through the wire mesh, dropping his face into his ink-stained palms.

"The Providentor did not record that observation in the official gazette," Shen murmured cautiously.

"He did not record it for the syndicate directors," Marcus said. "He looked at the brass counting-dials clicking off the births in Hankow and Osaka, and he took me by the elbow—his grip could still bruise the bone through a wool tunic then—and he said: *'Marcus, your father and I built the frame of this house with frontiersmen and Rebel veterans because they were the timber nearest the axe. Look at the numbers in that book. Three hundred million souls cannot be held by a handful of New York bankers’ nephews and Satsuma cousins sitting on velvet cushions. Within ten years, the blood that built this empire will be a drop of tallow in an ocean of brine. If you let Schuyler and Takashima turn the prefectures into family pastures after I am under the stone, the three hundred million will tear the fences down in a single night. Grind the names out of them, boy. Make the ledger the only father a magistrate has.'*"

Marcus looked back down at the glowing green dial on his wrist. The second-hand swept across the twelve. forty minutes had not elapsed, yet Candidate Four-Four-Zero-Nine had already upset his porcelain ink-pot across the blank pages of his Siberian coal calculation, the black fluid soaking into the coarse gray duck of his sleeve as his shoulders shook with dry, silent sobs.

"A candidate who deliberately spoils his examination folio before the siren forfeits his remaining time under Article Nine," Marcus noted clinically, pulling the heavy iron lever of the sector-alarm down until the copper contacts bit.

Below them, along the wet concrete alley of the third Canton row, the electric gong over Cell Four-Four-Zero-Nine gave two short, strident clangs. Before the echo had died against the corrugated Birmingham iron, two Cantonese orderlies and a Hawaiian provost-corporal trotted down the narrow passage with a key-ring and a pair of canvas-webbing ankle-straps. The heavy drop-bar clattered up; the cell door swung outward into the drizzle.

"Let us go down to the turnstile, Magistrate Shen," Marcus said, turning on his heel and descending the cleated iron steps of the catwalk with the brisk, unhurried stride he used on the parade-ground of the Imperial Military Academy at Monterey. "Comptroller Schuyler has been sitting in his brougham since four o’clock with a hot-water brick at his feet, expecting to drive his grandson up to Nob Hill for supper. It would be discourteous to keep a member of the Regency Council waiting in the mud."

At the main eastern gate, where the double stockade of electrified barbed wire parted before a guardhouse of gray Sierra granite, the air smelled strongly of wet horse-manure, ozone from the transformer-sheds, and the carbolic wash tracking off the boots of the guard-relief. 

Inside the fenced courtyard behind the guardhouse—which served both as the processing-pen for failed candidates and as the primary coastal depot for the Cadet Corps of the Imperial Military Academy—four hundred eighteen-year-old youths stood drawn up in four hollow squares under the sizzling blue glare of the carbon-arc lamps. Marcus had spent the morning inspecting their drill before crossing the bay to the Examination Sheds, and as he stepped off the catwalk stairs onto the wet gravel, the cadet-captains brought their squads to rigid attention with a single, synchronized slap of leather rifle-slings against coarse blue wool.

They were the physical incarnation of the census ledger Elias Thorne had read in the subterranean vaults: in the first rank of the right-hand square stood a six-foot youth from the Shensi hill-country beside the dark-skinned son of a Samoan harbor-chief and a red-haired boy from the Pennsylvania iron-towns; in the second stood a samurai cadet from Hizen flank-to-flank with a Tagalog from Luzon and a boy from the Melbourne sheep-downs. None of them bore a surname upon his brass collar-plate—only the Roman numeral of his birth-canton and the four digits of his Academy matriculation. Since their twelfth year, when the Triennial Assessors had taken them from their parish schools, they had not spoken their mother-tongues except as tactical exercises; they ate the same ration of pressed bean-curd and salted beef, slept on the same iron cots, and recited the *Maxims of the Providentor* in unison every morning before the sun-and-anchor rose above the parade-ground.

"Present—*arms!*" barked the cadet-adjutant—a youth born in the conquered ruins of Atlanta who spoke with the clipped, nasal accent of the New Edo staff schools.

Four hundred magazine-rifles snapped vertical before four hundred identical chests, the bayonets gleaming like a row of wet icicles in the drizzle.

Marcus returned the salute with two fingers to his oilskin cap-brim, his cold eyes sweeping the line with quiet satisfaction. His father had been forced to bribe Missouri bushwhackers with silver bags and threaten Hawaiian kings with Gatling guns to keep his columns moving; these boys in the yard behind him had never heard of the United States Constitution, had never seen a Tokugawa shogun, and would shoot their own fathers upon the church steps of Boston or Kyoto if the order came down the pneumatic tube bearing the stamp of the Chancery.

Outside the iron turnstile, the door of the black syndicate carriage swung open. Old Cornelius Schuyler, leaning heavily upon his gold-headed ebony cane and the arm of a liveried footman, stepped down onto the plank walk laid across the mud. Beside him—having ridden up from the Oakland ferry-slip in an Admiralty steam-phaeton whose boiler was still hissing softly behind the hedge—walked Grand-Admiral Marquis Takashima, wrapped in his heavy naval boat-cloak.

"General Vance!" Schuyler called out, his wheezing voice rising sharp and anxious through the iron bars of the gate as he peered past Marcus’s shoulder into the processing-yard, where the two Cantonese orderlies were just emerging from the third alley, gripping the elbows of a stumbling, bare-headed boy in a stained gray prison-duck tunic. "Why is Arthur being brought out by the hospital-men before the six o’clock siren? Is the boy taken ill with the chill? Bring him to the carriage at once—my physician is inside with hot brandy!"

Marcus stopped three feet behind the locked iron turnstile, his hands clasped neatly behind the small of his back, while Chief Examiner Shen stepped to his left elbow holding the wet, ink-blotted examination folio between two pairs of brass tongs as if it were a dead rat.

"There is no Arthur Schuyler in this compound, Comptroller," Marcus said pleasantly. "If you refer to Candidate Four-Four-Zero-Nine of the Seventh Maritime District, his examination concluded nine minutes ago when he overturned his ink-horn upon the third sheet of the Siberian logistics problem. Under the Statute of the Hundred and Twenty-Four States, which you and the Marquis countersigned in the Rotunda two months ago, a candidate who fails the polytechnic minimum by reason of wilful defacement is automatically inducted into the Second Class Pioneer Reserve for seven years’ service on the southern frontier."

The boy between the orderlies raised his pale, tear-streaked face as the arc-light struck his cropped yellow hair. "Grandfather!" he choked out, wrenching furiously against the Cantonese corporals’ grip as a Hawaiian blacksmith stepped forward from the induction-shed with a pair of heavy steel shears to clip the candidate’s number-patch from his shoulder and replace it with the yellow canvas brassard of the Sumatra rubber-battalions. "Grandfather, don't let them put me in the steamer! The logarithms were for sixty-below temperatures—nobody taught us the Siberian tables at the New York grammar school! They changed the questions on purpose!"

Old Schuyler’s face went the color of wet tallow, then swelled to a mottled, apoplectic purple beneath his white side-whiskers. He struck the iron bars of the turnstile with the ferrule of his ebony cane.

"Unlock this gate, Major Shen!" the seventy-year-old financier roared, his voice cracking in the wet dusk as two of the young Academy cadets inside the fence automatically took a half-step forward, their thumbs resting on the safety-catches of their magazine-rifles. "General Vance, have you lost your senses? That boy is the sole heir to the Schuyler-Livingston banking trust! His father underwrote forty million thalers of the Yukon Gold Reserve when you were in short trousers! You cannot ship the grandson of a Regent of the Realm to dig ditches in a malarial swamp alongside coolies and felons because he missed a sum in algebra!"

Beside Schuyler, Marquis Takashima stepped forward to the wet bars, his narrow dark eyes passing from the weeping boy to the four hundred multi-ethnic cadets standing like bronze statues in the yard behind Marcus’s back. The old Satsuma warlord’s voice was low and vibrant with menace.

"My own grand-nephew, Shimazu Tadao, sits in the ninth row of that shed tonight, General Vance," Takashima said. "Am I to understand that if a clerk from Peking marks his Chinese syntax deficient at six o’clock, the heir of the Satsuma house is likewise to be sheared like a sheep by your Hawaiian turnkeys? While the Providentor breathed, there was respect for the blood that forged the sword."

"While the Providentor breathed, Marquis, he was forced to humor the pride of old men who remembered the world before the Pivot," answered a clear, musical voice from the shadow of the Granite guardhouse.

Lady Kaiulani stepped out from beneath the stone arch onto the wet gravel beside Marcus Vance. She had come across from San Francisco on the five-thirty launch; she wore her high-collared black bombazine beneath a cloak of dark sea-otter fur, and behind her walked Colonel Kalakaua and six troopers of the Insular Guard with holstered self-loading pistols at their belts.

She walked straight to the iron bars until less than twelve inches of rainy air separated her pale, severe face from the noses of her two fellow Regents.

"The Providentor is in his granite box at Monterey, gentlemen," Kaiulani said softly, her dark eyes holding Takashima’s gaze without a tremor while the Hawaiian blacksmith behind them forced young Schuyler to his knees on the wet concrete and closed the iron rivet of the Sumatra identification-collar around the boy’s neck with a sharp *clink* of his hammer. "Before he closed his eye on the gallery, he gave us the Statute of the Hundred and Twenty-Four States so that there would be no Schuyler banking trust and no Satsuma clan ten years from tonight. If I spare Mr. Schuyler’s grandson from the rubber-boats at six o’clock, how shall General Vance command those four hundred boys behind him to die at the Yenisei trenches at seven?"

"This is a coup d'état against the Council of Regency!" Schuyler gasped, his plump hands gripping the wet iron palings as his grandson was hauled to his feet and pushed toward the covered gangway leading down to the quarantine wharf, where the lights of the Batavia transport were already glowing green and red through the fog. "Marquis—you have the Second Cruiser Squadron anchored off Goat Island! Order your captains to land six hundred marines at the ferry-slip before that transport clears the pier! And I will wire the Clearing House in New York and Osaka to stop payment on every garrison draft from here to Irkutsk at nine tomorrow morning! We will see how long Her Highness and this boy-general can play at being Caesar without a silver thaler in the chest or a ship in the bay!"

Takashima’s right hand dropped to the hilt of his sword, his nostrils flaring as he turned half around toward his waiting steam-phaeton on the road. "My launch is at the foot of the hill, Comptroller. Once I am aboard the *Kamehameha II*—"

"Your launch was impounded by the cadets of the Third Maritime Company twenty minutes ago, Marquis," young Marcus Vance interrupted, not raising his voice half a tone as he drew a folded white telegraph-form from his khaki breast pocket and held it up against the iron grate where the blue arc-light fell across the wet ink. "And as for the Second Cruiser Squadron off Goat Island—you are quite right that a divided fleet is a danger to the public peace. At four-fifteen this afternoon, acting under the Emergency Integration Warrant signed by the Chancellor, the newly commissioned cadet-officers of the Naval Polytechnic relieved every Satsuma post-captain in the bay of his command. Your cruisers are currently under the guns of the Alcatraz eighteen-inch batteries with mixed crews of Californian, Cantonese, and Hawaiian artificers at the throttles."

Takashima froze, his boot suspended an inch above the mud of the road, his bronze cheek turning the color of old tallow under the lamp. "My captains... relieved by schoolboys?"

"By Imperial Citizens, Marquis," Kaiulani corrected him gently, her gloved hand resting upon the iron turnstile lock while down at the wharf the deep, mournful blast of the Batavia transport’s steam-whistle announced the casting off of the conscript-barges. "And you need not trouble the telegraph operators in New York tonight, Mr. Schuyler. At noon today, the Bureau of Integration foreclosed upon the private shares of the Schuyler-Livingston Syndicate for arrears on the Siberian war-assessment. Your clerks on Montgomery Street are now civil servants of the Fifth Fiscal Grade, answering directly to Magistrate Shen."

She nodded once to Colonel Kalakaua. The heavy iron gate of the guardhouse did not open to let the two old men inside; instead, twenty cadets of the Imperial Academy marched out of the side sally-port in double file, their bayonets fixed, and surrounded the black syndicate carriage and the Admiralty phaeton in the muddy lane.

"You will not be harmed, my lords," Kaiulani said as the rain began to beat harder against the ten thousand iron roofs of the Examination Sheds behind her, drowning the faint, desperate cries of young Schuyler from the wharf below in a vast, metallic drumming that sounded like the marching of three hundred million feet. "The Empire does not make martyrs of its bookkeepers. You will drive back to the ferry under the escort of General Vance’s cadets, and tomorrow afternoon at four you will sit in your accustomed chairs upon the high balcony of the Chancery beside me to review the autumn parade. The people of San Francisco must see that the Triumvirate is united—even if only two of us still hold the pen."

***

By three o’clock the following afternoon, the October gale had blown itself clear out to sea, leaving the sky above the Golden Gate scoured to a hard, brilliant dome of imperial blue that curved unbroken from the redwoods of Marin to the smoking slag-heaps of the Contra Costa shore.

High upon the western facade of the Citadel on Rincon Hill—seventy feet above the granite terrace where the bronze statue of Elias Thorne, cast thirty feet tall from the melted cannon of Washington, London, and St. Petersburg, stood looking out toward the sunset with his iron walking-stick planted upon the globe—the tall French doors of the Chancery balcony stood open to the salt wind.

Inside the threshold, just out of sight of the half-million subjects who packed the stepped avenues and roof-tops down to the water’s edge, Cornelius Schuyler and Marquis Takashima sat side by side in two high-backed chairs of carved Hawaiian koa-wood. To the binoculars of the foreign consuls down in the plaza, the two aged oligarchs appeared to be sitting in state beneath the silk canopy of the Rising Sun, wearing their full gold-braided collars and the broad blue ribands of the Order of the Golden Gate. Only when one stood within three paces of the balcony rail could one see that their ankles were strapped to the chair-legs behind the velvet valance with heavy canvas webbing, and that two twenty-year-old cadet-lieutenants of the Academy—one a broad-faced youth from the Amur Cossack settlements, the other a dark-eyed boy from the Cantonese dock-guilds—stood directly behind their headrests with cocked nine-shot pistols hidden beneath their dress capes.

Lady Kaiulani walked out past their knees to the stone balustrade, General Marcus Vance the younger stepping precisely to her left elbow.

Below them stretched the City of the World—no longer an American seaport, nor an Asian colony, but the monumental, smoking capital of the Great Arena. For twelve miles around the vast horseshoe of the bay, the chaotic wooden shanties of the gold-rush era had been swept away by the straight-edge of the Imperial Engineers. From the foot of Telegraph Hill to the southern slips of Hunters Point ran a continuous, three-tiered embankment of gray Sierra granite and red brick: on the lowest level, sixty ocean-going cargo-liners and armored depot-ships lay moored bow-to-stern beneath a forest of hydraulic gantry-cranes that clanked and hissed in unified cadence, swinging bales of raw Kiangsu silk, ingots of Broken Hill silver, and crates of Lowell textiles directly onto the electric freight-cars of the Belt Line; on the second tier, elevated thirty feet above the mud upon cast-iron colonnades, thundered the broad-gauge express trains arriving directly from Boston, Irkutsk, and Peking via the Bering Bridge without a single change of locomotive; and rising up the steep hills behind the smoke-canopy stood the geometric terraces of the ministries—white marble Roman porticoes crowned with sweeping green copper roofs in the style of Kyoto and Peking, their avenues shaded by alternating rows of Australian eucalyptus and California palms.

And down the hundred-foot width of Market Street, between twin walls of dark blue-and-gold banners that snapped taut in the wind off the water, marched the autumn levy of the Hundred and Twenty-Four States.

There were no regimental colors bearing the names of Virginia, Satsuma, or New South Wales. As the forty-piece brass bands at the head of each brigade crashed out the slow, metallic chords of the Imperial Anthem—the heavy European tubas answered by the deep boom of *taiko* drums and the wail of island conches—ten thousand men in identical tunics of slate-gray and navy wool stepped across the granite paving-stones as a single machine. The sun, dropping toward the Farallones in a blaze of clear sunset gold, caught the forest of eighteen-inch bayonets and turned the avenue into a river of moving fire,

while the air rising up to the balcony carried the mingled, unmistakable breath of the finished realm: salt spray from the Gate, the sharp ozone of the electric street-railways, burned Borneo fuel-oil from the battleships anchored off Alcatraz, and the heavy aloeswood smoke drifting from the great Cathedral of the Sun and St. Michael on the crest of Nob Hill.

"The transport from Batavia cleared the heads at dawn, Your Highness," young Marcus Vance said, his clipped voice pitched just above the roar of the brass bands below as he rested his gloved hand upon the cold stone balustrade beside hers. "And the new prefects from the Berkeley examination will take their oaths in the Rotunda at six. Of the ten thousand who entered the sheds on Monday, twelve hundred passed the third modulus. Not one of them bears a family name that appeared in the peerage rolls of sixty-five."

Behind them in the shadow of the canopy, Cornelius Schuyler’s head drooped forward onto his gold-laced breast, a thin trickle of saliva wetting his white cravat as he stared down through blurred, watery eyes at the gray bayonets of the youths who had taken his bank and his grandson in the same night. Beside him, Marquis Takashima sat rigid as an idol of lacquered wood, his eyes fixed not on the street, but upon the thirty-foot bronze shoulders of Elias Thorne’s statue towering at the foot of the terrace.

Kaiulani looked out past the bronze head of the dead Titan, across the mile of sparkling blue water where the eighteen-inch turrets of the *Elias Thorne* and the *Kamehameha II* swung their fifty-foot barrels skyward to fire the sunset salute. She was fifty years old; her youth lay buried under the coral blocks of Fort Street in Honolulu, and the man who had broken her kingdom and chained her to his chariot was rotting under five tons of stone at Monterey. Yet as the first blank charge from the fleet roared across the bay—shaking the glass in the conservatory dome overhead and making the half-million faces down in the plaza turn upward toward her black-robed figure on the balcony as if she were the sun itself—she felt the cold, terrible exultation that Elias had felt on the snowy lip of the Sierra forty-three years before.

The carpenter was dead, and the wood had forgotten it had ever been trees; there remained only the iron, and the hand that held the gauge.

"General Vance," Kaiulani said, not turning her head from the blinding gold of the western water as she reached into her black bombazine sleeve and drew out the small brass cylinder containing the winter mobilization tables for the Southern Isthmus, holding it out toward the young marshal while the second cannon-salute thundered off the hills, "when the parade has passed the Mint, you will have the surgeons certify that Comptroller Schuyler and Marquis Takashima have suffered a grave exhaustion from the afternoon’s ceremonies, and remove them to the sanatorium at Santa Cruz. And when you have locked their doors, order the special train for the Tehuantepec and Darien line. Before the old man took to his bed in eighty-four, he stood with your father’s engineers upon the red clay of Culebra and swore that the Atlantic ships would pass into our ocean through an iron trough of his own cutting. The northern bridge is bolted; you and I are going south to inspect the final ditch."

***

In the private diaries of the Providentor, which Lady Kaiulani carried southward in her velvet dispatch-box aboard the coastal packet *Culebra* during that first week of November, the entry for the nineteenth of March, 1884—written during the last journey Elias Thorne had ever made upon his own two feet before the dropsy chained him to the conservatory—remained blotted with the brown stains of Darien mud.

He had stood that afternoon upon the high, blasted ledge of Gold Hill, fifty miles south of the Caribbean surf, leaning both hands upon his iron walking-stick while the equatorial sun beat down through a yellow fog of dynamite fumes and pulverized red cucaracha shale. Below his boots, where the French canal syndicate of Monsieur de Lesseps had gone bankrupt in eighty-two before the Pacifica gunboats foreclosed upon the Colombian concessions, stretched a steaming, mile-wide wound torn straight through the green spine of the Americas.

It was not a river-valley; it was an open-pit slaughterhouse of stone and steam. Three hundred feet down in the boiling red trough of the Cut, seventy Bucyrus-Nagasaki steam-shovels—monstrous iron crabs weighing ninety tons apiece, their dipper-buckets armed with forged manganese-steel teeth—chewed relentlessly into the sliding clay terraces. With every biting swing of their crane-booms, the machines belched thick columns of coal-black smoke and white exhaust-steam that refused to rise in the ninety-eight-degree humidity, hanging instead between the raw red cliffs like the breath of a subterranean dragon. Mile-long dirt-trains, drawn by geared Baldwin locomotives whose brass bells clanged in an endless, deafening chorus, crawled along seven tiers of narrow-gauge track notched into the mud walls, hauling the disemboweled guts of the Cordilleras out toward the Pacific dump-heaps at Naos Island.

"The Frenchmen tried to dig a sea-level ditch with donkey-carts and Martinique spades, Protector," Major Sterling had shouted into Elias’s ear over the roar of forty pneumatic rock-drills hammering into the basalt shelf twenty yards below them. Even then, three years before his death, Elias’s breath had come in thick, whistling pulls against the wet heat that smelled of rotting jungle lianas, nitro-glycerine headaches, and the sour tallow of the shovel-gears. "Their clay slides came down from Contractor’s Hill faster than their buckets could lift the muck! We have stepped the banks back at forty-five degrees, laid eighty-pound broad-gauge rail on every bench, and put sixty thousand Cantonese, Jamaican, and Georgian convict-navvies into the trench in three eight-hour relays under electric arc-lamps!"

Elias had wiped the hot red mud-spatter from his cheek with a rough thumb, his solitary clear eye squinting down through the sulfur-haze toward the southern end of the gorge, where the colossal twin concrete chambers of the Miraflores Locks rose like the unfinished temple-pylons of Karnak above the mangrove swamps.

"Do not talk to me of the Frenchmen, Sterling," Elias had rasped, planting his stick deeper into the greasy red clay as a five-ton charge of blasting-gelatine detonated at the bottom of the Bas Obispo reach, sending a dull, subterranean thump up through the soles of his cavalry boots and raining splinters of blue trap-rock across the tin roofs of the guard-sheds. "De Lesseps was a stock-jobber digging a turnpike for Liverpool tramp-steamers. I am cutting a sally-port for the Battle Fleet. How wide are those lock-chambers at the sill?"

"One hundred and twenty feet clear between the concrete walls, sir, and a thousand feet from mitre-gate to mitre-gate," Sterling had answered, opening his oilskin plan-roll against the drizzle that fell every afternoon at three o’clock like warm soup from the Chagres hills. "Wide enough to pass the *Elias Thorne* or the *Imperator* with ten feet of water to spare on either beam, and fed by the artificial lake we have dammed behind the Gatun spillways. When the eighty-foot steel leaves of those gates swing shut, Protector, the Atlantic Ocean ceases to be an ocean. It becomes a back-canal of the San Francisco Admiralty. A squadron of our turret-ships can steam out of the Golden Gate, pass through this hill in nine hours without coaling, and lay their eighteen-inch guns off the mouth of the Thames or the Narrows of New York before the European cables know they have cleared Balboa."

Elias had looked down at the swarming floor of the Cut, where a gang of two hundred bare-chested men in the striped duck trousers of the Atlantic draft-dodgers were straining with iron crowbars to shift a section of muddy track before the next dirt-train backed down the switch. One of the men slipped in the red slime; before the corporal’s whistle could blow, the flange of a loaded dump-car took him across the thighs, and two Cantonese stretcher-bearers trotted out of the steam-fog with a canvas sack and a lime-bucket, shoveling the red clay over the spot without halting the locomotive’s bell for a single stroke.

"Pour the concrete at night, Sterling," Elias had said, turning his heavy, failing frame back toward the armored inspection-car waiting on the upper spur. "My ankles are filling with water, and this heat rots a man’s liver. I will not live to see the first battleship pass the sill—Make sure the lock-walls are twelve feet thick at the base. When my stone is laid in Monterey, this ditch is the padlock on the eastern door; I want no Englishman with a bag of powder knocking the hinges off after I am gone."

***

Now, in the November of 1887, the old man’s diary lay closed upon the brass table of the *Culebra*’s deck-saloon, and as the steamer rounded the fortified volcanic bastion of Flamenco Island into the anchorage of Panama Bay, the Chronicler who accompanied the Regent’s suite looked out upon the monstrous realization of that afternoon’s command.

In the annals of the older empires, great public works—such as the wall of Hadrian or the Grand Canal of the Sui—left behind them only the quiet bones of their builders buried under the turf. At the southern mouth of the Isthmian trench, however, the collision of forty million gold thalers in annual payroll with the human dregs of four continents had spawned a brick-and-corrugated-iron cancer that the engineers called the Fourth Naval Canton, and the sailors of the world called the *City of the Cut*.

Where the sleepy, moss-grown Spanish battlements and tumbledown adobe convents of old Panama City had rotted beside the tidal mud-flats twenty years earlier, a geometric metropolis of two hundred thousand souls now festered beneath a permanent canopy of yellow coal-smoke, mosquito-smudge, and crude petroleum vapor. The city was laid out not for habitation, but for the processing of muscle and the extraction of silver. Along the three miles of newly blasted basalt quays at Balboa, where the giant floating caisson-gates of the Pacific entrance-locks loomed eighty feet above the low-tide slime like cliffs of grey cast iron, stood the monumental, windowless storehouses of the Isthmian Commissariat: cold-storage beef-vaults cooled by ammonia-engines from Chicago, quinine-distilleries, and the six-story red-brick barracks of the Satsuma and Hawaiian garrison regiments.

Yet behind that rigid frontage of Imperial Blue and Sunset Gold, stretching back up the steaming red-clay slopes of Ancon Hill toward the mouth of the Culebra gorge, lay the *Boca*—four square miles of two-story timber shanties roofed with flattened kerosene-tins, raised eight feet above the black, bubbling sewage-ditches upon creosoted Oregon pilings, and connected by narrow plank catwalks slick with fish-offal and spilled palm-gin.

To walk the elevated boardwalks of the Avenida Central at eight o’clock in the evening, when the six-o’clock shift-trains had vomited thirty thousand mud-caked laborers out of the Cut, was to descend into a polyglot furnace where the syncretism of the Empire had rotted into pure, commercialized delirium. The air under the sizzling blue carbon-arc lamps was ninety-two degrees and thick as wet flannel: it smelled of fried plantains, scorching human hair from the barber-stalls, the sharp carbolic-and-lime wash that the Chinese sanitary gangs pumped into the open gutters every four hours to kill the yellow-fever larvae, and the heavy, sickly-sweet fumes of Yunnan opium mixed with cheap Monongahela whiskey.

Here, beneath painted canvas signs written simultaneously in English, Spanish, Japanese *katakana*, and Cantonese characters, every vice of the Great Arena was sold by the stopwatch and taxed at twenty percent by Magistrate Shen’s municipal excise-clerks. In the vast, open-sided timber sheds of the *Saloon of the Two Oceans*, five hundred negro shovel-men from the Mississippi protectorates and scar-faced Irish navvies from the Massachusetts levies drank green wormwood absinthe at zinc bars alongside bare-footed Tagalog dynamite-drillers and tattooed Marquesan boatmen, while up on the sawdust stage a troupe of bankrupt actresses from the New York theaters danced the can-can to the accompaniment of a Bavarian brass tuba and a Cantonese two-stringed fiddle. Next door, separated only by a partition of quarter-inch redwood board through which the swearing and the clink of silver tenths sounded without pause, stood the licensed bath-houses and brothels of the Yoshiwara Concession—where four hundred girls brought over on five-year treasury indentures from the starving fishing-villages of Kyushu and the orphanages of Charleston sat behind wooden lattices in kimonos of cheap Lowell cotton, their health-tickets stamped every Tuesday morning by a former surgeon of the Union Army wearing the brass armband of the Pacifica Sanitary Police.

No man in the City of the Cut owned the roof over his bunk, and no man walked three hundred yards without passing beneath the shadow of the overhead wire-tramways that carried the red rock of Culebra day and night across the housetops toward the breakwater dumps—an endless, rumbling iron conveyor that dropped flakes of wet shale into the soup-bowls of the eating-houses and shook the plank walls with the eternal vibration of the ditch. And at the foot of every street, where the boardwalks met the double-track railway embankment, stood the concrete pillbox of the Provost Guard, its loopholed steel shutters half-open to show the gleaming brass water-jacket of a Maxim gun trained straight down the gutter.

***

On the morning of the fourteenth of November, the rain did not fall upon the City of the Cut in drops; it came down from the black clouds over the Chagres valley in solid, lukewarm sheets that flooded the carbolic ditches to the level of the boardwalks and washed three dead rats against the iron steps of the Sanitary Headquarters at Empire Station.

Inside the high, whitewashed operating-hall of the former French hospital—whose verandas were now enclosed in double envelopes of fine brass copper-screening to keep out the *Stegomyia* mosquitoes—General Marcus Vance the younger stood before a long pine trestle-table covered in glass specimen-jars and wet yellow morning reports. He wore his khaki tunic buttoned to the chin over a rubberized apron; the air in the screened room was stifling, reeking of iodoform, boiling corrosive sublimate, and the unmistakable, sour-sweet stench of the *vomito negro*—the black blood-vomit that drifted through the louvers from the quarantine-wards down the hill.

Across the table stood Colonel Gorgas, Chief Surgeon of the Isthmian Works, his white linen duck trousers splashed to the knees with yellow clay and crude petroleum, and Major Kuroda of the Satsuma Garrison Brigade.

"Fourteen new cases in the Gorgona barracks since midnight, General, and twenty-two among the Italian and Georgian mason-gangs at the Pedro Miguel lock-pit," Colonel Gorgas said, his fingers trembling with exhaustion and forty grains of daily quinine as he laid a fever-chart stained with black spots before Marcus’s slide-rule. "The October slides in the Cut dammed the east diversion-channel and created forty acres of stagnant brush-swamp right behind the coolie-lines. My oil-gangs cannot spray the puddles because the three thousand Jamaican and Georgia shovel-men in Sector Four threw down their picks at daybreak! They have barricaded themselves inside the timber-shanties along the Las Cascadas ridge—they say the doctors are poisoning the well-water with carbolic to kill off the sick men and save their back-pay for the Mint, and they shot two of my Hawaiian hospital-orderlies who tried to bring the sulphur-pots into the street!"

Marcus did not touch the stained fever-chart; he picked up a pair of nickel-plated forceps, lifted the corner of the paper to examine the daily mortality curve on the sheet beneath, and let it drop.

"How many cubic yards of rock did Sector Four send to the Naos dump yesterday, Major Kuroda?" Marcus asked, his clipped, metallic voice cutting across the surgeon’s report as if the black vomit were merely an error in coal-consumption.

"Eleven thousand two hundred, sir," Kuroda answered, consulting his pocket-book. "Sixteen thousand below the daily quota required to clear the lock-sills before the February fleet-maneuvers. And the strike is spreading down the line toward Balboa—the Irish mechanics at the Gorgona machine-shops have banked their forge-fires and are demanding that the quarantine-cordon be lifted so they can take the Friday steamer back to New Orleans before the yellow jack gets into the white quarters."

Marcus pulled his ivory slide-rule from his breast pocket. For ten seconds the only sound in the copper-screened hall was the drumming of the tropical deluge upon the corrugated tin roof and the dry *slick-slap* of the celluloid cursor sliding between the young general’s steady fingers.

"A single skilled steam-shovel engineer from the Gorgona shops costs the Bureau twelve hundred thalers to train and six months to replace from Sacramento," Marcus said, reading the figure off the rule before slipping it back into his pocket. "A Jamaican or Georgian pick-man in the Las Cascadas shanties costs thirty thalers in bounty-money, and we have twelve thousand fresh Shantung coolies waiting in the quarantine-hulks at Taboga Island whose resistance to the Chagres fever is eighteen percent higher by the August tables. We will not risk the machine-shop crews by letting the *Stegomyia* mosquitoes breed in the Las Cascadas thatch for another twenty-four hours."

Colonel Gorgas blinked through his rain-speckled spectacles, his gaunt face paling beneath his tropical tan. "General, there are four thousand men—and three hundred women and children from the old French camp—huddled inside those timber tenements on the ridge! If my orderlies cannot go in with the sulphur-pans and the wire-screens because of the strikers’ rifles, it will take two weeks of house-to-house parley to segregate the infected cases!"

"We do not have two weeks, Doctor; Lady Kaiulani’s battle-squadron passes the locks on the tenth of February, and a mosquito does not listen to parley," Marcus replied, turning to the wall-map of the Culebra reach where the red pins of the fever-outbreak clustered thickest along the wooden shantytown of Las Cascadas. "When a gangrene appears in a toe, my father did not poultice the boot; he took the leg off below the knee so the trunk could march. Major Kuroda."

"General?" The Satsuma officer clicked his heels on the wet pine boards.

"Take the First and Second Battalions of the Choshu Infantry and the four armored oil-train flatcars up the east berm-track to the Las Cascadas switch," Marcus ordered, unbuckling his rubberized apron and tossing it onto the specimen-table as he reached for his oilskin cap. "Do not send a single soldier into the boardwalks where a man with a shotgun can shoot him from a window, and do not arrest the strike-committee. Surround the entire four-hundred-yard perimeter of the Las Cascadas shantytown with two rows of portable barbed-wire hurdles and eight Maxim guns. Give the inhabitants fifteen minutes by the locomotive whistle to walk out naked through the carbolic dipping-troughs at the railway-cut. Every man who comes out through the trough goes into the iron boxcars for thirty days’ solitary quarantine on the Naos rock-pile at half-rations."

Colonel Gorgas took a step forward, his hand catching the edge of the table as he stared at the twenty-nine-year-old general’s bloodless profile. "And those who are too sick with the fever to crawl out of their bunks in fifteen minutes, General Vance? Or the strikers who refuse to leave the barricade?"

"At the sixteenth minute," Marcus said, already walking toward the double-screened door where his horse-holder waited in the pouring rain beside the railway-handcar, "Kuroda’s engineers will turn the high-pressure hoses from the four oil-cars onto the shingle roofs, soak the entire Las Cascadas quarter with ten thousand gallons of unrefined Borneo crude, and fire four thermite canisters into the center alley. Fire sterilizes both the mosquito-larvae and the mutiny in a single operation, Doctor, and the ashes will serve to dry up the stagnant puddles in the diversion-ditch. Come along with your microscope; I want the ground inspected for live pupae as soon as the tin cools."

Twenty minutes later, the geared inspection-locomotive pushed Marcus’s armored flatcar up the four-percent grade of the Las Cascadas spur, its brass driving-rods flashing through the grey curtain of the tropical downpour while the wheels ground over red shale that was already sliding like melted butter across the ties. 

Ahead of the cow-catcher, perched upon the raw clay shelf between the three-hundred-foot abyss of the Cut on the left and the steaming green wall of the virgin jungle on the right, stood the shantytown of Sector Four: two hundred densely packed, two-story tenements of unpainted pine and corrugated iron, their upper galleries hung with soggy red blankets and hand-lettered boards reading *SILVER OR STEAMSHIPS—NO MORE LIME-PITS.* 

Down on the main broad-gauge track below the plank-walks, four companies of Choshu infantry in dark blue oilskin capes had already uncoiled six-foot concertinas of rusted barbed wire across the approaches, while on the embankment directly opposite the town’s central market-shed, two massive eight-wheeled steel tank-cars—each bearing the yellow stencil of the *Imperial Sanitary & Petroleum Commission*—hissed and throbbed as their steam-pumps built pressure to two hundred pounds on the dial.

Marcus did not step down into the mud; he stood beneath the bolted steel canopy of the flatcar, his gloved hand resting beside the breech of the brass three-pounder Hotchkiss mountain-gun mounted on the forward pedestal. Fifty yards away, perched upon the corrugated tin roof of a grog-shop above a barricade of overturned dump-carts, a red-bearded Georgian mechanic in a faded Confederate forage cap—a man who had lost three fingers of his left hand to a rock-drill at Bas Obispo—leveled a stolen Winchester repeating rifle across the rain-swept wire.

"You hear me down there in the iron car, General Vance!" the Georgian roared, his voice cracking over the hiss of the oil-pumps and the wailing of two hundred fever-stricken men and women whose yellow, blood-streaked faces pressed against the unscreened wooden shutters of the upper bunk-houses behind him. "We got eighty kegs of giant-powder stacked under the floor of this saloon, and we got four hundred white men and Jamaicans behind these carts with dynamite-sticks in their shirts! You turn those yellow devils loose on us with bayonets, or you try to lock us in the fever-cars for Naos, and we’ll blow this whole clay bank straight down into your ditch and bury ten of your steam-shovels fifty feet deep! Bring the pay-wagons up the track and give us clearance papers for the New Orleans packet, or by God—"

Marcus looked down at his wrist. Twelve minutes had elapsed since the locomotive’s first warning blast had echoed down the gorge; only forty-six men—mostly Cantonese water-carriers who knew the ways of the Provostry—had crawled out through the mud to strip off their rags and plunge through the smoking vats of carbolic acid by the switch-tower. Up in the second-story windows of the shanties, he could see the dark swarms of mosquitoes rising like grey smoke from the rain-barrels under the eaves whenever a sick man’s arm struck at the air.

"He is standing directly over the main drainage-culvert of the upper bench, Major Kuroda," Marcus observed calmly, not raising his voice toward the Georgian on the roof as he reached down and turned the brass elevating-screw of the Hotchkiss three-pounder two turns to the left. "If he detonates eighty kegs of nitro-glycerine powder under that grog-shop, the concussion will shear the clay toe of the embankment and cost us three weeks of steam-shovel time to clear the slide before the Regent’s steamer arrives tomorrow. We will not wait for the fifteenth minute."

"The women are still on the lower porch, General," Colonel Gorgas said from the rear of the flatcar, his hand gripping the wet iron stanchion so hard his knuckles went white.

"They are carriers of the Stegomyia parasite, Doctor, and they are standing on eighty kegs of government blasting-powder," Marcus replied, sighting down the wet brass barrel of the mountain-gun until the front blade rested squarely upon the buckle of the Georgian mechanic’s belt fifty yards away. Yet before his right thumb could depress the firing-lanyard, the field-telegraph box bolted to the rear bulkhead of the flatcar began to clatter with the sharp, urgent triple-spark of the Regent’s personal launch.

Major Kuroda snatched the wet paper ribbon from the brass spool and stepped to Marcus’s elbow. "From Her Highness aboard the Culebra at the Balboa quarantine-buoy, General. You are to hold the thermite batteries. The Envoys of the Andean and Caribbean Republics are riding up the gorge on the noon observation-train with the Regent, and she refuses to have them choke on roasted Georgian meat while she is negotiating the Darien Hinterland Buffer."

Marcus slowly took his thumb off the brass lanyard, though he did not alter the elevation of the gun by a hair’s breadth. He straightened his spine beneath the dripping steel canopy and looked back toward the winding red-clay throat of the gorge, where the white plume of the Regent’s geared mountain-locomotive was already rising above the wet banana-fronds.

"Turn off the steam-heaters in the oil-vats, Major," Marcus said, pulling a clean square of linen from his pocket to wipe the rain from his slide-rule. "Pump the Borneo crude cold through the hoses at two hundred pounds pressure. Knock the Georgian off the tin with the water-stream, flood the cellar under the saloon until their giant-powder is wet porridge, and let the Choshu battalions go over the carts with clubs and pick-handles. If Her Highness wishes to show the South Americans a surgical camp instead of a furnace, we will give them cold iron."

***

It was during that same three-o’clock deluge of the previous autumn—six months before the final silence in the Monterey crypt, when Elias Thorne had still been able to sit propped among his horsehair cushions before the bronze map in San Francisco—that the first spark had passed unbroken beneath the mud of the Isthmus from the Atlantic water to the Golden Gate.

In the annals of the Chancery, that October afternoon of 1886 is remembered not for any battle, for the battles were over, but for the strange, suffocating quiet inside the fourth-floor Map Room when Major Sterling uncoiled the insulated gutta-percha lead that connected the Rincon Hill repeater directly to the newly submerged trans-isthmian cable at Colón. Outside, the San Francisco autumn had been clear and sharp with the smell of crushed wine-grapes coming down on the Sacramento barges and the coal-smoke of the Potrero rolling-mills; inside, the air was heavy with the camphor and burnt stramonium that kept the Providentor’s congested lungs drawing breath.

Elias had sat in his wheeled chair of Hawaiian koa-wood, his swollen ankles wrapped in gray flannel beneath his unlaced cavalry boots, his solitary wide eye fixed not upon Cornelius Schuyler or Marquis Takashima, who stood whispering beside the porphyry table over the autumn silver-tallies, but upon the small brass sounder set upon a block of green serpentine marble beside his right elbow.

"The siphon-recorder at the Balboa lock-house is linked through the Culebra conduit to the Limon Bay breakwater on the Caribbean side, Protector," Major Sterling had said, his one-eared head bent low over the galvanometer needle as it trembled under the first test-current from three thousand miles south. "General Vance’s sappers laid the last splice through the Gatun spillway trench twenty minutes ago. For the first time since the creation of the earth, the tide-gauges of the two oceans are beating on the same wire."

Across the room, old Cornelius Schuyler had looked up from his discount-sheets, his gold pince-nez slipping down his nose as he peered at the little brass machine. "A triumph of engineering, Major, no doubt—though until the Culebra clay-slides are dredged to forty feet, a copper wire through the mud does not pay the four-percent coupon on the Isthmian Canal Debentures. The London underwriters are still betting at Lloyd’s that the Chagres river floods will wash our concrete lock-sills into the Caribbean before a single keel crosses the divide."

Elias had not looked at the banker. His right hand—the only hand that still obeyed the iron will locked behind his scarred brow—rested upon the leather arm of his chair, the thick, yellowed fingernail tapping a slow, uneven measure against the wood. Beside his wheel, Lady Kaiulani stood in her rustling black bombazine, her dark eyes watching the galvanometer mirror flash a tiny spot of green light across the wall.

Then the armature clicked.

It was not the hesitant,relay-weakened stutter that had come round the Horn through Valparaiso or across the torn wires of the old Eastern states. It struck the brass anvil with a sharp, metallic ring that filled the high-arched room like the cocking of a Paterson revolver.

*Clack-clack-clack. Clack-clack.*

Sterling did not wait for the clerk to write the words upon a form; he read the dots directly off the brass tongue as they leaped from the Caribbean surf across the mountains of Mexico and up the granite spine of California:

"*'From Port-Captain, Atlantic Terminus, Cristóbal Mole, to the Providentor at San Francisco,'*" Sterling’s voice trembled in the hush. "*'High water on the Limon Bay gauge stands at twenty-two inches above mean datum. The Pacifica gunboat* Culebra *passed through the temporary diversion-channel from the Pacific side at noon and has just dipped her ensign in salt water off the Toro Point lighthouse. The Atlantic Squadron salutes the Throne. There is no longer a Cape Horn.'*"

Marquis Takashima had taken a single step toward the bronze relief-map on the wall, his narrow eyes widening as he looked at the thin silver wire inlaid across the waist of the Americas. "A gunboat in the Caribbean," the old samurai had murmured in his stiff English. "Within six days’ steaming of Havana and the mouth of the Mississippi, without touching a British coaling-station."

Elias had slowly lifted his right hand from the koa-wood armrest. With a heavy, dragging motion that cost him three ragged pulls of breath through his open teeth, he reached out and laid his scarred palm directly over the vibrating brass sounder on the marble block, feeling the electric pulse of the Atlantic Ocean beating like a captured bird against the callouses that had once worked Red Higgins’s ash sweep on the muddy Mississippi.

He had never seen the Atlantic. Forty-nine years ago, when the bailiff from Philadelphia had burned his mother’s loom in the Kentucky clover and ridden back across the Alleghenies toward the counting-houses of Boston and New York, that eastern sea had been the invisible throne of his enemies—the cold, arrogant water from which the laws, the bank-writs, and the ships of the old world came forth to master the wilderness. For half a century he had turned his back upon it, building his house around the vast, roaring bowl of the sunset until the West was too heavy for the East to bear.

Now the eastern sea was nothing more than a mill-pond at the back door of his canal, and its water was ticking under his thumb.

"Write the reply, Kaiulani," Elias had whispered, his voice scraping like dry gravel from the bottom of his congested chest while his solitary clear eye burned across the baize at Schuyler and Takashima. "Tell the Port-Captain at Cristóbal to unlimber two sixteen-inch Krupp rifles on the Toro Point mole facing north toward Jamaica and New York. And tell the underwriters at Lloyd’s that the Grand Confederation is no longer a Pacific state. Where the water runs, the law is one."

***
