Now, thirteen months after that spark had rattled the brass sounder under the dead Titan’s palm, the rain over the Las Cascadas ridge had slackened to a warm, dripping mist that smelled of wet Borneo petroleum, bruised banana-leaves, and the sharp carbolic vapor rising from the quarantined shanties.

High above the smoking red trench of the Culebra Cut, upon the glass-enclosed observation veranda of the Regent’s armored salon-car parked on the Bishop’s Hill siding, Lady Kaiulani sat before a table of polished Nicaraguan mahogany. Around the curve of the brass rail below the windows, five hundred feet down through the swirling yellow steam of the Bucyrus shovels, the four Battalions of the Choshu Infantry were marching the last of the stripped, oil-blackened Georgian and Jamaican strikers down the railway ties toward the iron boxcars at Empire Station. Not a shot had been fired; only the rhythmic *thwack* of pick-handles and the hiss of the cold petroleum hoses rose through the wet afternoon to remind the passengers in the saloon-car how the Bureau of Integration settled labor disputes.

Across the mahogany table from Kaiulani sat four gentlemen in faultless Parisian broadcloth whose high starched collars were wilting in the ninety-degree greenhouse air: Don Rafael Núñez, President of the Colombian Confederation at Bogotá; General Guzmán Blanco of Venezuela; and the plenipotentiaries of Costa Rica and the Nicaraguan lakes. They had been brought up from the Balboa wharf behind General Vance’s locomotive to see the ditch before they signed the parchment.

"You observe, Excellencies, that the Regency does not waste powder when water will serve," Kaiulani said, her musical voice cool and even as she poured dark Bogota coffee from a silver pot into four tiny porcelain cups, her black bombazine mourning-sleeves brushing the corner of the map where the new red boundary-line of the *Isthmian Neutrality Zone* swept in a two-hundred-mile arc from the Gulf of Urabá to the Chiriquí lagoon. "Had General Vance allowed that lunatic on the grog-shop roof to fire his Winchester, eighty kegs of nitro-glycerine would have slid half a million cubic yards of red clay back into the channel, and the commercial dividends of your republics would have been delayed until the spring equinox."

Don Rafael Núñez did not touch his coffee. His thin, scholarly face—the face of a poet who had spent thirty years trying to govern mountain caudillos with French philosophy—was grey as he looked down through the plate glass at the long file of naked, shivering mechanics being driven through the carbolic troughs by Japanese soldiers half their height.

"When the French company of Monsieur de Lesseps dug in this valley, Madame la Régente," Núñez said in Spanish, his voice trembling slightly as a ninety-ton steam-shovel directly below the cliff bit into the shale with a shriek of iron teeth that made the coffee-spoons chime against the saucers, "they leased a strip of ten kilometers along the Chagres River and paid the Treasury at Bogotá two hundred and fifty thousand gold francs a year in transit-dues. Now the Providentor is dead in California, and you lay before us the *Treaty of the Darien Hinterlands*. You demand not ten kilometers, but the sovereign police-administration of the entire watershed from the Atrato River to the Costa Rican frontier, the abolition of our municipal customs at Cartagena and Barranquilla, and the right to garrison the Andean passes with your Asian regiments! In Bogotá, madam, they will call this the extinction of Bolívar’s republic!"

"In Bogotá, Don Rafael, your treasury has not paid the interest on its London railway bonds since the year seventy-nine," Kaiulani replied, resting her ungloved hands—slender, dark, and adorned only with the heavy whale-ivory ring of Oahu—upon the edge of the treaty scroll. "And last month, while your Liberal and Conservative generals were shooting each other in the plaza at Medellín over a church-tax, three British cruisers from the Jamaica station anchored off Cartagena and offered to buy the Atrato river-concession as a rival canal-route. Do you imagine that the empire which bridged the Bering Strait and sank Admiral Hornby in the Coral Sea will permit seven bankrupt republics to sit above the lock-chambers of our main arterial road, waiting to sell the high ground to London or Berlin whenever a local colonel needs silver to pay his ragged lancers?"

General Guzmán Blanco of Venezuela leaned forward, his heavily pomaded black beard brushing the gold braid of his uniform chest. "We are sovereign states of the Latin race, Your Highness! Even when the old United States in Washington proclaimed their Monroe Doctrine, they did not ask us to put Hawaiian magistrates in our custom-houses or rebuild our mountain railways to a six-foot California gauge! If we refuse this protectorate and retire to the cordilleras, will you send your Choshu infantry to climb twelve thousand feet into the Andes after us, as your Marshal did in Siberia?"

A faint, almost sorrowful smile touched the corners of Kaiulani’s mouth. She looked past the Venezuelan general’s shoulder toward the door of the car, where young General Marcus Vance had just stepped onto the rear platform out of the rain, stripping off his wet oilskin cape and handing it to his orderly without a spot of mud upon his khaki tunic.

"General Vance does not climb mountains when he can close the beach, Excellency," Kaiulani said softly. "Look down at the bay behind us. Every sack of coffee that leaves Guayaquil or Maracaibo, every hide from the Orinoco, and every bar of silver from the Cauca mines reaches the markets of the world in bottoms registered at San Francisco, Osaka, or Shanghai. If you return to Bogotá and Caracas tonight without signing the Hinterland Concordat, not a single Pacifica rifle will march up your mule-trails. Instead, at noon tomorrow, the Bureau of Integration will place a one-hundred-percent quarantine tariff upon every port between Vera Cruz and Valparaiso that does not fly the customs-pennant of the Triumvirate, and Mr. Schuyler’s banks will sell your defaulted European debt at auction to the coffee-planters of Java and Brazil."

She picked up a small leather case from beside the coffee-tray and clicked open the lid, revealing four heavy gold stars of the *Imperial Order of the Two Oceans*, each set with a central nugget of unworked Yukon bullion.

"On the other hand," she continued, her voice dropping into the velvet cadence she had learned thirty years ago in the candle-lit salas of Sonora and Monterey, "if the Presidents of the Hinterland Republics enter the Customs Union today as Hereditary Wardens of the Southern Approaches, the Market Street Mint will immediately assume your London debt at par, advance twelve million silver thalers for the completion of the Quito-Bogotá broad-gauge spur, and guarantee your present presidential administrations for life against all domestic insurgents by stationing two cruisers of the Insular Fleet permanently at Cartagena and La Guaira. You may keep your flags, gentlemen; you may keep your cathedrals and your Spanish courts; we ask only for the gauges of the track, the keys of the quarantine-stations, and five thousand of your mountain youth every spring to serve in the Amur garrisons where they cannot plot revolutions at home."

General Vance stepped through the mahogany sliding-door into the salon, the smell of wet wool and raw Borneo petroleum following him into the fragrance of coffee and cigar-smoke. He bowed slightly from the neck to the four Latin envoys, his pale eyes resting for an instant upon the gold medals on the table before he laid a damp engineer’s report beside Kaiulani’s saucer.

"The Las Cascadas bench is cleared, Your Highness," Marcus said in his flat, rapid voice. "Four hundred and twelve laborers have been processed through the carbolic vats and entrained for the Naos rock-quarries; the shanties have been pulled down by the steam-winches to prevent mosquito-breeding in the timber, and the six-o’clock shift from the Shantung depot is already moving into the cut with fresh drill-steels. If these gentlemen have concluded their inspection of the earthworks, the pilot-engine iscoupled to take us down to the Miraflores lock-sill before the tide turns."

Don Rafael Núñez looked up at the twenty-nine-year-old general whose father had burned the ice of Lake Baikal, and then back at the fifty-year-old Polynesian princess in her black dress who held the gold pen poised between her slender fingers. Outside, the ninety-ton steam-shovels had already resumed their rhythmic, iron-jawed chewing into the red bowels of the continent, shaking the floorplates of the car with every bite.

"Give me the parchment, Madame," the President of Colombia whispered, reaching for the pen.

***

Twelve years later—when Don Rafael Núñez and old Cornelius Schuyler and Marquis Takashima had all gone down into the quiet earth to join the first generation of the conquerors, and the nineteenth century itself was dying in the glare of ten thousand blast-furnaces—the great ditch was done.

On the morning of the first of January, 1900, the tropical sun rose out of the Caribbean and climbed over the drowned jungles of Gatun Lake to look down not upon a red-clay trench of screaming steam-shovels and fever-shanties, but upon a straight, silent canyon of dressed Sierra granite and poured gray concrete fifty miles long, through whose hundred-foot channel the green waters of the two oceans mingled without a ripple.

At the Pacific entrance of the Balboa reach, where the twin eighty-foot steel mitre-gates of the lower Miraflores chamber stood open to the morning flood, rose the colossal Arch of the Pivot—two hundred feet of white California marble and green Japanese bronze spanning the lock-walls like the legs of the Rhodesian Colossus, bearing across its frieze in six-foot letters of gilded cast iron the three words from the Providentor’s Sacramento speech of fifty-two:

*BEHIND US LIES THE PAST.*

Upon the high stone reviewing-tribune built directly into the western abutment of the lock-wall, shaded from the blinding equatorial glare by an awning of imperial blue silk, stood the two survivors who kept the gauge of the completed world: Lady Kaiulani, now in her sixty-third year, her hair white as the foam on the Honolulu reef above her unchanging black bombazine and the gold collar of the Sole Regency; and beside her, General-in-Chief Marcus Vance, forty-two years old, his temples silvered above the unadorned slate-gray tunic of the Imperial Staff, the ivory cursor of his slide-rule still protruding half an inch from his breast pocket.

Below them, lining the five miles of stepped concrete embankments from the foot of Ancon Hill to the breakwater of Naos Island, stood no cheering rabble with paper flags, but one hundred thousand soldiers and civil prefects of the Hundred and Twenty-Four States drawn up in silent, motionless blocks of blue and gray: regiments of Manchurian and Siberian Riflemen standing shoulder-to-shoulder with battalions from the Massachusetts and Virginia cantons; graduates of the Berkeley and New Edo examination-sheds in their dark alpaca robes with the five-digit silver numerals gleaming on their collars; and ten thousand Cantonese and Jamaican canal-masons holding their iron rock-drills at the present like muskets.

The air above the water was ninety degrees, yet there was not a single mosquito along the concrete banks; the breeze off the bay carried only the clean, hot smell of ozone from the five-thousand-horsepower hydroelectric turbines humming inside the dam-spillways, the sharp tang of salt brine, and the heavy, resinous smoke of aloeswood rising from the bronze braziers at the corners of the Arch.

And gliding dead-slow into the upper chamber between the concrete walls—towed not by puffing steam-tugs, but by four noiseless, thirty-ton electric cog-locomotives whose copper contact-shoes hissed blue sparks along the rack-rails on the coping—came the first vessel to cross the severed spine of the earth.

She was the thirty-thousand-ton dreadnought battleship *Elias Thorne*—the third flagship of the name, launched from the slips of Potrero Point six months before, driven by Parsons steam-turbines burning refined Sumatra oil, and carrying twelve twenty-inch breech-loading rifles in four triple turrets of Krupp cemented steel.

Yet it was not the twenty-inch guns upon which the hundred thousand pairs of eyes along the concrete banks were fixed as the monstrous blue steel hull settled into the water of the lock-chamber. High upon the forward armored barbette, directly ahead of the conning-tower where Rear-Admiral Shimazu Tadao—Candidate Seven-One-Zero-Two of the class of eighty-seven—stood at attention with his hand at his visor, the ship’s carpenters had bolted a massive, ten-ton throne of cast bronze.

Seated upon that chair, thirty feet above the scorching steel deckplates and facing straight southward toward the open gate of the Pacific Ocean, rode the founder of the Empire.

He was not flesh, though the simple Cantonese coolies down on the lower steps dropped to their knees on the concrete and touched their foreheads to the stone as the shadow of the bow fell across them. Five years earlier, when the last whispers of a Republican restoration had flickered in the cellars of Boston and Kyoto, Kaiulani and Marcus Vance had ordered the lead casket in the Monterey Basilica unsealed; the embalmed corpse of the Providentor had been encased in an airtight shell of electro-plated copper and bronze molded directly from his death-mask, dressed in the bronze facsimile of his plain Engineer’s coat with the iron walking-stick welded upright between his knees, and bolted to the prow of the Fleet so that the Sovereign of the Realm might inspect his provinces forever without the inconvenience of a beating heart.

As the eighty-foot steel leaves of the upper gate swung silently shut behind the dreadnought’s stern, driven by the subterranean hydraulic rams without the clank of a single chain, the water in the thousand-foot granite trough began to drop toward the level of the Pacific tide.

Foot by foot, as the green Caribbean water drained through the eighteen-foot culverts beneath their boots with a deep, organ-like roar that vibrated through the marble tribunal, the towering steel superstructure of the *Elias Thorne* sank lower between the walls—until the bronze head of the dead Caesar, crusted white along the cheekbones with the dried salt-spray of the Atlantic passage from New York and Havana, came level with the stone parapet where Kaiulani and Marcus stood.

Only twenty feet of hot, sunlit air separated the woman on the wall from the metal figure on the turret. She could see the exact, pitiless fold of the bronze eyelid that the sculptor had copied from the paralyzed left side of his face; she could see the square, blunt thumb welded over the head of the iron stick.

*We have brought your ship through the mountain, Elias,* she thought, her withered, ivory-ringed hand tightening upon the scorching marble of the balustrade while the hydroelectric sirens atop the Arch of the Pivot began to sound the noon hour in a single, deafening chord that drowned the screaming of the sea-birds all the way to Taboga. *From the ice of the Yenisei to the reefs of Melbourne, from the ruins of the Potomac to the gates of this lock, there is no king, no parliament, and no tribal chief left standing who can say no to your clerk’s ink. We have ground the names out of the boys; we have turned the ocean into a cistern; we have bolted the world together so tight that even your corpse can steer it.*

Beside her elbow, General Marcus Vance raised his left wrist, checking the green radium hands of his chronometer against the drop of the water-gauge on the lock-wall as the lower mitre-gates parted outward toward the blinding blue expanse of Panama Bay. "Eight hours and forty-two minutes from the Toro Point breakwater to the Pacific sill, Your Highness," Marcus said, his tone clear and unmarked by age or awe as the fifty-foot gap between the steel leaves widened to reveal the waiting double columns of the First and Second Battle Squadrons—forty-eight blue-hulled dreadnoughts and armored cruisers stretching out to the western horizon beneath a solid canopy of oil-smoke. "Twelve minutes faster than the Admiralty tables calculated for a thirty-thousand-ton displacement. The First Atlantic Division will clear the locks by sunset, and by the fifteenth of next month we can transfer sixty-four capital ships from the Yellow Sea to the mouth of the English Channel in twenty-one days without asking permission of the winds." He pulled a folded white wireless-telegraph flimsy from his belt-pouch—received ten minutes earlier from the high-frequency spark-towers on Ancon Hill—and held it out between two gloved fingers as the four electric towing-locomotives on the coping gave two short bells and began to haul the *Elias Thorne* forward through the open gates into the Pacific swell. "Before we go down to the state barge to follow the flagship out, Madam," Marcus continued, not looking at the bronze effigy gliding slowly past their faces in the glare, "the Prefect of the Seventy-First Canton at Irkutsk wirelessed at eleven that the German and French boundary-commissioners at Omsk have refused to countersign the new tariff-schedule for the Trans-Siberian and Ural potash mines, and the Kaiser in Berlin has ordered three army corps to the Polish border to support the Moscow grain-syndicate. If we divert the third transport-flotilla from Manila to the mouth of the Obi before the spring thaw—" Kaiulani did not take the wireless slip from his fingers. She stood at the extreme edge of the granite wall, the hot wind off the Pacific lifting the white braids beneath her black mourning-veil as the bronze back of the Providentor’s chair passed through the shadow of the great Arch and rode out onto the long, rolling heave of his own ocean, while behind the flagship the upper lock-gates were already swinging open a second time to receive the bow of the *Kamehameha III*. "Let the Prefect at Irkutsk double the transit-duty on the Ural ore-trains at midnight, Marcus," Kaiulani said, turning slowly away from the parapet and walking toward the stone steps where her palanquin-bearers in the blue-and-gold livery of the Chancery stood waiting beside the electric elevator-shaft, her hand rising to shade her tired dark eyes from the intolerable, brassy glare of the twentieth-century noon as the twenty-inch turrets of the battle-fleet outside the islands began to fire the first salvo of the new hundred-year ledger, "and tell the German Ambassador when he calls at Monterey on Tuesday that the Providentor’s rails do not stop at the mountains; they stop where the iron runs out." *** Yet before the iron ran out—and before the bronze effigy upon the turret of the *Elias Thorne* had ever tasted the tropical spray of the Miraflores locks—there had lain that strange, luminous decade of the late seventies and early eighties which the school-primers of our own century still call the Antonine Peace. History, in its haste to record the cracking of the foundations, too often passes lightly over the noon-hour when the mortar appeared dry and eternal. When I returned to San Francisco in the autumn of 1879 from my first post as Junior Assessor of Customs at the Hankow landing, I did not find the mud-spattered military camp that my uncle had described from the fifties, nor had the city yet hardened into the grim, numbered barracks of the Regency. It was the Golden Age of the Protectorate—that brief, breathless equinox between the conquest of the circumference and the calcification of the soul, when the silver of five continents poured into the Golden Gate faster than the Market Street Mint could stamp it, and no man yet whispered in the taverns that the Emperor on Rincon Hill had no heir of his body. For ten years following the truce along the Yenisei and the pacification of the Chinese river-ports, the great guns of the fleet fired only at target-hulks off the Farallones. Peace lay over the seventy million square miles of the Great Arena like a warm, golden afternoon. In San Francisco, the raw redwood palisades of Clark’s Point had vanished beneath the marble colonnades of the Imperial Exchange, where merchants in silk kimonos from Osaka, broad-hatted cattle-factors from the Sonora cantons, and pale, chastened brokers from the Boston protectorates bought and sold the harvests of half the earth without raising their voices above a polite murmur. A man could board a sleeping-car at the Oakland mole on a Monday morning, eat fresh Columbia salmon chilled in ammonia-ice while his train climbed the Sierra snow-sheds, and step down on the following Saturday onto the granite platform of the Potomac Depot without once showing a passport or exchanging a single Pacifica thaler for local paper. Along the terraced hills above the bay, the rough mining-captains who had ridden with Elias Thorne at the Rio Frio or marched with the elder Vance through the red clay of Virginia had built themselves palaces of pale Sierra granite and red Hawaiian koa-wood, their conservatories heated by steam-pipes and lit by the new Swan incandescent lamps. Yet even in that meridian splendor, when the treasury vaults held four hundred million thalers in uncoined bullion and the grain-fleets whitened the sea from Melbourne to Sitka, the thoughtful observer could detect a curious hollowness beneath the gilt. In the coffee-houses along Montgomery Street, when the four-o’clock chimes rang from the syncretic basilica on Nob Hill and the afternoon editions of the *Gazette* were laid upon the marble tables, the old men did not read the shipping manifests first. They turned in silence to the brief, three-line bulletin at the top of the court column: *The Providentor walked for twenty minutes upon the south terrace at noon.* Everything—the price of Hankow tea, the peace of the Boston streets, the obedience of the Satsuma admirals—hung upon the pulse of a single sixty-two-year-old chest. We walked through our marble gardens like guests at a summer banquet who hear, far off beyond the cypress hedges, the first low rumble of an autumn thunderhead, and therefore drink their wine all the faster before the rain begins. *** Nowhere did that late-afternoon sunlight shine with a more deliberate, cultivated brilliance than upon the white limestone quadrangles of the Imperial University on the Berkeley slopes across the bay. On a crisp afternoon in May of that same year, 1881, Lady Kaiulani walked slowly down the central aisle of the Grand Exhibition Hall, her hands folded within the wide sleeves of a gown of deep imperial-blue brocade woven in the looms of Kyoto, while at her throat gleamed the ancient whale-ivory clasp of Oahu. She had not yet put on the perpetual black bombazine of her later Regency; at forty-four, her dark hair showed only the first faint threads of silver above her temples, and though the ghosts of Fort Street never left her eyes, she had set herself with all the fierce, subtle intelligence of her race to give the iron skeleton of Elias’s empire a living skin of marble and paint. Behind her walked the Rector of the University—a former professor of aesthetics from Harvard College named Norton, whom the Chancery had brought west after the closing of the Massachusetts schools—and Master Kano Hogai, the court painter summoned from Edo to direct the Academy of the Two Shores. "You see, Your Highness, how the students of the fourth year have abandoned both the dry academicism of the European salons and the narrow brush-traditions of the old Tokugawa guilds," Rector Norton was saying, his thin Bostonian voice trembling with genuine enthusiasm as he gestured toward the forty-foot mural of wet fresco that covered the eastern wall of the rotunda. Upon the plaster, a score of young apprentices—boys from California, Canton, and the Hawaiian valleys working side by side on bamboo scaffolds—were laying gold leaf into the wet lime. The painting depicted the *Apotheosis of the Pacific Pivot*: in the foreground, painted with the muscular, anatomical realism of the Italian Renaissance, stood the bronze-cast figures of American iron-puddlers and Polynesian navigators hauling at the capstans of a colossal dreadnought; yet the sea and sky behind them were rendered not in the muddy oil-shadows of Europe, but in the sweeping, mist-veiled ink-washes and hammered sunset-gold leaf of the classic Kano screens, while above the ship’s funnels the Christian archangels and the wind-gods of Ise rode the same stylized, coiling cloud-bank. Kaiulani stopped before the scaffold, the smell of wet lime, turpentine, and ground lapis lazuli filling her nostrils instead of the coal-soot of the dockyards. "It has grandeur, Master Kano," Kaiulani said, switching effortlessly from English to the courtly Japanese of the Kyoto studios as she looked at the aged master beside her, whose silk *hakama* were spotted with Prussian blue and vermilion tempera. "Yet look at the faces of the foundrymen at the capstan. The boy from Philadelphia who painted that left group has given the Americans the brows of Roman senators, and left the Cantonese stokers in the shadow of the boiler like beasts of burden. Tell him to scrape the plaster before it dries tonight." Master Kano bowed low, a sharp glint of approval in his narrow dark eyes. "I told the youth this morning, High Commissioner, that in the Pacific style there is no foreground for one blood and background for another. The line must carry the same weight from the corner of the frame to the center." "More than the line, Master Kano—the memory," Kaiulani replied softly, stepping closer to the wet wall where a young Hawaiian student from Maui was carefully laying strips of crimson and yellow bird-feather patterns into the painted border of the architrave. "For thirty years the Providentor has bound these provinces together with broad-gauge rail and provost-courts. An empire that lives only in the tax-ledger and the guardhouse is a prison that men tear down the moment the turnkey nods. If our grandchildren in Boston and Nagasaki are to bleed for this ocean when we are gone, they must look up at the walls of their courts and see a beauty that neither England nor the old Shogunate could have imagined alone." She turned toward the center of the hall, where the sculptors’ models for the new district capitals were ranged upon velvet pedestals: scale-models of railway stations whose cast-iron arches curved like the hulls of Samoan war-canoes, and municipal basilicas where the stained-glass windows of Chartres were set into earthquake-proof frames of interlocked Japanese cedar. "Rector Norton," she said, her clear voice echoing through the sunny vault as a class of young cadet-architects in their blue wool tunics paused at their drafting-boards to bow, "you will double the bursaries for the School of Imperial Letters and the Conservatory of Music from the Honolulu sugar-fund this autumn. I want the history of the Atlantic Rebellion rewritten in three-part verse for the grammar schools before winter—not as a conquest of states, but as the Deliverance of the Continent from chaos. Let them sing it to the tune of the island chants and the brass cornets together. When a boy has learned to love the shape of the temple, he does not ask whose bones are buried beneath the cornerstone." *** Yet while the apprentices at Berkeley were laying sunset gold into the wet plaster to make a god of him, the god himself sat forty miles south among the deep, primeval gloom of the Santa Cruz mountains, trying to catch his breath in the cold resinous dark beneath trees that were already two thousand years old when Julius Caesar crossed the Rubicon. Nobody in the city below knew that the armored private car on the Monterey spur had stopped at the Felton siding three nights ago. To the foreign consuls and the brokers on Montgomery Street, the Providentor was still behind the closed doors of the Rincon Hill Citadel, reviewing the Siberian timber-schedules. Here, inside the five-thousand-acre cordon of the Big Basin reserve—where two battalions of the Life Guard patrolled a triple perimeter of barbed wire through the sword-ferns and not even a telegraph wire was permitted to hum among the branches—there was no sound of drop-forges, no smell of coal-tar, and no sight of the sea. Only the redwoods stood around the low, unpainted cedar bungalow: monstrous, fluted columns of dark red bark twenty feet thick at the butt, rising three hundred feet straight up to shut out the sky and turn the noon sun into a series of thin, dusty shafts of cathedral twilight. The air on the wide timber veranda was fifty-five degrees and smelled exclusively of damp leaf-mold, cold brook-water, and the sharp, clean camphor of fallen needles. Elias sat in an oversized hickory rocking-chair near the rough-barked railing, a gray army blanket from the old Mexican war folded across his knees. He wore no uniform—only a loose flannel shirt open at the corded, weather-scarred neck, and a pair of soft elk-skin moccasins that gave room to the dull, doughy swelling around his ankle-bones. He was sixty-four that summer. For the first time since the afternoon he had pried the hot iron hinges from his father’s threshold in Kentucky half a century ago, his hands were entirely empty. Across the unpainted redwood table sat his oldest friend—Brigadier Caleb Vance, now past seventy-five, nearly blind with cataracts in his left eye, his white beard reaching to the brass buttons of his faded reserve waistcoat as he slowly pared the rind from a green Pippin apple with a bone-handled pocket-knife. "The doctor from Monterey says if you stay up here in the timber till October and leave the salt-fish and the telegraph-ribbons alone, the water’ll go out of your shins by frost, Elias," Caleb said, his voice a cracked, peaceful wheeze that belonged to campfires that had gone cold forty years ago. He cut a wedge of white apple on his thumb and held it out on the flat of the blade. "Says a man’s heart ain't made of Bessemer plate. Even an old mule on the Santa Fe trace had to be turned out to the vega grass once in seven years, or he’d drop in the harness with the blind staggers." Elias did not take the apple. His broad, grey-stubbled jaw was set against the slow, heavy thudding behind his ribs—a rhythm that felt less like blood than like warm mercury sloshing inside a cracked leather flask. He looked out past the veranda steps, where a clear mountain creek brawled over grey granite boulders between banks of five-finger fern, and up along the sheer, vertical cinnamon-colored trunk of a giant *Sequoia* that stood ten paces from the porch. "That tree was standing there when the Romans were fighting the Carthaginians, Caleb," Elias said. His voice was low, rough, and surprisingly quiet without a vaulted ceiling to throw it back at him. "No bailiff ever nailed a paper to it. No clerk ever entered its board-feet in a book. When the lightning struck the top out of it five hundred years ago, it didn't call a council; it just grew a new crown out of the side branch and kept on standing." Caleb chewed his apple slowly with his back teeth, squinting his one good eye across the porch at the tall, stoop-shouldered figure in the flannel shirt. "You’re talking like an old man, boy. I never heard you look at a pine tree before without asking how many railway ties she’d saw out to the hundred-foot log." "I am sixty-four, Caleb, and when I tried to pull my boot on Tuesday morning at the Citadel, my left fingers wouldn't close on the strap," Elias said, looking down at his wide, square-nailed left hand resting on the hickory arm

of the chair. The skin across his knuckles was shiny and tight, like tallow stretched over a bladder, and a slight, rhythmic tremor shook his thumb whenever he took his mind off it. "Marcus died in the snow ten years ago because I drove him till his lungs burst. Now his boy is twenty-three, sitting down at the Monterey Academy with a slide-rule in his pocket and a face like a steel trap, waiting for me to hand him the reins; and down in the city, Schuyler and Takashima have their clerks counting how many drops of foxglove-water the apothecary sends up to my room every week."

"Then hang Schuyler before supper and send the Jap back to his islands in a rowboat," Caleb grunted, shutting his pocket-knife with a sharp *snap* and laying it on the plank table. "You got forty regiments of the old boys’ sons between here and the Sacramento who’d burn the Mint down if you lifted your finger."

"And who runs the Mint the morning after they burn it—you and me with a pair of skinning-knives?" Elias asked, a dry, humorless chuckle catching in the fluid at the bottom of his throat and turning into a long, rasping cough that forced him to grip the rough cedar rail until the gray blanket slipped from his swollen knees onto the floorboards.

Before Caleb could rise from his bench to lift the wool, the screen-door at the end of the veranda gave a quiet creak, and Lady Kaiulani stepped out onto the planks. She had ridden up the mountain bridle-path from the Felton station on a mule, leaving her escort of Hawaiian guardsmen at the lower creek-crossing; she wore a plain riding-habit of dark forest-green wool, her black hair loosened by the pine-boughs, carrying a small wicker basket of fresh figs from the Santa Clara mission orchards over her arm.

"The Brigadier has been giving you salt-meat again, Elias, or you have been trying to walk down to the brook without your stick," she said, setting the basket upon the table and bending down with effortless grace to lift the Mexican blanket and tuck it back around his thick, cold ankles. As her warm fingers brushed his shin through the elk-skin moccasin, Elias looked down at the crown of her dark head, and for a single, unguarded instant in the green twilight of the redwoods, the Emperor of the Pacific looked merely like a tired frontier wolf who had crawled into the brush to hide his grey muzzle from the pack.

"I was telling Caleb that the trees don't care who sits in the Chancery at Monterey," Elias said, his rough hand coming down lightly upon her shoulder as she straightened up beside his chair.

Down by the lower creek-crossing, a sudden challenge from the Life Guard pickets echoed through the silent cathedral of the trunks, followed by the metallic clatter of a horse’s iron shoes striking the granite boulders of the forbidden trail—not a panic-stricken courier, only young Captain Marcus Vance riding up at a measured trot on a lathered bay mare, his academy tunic buttoned neat to the throat.

"Why are you out of the schoolhouse, boy?" Caleb called down from the porch as his grand-nephew dismounted by the fern-bank and tied his reins to a redwood root.

"The Protector’s vacation ended at noon, Uncle," young Marcus said, climbing the cedar steps with a rolled linen blueprint under his arm and bowing slightly to Kaiulani. "The Benicia Balloon Works has finished the hydrogen-cells for the first aerial cruiser, and the German and French trade delegates have arrived at the Oakland mole asking for an audience before the autumn tariffs close the Rhine. If the Protector does not show his face on the field tomorrow, Comptroller Schuyler intends to sign the European cotton-quotas himself."

Elias looked from the cold, unblinking youth on the steps to the ancient trees rising into the mist. There would be no rest in the timber; an empire was a bicycle that fell into the ditch the moment the rider took his feet off the pedals.

"Help me up, Caleb," Elias said, reaching for his stick.

***

Two mornings later, the salt-marsh grass of the Imperial Arsenal at Benicia lay flattened beneath a hot, violent smell of sulphuric acid, iron-turnings, and scorched castor-oil.

Inside the cavernous, open-ended shed that rose two hundred feet above the Carquinez Strait—a cathedral of riveted angle-iron large enough to swallow two ships of the line side by side—young General Marcus Vance walked slowly beneath the belly of the *Aeolus*. Above his visored cap hung six hundred feet of yellow rubberized silk stretched drum-tight over an internal skeleton of tubular duralumin and split Tonkin bamboo. The gas-bag did not sway; anchored to fifty-ton concrete blocks by forty hemp mooring-lines, the monster pulsed slightly in the draft from the bay like the lung of a sleeping whale.

Suspended thirty feet below the silk envelope by a web of piano-wire rigging hung the gondola: a long, narrow boat-hull of corrugated sheet-aluminum, housing a twin-cylinder flash-boiler fired by atomized Borneo benzine that drove two four-bladed propellers of laminated ash as tall as windmills.

"The gross lift at sixty degrees Fahrenheit is forty-two tons, General," said Chief Engineer Loewe, a former Prussian balloonist from the siege of Paris whom the Chancery had hired out of a Berlin debtor’s prison three years prior. Loewe’s linen duster was eaten full of small round holes from the acid-vats where eighty tons of iron shavings were still dissolving in lead-lined troughs to fill the stern ballonet. "With four hundred gallons of benzine in the gravity-tanks and twenty hundredweight of water-ballast, we can carry a crew of twelve, two Maxim machine-guns on swivel-mounts, and forty hundred-pound melinite drop-bombs in the central rack."

Marcus did not look up at the silk; he tapped the aluminum skin of the gondola with the knuckle of his gloved forefinger. It gave back a thin, tinny *ping*.

"A Cheyenne dog-soldier on the Powder River or a Kirghiz horseman on the Yenisei can put a .45-caliber lead slug through sixteenth-inch aluminum at four hundred yards, Herr Loewe," Marcus said, his clipped voice echoing against the vast curvature of the gas-bag overhead. "And if a single incendiary bullet from a British Martini-Henry pierces that hydrogen envelope while the craft is hovering below three thousand feet, you have built me a four-hundred-thousand-thaler Roman candle."

"We do not intend to hover below three thousand feet, Excellency," Loewe replied, wiping his spectacles with an oily rag as two Cantonese mechanics in asbestos aprons climbed into the gondola and lit the pilot-burners under the flash-boiler with a sharp *whuff* of blue vapor. "At five thousand feet, no rifle on earth can touch the envelope, and the wind-drift over the interior plains is steady from the west. Think of the economy, General! Right now, to police the three thousand miles of desert between the Salt Lake and the Obi, you keep eighty regiments of cavalry eating six-thaler oats in mud forts every fifty leagues. With six air-cruisers of the *Aeolus* class moored at Denver, Sitka, and Irkutsk, a single lieutenant with a pair of Zeiss glasses and a wireless-spark key can patrol five hundred square miles of steppe between breakfast and noon."

"And when he sees a band of insurgents tearing up the broad-gauge track, what does he do from five thousand feet—drop a melinite bomb into a prairie five miles wide and hope the horse stands still while the shell falls for eighteen seconds?" asked old Brigadier Caleb Vance, who had ridden out from the Presidio on a quiet mule to watch his grand-nephew’s new toy and now stood leaning on his hickory stick near the open shed-doors, spitting tobacco juice into the marsh-reeds.

Young Marcus turned his pale eyes upon the old frontiersman. Between the seventy-five-year-old veteran of the Platte snowdrifts and the twenty-three-year-old polytechnic graduate lay the entire gulf of the century.

"He does not drop bombs on horsemen, Uncle," young Marcus said patiently, pulling his ivory slide-rule from his breast pocket. "A horseman requires a village to winter in, a corral for his remounts, and a well of sweet water within twenty miles. The air-cruiser does not fight the guerrilla; it follows him at night by the glare of his campfires, marks the map-coordinates of his winter *aoul* or his adobe sanctuary, and drops four hundred pounds of white phosphorus and arsenic canister into his granary and his water-hole while he sleeps. It reduces the policing of a continent from a cavalry campaign to a problem in municipal sanitation."

He stepped up the narrow aluminum ladder into the gondola’s forward control-car, where Major Kuroda was already checking the mercury barometer and the brass speaking-tubes leading to the engine-cage.

"Cast off the bow-lines, Herr Loewe," Marcus ordered, strapping a leather chin-stay under his cap as the flash-boiler behind him built to six hundred pounds of superheated steam with a high, whistling shriek that sent the marsh-ducks exploding out of the tules along the strait. "We will take her up to four thousand feet over the bay and drop three dummy sand-casks onto the Alcatraz target-raft before the Protector’s barge reaches the Mint slip. I want the old men on Montgomery Street to look up from their ledgers at noon and see that there is no longer a roof over their heads that my guns cannot look through."

***

At that very noon, while the monstrous yellow cigar of the *Aeolus* rose slowly out of the Benicia marshes and turned its twin wooden screws toward the Golden Gate against the upper sea-breeze, Lady Kaiulani did not look up at the sky. She was standing three stories below the street-level of San Francisco, in the cool, grease-scented gloom of the Imperial Assay and Ration Vaults beneath the Custom House, watching a clerk weigh a dead man’s thumb.

It was not a real thumb, though the Cantonese coolie-broker who stood trembling before the iron grillwork looked as if he would gladly have hacked off his own digit to be out of the cellar. It was a brass identification-tally—Number Seven-Seven-Four-Two of the Washoe Silver Reserve—stamped with the sun-and-anchor and crusted along its rim with green verdigris from the lime-pits of Virginia City.

"Read the voucher attached to that disk again, Auditor Shen," Kaiulani said.

She wore her dark blue riding-habit from the Santa Cruz mountains, the skirt pinned up out of the damp sawdust of the vault floor, a single electric hand-lamp held in her gloved fingers to illuminate the open double-entry folio on the stone table. After three days in the clean, ancient silence of the redwoods with Elias, the air of the capital’s basement tasted to her like the bilge of an old slave-ship: wet cement, ozone from the Hollerith sorting-machines clattering in the next room, and the rank, sweetish pomade used by the third-grade fiscal clerks.

Shen—then a thirty-year-old assessor newly promoted from the Hankow customs—adjusted his horn spectacles and held the yellow treasury warrant close to the bulb. "Dated the twelfth of August, Your Highness, and countersigned by Deputy-Comptroller Schuyler the younger," Shen read in his precise, uninflected court English. "'To the Factors of the Six Companies Guild, Sacramento: four hundred and eighty silver thalers, being full settlement of five-year accumulated wages and rice-bounty for Coolie Seven-Seven-Four-Two, discharged in good health upon completion of his Comstock tunnel-indenture.'" "And now read the burial-register from the Mount Davidson typhus-ward that my Hawaiian provosts seized from the mine-superintendent’s safe on Tuesday," Kaiulani commanded. Shen turned the leaf of a smaller, grease-stained book bound in rough calfskin. "'Coolie Seven-Seven-Four-Two, native of Swatow: died of the black lung and spotted fever in Shaft Four, November nineteenth, eighteen-seventy-seven. Buried in Trench C without kin.'" A thin, whistling sigh escaped the fat Cantonese broker outside the iron bars; he dropped to both knees on the concrete, his silk skull-cap rolling into the sawdust as he knocked his forehead against the lower rail. "Mercy, High Commissioner!" the broker babbled in the Kwangtung dialect, his plump hands clawing at the iron palings. "It was not the Guild that kept the silver! When a coolie dies in the deep levels before his third year, the white superintendents and Mr. Schuyler’s audit-clerks do not strike his number from the Hollerith cards! They keep his brass tag on the hook, draw his four pounds of salt pork and his two silver thalers a day from the Crown Commissariat for the remaining three years, and give our Guild ten percent to sign the discharge-mark with a dead man’s ink-thumb! There are six thousand ghosts drawing rations on the Comstock rolls today, Lady—and ten thousand more on the Puget Sound timber-books! If I had refused to stamp the paper, Mr. Schuyler’s provosts would have revoked my rice-license and sent my sons to the rock-piles!" Kaiulani did not answer the broker. Slowly, she straightened her spine beneath the low brick arch of the vault, letting the electric lamp hang down against her dark blue skirt so that their faces were thrown into deep upward shadow. Here was the truth of the Antonine Peace that Rector Norton’s apprentices were painting in gold leaf and lapis lazuli across the water at Berkeley. From the deck of a battleship or the window of a Pullman car, Elias’s empire looked like a seamless monument of granite and Bessemer steel. Down here in the cellar, where the oil met the gears, the monument was already being eaten hollow by its own bookkeepers. Because no newspaper dared print a line without the censor’s stamp, and because no workman dared strike a blow without facing Marcus Vance’s Gatling guns, the thirty thousand clerks, syndicate-nephews, and Satsuma quartermasters who kept the ledgers had discovered a gold-mine richer than the Klondike: an empire of paper phantoms. Dead coolies ate government beef in Nevada; phantom regiments of Missouri militia drew Spencer carbines that were quietly sold off the back of lighters at Manila to the Borneo pirates; and the very mortar of the state was being ground into private silver dust before the founder's eyes had even closed. Yet above the basement arches, up in the sunlit halls of the Rincon Hill Citadel, the outer crust of the colossus still shone with blinding, terrifying splendor. That same afternoon, when Elias Thorne returned from the redwoods to take his place in the Hall of the Council—the vast, redwood-vaulted throne room whose tall casements looked straight out through the Golden Gate—he did not look like a man whose cellars were full of rats. He sat upon the raised silver curule chair with his heavy cavalry boots laced tight over his bandaged calves, his broad shoulders squared inside the unadorned navy wool of his Engineer’s tunic, while below the porphyry steps stood the begging bowls of Europe. They had come around the Horn on a leased Hamburg packet because they could no longer afford the coal to steam via Suez: Count von Hatzfeldt from Berlin, Monsieur Challemel-Lacour from the French Republic, and Sir Julian Pauncefote of Whitehall. For three days they had waited in the anterooms of the Palace Hotel like provincial tax-collectors while Elias rested his knees among the Santa Cruz ferns; now, as the late sun struck through the western glass and turned the brass fasces behind his head into pillars of sunset gold, the three envoys bowed from the waist before the Kentucky squatter’s son. "The winter harvests in Prussia and the Loire have failed for thesecond year, Excellency," Count von Hatzfeldt began, his high boots creaking on the koa-wood parquet as he laid a vellum schedule upon the lowest step of the dais. Though he wore the white cuirassier tunic of Bismarck’s Reich, the gold braid at his cuffs was tarnished by salt-damp, and his voice lacked the iron ring of the seventies. "With the Russian steppes closed by your Siberian truce-lines and the Chicago elevators shipping exclusively to Canton, the price of wheat in Berlin has doubled since August. Furthermore, our electrical works at Siemens and the Krupp rolling-mills at Essen are standing at half-time for want of Malaysian gutta-percha and Peruvian nitrates. The European Concert asks no territorial revision in the Pacific; we ask only that Your Excellency lift the forty-percent differential duty upon non-Confederation hulls at Manila and Guayaquil, and release twenty million bushels of San Joaquin red wheat against sixty-day bills drawn upon the Reichsbank and the Bank of France." Elias did not reach for the vellum. His right hand rested upon the head of his iron walking-stick; behind his ribs, the heavy, sloshing mercury of his pulse beat a slow measure against his wool vest, and the air in the crowded hall smelled to him of French pomade, damp broadcloth, and the faint, metallic ozone drifting up from the cable-vaults below. "Sixty-day paper drawn on Berlin and Paris," Elias said, his low, rough voice carrying clearly down the length of the silent chamber where Cornelius Schuyler and Marquis Takashima stood beside the serpentine pillars. "When my father owed sixty-two dollars on his land in thirty-seven, Count, the bailiffs did not take sixty-day paper. They asked for hard coin, and when we had none, they burned the logs." Sir Julian Pauncefote shifted his weight, his pale English cheeks flushing beneath his gray whiskers. "Surely the Providentor does not compare the sovereign credit of Great Britain, France, and the German Empire to a frontier mortgage. We offer the treasury bills of three hundred million civilized people." "You offer the promises of three armed camps sitting on a worn-out peninsula," Elias replied, leaning forward half an inch upon his stick until his pale eyes fixed the Englishman to the floor. "You spend forty million pounds a year building fortresses against each other along the Rhine and the Alps, and then come to my wharf with your hats in your hands to ask for bread and copper-insulation on credit. My granaries at Vallejo are full to the rafters, gentlemen, and my nitrate-hulks at Callao are riding deep in the water. You may have twenty million bushels of wheat before the November gales, and ten thousand tons of Sarawak rubber." Count von Hatzfeldt’s narrow chest relaxed slightly. "On the security of the Reichsbank notes, Excellency?" "On the security of your blast-furnaces and your naval slips," Elias said. "I take no European paper. For every bushel of California wheat that enters Hamburg or Havre this winter, your governments will deliver to my agents at Antwerp fifty tons of rolled Bessemer rail-iron at forty percent below the Essen market price, or sign five-year indentures transferring four hundred master optical-grinders and chemical engineers from Jena and Lyons to the polytechnic schools at Berkeley. And as for the differential duty—any European steamer that wishes to load nitrates at Callao or tin at Batavia without paying the sixty-percent foreign impost need only haul down her national rag at the harbor-mouth, register fifty-one percent of her hull with Mr. Schuyler’s maritime board in San Francisco, and carry a Hawaiian port-officer on her bridge. Those are the terms of the trough. You may sign them at the Chancellor’s desk before the five-o’clock gun, or you may go home and explain to your weavers why their bread is made of turnip-meal this Christmas." He did not wait to watch them bow. Rising from the silver seat by driving his right arm straight down upon the iron ferrule of his cane—a movement so practiced and rigid that none of the three Europeans saw how his left boot dragged across the velvet carpet—Elias turned his back upon the ambassadors of the Old World and walked slowly through the bronze doors behind the dais. *** Only when the double oak panels of his private bedchamber on the third floor had been bolted on the inside by Brigadier Caleb Vance did the iron go out of his knees. The room was small, austere, and windowless on the seaward side to keep out the draft, heated by a single porcelain stove burning smokeless anthracite. There was no gilded canopy here; against the whitewashed plaster wall stood the narrow gas-pipe camp-cot from Vicksburg, a washstand with a tin basin, and a leather armchair smelling of old horse-sweat and camphor. Elias got three paces past the threshold before his right elbow buckled on the stick. "Easy, boy," Caleb whispered, catching Elias’s two-hundred-pound frame beneath the left armpit with his own gnarled, seventy-five-year-old shoulder and easing him down into the leather chair beside the stove. "You held your breath too long out there in front of the quality. Let me get the knife to these laces." Elias could not answer him at once. His chin was tipped back against the greasy leather headrest, his mouth wide open as he fought to pull air through a windpipe that felt as though it had been plugged with hot wet wool. The room smelled of carbolic soap and the dried stramonium-leaves smoldering in the brass saucer on the washstand, yet behind those familiar odors he smelled something strange and sharp—like scorching copper wire or burned feathers—that was not in the room at all, but inside the left hemisphere of his own skull. "The... the German," Elias formed the words slowly, his tongue feeling thick and dry as a salted boot-tongue in his mouth while Caleb knelt on the rug, his cataract-clouded eye bent close to the floor as he cut the tight leather thongs of Elias’s boots with his pocket-knife. "Did you see his coat, Caleb? White wool... and brass eagles... and begging for twentyshiploads of flour like a teamster at the fort gate." "I seen him," Caleb grunted, stripping the split calfskin off Elias’s swollen, purple-mottled ankle and wrapping the cold flesh in warm flannel from the stove-fender. "They’re all whipped, Elias. The whole kit and boodle of ’em from here to Jerusalem. Now keep your jaw shut and drink this foxglove-water before the Princess comes up from the cellar and skins me alive for letting you stand on the steps." Caleb rose stiffly from his knees and held the small blue glass measure to Elias’s lips. Elias reached up with his left hand to steady the old man’s wrist—and the hand did not rise. It lay on his flannel thigh like five pounds of dead salt pork wrapped in yellow hide. He stared down at his own fingers in the dim light of the stove-grate. He commanded the thumb to twitch, just as he had commanded forty Rangers to wheel at the Rio Frio and sixteen battleships to steam past Kanagawa; the nerve sent the spark down the arm, and nothing answered. At the same instant, the scorching smell of burned feathers flared behind his left eye into a silent, blinding flash of white magnesium light. The porcelain stove, Caleb’s white beard, and the tin washbasin tilted sideways without a sound; the left side of his jaw sagged open, spilling the bitter digitalis down the front of his navy tunic, and when he tried to call out his friend’s name, his throat produced only a thick, wet, bubbling rattle that died on his chin. Caleb did not drop the glass. The old artilleryman stood frozen for two seconds, looking down at the twisted, half-stone mask of the boy he had pulled out of the frozen mule on the Platte fifty years before. Then, moving with a terrifying quietness for a man of seventy-five, Caleb stepped to the chamber door, drew the heavy iron night-bolt across the jamb so that none of the corridor pages could enter, and walked into the adjoining dressing-closet where Lady Kaiulani was waiting beside the private hydraulic lift from the Assay Vaults. "Don't call the garrison surgeon, ma'am," Caleb said, his cracked voice steady as he closed the closet door behind him and held up his wet, medicine-stained sleeve in the yellow lamp-light. "His left side’s gone dead as a wedge, and he’s lost his tongue. If Takashima’s orderly out in the passage hears a doctor running up the stairs with a lancet-case, the Japanese cruisers will be clearing for action before the six-o’clock bell." Kaiulani did not gasp, nor did her hand tremble as she laid the brass identification-tag of the dead Comstock coolie down upon the dressing-table. For ten years she had known this hour was coming up the stair; now that it stood in the room, her dark face settled into an icy, impenetrable calm. "Can he see you with his right eye, Brigadier?" she asked softly, already stripping the long silver hat-pin from her riding-bonnet. "Looks right through me like a bored cannon," Caleb said. "Then he is still on the throne," Kaiulani said, walking past him into the bedchamber where the great figure slumped crookedly in the leather chair, his solitary gray eye staring fiercely out from the ruined mask at the locked oak door. "Put fresh coals in the grate, Caleb, and go out onto the gallery landing with your pipe. Tell the household chamberlain that the Providentor has ordered a cold supper laid in his study and wishes no disturbance while he drafts the Berlin grain-warrants with me. Nobody enters this wing until my nephew brings the Hawaiian Guard up from the Mint at midnight." *** Yet an empire wired together with six thousand leagues of copper nerve-fiber cannot have its brain struck half-dead at five o’clock without the twitch being felt in the extremities before six. A corridor page from the Osaka delegation had seen the European envoys dismissed ten minutes early; a laundry-woman in the basement had noticed that no hot water was called for in the third-floor bath; and at a quarter past seven, the apothecary’s boy from the Presidio hospital was intercepted at the side gate by one of Marquis Takashima’s marine orderlies while carrying two cylinders of compressed oxygen wrapped in an army blanket. By nine o’clock that night, while the city of San Francisco drank its beer in the gas-lit gardens along Market Street and celebrated the humiliation of the German Count, a heavy, unnatural quiet had settled over the subterranean War Room forty feet beneath the granite foundations of the Monterey Staff College Annex on Telegraph Hill. Here there were no windows to let in the fog, and no redwoods. The vaulted concrete chamber—built to withstand the direct hit of a sixteen-inch naval shell—hummed with the low, continuous vibration of the rotary ventilation-fans and smelled sharply of damp Portland cement, ozone from the twenty telegraph repeaters clicking softly in the rear alcove, and the rank, oily smoke of the Manila cheroots that Colonel Armistead was chewing unlit in the corner. Around the massive slate plotting-table in the center of the floor stood five men: young General Marcus Vance, still wearing the oil-spotted khaki tunic in which he had descended from the gondola of the *Aeolus* at sunset; Marquis Takashima in his dark naval cape; Colonel Armistead of the Second Virginia Auxiliary; General Saigo of the Choshu Guard; and Major Kuroda. Upon the black slate between them lay not the charts of the German or Russian frontiers, but the purple-inked mobilization grid of the city of San Francisco and the domestic rail-junctions of the Sacramento Valley. "The oxygen cylinders went up the private bullion-hoist from the cellar at seven-thirty, General Vance," Marquis Takashima was saying, his narrow bronze face gleaming like old lacquer under the green-shaded incandescent bulbs as his gloved finger tapped the red square marking the Rincon Hill Citadel. "And my personal physician has interviewed the apothecary’s assistant. Three cylinders of pure oxygen and ten grains of strychnine sulfate. A physician does not administer strychnine and oxygen to a man of sixty-four unless the respiratory center of the brain has been struck by cerebral hemorrhage. The Providentor is either dead behind that locked oak door, or he is a mute paralytic under the thumb of the Hawaiian woman and your dottering uncle." "Old Caleb Vance has two companies of the Life Guard sitting on the stairs with loaded Spencers, Marquis," growled Colonel Armistead, spitting a shred of tobacco leaf onto the concrete floor as he leaned his scarred knuckles on the edge of the slate. "I rode up to the south gate at eight to present the evening guard-report in person. Caleb came out to the wicket himself with a Colt forty-five in his waistband—told me Elias was asleep after the German parley and that any officer who brought an armed file within two hundred yards of theMason Street wall before morning would be blown out of his saddle. Meanwhile, Comptroller Schuyler has locked himself inside the Bank of California with forty hired Pinkerton riflemen and is burning his private Comstock ledgers in the furnace boiler." General Saigo of the Choshu division rested his left hand upon the hilt of his saber, his dark eyes passing coldly over the Virginian’s shoulder to meet young Marcus’s gaze. "If the breath leaves the Providentor’s body before the succession is regulated by the Sword, General Vance, the Comptroller’s syndicate-clerks and the Hawaiian Princess will proclaim a civilian Regency from the balcony at dawn. Within a week, the

eastern provinces will stop the tribute-trains, and the Diet will vote to cut the naval estimates in half. I have four battalions of the Choshu and Satsuma infantry under arms at the Presidio barracks tonight, and Admiral Takashima’s cruisers have steam up off Goat Island. We require only your counter-signature on the Riot Warrant to occupy the Mint, the Telegraph Exchange, and the Rincon Hill gates before midnight." Young Marcus Vance did not look up from the slate table immediately. He stood directly beneath the central lamp, the green light catching the pale, beardless planes of his twenty-three-year-old face and the ivory tip of the slide-rule in his breast pocket. All evening he had listened to the old warlords—the samurai who remembered the Shogun’s wars and the Virginian who remembered Chancellorsville—talking of barricades and palace gates as if power were a physical chest of silver that could be carried off in an ambulance-wagon. "You propose to march four Japanese battalions down Market Street at midnight to shoot down Brigadier Caleb’s Missourians at the Palace gate, General Saigo?" Marcus asked, his clinical voice cutting through the hum of the ventilating-fans without a trace of heat. "To secure the person of the Sovereign from insular usurpers," Takashima replied smoothly, stepping closer to the youth’s elbow. "Under a Provisional Military Directorate: yourself as Chief of the Continental Staff, myself as High Admiral of the Ocean, and Mr. Schuyler retained at the Treasury under our audit to keep the New York banks quiet. Once our sentries are inside the bedchamber, whether the old man can speak or not is immaterial; we will issue the proclamations over his stamp." Marcus reached out with two steady fingers and picked up a small brass marker representing the experimental air-cruiser *Aeolus*, setting it down squarely upon the inked outline of the Citadel conservatory dome. "If your Choshu infantry fires a single volley at the Life Guard on Mason Street tonight, Marquis," Marcus said, looking from the Japanese admiral to the scarred Virginian beside him, "Colonel Armistead’s four regiments of Atlantic Auxiliaries in Oakland will cross the bay on the ferry-barges by four in the morning to shoot your sailors in the back, and by noon tomorrow half of San Francisco will be in ashes while the British fleet steams out of Esquimalt to retake Puget Sound. My father did not die in the ice at Baikal so that his son could preside over a Mexican *pronunciamiento* in a street-gutter." "Then what is your calculation, boy?" Armistead demanded, his hand tightening on his belt as the telegraph repeater in the rear alcove suddenly began to clatter with an incoming priority wire from the Citadel. "If we stand on our thumbs till daylight while Kaiulani and Shen lock the doors—" "We do not touch the doors, Colonel; we take the wires," Marcus said, turning half a pace toward Major Kuroda as the aide tore the wet blue ribbon from the spool and brought it to the slate table. Marcus read the cipher once, then laid it face-up beneath the green lamp. It bore the private seal of Lady Kaiulani from the Assay Vaults: she had already placed forty tons of nitro-glycerine under the Market Street bullion-cellars and wired the torpedo-boats at Mare Island to sink any cruiser off Goat Island that moved an anchor-fluke without her counter-sign. "You see, gentlemen," Marcus said softly, "the High Commissioner understands engineering better than you do. If we fight her tonight, we inherit a crater. Tomorrow morning, I will walk into the conservatory alone and sign a compact with Her Highness to preserve the Triumvirate for as long as the old man’s chest can be kept moving by oxygen and strychnine—five years, perhaps six, until my polytechnic cadets are old enough to take the ships out of your hands without firing a shot." *** It was by that secret subterranean compact of eighty-one that the phantom peace was bought, and the terrifying, half-paralyzed twilight of Elias Thorne’s reign was stretched across the middle eighties like a drumhead tightened to the splitting-point. Yet before the final calcification of the Hundred and Twenty-Four States could be proclaimed over his death-bed—during those last, suspended summers of eighty-five and eighty-six when the old Titan still sat propped beside the carp-pool and the world waited for the inevitable stroke—Lady Kaiulani made one final, unrecorded effort to discover whether blood might yet spare the Empire the tyranny of the examination-shed. On a warm afternoon in the late summer of 1886, ten months before the Coral Sea and the final silence at Monterey, she walked alone through the terraced bamboo and cypress alleys of the Palace Gardens on the southern slope of Nob Hill. Here, behind twenty-foot walls of rusticated Sierra granite patrolled by her silent Oahu riflemen, the roar of the Potrero rolling-mills and the constant, brassy clanging of the cable-cars along California Street were muted to a drowsy, insect-like hum. The air smelled of crushed lemon-verbena, hot Monterey pine-needles, and the salt mist that drifted lazily through the red-lacquered torii gates bordering the lotus ponds. Across the clipped emerald turf of the lower bowling-green, beneath the shade of a weeping *waringin* tree transplanted from Batavia, sat the three young men whom the court whispers called the Left-Handed Princes. Elias Thorne had never married. A king who weds a daughter of Boston insults Edo; a conqueror who takes a princess of Satsuma or Oahu to his lawful bed turns his own frontier marshals into rebels. Instead, across forty years of camps and chanceries, the Providentor had left his rough, hawk-nosed stamp upon three women of the three great races he had welded into his realm—and because he regarded human beings as timber to be tested for its grain before being mortised into the state, he had brought the three boys up within the garden walls under the eyes of the Chancery tutors, unacknowledged by statute yet clothed in the purple-bordered tunics of Imperial Wards. Kaiulani paused beside a carved stone lantern, her black silk parasol tilted against the glare of the western water, watching them through narrowed, clinical eyes. The eldest, Silas—born in fifty-nine to a dead widow of the Virginia Auxiliaries during the Denver winter—was twenty-seven now. He had his father’s broad, ox-like shoulders and thick wrists, yet as he lounged in a wicker garden-chair with a silver flask of Monongahela rye uncorked beside his knee, tossing bits of sugared biscuit to the golden carp, his face showed none of the freezing Kentucky iron. It was soft, florid, and petulant around the mouth; he had spent the morning losing four thousand thalers at the Jockey Club races at Ingleside, and his riding-boots were still crusted with turf-mud. Ten paces away, kneeling upon a straw *tatami* mat spread over the grass, the second son—Kiyoshi, born to a lady of the Choshu house after the treaty of Shimoda—was methodically dismantling the breech-mechanism of a new Sacramento repeating rifle with a pair of oiled chamois gloves, his narrow, shaved head bent so low over the steel springs that the sun caught the small, livid scar where a court surgeon had trepanned his skull after a childhood bout of the falling-sickness. And standing apart by the marble balustrade overlooking the harbor, dressed in white linen flannel and sketching the distant smoke of an incoming Canton tea-liner in a small calfskin water-color book, was the youngest: Kalanimoku, her own second cousin’s child, born in the year after the Honolulu barricades—a boy of eighteen with Elias’s pale, startling gray eyes set inside the warm bronze skin of an island chief. "Your Highness walks late in the sun," Silas said, not rising from his wicker chair as her shadow fell across the turf, though he lazily pushed the silver whiskey-flask behind a flowerpot with the toe of his boot. "Have you come down from the conservatory to tell us whether the old man’s left thumb twitched after dinner, or has young General Vance decided to turn this garden into a balloon-shed?" "I have come to see how the sons of the house employ their afternoon while the grain-brokers in the city below are betting ten to one that the Providentor will not see September," Kaiulani said, her musical voice cool and level as she closed her parasol with a sharp *snap*. "Did you attend the sitting of the Maritime Tariff Committee at noon, Silas, as the Chancellor requested?" Silas laughed—a thick, wet sound that smelled of sour mash even at three paces—and flicked a pebble into the lotus pond. "To sit for four hours between old Schuyler’s nose and Auditor Shen’s abacus, listening to how many barrels of salt-pork go to the Sitka mines? Let the Berkeley examination-clerks count the pork, Aunt. When my father’s breath stops, theFirst Virginia and the California Lancers will not ask a man how many logarithms he knows before they hoist him onto his saddle. They will look for a white man who carries the Thorne jaw and knows how to spend gold in the canteens." Beside the mat, Kiyoshi did not look up from the disassembled rifle-bolt, though his thin fingers began to twitch with the rhythmic, involuntary tic that preceded his seizures. "The Virginia regiments are garrisoned at Hankow and the Yenisei, Elder Brother," the Choshu youth said in his high, strained English, his thumb clicking the firing-pin three times against the steel sear. "In San Francisco there are only the Satsuma Marine guards and the Academy cadets. When the breath stops, Marquis Takashima will clear the palace with the bayonet, and if a man does not wear the sword-belt of the Western Clans, his throat will be cut before he reaches the stable." Down by the balustrade, young Kalanimoku closed his water-color pad with a quiet sigh and turned his pale gray eyes—Elias’s own eyes, stripped of all their pitiless ambition—toward Kaiulani. "Do not listen to them, Aunt," the boy said softly in the Hawaiian tongue. "One dreams of a tavern-camp, and the other dreams of a shogun’s slaughterhouse. If the throne is an iron chair where a man must sit with a pistol in his lap and watch his brothers’ cups for arsenic, let General Vance and his slide-rules have it. Give me a schooner and twenty islanders, and let me sail back to Kauai to plant taro in the quiet valleys." Kaiulani looked from one to the other across the manicured grass: the drunken roaring-boy of the old frontier, the epileptic fanatic of the barracks, and the gentle painter who wanted to go home to a garden that had been paved with coal-dredges twenty years ago. For forty years Elias had felled every tall tree between the Potomac and the Yellow Sea so that none might cast a shadow across his camp-cot; and in the shade of that solitary, monolithic oak, nothing had been able to grow save toadstools and weeds. If she crowned Silas at dawn, Takashima’s battleships would shell the Citadel by noon; if she crowned Kiyoshi, the American provinces would rise from Boston to Sacramento; and if she placed the gold collar upon Kalanimoku’s slender neck, young Marcus Vance would have him strangled with a telegraph-wire before the ink was dry on the proclamation. There was no blood left that could hold the circle. The dynasty had died before it was born, crushed beneath the sheer, unyielding tonnage of the father’s personality. *** And down beyond the twenty-foot granite wall of the garden, in the steep, grid-iron canyons of brick and redwood that tumbled from the skirts of Nob Hill to the oily waters of the bay, the great beast of seven hundred thousand souls was already smelling the sickness in the upper rooms. To the Chronicler who mingled with the crowds along Kearney and Market streets during those sultry, oppressive days of late August—when a freakish calm off the Farallones left the coal-soot of the foundries hanging motionless between the cornice-stones like a ceiling of dirty yellow flannel—the transformation of the public temper was as rapid and terrifying as the souring of milk before a thunderstorm. For twenty years the people of the capital had lived inside the iron parenthesis of the Providentor’s will. Because nobody had seen Elias Thorne walk down the steps of the Chancery since the spring of eighty-four, and because the official *Gazette* printed every morning the same unvarying three-line formula regarding his afternoon audiences in the conservatory, the lower wards had come to regard him less as a mortal magistrate of flesh and bone than as an eternal, subterranean boiler that kept the silver thalers circulating and the grain-elevators full. Now, without a single line appearing in the censored press, the invisible telegraph of the streets—the whispers of laundry-coolies coming down from the Mason Street service-gates, the guarded talk of apothecaries’ clerks over their beer-mugs in the German cellars of Bush Street, the sudden doubling of the Hawaiian sentry-posts around the Sub-Treasury—ran through the tenements from the Mission to the Barbary Coast. *The old man’s tongue is black,* the Irish dock-wallopers muttered as they leaned on their bale-hooks beside the silent hydraulic cranes at the Pacific Mail wharf, watching two Satsuma torpedo-boats slip their moorings off Goat Island with their battle-lanterns hooded in broad daylight. *He’s been dead since the German Count came to town, and the Kanaka witch is keeping him packed in rock-salt up in the glass house while the New York bankers ship all the flour out to Canton!* By the third morning of the rumor, the terror had translated itself into the only language a metropolis understands: the price of bread. Although the vast stone granaries at Vallejo and Port Costa were bursting with forty million bushels of the summer harvest from the San Joaquin, the syndicate grain-jobbers along California Street—men who took their secret cues from Cornelius Schuyler’s private discount-desk—had quietly locked their warehouse receipts inside their iron safes, refusing to release a single barge-load of red wheat against the standard silver-paper certificates of the Municipal Commissariat until they knew whose signature would stand on the Treasury warrants on Monday morning. Within forty-eight hours, the two-pound loaf of regulation barley-and-wheat bread, which had stood fixed by provost-statute at one silver tenth since the year of the Sitka purchase, vanished from the bakers’ counters. At six o’clock in the evening, when the shift-whistles blew at the Potrero Point armor-works and the Union Iron Foundry, ten thousand soot-streaked puddle-men, Cantonese sandal-makers, and discharged veterans of the eastern campaigns did not go home to their boarding-houses. They packed the cobbled triangle before the closed bronze doors of the Old Mint and the neighboring bakeries along Commercial Street, where wooden shutters had been bolted over the broken glass and armed squads of the Tripartite Municipal Police stood ankle-deep in spilled flour and horse-dung with their repeating carbines held across their chests. "Four silver tenths for a ten-ounce loaf of sour corn-meal at the Italian’s on Dupont Street!" roared a massive, grey-bearded hammer-man from the Risdon boiler-shops, standing on the hub of an overturned dray and waving a hard, mildewed ship’s biscuit above the sea of greasy bowler hats and blue coolie-blouses. "And when I laid down a five-thaler Treasury note with the Protector’s own face on the paper, the shopkeeper spat on the counter and said the bank wouldn't give him sixty cents in copper for it because Elias Thorne is nailed up in a lead box at Monterey and the Japs are going to divide the Mint with the Wall Street sharks tonight!" "Show us the Old Man!" a woman screamed from the steps of the closed savings-bank opposite, holding an empty flour-sack above her shawl while three hundred voices along the curbstone took up the cry in a ragged, rhythmic chant that echoed off the iron shutters of the counting-houses: *"Show us the Protector! Open the balcony, or we’ll bring the sledges to the gate!"* *** Up on the third floor of the Citadel, inside the windowless, anthracite-heated bedchamber where the air bit the nostrils with the sharp, medicinal stench of spilled strychnine, camphor-ice, and scorching copper from the galvanic battery-box on the washstand, Elias Thorne heard the roar of the street-mob coming up through the stone ventilating-shafts like the grumbling of ice-floes jamming against a bridge-pier. He was not in a lead box, though as Brigadier Caleb Vance and two tight-lipped naval surgeons finished strapping his torso into the hinged whalebone-and-steel orthopedic corset beneath his dark blue Engineer’s tunic, the distinction between a living sovereign and an iron effigy had grown narrower than a knife-blade. Since the second stroke had taken his left arm and his speech after the German audience forty-eight hours ago, Elias had existed inside a terrifying, vertical prison. His mind behind his brow was as clear and pitiless as the winter sun over the Wind River mountains; he could calculate the tonnage of the Vallejo wheat-bins to the hundredweight, and he knew to the penny why Cornelius Schuyler’s brokers had locked the flour-barges to force a Regency crisis before the weekend. Yet when he commanded his vocal cords to form the order that would hang twenty grain-jobbers from the California Street lamp-posts, his ruined throat produced only a dry, hissing click; and his left leg and arm hung from his shoulder-socket like fourstones of wet clay bolted to a pine post. "Pull the lower buckle another notch, Doctor," Lady Kaiulani commanded, standing at the foot of the dressing-chair in her dark blue brocade gown, her face pale and immovable as she held the gold-braided collar of his greatcoat open in her hands. "If his knees bend an inch when the hydraulic platform rolls out onto the stone flags of the balcony, ten thousand men down in the plaza with opera-glasses will see it, and by midnight the Presidio garrison will be marching on the Mint." The senior surgeon—a man whose fingers were stained yellow with picric acid and who knew that if the patient died under his wrench, old Caleb Vance would shoot him before he reached the corridor—pulled the leather strap across Elias’s lower ribs until the steel stays groaned against his swollen liver.
