"Highness, the fluid in the pleura is pressing directly upon the aorta," the doctor whispered, wiping the sweat from his forehead with his cuff as he pointed to the two copper electrodes of the portable galvanic battery that he had taped with gutta-percha plaster to the muscles of Elias’s paralyzed left neck and shoulder. "With forty grains of digitalis and a twentieth of a grain of strychnine in his veins, his heart is beating like a trip-hammer against a closed valve. If we lock his spine upright in this iron frame for fifteen minutes in the cold wind off the bay, and pass a galvanic current through the cervical nerves to keep his chin from sagging onto his chest, the blood-pressure in the carotid may rupture the remaining vessel in the brain before the crowd clears the square!" Elias did not wait for Kaiulani to answer the sawbones. With his live right hand—the broad, scarred hand that had held the squirrel-rifle in Kentucky and the Paterson Colt on the Rio Frio—he reached out from the sleeve of his tunic, seized the surgeon’s linen lapel in a grip that twisted the cloth into a knot, and jerked the man’s face down within six inches of his own. From the right side of Elias’s face, a single wide, water-clear eye blazed out of the grey, half-dead mask with such volcanic fury that the physician went white to the lips. Elias released the lapel and struck his own iron-corseted breastbone twice with his right fist—*thud, thud*—a hollow sound like a mallet striking a keg of nails. "He’s telling you he’d rather burst his skull standing up in the wind than rot in the bedsheets while Schuyler steals his horse," Brigadier Caleb Vance said, his one good eye glinting fiercely beneath his white bushy brow as he knelt and locked the hinged steel leg-splints inside the wide tops of Elias’s cavalry boots, hiding the iron joints beneath the dark blue trouser-cuffs. "Put the coat on him, Princess, and give me the switch to that spark-box. I walked beside him when we didn't have mule-tallow to grease our moccasins, and by God, I’ll hold his chin up for the last parade." Five minutes later, at the exact stroke of six upon the bronze bell of the Nob Hill basilica, the tall, twenty-foot French casements of the Western Balcony above the Citadel plaza swung slowly inward. Down in the vast, stepped granite amphitheater below—where fifty thousand mechanics, dock-laborers, and off-duty soldiers stood wedged shoulder-to-shoulder between the thirty-foot bronze statue of the Providentor and the cordons of young Marcus Vance’s Academy cadets—the angry, roaring chant of *"Bread or blood!"* died away into a sudden, intake of breath that sounded like the surf drawing back down a gravel beach before a tidal wave. Out through the dark arch of the doorway, moving at a slow, stately pace that no man on the pavement below could tell was driven by a noiseless hydraulic worm-gear sliding through a groove in the marble flags rather than by human steps, came the Sovereign of the Pacific. He was not sitting in a wheeled chair. Bolted upright from heel to hip inside the hidden steel stirrups of the sliding platform, his broad shoulders squared by the whalebone stays beneath his plain, unadorned Engineer’s tunic, Elias Thorne appeared to walk straight to the stone balustrade and stop with his right hand planted squarely upon the coping. To his right stood Lady Kaiulani in the full crimson-and-yellow feather mantle of the island kings; to his left stood young General Marcus Vance and old Caleb, whose gnarled hand inside his coat-pocket gripped the vulcanite rheostat of the galvanic wire

running up beneath the skirt of the Providentor’s greatcoat. Down in the front rank of the crowd by the fountain, five hundred binocular-lenses and spyglasses clicked up simultaneously in the red, level rays of the setting sun. For ten seconds, nobody breathed. The wind coming in through the Golden Gate was cold and sharp with salt-kelp and foundry-smoke; it whipped Elias’s short-cropped white hair against his temples and flattened the blue wool against his chest. Inside the iron corset, Elias felt as if he were being sawed in half by red-hot wires. Every beat of his strychnine-lashed heart sent a blinding, crimson stroke against the back of his eyeballs, turning the fifty thousand upturned white faces down in the plaza into a shimmering lake of molten brass; the water in his lungs rose into his throat with the taste of warm copper pennies, and he knew that if he let his right knee slacken by the thickness of a sheet of paper against the steel splint, the whole monstrous lie would pitch forward over the stone rail into the street. Below the balcony, in the reserved loggia beside the Mint gates, old Cornelius Schuyler half-rose from his carriage-seat, his mouth falling open as he stared up at the erect, broad-shouldered figure towering against the sunset gold. "He is standing on his own boots!" Schuyler whispered hoarsely to Marquis Takashima, his trembling fingers dropping the key to the Vallejo grain-safes into the straw at his feet. "The apothecary lied to your doctor—he has ten years of iron in him yet!" Up on the balcony, Elias’s left cheek began to sag toward his collar as the nerve tired. Instantly, Caleb Vance turned the brass screw in his pocket half a notch to the right. A silent, scorching bolt of galvanic electricity leaped from the wet battery-sponge into the dead muscles of Elias’s neck; his jaw locked shut with a click that nearly cracked his molars, his head jerked upright toward the western sky, and with a superhuman wrench of his live right shoulder, he lifted his heavy iron walking-stick three inches off the marble balustrade and brought the ferrule down upon the stone. *Crack.* The sharp, metallic report echoed across the hush of the fifty thousand. He did not need a voice; for thirty-five years that stick striking a floorboard had been the only constitution the Pacific knew. Turning his head half an inch through the fiery agony of the electric current so that his wide, unblinking right eye looked straight down into the loggia where Schuyler sat, Elias raised his right arm and pointed the iron stick down the slope of California Street toward the locked grain-piers—and as fifty thousand throats below erupted in a single, terrifying roar of *"Thorne! Thorne!"* that shook the glass in the conservatory dome and sent the sea-gulls wheeling in panic out over the dark water of the Gate, Kaiulani leaned close to his stiffened shoulder while the red sun touched the horizon line and whispered the compact that young Marcus Vance had sealed with her in the cellar an hour before.

"Hold the rail for thirty seconds more, Elias," she murmured against the howling triumph of the square, her hand steadying the hidden hydraulic lever behind the velvet drape. "Schuyler’s clerks are already running to unlock the Vallejo wheat-barges, and Marquis Takashima has signaled his cruisers to bank their fires. We have bought your empire its six years of breath."

***

Those six years of borrowed twilight—bought by galvanic wire in eighty-one and spent in the long, grinding encirclement of the southern waters—came to their final accounting on a moonless night in late August of 1887, forty-eight hours after the promulgation of the Hundred and Twenty-Four States in the Rotunda. 

Inside the Private Library on the third floor of the Rincon Hill Citadel, the electric bulbs had been turned off by the Providentor’s own gesture. Only a roaring fire of seasoned Sierra pitch-pine and black Nanaimo lump-coal blazed in the deep granite hearth, filling the book-lined vault with the resinous, popping music of that first Kentucky autumn fifty years before. The room smelled of scorched calfskin, wood-ash, and the sharp camphor-spirit that Brigadier Caleb Vance had rubbed into Elias’s chest before being ordered from the room.

Elias sat alone before the iron hearth-grate in his rubber-tired koa-wood chair, the brake-levers locked fast against the floor-tiles. The transient paralysis of eighty-one had yielded in his middle eighties to a slow, suffocating calcification of the pericardium, only to return threefold after the Coral Sea; yet tonight, with sixty grains of strychnine and brandy burning through his arteries for the last time, he had forced his swollen right hand to obey the chisel of his brain. Across his lap, resting upon the sea-otter fur, lay the brass-bound mahogany chest that had traveled under his bunk from the adobe blockhouse at Clark’s Point to the Forbidden City.

Inside it lay forty years of unvarnished memory: the greasy pocket-ledgers in which he had tallied the stolen Dupount powder on the Llano Estacado; the secret correspondence with Major St. Clair of the Golden Circle before the betrayal of Richmond; the true casualty rolls of the Chilkoot ice-steps before Auditor Shen’s clerks had scrubbed the numbers for the Diet; and the three small, salt-stained notebooks bound in Mexican pigskin wherein, during the long nights off the Peiho bar and the vigil at Sitka, he had written down in his cramped, phonetic frontier hand his private meditations upon the creatures who served him.

He picked up the first of the pigskin books with his thick, purple-mottled right fingers. The firelight caught the faded brown ink on the flyleaf: *No law holds past the range of the gun that wrote it. If Kaiulani lives ten years after my breath stops, she will turn the Legion into a priesthood of eunuchs; if young Vance gets the seal, he will measure men’s skulls with a caliper until the boiler splits.*

Elias stared at the page with his wide right eye. Down in the subterranean archives beneath the Mint, Rector Norton’s historians and Magistrate Shen’s scribes were already engraving the official steel plates of the *Annals of the Providentor*—how the American Caesar had been guided from his fourteenth year by an unerring, mathematical vision of oceanic harmony, moving from the Platte to the Yenisei without a doubt in his breast or a blot on his escutcheon. 

If he left these pigskin books in the mahogany box, fifty years hence some spectacled clerk from the Berkeley sheds would pry open the brass lock. They would read that the founder of the Grand Confederation had not cared a copper real for their Three Harmonies; that he had built an empire across half the earth for the same reason he had shot Cortina’s horse between the eyes in the Rio Frio—because he could not endure the sound of another man’s whip cracking over his head. They would see the joints in the armor. They would learn that the god in the bronze coat had been a mortal man who feared the dark water rising in his own ankles, and the moment the provinces learned that the mortar had been mixed by human hands, they would begin to pick at the stones.

History did not require the truth. History required an iron die that never varied by the thousandth of an inch.

Using the hooked ferrule of his walking-stick, Elias pushed the heavy brass fender aside and wheeled his chair two feet closer to the open grate until the heat of the pitch-pine blistered the dry skin of his cheekbones and made the grease on his cavalry boots smoke. He did not tear the pages out; a single sheet blown up the chimney onto the roofs of Mason Street might buy a printer’s boy a rope. He lifted the entire pigskin volume in his right fist and pitched it straight into the white-hot hollow between two burning logs.

The dry Mexican leather curled backward with a sharp, greasy hiss, weeping black tallow into the coals before bursting into a tall, yellow-green sheet of flame as the copper-gall ink caught fire. 

One after another, moving with a slow, mechanical deliberation that made the sweat pour down his paralyzed left cheek into his white stubble, Elias fed his life into the stone. In went the secret receipt from Governor Pesqueira for the Tucson Springfields; in went the original surgeon’s certificate from Shanghai showing that the Master of the Ocean had lain helpless on his back for eleven days while a Polynesian woman forged his cipher; in went the water-color sketch of the Kauai valley that young Kalanimoku had laid upon his knee the week before the boy died of the winter pleurisy at Monterey.

For twenty minutes nothing sounded in the library save the heavy, whistling scrape of Elias’s breath and the roar of the chimney draft sucking forty years of blood and ink up into the San Francisco fog. When the last mahogany partition of the box had been splintered with the butt of his iron stick and laid upon the grate, he leaned forward and poked the black, fluttering skins of carbonized paper with the ferrule until they dissolved into gray powder among the pine-ash.

There was nothing left of Elias Thorne now except the bronze statues in the squares and the laws stamped in steel. He had burned the carpenter out of the house; let the tenants worship the beams.

As he drew the iron stick back from the grate, the heavy, mercury-filled sack behind his breastbone gave a single, monstrous heave—not a pain, for he had lived with the hot wire in his ribs so long that pain was merely the weight of his coat, but a sudden, total stopping of the piston at the top of the stroke. The iron cane slipped from his numb right fingers and struck the hearth-stones with a loud *clang* that echoed through the oak panels of the door. Above the mantel, the gilded face of the bulkhead clock swam backward into a rushing wall of coal-black smoke that smelled of cured hog-fat, frost-bitten Kentucky clover, and the vast, roaring salt-spray of an unbroken sea.

***

To the Chronicler who walked homeward through the quiet, fog-drenched streets of the capital at four o’clock on that morning of the twenty-second of August, 1887—or who looked back upon that night thirteen years later from the completed concrete ramparts of the Panama locks—the passing of the founder did not announce itself with the ragged musketry of a revolution. It came out of the upper mist like the voice of the bronze ocean itself.

For three hours after midnight, while the physicians and the three Regents stood behind the bolted doors of the third-floor library, every telegraph wire and submarine cable between the Golden Gate and the outer pickets on the Yenisei and the Coral Sea had been held open on a dead, continuous current—forbidding a single private syllable to pass through the repeaters until the garrisons at Boston, Edo, Peking, and Sydney stood under arms at their magazine gates. 

Then, at seventeen minutes past four, while the stars were still drowned in the cold sea-smoke pouring over the Marin hills and the seventy foundry-stacks along the Potrero shore were just beginning to redden the low sky for the morning shift, the great twelve-ton bell of the Syncretic Cathedral of St. Michael and the Sun Goddess on the crest of Nob Hill gave a single, booming stroke.

It was not the brisk, silvery chime that called the clerks to the counting-houses at six, nor the double alarm-clatter of a dockyard fire. Cast from the bronze twenty-four-pounders that Marshal Vance had captured at Tucson and Vicksburg, the hammer fell upon the lip of the metal with a deep, subterranean vibration in the key of C-minor that seemed to travel downward through the granite bedrock of the peninsula rather than outward through the air.

For sixty seconds by the watch, the first stroke hung alone in the wet darkness, humming through the iron rails of the cable-car tracks and rattling the loose window-sashes in the brick tenements of the Mission.

Then, before the bronze murmur had quite died against the water of the bay, the second stroke fell—and with it, as if a single electric key had closed the circuit of the world, came the answer from the water and the hills. Down in the deep channel off Alcatraz and Clark’s Point, the eighteen-inch turret-guns of the *Elias Thorne* and the *Prometheus* began to fire the minute-salute with blank charges of smokeless powder, each flat, slamming concussion tearing the fog-bank into yellow rags and setting the ten thousand wooden prayer-gongs in the Japanese and Cantonese barracks along the Embarcadero beating in a slow, funereal cadence. From the Presidio batteries, from the limestone casemates of Fort Point, from the foundry whistles at Hunters Point and the giant bronze *bonsho* bells of the Buddhist temples on the Berkeley slopes, the sound rolled together into a single, continuous ocean of mourning iron.

Along Market and Montgomery streets, five thousand gas-lamps and carbon-arc globes were extinguished by sectors as the municipal engineers pulled the master-switches in the power-stations, plunging the marble porticoes of the Exchange and the thirty-foot bronze statue before the Citadel into sudden, pitch-black eclipse, only to have the darkness split ten seconds later by twenty vertical beams of white electric searchlight rising straight into the fog from the decks of the anchored battle-fleet.

People did not run into the streets screaming as they had during the bread-panic of eighty-one. As the windows of the boarding-houses and the palaces on Mason Street slid up in the gloom, seven hundred thousand men and women looked out into the throbbing, cannon-shaken mist in absolute silence. Along the curb below my lodgings on California Street, a night-shift of Irish track-layers and Shantung street-sweepers who had been re-bolting a frog in the cable-slot slowly laid their iron crowbars down upon the granite sets; without a word from their Hawaiian provost-corporal, the white men took off their greasy bowler hats and the Chinese dropped to their knees in the wet coal-mud, facing toward the dark mass of Rincon Hill.

No man under forty in that street could remember a morning when Elias Thorne had not sat above the city. To the youth who had been numbered in the Berkeley sheds, and to the coolie who carried his brass ration-tag around his neck, it was as if the Sierra Nevada itself had quietly slid into the sea while they slept. The providence that had burned a cabin in Kentucky fifty years ago had completed its arc; the mortal hand was cold, and across twelve thousand miles of wire—from the frozen blockhouses of the Obi to the steaming red ditches of Culebra—eight hundred million souls stood still in the dark to hear whether the iron roof above their heads would hold or fall.

***

Inside the Hall of the Council on the second floor of the Citadel, the roof was already groaning before the cathedral bell on Nob Hill had finished its twentieth stroke.

They had not waited to carry Elias’s body down to the embalming-tables in the cellar; he still sat behind the locked doors of the library upstairs, his chin propped on his leather collar and the ashes of his journals cooling in the grate, while down in the vast, redwood-vaulted throne room the lamps burned at full pressure against the gray dawn filtering through the seaward casements. The air smelled of wet military wool, warm beeswax from the ceremonial tapers lit on either side of the empty silver curule chair, and the sharp, metallic tang of pistol-oil.

Lady Kaiulani stood upon the third porphyry step of the dais, directly in front of the vacant silver seat. She had taken off the blue brocade of the court; she wore the severe, high-necked black bombazine that she would never again lay aside until the afternoon of the twentieth century when she stood above the Miraflores locks, and around her throat hung the heavy gold collar of the Insular Chancelleries. 

Below her, the semicircular floor of the Council Chamber was not filled with the sixty senators of the Diet—for young General Marcus Vance’s Academy cadets had barred the outer plaza gates to the civilian delegates at four o’clock—but with eighteen men in the mud-spattered, gold-braided uniforms of the High Command and the Fiscal Boards, standing in three tight, hostile clusters that refused to mingle across the inlaid brass meridians of the floor.

To the left, beneath the marble bust of the elder Marshal Vance, stood Colonel Armistead of the Virginia Auxiliaries and four gray-bearded continental division commanders, their heavy cavalry sabers unhooked from their saddle-chains so that the steel scabbards clinked against their spurs with every shift of their boots. To the right, grouped around Grand-Admiral Marquis Takashima and General Saigo, stood six post-captains of the Satsuma and Choshu fleets, their white gloves stained with coal-smut from the Goat Island launches. And in the center, behind the green baize table where the bronze seal-press of the Realm sat with its lever locked by a steel pin, stood Cornelius Schuyler and three directors of the Market Street Clearing House, their faces gray and pouchy in the competing glare of the electric bulbs and the wet morning sky.

"The Statute of the Hundred and Twenty-Four States was never enrolled upon the parchment books of the Chancery, Madame!" Colonel Armistead’s voice boomed out against the redwood rafters, loud enough to drown the distant, rhythmic thud of the Alcatraz salute-guns shaking the window-panes. He took a heavy step across the brass meridian of the Tropic of Cancer, his scarred hand slamming down upon the green baize within six inches of Auditor Shen’s ink-stand. "You and the boy-general bullied a dying man into croaking two words from a balcony while his brain was drowned in apoplexy! By the Military Articles of Sixty-Two—written by the Providentor’s own hand at Sacramento—when the Sovereign dies without a named successor of his loins, the supreme executive authority reverts to the Council of Continental Marshals until the army camps have voted!"

"The Articles of Sixty-Two were written for a frontier province of five million white miners before a single keel of the Battle Fleet was laid at Yokosuka!" General Saigo snapped back, his small, muscular frame stepping forward from the Japanese cluster until the gold chrysanthemum upon his cuff brushed the Virginian’s elbow. Behind Saigo, the six Satsuma captains simultaneously shifted their weight onto their left feet, freeing their sword-hilts. "Who holds the sea-lanes from Melbourne to the Kuriles tonight, Colonel? Not your Missouri mule-skinners! Seventy percent of the armored tonnage in the Pacific carries the flag of the Western Clans! If there is to be a Lord Protector of the interregnum, he must be named by the Joint Admiralty Board, with Grand-Admiral Takashima as Regent of the Sword!"

"And whose silver pays the coal-bills for your battleships, General Saigo?" wheezed Cornelius Schuyler, his plump, trembling hands clutching the edge of the seal-table as if he meant to carry the bronze press out under his coat. His watery eyes darted in terror from the Virginian’s saber to the samurai’s katana. "If you set up a drumhead dictatorship of camp-commanders or Japanese admirals this morning, the Clearing Houses in New York, Frankfurt, and Hong Kong will refuse the autumn treasury warrants before noon! The Regency must be vested in the Fiscal Commission—three civilian syndics with the power of the purse—"

"And young Silas Thorne in the silver chair to give the rabble a name they know!" shouted Armistead, wheeling upon the banker with the veins standing out like blue whipcord along his grizzled neck. "My Virginians are at the Presidio gate right now with four batteries of three-inch rifles! Put Elias’s eldest son on the horse before six o’clock, or by God, I’ll march them down Mason Street and clear these counting-house rats out with the bayonet!"

"Bring young Silas out of the garden, Colonel," Marquis Takashima said, his voice dropping to a low, lethal hiss as his thumb released the brass catch of his scabbard with a sharp *snick* that made Schuyler flinch backward against the table, "and my marine gunners at the foot of the hill will blow his head off his shoulders before his boot touches the stirrup. If blood is to be the title-deed, my nephew Kiyoshi carries the Providentor’s blood and the Choshu seal!"

Up on the third porphyry step, Lady Kaiulani did not move a muscle of her dark face, nor did she raise her voice to stop them. With her hands folded quietly beneath the heavy gold links of her collar, she looked down at the eighteen old men snarling across the brass lines of the globe like mastiffs over a butcher’s tub.

*Look at them, Elias,* she said silently to the cold figure sitting upstairs in the dark library. *Your body has not been cold for ninety minutes, the cannon are still roaring your name across the water, and already the timber is splitting along the grain. Thirty years of syncretism—thirty years of Three Harmonies and Imperial Anthems—and the instant your thumb is off the lever, the Virginian wants a border-camp, the samurai wants a shogunate, and the banker wants a mortgage-deed.*

She did not reach for the gavel on the clerk’s desk. Instead, she lifted her eyes past the gleaming bald crown of Cornelius Schuyler’s head, past the drawn blades by the door, toward the tall mahogany clock above the northern gallery. It lacked two minutes of five.

General Marcus Vance was not in the room.

***

Three hundred yards down the northern slope of Rincon Hill, inside the brick-and-iron rotunda of the Central Telegraph and Guard Headquarters that straddled the main cable-conduits between the Citadel and the Mint, the air did not smell of beeswax tapers; it smelled of hot lubricating oil, wet ozone, and the sharp, vinegary reek of fifty brass telegraph sounders hammering at full speed under a low ceiling of structural steel.

General Marcus Vance the younger stood upon the raised iron grating in the center of the floor, directly between the master switchboard of the Continental Trunk Lines and the pneumatic tube-terminal that fed the harbor forts. He had not put on mourning crape, nor did he wear the gold-braided dress coat in which his elders were quarreling up in the throne room. He wore his plain, slate-gray Academy field-tunic, a nickeled nine-shot pistol holstered at his hip, and his radium-dialed chronometer strapped outside his left cuff.

All around the circular brick wall, forty twenty-year-old cadet-lieutenants of the Polytechnic Corps—boys with five-digit silver ciphers on their collars and no family names in the peerage book—sat on iron stools before the repeaters, their vulcanite headphones clamped over their cropped skulls as they intercepted every wire passing out of the peninsula.

"The commander of the Second Virginia Auxiliary at the Presidio has just wired Colonel Armistead’s adjutant at the Mason Street gate, General," reported Major Kuroda, tearing a yellow manifold-sheet from the local military circuit and stepping up onto the iron grating. "He asks whether the horse-artillery batteries are to limber up for a march on the Sub-Treasury at five-thirty. And a signal-launch from the cruiser *Satsuma* off Goat Island is flashing the Naval Annex by shutter-lamp, requesting Marquis Takashima’s personal warrant to land four hundred marines at the Folsom Street wharf."

Marcus did not look at the yellow paper. His pale, unblinking eyes were fixed upon the great illuminated glass map of the San Francisco peninsula bolted to the iron stanchions before him, where tiny red and green electric bulbs showed the exact position of every street-railway power-house, water-main valve, and Academy cadet-company between the Golden Gate and San Mateo.

"My father told me before he went to Lake Baikal that when a horse breaks its leg in the traces, you do not hold a committee meeting with the mules behind it; you shoot the horse and lock the wagon-brake before the load goes over the cliff," Marcus said, his clipped, metallic voice cutting cleanly through the rattling din of the sounders. He pulled his ivory slide-rule half an inch from his breast pocket and pushed it back with a dry *click*. "Colonel Armistead and Marquis Takashima are still living in the year sixty-five. They think a city of seven hundred thousand souls is captured by marching men with flags down the middle of the street."

He turned to the master switch-panel behind him, where a Cantonese cadet-engineer stood with his rubber-gloved hands resting upon three heavy copper knife-switches painted red.

"Cut the commercial and municipal telegraph trunks to Oakland, Sacramento, and the Presidio," Marcus ordered. "Leave only the underground armored lead to Alcatraz, Mare Island, and the Citadel guard-posts open on my personal cipher. Have the cadets at the Potrero generating-station pull the breakers on the Market and California street-railway lines so not a single cable-car or electric dray moves between the ferry-slips and the hills; and tell Captain Kalakaua’s detail at the Spring Valley water-gate to drop the iron sluices on the Presidio main. If Colonel Armistead’s Virginians wish to march into town this morning, they may start by drinking their own horse-troughs dry."

With three rapid, spitting flashes of blue electric arc, the copper switches dropped from their jaws. Instantly, half the brass sounders along the wall went dead and silent.

Marcus stepped to the central transmitting desk, where the master-key of the Municipal Provost Network waited under a glass hood. He did not dictate to a clerk; he laid his own steady, square-nailed fingers upon the vulcanite knob and began to send in the rapid, machine-like military code of the Monterey Staff College—a signal that was simultaneously printed upon the ticker-tapes of all forty-two police precincts, harbor batteries, and railway depots around the bay:

*PROCLAMATION ONE. BY ORDER OF THE IMPERIAL STAFF AND THE BUREAU OF INTEGRATION. TO ENSURE THE PEACEFUL TRANSITION OF THE REALM AND PREVENT FOREIGN SABOTAGE DURING THE OBSEQUIES OF THE PROVIDENTOR, A STATE OF SIEGE AND MARTIAL LAW IS HEREBY DECLARED THROUGHOUT THE METROPOLITAN PREFECTURE OF SAN FRANCISCO FROM FIVE O’CLOCK THIS MORNING. ALL CIVIL COURTS, SYNDICATE EXCHANGES, AND MUNICIPAL ASSEMBLIES ARE SUSPENDED. ANY ARMED DETACHMENT OF THE AUXILIARY OR CLAN FORCES MOVING FIVE HUNDRED YARDS BEYOND ITS BARRACKS PERIMETER WITHOUT THE COUNTER-STAMP OF THE ACADEMY PROVOST WILL BE ENGAGED IMMEDIATELY WITH HIGH-EXPLOSIVE SHELL BY THE HARBOR FORTIFICATIONS. CITIZENS WILL REMAIN WITHIN THEIR WARDS. THE RATION-DEPOTS WILL OPEN AT EIGHT UNDER CADET GUARD.*

He lifted his finger from the key as the bulkhead clock clicked onto the hour of five. Outside in the damp courtyard of the Telegraph Annex, the steam-sirens of twenty armored traction-lorries—each mounting twin water-cooled Maxim guns behind quarter-inch nickel-steel shields and manned by multi-ethnic squads of the First Cadet Brigade—began to hoot through the lifting fog as the heavy iron gates swung open onto Montgomery Street.

"Take two companies of the Shensi and Samoan cadets up the bullion-hoist to the second-floor corridor of the Citadel, Major Kuroda," Marcus said, drawing on his gray buckskin gloves and smoothing the leather over his knuckles. "Do not enter the Throne Room until I tap the glass of the door. Let the old men shout themselves hoarse for ten minutes more; a boiler that has blown off its superfluous steam is much easier to bolt down."

***

Yet while General Vance’s cadets could sever the copper wires of the San Francisco peninsula with three strokes of a rubber-gloved hand and lock seven hundred thousand metropolitan subjects inside their brick wards before breakfast, not even the Polytechnic Staff could repeal the physics of distance across an empire that spanned one hundred and eighty degrees of longitude.

To the Chronicler who examines the unexpurgated cable-logs of that terrible autumn of 1887—preserved in the lead-lined vaults of the Monterey Chancery where no schoolboy ever sees them—the death of Elias Thorne did not travel outward from California like the ripple of a stone dropped into a quiet pond; it traveled like a spark running down a train of damp, imperfectly mixed blasting-powder, sizzling silently beneath the water for three thousand leagues only to detonate with blinding violence wherever the concrete of the new order had not yet set over the ancient rock.

In the home provinces of the Pacific coast, and across the exhausted, garrisoned plains of the Atlantic protectorates where two generations of white men had been bled white by the Sacramento conscriptions, the news was received with the dull, fatalistic stupor of draft-oxen who hear the driver fall from the wagon-box yet keep walking between the ruts because the iron yoke is still bolted to their necks. In Boston and Philadelphia, the shutters stayed up on the counting-houses, and the people waited indoors for the provost’s bread-carts.

It was at the raw, bleeding outer rim of the circumference—in the newly swallowed continent of the Southern Ocean and along the vast, muddy arteries of the middle Yangtze—that the iron hoop snapped before the funeral tapers in San Francisco were half burned down.

Because the nineteenth meridian of August on the Pacific coast was already the afternoon of the twenty-second across the international date-line in Australia, the sun was dropping red and smoky behind the eucalyptus ridges of the Blue Mountains when the submarine cable from Noumea brought the dead current into the repeater-office at Sydney.

For twelve weeks since the May morning when Prince Kalakaua and young Marcus Vance had landed their marines at the Man-o'-War Jetty, the three million Anglo-Saxon colonists of New South Wales and Victoria had lived under the cold, suffocating lid of the Eighteen-Inch Gun. Their coastal parliaments had been padlocked; their wool-clips had been seized against silver-paper receipts of the Market Street Mint; and forty thousand Cantonese and Irish railway-navvies, protected by Satsuma infantry cordons, had been tearing up the colonial tracks from Parramatta to Melbourne to re-lay the broad six-foot gauge of the Empire. So long as Admiral Hornby’s British fleet was rotting at the bottom of the Coral Sea and the terrible old man on Rincon Hill held the lanyard, the sheep-barons and the gold-miners of the interior had chewed their bitterness in silence.

Then, at four-ten in the afternoon, a nineteen-year-old Australian telegraph-clerk in the Bathurst railway-shed—a boy whose father had died aboard the British corvette *Wolverene* in June—listened to the official Monterey death-cipher passing down the wire toward the garrison headquarters at Ballarat.

He did not deliver the slip to the Japanese provost-captain on the platform. Instead, before the Choshu sentry outside the window could unslings his carbine, the youth cross-plugged the main pastoral trunk-line into the local railway-bell circuit and hammered out five words in plain English Morse to every sheep-station, gold-camp, and locomotive-roundhouse across twelve hundred miles of bush from Brisbane to Adelaide:

*THE YANKEE CAESAR IS DEAD.*

Within thirty minutes, before the Satsuma colonel commanding the Ballarat mining-district had even finished decoding his cipher from Sydney, the deep, hoarse steam-whistles of the Eureka Deep-Lead Gold Pits began to blow the old colonial assembly-call—not the regulated noon blast of the Imperial Assessors, but three short, frantic shrieks repeated over and over against the darkening winter sky.

Down in the timbered galleries eight hundred feet beneath the red gravel of Ballarat, four thousand Cornish, Irish, and native-born Australian sinkers dropped their pneumatic drills into the sump-water. They did not come up the cages with empty hands; they broke open the company powder-magazines with their sledges, slung canvas sacks of Nobel’s blasting-gelatine and coiled safety-fuse over their flannel shirts, and swarmed out of the shaft-heads into the frosty dusk just as the six-o’clock bullion-train for Melbourne was taking water at the wooden tank.

"Hold the engine, boys!" roared Timothy Lalor, a one-armed veteran of the old fifty-four stockade whose nephew had been shipped to the Bering tunnel-gangs by Magistrate Shen’s assize the week before, leaping onto the tender-pile with a lighted miners’ flare in his fist and a stolen Martini-Henry rifle crooked in his stump. Around the red-brick station-house, the fifty Choshu riflemen of the treasure-guard were already running out of their guardroom, their brass bugle sounding the alarm as their officer screamed orders in Japanese to unlimber the Maxim gun on the flatcar.

The miners did not form ranks to be mowed down by machine-gun fire as the Dutch soldiers had done in Java. Scattering behind the forty-foot mounds of white quartz-tailings that towered directly above the railway cutting, two hundred veteran blaster-men lit the thirty-second fuses of their gelatine-cartridges from their hat-lamps and hurled a hail of smoking, hissing iron cylinders straight down onto the roofs of the armored bullion-vans.

The earth of Victoria split open in a continuous, rolling sheet of yellow-white nitro-glycerine flame that blew the six-foot broad-gauge rails into twisted corkscrews of Bessemer steel, hurled the Maxim flatcar upside down into the slime of the cyanide-vats, and buried the Japanese guard-company beneath four hundred tons of shattered brick and quartz gravel.

And six thousand miles to the northwest, where the hot, yellow flood of the Yangtze-Kiang rolled past the stone bund of the Pacifica Concession at Hankow, the same hour of dawn that saw Ballarat in flames looked down upon a darker, vaster convulsion.

There, in the heart of the Forty-Eighth River Canton—where three million Chinese iron-workers and tea-packers labored beneath the brick chimneys of the Hanyang Arsenal to cast railway-chairs for the Siberian line—the secret lodges of the *White Lotus* and the *Righteous Harmony Fists*, who for ten years had bowed their heads before the mandate of the invincible Western Emperor, learned from the Cantonese river-pilots at midnight that the Dragon Chair across the Eastern Sea was empty.

At daybreak, while the Imperial Paddle-Monitor *Monocacy* lay moored off the Hanyang iron-wharf with her boilers banked and half her mixed crew ashore in the tea-houses, the low, muttering roar of three hundred thousand voices rose out of the maze of narrow mud-brick alleys behind the foreign compound. They carried no modern magazine-rifles; they bore eight-foot iron pikes forged in secret during the night-shifts at the rolling-mills, red silk banners inscribed with charms against foreign lead, and ten thousand earthenware jars of kerosene stolen from the Standard-Pacifica godowns.

Up on the granite steps of the Customs Inspectorate overlooking the bund, Junior Prefect Hoshino—Candidate One-One-Zero-Eight of the Berkeley class of eighty-four—stood in his immaculate black alpaca gown beside a detachment of forty Hawaiian and Californian provost-guards. His horn-rimmed spectacles reflected the red glare of the burning tax-sheds along the riverfront as a solid, mile-wide wall of blue-bloused iron-puddlers and boatmen surged across the bridge of boats, swinging their heavy foundry-sledges against the iron palings of the Concession gate.

"Open the magazine-locks on the three-pounder Hotchkiss guns, Sergeant!" Hoshino shouted in English, his high, scholarly voice cracking for the first time since he had left the examination-cells as a paving-stone thrown from the front rank of the mob shattered the glass lamp-globe above his head and showered his shoulders with splinters. "Where is the steam-launch from the *Monocacy*? Why doesn't the monitor open fire with shrapnel down the avenue?"

The Californian provost-sergeant—a grizzled forty-year-old veteran of the Canton river-patrols who was frantically jamming a brass clip of smokeless cartridges into the receiver of his rifle while his boots slipped in the blood of two slain customs-clerks on the lower step—pointed a shaking thumb out toward the yellow river-mist.

Out in the middle of the stream, the *Monocacy* was not swinging her turrets toward the shore. From her quarterdeck rose the sharp, crackling rattle of small-arms fire and the flash of cutlasses: the American engine-room artificers and the Satsuma deck-guards aboard the monitor, having heard two contradictory rumors off the telegraph-barge—one that Marquis Takashima had seized the throne in San Francisco, the other that the Virginia regiments had proclaimed Silas Thorne—had turned their revolvers upon each other across the open engine-hatches while forty Cantonese fire-junks, chained together in pairs and piled to the mastheads with blazing pitch-barrels and oil-soaked cotton-bales, drifted straight down the five-knot current against the monitor’s unprotected wooden sponsons.

"The fleet’s fighting itself in the river, Prefect!" the sergeant yelled over the deafening crash of the Concession’s main iron gates giving way under the blows of a six-ton cast-iron girder swung by fifty Hanyang foundrymen. "And there’s forty thousand of ’em coming through the courtyard with kerosene-pots! Get out of that clerk’s dress and get behind the parapet before—"

A hundred jars of burning Borneo naphtha arched over the shattered iron palings at once, turning the white granite steps of the Customs House into a roaring cataract of liquid fire that swallowed the Berkeley graduate, his slide-rule, and his forty provosts before the first fire-junk struck the *Monocacy*’s side.

***

In San Francisco, no word of the burning of Hankow or the dynamiting of the Ballarat rails was permitted to escape the concrete basement of the Telegraph Annex. On the afternoon of the twenty-fifth of August, as the gun-carriage bearing the soldered lead casket of Elias Thorne rolled slowly down the steep granite pitch of Rincon Hill toward the Monterey funeral-train waiting at the Townsend Street depot, the capital of the Great Arena lay wrapped in a silence more terrifying than artillery.

It was not the triumphant, brass-throated silence of the October reviews, nor the devout hush that the later school-books described when the bronze effigy had been bolted to the battleship turret at the turn of the century. The Chronicler who stood that day upon the roof of the Mint looked down upon a city locked in rigor mortis.

Behind the triple cordons of young Marcus Vance’s Polytechnic Cadets—who lined Market Street at two-pace intervals with fixed bayonets and their backs turned not toward the coffin, but outward toward the tenements—half a million citizens stood behind shuttered windows and barred shop-doors. The air was cold with the grey August fog blowing through the Gate, smelling of wet crape, unburned coal-dust from the banked factory chimneys, and the heavy, suffocating clouds of Hawaiian sandalwood and Japanese aloes that poured from the bronze thuribles carried by sixty priests of the Syncretic Basilica.

Twelve black Clydesdale stallions from the Oregon artillery-depots, draped to the fetlocks in purple velvet housings embroidered with the golden sun-and-anchor, drew the six-ton caisson of an eighteen-inch coastal cannon. Upon the iron cradle where the barrel should have lain rested the long, narrow box of Sierra granite and sheet-lead, covered only by the faded blue wool of Elias’s old Mexican War Engineer’s coat and the iron walking-stick tied across the lid with white silk cord.

Three paces behind the rear axle walked Lady Kaiulani.

She walked alone upon the fifty-foot breadth of the granite sets, her long train of dull black mourning bombazine whispering over the wet stones, the whale-ivory clasp of Oahu cold against her throat. Behind her, separated by a file of twenty armed Oahu guardsmen so that they could neither whisper to one another nor gesture to the rooftops, walked the nominal regents and marshals of the broken house: old Brigadier Caleb Vance leaning heavily upon the arm of his grand-nephew Marcus; Cornelius Schuyler, his face the color of lard beneath his tall silk hat; Marquis Takashima in full Satsuma armor covered by a black naval cloak; and behind them, the three Left-Handed Princes—Silas sweating sour whiskey through his black gloves, Kiyoshi staring fixedly at the back of Takashima’s neck, and young Kalanimoku looking up at the grey gulls circling above the cornice-stones.

With every slow, measured *clomp* of the twelve iron-shod horses, Kaiulani felt the emptiness opening beneath her slippers.

For twenty-five years she had hated the man in the lead box with the dry, undying passion of a princess whose islands had been turned into a coaling-hulk; and for twenty years she had governed beside him because she knew that his terrible, scarred right hand was the only bolt holding three hundred million human beings from tearing one another’s throats out in the dark. He had not built a state; he had built an arch of unmortared basalt blocks that stood solely because his own two-hundred-pound carcass was wedged into the keystone.

Now the keystone was six feet of cold tallow and strychnine rolling down the hill toward a vault in Monterey. Look where she might along the five-mile avenue—at the white, hungry faces of the unpaid foundrymen pressed against the upper garret-panes of the Mission; at the yellow-braided Virginia cavalrymen sitting their horses at the cross-streets with their carbines unslung and their eyes fixed hatred-wide upon the Japanese marine detachments opposite; at the silent, lowered cranes along the Embarcadero where forty grain-ships waited for a clearance-stamp that no foreign consul would honor—she saw the vacuum rushing in.

A gust of salt wind off the bay caught the corner of the dead man’s blue coat on the caisson ahead of her, lifting the empty left sleeve so that it flapped once against the lead and fell back lifeless.

Beside her right shoulder, old Caleb Vance stumbled slightly on a slick cable-rail, his cataract-blinded eye weeping in the cold wind as he muttered under his breath—not to Kaiulani or to the boy beside him, but to the box on the gun-carriage: *"You left the gate unlatched, Elias. We’re eighty miles from the fort, and the wolves are in the horses."* 

Young Marcus Vance did not look at his great-uncle; his pale, unblinking eyes beneath his visored cap were fixed upon the signal-mast atop the Goat Island naval depot two miles out in the bay, where a small string of red and yellow bunting had just broken out against the fog—a fleet-cipher that was not in the Monterey Polytechnic code-book.

***

The casket had not yet reached the turntable of the Townsend Street station—and the priests of the Basilica were still chanting the *De Profundis* beside the smoking sandalwood braziers on the platform—when the polite mask of the funeral procession dissolved behind the closed bronze doors of the Capitol Rotunda on Rincon Hill.

Marcus Vance had not gone down to the train with the mourners. Turning his horse out of the cortege at the corner of Third Street as soon as the Goat Island flags broke the mist, he had ridden back up the empty, cadet-lined hill at a hard gallop, the iron shoes of his bay striking red sparks from the granite sets while Major Kuroda and six mounted telegraph-orderlies clattered behind him.

When Marcus walked into the lower Rotunda—his grey field-tunic damp with sea-fog, his left hand resting not on a mourning-sword but upon the unbuttoned leather flap of his nine-shot pistol holster—he found that the eighteen marshals and syndicate-directors of the morning had grown to forty.

The great circular chamber beneath the bronze relief-map smelled of wet boots, hot tallow, and the raw electricity of men who knew the guns were already loaded outside. Marquis Takashima had not ridden to the depot; he stood beside the porphyry table in the center of the floor, surrounded not by his old Satsuma post-captains, but by thirty younger divisional commanders of the Japanese-Pacific Fleet and the Continental Choshu Brigades. Foremost among them stood General Kaito of the Third Amur and Insular Division—a forty-year-old graduate of the Yedo artillery schools who had lost two fingers of his left hand at the storming of Vladivostok and who wore across his chest neither the riband of the Golden Gate nor the cipher of the Berkeley sheds, but the pure white silk sash of the League of the Rising Sun.

And on the opposite side of the brass meridian, hemmed into the alcove beneath the telegraph gallery by twelve of Kaito’s marine-guards with fixed bayonets, stood Colonel Armistead and Auditor Shen.

"You have left the funeral before the earth is over your master, General Vance," Kaito said as Marcus’s spurs rang across the marble flags toward the center table. Kaito did not salute the twenty-three-year-old Chief of Staff; he stood with his booted legs planted wide across the inlaid brass line of the Equator, his right thumb hooked into his sword-belt, a wet blue cable-flimsy from Yokohama held in his maimed left hand. "Perhaps your schoolboys in the Telegraph Annex forgot to deliver the two-o’clock relay from Nagasaki and Hankow."

Marcus stopped four paces from the porphyry table. Behind him, Major Kuroda and the six Polytechnic cadets halted in a neat, silent file inside the doorway, their magazine-carbines held port across their chests.

"The Hankow repeater went dead at six this morning, General Kaito," Marcus said, his clipped, level voice dropping into the high vault without an echo. "And the commercial cable from Nagasaki was ordered closed by the Bureau of Integration at five. By what authority have your marine signalmen opened the Goat Island relay during a state of siege?"

Kaito laughed—a short, barking sound that made the six Choshu colonels behind him shift their hands to their scabbards. He tossed the blue cable-ribbon onto the porphyry table beside the locked bronze seal-press.

"By the authority of sixty-four armored ships of the line and a hundred and twenty thousand bayonets of the Japanese-Pacific Division who do not take their orders from a boy’s slide-rule or a Hawaiian woman’s ink-pot!" Kaito said, his voice rising until it rang off the thirty-foot bronze plates of Elias Thorne’s map on the wall above them. "Hankow is in ashes, General Vance! The Chinese iron-guilds have burned the *Monocacy* at her moorings and butchered your Berkeley examination-clerks on the steps of the Custom House because your American artificers shot our Satsuma deck-officers in the back! At Ballarat, the white miners have blown up the broad-gauge track with dynamite and hung the Choshu garrison from the water-tanks! And ten minutes ago, the Imperial Council at Kyoto cabled Marquis Takashima that if the Statute of the Hundred and Twenty-Four States is enforced to dissolve the domains of Satsuma and Choshu into numbered coolie-cantons, the Japanese homeland withdraws from the Treaty of Edo at sunset!"

Over in the alcove, Colonel Armistead strained forward against the crossed bayonets of Kaito’s marines, his scarred face purple above his gray beard. "Let ’em withdraw to hell, Marcus! Give my Virginians the word to open the Presidio magazines, and we’ll drive every yellow-belly on this coast into the surf before the moon rises!"

Marcus did not look at Armistead; he did not even look down at the Nagasaki cable on the stone. His pale eyes remained fixed upon the white silk sash across Kaito’s breast, measuring the distance between the general’s fourth brass button and the door with the cold, practiced habit of a surveyor setting a stake.

"The Tenno at Kyoto signed away his foreign war-powers in sixty-eight, General Kaito," Marcus said softly. "And there is no Japanese-Pacific Division on the muster-rolls of this morning. There are only the Seventh, Twelfth, and Nineteenth Imperial Brigades, whose coal is in my bunkers at Mare Island and whose ammunition-lighters are under the guns of Alcatraz. You are twenty minutes away from mutiny."

"Mutiny against whom, boy?" Kaito sneered, taking one step across the brass meridian until the smell of his wet wool cloak and clove-oil filled Marcus’s nostrils. "Against a dead frontier bandit in a lead box? Elias Thorne conquered this ocean with our ships and our blood while you were sucking milk in a Sacramento nursery! Now that his heart has stopped, do you think the samurai who took Peking and sank the British at the Coral Sea are going to stand in iron cubicles at Berkeley to be numbered like cattle by a Polynesian widow and a twenty-three-year-old schoolmaster?"

Kaito’s right hand dropped from his belt and struck the hilt of his two-handed *katana*, drawing six inches of mirror-bright steel from the scabbard.

"The Regency of the clerks is ended, Vance! Marquis Takashima has boarded the flagship *Yamato* off Goat Island twenty minutes ago. My four regiments of the First Insular Division have seized the Folsom Street wharves and the Mint bullion-vaults, and our twelve-inch turrets in the stream are trained upon this dome! Sign the warrant restoring the Asian Prefectures and the Fleet Admiralty to the Western Clans before the five-o’clock bell, or when I walk down those steps and hoist the red lantern on the plaza flagpole, the *Yamato* will drop ten hundredweight of shimose shell straight through that glass roof onto your head!"

Marcus’s hand did not move from his holster-flap. He pulled his radium-dialed chronometer half an inch from his cuff and glanced at the sweeping second-hand.

"It is four-fifty-two, General Kaito," Marcus said. "If Marquis Takashima boarded the *Yamato* at four-thirty, he has had twenty-two minutes to raise steam in cold boilers against a four-knot ebb tide, while my cadet-crews aboard the *Elias Thorne* and the *Prometheus* have been lying off Clark’s Point with superheated oil-burners at three hundred pounds pressure since midnight. You may keep your red lantern in your pocket. Major Kuroda—shoot this man."

***

Kuroda—born in the shadow of Kumamoto Castle, taken from his clan at twelve by the Triennial Assessors, and bearing upon his collar only the silver cipher *Zero-Four-One-Nine* of the Monterey Polytechnic—did not blink.

Before General Kaito’s blade could clear the scabbard, Kuroda’s nine-shot automatic pistol barked three times from the hip—*crack-crack-crack*—the smokeless nitro-powder filling the Rotunda with a sharp, chemical slap that blew two brass buttons and a spray of dark arterial blood out the back of Kaito’s white silk sash.

Kaito pitched forward onto his knees across the brass line of the Equator, his forehead striking the inlaid copper outline of the Galapagos Islands with a dull *thud* as the thirty Japanese officers and the twelve marine guardsmen in the alcove erupted into a simultaneous, screaming tangle of drawn sabers and leveled rifles.

"Drop the bronze shutters!" Marcus barked, already vaulting backward over the porphyry table and kicking the heavy oak council-board onto its side as a ragged volley from the Choshu marines shattered the marble bust of his father behind him and sent chips of white stone whistling past his ear.

Up in the iron gallery surrounding the dome, twenty Polytechnic cadets—boys from Pennsylvania, Canton, and Oahu who had been lying flat behind the balustrade since four o’clock—rolled two water-cooled Maxim guns to the rail and pressed their thumbs against the brass firing-levers.

For forty seconds the Rotunda of the Grand Confederation ceased to be a parliament and became an iron cauldron of flashing muzzle-blast and ricocheting lead. Beneath the thirty-foot bronze gaze of the world Elias Thorne had bolted together, the synchronized *tat-tat-tat-tat* of the six-hundred-round-a-minute belts scythed straight down into the gold-braided cluster around the table, tearing through Satsuma silk and Virginia broadcloth alike—for Colonel Armistead, seizing a fallen marine’s carbine in the smoke, had tried to shoot his way out the eastern door toward the Presidio horses and took three .30-caliber nickel-jacketed bullets through his gray beard before his boot touched the threshold.

Marcus did not stay to watch the floor cleared. Leaving Kuroda’s cadets firing downward through the yellow cordite haze into the writhing heap of plumed hats and blood-soaked sashes around the seal-press, he sprinted through the narrow armored passage behind the dais, threw open the iron casement of the seaward observation-tower, and stepped out onto the wind-swept granite parapet seventy feet above the bay.

Below him, the fog had torn apart under the rising sunset wind, and the heart of the Empire was tearing itself in two across three miles of white-capped water.

Aboard the ten-thousand-ton armored cruiser *Yamato*, lying eight hundred yards off Goat Island with the gold chrysanthemum of Satsuma newly hoisted to her maintruck above the torn blue-and-gold ensign of Pacifica, Marquis Takashima had not waited for Kaito’s red lantern. At the first muffled rattle of the Maxim guns inside the Citadel dome, the forward eleven-inch turret of the *Yamato* swung shoreward and spat a blinding, orange-black billow of shimose high-explosive.

The eight-hundred-pound shell screamed directly over the roofs of the Embarcadero coffee-warehouses and detonated squarely against the granite plinth of Elias Thorne’s thirty-foot bronze statue in the plaza below Marcus’s boots.

With a roar that shattered every pane of glass for six blocks down Market Street, the cast-bronze legs of the American Caesar sheared at the knees; the thirty-ton metal giant tilted slowly forward through the boiling yellow smoke and crashed face-down across the cable-car tracks, its iron walking-stick snapping in half against the cobbles.

"Signal the *Elias Thorne* and the Alcatraz disappearing-carriages!" Marcus shouted into the brass speaking-tube bolted to the parapet wall, the hot wind whipping the granite dust of the shattered monument across his bloodless cheeks as five more Japanese cruisers in the middle anchorage slipped their cables and began to open fire with their secondary batteries upon the Folsom Street barracks, while half a mile to the north the eighteen-inch turrets of his own cadet-manned flagship swung their fifty-foot barrels down to point-blank depression against their sister ships. "Do not waste armor-piercing shell on their waterlines—the channel is too shallow, and their hulls will block the grain-slips if they sink in the fairway! Load cast picric-acid high-capacity and fire into their upper bridges and boiler-uptakes at sixteen hundred yards! And tell Captain Kalakaua at the Mare Island torpedo-station to release the Brennan wire-guided mines into the ebb-tide!"

He did not wait for the acknowledgment bell from the casemate below; the first two-thousand-pound broadside from the *Elias Thorne* erupted across the water with a concussion that tore the speaking-tube out of its mortar and rained burning splinters of the *Yamato*’s fore-bridge across the ferry-slips.

***

Two thousand one hundred miles to the southwest, where the oil-smoke of the burning San Francisco wharves could not stain the trade-wind clouds, the dispatch-cruiser *Liliuokalani* steamed through the narrow coral jaws of the Honolulu channel at daybreak on the fourth of September, her white hull blistered to the waterline by six days of forced-draft steaming at twenty-two knots.

Up on the flying bridge, her hands gripping the salt-crusted brass rail behind the splinter-shield while the red sun rose over the volcanic crater of Diamond Head, stood Lady Kaiulani.

She had not gone down to Monterey with the funeral train. When the first eleven-inch shell from the *Yamato* had brought the bronze Caesar crashing into the Market Street cobbles and set the Virginia cavalry galloping down from the Presidio to loot the Sub-Treasury, she had recognized in the flash of a single second that the machine she and young Marcus had perfected in the examination-sheds was too brittle to survive its own first turn of the wheel. Marcus would fight for the continental rail-heads with his numbered boys until every furnace from Sacramento to the Ohio was cold slag; Takashima would burn the dockyards to keep his ships. If the whole Pacific was not to go down into the dark together, someone had to cut the cable before the fire ran down the wire to the islands.

At the foot of the Fort Street mole—where twenty-eight years before she had watched Elias’s marines land in the rain—four thousand men of the First Insular Guard and two hundred Cantonese and Portuguese sugar-factors stood waiting beneath the royal palms, their faces turned anxiously toward the cruiser’s signal-yard.

Kaiulani did not wait for the gangplank to be lashed. Stepping onto the coral quay in her salt-stiffened black bombazine, with young Kalanimoku carrying the iron strongbox of the Oahu Chancery seals behind her and Colonel Kalakaua’s riflemen forming a hollow square around her skirts, she walked straight to the stone base of the Harbor Telegraph House.

Inside the open door, the brass siphon-recorders of the San Francisco and Manila submarine cables were still chattering furiously—one key hammering out General Vance’s peremptory conscription-warrants for ten thousand island laborers, the other screaming Admiral Takashima’s orders to the Pearl River coaling-hulks to seize the Honolulu dry-docks in the name of the Western Clans.

"Bring the cold-chisel and the sledge from the quartermaster’s dray, Colonel," Kaiulani said, her voice clear and musical above the surf booming on the outer reef, though her dark eyes were rimmed with the gray ash of four sleepless nights. 

Two Hawaiian pioneers in blue wool tunics stepped forward to the heavy lead-sheathed trunk-cables where they rose out of the coral sea-wall into the gutta-percha junction-box.

"Your Highness," stammered Director Damon of the Bishop Sugar Syndicate, pushing his white linen helmet through the cordon of rifle-butts as the blacksmith set the steel edge of the chisel against the San Francisco line. "If you sever the Monterey wire and refuse the fleet requisitions, both Vance and Takashima will declare Oahu in rebellion! Half our autumn sugar-crop is sitting on the wharves waiting for the Oakland steamers, and we have only six weeks of California flour in the komisariat vaults! How can four islands stand alone between two hundred warships?"

"By ceasing to be their coal-bin, Mr. Damon," Kaiulani answered, taking a folded parchment from her sleeve—written not in the three languages of the *Codex Pacificus*, but in the old Hawaiian and English of her brother’s court—and handing it to the herald beside the flag-staff. "For thirty years we gave the Providentor our harbor and our sons because his iron kept the peace of the sea. Now the carpenter is dead, and his apprentices are burning down the workshop with their own kerosene. Strike the iron, Corporal."

The twelve-pound sledge fell twice—*clang, clang*—shearing through copper core and gutta-percha insulation alike in a shower of blue sparks that silenced the San Francisco sounder mid-syllable.

"Raise the old ensign of the Eight Stripes over the battery at Punchbowl," Kaiulani commanded as the herald nailed the *Proclamation of the Insular Sanctuary* to the teak door of the Custom House. "From this hour, the Hawaiian Archipelago and the Polynesian Reefs are an inviolable Neutral Zone, closed to every warship carrying a gun larger than a six-pounder salute-piece. Any disabled vessel from California or Japan that enters Pearl Lochs to escape the storm will have its breech-blocks dropped into thirty fathoms of water and its crew interned in the taro-valleys until peace is signed. Close the sugar-mills, Mr. Damon, and turn the cane-fields back to sweet-potatoes and upland rice before the rain tonight. We are going to lock the garden gate while the mainland eats itself."

***

It was well for those small islands that the Princess severed the copper nerve when she did; for across the continental immensity of the American and Asian provinces, the autumn of 1887 and the bitter winter of eighty-eight brought down upon three hundred million souls that catastrophic paralysis which our surviving parish-registers call the *Time of Troubles*.

To the Chronicler who had marveled only six years earlier at the clockwork majesty of the Great Arena—when a bushel of San Joaquin wheat or a pig of Hankow iron moved five thousand miles by broad-gauge rail and turbine-steamer without varying a tenth of a silver thaler in price—the speed with which the nineteen-century civilization rotted back into the twelfth was the most terrible lesson of the Pivot.

Elias Thorne and Lady Kaiulani had constructed their state upon a single, pitiless principle: that no canton should be able to feed, clothe, or arm itself without the counter-stamp of Monterey. To prevent rebellion, the Seventy-Second Agricultural Prefecture in the Mississippi valley had been forbidden to build iron-forges or textile-looms, shipping its raw corn and hogs west to the Rocky Mountain depots in exchange for Lowell cottons and Osaka hardware; the mining-towns of the Sierra and the Urals grew not a blade of cabbage, living entirely upon canned Columbia salmon and Australian mutton brought up the mountain grades every forty-eight hours by the commissariat trains; and not a local bank from Boston to Irkutsk held five thousand dollars in hard specie, clearing every wage-bill by telegraph through the central Hollerith ledgers beneath the San Francisco Mint.

When the battle in the Golden Gate burned the Mint cable-terminal to the water’s edge on the twenty-sixth of August, and three rival Regents in three days—General Vance at Sacramento, young Silas Thorne among the Virginia cavalry at Denver, and Admiral Takashima aboard his battered fleet off Santa Barbara—simultaneously declared one another’s treasury-notes to be treasonable waste-paper, the circulation of the human body stopped between sunrise and sunset.

Along six thousand miles of broad-gauge track from the Missouri to the Amur, the freight-conductors found that the paper warrants in their pouches would no longer buy a cord of wood or a tank of water at the way-stations. Within a week, the great transcontinental arteries were choked with dead iron: at the Ogden and Cheyenne junctions, forty miles of double-track siding stood solid with stalled refrigerator-cars in which ten thousand tons of dressed Chicago beef and California fruit rotted into black, buzzing slime under the September sun because the engineers had uncoupled their locomotives and ridden off with stolen coal-tenders to join the local militia-bands.

In the factory-cantons of Massachusetts and the iron-valleys of Pennsylvania, where two million mechanics lived from Saturday ration-card to Saturday ration-card, the silence of the railway-whistles meant immediate famine. By October, the traveler who ventured along the old turnpikes between Philadelphia and Pittsburg no longer saw the blue coats of the Tripartite Police; the Berkeley prefects—boys born three thousand miles away who spoke the local dialect like foreigners—had been hung from their own telegraph-poles by the starving iron-puddlers during the first week of the frost. Every county line had become a bristling palisade of felled telegraph-poles and overturned street-cars, behind which former colonels of the Atlantic Auxiliaries or self-appointed committee-chairmen levied thirty-percent toll in salt pork and rifle-cartridges upon every farm-wagon that tried to pass from one township to the next.

On the high plains of the Humboldt and the Platte, where the golden spikes of the Protector’s first rail had been driven thirty years before, the Cantonese and Irish section-gangs, abandoned without pay or flour three hundred miles from the nearest orchard, tore up the eighty-pound Bessemer rails to forge pikes and butcher-knives over fires built from the redwood sleepers. Bands of three hundred men—wearing tattered remnants of the Imperial slate-gray uniform mixed with buffalo-hides and stolen church-vestments—roamed the alkali valleys behind traction-engines converted into crude armored forts, burning the lonely ranch-houses for a sack of seed-corn and fighting pitched battles with the Paiute and Cheyenne horse-tribes, who had come down out of the reservation hills for the first time in a generation to graze their ponies across the unguarded ruins of the telegraph-stations.

The Great Arena had not broken into nations; for Elias Thorne had ground the nations into dust too fine to cohere again. It had broken into ten thousand starving parishes, each sitting in the cold dark beside a dead locomotive, waiting for a train from the coast that would never come.

***

By the nineteenth of November, the only army east of the Pacific surf that still kept the six-foot gauge open and the five-digit ciphers upon its collars was the First Polytechnic Corps of General Marcus Vance—and at four o’clock that afternoon, three miles below the granite summit of the Donner Pass in the high Sierra Nevada, the snow was burying his slide-rules six inches deep an hour.

Marcus stood beside the cab of the armored rotary snow-plow *Polyphemus* at the mouth of Snow-Shed Fourteen, his slate-gray greatcoat stiff as sheet-iron with frozen sleet, the green radium dial of his wrist-chronometer glowing dimly through the driving white twilight. The air at seven thousand feet was twelve degrees above zero and smelled of wet wood-smoke, scorched cylinder-oil, and the raw, butcher-shop stench of the forty artillery mules that his Cantonese pioneers had just shot and gutted in the ditch behind the tender to feed the boiler-fires with their fat.

Three months of mathematical war had pared the twenty-three-year-old Marshal’s cheeks down to the tight, grey bone of his dead father’s skull. He had burned Takashima’s cruisers out of San Francisco bay in September, only to find that a fleet without Nagasaki coal-colliers and a capital without San Joaquin grain-barges was a steel trap that starved its own garrison. When Silas Thorne—proclaimed *Protector of the Free States* by seventy thousand mutinous Virginia, Missouri, and Australian veterans at Salt Lake—had shut the eastern portals of the Sierra tunnels in October and cut the Sacramento aqueducts, Marcus had marched his twelve thousand Polytechnic cadets and his six remaining batteries of eighteen-pounder Krupp field-guns up the icy granite gorge of the Truckee to blow the eastern door open before winter locked him against the coast.

He had calculated the coal-tonnage to the pound; he had calculated the ballistic tables for seven thousand feet of altitude; he had forgotten only that a boy who has spent three years in an iron examination-cell at Berkeley does not shoot as straight when his toes are black with frostbite and the timber roof above his head is raining burning pitch.

"The rotary-blades are jammed solid in the cut ahead, General!" shouted Major Kuroda, stumbling back down the six-foot ties out of the blinding smoke of Snow-Shed Fourteen with his left sleeve burned to the elbow and a smear of frozen blood across his horn-rimmed spectacles. "Silas Thorne’s Cornish miners didn't just drop the granite roof of the tunnel—they chained three loaded coal-gondolas across the grade and poured ten thousand gallons of Washoe rock-oil down the timbers before they lit the fuse! The shed is a furnace for half a mile, and the heat is melting the snow-pack on the upper ledges directly over our ammunition-cars!"

Marcus did not step back under the shelter of the locomotive tender. He pulled his ivory slide-rule from his stiffened breast pocket with two frost-blistered fingers; the celluloid cursor was cracked across the logarithmic scale where a spent .45-70 slug had struck his chest at the Cisco switch two hours before, yet he pushed the slide to the mark with mechanical precision.

"If the shed timbers are burning at twelve hundred degrees, the draft through the eastern portal will burn the pine arches out in thirty-eight minutes," Marcus said, his clipped voice flat and breathless in the thin mountain air as the heavy, booming *crump* of Silas’s three-inch mountain-howitzers echoed down from the invisible granite crags above the tree-line, sending a fresh shower of pine-boughs and ice-shrapnel rattling off the steel roof of the plow. "Unlimber the two six-inch siege-mortars on the flatcars, Major, and elevate to sixty-five degrees against the north ridge. Have the Third Shensi and Pennsylvania Cadet Battalions fix bayonets and go up the granite chute to the left of the shed in open skirmish-order. Once they clear the rifle-pits above the portal—"

"General, the Third Battalion cannot climb the chute," Kuroda interrupted, his hand dropping to the ice-crusted frame of the locomotive as a four-pound shrapnel shell burst thirty feet overhead in the swirling snow-fog, driving three lead balls with a sharp *whack-whack-whack* through the wooden cab behind them and spilling the dead fireman out across the coal-apron. "Four hundred of the southern and Cantonese boys sat down in the snow by the water-tank ten minutes ago and took their boots off. Their feet are frozen to the ankle-bones, and we haven't issued a hot ration since the Emigrant Gap depot burned on Tuesday! And the aerial cruiser *Aeolus*—"

Kuroda pointed a trembling, soot-blackened finger upward toward the narrow rift between the granite walls where the storm-wind howled down from the summit at fifty miles an hour.

Through a sudden, ragged tear in the snow-clouds two thousand feet above the pass, the monstrous yellow silk belly of the dirigible *Aeolus*—which Marcus had ordered up from Benicia at dawn to drop white phosphorus upon Silas’s hidden howitzer-batteries—appeared for five seconds, pitching wildly nose-down like a harpooned whale in the freezing downdraft. Her twin wooden propellers were feathered and motionless, frozen solid in their bearings by the Sierra sleet; even as Marcus raised his chin, a gust off Donner Peak caught the six-hundred-foot hydrogen bag broadside, tore the aluminum gondola clean out of its piano-wire rigging, and slammed the silk envelope against the jagged granite teeth of the Palisades.

A silent, dirty-orange mushroom of burning hydrogen blossomed against the snow-field, lighting up the canyon walls for three miles around—and in that brief, apocalyptic glare, Marcus saw what no logarithmic table at Monterey had predicted.

Up along the blasted granite benches on both sides of the railway cut, where Elias Thorne’s Chinese coolies had chipped the grade out of the living rock with hand-drills twenty-five years before, stood not a ragged mob of mutineers, but six thousand men of the old frontier legions—the sons of the Rio Frio Rangers, the bearded veterans of the Baikal sledges, and the Cornish blaster-men of the Comstock—wrapped in buffalo-coats and stolen grey army blankets, rolling hundred-pound kegs of black blasting-powder with lighted fuses straight over the granite lip onto the roofs of his stalled troop-trains.

"Get the locomotive reversed, boy!" roared a cracked, furious voice from the open door of the staff-car behind the tender.

Old Brigadier Caleb Vance, seventy-six years old and blind in one eye, stood upon the icy iron steps of the platform with his white beard blowing across his shoulder and an archaic single-shot Springfield musket braced against his hip. He had refused to stay behind in the Sacramento hospital when the column marched; now, as the first powder-keg bounced down the granite talus and blew the wheels out from under the third cadet-coach in a geyser of red fire and mangled seventeen-year-old limbs, the old man reached out and caught his grand-nephew by the collar of his slate-gray coat.

"You’re in a box-canyon with the snow sliding, Marcus!" Caleb yelled over the screaming of the wounded cadets in the ditch and the roar of the burning snow-shed ahead. "Your little schoolboys don't know how to fight in the brush when the track’s gone! Uncouple the engine from the flatcars and run her backward down the grade to Auburn before Silas drops the whole mountain behind your tail!"

Marcus wrenched his collar out of the old man’s grasp, his pale face twitching for the first time as a second avalanche of rock and powder-smoke buried the mortar-flatcar fifty yards down the line, cutting his column in half. In his breast pocket, his fingers closed convulsively around the broken ivory slide-rule.

"The track is the Empire, Uncle!" Marcus shouted back, drawing his nickeled nine-shot pistol from its holster as a hundred bearded Missouri riflemen in captured blue coats came sliding down the snowy embankment through the pine-smoke, swinging clubbed carbines and roaring Silas Thorne’s name. "If we abandon the six-inch guns on this grade, we have no siege-train left between here and the bay! Major Kuroda—form the headquarters company across the tender-apron! Fire by volleys at fifty yards—"

Before Kuroda could raise his whistle to his frost-split lips, the granite cliff three hundred feet above Snow-Shed Fourteen gave a deep, subterranean groan as the heat of the burning oil-cars below melted the foot of the overhanging glacier. Five thousand tons of blue ice, granite boulders, and burning pine-timbers sheared away from the mountain wall at once, plunging downward toward the track with a roar that drowned the musketry as Caleb Vance threw his heavy, seventy-six-year-old body squarely against Marcus’s chest, driving the young general backward over the iron coal-gate of the reversing tender just as the world went white and the coupling-pins sheared like icicles beneath the weight of the falling peak, sending the solitary locomotive hurtling backward down the five-percent grade into the Sacramento fog while old Caleb Vance’s body remained behind under forty feet of Sierra drift.

***

It was the exhaustion of that winter—when Marcus Vance’s frostbitten remnant limped back into the cold foundries of Oakland without a single siege-gun, while Silas Thorne’s frontier regiments starved behind the snow-blocked tunnels of Nevada and Marquis Takashima’s cruisers lay anchored off Santa Barbara with empty coal-bunkers and foul bottoms—that brought the three wolves of the broken house to the coral reef of Oahu in the spring.

They did not come out of love for the Princess; they came because the only dry coal-heaps and the only unburned rice-granaries between the Rocky Mountains and the Yellow Sea lay behind the mine-fields of Pearl Lochs, in the newly christened neutral sanctuary that the islanders called *Thalassia*.

On the twelfth of April, in an open-sided pavilion of spliced bamboo and dark Hawaiian koa-wood erected upon the neutral spit of Sand Island—where every officer was searched to the skin for derringers by six-foot Marquesan spear-men before stepping off his gig—Lady Kaiulani sat alone at the head of a semicircular table of polished basalt. The trade-wind coming off the outer rollers smelled of wet coral, crushed plumeria blossoms, and the clean, stinging salt spray that had washed the blood of the continent from the air.
