Before her sat the three men who had spent seven months tearing Elias Thorne’s coat into rags: General Marcus Vance, his left arm still in a black silk sling from the Donner avalanche, his slate-gray tunic threadbare at the cuffs; Silas Thorne, bloated with dropsical whiskey and wearing a tarnished gold-laced coat of the Virginia Auxiliaries over muddy cavalry boots; and Grand-Admiral Marquis Takashima, gaunt and yellow-cheeked from three months of scurvy rations aboard the *Yamato*.

"You have six days of Welsh steam-coal left in your bunkers at San Pedro, Marquis," Kaiulani said, her musical voice barely raised above the hiss of the surf along the reef as she laid three identical sheets of Oahu mulberry-parchment upon the dark stone. "And you, Silas, have forty thousand Missourians at Carson City eating boiled mule-hide because the Cantonese railway-masons have blown up the Humboldt bridges behind you; while General Vance is minting iron ration-tokens in San Francisco that the fishermen at the wharf refuse to take for a basket of smelts. You have proved that none of you is tall enough to wear the dead man’s boots alone."

Silas struck the basalt table with his bandaged fist, making the ink-horns rattle. "Give me ten thousand tons of Honolulu sugar-silver and open the Sacramento wire, Aunt, and I’ll hang every Berkeley clerk between the Sierra and the Gate before June! I am Elias Thorne’s blood!"

"You are a tavern-captain whose own regiments sold your artillery-horses to the Mormons last Tuesday for three hundred sacks of corn-meal," Kaiulani replied without looking at him, her dark, severe eyes passing from Takashima’s sunken temples to the broken ivory slide-rule still pinned inside Marcus Vance’s breast pocket. "Neither blood nor logarithms will put this ceiling back up alone. If you leave this island tonight without signing the Truce of Thalassia, I will open the Pearl Lochs coal-docks tomorrow morning to whichever one of you brings me the heads of the other two—or, if you prefer to die together, I will wire the British Viceroy at Calcutta that the Pacific Fleet has no powder for its twelve-inch guns."

Takashima’s dry lips parted over his blackened teeth. "And what is the price of the coal, Your Highness?"

"A tripod of iron," Kaiulani said, drawing the whale-ivory seal of Oahu from her black bombazine sleeve and setting it between the ink-pots. "Silas returns to Denver as Hereditary Marshal of the Interior Cantons, with ten million silver thalers a year from the Mint to keep his horsemen drunk and off the tracks. Marquis Takashima retains the High Admiralty of the Western Waters, provided every battleship carries a Polytechnic engineer at the throttles and clears its customs through Monterey. And General Vance remains Chancellor of the Gauge in San Francisco, under my Regency, until we have rebuilt the ditch at Panama and welded the hoop so tight that it will take twenty years of peace before your grandsons are rich enough to finish this war."

***

To the Chronicler who writes these closing pages in the autumn of 1915, looking down from the library windows of the Berkeley Polytechnic upon a bay that has known twenty-seven years of armed, sleepless convalescence since that morning on Sand Island, the wisdom of Lady Kaiulani’s tripod is visible in every smoke-stack along the shore.

For twenty-six years—through the long, gray afternoon of her Sole Regency, while the canal at Panama was poured in concrete and the bronze corpse of the Founder rode the turrets of the fleet to keep the provinces in awe—the truce of Thalassia held the hundred and twenty-four states together like a splint of iron wire bound around a fractured thigh-bone. One by one, the wild beasts of the first succession died off in their cages: Silas Thorne drowned in his own dropsy and sour mash at the Denver palace in ninety-nine; old Marquis Takashima went to his ancestors before the Miraflores locks were opened; and by the spring of the last year, only the aged Princess and the gray-haired, fifty-six-year-old Marshal Marcus Vance remained alive of those who had heard Elias Thorne’s stick strike the floorboards.

Yet a splint is not a bone; and by the summer of 1914, when the eighty-year-old Regent knew that her own breath was failing in the Honolulu trade-winds, the Great Arena had grown too heavy to be governed by a dead man’s bronze statue and a college of unnamed clerks. The third generation had arrived—three hundred and eighty million souls who had never seen the frontier or the shoguns, who spoke the clipped, hybrid court-pidgin of the examination-sheds, and who demanded a living magistrate upon the dais.

It was at the Grand Conclave of May, 1914—held not in the blood-stained Rotunda of San Francisco, nor in the fragile bamboo pavilions of Oahu, but upon the artificial granite island of the Miraflores Lock-Spillway at Panama, where the Atlantic and Pacific squadrons lay moored gun-wale to gun-wale in the fresh water of the continent’s spine—that the *Settlement of the New Century* was sealed.

On that blistering noon, before the assembled Prefects of the Hundred and Twenty-Four States and the gray-templed Polytechnic Admirals, Lady Kaiulani walked for the last time to the stone parapet beneath the Arch of the Pivot. leaning upon the steel arm of Field-Marshal Marcus Vance. She did not bring forth the bronze effigy from the flagship; at dawn that morning, by her final warrant, the copper-plated corpse of Elias Thorne had been unbolted from the barbette of the dreadnought and lowered with twenty tons of pig-lead into the four-thousand-fathom abyss of the Marianas Trench, where no rebel could ever melt him down and no clerk could use his dead thumb for a stamp.

Instead, she led forward two twenty-four-year-old youths in the plain slate-gray wool of the Imperial Service: Prince Kalanimoku the younger—the son of her gentle cousin who had died in the Monterey pleurisy, carrying in his veins the mingled blood of the Kentucky Protector and the ancient kings of Maui—and beside him as Imperial Consort, the Lady Chiyo, grand-niece of Marquis Takashima and First Wrangler of the Kyoto Mathematical Synod.

Thus was established the *Syncretic Dynasty of the House of Thorne-Kamehameha*, under the perpetual constitutional guardianship of the Polytechnic Staff. The Caesar of the frontier was gone into the deep water; in his place sat a bronze-skinned, gray-eyed Sacred Emperor who reigned from the coral palaces of Thalassia like the heaven-descended sovereigns of the East, signing no death-warrants and touching no tax-rolls, while in the concrete vaults of Monterey, Marshal Vance’s ten thousand numbered prefects worked the Hollerith engines that moved the grain and the coal.

The Empire had survived its maker’s death by shedding its skin: what had begun in the mud of the Rio Frio as the personal raid of an American border-captain had hardened, sixty years later, into an immortal, self-winding priesthood of bronze and steam.

***

And because an engine that cannot break inward must inevitably grind outward until it consumes the last unnumbered acre of the globe, the new dynasty was scarcely six months upon the lotus-throne of Thalassia before the long-delayed reckoning with the fragments of the Old World sounded across the western straits.

For forty years since the disaster in the Coral Sea and the closing of the Suez approaches by the Pacifica tariff-leagues, the remnants of the British Empire had crouched behind the basalt bastions of Singapore and the Himalayan passes like an aged lion driven into its last thorny brake. Stripped of Canada, shut out of the Yangtze and the Australian downs, the House of Windsor and the remnant of the London Parliament had transferred their ragged exchequer, their surviving dreadnoughts, and two million conscripted English and Sepoy riflemen to the peninsula of Hindostan—proclaiming at Delhi the *Imperial Federation of the Indian Ocean*, the last autonomous fortress of the Atlantic race upon the earth.

In the autumn of 1914, when the British Viceroy at Calcutta refused to admit the Monterey census-assessors into the jute-mills of Bengal and mined the Straits of Malacca against the Sumatra oil-tankers, the great brass telegraph-keys in the cellar of Rincon Hill did not stutter with ultimatums as they had in the days of the Tsar.

Field-Marshal Marcus Vance, fifty-seven years old now and cold as the Sierra glacier that had killed his uncle, simply walked to the illuminated glass wall-map of the hemisphere, pulled his cracked ivory slide-rule from his tunic pocket, and moved four brass markers three inches to the west.

To the Chronicler who accompanied the headquarters staff aboard the eighty-thousand-ton super-dreadnought *Pacifica* as the Combined Fleets forced the Nicobar channel in the red monsoon dawn of November, the *Great Indian War* bore no resemblance to the desperate, smoky brawls of Vicksburg or Vladivostok. It was the collision of a continental trip-hammer with a wall of dry brick.

Over the churning, slate-green rollers of the Bay of Bengal came not a column of ships, but a floating industrial city twenty miles wide: forty turbine-driven dreadnoughts burning refined Borneo petroleum, flanked by twelve flat-decked *aeroplane-tenders* from whose five-hundred-foot timber flight-strips rose swarms of twin-engined Curtiss-Nakajima biplanes armed with two-hundred-pound picric-acid torpedoes, while five thousand feet above the mastheads rode the twelve rigid duralumin air-cruisers of the *Aeolus III* class, their wireless-antennas sparking blue against the monsoon clouds as they corrected the fall of the twenty-inch shells by trigonometry from thirty miles out at sea.

At six o’clock on the morning of the fourteenth of November, off the sand-heads of the Hooghly estuary below Calcutta, the last battle-fleet of the Atlantic world—twenty-two coal-burning British battleships of the *King Edward* and *Viceroy* classes, their black smoke-columns trailing low across the rain-squalls and the White Ensign of St. George nailed to their mainmasts—steamed out between the mine-fields to die in deep water.

Up on the armored signal-bridge of the *Pacifica*, three stories above the triple twenty-inch turrets where the hydraulic rammers were already seating the two-ton armor-piercing projectiles into the breeches with a greased, pneumatic hiss, stood not Field-Marshal Marcus Vance, for the fifty-seven-year-old Chancellor of the Gauge had surrendered his baton to the third generation that autumn, but his thirty-year-old former Chief of Operations, Fleet-General Kuroda the younger—Candidate Zero-Zero-One-Four of the class of nineteen-six.

Through the three-inch Zeiss slit of the conning-tower, the distant British line was visible only as a row of tiny gray smudges nineteen miles to the northwest, where the muddy brown outflow of the sacred Ganges stained the green ocean water like a widening pool of rust.

"The flagship *New Delhi* has just hoisted the old Nelson signal at the fore, General," the flag-lieutenant—a boy born in the Massachusetts cantons whose collar bore the cipher *Eight-Eight-One-Two*—reported, his eye pressed to the stereoscopic range-finder while the plot-table ticks clicked off the decreasing yards in red electric numerals along the bulkhead. "And their coastal batteries at Diamond Harbor and Saugor Island are opening fire with thirteen-inch cordite at extreme elevation. The shells are falling four thousand yards short in the outer channel."

Young Kuroda did not look through the armored slit. The air inside the conning-tower smelled of warm transformer-oil, ozone, and the faint, sweet scent of the Honolulu sandalwood paper upon which the morning dispatches from the Sacred Emperor Kalanimoku were printed. In his right hand, Kuroda held the standard-issue duralumin circular calculator of the Monterey Staff—an instrument that calculated wind-drift, barometric density, and the Coriolis rotation of the earth without the need for a human thumb to slide an ivory stick.

"They are burning Cardiff and Bengal lump-coal in hand-stoked Scotch boilers, Lieutenant," Kuroda said, his voice dry, unhurried, and quiet as the hum of the gyro-compass between his boots while the first British salvo threw up four harmless white water-spouts two miles ahead of his bow. "After forty minutes at twenty knots against the monsoon swell, their stokers will be fainting on the floor-plates and their speed will drop to sixteen. We will not close within the range of their thirteen-inch guns to give their newspapers a Trafalgar."

He turned the knurled brass dial of the ballistic computer two clicks to the left, checking the wireless telemetry ribbon unspooling from the air-cruiser hovering above the Hooghly mud-banks.

"Alter course four points to port and hold the range at twenty-six thousand yards," Kuroda ordered, laying his gloved finger upon the brass firing-circuit of the master director-tower as the sixty twenty-inch rifles of the First Squadron rose in synchronized unison against the wet gray sky of Bengal, their muzzles pointing toward the invisible shoreline where three hundred years of European dominion waited behind the mud-forts.

***

Seven thousand eight hundred miles to the east, where the November afternoon was already sinking into the cold salt fog of the Golden Gate, the salvo that broke the spine of the *New Delhi* registered only as a tiny, silent jump of a siphon-needle upon a glass drum.

Inside the high, glass-walled solarium atop the retired officers' pavilion at the Presidio—a quiet house of unpainted redwood and Sierra stone overlooking the same mile-wide strait where Elias Thorne had watched the *Oregon* steam in sixty-four years before—Field-Marshal Marcus Vance sat alone beside an unlit anthracite grate.

He was fifty-seven years old, though the rheumatic frost of the Donner avalanche had stiffened his left knee until he walked with a steel brace inside his trouser-leg, and the hair above his temples was as white as the salt-crust on the Farallones. He wore no uniform; when the Synod of Prefects had voted him the Gold Baton of Emeritus Guardian in October and promoted young Kuroda to the supreme command of the Western Expedition, Marcus had folded his slate-gray tunic into a camphor-chest and put on the plain dark alpaca coat of a retired polytechnic assessor.

Before his knees stood a small mahogany receiver-table connected by a courtesy wire to the Telegraph Annex on Rincon Hill. Every three minutes, the automatic printer beside his elbow gave a soft, oiled *whir* and spat out four inches of perforated yellow tape.

Marcus did not need a codebook to read the holes in the paper. Resting across his grey wool thigh lay the cracked ivory slide-rule that had stopped the .45-70 slug at Cisco switch during the winter of the Troubles.

*16:12 GMT,* the holes said. *SQUADRON ONE. ELEVATION FOURTEEN DEGREES. CONSUMPTION OF PICRIC-ACID SHELL, TWELVE HUNDRED TONS. BRITISH UNITS SUNK OR BURNING ON SAGAR BAR: SIXTEEN. OWN CASUALTIES: ONE CURTISS TORPEDO-PLANE LOST TO ENGINE FAILURE.*

Marcus picked up the ivory rule between his stiff, square-nailed fingers and pushed the cracked celluloid cursor half an inch along the wood. His pale eyes lifted from the yellow paper to the wide plate-glass window.

Down below the bluff, across the dark green heave of the bay, the three-tiered granite embankments of San Francisco were lighting their five o’clock carbon-arcs against the dusk. A ten-thousand-ton automated grain-collier from the Sacramento delta was sliding silently beneath the hydraulic gantry-cranes at the Mint slip, while up on the Berkeley slopes the white marble quadrangles of the Examination Sheds glowed like a row of lighted factory furnaces.

For forty years he had worked to take the human passion out of war—to purge the army of his father’s bloody frontier charges and old Caleb’s whiskey-soaked camps, replacing the saber and the family name with the logarithm and the five-digit collar cipher. He had designed the examination cubicles; he had calculated the ration-tables; he had trained young Kuroda and ten thousand boys like him to regard the burning of a city or the sinking of a fleet not as glory, nor even as cruelty, but simply as the balancing of an equation in coal and nitrogen.

And now the equation had balanced him out of the room.

They did not hate him down in the concrete vaults of Monterey; they revered his portrait in the mathematics hall alongside Elias Thorne’s iron walking-stick. Yet when he had gone down to the Admiralty wharf in October to argue that the Empire’s natural circumference stopped at the Straits of Malacca—that to swallow three hundred million starving Bengali peasants and two thousand miles of Indian railway on a five-foot-six gauge would overstrain the silver reserves of the Market Street Mint by fourteen percent—the young prefects of the class of nineteen-ten had listened to him with the polite, stone-faced patience that he himself had shown to Cornelius Schuyler and Marquis Takashima at the iron turnstile twenty-seven years ago.

*The turbines at Balboa and the blast-furnaces at Hanyang are producing a twenty-percent surplus of steel plate and picric acid, Marshal,* Candidate Zero-Zero-One-Four had answered him, tapping a duralumin calculator that did not have a bullet-crack across its face. *An industrial machine that does not expand its market-radius by four percent per annum chokes upon its own pig-iron. We do not invade Hindostan for glory; we invade it to absorb the surplus output of the Osaka rolling-mills.*

The ticker-machine beside Marcus’s elbow whirred again.

*16:20 GMT. DIAMOND HARBOR FORTS SILENCED BY AERIAL PHOSPHORUS. VICEROY AT CALCUTTA REQUESTS FORTY-EIGHT HOUR ARMISTICE TO EVacuate EUROPEAN WOMEN. FLEET-GENERAL KURODA REPLIES: THE TIDE SERVES AT SIX. UNCONDITIONAL CAPITULATION OF THE PENINSULA OR THE DREADNOUGHTS ENTER THE RIVER.*

Marcus looked down at the cracked ivory stick in his lap. His father had ridden a lathered horse into the red mud of Vicksburg to make a king; he himself had frozen his toes in the Sierra snow to turn that king into a machine; and now the machine was rolling westward across the warm oceans of the earth under its own steam, with nobody left at the throttle who remembered why the fire had been lit in the boiler.

A quiet tap sounded at the glass door of the solarium. An orderly—a seventeen-year-old boy from the Amur Cossack cantons wearing the blue brassard of the hospital service—stepped inside with a steaming porcelain mug upon a tin tray.

"Your five-o’clock beef-tea, Marshal," the boy said in the flat, accentless English of the primary sheds, setting the mug down directly atop the uncoiling yellow tape from the Bay of Bengal without glancing at the holes. "The surgeon says the damp fog is bad for your knee-joint if you sit by the glass after sunset. Shall I draw the blackout curtains?"

Marcus slowly slid the broken ivory rule back into his alpaca breast pocket, where there were no brass buttons to catch the light.

"Draw them, Corporal," Marcus said.

***

Three weeks later, on the morning of the sixth of December, the northeast monsoon blew clear and hot down the muddy yellow reaches of the Irrawaddy River, carrying the smell of charred teakwood, stagnant paddy-slime, and the heavy, sweetish smoke of the Rangoon oil-refineries that the retiring British garrison had tried in vain to burn before the Choshu marine-brigades landed at Syriam.

High above the brown water, upon the vast, brick-paved terrace of the Shwedagon Pagoda—where the three-hundred-foot bell-shaped stupa of solid gilded masonry blazed against the tropical sky in a glare of Sunset Gold that outshone the domes of San Francisco—a pavilion of imperial-blue silk had been pitched between the plaster statues of the guardian *chinthe* lions.

Lady Kaiulani did not walk up the four hundred stone steps from the cantonment road. She was eighty years old that winter; her bones were as light and dry as the bamboo ribs of a fan, and the tropic heat that had once been the breath of her Honolulu youth now pressed upon her shrunken chest like a hot iron weight. Four six-foot guardsmen of the Oahu Household carried her up the southern stairway in an open palanquin of black-lacquered koa-wood, her tiny figure upright among the velvet cushions in her unchanging gown of severe black bombazine, the ancient whale-ivory *lei niho palaoa* resting against the withered parchment of her throat.

As the bearers set the poles down upon the scorching red brick of the platform, Kaiulani raised her dark, sunken eyes—still as clear and merciless as obsidian beneath her white braids—and looked out past the golden lotus-spire toward the city below.

Across the miles of green palm-groves and flooded rice-delta, the Union Jack had vanished from the earth. Over the teak-wharves of the Irrawaddy Flotilla Company, over the red-brick barracks of the cantonment and the high iron roofs of the Burmah Oil tanks, snapped ten thousand banners of Imperial Blue and Gold, while out in the main stream lay the gray, triple-turreted bulk of the cruiser *Kamehameha IV*, her twenty-inch guns trained steadily upon the gilded roofs of the Viceregal residency.

Inside the open silk pavilion, waiting on the shady side of a thirty-ton bronze temple-bell that the Burmese kings had cast a century before, stood a delegation of five men in stained white tropical drill and tarnished gold lace: Lord Hardinge of Penshurst, the last British Viceroy of India; General Sir Beauchamp Duff, Commander-in-Chief of the shattered Bengal Army; and behind them, three silk-turbaned native princes—the Nizam of Hyderabad, the Maharaja of Gwalior, and the Gaekwar of Baroda—whom Fleet-General Kuroda’s air-cruisers had brought down from Delhi under polite escort the night before.

Kaiulani did not rise from her palanquin chair. The bearers stepped back three paces andgrounded their magazine-rifles on the brick; beside her right elbow, Fleet-General Kuroda unrolled a six-foot linen map of the Indian subcontinent across the teakwood table, weighting the corners not with ink-horns, but with four brass fuse-caps from the twenty-inch shells that had sunk the *New Delhi*.

"Your Highness has brought us to a temple of idols to sign away the inheritance of Queen Victoria," Lord Hardinge said, his voice trembling with the quinine-ague and the humiliation of a race that had not signed a treaty under the muzzles of foreign cannon since Yorktown. His white linen cuff was frayed where a splinter had struck his launch at Diamond Harbor, and he refused to look at the three Indian princes standing silently behind his shoulder. "In November you promised at Singapore that if the Home Fleet ceased fire in the Hooghly, the sovereignty of the Crown over the interior provinces west of the Ganges would be respected under a commercial customs-union."

"In November, My Lord, your sappers had not yet blown up the broad-gauge tunnels in the Khyber Pass or invited the Russian remnants at Tashkent to occupy the Punjab," Kaiulani replied. Her voice was no longer the clear, bell-like contralto that had charmed the Mexican governors at Monterey fifty years ago; it was a dry, musical whisper, like wind rustling through dead palm-fronds, yet every syllable cut through the hum of the temple flies. "When an house-holder sets fire to his own thatch to spite the bailiff, the municipality does not leave him in possession of the kitchen. General Kuroda, read the lines of the Partition."

Kuroda did not look at the Englishman; he tapped the linen map with the tip of his steel dividers.

"From the first of January, nineteen-fifteen, the corporate entity known as the British Indian Empire ceases to exist," Kuroda read in his flat, Polytechnic cadence. "The littoral provinces of Burma, Bengal, Madras, and Ceylon are incorporated directly into the Grand Confederation as the One Hundred and Twenty-Fifth through One Hundred and Thirtieth Maritime Cantons, under the civil code of Monterey and the six-foot railway gauge. The interior plateau of the Deccan and the Rajput states—" here Kuroda inclined his cropped head half an inch toward the three silent maharajas in their jewel-crusted turbans "—are constituted as the Autonomous Princely Protectorate of Hindostan, answering directly to the Insular Chancery at Thalassia, with native garrisons officered by graduates of the New Edo and Berkeley academies."

Lord Hardinge’s gaunt face went the color of wet chalk under his sun-burn. "And the British Crown? The two hundred thousand Englishmen and women in the civil service and the hill-stations—the tea-planters of Assam, the regimental depots at Meerut and Bombay?"

"The port of Bombay and a ten-mile radius around the Malabar cotton-mills will remain a Free Leasehold Factory of the London Exchequer for twenty years, to liquidate the sterling debt owed to the Market Street Mint," Kaiulani said softly, resting her tiny, blue-veined hand upon the whale-ivory clasp at her throat as a flight of three Curtiss-Nakajima biplanes droned low over the golden spire of the pagoda, their twin propellers beating the hot incense-smoke down into the pavilion. "Your soldiers will lay down their Lee-Enfield rifles at the Calcutta docks before the winter solstice and embark upon the Pacific Mail colliers for Southampton at our expense. As for your civil magistrates, My Lord—any young Englishman under the age of twenty-two who wishes to remain in Asia may present himself at the Rangoon examination-sheds on Monday morning, shave his head, and sit for the third-class polytechnic logarithm paper alongside the sons of his Bengali sweepers."

Behind the Viceroy, the Nizam of Hyderabad stepped forward across the carpet, bowing low until his emerald-plumed turban touched the shadow of the koa-wood palanquin.

"And the salt-tax of the English, Great Lady?" the Nizam asked in careful French.

"Abolished at noon, Highness," Kaiulani answered, turning her dark eyes upon the Indian prince with the cold, maternal smile that had once locked Don Rafael Núñez into the Panama saloon-car. "You will pay no tribute to London again. You will merely send ten thousand of your Rajput horsemen each spring to patrol the Ural timber-lines for General Kuroda, and buy your locomotives from the Osaka works. Give the Viceroy the pen, General; the sun is rising on the brick, and I wish to be aboard the steamer before the noon heat."

***

To the Chronicler who stood seven days later upon the stone *ghats* of Benares—watching a battalion of Cantonese and Californian railway-surveyors drive their red-and-white leveling-stakes into the sacred mud of the Ganges while a squad of Choshu military police superintended the stacking of ten thousand surrendered British Martini-Henry and Lee-Enfield rifles upon the temple steps—the scene required neither commentary nor tears.

In the history of mortal empires, there is always an afternoon when the tide reaches its highest watermark upon the sea-wall, pauses for the space of a single heartbeat in the sun, and begins its long, invisible retreat toward the mud-flats. For the race of the Atlantic islands—those bold, red-coated shipbuilders who had sailed out of the Thames and the Bristol Channel three centuries before to girdle the globe with their counting-houses and their steam-engines—that afternoon fell on the thirteenth of December, 1914, along the broad, corpse-strewn flood of the Mother River.

The *Treaty of Rangoon* was not printed in the London newspapers until the following month, for the submarine cables through the Red Sea had been dredged up and cut by the Pacifica cable-ships off Aden; yet along the twelve hundred miles of the Grand Trunk Road from Delhi to the sea, the end of the European millennium was already written in iron.

All morning, under a pale, dusty winter sky that smelled of burning cow-dung, crushed marigolds from the Hindu shrines, and the sharp, unmistakable coal-tar of the Monterey disinfectant-carts, the last regiments of the British Raj marched down the stone steps to the river-barges.

There were no brass bands playing *The British Grenadiers*, and no silk colors flying above the mist; by the fourth article of Fleet-General Kuroda’s military convention, the regimental standards of the Black Watch, the Coldstream Detachments, and the Bengal Lancers had already been soldered inside leaden cylinders at the Allahabad arsenal to be shipped eastward as curiosities for the Rotunda museum in San Francisco. In absolute silence, four thousand sun-blackened Yorkshiremen and Scots in faded khaki drill—the grandsons of the men who had blown open the Kashmir Gate in fifty-seven and held the bloody ridge above Delhi—filed down the ancient stairs between twin ranks of twenty-year-old Imperial Cadets wearing the unadorned slate-gray wool and five-digit silver collar-ciphers of the Great Arena.

At the foot of the Manikarnika Ghat, where the sandalwood funeral pyres of the Brahmans smoked lazily beside the oily brown water, I paused behind the shoulder of Prefect-Assessor Shen the younger—son of that Auditor Shen who had weighed the dead coolie’s brass thumb in the San Francisco cellar thirty-three years ago—as he sat before a folding camp-table of stamped duralumin, checking the British embarkation-rolls against a portable Hollerith card-punch.

"Eight hundred and forty-two rank-and-file of the Second Battalion, West Riding Regiment, Citizen-Prefect," reported an English major with an empty left sleeve pinned across his tunics, halting before the table and laying his rusted Webley service revolver upon the aluminum sheet beside Shen’s brass ink-pot. The officer’s eyes were bloodshot from the coal-smoke of the burned cantonments at Cawnpore; as he looked past the Chinese magistrate’s horn-rimmed spectacles toward the middle of the river—where a colossal floating steam-hammer towed by an Osaka tug was already driving creosoted Oregon pilings straight through the sacred bathing-pools to carry the new six-foot-gauge railway bridge—a muscle twitched violently in his hollow cheek. "We have left two hundred men down with the enteric fever in the garrison hospital at Lucknow. By the terms of Lord Hardinge’s capitulation on the pagoda steps, they are to receive full quinine rations and homeward passage aboard the January hospital-transport."

Prefect Shen did not look up from his perforated manila cards. With two deft, practiced fingers, he lifted the Englishman’s revolver by the trigger-guard, dropped it into a tarred wicker basket filled with broken Wilkinson sabers and brass crown-badges that two Hawaiian orderlies were carrying down to the ballast-lighters, and stamped a violet serial numeral across the major’s parchment clearance-sheet.

"The military hospital at Lucknow was reclassified at six this morning as District Quarantine Station Four-Zero-Nine, Major," Shen said in his smooth, accentless Berkeley English, his right palm depressing the steel lever of the card-punch with a sharp *clack* as the next file of disarmed Highlanders stepped onto the gangplank of the waiting stern-wheeler. "Your sick will be processed according to the Pacifica Sanitary Code. Those whose temperatures return to the normal curve before the fifteenth of January will be embarked on the colliers at Calcutta; those whose fevers prove chronic will be assigned third-class clerical duty in the Assam tea-cantons to defray the cost of their municipal quinine. Step down to the lower deck, please, and instruct your sergeants not to throw their empty biscuit-tins over the rail; the channel is being dredged to sixteen feet for the Hanyang ore-barges."

The one-armed major stood motionless for three seconds upon the slimy stone step, the hot winter wind lifting the skirt of his torn khaki coat while high above his head, from the topmost balcony of the great Mosque of Aurangzeb, a signal-squad of the Choshu Corps unrolled the thirty-foot banner of Imperial Blue and Sunset Gold, letting the heavy silk drop down across the ancient red sandstone until the old world vanished beneath the hem.

***

While the soldiers of the Atlantic island were filing onto the river-lighters at Benares, Lady Kaiulani remained behind at Rangoon for three days to lock the cellar doors of the conquered continent before the monsoon broke.

She did not hold her court upon the scorching bricks of the pagoda a second time. On the afternoon of the sixteenth of December, she sat within the high, teak-paneled counting-room of the former Jardine-Matheson Godown No. 1 along the Strand Road—a cavernous vault of dark Burmese timber whose iron-barred windows looked out upon the forest of hydraulic dock-cranes and the gray, armored flanks of the transport-fleet. The room was cool and dim, smelling powerfully of raw Patna opium-chests, dried Pekoe tea-brick, and the sharp, biting naphtha that the sanitation gangs were spraying across the wharf-timbers outside to kill the plague-fleas.

Before her table of polished camphor-wood stood four men whose knees trembled slightly inside their immaculate tropical broadcloth and silk robes: Sir Catchick Paul Chater, senior partner of the Hong Kong and Calcutta opium-syndicates; Mr. David Sassoon the younger of the Bombay exchanges; and two corpulent Marwari silver-bankers from the Burrabazar whose fathers had financed the East India Company’s regiments a century before.

"The political sovereignty of the peninsula does not concern our houses, Your Imperial Highness," Sir Paul Chater was saying, his pale, heavily lidded eyes fixed greedily upon the open iron strongbox beside Kaiulani’s foot where the new bronze Revenue Seals of the One Hundred and Twenty-Six Maritime Cantons lay nested in green velvet. "Whether the customs-guard at the Hooghly wears a red coat or a slate-gray tunic, the eighty thousand chests of Bengal and Malwa opium now lying in the Ghazipur maturing-sheds represent twelve million pounds sterling in private commercial paper, hypothecated to the London and Bombay discount-banks. And the Assam tea-clip for the coming spring is already contracted in advance to the Mincing Lane brokers at fourpence the pound. We ask only that the Regency validate our existing export-warrants under the commercial clauses of the Treaty of Rangoon."

Kaiulani did not answer him at once. At eighty years of age, her tiny, shrunken figure inside the rustling black bombazine seemed almost swallowed by the high-backed chair of carved teak; yet as she lifted a single, fist-sized ball of dark, gummy Behar opium from the sample-tray on the desk and turned it slowly between her withered, ivory-ringed fingers, the four millionaires in front of the table held their breath like schoolboys before a switch.

"For seventy years, gentlemen," Kaiulani said, her dry, musical whisper carrying clearly over the rhythmic *clank-hiss* of the Osaka steam-winches loading rice-sacks outside the window, "you and the English factors at Canton poisoned the rivers of China with this black mud so that your banks in London might buy Indian cotton and pay the dividends of Whitehall. When Elias Thorne took the Yangtze valleys into his protection in seventy-four, your gunboats stood behind the Singapore straits and smuggled forty thousand chests a year through the Hainan junks to rot the brains of our iron-workers at Hanyang."

Mr. Sassoon took a hasty step forward, his manicured hands fluttering above his white waistcoat. "The trade was licensed by Royal Charter, Madam! If the Ghazipur opium-factories are closed without compensation, forty thousand poppy-cultivators in Behar will default on their land-rents before March, and every bank from Bombay to Singapore will suspend specie payments!"

"The factories at Ghazipur will not be closed, Mr. Sassoon," Kaiulani replied softly, letting the black ball of gum drop back into the brass scale-pan with a dull *thud*. "An empire of four hundred million labourers requires three hundred tons of morphia and laudanum a year for its field-hospitals and its veterinary depots. From noon today, however, every poppy-field in the Ganges valley and every tea-garden from Darjeeling to the Brahmaputra becomes an exclusive Crown Monopoly of the Bureau of Integration."

She signed a brief gesture with her left hand; beside the door, a twenty-two-year-old Polytechnic fiscal prefect stepped forward and laid four printed indentures across the camphor-wood.

"The word *private* is struck from the commercial dictionary of the Indian Ocean," she continued, her obsidian eyes passing coldly across their grey, slack-jawed faces. "At six o’clock tonight, my Hawaiian provosts will burn sixty thousand chests of your smoking-opium in the lime-kilns at Kidderpore so that no Cantonese furnace-man ever sucks a pipe of English poison again. The remaining twenty thousand chests will be refined into surgical alkaloids at the Monterey laboratories under military seal. As for the Assam and Ceylon tea-harvests—not a single leaf will sail for the Thames in a European bottom. The entire crop is requisitioned in perpetuity by the San Francisco Commissariat at a fixed assessment of two silver tenths the pound, payable in forty-year canal-script."

"Two tenths in paper!" gasped Sir Paul Chater, his hand clutching at his silk cravat as if the cord were tightening around his windpipe. "That is twenty percent below the cost of the coolie-hire on the hills! You are confiscating the capital of the City of London by a stroke of the pen!"

"Fleet-General Kuroda confiscated your capital with twenty-inch picric-acid shells off Sagar Island three weeks ago, Sir Paul; I am merely giving you a receipt for the ashes," Kaiulani said, reaching for the whale-ivory seal at her wrist. "If you and your partners sign the transfer-deeds before the four-o’clock gun, you will be retained as salaried factors of the Seventh Tea and Chemical Trust at three thousand thalers a year, with permission to reside in your Calcutta villas under cadet supervision. If you prefer to plead the law of Mincing Lane, the convict-transport *Michigan* is coaling at the jetty to take four hundred railway-masons to the northern Ural mines at daybreak, and Auditor Shen informs me that the winter gang-rolls are still four names short."

***

It was the arrival of that same news at the mouth of the Thames—brought not by the severed Red Sea wires, but carried slowly around the tempestuous winter swells of the Cape of Good Hope aboard the overcrowded, coal-starved hospital-colliers that limped into Southampton Water in the February of 1915—that let down the final, iron curtain of the *Long Mourning* upon the island of Great Britain.

To the Chronicler who traveled to England in the following spring as an attaché of the Pacifica Debt-Liquidation Commission, no ruin in the ancient world—neither the grass-grown quays of Carthage nor the shrunk brick villages that huddled inside the shell of Diocletian’s palace—offered a spectacle more solemn or instructive than the twilight of the Atlantic metropolis.

There had been no sack of London; not a single shell from Kuroda’s dreadnoughts had ever fallen upon the chalk cliffs of Kent. Yet as our turbine-packet steamed up the yellow reaches of the lower river past Gravesend and the Isle of Dogs, we looked out upon a city that had died of an embolus in its distant arteries without a stone of its walls being scratched.

For two miles along the West India and Tilbury Docks—where thirty years before the forest of masts and red-and-black funnels had stood so thick that a man might walk across the river on the decks of the tea-clippers and the Australian wool-fleets—the grey granite basins lay as empty and still as highland tarns. Four hundred rust-streaked tramp-steamers, stripped of their brass fittings to pay the harbour-dues, rotted four-abreast against the rotting timber jetties with seagulls nesting in their cold smokestacks; the hydraulic cranes stood locked at forty-five degrees in the freezing drizzle, red with flaking iron-oxide; and along the endless brick vaults of the spice- and tea-warehouses, the bolted iron shutters bore only the stenciled white padlock of the *San Francisco Receivership Board*.

Because the gold of the Rand was cut off by the Pacifica cruisers at Delagoa Bay, and because the cotton of the Mississippi, the wool of Melbourne, and the tea of Assam now cleared exclusively in silver thalers through the clearing-houses of Market Street and Osaka, the pound sterling—which for two hundred years had been the measure of human labor from Archangel to Valparaiso—had fallen in six weeks to the value of provincial waste-paper.

When I walked up Threadneedle Street toward the Bank of England on a raw, sleet-swept Tuesday noon in March, the air did not smell of roasting coffee-beans, sea-coal, and opulent cigar-smoke as my father had remembered it before the fall of the East. It smelled of boiled turnip-tops, wet shoddy wool, and the sour sweat of fifty thousand idle dock-laborers and discharged clerks who stood in silent, four-deep queues along the granite curb, waiting in their threadbare black frock-coats and battered top-hats before the municipal soup-booths that the Pacifica Quaker Relief Mission had set up beneath the portico of the Royal Exchange.

Inside the great domed rotunda of the Stock Exchange, where once the roar of the jobbers had shaken the plaster whenever a gun was fired on the Indus, forty old men in black mourning-armbands sat around a single coke-brazier, trading fractional parcels of Welsh coal-scrip and Irish potato-warrants in whispers so low that the drip of the London rain through the unmended skylight sounded like a drum-roll on the flagstones.

No riots disturbed the streets of Westminster; the fierce, hot blood of the island had been drained away into the mud of the Hooghly and the prison-hulks of the Coral Sea, or had emigrated ten years ago on the steerage-packets to seek a five-digit collar-number in the foundries of Seattle and Nagasaki. What remained behind was an island of widows, grey-haired pensioners, and silent children in wooden clogs, walking beneath the soot-blackened monuments of Nelson and Wellington like the fifth-century Britons wandering among the cold hypocausts of Londinium after the eagles had gone back to Rome.

History had not destroyed the Atlantic; it had simply turned its back upon the cold gray ditch, and the light had gone out of the windows.

***

And where the light had gone, the stone followed.

If San Francisco had been the forge where Elias Thorne hammered the red-hot links of the circumference together, and Monterey had been the subterranean vault where Marcus Vance’s clerks counted the rivets, neither the fog-swept peninsula of California nor the earthquake-shaken islands of Japan could remain forever the ceremonial heart of an ocean that now reached from the gateway of the Red Sea to the locks of Panama. A ring of ten thousand leagues required an axle in the middle of the water.

Already, in the third year after the Settlement of 1914, the traveler whose turbine-liner raises the blue volcanic peaks of Oahu at daybreak no longer looks upon the sleepy Polynesia of the old songs, nor even upon the fortified coaling-station where Lady Kaiulani cut the telegraph cables during the Time of Troubles. He looks upon *Thalassia*—the City of the Pivot, the marble navel of the twentieth-century earth.

Where the shallow coral flats and the green taro-marshes of Waikiki and Pearl Lochs once drowsed beneath the kiawe trees, sixty thousand Cantonese stone-masons, Italian concrete-pourers, and Samoan diver-gangs are rearing a geometric Venice of white Sierra granite, black volcanic basalt, and green Japanese bronze that stretches for twelve unbroken miles from the fortress-crater of Diamond Head to the naval slips of Waipahu.

There is no coal-smoke permitted to stain the trade-wind clouds above the Sacred Emperor’s water. Thirty miles away, on the windward cliffs of Molokai and the boiling lava-slopes of Hawaii, four hundred thousand horsepower of geothermal steam-turbines and ocean-wave dynamos send their high-tension current beneath the channel through lead-armored conduits; so that as our vessel glides between the twin hundred-foot bronze lighthouses of the Honolulu Passage, the city rises out of the peacock-blue rollers without a single chimney-stack, humming only with the deep, orchestral vibration of unseen transformers and smelling of salt spray, warm ozone, and the ten thousand acres of white ginger and sandalwood terraced into the Punchbowl hills.

On the morning of the eighteenth of October, 1916, I stood beside the aging Field-Marshal Marcus Vance upon the high, unfinished basalt causeway of the *Via Triumphalis*—the two-hundred-foot ceremonial mole that runs straight across the dredged lagoon of Kalihi toward the artificial island where the Imperial Palace of the Double Horizon is rising forty courses above the tide.

Below our boots, suspended from electric gantry-cranes that spanned the canal-basins like bridges of silver lace, massive twenty-ton blocks of red Rajasthan sandstone—quarried from the demolished forts of the Mogul emperors at Agra and brought eastward as ballast in the returning tea-fleets—were being lowered into the wet Portland cement alongside columns of Californian porphyry and beams of copper-sheathed Taiwanese camphor-wood.

"They are laying the stones of Delhi into the sea-wall at twelve hundred thalers the cubic yard, Citizen-Historian," Marcus Vance said, leaning his weight upon his steel-braced left leg while the warm, scented trade-wind lifted the thin white hair beneath his plain alpaca cap. He had come out from his Presidio solarium on the autumn steamer at Lady Kaiulani’s final summons; his face was gaunt and yellow as old parchment against the blinding white glare of the coral dust, yet his pale eyes still measured the swing of the electric cranes with the old, incurable calculation. "With the concrete poured into that single bastion to carry the Sacred Emperor’s lotus-pavilion, I could have lined forty miles of the Baikal tunnel or built three dreadnoughts of the *Pacifica* class."

Before I could answer the old Marshal, the rhythmic *clack-clack* of iron-shod bearer-poles echoed along the marble paving behind us, and the black-lacquered koa-wood palanquin of the Queen-Mother Kaiulani halted at the edge of the mortar-trough.

She was eighty-two now, so small and shrunken beneath her black bombazine and her white veil that she looked like a royal mummy brought up from the burial-caves of Kona to inspect the living; yet as the twenty-six-year-old Sacred Emperor Kalanimoku—tall, bronze-skinned, and magnificent in his ceremonial mantle of yellow *mamo* feathers and silver Polytechnic braid—stepped down from his electric launch to assist her, she waved his young hand aside and leaned over the side of her chair toward Marcus.

"You are still counting the coal-tons, Marcus, when the winter is over," Kaiulani whispered, her tiny, claw-like fingers pointing past the swinging block of red Indian stone toward the center of the lagoon, where four hundred graduates of the Kyoto and Berkeley academies were raising the bronze scaffolding of the Great Gnomon—the zero-meridian obelisk from which all time and longitude upon the planet were henceforth to be reckoned. "Elias built the walls of the barn with iron because the wolves were in the timber; you and I kept the roof up with numbers because the mortar was still wet. Look at my grandson’s eyes."

Marcus turned his head half an inch to look at the young Emperor Kalanimoku, who stood ten paces away beside his Japanese consort, pointing out the curve of the Samoan-arched senate-house to a group of white-robed Bengali and Virginian prefects while a flight of silver-winged patrol-hydroplanes banked overhead in the sun.

"He has Elias’s eyes, Madam," Marcus said flatly, his hand slipping by forty years’ habit toward his breast pocket where the cracked ivory slide-rule lay hidden beneath the cloth, "and he has never heard a shot fired in anger or seen a man die of the black vomit in a ditch. Within fifty years, these boys in their feather cloaks will forget that the ocean has teeth."

"That is why we are building the walls twenty feet thick out of the stones of the kings we broke, Marshal," Kaiulani answered, her dark eyes closing for an instant against the salt dazzle of the lagoon as the giant electric crane above us gave two sharp warning bells and began to lower the twenty-ton block of Agra sandstone down toward the bed of gray California lime, "so that when the boys grow soft in the sun, the sheer weight of the arch will hold them in their chairs whether they have iron in their spines or not. Now come out of the wind, Marcus. The glass is glazed in the upper dome, and I will not have the first parliament of the ocean wait while two ghosts argue over the price of cement."

***

Two hours later, when the noon sun stood directly above the bronze tip of the Great Gnomon and the geothermal sirens along the reef sounded the meridian chord, the bearers carried her palanquin up the spiral ramp into the Whispering Gallery of the Crystal Palace.

From her cushioned seat behind the pierced screen of gilded Japanese cedar, eighty feet above the inlaid basalt floor, Lady Kaiulani looked down through the blue-tinted prism of the dome upon the finished harvest of her eighty years.

No stone wall shut this chamber from the element that had given it birth. Supported by sixteen monumental ribs of cast Pittsburgh duralumin curved in the high, sweeping parabola of a Samoan council-house, the vault of three-inch Jena glass rose two hundred feet into the tropical sky, cooled by forty noiseless water-curtains of chilled mountain rain that sheeted down the exterior panes and turned the equatorial glare into a cool, submarine twilight of Imperial Blue and pale emerald.

Below her, ranged in five concentric amphitheaters of red Hawaiian koa-wood around the central porphyry rostrum, sat the six hundred Conscript Fathers of the First Pan-Pacific Senate.

They had not been chosen by the brawling ballot-boxes that Elias Thorne had burned at Sacramento in fifty-four, nor were they the rough, mud-stained camp-commanders who had drawn their sabers around his coffin on Rincon Hill. Each of the Hundred and Thirty Cantons—from the fog-bound timber-wards of Massachusetts and the sheep-downs of Victoria to the steaming jute-deltas of Bengal and the copper-mines of the Amur—had sent up four representatives: two Elder Assessors elected for life by the provincial chambers of commerce and agriculture, and two Senior Prefects of the First Class who had stood for thirty years without a blot upon the Hollerith ledgers of the Bureau of Integration.

As the fragrance of burning Mysore sandalwood and fresh white ginger-blossoms drifted upward on the conditioned draft to meet the faint, omnipresent tang of transformer-ozone, Kaiulani rested her chin upon her withered, ivory-ringed fingers and watched the floor.

*Here is the cage I promised myself on the morning the* Oregon *broke the reef,* she thought, her old heart beating with a slow, thin flutter against her black bombazine ribs while down on the rostrum the Grand Herald of the Chancery struck the floor three times with a staff—not Elias’s rough iron stick, which lay four miles deep in the Marianas mud, but a ceremonial rod of braided whalebone and Damascus steel. *For sixty years we have ruled this basin by the telegraph-warrant and the provost’s carbine, and the first time the hand on the wire went cold, the continent tore itself open from Ballarat to the Donner snow-sheds. No bayonet can hold four hundred million men forever. If the House of Thorne-Kamehameha is to outlast my breath, the provinces must have a temple where their grey-beards can bring their petitions, count the silver in the daylight, and believe that the law is their own work.*

Down in the third tier of the southern arc, the Senior Senator for the Eighty-Second Canton—a broad-shouldered, white-bearded pastoralist from Melbourne named MacArthur, whose father had lost an arm fighting Prince Kalakaua’s marines at Sydney Heads in eighty-seven, yet who now wore the blue silk sash of the Imperial Wool Board over his grey colonial broadcloth—rose in his place as the Herald called the first order of the Ways and Means.

"If it please the Throne and the Conscript Prefects," MacArthur’s deep, gravelly bush-voice rang out, amplified without distortion by the parabolic bronze acoustic-shells built into the duralumin ribs above the dais. "Before the Senate ratifies the quinquennial grain-and-coal assessment for the Ural railway extensions, the delegates of the six Australian and New Zealand cantons lay upon the table a Bill of Right regarding the local appointment of harbor-magistrates. For twenty-nine years since the Pacification, every customs-assessor at Melbourne and Auckland has been sent out from the Berkeley or New Edo sheds without asking the warranty of our provincial guild-councils. Now that the British flag is down at Calcutta and the peace of the ocean is perpetual, we ask that the Constitutional Statute of Nineteen-Sixteen be amended: namely, that no fiscal levy exceeding ten million silver thalers shall pass into law without a two-thirds division of this floor, and that the local guilds shall submit three names from their own blood for every vacant prefecture!"

Along the upper benches of the American and Cantonese tiers, a low, approving murmur ran through the koa-wood stalls; two merchants from the Shanghai tea-syndicate and a grey-haired iron-master from the Pittsburg valley leaned forward, their hands rising toward the brass voting-levers on their desks.

Behind the cedar lattice in the gallery, Kaiulani’s shrunken fingers tightened upon the arm of her palanquin. *Let them debate it,* she urged silently, her eyes darting across the gulf toward the imperial tribune opposite, where young Emperor Kalanimoku sat beneath his canopy of yellow *mamo* feathers. *Give them the harbor-clerks in Melbourne, Kalanimoku. Let the old sheep-man go home to Victoria and tell his sons that his voice moved the needle in Thalassia. That is how Augustus bound the Roman provinces when the legions grew tired—by letting the conquered wear the toga and vote the salt-tax.*

***

To the Chronicler who sat four benches below the Queen-Mother’s screen in the gallery reserved for the Historiographers of the Academy, the rising of the Australian senator beneath that soaring canopy of glass and duralumin seemed, for the space of five minutes, the very consummation of human history.

Even before a single vote had been recorded upon the electric tally-boards, the building itself spoke a language that neither Pericles nor the builders of the Forbidden City had possessed the vocabulary to imagine.

Our scholars in the Berkeley aesthetics schools have called this the *Thalassian Style*—that late, ripe blossom of Imperial Syncretism which reached its perfection between the opening of the Panama Locks and the partition of India. In the early decades of the Protectorate, when Elias Thorne was still alive to growl at architects’ bills, the fusion of the shores had been an awkward, military marriage of convenience: an American brick custom-house with a tiled Chinese roof nailed over the rafters, or a Christian garrison-chapel with a wooden Shinto *torii* standing before the porch like a captured trophy.

Here in the Senate House of Thalassia, the seams had vanished into the metal.

Look where one might around the vast, sun-filtered rotunda, no eye could separate the East from the West, or the island from the continent. The sixteen colossal ribs of the vault were cast from Pennsylvania and Hanyang steel, yet their structural cross-bracing followed the intricate, earthquake-defying *kigumi* joinery of the Nara temples without a single visible rivet-head, while their bases rested upon octagonal plinths of black Oahu basalt carved with the spiral *koru* reliefs of the Maori navigation-schools. Above the main rostrum, where in a European parliament would have hung a painted canvas of kings or battles, rose a forty-foot mosaic executed in crushed Mexican turquoise, sunset-gold leaf, and mother-of-pearl from the Arafura Sea: it showed neither Christ nor Amaterasu nor George Washington, but the *Sacred Compass of the Pivot*—a blazing golden sun rising out of the centre of the Pacific water while the four winds, wearing the bronze faces of the Polynesian, the Mongol, the Anglo-Saxon, and the Hindoo, poured the rivers of the four continents into a single crystal bowl.

Even the dress and speech of the six hundred men upon the koa-wood benches below bore witness to the melting of the old world’s coins in Elias’s crucible.

Senator MacArthur of Melbourne had spoken in English, yet it was no longer the nasal colonial dialect that his grandfather had brought out from Yorkshire; his sentences were measured by the crisp, mathematical syntax of the Monterey primers, and when he spoke of the customs-levy, he used without embarrassment the Sino-Japanese fiscal terms—*lijin*, *koku-unit*, and *kapu-warrant*—that had been the legal tender of the sea for forty years. Across his grey broadcloth chest, the Australian wore a collar of woven Samoan hibiscus-fiber dyed Imperial Blue and fastened with a clasp of Klondike gold; beside him, the Senior Prefect from the Kyoto silk-wards wore Boston-cut trousers of dark navy wool beneath a short, stiff *haori* jacket embroidered with the five-digit silver cipher of the Polytechnic Corps.

The very air they breathed was an artifact of the unified globe: chilled by ammonia-compressors forged in Osaka, scented with the bruised sandalwood of conquered Mysore, and humming with the steady sixty-cycle pulse of the Molokai lava-turbines.

To a young cadet looking down from the doorway, it appeared that the long tragedy of the human races was ended—that the frontiersman’s rifle and the samurai’s sword had indeed been beaten into a mighty, translucent greenhouse wherein all the tribes of the Great Arena might sit in eternal, well-ventilated harmony to regulate the price of rice and copper.

Yet up behind the gilded cedar screen of the Whispering Gallery, an eighty-two-year-old woman who had seen the foundation-trenches dug in blood was not looking at the turquoise mosaic on the wall.

***

Lady Kaiulani was looking at her grandson’s right hand.

Across the rotunda, beneath the flaring crimson-and-yellow feather canopy of the Imperial Tribune, the twenty-six-year-old Sacred Emperor Kalanimoku had not inclined his head in the prescribed constitutional nod to signify that the Australian senator’s bill was admitted to the floor.

He sat very straight upon the curule chair of cast bronze and whale-ivory, his broad, island-born shoulders draped in the heavy mantle of *mamo* feathers that three generations of Hawaiian bird-catchers had died in the mountain rain to gather for her dead brother’s line. Beside him sat his consort, the Lady Chiyo of Kyoto, her face painted white and motionless as a porcelain Noh mask, her small hands hidden within her silver-brocade sleeves; and two steps below the feather footstool stood Fleet-General Kuroda the younger, his thumb resting lightly upon the duralumin hilt of his staff-sword.

When Senator MacArthur finished speaking and sat down upon the Melbourne bench, a hush fell over the six hundred stalls. By the *Organic Charter of the Senate*—which Kaiulani herself had drafted with Rector Norton’s clerks during the winter after Rangoon—the Chancellor of the Floor should now have called upon the Fiscal Assessor of the Treasury to reply with the balance-sheets, leaving the Sacred Emperor above the battle like the sun above the clouds.

Instead, Kalanimoku lifted his right hand from the ivory armrest.

He wore no iron walking-stick at his knee; he held a slender, twelve-inch baton of polished duralumin wired directly to the electric annunciator-board above the rostrum. And as his pale gray eyes—Elias Thorne’s cold, unblinking Kentucky eyes, set like two chips of glacier-ice inside the warm brown velvet of his Polynesian face—looked down across the blue twilight at the white-bearded Australian, the young man did not smile.

He pressed the button in the butt of his baton once.

Instantly, with a sharp, metallic *clack* that echoed through the glass vault like the cocking of a giant rifle, the great red semaphore-arm above the rostrum dropped across Senator MacArthur’s canton-number, cutting the current to the acoustic microphones on the southern benches.

Kalanimoku did not wait for the Herald. He rose to his full height of six feet two inches beneath the feather canopy, the sunset gold of his cloak spilling over the porphyry steps, and spoke into the golden amplifier at his breast. His voice was not the high, chanting cadence of the island chiefs, nor the dry academic Latinity of the Berkeley sheds; he had practiced in secret before the phonograph-cylinders in the Monterey archives until he had caught the exact, gravelly, short-breathed bark of the grandfather he had never seen.

"The Eighty-Second Canton is four thousand tons in arrears upon its autumn tallow-and-mutton delivery to the Manila fleet-freezers," Kalanimoku said, the amplified iron of his twenty-six-year-old voice rolling down from the sixteen bronze horns in the ceiling until the chilled water-curtains on the glass panes trembled. "When my grandfather took Sydney into the peace of the Ocean, he did not ask the sheep-graziers of Victoria whom he should send to weigh their wool. He sent men with numbers on their collars who could not be bribed with colonial claret."

Down on the southern tier, old MacArthur half-rose from his koa-wood desk, his weathered face flushing dark crimson above his blue sash. "Majesty! By the Charter of the Settlement of Nineteen-Fourteen, a Bill of Right presented by six cantons cannot be struck from the order-book by the Chair without a division of the Conscript Fathers!"

Up behind the cedar screen, Kaiulani leaned forward so sharply that the whale-ivory clasp at her throat struck the lattice with a dry *tap*. Beside her palanquin, old Field-Marshal Marcus Vance did not move; he stood leaning on his steel leg-brace in the shadow of the curtain, his pale eyes fixed not on the Emperor, but upon the four galleries above the entrance-doors, where eighty young cadets of the Palace Guard—boys wearing the new gold-and-crimson shoulder-cords of the *Emperor’s Own Household Regiment*—had quietly stepped up to the brass rails with their hands on their pistol-holsters.

"Look at the floor, Madam," Marcus murmured under his breath, so low that only Kaiulani heard him above the hum of the air-ducts.

Kaiulani looked down at the five concentric rings of koa-wood desks.

The two Shanghai tea-merchants and the Pittsburg iron-master who had raised their hands to second MacArthur’s motion three minutes before were not reaching for their voting-levers now. Slowly, as their eyes traveled upward from the tall figure in the yellow feather cloak to the four machine-gun apertures concealed behind the bronze wind-gods of the mosaic—and then sideways toward Fleet-General Kuroda’s cropped head below the dais—their hands dropped back into their laps.

Across the central aisle, Prefect-Senator Shen the third—grandson of the old auditor, representing the First Metropolitan Canton of San Francisco—rose smoothly in his black alpaca robe and bowed until his forehead touched the brass rail of his desk.

"The First Canton moves that the petition of the Australian delegates be referred without debate to the Imperial Household Chancellery for ten-year archival review," young Shen said in his oiled, faultless voice, "and that this Senate proceed immediately to ratify by acclamation the Sacred Emperor’s warrant for the construction of the four new dreadnoughts of the *Kalanimoku* class at Yokosuka, Together with a special benevolence of forty million silver thalers to be placed at His Majesty’s personal disposal for the fortification of the Persian Gulf."

"Second the motion!" barked thirty voices at once from the Satsuma, Choshu, and Californian military benches—men whose sons held commissions in Kuroda’s new Western Fleets and whose canton-assessments had been quietly halved by the Palace Secretariat the night before.

Kalanimoku did not ask for the nays. With a single downward sweep of his duralumin baton, he closed the master-circuit on his armrest. Around the circular wall, five hundred and eighty green electric bulbs flashed on simultaneously beside the canton-numbers; only the twenty-four lamps of the Australian and New England benches remained dark.

"The benevolence is voted without division," Kalanimoku said, sitting back down upon the bronze curule chair and pulling the yellow feather cloak across his knees with the exact, heavy-shouldered movement that Elias Thorne had used when wrapping his Mexican blanket around his swollen ankles in the redwoods thirty-five years ago. "Let the Melbourne delegates take notice: the Senate is assembled to register the harmony of the circumference, not to haggle over the gauge of the track. The Chancellery will appoint the Sydney harbor-masters at six."

Behind the cedar screen in the Whispering Gallery, the air smelled suddenly suffocating to Kaiulani—no longer of fresh mountain rain and white ginger, but of cold mutton-tallow, burned stramonium, and the damp, airless concrete of a tomb.

She had buried Elias Thorne’s copper-plated corpse four miles deep in the Marianas Trench so that no man could rule by his dead bones; she had mixed the blood of Oahu and Kyoto with his frontier clay to soften the iron; she had built a palace of crystal in the middle of the warm sea and called six hundred elders from the four corners of the earth to make a law that would not need a tyrant.

And out of the womb of her own gentle cousin’s son, backed by the logarithm-wheels of the third generation, the Kentucky wolf had simply climbed back onto the chair in a cloak of island feathers.

These six hundred men in their silk sashes and alpaca robes were not a parliament; they were a chorus of frightened clerks hired to clap their hands in unison whenever the great bronze machine in the center of the ocean required another forty million thalers of coal and blood to grind its way from the Persian Gulf to the Cape of Good Hope.

"Take me down from this bird-cage, Marcus," Kaiulani whispered, her tiny, eighty-two-year-old hand reaching out blindly through the cedar gloom to catch the sleeve of the retired Marshal’s plain alpaca coat as the six hundred senators below rose to their feet and began to chant the three-part Polynesian-Latin hymn of the *Pax Pacifica* while the great pipe-organ in the dome thundered out the brassy chords of the Imperial Anthem.

Marcus Vance laid his square, age-spotted fingers over her cold knuckles upon the palanquin rail, though he did not signal the Hawaiian bearers to lift the poles.

"There is nowhere left to go down to, Your Highness," the old general said quietly, looking through the diamond-shaped openings of the lattice at the tall, gray-eyed youth on the throne below, who was already leaning over the side of the dais to trace with Fleet-General Kuroda’s steel dividers the red line of the Suez and Cape railway concessions across the map of Africa while the Senate sang, "for the land is only the wharf now, and the wharf belongs to the water."

***

To understand the literal truth of the old Marshal’s words, the Chronicler needed only to walk three miles westward from the crystal dome of the Senate that same afternoon, along the broad basalt causeway of the *Via Triumphalis*, to the inner basins of the Pearl Lochs Imperial Dockyard.

In the ancient empires of the continent—in the Rome of the Antonines or the China of the Ming—the ultimate measure of sovereignty had always been the road and the wall: the paved military highway down which the foot-soldier marched with his pike, and the masonry rampart behind which the tax-collector sat safe from the nomads of the steppe. Even in the first generation of our own Protectorate, when Elias Thorne and the elder Vance were spiking the six-foot gauge across the alkali deserts of Nevada and the frozen birch-forests of the Yenisei, the sea had been regarded merely as a salt ditch to be bridged by steam-packets so that one railway terminal might feed another.

Here at Thalassia, in the autumn of 1916, the element had swallowed the road.

As I stood upon the upper observation gallery of Dry-Dock Number Four—a cyclopean trough of poured California concrete fifteen hundred feet long and two hundred feet deep, hewn straight out of the ancient coral limestone of Waipahu—the land upon which I planted my boots felt like a fragile, temporary raft moored beside the real architecture of the state.

Below me, riding in forty feet of oiled, emerald-green harbor water along the three-mile curve of the Battleship Quay, lay the First Battle Division of the *Thorne*-class super-dreadnoughts: the *Providentor*, the *Golden Gate*, the *Sakurajima*, and the newly commissioned flagship *Thalassia*.

They bore no more resemblance to the low, monitors-hulled ironclads that had battered the forts of Vladivostok than a cathedral bears to a frontier blockhouse. Each of those four hulls displaced sixty-four thousand tons of Krupp cemented nickel-steel, painted the dark, pitiless Imperial Blue that turned almost black in the shadow of the cranes, with a gilded bronze sun-and-anchor thirty feet wide bolted across the flared clipper bow. They carried no coal-bunkers; deep beneath their triple-layered torpedo-blisters, twelve high-pressure Yarrow boilers fired by atomized Borneo and Persian petroleum fed ninety thousand horsepower to four geared Parsons steam-turbines, capable of driving that mountain of armor through a typhoon swell at twenty-eight knots for twelve thousand miles without once dropping anchor at a shore depot.

Along the eight-hundred-foot flush deck of the *Thalassia*, rising in four superimposed tiers fore and aft of the massive tripod lattice-masts, sat the true legislators of the Hundred and Thirty Cantons: sixteen twenty-two-inch breech-loading rifles housed in four quadruple turrets of eighteen-inch hardened steel.

As the four-o’clock dockyard bell sounded across the lagoon, the hydraulic testing-pumps inside the flagship’s barbettes began their afternoon calibration. Without a single sailor appearing upon the scorching teak planks of the deck, the four forward turrets—each weighing three thousand tons, the weight of an entire regiment of artillery with its horses and caissons—swung forty-five degrees to port with a low, greased, subterranean hum that vibrated through the basalt quay wall, while the sixty-foot steel barrels elevated in unison toward the western clouds.

The air above the basin did not smell of the land. Though the green volcanic peaks of the Koolau range rose only five miles behind the machine-shops, the trade-wind across the docks carried exclusively the hot, greasy breath of refined fuel-oil, the sharp metallic bite of red-lead paint baking on five-inch deck-plate, and the omnipresent blue ozone of the two-hundred-ton electric gantry-cranes that moved back and forth along the coping like iron spiders, lowering thirty-ton crates of frozen Melbourne mutton and Hanyang cordite straight into the armored bowels of the fleet.

A shore garrison could mutiny, as Colonel Armistead’s Virginians had done in eighty-seven; a railway track could be torn up in a night by three hundred starving miners with crowbars and blasting-gelatine. But a sixty-four-thousand-ton floating fortress whose freshwater condensers distilled five hundred tons of drinking water a day from the brine, whose refrigerating-vaults held six months of meat, and whose twenty-two-inch guns could drop a three-thousand-pound high-capacity picric shell onto a city hall twenty-four miles inland from the five-fathom line required neither the love nor the consent of the earth.

The continent had become merely a quarry to dig the ore and a plantation to press the oil; the throne of humanity floated upon sixty feet of salt water, and any province from Boston to Calcutta that displeased the five-digit ciphers in the conning-tower could be starved into the twelfth century or blown into red brick-dust before its militia could march within sight of the surf.

***

Late that night, when the electric gantry-cranes down at the Waipahu basins had finally ceased their rhythmic clanking and only the green and red riding-lights of the sixty-four-thousand-ton dreadnoughts glimmered across the five miles of dark water like a second, geometric constellation fallen into the lagoon, Lady Kaiulani sat alone upon the high seaward balcony of the Coral Pavilion.

She had dismissed her Oahu tire-women and forbidden even old Marcus Vance to follow her through the sliding doors of Hawaiian koa-wood. Wrapped to the chin in a heavy mantle of black silk and gray sea-otter fur—for at eighty-two the blood in her veins ran so thin and slow that even the warm October trade-wind of her childhood felt to her like the draft from the Donner snow-sheds—she rested her withered hands upon the broad volcanic basalt of the parapet and looked up at the sky.

Above the black, saw-toothed silhouette of the Waianae mountains, where no electric arc-lamp had yet been bolted to the rock, hung the ancient stars of the Polynesian navigators: *Hokulea*, the Star of Gladness, and the long, tilting diamond of the Southern Cross dipping low toward the Line.

Sixty years ago, before the *Oregon* had ever stained the reef with coal-soot, her grandfather’s canoe-steersmen had read those fires without a sextant or a logarithm table, guiding their double-hulled koa dugouts across two thousand miles of empty blue swell from Tahiti to Hawaii by the warmth of the current against their dip-nets and the angle of the constellations above the masthead. In those days, the ocean had possessed a rim. A chief sailed until he found an island where the taro grew sweet in the black mud and the reef kept the sharks from the bathing-pool; and there he drove his ridge-pole into the earth and called his boundaries good.

Now, as Kaiulani lowered her gaze half an inch from the Southern Cross, two vertical beams of ten-million-candlepower carbon searchlight—mounted upon the fore-top of the super-dreadnought *Providentor* three miles out in the roadstead—swept slowly across the underside of the trade-wind clouds, wiping the ancient stars out of the heavens in a white, chalky glare while the high-frequency spark-transmitters atop the Great Gnomon crackled with a continuous, violet hiss, relaying the midnight tallies from the newly conquered customs-sheds of Madras and Colombo.

*Will it ever be enough for them, Elias?* she asked the dark water, her small, shrunken chin sinking down upon the whale-ivory hook at her throat as the night breeze brought up from the harbor not the scent of the bruised night-blooming jasmine in the palace courts below, but the faint, greasy tang of hot Borneo bunker-oil from the fleet.

She knew the answer before the wind died against the stone. She had heard it that very afternoon in the crystal dome when her grandson Kalanimoku had struck the Melbourne petition from the table; she had seen it in the cold, unblinking eyes of Fleet-General Kuroda as his steel dividers walked across the map from the mouths of the Indus toward the red sands of Aden and the silver mines of the Transvaal.

When Elias Thorne had ridden into Sacramento in fifty-two, he had sworn that the Sierra Nevada was wall enough to keep his house safe from the eastern bailiffs. Then the wall had required the sea-coast to feed the forts; and the sea-coast had required the islands to coal the cruisers; and the islands had required the rivers of China and the sheep-downs of Australia to pay the interest on the ironworks; and the ironworks had required the three hundred million souls of India to consume the surplus steel of the rolling-mills.

Now the circumference stood at the Bab-el-Mandeb and the Ural crests, and already the young men with the five-digit silver numerals on their collars were complaining in the Chancellery corridors that the German tariffs on the Rhine and the petty wars of the French generals along the Seine were disturbing the price of Pacifica nitrates at Antwerp.

An empire built upon the steam-piston and the clearing-house had no skin to hold it in; unlike a living tree that stops growing when its crown reaches the light of the forest, this monster of cast bronze and numbered clerks could only keep its balance by falling forward into the next continent. Tomorrow Kalanimoku and Kuroda would take the Suez ditch and the gold-reefs of Africa to protect the Indian tea-ships; ten years hence, when her bones were dust in the Kona caves, they would steam through the Pillars of Hercules and turn the Mediterranean into a numbered barge-canal; and when they had ground London and Berlin and Paris into the same grey, sanitary mortar as Hankow and Boston, when there was not a single unnumbered village or unmeasured bushel of wheat left between the rising and the setting of the sun—what would the machine eat then, except its own iron bowels?

A cold spasm of coughing shook her tiny frame beneath the sea-otter fur. She did not ring the silver bell on the table behind her. Gripping the rough basalt of the rail until her ivory rings clicked against the stone, the last Queen of the Islands stared out into the blinding white sweep of the battleship searchlights, watching the empty sky where the stars had been.

***

Yet if the aged Queen-Mother upon her Hawaiian terrace trembled before the specter of an infinite, all-devouring order, the Chronicler who crossed the Atlantic protectorates three months later—accompanying the Third Diplomatic Mission sent out by Emperor Kalanimoku in the winter of 1917 to inspect the defaulted European grain-mortgages—soon discovered that the opposite end of history’s balance-beam offered a spectacle far more hideous.

For as the Pacific basin had consolidated over sixty years into a single, blinding sun of regulated bronze and hydroelectric power, the old peninsula of Western Europe, stripped of its oceanic colonies, cut off from the rubber of Malaya, the oil of Sumatra, and the silver of the Americas, had not sunk everywhere into the quiet, widow-like senility that I had witnessed along the rotting docks of London.

On the continent across the Channel, the starvation of the body had bred the delirium of the brain.

When our armored sleeping-car—hauled from the Pacifica leasehold-wharf at Havre behind an old, coal-burning French locomotive whose leaky brass flues showered the frosty Normandy hedgerows with cinders—rolled into the Gare Saint-Lazare in Paris on the afternoon of the nineteenth of January, 1917, we stepped down into a capital that smelled of horse-dung, wet charcoal-smoke, unwashed sheepskin, and the sour, unmistakable stench of a nineteenth-century siege.
