No sixty-cycle electric turbines hummed beneath these streets. Because the German Syndicates had seized the Saar coal-fields during the Tariff War of nineteen-twelve, and the British colliers could no longer spare a ton of Cardiff steam-coal across the water, the great boulevards that Baron Haussmann had carved through the stone of Paris sixty years ago lay in a perpetual, freezing twilight. The bronze gas-standards along the Rue de Rivoli had been stripped of their mantles; in their place, at every third cross-street, squads of frostbitten boys in tall, brass-fronted shakoes and sky-blue greatcoats tended open iron braziers of smoking peat and split boulevard-chestnuts.

Yet it was not poverty alone that struck the observer from the Great Arena as our carriage rattled over the broken wood-paving of the Place de la Concorde under an escort of twelve cuirassiers whose horses showed every rib beneath their tarnished steel breastplates. It was the frantic, theatrical ghosts that these starving Europeans had summoned out of their grandfathers’ closets to warm their hands.

The Third Republic had perished five winters ago in the bread-riots following the collapse of the Suez Canal shares. In its stead—ruling over a shrunken, bankrupt France whose southern departments around Marseilles and Lyons had already seceded under an autonomous *Commune of the Rhone* financed by smuggled Pacifica silver—reigned the *Fourth Plebiscitary Empire* of Marshal-Protector Jean-Baptiste Victor, a former colonial brigadier from Algiers who had married a grand-niece of the house of Murat and now styled himself *Regent of the Eagle*.

Every crumbling limestone facade along the Rue Royale, where the plate-glass windows of the dead luxury-shops were boarded up with rough deal planks, was plastered ten feet high with wet, screaming lithographs in red, white, and blue ink, showing the spiked helmet of the German Kaiser and the golden sun-and-anchor of Pacifica being trampled beneath the hooves of a white Marengo charger, above the legend: *YEAR V OF THE NATIONAL REVANCHE—IRON FOR BREAD, BLOOD FOR GLORY!*

"You see, Citizen-Historian, what happens to a house when the roof-beam is sawed through and the tenants are left to stew in their own sour wine," observed Prefect-Legate Shen the third, sitting opposite me upon the faded crimson velvet cushions of our hired landau with a fur muff drawn up to his chin and his horn-rimmed spectacles misted by the raw Seine fog. Through the cracked window-glass, we watched a column of three hundred French conscripts—boys of sixteen and grey-beards of fifty wearing the red trousers of eighteen-seventy and carrying obsolete single-shot Gras rifles with twenty-inch triangular bayonets—tramping through the slush behind a deafening battery of twenty brass drums and brazen bugles. "They have no Borneo benzine for an aeroplane; their treasury-francs sell at forty-two to the silver thaler in the Zurich alleys; and yet they spend their last three百 tons of foundry-brass casting eagles for their hats and marching up and down the cobbles to keep from freezing."

Before I could reply, our carriage swung through the gilded iron gates of the Cour du Carrousel at the Tuileries—rebuilt in cheap, flaking stucco over the burned stones of seventy-one—and pulled up before the Grand Staircase.

Inside the Salle des Maréchaux, where the cold draft from the river rattled the painted canvas ceilings and the only heat came from four huge porcelain stoves stuffed with green poplar logs that wept black creosote down the marble pilasters, the court of the new Bonaparte stood assembled to receive the creditors of the earth.

There were two hundred of them packed between the peeling gold caryatids: marshals in high jackboots and white buckskin breeches stained with stable-mud; frantic-eyed journalists and poets of the *Ligue de la Patrie* wearing tri-color sashes over their frayed evening-coats; and bony-shouldered duchesses of the Faubourg whose diamonds had long since gone into the vaults of the Market Street Mint, leaving only paste tiaras and dyed ostrich-plumes trembling above their rouged, hungry cheeks. At the head of the room, upon a gilded pine platform draped in crimson cotton velvet, stood Marshal-Protector Victor himself—a short, bull-necked man of sixty with waxed mustaches dyed jet-black, his chest entirely covered from collarbone to

belt with enameled tin crosses of the Legion of Honor, his left hand resting upon the guard of a curved Mameluke saber while his right remained thrust inside the breast of his green general’s coat in slavish imitation of the Corsican.

"The Legate of the Pacifica Chancellery will approach the Eagle!" bawled the Grand Chamberlain, striking the parquet with an ebony staff tipped with a gilded lead bird.

Prefect Shen did not remove his fur gloves, nor did he bow from the waist as the European ambassadors had bowed before Elias Thorne on Rincon Hill thirty-six years ago. Walking at his measured, unhurried Berkeley pace across the cold floor in his plain, high-collared tunic of dark slate-gray wool with the silver cipher *Zero-One-Zero-Two* gleaming at his throat, Shen halted six paces from the pine dais and drew a single folded sheet of blue Monterey bond from his leather portfolio.

"To the Provisional Magistrate of the Seine Municipalities," Shen began in his flat, nasal French, deliberately omitting every imperial title while a furious, hissing murmur ran through the crowd of plumed marshals around the stoves and Protector Victor’s fleshy jowls turned the color of raw beef-liver above his gold collar. "The Bureau of Integration at Thalassia acknowledges receipt of your December memorandum requesting a further moratorium upon the eighty million silver thalers advanced by the Osaka and San Francisco syndicates during the famine of nineteen-fourteen, together with your application for the purchase of four hundred thousand barrels of California mess-pork and twenty thousand tons of Chile saltpeter against ten-year bonds of the French Customs."

Protector Victor took half a step forward to the edge of the pine platform, his hand coming out of his waistcoat to slap the hilt of his curved saber with a loud metallic *clack*.

"France does not beg for pork like a coolie canton, Monsieur l'Assesseur!" Victor roared, throwing his head back so that the gallery of journalists behind the pillars might catch the full Napoleonic thunder of his voice. "The sword of Austerlitz and Jena holds the balance of the Rhine! If the German Emperor marches into Belgium this spring to seize the Antwerp docks, who stands between your merchant-hulks and the Prussian artillery? Five hundred thousand French bayonets! We offer the Grand Confederation an alliance of equals—the Grand Army of the Continent and the Fleet of the Ocean—provided the nitrate-ships unload at Brest before the first of March without prior hypothecation of our state railways!"

Shen did not blink behind his spectacles; he simply turned the blue sheet over between his gloved fingers.

"The Bureau of Integration has no interest in whether the German customs-guards or your own occupy the mud-flats of Belgium, Magistrate," Shen said, his quiet voice cutting cleanly across the theatrical echo of the vault as two young Polytechnic naval lieutenants behind me stepped forward with a brass tripod-case, "and a bayonet is worth precisely four cents in scrap-steel at the Hanyang furnaces. As for your state railways from Havre to Dijon, they were forfeited to the Market Street Clearing House at midnight on the first of January for non-payment of the rolling-stock annuities. If a single barrel of Chile saltpeter is unloaded at Brest before our receivers take possession of the roundhouses, the cruiser squadron at Cherbourg will shell the custom-house into the harbor."

***

While Prefect Shen was locking the bailiff’s padlock upon the rusted gates of Paris, a far more dangerous chemistry was brewing five hundred miles to the east, in the soot-darkened winter twilight of Berlin.

Against the prayers of her physicians—who warned her that the frost of the North German plain would stop an eighty-two-year-old heart that had beaten all its life among the hibiscus and the redwoods—the Queen-Mother Kaiulani had come across the continent from Genoa in the heated observation-car of the Imperial Chancery train. She had not come to collect debts; she had come because her own secret agents in the Warsaw and Moscow telegraph-sheds had warned her that the two wounded giants of the Eurasian heartland, stripped of their oceans by Elias Thorne’s iron ring, had finally turned back to back in the snow.

On the afternoon of the twenty-fourth of January, inside the gloomy, brown-varnished Congress Hall of the Reichskanzlei on the Wilhelmstrasse, the air smelled of wet military broadcloth, synthetic coal-tar benzine, and the harsh, coarse Makhorka tobacco of the Omsk steppes.

Kaiulani sat in her wheeled koa-wood chair beside the roaring porcelain stove, wrapped to her white braids in double cloaks of sea-otter fur, her tiny, obsidian eyes looking across the green baize table at the two men who held three hundred million white peasants under their boots: Chancellor von Bethmann’s successor, Field-Marshal von Mackensen of the German Syndicates, wearing the black-and-silver skull busby of the Death’s Head Hussars upon his bony knee; and beside him, buttoned to the chin in a long, grease-stained Cossack caftan of grey camel’s-hair, Generalissimo Brusilov of the Directory of All the Russias—that grim, xenophobic military dictatorship which had risen out of the ashes of the eighty-seven revolution after Elias Thorne locked the Siberian gates at the Obi.

"Your Imperial Highness has traveled six thousand leagues through the winter to offer us the crumbs from your grandson’s table," Marshal von Mackensen said, his voice a dry, metallic rasp as his gloved finger pushed Kaiulani’s draft treaty—offering a twenty-percent reduction on Malaysian rubber duties and five million bushels of Manchurian soy-beans—back across the green baize. "For thirty years, ever since the old bandit in San Francisco cut Russia off from the Pacific and closed the China seas to German keels, you have treated the two greatest military empires of the white race like bankrupt tenants in an alley. Our Krupp furnaces at Essen have iron ore, Madam, and General Brusilov’s Directory from Moscow to the Urals has twelve million marching men who do not need a five-digit collar-tag to carry a rifle."

"And you have neither copper for your shell-casings nor nitrates for your smokeless powder, Marshal," Kaiulani replied in her thin, musical whisper, not touching the rejected parchment. Under the sea-otter fur, her withered fingers gripped the whale-ivory hook at her throat; she felt as if she were sitting in a powder-magazine while two blind men struck flints over an open keg. "Because your banks cannot pay silver in Market Street, you have signed the Pact of Breslau with the Moscow Directory to pool your coal and your conscripts. You think that by marching west across the Rhine this spring to plunder the French railways and seize the Antwerp docks, you will break out of the box Elias Thorne built around you."

Generalissimo Brusilov leaned his broad, bearded face toward the lamp, the old shrapnel-scar from the Yenisei winter campaign gleaming white across his cheekbone. "When a wolf is walled up in a stone cellar, High Commissioner, he does not ask the mason’s permission before he eats the sheep in the next stall. You took the Amur and the Baikal mines from us when the Tsar fell; you took the oceans from the Germans. Europe is all that is left on the board. If Thalassia wishes peace on the Atlantic seaboard, lift the blockade on the Silesian munition-trusts and return the Vladivostok railway to Moscow before the thaw!"

"Return a single verst of the Siberian gauge, General, and Fleet-General Kuroda’s thirty air-cruisers at Irkutsk will turn every timber-town between the Obi and the Volga into a pillar of white phosphorus before Easter," Kaiulani said, her small chin rising an inch from the fur collar with a flash of the old Honolulu pride. "I did not come to Berlin in my winding-sheet to bargain away the Providentor’s border-stones. I came to tell you what will happen if your Prussian divisions cross the Meuse to strangle this pantomime Bonaparte in Paris. You will not win a six-week promenade as Bismarck did in seventy. You have no Peruvian saltpeter; you are making your nitric acid out of the air with coal-furnaces that eat half your harvest-labor. Within six months, you and the French will be bleeding each other to death in flooded ditches from the North Sea to the Alps—and when both your armies have eaten their horses, my grandson’s young prefects at Monterey will come through the Suez canal with sixty-four-thousand-ton dreadnoughts and turn Berlin and Moscow into numbered cantons like Calcutta!"

Mackensen rose stiffly to his feet, lifting his black hussar busby from his knee while Brusilov’s heavy boot-spurs clinked together behind the table.

"Then let your grandson’s clerks bring their slide-rules to the Rhine, Madam," the Prussian said coldly, bowing from the neck as the double doors at the end of the hall were thrown open by two giant Pomeranian grenadiers. "It is better to die in the iron than to rot in a coolie-shed paying sixty-percent tribute on a pound of Java coffee. The mobilization telemetry for the Western Army Group was transmitted to Cologne twenty minutes before your train crossed the Spree."

***

To the Chronicler who fled westward out of Germany aboard the last diplomatic special permitted to pass the frontier bridge at Herbesthal on the night of the third of February, 1917, the bursting of the European dam did not resemble the clean, mathematical slaughter that we had witnessed from the conning-tower of the *Pacifica* in the Bay of Bengal.

In the Great Arena, war had become a branch of municipal engineering—a silent, twenty-mile-distant calculation of oil-pressure and gyroscopic angles conducted by beardless youths who smelled of soap and ozone. Here in the narrow, over-populated cockpit of the old continent, where three hundred million starving, pride-maddened Europeans had been penned behind Elias Thorne’s tariff-walls for half a century without an outlet to the sea, war returned as a mediaeval plague armed with the cast-offs of the machine age.

At four o’clock on the freezing, sleet-lashed morning of the fourth of February, our train was shunted onto a high stone viaduct overlooking the gorge of the Meuse three miles below Liège, while the Belgian customs-guards tore up the track ahead of us with crowbars.

Down in the pitch-black valley below our carriage windows, the air smelled of wet coal-slag, burning beet-sugar factories, and the rank, ammoniacal reek of forty thousand Russian and Prussian draft-horses churning the frozen turnip-fields into mud. There were no searchlights sweeping the clouds from sixty-four-thousand-ton ships; there were no duralumin air-cruisers hovering at five thousand feet to correct the fire by wireless.

Instead, across five miles of river-mist, the night split open with the low, continuous, red-orange sheet-lightning of three thousand short-range Krupp and Putilov field-howitzers firing black-powder and cheap, smoky ammonal shells hub-to-hub from the apple-orchards.

Through my field-glasses, by the blinding magnesium flare of the parachute-rockets that the Belgian fortress-gunners were firing from the concrete cupolas of Fort Barchon, I saw the first waves of the German-Russian *Sturm-Korps* go down to the riverbank.

They did not advance in open skirmish-lines like our Polytechnic cadets in the Sierra. Driven forward by the famine in their bellies and the revolvers of their syndicate-officers behind them, sixty thousand grey-coated Brandenburgers and sheepskin-clad Don infantrymen charged shoulder-to-shoulder in dense, nineteenth-century phalanxes across the pontoon-bridges, singing old Lutheran hymns and Tsar’s marches while the French divisions of Marshal-Protector Victor—who had marched north from Sedan three days earlier in their bright red trousers and tarnished brass cuirasses—met them on the western dike with fixed twenty-inch bayonets and hand-cranked Mitrailleuse batteries.

When the two walls of starving men collided in the red mud between the burning farmhouses, the artillery on both ridges did not cease fire; the Prussian and French batteries simply lowered their sights and pumped shrapnel straight into the screaming, locked mass of their own infantry.

In twenty minutes, the ice-choked channel of the Meuse below our viaduct was jammed from bank to bank with a solid, undulating weir of sky-blue coats, grey sheepskins, and disemboweled artillery-mules, over whose backs the second reserve regiments of Moscow and Lyons were already scrambling with clubbed rifles and butcher-knives.

"Close the mahogany shutter, Citizen-Historian," Prefect-Legate Shen said behind me in the warm, electrically lit saloon-car, not rising from his leather armchair where he was methodically entering the morning depreciation of the Paris-Orleans railway shares into his pocket ledger with a gold-nibbed fountain pen. "There is no military instruction to be derived from watching paupers beat each other to death with iron bars in a ditch. The old man in San Francisco pulled the linch-pin out of their wagon forty years ago when he turned the trade-routes into the Pacific; now the wheels have come off on the hill, and the load is going into the ravine. Let us hope the engine-driver clears the Calais switch before noon, or we shall miss the *Empress of Oahu* at Southampton."

***

Yet when our fast turbine-liner steamed through the Golden Gate twenty-two days later, on the first morning of March, we found that the smoke of the burning Meuse had traveled faster through the submarine cables than our propellers could cut the water.

For the first time since the funeral of Elias Thorne in eighty-seven, the Imperial Court had left the warm coral lagoons of Thalassia to sit in the cold stone fortress of the continental forge.

Up on the crest of Rincon Hill, above a San Francisco where every dry-dock at Hunters Point and every blast-furnace along the Potrero shore was roaring day and night under a low ceiling of greasy black oil-smoke, the great bronze doors of the Council Chamber stood bolted against the spring rain. Inside the redwood-vaulted hall—where the old silver curule chair had been replaced by a raised metallic tribune wired directly to the subterranean telegraph-vaults below—the twenty-six-year-old Sacred Emperor Kalanimoku did not sit in his yellow *mamo* feathers.

He wore the dark blue, double-breasted coat of an Admiral of the Ocean, his broad brown hands planted flat upon the illuminated glass chart of the North Atlantic that had been bolted over the old porphyry steps. Around him stood the young wolf-pack of the third generation: Fleet-General Kuroda, his duralumin calculator gleaming at his belt; Prefect-Chancellor Shen; and twelve thirty-year-old Polytechnic Marshals of the Aerial and Submarine Boards, their silver five-digit collar-ciphers catching the cold gray light from the seaward casements.

Only two figures in the room belonged to the century that had built the walls: old Field-Marshal Marcus Vance, sitting stiff-legged upon a camp-stool by the dead hearth with his hands folded over his cane; and in the center of the brass meridian lines, wheeled straight up to the edge of the glass map in her black koa-wood chair, the Queen-Mother Kaiulani.

She had survived the Atlantic gale and the snowy crossing of the Rockies on five grains of digitalis a day; her face beneath her black bombazine hood was the color of wood-ash, and her breathing sounded like dry leaves scraping across a gravestone, yet her small, shrunken hand struck the brass rim of the Atlantic chart with a force that made the red glass markers along the English Channel rattle.

"Twelve armored divisions of the First and Fourth Continental Armies, and thirty dreadnoughts of the *Thorne* and *Kalanimoku* classes to assemble at Halifax and the Azores by the fifteenth of April!" Kaiulani’s dry, whistling contralto cut through the hum of the chart-transformers as she read the mobilization warrant lying beneath her grandson’s palm. "Have the fumes of the Osaka furnaces rotted the brains in your skulls? Why are there Pacifica transport-markers laid down upon the ports of Brest and Antwerp?"

Fleet-General Kuroda did not lower his eyes before the eighty-two-year-old woman who had signed his father’s commission. He tapped the red-lit cluster of bulbs marking the mouth of the Scheldt with his steel dividers.

"On Tuesday morning, Your Imperial Highness, Field-Marshal von Mackensen’s Russo-German spearheads broke the French line at Namur and entered Brussels," Kuroda said in his flat, uninflected Monterey voice. "Marshal-Protector Victor is surrounded in the Lille fortresses with the remnant of the French army, and the German vanguard is four leagues from the Antwerp quays. Within ten days, the Berlin-Moscow Directory will hold every deep-water slip and coal-mine from the Baltic to the Bay of Biscay. Our clearing-houses in San Francisco and Canton hold four hundred and eighty million silver thalers in defaulted French and Belgian railway-mortgages, and thirty percent of our surplus nitrate and copper exports depend upon the Rotterdam barge-traffic. If we allow Mackensen and Brusilov to weld the European continent into a single autarkic fortress, the Atlantic market is closed to our factories forever."

"Then let the Atlantic market sink into the mud where Elias Thorne left it!" Kaiulani cried, leaning forward in her wheeled chair until her whale-ivory clasp swung clear of her shrunken breast, her obsidian eyes blazing past Kuroda straight into the cold, pale-gray eyes of her grandson Kalanimoku. "Listen to me, boy! I sat beside your grandfather on this very floor when the German Count and the Englishman came begging for twenty shiploads of California flour! Do you know why Elias tore up the tracks in Pennsylvania and turned his back on New York? Because he knew that the Atlantic is a tar-pit! For three hundred years the white tribes of that peninsula have done nothing but cut one another’s throats over five acres of turnip-mud along the Rhine!"

Kalanimoku did not flinch under his grandmother’s stare; his heavy jaw—the unmistakable, square-hewn jaw of the Kentucky squatter’s son, strange and terrifying beneath the smooth bronze skin of a Maui king—set hard against his gold-braided collar.

"When my grandfather sat in this room, Grandmother, a steamer took nineteen days to cross from Yokohama, and an army fought with horses and black powder," the young Emperor said, using that practiced, gravelly bark that made old Marcus Vance’s white eyebrows twitch beside the hearth. "Today, if von Mackensen puts German submarines into the Brest pens and Russian conscripts into the Essen rolling-mills, within five years their long-range dirigibles will be dropping picric-acid shells onto the locks at Panama and the oil-wells at Baku! There is no longer room upon this planet for two balance-sheets. Either Thalassia audits the books of Berlin before harvest, or our sons will be fighting the Europeans along the Mississippi and the Indus!"

"You are not marching to protect Panama, Kalanimoku—you are marching because you have built leviathan hammers at Waipahu and your clerks cannot bear to see an unflattened nail on the other side of the earth!" Kaiulani’s voice cracked into a harsh, tearing cough that stained her black lace handkerchief with a bright fleck of scarlet; she crushed the linen in her fist before the chamberlains could step forward, her trembling right index finger pointing down at the inlaid brass circle of the Pacific Ocean beneath her wheels. "Look at the floor under your boots! From the ice of the Bering Bridge to the reefs of Tasmania, from the temples of Benares to the locks of Darien, you hold four hundred and fifty million human beings in the palm of your hand! You have the rice, the gold, the oil, and the iron of three-quarters of the globe! If you send two million of our boys across the Atlantic ditch to police the ruins of Paris and Moscow, you will never bring the legions home again! The pivot will slip from the sea back to the land, and this empire will bleed its heart out in the snows of Poland just as Bonaparte did!"

Across the hearth, old Field-Marshal Marcus Vance slowly raised his white head from his cane.

"Her Highness’s logistics are correct, Majesty," the fifty-nine-year-old Marshal said quietly, his voice sounding like two dry stones rubbed together in the silence of the vault. "To maintain forty divisions across three thousand miles of Atlantic water against twelve million Russian and German rifles will consume eighty thousand tons of Borneo fuel-oil and four million silver thalers a day. Within eighteen months, you will have to double the rice-tax in Hankow and re-introduce the blood-conscription in the American cantons. The boiler is not riveted for that pressure."

Young Emperor Kalanimoku looked slowly from the broken old general by the cold fireplace to the dying eighty-two-year-old woman in her chair. Then, without a word, he turned his head toward Fleet-General Kuroda and Prefect Shen.

"The Marshal Emeritus and the Queen-Mother are tired after their voyage from Europe," Kalanimoku said, his hand descending toward the heavy bronze seal-press on the glass table while outside in the rain-swept plaza of Rincon Hill the steam-whistles of the Potrero troop-trains began to blow the assembly-call, "and they are thinking of an ocean that still had two shores. Chancellor Shen—prepare the Imperial Warrant for the Armed Neutrality Escort. Fleet-General Kuroda will assume command of the vanguard at Gibraltar on the first of May, and he will hold the Rock and the Channel approaches until both European wolves have bled themselves white enough to beg for our bailiffs."

***

To the Chronicler who went back across the Atlantic that May aboard the supply-colliers of Kuroda’s vanguard—watching the gray, turbine-driven mountains of the Pacifica fleet drop their anchors across the mouth of the Tagus and the Strait of Gibraltar like turnkeys locking the iron grate of a madhouse—the wisdom of the young Emperor’s delay soon manifested itself in a horror that neither Thucydides nor the prophets of Israel had ever been required to set down in ink.

For Kuroda did not land a single marine upon the beaches of France or Flanders that summer. Anchored six miles off the chalk cliffs of Dover and the sand-bars of the Scheldt, with their twenty-two-inch rifles trained indifferently upon the shore and their wireless masts intercepting every frantic cipher between Berlin, Paris, and Whitehall, the squadrons of the Great Arena simply kept the ring while the tribes of the Atlantic tore their own ancestral house down upon their heads.

It was in the first week of June, 1917, after Marshal-Protector Victor’s desperate counter-offensive along the Somme had shattered against the Russo-German barbed wire and the starving British Cabinet in Westminster had secretly leased the Harwich coaling-slips to the Prussian torpedo-flotillas in exchange for ten shiploads of Pomeranian rye, that the dying Bonapartist regime in Paris struck its last, blind blow across the ditch.

I was standing at midnight on the sixth of June upon the roof-leads of the Pacifica Debt-Receivership House at Greenwich, four miles down the river from St. Paul’s, where our numbered Cantonese and Virginian clerks were cataloguing the impounded bullion-books of the Royal Naval College by the light of portable storage-batteries. The night was moonless, warm, and stiflingly still; down in the dark, unlighted bend of the Pool of London, where no coal-fire had burned since the winter defaults, the smells of low-tide mud, rotting wharf-pilings, and the sour turnip-gruel of three million sleeping paupers hung motionless between the brick warehouses.

At twelve minutes past midnight, the silence above the Surrey hills broke—not with the clean, high-pitched hum of our Osaka turbine-planes, but with the heavy, rattling, lawn-mower throb of two hundred low-compression Renault and Gnome petroleum-engines burning crude shale-naphtha.

Out of the low cloud-bank over Croydon, flying at barely nine hundred feet above the chimney-pots because their warped wooden propellers could lift their loads no higher, came the last reserves of the *Flotte Aérienne de la Revanche*: forty lumbering, canvas-covered Voisin triplanes and twelve sausage-shaped, non-rigid hydrogen dirigibles painted dead coal-black with lamp-soot.

There were no anti-aircraft batteries left upon the Parliament embankments; the British twelve-pounders had been shipped to the Bengal front three years ago and now sat as rusting trophies in the parks of Monterey. Only a single ragged volley of Lee-Enfield rifle-fire crackled up from the veteran watchmen at the Tower of London before the lead French dirigible—commanded, as we learned afterward from the wreckage, by a nineteen-year-old tubercular count from Lyons who had chained himself to the steering-wheel—dropped its nose to five hundred feet above the timber-yards of Southwark and pulled the brass trip-cord of its ballast-racks.

They did not drop high-explosive steel shells; the French arsenals at St. Etienne had run out of copper driving-bands and picric acid in April. They dropped five thousand forty-gallon iron drums filled with a thick, syrupy mixture of boiled Gascon pine-turpentine, white phosphorus, and raw Baku petroleum residue that they had hoarded since the tariff blockade.

The first hundred drums struck the dry, tarred deal roofs of the Bermondsey tea-wharves and the medieval timber-framed tenements along Thames Street simultaneously.

There was no deafening concussion—only a hollow, drumming roar like giant hailstones smashing through rotten slate, followed three seconds later by a mile-wide curtain of blinding, greenish-white phosphorus flame that leaped two hundred feet straight into the air and turned the lead dome of St. Paul’s across the water into a globe of blood-red copper.

Through my binoculars, as the heat-draft from the river struck our faces four miles away at Greenwich like the opening of an iron-foundry door, I watched the second French airship take a stray Maxim bullet from the Victoria dock-guard directly through its hydrogen-valve.

The two-hundred-foot envelope did not merely burn; it split from bow to rudder in a rolling, saffron-colored thunderbolt that rained two tons of flaming rubberized silk and melting aluminum girders straight down onto the crowded shingle roofs of Cheapside and Threadneedle Street.

Within forty minutes, the fire-storm had created its own hurricane. Because the hydraulic pumping-stations at Wapping had been stripped of their brass pistons to pay the autumn rice-warrants, the bucket-brigades of old men and women in the streets below could only stand in the boiling white smoke with empty wooden pails while a sixty-mile-an-hour gale of superheated air sucked the flames through the narrow lanes from the Bank of England to the Fleet Ditch.

We heard the bells of St. Mary-le-Bow and St. Bride’s begin to ring as the oak belfries caught—not tolled by human hands, but swinging wildly in the hurricane draft until the ancient bronze melted in its cages and poured down through the burning rafters like white-hot syrup. Down onto the muddy foreshore of Queenhithe and Blackfriars tumbled five hundred thousand screaming, half-naked shadows, driving horses, hand-carts, and hospital-stretchers into the oily river while above their heads the stone arches of London Bridge disappeared behind a solid cataract of burning turpentine that floated across the surface of the Thames from bank to bank.

Beside me on the Greenwich roof, Junior Prefect Adams—Candidate Three-Three-Zero-Nine of the Seattle class—did not take his eye from the brass theodolite with which he was plotting the bearing of the fallen French airship.

"The Royal Exchange roof has just collapsed into the bullion-vaults, Citizen-Historian," the boy remarked calmly, wiping a flake of greasy black Thames soot from his celluloid collar while the roar of the dying metropolis four miles upstream shook the lead plates beneath our soles. "That will save our engineering gangs three weeks of demolition-dynamite when the foreclosure warrant takes effect in July. If the wind holds from the south-southeast until daybreak, the entire commercial parish from the Tower to the Temple will be cleared to the Roman brick."

***

Nine thousand miles away from that pitch-black cauldron on the Thames, the June morning broke over the coral lagoons of Thalassia in a haze of pale pearl and Sunset Gold so pure that the distant smoke of the inter-island fruit-steamers looked like strokes of a sable brush across Chinese silk.

Lady Kaiulani did not sit in the Whispering Gallery of the Senate anymore. During the three months since her return from San Francisco, her small body had shrunk until she weighed scarcely more than a ten-year-old child; the dropsy had risen above her knees, and the physicians had forbidden her wheels to leave the tiled, shady veranda of the Queen’s Marine Audit Pavilion—a low, open-sided loggia of white coral stone and dark koa-wood built directly atop the sea-wall at the entrance to the Waipahu commercial basin, where the trade-wind came in clean and damp over the breakers.

Yet though her body was anchored to the stone like a barnacle, her dark, sunken eyes beneath her white linen sun-veil had not lost a fraction of their terrible focus. Across her knees, resting upon a light board of polished cedar, lay the daily clearing-sheets of the Neutrality Syndicate, printed in violet ink upon thin rice-paper.

Fifty yards below her veranda balustrade, the deep-water channel of the Pearl Lochs commercial canal was so packed with incoming and outgoing merchant hulls that the green harbor water was churned into a permanent creamy lather of propeller-wash, smelling of warm coconut-oil, wet hemp, and the sharp, unmistakable tang of fresh red-lead paint.

A ten-thousand-ton Swedish-flagged tramp-steamer—her rusty iron plates newly painted with the broad white vertical stripes of the *International Relief Commission*, though her waterline sat four feet below the Plimsoll mark with the weight of the Hanyang pig-iron and Sacramento nitro-cellulose in her holds—was gliding slowly past the customs-buoy under the tow of two electric harbor-tugs. Scarcely a cable’s length astern of her followed a Dutch four-masted auxiliary bark out of Rotterdam, her deck-winches clanking rhythmically as the Cantonese stevedores hoisted crates of seized French gallery-paintings, Sèvres porcelain, and stripped church-bell bronze out of her hatches onto the Mint lighters.

"Read me the Lisbon and Gothenburg transfer-totals again, Malia," Kaiulani whispered, her thin, blue-veined hand resting motionless beside the untouched cup of papaya-broth on her tray while her niece—a forty-year-old woman in the severe gray linen dress of the Insular Secretariat—turned the ledger-page against the breeze.

"For the week ending June the ninth, Aunt," Malia read in her low, clear Hawaiian voice, "the Neutrality Clearing Board at the Azores delivered to the Swedish intermediaries at Gothenburg forty-two thousand tons of refined Chilean nitrates, eighteen thousand barrels of Borneo lubricating-oil, and four hundred thousand obsolete model-ninety-eight Sacramento magazine-rifles, against payment of sixty-four million gold marks drawn upon the collateral of the Krupp and Siemens machine-tool patents and the freehold deeds of the Westphalian coal-seams."

"And the Spanish frontier account at San Sebastian?" Kaiulani asked, watching the Swedish steamer dip her patched blue-and-yellow ensign to the bronze statue of the Providentor on the canal-head.

"Delivered to the agents of Marshal-Protector Victor via the Pyrenees narrow-gauge," Malia continued, her finger sliding down the violet column, "thirty thousand tons of Manchurian soy-meal, twelve thousand cases of Monterey picric-acid boosters, and six hundred reconditioned Curtiss rotary-engines, against the mortgage of the Lyons silk-looms and the final surrender of the Madagascar and West African harbour-leases. The net specie balance accruing to the Thalassia Treasury for the seven days—after deducting the coal-charges of Fleet-General Kuroda’s blockade squadrons at Gibraltar—stands at nineteen million, four hundred thousand silver thalers."

Kaiulani closed her eyes against the blinding dazzle of the sun on the water.

*Nineteen million thalers a week,* she thought, listening to the deep, musical hum of the electric gantry-cranes across the lagoon as they swung another twenty-ton load of Sacramento guncotton down into the belly of a neutral Norwegian hull. *In San Francisco three months ago, I wept blood into my handkerchief to keep Kalanimoku from sending our boys to die in the mud of the Meuse. I thought I was saving the Pacific from the furnace.*

She opened her eyes and looked down at the violet figures on the rice-paper—figures that were cleaner, neater, and infinitely more lethal than the sixty-four-thousand-ton dreadnoughts lying off Dover.

Kalanimoku and young Chancellor Shen had not needed to land a single cadet in France after all. By locking the gates of the ocean at Gibraltar and opening a pawnbroker’s wicket in the Azores, the priesthood of the slide-rule had discovered a way to conquer Europe without firing a single Pacifica rifle.

Whenever the Russo-German divisions pushed too close to the Channel ports, Shen’s agents at San Sebastian released ten thousand tons of Californian smokeless powder to the French at three hundred percent interest so that Marshal Victor’s conscripts might blow another fifty thousand Brandenburgers into the mud; and the moment the French bugles began to sound too loud along the Somme, the Swedish steamers unloaded fortyshiploads of Hanyang shell-steel and Montana copper at Gothenburg to keep Field-Marshal von Mackensen’s howitzers barking until autumn.

They were not mediating the war; they were tending it like a pair of Cantonese lime-burners feeding wet brushwood and coal-slack into a kiln, adjusting the draft with a turn of the telegraph-key so that the fire never went out until every ounce of gold, every title-deed, every factory-lathe, and every twenty-year-old boy between the Atlantic surf and the Ural mountains had been rendered down into grey ash and mortgaged paper in the vaults of Market Street.

"Look at the Dutch ship at the third slip, Malia," Kaiulani murmured, her withered chin trembling slightly as the electric crane hoisted a massive, eight-foot bronze altar-cross and four bundled tapestries from the Cathedral of Rheims out of the Hollander’s fore-hold in a cargo-net and swung them over the concrete coping toward the disinfection-sheds. "When Elias took the silver out of the Comstock, he left the rock in the mountain. My grandson is buying the skin off their dead children’s backs with our spoiled warehouse-powder, and calling it the Peace of the Pivot."

***

By the winter of 1918, the kiln was cold.

There was no Waterloo to end the European Civil War, nor even such a formal, sword-surrendering ceremony as we had witnessed upon the sun-baked bricks of the Shwedagon Pagoda four years earlier. The fire on the continent simply went out for want of timber to burn.

After the typhus and the black influenza of the second winter had carried off four million half-starved soldiers in the flooded trenches along the Rhine, and the great peasant mutinies of March had hung Generalissimo Brusilov from the Kremlin wall and driven Marshal-Protector Victor to blow his own brains out in a cellar at Tours, there remained neither a government in Berlin nor an army in France with the strength to lift a rifle.

When Fleet-General Kuroda’s white-painted hospital-cruisers and engineering-transports steamed up the Scheldt into the blackened, silent basins of Antwerp on the tenth of May, 1918, not a single coastal battery challenged the sun-and-anchor flag. Instead, along five miles of ruined stone quays, two hundred thousand emaciated Belgian, French, and German deserters—men in rotting rags of sky-blue and field-gray who had thrown their rifles into the canal—knelt side by side on the cobbles in the spring drizzle, holding out rusty tin pannikins toward the steam-winches as our Cantonese quartermasters lowered the first nets of California salt-pork and San Joaquin barley-biscuit.

To the Chronicler who sat four months later in the newly whitewashed hall of the old Reichstag in Berlin—watching Prefect-Chancellor Shen and the twenty-eight-year-old Sacred Emperor Kalanimoku promulgate the *Organic Act of the European Protectorate* before the assembled municipal receivers of the Western Peninsula—the scene possessed the quiet, antiseptic finality of a surgical amphitheater after the amputation is done.

All traces of the old monarchies and republics had been swept into the dust-bins with the broken plaster of the victory columns. Outside in the Tiergarten, where the bronze statues of the Hohenzollerns and Bismarck had already been unbolted from their red granite pedestals and loaded onto flatcars for the Hanyang scrap-furnaces, gangs of former Prussian guardsmen and French cuirassiers in identical, unbadged overalls of coarse gray Canton denim were widening the Charlottenburg railway embankment from the old European four-foot-eight gauge to the six-foot Imperial standard, under the quiet eyes of Samoan and Californian provost-corporals.

Inside the chamber, the air smelled strongly of carbolic whitewash, fresh Oregon pine-varnish, and the faint, omnipresent ozone of the sixty-cycle transformers that our Osaka engineers had installed in the cellar to replace the burned-out German dynamos.

There were no kings, no marshals, and no parliaments upon the floor. Ranged upon twelve rows of plain, numbered iron benches sat the newly appointed *Syndics of the Fourteen European Cantons*—sixty gaunt, hollow-cheeked former civil-servants, railway-directors, and municipal engineers from London, Paris, Berlin, Vienna, and Warsaw, each wearing a dark gray alpaca coat with a brass six-digit debtor-cipher pinned to his left lapel.

"Under Article Seven of the Brussels Liquidation Accord," Prefect-Chancellor Shen was reading from the steel podium, his horn-rimmed spectacles flashing in the white electric glare of the skylight as his flat, unhurried voice echoed across the silent benches, "the historical boundaries and customs-barriers of the kingdoms and republics heretofore known as Great Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Austria, and Western Russia are abolished in perpetuity. From the first of October, nineteen-eighteen, the peninsula west of the Vistula and the Dnieper is constituted as the Autonomous Fiscal Territory of the *European Confederation*, divided into fourteen numbered industrial and agricultural cantons under the supreme supervision of the High Commissioner at Antwerp."

Down in the second row, the Syndic for the Third Rhine Canton—a former director of the Essen steel-works named Hugenberg, whose left cheek still bore a purple carbuncle from the winter turnip-scurvy—slowly raised a trembling hand holding a printed balance-sheet.

"Citizen-Chancellor," the German said in thick, hesitant English, rising half out of his iron seat as two Polytechnic cadets by the wall shifted their hands to their pistol-belts, "by the schedule attached to Article Nine, eighty percent of the coal and pig-iron output of the Ruhr and Silesian basins is hypothecated for ninety-nine years to the Market Street Mint to service the Neutrality War-Loans, while our universities at Jena, Göttingen, and Paris are forbidden to maintain laboratories of chemistry or ballistics above the third primary grade. If our young men are excluded from the Monterey and New Edo polytechnic examinations, and our blast-furnaces work only for export to Osaka, by what trade are the two hundred million inhabitants of these fourteen cantons to purchase their winter wheat?"

Up on the dais, beneath the newly erected bronze relief of the *Sacred Compass*, Emperor Kalanimoku did not reach for his electric baton. He sat with his heavy, bronze-skinned hands resting calmly upon his knees inside his dark blue Admiral’s coat, his cold, pale-gray eyes looking past the German’s bald head as if he were gazing out over four thousand miles of empty salt water.

It was Prefect Shen who answered, without lifting his eyes from the parchment.

"The demographic census completed by Assessor Adams in August indicates that the urban population of the European peninsula exceeds the agricultural carrying-capacity of its soil by sixty-two million souls, Citizen-Syndic," Shen replied smoothly, turning the page with a dry rustle of his fingers while outside in the Friedrichstrasse the deep, brassy hoot of a broad-gauge Baldwin locomotive announced the departure of the noon labor-train for the Siberian timber-camps. "To relieve your municipalities of that burden, the Bureau of Integration has authorized a permanent annual draft of four million unmarried European males and females between the ages of sixteen and twenty-six to be transported via the Suez and Panama liners to the rubber-plantations of Borneo, the guano-beds of Peru, and the new irrigation-trenches of the Australian interior. Those who remain behind in the fourteen cantons will find ample subsistence in maintaining the tourist-monuments of Rome and Paris for our vacationing prefects, and weaving flax-linen for the Commissariat. Citizen Hugenberg, you may sit down; the High Commissioner’s train for Geneva leaves at four, and we have still to sign the indenture for the removal of the Louvre and Vatican collections to the museum at Thalassia."

As the German sank back onto the iron bench with his grey face buried in his hands, I looked up from my historiographer’s desk toward the tall window behind the dais—where, through the rain-streaked glass, a squad of Cantonese and Hawaiian riggers were hoisting the thirty-foot banner of Imperial Blue and Sunset Gold to the top of the Brandenburg Gate—and it seemed to the Chronicler that the long, bloody river of human history, which had begun three thousand years ago when the Greeks sailed out of Aulis toward the East, had finally run backward into the great ocean and frozen into a single, shoreless sheet of blue ice.

"Hand me the crimson sealing-wax, Citizen-Historian," Prefect Shen said, turning half a pace from the podium to hold his brass stamp over the alcohol-lamp on my table while his cold, spectacled eyes met mine across the tiny blue flame. "The local syndics have accepted the liquidation schedules. All that remains is for the Queen-Mother’s train to meet the Atlantic Expeditionary transports at the Swiss lakes so her hand may close the ledger."

***

Seven days later, the October wind coming down off the snow-fields of Mont Blanc swept across the grey, choppy waters of Lake Leman, carrying not the quiet chime of Alpine cow-bells, but the raw, sulfurous stench of Welsh slack-coal and the rhythmic, metallic pounding of ten thousand Cantonese railway-navvies re-laying the Geneva marshaling-yards to the six-foot Imperial gauge.

Inside the glass-walled conservatory of the Hôtel Beau-Rivage—where sixty years before the idle dukes of the old continent had sipped their mineral waters before Elias Thorne’s tariffs broke their banks—Lady Kaiulani sat before a long table of polished Swiss walnut. She was eighty-four years old this autumn; the Atlantic crossing from Halifax aboard the rolling flagship of the Expeditionary Force and the jolting military train up from the ruined docks of Marseilles had drained the last drop of warmth from her shrunken limbs. Dressed in a heavy gown of severe dark mourning silk, with a cape of Russian sable drawn tight around her narrow shoulders and the ancient carved tooth of the Oahu chiefs resting cold against her collarbone, she looked less like a living regent than an obsidian idol carried in the baggage-train of her grandson’s legions.

Outside on the stone quay, the logistical friction of the Atlantic deployment ground on without pause: a column of forty steam-traction lorries belonging to Fleet-General Kuroda’s Gibraltar Vanguard rumbled past the iron palings, their solid rubber tires crushing the frozen dahlia-beds as squads of Samoan and Californian military police unloaded crates of Hollerith sorting-machines and spools of copper field-wire into the requisitioned casino.

Before her table stood the last titular magistrates of the Western world: a trembling sub-deacon of the Roman Curia in a mud-stained soutane; a former federal councillor of the Swiss cantons whose gold watch-chain had been replaced by a piece of hempen twine; and General von Seeckt of the dissolved German Quartermaster Staff, his left arm strapped in a pasteboard splint.

"The military railway from Marseilles to Basel passed the load-test at six this morning, Your Imperial Highness," Fleet-General Kuroda reported, stepping in from the terrace with the lake-sleeting melting upon the dark blue shoulders of his boat-cloak. He laid a heavy parchment folio—bound not in velvet, but in grey vulcanized gutta-percha—directly across the walnut table. "The first six-foot-gauge grain-trains from the Genoa grain-elevators are already unloading San Joaquin barley at Zurich, and our garrison gunboats have been lowered by crane into the lake. The delegates have examined the *Geneva Accord*."

Kaiulani did not look up at the young Fleet-General; her dark, sunken eyes remained fixed upon the parchment title-page, where the double-headed eagles of Austria and Russia and the lilies of France had been erased by the scraper to make room for the single, geometric Sun-and-Anchor of the Pivot.

*So it is finished, Elias,* she thought, the cold draft from the terrace making the dry skin of her knuckles ache as her hand reached slowly toward the gold fountain-pen in the stand. *Sixty-five years ago you sat in a leaky adobe hut at Clark’s Point with a stolen map of the Sacramento river on your knee and told Caleb Vance that the East was a dead tree waiting for the axe. You died in your iron corset before you could cross the Mississippi, and I buried you under four miles of salt water so your shadow would not swallow the sun. Yet your dead hand has reached across two oceans and locked the doors of Charlemagne’s house.*

"Does the Chancery of Thalassia guarantee the municipal salt-ration if we sign away the customs of the Rhine and the Danube?" General von Seeckt asked hoarsely, his solitary hand twitching toward the hilt of a sword that was no longer at his belt.

"The Bureau of Integration guarantees three hundred grams of barley-meal and twenty grams of cured pork per diem to every registered laborer who presents his brass thumb-tag at the cantonment wicket," Kaiulani replied, her voice a dry, papery whisper that barely cleared the rim of her sable collar. She did not wait for the German to bow. Pressing the gold nib to the gutta-percha vellum, she traced the single, spiky Hawaiian word—*Kaiulani R.*—beneath the seal of the Protectorate.

***

To the Chronicler who traveled southward from Geneva that November by the newly widened military track through the Mont Cenis tunnel, and embarked at Genoa aboard the dispatch-cruiser *Manila* to inspect the winter moorings of the Gibraltar Vanguard, the transformation of the ancient world’s cradle surpassed all the marvels of the Indian war.

For three millennia, the inland sea that washes the marbles of Athens and the basalt moles of Ostia had been the private lake of the Caucasian race. Upon these blue, tideless waters the triremes of Themistocles had broken the Persian king; across these swells the legions of Scipio had carried the bronze wolf to Carthage, and the galleys of Venice and Don John had locked their oars against the Turk. To the European mind, the Mediterranean was the very *Mare Nostrum*—the warm hearth-fire around which all philosophy, law, and dominion had been warmed while the outer oceans lay in darkness.

Now, on a clear, sharp morning in late November, 1918, I stood upon the armored bridge-wing of the *Manila* as our squadron steamed at fourteen knots through the narrow Strait of Messina between Sicily and the toe of the Italian boot.

The air smelled neither of lemon-blossoms nor of the olive-wood fires of the Calabrian shepherds; it smelled of hot Borneo fuel-oil, stinging salt spray, and the sharp, chemical tang of the picric-acid smoke-floats that our torpedo-destroyers were dropping along the five-fathom line to calibrate the coast-defense range-finders.

Ahead of our clipper bow, riding in single-line-ahead formation across the exact channel where Ulysses had steered between Scylla and Charybdis, steamed the Second Battle Squadron of the Pacific Fleet: the *Kamehameha*, the *Satsuma*, the *San Joaquin*, and the *Monterey*. Their towering, pagoda-like tripod masts and dark Imperial Blue hulls cast shadows half a mile long across the wine-dark water; from their maintrucks snapped the Golden Sun, while upon their broad teak quarterdecks, companies of Japanese and Hawaiian marines in slate-gray wool performed their morning bayonet-drill to the brassy, syncopated blare of the Imperial Anthem.

Not a single European warship remained afloat between the Pillars of Hercules and the mouth of the Nile. At the foot of the white limestone cliffs of Taormina, beneath the broken brick arches of the Greco-Roman theater where Aeschylus had once been recited to the colonists of Syracuse, two hulking, rust-streaked Italian dreadnoughts—the *Dante Alighieri* and the *Conte di Cavour*—lay beached upon the shingle with their twelve-inch turrets cut open by oxy-acetylene torches, while four hundred Cantonese scrap-cutters swarmed over their decks like blue ants, loading the Krupp armor-plate into Osaka ore-barges to be shipped back through the Suez ditch and melted down into railway-chairs for the Manchurian branch-lines.

"The semaphore station atop Mount Etna reports the grain-convoy from Alexandria has cleared the Malta channel, Citizen-Historian," remarked Commander Hirose at my elbow, lowering his Zeiss binoculars and glancing down at the duralumin gyro-repeater beside the binnacle. Born in the Nagasaki naval wards and educated at the Berkeley sheds, the thirty-two-year-old captain looked up at the snow-streaked volcanic cone of Sicily with the mild, detached curiosity of a botanist examining a pressed fern. "Have you been ashore at Naples yet? The Prefect of the Seventh Italian Canton has cleared the beggars out of the Pompeii excavations and laid an electric tramway from the quay to the forum. Our stokers go up in parties of fifty on Sundays to photograph one another beside the plaster casts."

I looked out past the swinging twenty-two-inch muzzles of our forward turret toward the ancient Calabrian hills, where a giant whitewashed cipher—*CANTON XI : SECTOR 4*—had been painted in fifty-foot numerals across the granite cliff below a ruined Norman watchtower.

The wheel of providence had completed its full, pitiless revolution. The barbarians of the outer water—the children of the Polynesian coral-reefs, the Japanese fishing-villages, and the Californian gold-gulches that neither Caesar nor Alexander had ever dreamed existed beyond the rim of the flat earth—now kept the peace of the Roman sea with turbine-driven iron, while the descendants of the senators and the doges stood bareheaded on the seawall, waiting to sell a basket of oranges for a copper token stamped in San Francisco.

***

Yet the earth is older than the slide-rule; and when an empire bolts the doors of the world so tight that not a single rifle can be lifted against its prefects from the Vistula to the Sacramento, nature herself reaches into the mud for a weapon that cannot be stopped by eighteen inches of Krupp steel.

It was not until the middle of January, 1919—six weeks after the Queen-Mother Kaiulani had been brought home from Marseilles through the Suez locks aboard the hospital-liner *Solace*, never again to leave her wheeled chair upon the seaward veranda of the Coral Pavilion—that the first queer, unindexed numbers began to appear upon the perforated manila cards of the Bureau of Integration at Thalassia.

On a sultry, overcast afternoon when the trade-wind had died completely away, leaving the peacock-blue water of the Pearl Lochs lagoon as flat and oily as a sheet of warm lead and filling the open-sided loggia with the heavy, sickening perfume of over-ripe night-jasmine and ozone from the Molokai transformers, Kaiulani lay propped among her linen pillows, listening to the slow, rhythmic *whir-click, whir-click* of the portable Hollerith tabulator that Prefect-Chancellor Shen had set up on the bamboo veranda table.

At eighty-four, her sight had begun to cloud with the white pearly cataract of the islands, so that the distant hulls of the super-dreadnoughts out in the Waipahu roadstead looked to her like grey ghosts floating in milk; yet her hearing remained as sharp as a night-heron’s.

"Why has the sorting-needle stopped on the Antwerp and Genoa cards, Shen?" Kaiulani asked, her thin, dark fingers resting upon the curved bone hook at her breast as the machine gave three sharp rejection-bells and the young Cantonese clerk beside the Chancellor pulled a handful of red-bordered mortality slips from the brass hopper. "You told the Emperor at noon that the winter wheat-ration had been distributed without a single bread-riot in the fourteen European cantons."

Prefect-Chancellor Shen did not answer immediately. He took off his horn-rimmed spectacles, wiped the equatorial sweat from the bridge of his nose with a silk handkerchief, and held three of the red-punched cards up to the grey light filtering through the palm-fronds.

"There are no riots, Your Imperial Highness," Shen said, and for the first time since Kaiulani had known his father’s house, she heard a tiny, hairline crack of uncertainty in the smooth Berkeley voice. "A starving man with a turnip in his belly does not throw paving-stones at a Maxim gun. This is the weekly sanitary telemetry from the embarkation-barracks at Antwerp, Brest, and Odessa, where the first draft of four hundred thousand European labor-conscripts is being held for the Borneo and Peruvian transports."

"Have they brought the lice-typhus out of the Russian trenches again?" Kaiulani murmured, her eyelids drooping in the stifling heat. "Tell Fleet-General Kuroda’s surgeons to double the cresol-baths at the pier-heads."

"It is not the louse-fever, Madam," said a rougher, older voice from the shadow of the koa-wood pillars behind her chair. Old Field-Marshal Marcus Vance stepped slowly out onto the tiles, leaning heavily upon his rubber-tipped cane, his steel leg-brace creaking softly at the knee. He held in his square, liver-spotted hand a long blue submarine-cable flimsy that had come in ten minutes before through the private military conduit from Monterey—a message that had not passed through Shen’s commercial sorting-frames. "Cresol does not kill this, Princess," Marcus said, hobbling to the edge of the veranda table and laying the wet blue paper directly over Shen’s perforated cards. "Read her the post-mortem dispatch from Chief Surgeon Takagi at the Gibraltar coal-hulks, Chancellor—and then read her the morning report from the Vallejo grain-docks in San Francisco Bay." Kaiulani’s clouded eyes turned sharply toward the old general’s grey, gaunt face. "Vallejo? What has Vallejo to do with the Belgian labor-draft?" Shen looked down at the blue military wire, his thin lips tightening until they were white around the corners. "On the twenty-eighth of December, Your Highness, the returning empty munition-collier *Suisun*—which had discharged nitrate cargo at Rotterdam and taken on two thousand German and French railway-conscripts for the Panama canal-locks—put into Gibraltar with three hundred men dead in the steerage holds. They did not die of the winter starvation or the trench-typhus. According to Surgeon Takagi’s autopsy, the lungs fill with black, frothy blood within twelve hours of the first shivering-fit; the skin turns the color of wet slate—" "They call it the *Rhine-Mud Grippe* in the Antwerp alleys," Marcus Vance cut in, his pale eyes fixed grimly upon the distant, smoke-wrapped funnel of a ten-thousand-ton transport that was just rounding the quarantine-buoy off Diamond Head with its yellow jack flying at the fore. "It bred in the flooded shell-craters along the Meuse last autumn, where half a million unburied horses and men were rotting in the chemical sludge of our own picric-acid shells. As long as the Europeans were locked behind their trenches, it stayed in the mud. Then we knocked the walls down in May, marched four million conscripts onto the broad-gauge trains, and packed them into the twenty-eight-knot turbine liners that Elias and I built to bring the world inside a fourteen-day circle." Marcus lifted his cane two inches off the tiles and pointed the rubber ferrule straight at the yellow-flagged steamer dropping anchor in the outer roadstead. "That is the fast troop-transport *Great Republic*, nine days out from Panama via San Francisco," the old Marshal said, as down at the naval landing-slip below the pavilion the brass alarm-bell of the Quarantine Launch began to clang frantically across the still, sultry water, and four marine orderlies in white carbolic-masks came running up the basalt steps toward the terrace with a red dispatch-case between them. "She touched at Vallejo on Tuesday to coal, and by Friday noon four hundred examination-clerks in the Berkeley sheds and half the stokers on the *Thalassia* were spitting black blood into their hammocks. Chancellor Shen—don't touch that telegraph key until the surgeon tells us whether the quarantine line at Gibraltar has held or if the Atlantic Vanguard has already carried the rot into the Danube basins."

***

It had not held. Yet in the strange, merciless arithmetic of the Bureau of Integration, the pestilence that the Fast-Transports carried out of the Meuse craters became, within ninety days of its outbreak, the very mortar with which the Chancellery sealed the cellar doors of Central Europe.

To the Chronicler who entered Vienna in the late March of 1919—riding in the disinfecting-van of the Tenth Sanitary Train after the newly laid six-foot tracks had pierced the Semmering Pass from Trieste—the old seat of the Hapsburg Caesars offered a lesson in imperial geometry that neither sword nor shell could have etched so deep. Where the Russo-German batteries had left the outer Ringstrasse standing, the black grippe had emptied the inner courtyards like a scythe.

We did not march into the Austrian capital behind brass bands or lowered bayonets. Our vanguard consisted of forty white-painted steam-lorries of the *Imperial Pacific Relief Commission*, their boilers burning clean Borneo oil that smelled of hot paraffin and ozone against the sour, fetid miasma of unburied dead and boiled cabbage that hung beneath the chestnut trees of the Prater. Across the broad, cracked flagstones of the Heldenplatz—directly between the bronze hooves of Prince Eugene’s charger and the shuttered, mortar-chipped windows of the Hofburg—our Cantonese and Californian engineer-companies had erected six长 rows of galvanized-iron triage sheds and twenty high-pressure field autoclaves.

"Keep the queue inside the whitewashed ropes, Sergeant, and do not permit the former municipal magistrates to enter the soup-line ahead of the tramway-stokers," ordered Senior Sanitary Prefect Watanabe, standing beside me upon the granite plinth of the Empress Maria Theresa’s monument with a clipboard of stamped aluminum in his gloved hand and a gauze pad soaked in eucalyptus-camphor tied across his mouth and nose. 

Below our boots, stretching for half a mile down the Mariahilferstrasse in the raw spring sleet, stood thirty thousand citizens of the Ninth Danubian Canton. There were former colonels of the Imperial-Royal Uhlans wrapped in ragged, lice-ridden horse-blankets; hollow-eyed professors of the university hugging empty leather briefcases to their ribs; and pale, barefoot girls in the faded silk ball-gowns of nineteen-thirteen. Nobody shouted; nobody cursed the blue-and-gold Sun banner snapping from the dome of the Kunsthistorisches Museum. When a man has buried three children in the frozen garden-mould behind his tenement and feels the first hot, dry tickle of the Rhine-mud fever in his own windpipe, the pride of a thousand years of Christendom melts awaybefore the smell of boiling mutton-tallow and synthetic quinine.

As each shivering family reached the duralumin turnstile at the head of the shed, they did not merely hold out their bowls to the Hawaiian hospital-orderlies. Before a ladle of San Joaquin barley-gruel or a five-grain tablet of Osaka coal-tar febrifuge crossed the counter, the householder was required to lay his old Austrian parish-papers, his land-deeds, and his guild-certificates into the iron hopper of a portable furnace beside the cauldron, receiving in return a square brass ration-plate stamped with a six-digit canton numeral and a lead wire that our blacksmith-corporals riveted permanently around the left wrist.

"You observe the economy of the transaction, Citizen-Historian," Prefect Watanabe remarked through his camphor-mask, his spectacles reflecting the bright orange flare of the paper-furnace where three centuries of Hapsburg feudal charters and municipal franchises were curling into black ash to heat the carbolic vats. "In Poland last autumn, General Kuroda’s regiments had to expend four hundred rounds of machine-gun ammunition for every village we cleared for the gauge-widening. Here, a pound of compressed salt-pork and two pennies’ worth of carbolic soap buy us the freehold of the Danube without exploding a single cap. A man who has been conquered by a bayonet remembers his grievance when his ribs heal; a man who has sold his father’s name at a turnstile for a tin of hot broth and a clean shirt is a numbered clerk for life."

Down at the third wicket, an aged Austrian archduke—his collar-less linen shirt flapping beneath a moth-eaten fur pelisse—hesitated for three seconds as the Samoan corporal took his parchment patent of nobility with a pair of iron tongs and held the cold brass wrist-shackle open over the anvil.

"Next in the file!" the corporal barked in the flat, clipped pidgin of the Monterey depots, tapping the iron rivet-hammer once against the block; and without lifting his eyes to the bronze eagles on the palace roof above him, the last cousin of Charles the Fifth thrust his wasted white wrist into the ring.

***

By the autumn of that same year, the brass wrist-rings of the Relief Commission had locked the last starving parish between the Baltic and the Adriatic; yet in the high, glass-roofed Chart-Vault of the Imperial Palace at Thalassia, five thousand leagues away from the Vienna soup-booths, the sheer weight of the ledger was breaking the tables.

On an afternoon in late October, 1919, Lady Kaiulani sat in her wheeled koa-wood chair at the center of the great circular floor. She had not worn her court silks since the spring; she was wrapped in a plain, heavy wrapper of dark gray Oahu wool, her white hair cropped short like a dying soldier’s to save her tire-women the labor of the comb, the ancient carved whale-tooth hanging loose upon a neck no thicker than a child’s wrist.

All around her, the marble rotunda that she and Marcus Vance had designed five years ago to hold the quiet, clockwork balance of the Pacific basin had been turned into a roaring, suffocating factory of unindexed paper. The cool submarine twilight of the dome was gone; to feed the eighty supplementary Hollerith tabulators and high-speed pneumatic sorting-frames that Chancellor Shen had bolted across the mosaic floor, four temporary copper power-cables had been dragged in through the shattered lower panes of the stained glass, filling the vault with the blinding blue flash of overloaded mercury-rectifiers, the smell of scorching gutta-percha insulation, and the deafening, unending hail-storm rattle of ten million manila cards passing through the brass needles.

"The repeater-cable at Aden has been jammed for nineteen hours with the quarantine tallies from the Third Rhine and Eleventh Danubian Cantons, Your Imperial Highness!" shouted Junior Assessor Adams, his linen shirt soaked through with sweat and machine-oil as he elbowed his way through a knee-deep drift of unfiled yellow telegraph-tape that had spilled out of the pneumatic chutes from the Monterey Annex. "Until the Vienna and Warsaw mortality-deductions are cleared off the main wire, I cannot transmit the October rice-warrants to the Hankow granaries! Thirty grain-hulks are lying idle in the Yangtze with their steam up because the Canton prefects have no cipher-authority to open the sluices!"

"Then clear the Hankow warrants over the Siberian land-line through Irkutsk!" snapped Prefect-Chancellor Shen from the raised steel podium, his horn-rimmed spectacles sliding down his sweat-greased nose while three Cantonese mechanics with iron wrenches worked frantically beneath his feet to unjam a smoking sorting-wheel that had chewed a bundle of Bengal salt-cards into pulp.

"The Irkutsk trunk-wire was cut sixty miles west of Omsk on Tuesday by forty thousand escaped European labor-conscripts who seized a broad-gauge timber-train when their guard-battalion came down with the black grippe!" Adams yelled back over the clatter of the bells. "And the High Commissioner at Antwerp wires that unless four hundred thousand tons of Argentine beef and Sacramento flour are diverted from the Osaka foundry-allocations before the November frost, the Ruhr coal-miners will abandon the pumps and let the Westphalian shafts flood to the collar!"

In the center of the floor, Kaiulani did not raise her voice; she could not have made herself heard six feet away through the iron din of the tabulators. She simply reached out with her rubber-tipped ebony cane and hooked the hem of old Field-Marshal Marcus Vance’s alpaca coat where he stood leaning against a marble pillar beside her wheels.

"Look at Shen’s hands, Marcus," she whispered, lifting her chin toward the steel podium.

Up above the sea of overflowing wicker baskets, the grandson of Elias Thorne’s imperturbable Chinese auditor—the man who had smiled when Paris starved and never blinked when London burned—was striking the brass housing of the master-telegraph printer with his clenched fist, his immaculate slate-gray cuffs black with carbon-smut, his mouth working silently against the roar of the seventy ventilators.

"We built a heart to pump the blood of one ocean, Marcus," Kaiulani murmured, closing her cataract-clouded eyes as a warm, greasy draft of ozone and burned lubricating-oil blew across her face from the overloaded Molokai transformers. "Now Kalanimoku has spliced the veins of three hundred million dead-weight Europeans and two hundred million Hindoos into the same brass pipe, and the valves are bursting in the cellar. It takes eleven days for a famine-report from the Vistula to pass through the sorting-frames at Monterey, and while the needle is hunting for the card in this room, the rice rots on the Hankow wharves and the mutineers tear up the Siberian sleepers."

Marcus Vance looked down at the mile of tangled yellow paper coiling around the wheels of her chair like dead kelp on a beach after a typhoon.

"Elias told me once at the Panama cut that an engineer can build a bridge across any river in the world, provided he doesn't make the span so wide that the iron breaks under its own weight before a single train crosses it," the old Marshal said heavily, his stiff knee popping as he kicked a jammed bundle of Antwerp debtor-cards out of the path of her wheels. "We have no reserve battalions left in California, Princess. Every boy from the class of nineteen-eighteen who survived the winter grippe in the Berkeley sheds has been shipped out to police the Rhine soup-kitchens or guard the Suez oil-docks—and this morning, Emperor Kalanimoku signed the field-orders for Fleet-General Kuroda to march six divisions from the Indus up into the Hindu Kush to close the last hole in the fence."

***

That hole in the fence was the Kingdom of Kabul.

To the Chronicler who stands today—in this bitter December of 1919—beside the frozen wreck of an Osaka armored traction-engine three miles below the summit of the Jagdalak Pass, while the snow-wind off the sixteen-thousand-foot peaks of the Hindu Kush screams through the empty eye-sockets of our unburied draught-mules, the folly of that final campaign requires no logarithmic demonstration.

Upon the illuminated glass charts in the Palace of Thalassia, the mountain massif between the Indus and the Oxus had appeared to young Emperor Kalanimoku and his Polytechnic staff as a mere thumb-smudge of unnumbered gray paper—an intolerable gap of four hundred miles where the six-foot Imperial gauge from Peshawar failed to meet the Russian broad-gauge military line coming down from Tashkent and Samarkand. *"An empire that leaves an unbolted door between its Indian jute-cantons and its Siberian timber-wards invites every bandit in Asia to cut the wire,"* Fleet-General Kuroda had written in his September memorandum from Delhi; and on the first of October, with sixty thousand men of the Combined Pacific Corps—veteran Satsuma infantry, Californian railway-pioneers, and newly conscripted Bavarian and Yorkshire debtor-battalions—he had marched up the dry, slate-walled furnace of the Khyber Pass behind forty steam-tractors pulling six-inch Krupp mountain-howitzers and ten thousand tons of creosoted Oregon pine sleepers.

For three weeks, so long as the column remained within the range of the flat-trajectory naval guns mounted upon our armored broad-gauge trains at Jamrud, the machine had rolled forward with the old, effortless grandeur of the Great Arena.

Then the six-foot track ended against the vertical black granite of the Kabul Gorge, and the winter came down out of Tartary.

Here there was no sea within eight hundred miles to float a dreadnought; here the air at ten thousand feet was so thin and dry that our twin-engined Curtiss-Nakajima biplanes could not lift a hundred-pound picric bomb over the passes, and the great rigid duralumin air-cruiser *Sakurajima II*—ordered up from Karachi to spot the tribal rifle-sangars among the crags—had her envelope ripped open from nose to tail by a ninety-mile-an-hour freezing gale above Jelalabad, crashing into a ravine where the Ghilzai herdsmen hacked her aluminum girders into horse-shoes before the staff-cars could reach the smoke.

At four o’clock on this afternoon of the eighteenth of December, the thermometer on the dashboard of Fleet-General Kuroda’s command-lorry stands at fourteen degrees below zero. The Borneo petroleum in the fuel-tanks of our forty traction-engines has frozen into a thick, yellow jelly that will not pass the brass injectors; the water-jackets of the Maxim guns have split open from the frost; and for five miles along the narrow, ice-glazed mule-track that winds between the two-thousand-foot limestone precipices of the Kurd-Kabul defile, the rear-guard of the Grand Confederation is dying in the snow.

"Break up the pine railway-sleepers from the third flat-sled and pile them under the crank-case of the tractor, Captain!" Fleet-General Kuroda shouts, his voice no longer the quiet, unhurried Monterey baritone that had sunk the British fleet at the Hooghly, but a cracked, frost-bitten rasp as he stands knee-deep in the blood-stained drift beside the stalled ammunition-train. His slate-gray greatcoat is stiff with frozen mule-slobber and black oil-soot; the duralumin circular calculator in his frost-blackened right hand is useless, for there is no wireless telemetry in this granite trough, and the enemy above us has no railway-bridges to shell.

Eight hundred feet overhead, invisible behind the grey limestone boulders that crown the knife-edged ridges on either side of the gorge, four thousand Afridi and Ghilzai tribesmen—men who have never seen a steamship, who carry no brass ration-tags upon their wrists, and who have lived for a month on a handful of parched barley and raw mutton-fat tucked inside their greasy sheepskin *postins*—are firing down into the packed, dark-blue mass of our stalled column with long-barreled, home-forged jezails and stolen Lee-Enfield rifles left behind from the old British wars.

*Crack—whir-r-r—thud.*

A heavy, soft-lead slug fired from a cliff a quarter of a mile away strikes the frozen iron boiler-plate of the traction-engine behind Kuroda’s shoulder, flattens into a jagged star the size of a silver thaler, and ricochets sideways through the throat of Junior Prefect Adams—who has come out from Thalassia with the November audit-rolls and now pitches face-first into the snow across a pile of unlaid eighty-pound Bessemer rails, his horn-rimmed spectacles snapping in two beneath his forehead while his purple blood freezes into red ice before it can soak through the manila cards spilling from his haversack.

"The Bavarian debtor-company at the rear-guard cairn has thrown down its carbines, General!" screams Colonel Kalakaua the younger—a thirty-year-old Oahu graduate whose brown Polynesian cheeks are grey and peeling with the high-altitude frostbite—as he stumbles down the icy boulders from the tail of the column, his left hand clutching a jagged, nine-inch Afghan *choora* knife-wound in his ribs through which his dark wool tunic is steaming in the zero air. "The tribesmen didn't wait for the artillery to unlimber—they came down the dry watercourse on the flank with their long knives while our boys were trying to thaw the grease in their rifle-bolts over burning telegraph-poles! They’ve hamstrung the mule-teams on the howitzer-sleds, and they’re cutting the brass number-tags off our wounded while they’re still breathing!"

Kuroda does not look down at the dead assessor at his boots. Drawing his nine-shot automatic pistol with his stiff, fingerless left glove, he steps up onto the frozen iron draw-bar of the stalled tractor, his cropped head bare to the whistling sleet as a second volley of jezail-balls spanks off the rock wall above us, showering his shoulders with granite splinters.

"Turn the two remaining three-inch mountain-guns around on the sled-runners and fire canister straight back down the defile through the Bavarian company!"
