Kuroda roars against the howling wind of the pass, pointing his pistol barrel toward the writhing, screaming tangle of grey sheepskins and slate-blue coats two hundred yards up the narrow gut where a thousand bearded hillmen are leaping from boulder to boulder like mountain-goats, their three-foot curved blades flashing dull red in the twilight as a three-hundred-pound boulder levered from the upper ledge crashes squarely upon the tractor's frozen steam-dome and crushes Fleet-General Kuroda into the iron before his thumb can press the trigger.

***

Command of the bleeding column passed in that instant of escaping steam and shattered cast-iron to Brigadier Marcus Vance the third—grand-nephew of the lame Marshal in the Presidio solarium, and first in the class of nineteen-twelve at the Thalassia Staff College.

At twenty-eight, the third Marcus had never smelled burning pine-tar in a snow-shed or watched an artillery mule gutted for its tallow. He had earned his silver collar-numerals in the air-conditioned glass vaults of Oahu, writing a celebrated thesis upon *The Trigonometric Optimization of Coal-Collier Turnaround in the Coral Sea*. Now, as he scrambled out of the overturned staff-lorry with his fur-lined gauntlets smeared with Kuroda’s brains and his gold-rimmed pince-nez dangling by its silk ribbon against his cheek, he stared up at the darkening limestone walls of the defile like a clerk whose counting-house roof has suddenly caved in.

"Form the hollow square by cantons!" young Marcus screamed, his voice pitching up into a thin, reedy falsetto as he fumbled inside his velvet-lined map-case for the printed *Manual of Mountain Pacification* that the Monterey presses had issued at Peshawar. "Where is the wireless operator? Signal the air-cruiser station at Jelalabad to lay a curtain of white phosphorus along grid-sector nineteen! Why aren't the Bavarian companies dressing their ranks by the telegraph poles?"

"There are no telegraph poles left standing for forty miles to the east, Brigadier!" barked Sergeant-Major O’Higgins—a sixty-year-old grey-bearded survivor of the elder Vance’s Donner Pass rear-guard, whose left ear had been left behind in the Sierra snow thirty-two years ago—as he grabbed the young general by his gold-braided shoulder-strap and dragged him bodily behind the dead carcass of a frozen camel just as a volley of hammered iron nails and telegraph-wire slugs tore through the canvas hood of the lorry. "The hillmen chopped the cedar posts down on Tuesday to roast their mutton, and the wireless dynamo is at the bottom of the Kabul River with its wheels in the air! Put that paper book back in your pocket, boy, or by God none of us will ever see the Indus again!"

Marcus tore his arm free from the old Irishman’s grip, his soft, indoor cheeks blotched purple and white with terror and the zero wind. Down in the trough of the trail, five hundred Satsuma and Californian cadets were huddled in a frozen, sheep-like herd around the stalled baggage-wagons—not firing back at the flashes on the ridge, because their Polytechnic drill-regulations forbade independent volley-fire without range-finder elevation from a section-officer, and the Afridi marksmen had systematically shot every youth carrying a brass sextant or a pair of Zeiss binoculars through the forehead during the first hour of the march.

"I am the senior surviving graduate of the First Class!" Marcus shouted, pulling a silver-plated revolver from his patent-leather holster with fingers so numb he dropped the weapon twice into the bloody slush before his thumb found the safety-catch. "By General Order Four-Zero-Two, no rolling-stock or Hollerith ledger-chests may be abandoned to an unnumbered population! Uncouple the surviving mules from the hospital ambulances and hitch them to the two treasury-vans! If we leave the November tax-rolls of the Punjab in the snow, the Audit Board at Monterey will strike my cipher from the peerage!"

"The Audit Board isn't up on that ridge with a three-foot *khyber* knife, you little counting-house fool!" O’Higgins roared back, swinging the butt of his heavy magazine-carbine to smash the padlock off an ammunition-limber and tossing double handfuls of loose brass cartridges to the shivering Cantonese pioneers in the ditch. "Your grandfather left six-inch Krupp mortars in the Donner drift to save his men's skins, and his uncle rode a raw-boned mule through the Comanche fires with nothing in his saddle-bags but parched corn! If you hitch the ambulance-mules to those paper-wagons, four hundred frost-bitten boys will have their throats slit before the moon rises!"

"Insubordination under fire!" Marcus shrieked, leveling his silver pistol not at the turbaned shadows now pouring down the shale-slides fifty yards away with the terrible, ululating war-cry of the hills, but at the chest of the sixty-year-old sergeant-major. "Hitch the mules to the audit-vans, Sergeant-Major, or I’ll have you shot against the wheel! The records of the Hundred and Twenty-Eighth Canton must reach the Peshawar wire before—"

He never finished the regulation. From the overhanging crag directly above the stalled treasury-van, an eighty-year-old Ghilzai grandfather in a greased wolf-skin coat didn't even bother to waste a lead bullet on the boy with the gold eye-glasses; he simply tipped a forty-pound fire-pot of blazing pine-resin and camel-dung over the lip of the rock.

The clay jar burst squarely atop the varnished roof of the audit-wagon, showering young Marcus Vance’s slate-gray shoulders with liquid fire and setting ten thousand perforated manila census-cards roaring up into the freezing night like a chimney-flue—a bright, orange beacon against the snow by whose light the hillmen came in among the baggage-train with the steel.

***

Twelve hundred miles west of that burning wagon in the Kabul gorge, the winter wind off the Elburz mountains rattled the loose, diamond-paned casements of the Golestan Palace in Tehran, blowing a fine, gritty dust of dried salt-marsh and pulverized brick across the faded Shiraz carpets of the Hall of Mirrors.

Lady Kaiulani did not sit in her wheeled chair; the jolting forty-hour journey up from the British-built railhead at Basra in an unheated military ambulance-van had inflamed the pleurisy in her eighty-four-year-old lungs until she could breathe only when propped upright at a forty-five-degree angle upon a camp-bed of folded grey army blankets set directly before the smoking charcoal brazier.

She wore neither the mourning silk of the Oahu court nor the sable cape of Geneva. Over her shrunken, fever-racked chest was buttoned old Field-Marshal Marcus Vance’s spare field-greatcoat of coarse Californian wool, smelling of camphor and stale tobacco, which the dying general had taken off his own shoulders at the Suez landing-slip when the cable arrived that his grand-nephew had lost forty thousand men and all the siege-trains in the snows between Jelalabad and Jamrud.

Across the brazier, sitting cross-legged upon a divan of tattered crimson brocade from which the gold thread had been picked out during the famine of nineteen-sixteen to buy Russian kerosene, reclined Ahmad Shah Qajar, the twenty-two-year-old King of Kings of Persia—a fat, sulky youth in a tall black astrakhan cap with an uncut three-carat diamond pinned to the front, flanked by four grey-bearded Mujtahids of the Shi’a clergy and the Warlord of the Bakhtiari horse-tribes, whose bandoliers of British .303 cartridges clinked against his silver-mounted dagger every time he scratched his lice.

"At Calcutta five winters ago, Great Lady, your Fleet-General Kuroda told the Nizam of Hyderabad that the Pacific Ocean needed no allies who rode horses," the Bakhtiari khan said in guttural, camp-fire Hindustani, spitting a husk of roasted pumpkin-seed straight into the charcoal embers between Kaiulani’s small, wool-stockinged feet. "Now Fleet-General Kuroda’s skull is nailed to the gate-post of the Bala Hissar in Kabul, and the Turkoman raiders from Merv have cut your broad-gauge track at Kushka and burned sixty of your oil-cars on the Oxus bank. Why does the grandmother of the Sacred Sun come coughing through the mud of Mesopotamia with ten mules of silver thalers at her tail, instead of sending the flying iron ships to blow the mountains flat?"

Kaiulani did not wipe the grey charcoal-ash from her chin. Beneath her cropped white hair, her cataract-milky eyes stared through the faceted glass reflections of the walls as if she were looking back across sixty-seven years of water and iron—back to the afternoon when Elias Thorne had ridden into Monterey with four batteries of brass twelve-pounders and dictated the law of the hemisphere to governors who crawled on their knees for a railway-station.

Then, the Empire had been young, and a single regiment of boys with repeaters could buy a kingdom for a handful of telegraph-wire. Now the iron hoop was stretched around twenty-five thousand miles of earth; the German and Russian debtor-cantons were taking three hundred thousand bayonets to hold down; the black grippe was rotting the examination-sheds at Berkeley; and here, in a freezing mud-walled room at the back of Asia, the last Regent of the Pivot had to beg a twenty-two-year-old mountain thief to guard her flank.

"The flying ships do not rise when the ice is on the wings, Sardar," Kaiulani whispered, every breath rasping in her throat like a rusty saw drawn through wet koa-wood, while beside her camp-bed Junior Prefect Hoshino the younger—whose father had burned in the naphtha on the Hankow steps thirty-two years before—held an open tin of warm Californian condensed milk that she could no longer swallow. "And my grandson has no desire to waste the boys of Oahu and Satsuma hunting goats among the rocks of Herat. Take the iron boxes off the pack-frames, Hoshino."

Four Hawaiian marine-guards—the last survivors of her personal household company, their blue tunics patched at the elbows with grey canvas and their boots tied together with copper telegraph-wire—stepped forward and pried open three unpainted pine chests with their bayonets, spilling a dull, heavy cascade of minted San Francisco silver thalers and five hundred new, grease-packed Sacramento magazine-carbines across the worn wool of the carpet.

"We do not ask the Shah-in-Shah to shave his head or sit in the examination-cubicles," Kaiulani continued, her thin, bluish lips curling in the ghost of that cold Polynesian smile that had once bought the kings of Peru and Siam. "Keep your astrakhan caps; keep your mullahs and your customs-houses at Bushire. The Chancery of Thalassia repeals the Mesopotamian Tariff-Ordinance of nineteen-fifteen. We will pay your Bakhtiari and Qashqai horsemen four million silver thalers a year out of the Abadan petroleum-royalties, and deliver twenty thousand magazine-rifles with five hundred rounds apiece at the Bandar Abbas wharf before the spring equinox—provided your tribesmen ride east to the Hari Rud river before Tuesday and cut the throat of every Afghan or Turkoman rebel who tries to cross the desert toward our oil-pipes at Basra."

Young Ahmad Shah leaned greedily forward over his bolster, his pudgy fingers digging into the pile of silver coins like a child in a sand-heap; but the old Bakhtiari khan did not touch the money. He picked up one of the new Sacramento carbines, worked the bolt twice with a practiced, oily *snick-snack*, and looked down at the dying old woman in the soldier’s coat.

"Four million thalers is the price of the spring grass, Lady," the khan said softly, resting the hot muzzle of the American carbine across his knee. "In the autumn, when the snow closes the Russian tracks again and your sick boys in the Basra hospital are dying of the marsh-ague, the price of the winter guard will be eight million—and the four twelve-pounder mountain-guns from your escort train."

Kaiulani closed her cloudy eyes and let her head sink back into the rough wool of Marcus Vance’s collar.

*Give them the guns,* she thought in the dark, listening to the Persian khan’s spurs jingling as his men began to drag the silver-chests out the door before the parchment was even signed. *That was how the Caesars at Ravenna paid the Goths when the legions forgot how to march in the snow. This year we buy them off with silver and carbines; next year Kalanimoku will make this horse-thief a Patrician of the Senate; and ten winters from now, when the Molokai turbines lose their pressure, they will ride down to the sea and stable their mares in the marble baths of Thalassia.*

***

Yet even the Bakhtiari horsemen whom the dying Queen-Mother hired with her silver could only patrol the flat salt-deserts along the Persian border; they did not dare ride ten leagues eastward into the jagged black teeth of the Hindu Kush, where the spring thaw of 1920 uncovered the reality of what our Monterey war-bulletins called the *Pacification of the One Hundred and Thirty-First Canton*, and what the soldiers in the armored blockhouses called the *Hidden War*.

To the Chronicler who remained at the fortified railhead of Peshawar through that burning May—watching the third-generation Polytechnic engineers attempt to repair by pure horse-power the prestige that young Brigadier Vance had left burning in the Kurd-Kabul snow—the struggle presented the most terrible paradox of our history: the total impotence of the world’s mightiest industrial machine when confronted by an enemy who possessed nothing worth bombarding.

In the Great Indian War, and again in the liquidation of Europe, the victory of the Pacific had been swift and mathematically certain because the English, the French, and the Germans lived inside the same nineteenth-century house of iron and paper as ourselves. When Fleet-General Kuroda dropped a two-thousand-pound picric shell into a railway junction at Calcutta or cut the telegraph-trunk outside Brussels, three million urban mechanics starved within forty-eight hours and came out with their hands up to beg for a brass wrist-tag.

Here in the labyrinth of dry limestone canyons and twenty-thousand-foot glaciers between the Indus and the Oxus, there was no nerve-center to sever. Kabul itself was only a sprawling mud-brick village whose bazaar could be burned to the ground on Monday and rebuilt out of river-clay on Thursday; there were no banks to foreclose, no factory-chimneys to range upon with our stereoscopic sights, and no parish registers in which to punch a Hollerith card.

When Emperor Kalanimoku, stung to fury by the loss of Kuroda’s column, ordered the Osaka and Pittsburg arsenals in March to send out the First Heavy Land-Flotilla—sixty forty-ton *Leviathan*-class steam-tanks, each plated in two inches of cemented nickel-steel, propelled by twin kerosene-fired flash-boilers on broad caterpillar-treads, and mounting a six-pounder Hotchkiss cannon and four water-cooled Maxim guns in revolving sponsons—the young prefects at Thalassia calculated that the mountain passes would be swept clean of bandits at a fuel-expenditure of twelve gallons to the linear mile.

On the twelfth of May, I rode in the armored observation-tender behind the vanguard of the Seventh Land-Flotilla as twelve of those rumbling, oil-belching iron tortoises crawled at four miles an hour up the dry boulder-bed of the Panjshir valley, forty miles north of the ruined Kabul cantonment.

The heat inside the steel hull was a hundred and thirty degrees Fahrenheit; the air smelled suffocatingly of vaporized kerosene, hot brass, scorching asbestos boiler-lagging, and the sour sweat of the eight Cantonese and Californian mechanic-gunners who sat half-naked upon the iron floor-plates, their eyes glued to the narrow prismatic periscopes while the sixty-horsepower steam-cylinders hammered like trip-hammers between their knees.

Outside in the blinding white glare of the noon sun, the valley was as empty and silent as a crater of the moon. Not a single turbaned head showed above the grey stone *sangars* on the ridges; the terraced mulberry-orchards and the flat-roofed mud villages along the stream had been abandoned three days before, their inhabitants carrying off every grain of barley and driving their sheep up into the twelve-thousand-foot snow-fields where no forty-ton machine could ever climb.

"Seven miles from the entrance of the gorge, Citizen-Historian, and we haven't seen a target worth a six-pounder shell," shouted Tank-Commander Lieutenant Sato—Candidate Zero-Nine-Two-Two of the class of nineteen-seventeen—wiping the black cylinder-grease from his chin as he leaned down from the forward turret-basket to tap the brass steam-gauge. "The tribesmen took one look at the two-inch Krupp plate at Charikar last week and ran for the Pamirs! Once our pioneer gangs lay the six-foot sleepers through this cut tomorrow, we can run the armored trains straight through to the Oxus!"

He had scarcely taken his fingers from the gauge when the lead forty-ton *Leviathan*—lumbering fifty yards ahead of our bow across a narrow, dry gravel-fan where a mountain torrent came down from the limestone cliffs—suddenly pitched its iron snout forty-five degrees downward into the earth with a dull, hollow *boom* of collapsing timber.

There had been no mine exploded; our electric induction-sweepers mounted on the front horns of the tank would have detected five pounds of iron casing three feet under the stones. Instead, four hundred Tajik and Ghilzai women and children, working by night with wooden shovels and goat-skin baskets without a single scrap of metal on their bodies, had dug a twenty-foot pit across the torrent-bed, roofed it over with split juniper-poles and river-shingle to match the dry wash, and lined the bottom with ten tons of loose, greasy soapstone boulders.

As the forty-ton iron monster crashed through the juniper roof, its left caterpillar-track sheared its bronze drive-pins against the soapstone; the flash-boiler pipe snapped at the flange, filling the sealed steel hull instantly with three-hundred-degree superheated steam that parboiled the eight numbered cadets inside like lobsters in a pot before a single hatch could be unbolted.

And before our second tank could reverse its steam-valves in the narrow defile, the empty, sun-baked cliff-face sixty feet above our roofs came alive.

No rifles were fired against our two-inch armor. From behind a hundred grey boulders that looked part of the mountain wall, three hundred ragged men in earth-colored wool leaped straight down onto the flat steel decks of the stalled machines where our gun-sponsons could not elevate to reach them.

Through the three-inch glass block of my periscope, I saw a barefoot sixteen-year-old boy with a tangled black beard and a tattered blue turban land like a mountain-cat directly atop the ventilator-grating of Lieutenant Sato’s turret. The youth carried neither a rifle nor a bomb; he held in his left hand a heavy iron shepherd’s crowbar, and in his right a greasy goatskin bag filled with ten pounds of fine, dry quartz-sand and powdered sheep-dung.

"Traverse the dorsal Maxim! Clear the roof!" Sato screamed, slamming the iron lever of the steam-siren as two more hillmen jammed their iron crowbars straight between the teeth of our rear drive-sprockets, locking the caterpillar-treads solid with a screech of stripping steel gears.

Up on the roof, the barefoot boy did not wait for the machine-gun turret to turn. Bracing his heel against the hot chimney-cowl, he poured the entire goatskin of dry quartz-sand and dung straight down the air-intake funnel of the forced-draft blower—and then, as the high-speed fan sucked the grit into the main engine-bearings and seized the pistons in a blinding cloud of black, oily smoke that filled our cabin to the roof, a second hillman stuffed a burning rag soaked in stolen kerosene down the periscope-shaft while the crowbars outside began to pry at the red-hot bolts of the forward hatch.

Only the arrival of the third observation-tender’s external shrapnel-howitzer—which fired a canister round directly across our buckled deck-plates, sweeping both the tribesmen and our own brass periscope-hoods into the gravel—allowed my driver to uncouple the armoured trailer and drag our crippled hull backward down the dry wash toward Charikar.

***

We left eleven forty-ton *Leviathans* smoking in the Panjshir stones that afternoon, at a cost to the San Francisco Treasury of four million silver thalers; and by the time the cable-summary of that week’s wastage passed through the submarine repeaters to the middle of the Pacific, the price of ten pounds of Afghan quartz-sand was shaking the marble floor of the Crystal Palace.

Lady Kaiulani had been brought back from the Persian Gulf in June aboard the hospital-cruiser *Oahu*, kept alive only by the oxygen-cylinders that the naval surgeons strapped beside her berth. On the nineteenth of July, 1920, against the frantic protests of her niece Malia, she ordered her bearers to carry her koa-wood chair not up to the screened privacy of the Whispering Gallery, but straight out onto the lower porphyry rostrum of the Pan-Pacific Senate, directly beneath the empty bronze curule chair of her grandson.

Emperor Kalanimoku was not upon the dais; he had secluded himself three miles away in the fortified Naval Chart-Room at Waipahu, refusing to meet the provincial assessors until the Osaka arsenals completed the eighty new *Titan*-class mountain-tanks he had requisitioned over the Treasury’s veto. Down in the five concentric rings of koa-wood stalls, however, the docile chorus of nineteen-sixteen had vanished.

The chilled mountain water-curtains were no longer sheeting down the outer Jena glass of the dome; the geothermal conduits from Molokai had been diverted since April to power the twin-shift electrolytic aluminum furnaces at Pearl Lochs, and the equatorial noon beat straight through the dry panes, heating the vast greenhouse to ninety-six degrees and filling the stagnant air with the sour smell of six hundred sweating wool robes, overheated transformer-varnish, and the bruised, rotting ginger-garlands wilting around the bronze pillars.

Nobody was chanting the *Pax Pacifica*. Five hundred andforty senators were standing upon their feet at once, not reaching for their green acclamation-levers, but waving long, violet-inked strips of canton clearing-house paper and shouting in English, Cantonese, and Japanese across the marble gulf at Prefect-Chancellor Shen.

"Fourteen percent discount upon the silver canal-scrip in the Shanghai rice-alleys since Tuesday!" roared Senior Senator Wu of the Forty-Sixth Yangtze Canton—not a rebellious colonial sheep-farmer like old MacArthur, who had died in the Melbourne grippe-wards the winter before, but a life-long graduate of the First Class whose collar bore the silver numerals of the Hankow Iron Trust. He stepped out into the central aisle, shaking a fistful of depreciated Market Street Treasury notes straight toward the steel podium. "For eight months you have requisitioned every ton of Hanyang pig-iron and every barrel of Borneo fuel-oil to build forty-ton steam-coffins that the hill-bandits in Kabul crack open with ten-cent crowbars! Our river-barges from Ichang to Nanking are tied up to the mud-banks for want of kerosene, our foundry-puddlers are being paid in unstamped paper that will not buy three ounces of salt-fish, and this morning the Chancery Assessors demand another ninety million silver thalers for a third winter mobilization on the Indus!"

"And the California orchards are rotting on the boughs!" shouted Assessor Miller of the Third Sacramento Canton from the upper tier, slamming the lid of his koa-wood desk so violently that the brass ink-horn leaped from its socket and rolled down the steps. "You took forty thousand of our Mexican and Cantonese harvest-hands in March to lay six-foot sleepers through the Khyber snow, and not five hundred have come back with their toes on their boots! The San Joaquin grain-syndicates will not honor another War-Benevolence warrant while the gold reserve in the Rincon Hill vaults sits below twenty percent!"

Up on the porphyry rostrum, Prefect-Chancellor Shen stood gripping the edges of the steel lectern, his spectacles fogged with sweat, the electric tally-board behind his head flashing a chaotic, stuttering blizzard of red refusal-bulbs as canton after canton broke the circuit.

"Conscript Fathers!" Shen’s amplified voice cracked across the vault with a harsh metallic feedback screech. "By the Constitutional Statute of Nineteen-Fourteen, military appropriations certified under the Sacred Emperor’s war-seal are exempt from provincial audit! If the Hankow and Sacramento chambers suspend the July silver-remittance, the Bureau of Integration will close the telegraph-clearing houses at six o’clock!"

"Close them and see who starves first, clerk!" bellowed thirty voices from the Satsuma and Osaka shipping-benches, as the great syndicate-factors who had grown fat on the looting of London now saw their own turbine-liners rusting empty at the buoys.

In her low chair beside the porphyry steps, eighty-five-year-old Lady Kaiulani slowly lifted her right hand from the grey wool lap-robe. She could no longer hold the heavy duralumin baton; she held only a light, hollow bamboo fan-stick, yet as she struck the bronze rim of the rostrum gong once—a thin, dry *ting* that barely reached the first row of benches—her niece Malia threw the master-switch of the dais microphones, and the amplification horns in the roof caught the rasp of the dying Queen’s breath.

"Be silent," Kaiulani whispered.

The roar of the six hundred stalls died away not out of fear of the Household Guards in the upper gallery—whose young officers stood looking nervously at one another with their hands off their holsters—but because the sound of that ancient, rattling throat falling from the sixteen bronze horns was like the voice of the dead century speaking out of the Marianas mud.

"You shout at Chancellor Shen because your paper thalers have lost fourteen cents on the dollar in the Shanghai alleys," Kaiulani said, her cataract-white eyes staring straight out into the shimmering, uncooled heat of the dome while a drop of sweat trickled down her shrunken brown temple and caught against the ancient carved bone hook at her neck. "Did you think, when you clapped your hands three summers ago to buy the cathedrals of France and the iron-works of the Ruhr with spoiled guncotton, that the wheel only turns one way? You wanted an empire without a rim. You voted the ships to break Calcutta; you voted the conscription-trains to empty Vienna; you sat in these koa-wood chairs and cheered when my grandson told you that the world was a single ledger."

She leaned an inch forward against the leather strap that held her upright in the chair, her small, claw-like fingers pointing down at the pile of rejected violet warrants on the floor.

"Now you have reached the rock where there is nothing left to steal," she rasped, her breath whistling through the fluid in her chest. "A forty-ton steam-tank costs sixty thousand silver thalers at the Osaka dock, and a boy in a sheepskin coat destroys it with a handful of sand that costs him nothing. You cannot balance this book by shouting at the clerk. Either you vote the ninety million thalers today and eat barley-husks in San Francisco until the snow melts on the Hindu Kush, or you tell my grandson to pull up the six-foot rails and admit to four hundred million debtors from Antwerp to Benares that the Pacific gun can be stopped."

***

They did not vote the ninety million thalers.

When the division-bell rang at four o’clock through the stifling, ninety-eight-degree twilight of the Crystal Palace, three hundred and ninety-two red bulbs burned upon the basalt wall against two hundred and eight green; and for the first time since Elias Thorne had bolted the eighteen-inch cannon to the Fort Point casemate sixty-six years before, the treasury of the Great Arena refused the warrant of the camp.

To the Chronicler who stood five weeks later—on the sultry, dust-choked morning of the twenty-eighth of August, 1920—upon the stone parapet of the Jamrud Fort at the eastern mouth of the Khyber Pass, the consequence of those three hundred and ninety-two red electric lamps unrolled across the baked gravel plain of Peshawar like a funeral cortege that had lost its coffin.

The official bulletin pasted that morning upon the lime-washed bulletin boards of theHundred and Thirty Cantons did not employ the word *retreat*. Drafted by Prefect-Chancellor Shen himself in the cool language of the Berkeley engineering primers, it announced merely a *Rectification of the Trans-Indus Metering Perimeter*: having completed the punitive topographical survey of the Kabul basin, the Seventh and Ninth Imperial Corps were retiring to the permanent broad-gauge terminal along the right bank of the Indus to economize winter fuel-allocations.

Yet the forty thousand dark-skinned Punjabi and Rajput peasants who lined the dry irrigation-ditches outside the Jamrud cantonment—watching in dead, stony silence behind the leveled bayonets of our Choshu provost-cordons—did not need to read English or carry a slide-rule to understand what was coming down out of the narrow red jaws of the hills.

For sixty-eight years, the law of the Pivot had rested upon a single, unanswerable demonstration: where the six-foot track was laid down, it never came up again. Kingdoms might burn, plagues might empty the tenements, and three hundred thousand men might die in the snow, but the broad Bessemer rail crept forward like the basalt lava of Hawaii, turning everything behind its sleepers into numbered stone.

Now, out of the shimmering, hundred-and-ten-degree heat-haze of the Khyber defile, came the last armored flatcar-train of the Western Frontier, backing slowly down the two-percent grade toward the Indus at three miles an hour.

It was not pushing sleepers into the mountains; it was eating its own road.

Behind the blackened, dented steel skirt of the locomotive—whose cab-plates were starred and pock-marked by ten thousand soft-lead jezail slugs, and whose water-tender leaked a steady, rust-colored stream of boiling radiator-scum across the ties—rolled four heavy crane-cars manned by soot-blackened Californian and Cantonese pioneer-gangs. As the train crept backward yard by yard, the steam-grapples dropped their iron claws over the tail-board, wrenched the eighty-pound Bessemer rails loose from the creosoted Oregon pine sleepers with a high, agonizing screech of drawn spikes, and swung the thirty-foot steel bars up onto the flatcars like a defeated giant gathering up his broken spears.

Behind the crane-train marched the remnant of the Ninth Polytechnic Division.

There were no brass bands playing the Imperial Anthem, as they had played on the marble quays of Messina; there were no rigid duralumin air-cruisers hovering overhead to cast the shadow of the Sun-and-Anchor across the dust. In ragged columns of fours—their slate-gray wool tunics stiff with dried salt-sweat and gray mountain lice, their boots bound up with strips of raw sheepskin, and the silver numerals torn from half their collars so the Afridi knife-men would not single them out as officers in the night—sixteen thousand frost-scarred, dysentery-hollowed boys from Seattle, Kyoto, and Canton limped out of the pass, dragging their six-pounder Hotchkiss guns behind them on hand-ropes because the last of the traction-engines had been blown up with our own dynamite at Landi Kotal to keep their bronze bearings out of the tribesmen’s forges.

And five hundred yards behind our rear-most pioneer-squad, walking leisurely down the middle of the torn-up roadbed before the dust of the departing flatcars had even settled upon the crushed ballast-stone, came three hundred Afridi and Shinwari horsemen.

They did not fire a single shot at the retiring train; they did not need to. Sitting high in their wooden saddles with our captured model-ninety-eight Sacramento magazine-carbines slung across their greasy sheepskin shoulders and necklaces of brass Imperial ration-tags clinking around their stallions’ throats, they halted at the exact whitewashed stone cairn that marked the old British boundary-line, dismounted in the hot sun, and began to pry the remaining Oregon pine sleepers out of the gravel with iron bars to build a bonfire for their noon tea.

Beside me on the Jamrud parapet, Senior Engineer-Prefect Sato—the older brother of that Lieutenant Sato who had been pulled half-blinded out of the Panjshir tank in May—stood with his hands gripping the scorching sandstone battlement. He did not raise his Zeiss binoculars to look at the tribesmen burning the ninety-cent sleepers; his eyes were fixed downward upon the inner courtyard of the fort.

There, in the shadow of the commissariat grain-sheds, a company of our own Autonomous Rajput Lancers—men whose fathers had bowed to the ground before Lady Kaiulani on the Shwedagon steps six winters ago—were sitting their horses with grounded lances. They were not mutinying; their tunics were buttoned to the chin in strict Monterey regulation. Yet as the last crane-car pulled the final pair of six-foot rails through the iron gates of the perimeter and the Cantonese blacksmiths swung the barriers shut, the Rajput subadar slowly turned his head and looked up at the pillar of black pine-smoke rising from the abandoned track half a mile away.

The Indian officer did not speak a word to his troopers; he simply spat a red stream of betel-juice squarely onto the stone threshold of the Pacifica telegraph-office.

"They have seen the iron go backward, Citizen-Historian," Prefect Sato said quietly at my shoulder, his fingers trembling so violently upon the sandstone that the duralumin circular calculator slipped from his belt-loop and struck the parapet flags with a tinny ring. "For sixty years we held three hundred million of them with ten thousand clerks because they believed our gauge was a law of nature, like the monsoon or the tide. Now a thousand barefoot goat-herds with iron crowbars have pried up the track in broad daylight, and before the moon is full tonight, every bazaar from Calcutta to the Amur will know that the circumference has a crack."

***

The bazaar-rumor did not walk on camel-back; it traveled by the very copper wires that Elias Thorne had strung across the world to bind his provinces together, and it reached the frozen birch-forests of the Sixty-Fourth Siberian Canton before the first September snow-squall blew down from the Sea of Okhotsk.

To the Chronicler who was ordered northward from Peshawar that autumn via the Tashkent-Irkutsk military junction—accompanying the Special Audit Commission sent out to investigate why the August deliveries of Lake Baikal copper-matte and Lena pit-props had fallen forty percent below the Hollerith projections—the journey across the Roof of Asia was like passing through the chambers of an enormous iron clock whose mainspring was slowly uncoiling in the dark.

Ever since the Brussels Liquidation Accord of nineteen-eighteen, the vast sub-arctic wilderness stretching from the Yenisei River to the Stanovoy Mountains had served as the subterranean ash-pit of the Great Arena. Into those three thousand miles of larch-swamp, permafrost, and open-cut copper-shale, Prefect-Chancellor Shen’s demographic tabulators had poured four million unassimilated European war-debtors—former Prussian artillerymen, French mechanics from the ruined Saint-Étienne arsenals, Yorkshire coal-hewers, and Russian veterans of Generalissimo Brusilov’s dissolved regiments—each wearing the riveted lead-and-brass shackle of the Relief Commission upon his left wrist, digging ore and felling railway-timbers at fourteen degrees below zero to pay the interest on their burned cities.

So long as the armoured broad-gauge trains rolled punctually every forty-eight hours out of the Vladivostok and Hanyang depots, bringing the winter tallow-tubs and the fresh relief-battalions of Satsuma and Californian cadets, the four million wrist-tags had swung their picks in silence.

Then came the summer of the Afghan drain, when the coal-colliers were held in port by the Senate’s treasury-veto and half the Siberian garrison-companies were stripped from the timber-stockades to hold the Indus line.

On the night of the fourteenth of October, 1920, our three-car armoured audit-train lay stalled on a high wooden trestle-siding at Mining-Sector Nine—the great *Krasny-Yar* copper-and-shale pit eighty miles north of the Chita junction, where sixty thousand German, Russian, and Polish debtor-masons worked in three eight-hour shifts beneath the glare of overhead carbon-arcs to feed the Osaka smelting-furnaces.

The air outside our double-glazed observation windows was twenty-two degrees below zero; there was no wind, and the smoke from the great brick roasting-kilns at the bottom of the two-mile-wide terraced canyon rose straight up toward the green, flickering curtains of the northern aurora like solid pillars of yellow sulfur, smelling of scorched iron-pyrites, frozen human night-soil, and boiled horse-tallow.

Inside the steam-heated saloon-car, Senior Auditor Hoshino—who had come up from the Persian gulf after leaving the dying Queen-Mother at Oahu—sat before a green-baize table covered with unpunched manila cards, his brow furrowed behind his spectacles as he tapped the dead brass key of the portable field-telegraph.

"The repeater at Nerchinsk has not answered the nine-o’clock parity-check, Citizen-Historian," Hoshino said, his breath frosting slightlyeven inside the heated car as the boiler-pressure in our locomotive dropped for lack of dry birch-cordwood. "And the pit-superintendent here has delivered only fourteen gondolas of crushed matte since noon instead of forty. Look down at the third gallery: why have they shut off the pneumatic rock-drills before the ten-o’clock bell?"

I wiped the rime from the inner pane with my fur gauntlet and looked down into the blinding, white-and-violet glare of the open-cut abyss five hundred feet below our trestle.

The rhythmic, deafening *chug-chug-chug* of the three hundred Ingersoll-Osaka steam-drills that usually shook the permafrost night and day had stopped dead. Along the icy, twenty-foot-wide granite ledges of the lower galleries, where the narrow-gauge ore-tubs ran on iron rails toward the central hoisting-shaft, twenty thousand men in padded grey canvas coats and frozen bast-shoes were standing motionless in the snow.

They had not thrown down their four-pound sledges or their six-foot steel crowbars; they held them balanced across their shoulders like pikes. Up on the timber guard-towers at the four corners of the pit, the solitary Choshu and Hawaiian sentries—boys of nineteen who had been kept on double-watch for three months without relief, their hands wrapped in greasy rags around the frozen water-jackets of their Maxim guns—were leaning over the pine rails, shouting down through tin megaphones into the yellow sulfur-fog.

"Shift Three to the rock-face!" bawled the megaphone from Tower Two, the thin, cracked voice of the Oahu corporal echoing across the silent canyon. "Clear the ore-switches on Gallery Four, or the night-gruel ration is forfeited!"

Down on the bottom step of Gallery Four, beside the red-hot cast-iron brazier where the drill-bits were tempered, a tall, gaunt man in the tattered, sleeveless coat of a former Prussian pioneer-major stepped out of the ranks.

Through my field-glasses, I saw him hold his left arm straight out over the white-hot coals of the forge—not to warm his fingers, but to lay the lead-and-brass debtor-shackle on his wrist squarely across the iron anvil beside the fire. With a single, measured blow of a ten-pound smith’s hammer, a bearded Russian forge-striker sheared the Monterey rivet in two; the Prussian raised his bleeding, liberated wrist high into the violet glare of the carbon-arcs and flung the stamped brass number-plate straight into the melting-pot.

"The Khyber track is up, brothers!" the German’s deep, baritone roar rolled from terrace to terrace up the frozen stone amphitheater, repeated instantly in Russian, Polish, and English by fifty voice-leaders along the galleries. "The hillmen have burned the tanks at Kabul, and there hasn't been a troop-train through Irkutsk since the September frost! There are sixty thousand of us in the ditch, and eighty sick boys on the wall with frozen water-guns!"

Up in Tower Two, the nineteen-year-old Oahu corporal slammed the brass thumb-piece of his Maxim gun forward.

A dull, metallic snap echoed across the rim.

The firing-pin fell upon a chamber locked solid with twenty-degree grease and frozen condensation; not a single cartridge exploded. Before the boy could draw his cleaning-rod or unbuckle his nine-shot pistol from beneath his sheepskin coat, forty Russian and Yorkshire quarry-blasters on the ledge directly beneath the tower-stilts did not climb the ladder—they simply swung two hundred-pound wooden boxes of thawing nitro-glycerine against the frozen larch-wood pilings and touched their red-hot drill-irons to the grease-paper.

The northern wall of the canyon vanished in a blinding, sky-high geyser of yellow flame and splintered timber that blew Tower Two and its Maxim gun three hundred feet into the air across the pit, severed the main high-tension copper power-line from the Chita dynamos in a sizzling shower of blue ten-thousand-volt sparks, and plunged the entire two-mile gorge into pitch blackness—save for the red glare of the forge-braziers and the sudden, terrifying roar of sixty thousand iron-shod boots charging straight up the timbered haulage-ramps toward our railway-siding.

"Reverse the locomotive! Cut the audit-vans loose from the coal-tender!" screamed Auditor Hoshino, leaping up from the green-baize table as the shock-wave of the nitro-glycerine blast shattered every double-paned window in our saloon-car and showered his unpunched Hollerith cards with jagged needles of frozen glass. He tore open the iron door to the forward platform, his horn-rimmed spectacles flying off into the dark as he hammered with both fists against the armored bulkhead of the engine-cab. "Engineer! Open the throttle for the Chita main-line before they reach the trestle switches!"

Ahead of us in the freezing dark, the cab-door of the giant six-foot-gauge Baldwin locomotive did not open to the Auditor’s knock. Instead, from the footplate where our two deportee firemen—a former locomotive-artificer from Lyons and a boilermaker from Essen—had been shoveling birch-logs since sunset, came the dull, heavy *thud* of an iron coal-pick striking flesh, and the body of our Californian cadet-engineer rolled lifelessly down the icy iron steps onto the snow-bank beside the track, while the tall figure of the French fireman leaned out of the cab window with a stolen service-revolver in his soot-blackened fist and fired twice into Hoshino’s chest, toppling the Senior Auditor backward over the coupling-chains just as my clerk dragged me out the rear vestibule door into the sub-zero scrub-pine.

***

Four hundred miles west of that slaughtered audit-train, where the black, unfreezing rapids of the Angara River boiled out of the ice-crust of Lake Baikal, Brigadier Marcus Vance the third did not risk his gold-rimmed pince-nez within reach of a deportee’s coal-pick.

He stood five thousand feet above the snow-buried stockades of the Irkutsk Timber-Canton, inside the electrically heated aluminum control-gondola of the rigid dirigible *Vengeance of Oahu*.

The scars of the Kurd-Kabul defile were still raw and purple across his soft cheeks where the burning pine-resin from the Afghan fire-pot had splashed him before Sergeant-Major O’Higgins dragged him onto a pack-mule; his left ear-lobe was missing, taken off by a surgeon’s shears at Peshawar to stop the gangrene, and his hands inside his wired silk flying-gloves twitched with a perpetual, rhythmic tremor whenever a gust of wind off the Stanovoy peaks made the duralumin deck-plates creak beneath his boots. Yet he had not been struck from the peerage. Because Emperor Kalanimoku could not admit to the rebellious Senate that a Vance had lost forty thousand men to barefoot goat-herds, the young brigadier had been quietly transferred northward across the Gobi by aero-transport to command the Aerial Suppression Flotilla of the Baikal Sector.

"The rebel column from the Chita copper-pits has broken into the central marshaling-yards at Innokentyevskaya, Brigadier," reported Flight-Captain Noguchi, his face illuminated from below by the pale green glow of the stereoscopic drift-sight set into the glass floor between their feet. "They have six captured broad-gauge locomotives under steam and are mounting the depot's two-inch Hotchkiss field-pieces onto flatcars. Our surviving garrison—three hundred Californian and Cantonese railway-guards—is barricaded inside the brick grain-elevator by the river, with forty thousand Prussian and Russian quarry-men piling oil-soaked sleepers against the walls."

Marcus did not look down through the glass floor-plate; the sight of tiny dark figures swarming over a stalled train in the snow made the burnt skin on his neck prickle with cold sweat.

Instead, he kept his eyes fixed upon the polished brass pressure-gauges of the chemical ballast-tanks lining the bulkhead. Around the *Vengeance of Oahu*, flying in a tight, twelve-point diamond formation across the bitter, starlit Siberian night, rode the eleven sister-ships of the Third Aerial Division—six-hundred-foot cigars of duralumin lattice and silver-doped silk, their forty-eight Maybach-Osaka petroleum engines humming with a deep, synchronized drone that shook the dry frost crystals from the birch-forests a mile below.

"What is the barometric temperature on the river-ice, Captain?" Marcus asked, his voice high and tight as he fingered the silver collar-numerals at his throat.

"Twenty-six degrees below zero, sir, with a four-knot thermal inversion trapping the coal-smoke at three hundred feet above the roofs," Noguchi answered, glancing up from the brass eyepiece.

"Then the liquid phosgene will not evaporate on impact; it will settle into the cellars and the railway-cuts like water in a trough," Marcus said, a tiny, wet smile twitching at the corner of his scarred lip. In the Hindu Kush, the hillmen had hidden under fifty feet of overhanging limestone where no bomb could reach them, and the wind had torn his airships to rags. Here on the flat, frozen plain of the Angara, sixty thousand escaped European debtors and their families were packed inside two square miles of wooden barracks and brick marshaling-sheds, without a single anti-aircraft cannon larger than an infantry rifle.

"Captain Noguchi, what is the replacement book-value of the Innokentyevskaya grain-elevator and the three hundred garrison-guards inside it?" Marcus asked, pulling his new, uncracked duralumin circular calculator from his fur-lined breast pocket.

Noguchi blinked behind his fur-trimmed goggles. "The grain-elevator holds forty thousand bushels of Manchurian barley, Brigadier, and the three hundred boys of the Seventy-First Guard are Berkeley third-year—"

"If the Chita mutineers seize the Baikal tunnel-mouths tomorrow morning, the demolition of the masonry arches will cost the Monterey Treasury fourteen million silver thalers and sever the Ural copper-supply for six months," Marcus interrupted, his trembling thumb spinning the logarithmic disc with frantic speed. "Three hundred third-class cadets and a brick granary represent less than half of one percent of the canton's capital capitalization. We will not attempt a low-altitude precision drop with picric-acid shells and risk a rifle-volley into our hydrogen cells. Signal the flotilla to open the main ballast-valves simultaneously."

"All twelve ships, sir?" Noguchi’s gloved hand hesitated half an inch above the brass telegraph-handle. "We are carrying eighty tons of pressurized chlorine-phosgene mixture and four thousand white-phosphorus incendiary cylinders! With this thermal inversion, the gas-cloud will drift straight across the municipal timber-workers' settlement and the hospital-stockade on the east bank—there are twelve thousand women and typhus-convalescents in those sheds who haven't joined the Chita column!"

"An unnumbered debtor who watches a mutiny from a window without lifting a shovel for the Emperor is a mutineer on half-ration, Captain!" Marcus shrieked, his voice breaking into the same reedy falsetto that had echoed through the Kurd-Kabul gorge before the fire-pot fell, his hand slapping the pistol-holster at his hip. "Open the valves across the entire grid-square, or I will log your cipher for court-martial before we touch the Vladivostok mooring-mast! Drop the phosphorus first to set the outer stockades burning, so they are driven inward toward the railway-cut—then dump the phosgene tanks into the middle of the funnel!"

Noguchi did not argue a second time with a Vance whose cheek twitched like a galvanized frog’s. He pulled the red master-lever three notches back against the brass quadrant.

Beneath the belly of the *Vengeance of Oahu*, the pneumatic bomb-bay doors parted with a sharp, greasy hiss of compressed air; and as the cold Siberian draft rushed up into the cabin, smelling of pine-needles and wood-smoke, twelve hundred fluted iron cylinders tumbled out of the racks of the squadron, trailing long, white-hot ribbons of igniting phosphorus down toward the yellow camp-fires of the railway yard.

Marcus stepped finally to the edge of the glass floor-panel and looked down between his boots.

A mile below, the wooden roofs of the hospital-sheds, the tarred timber stockades, and the stalled freight-cars erupted simultaneously into a geometric square of blinding, greenish-white fire that lit up the snow-plain for ten leagues around. Through the high-powered Zeiss lenses of the drift-sight, Marcus could see the dark, ant-like multitudes of the Chita rebels—along with the women dragging blankets from the burning barracks and the three hundred Californian cadets waving their blue-and-gold signal-flags frantically from the roof of the central grain-elevator—running wildly inward toward the only unburned ground in the canton: the deep, sunken granite trench of the six-foot railway cut.

Then the second flight of airships passed over the fire-ring and opened the two-inch brass stop-cocks of their chemical ballast-tanks.

No explosions followed; only a thick, heavy rain of pale yellow liquid that turned, the instant it struck the heat of the burning sleepers, into a dense, rolling fog of greenish-gray vapor five hundred yards wide and forty feet deep. Too heavy to rise through the freezing air, the cloud of phosgene and chlorine slid down the terraced snow-banks into the sunken railway-cut like liquid lead.

Within four minutes, the waving blue-and-gold flag atop the grain-elevator dropped over the parapet. Down in the trench between the six-foot Bessemer rails, the sixty thousand dark specks ceased to run; they did not fall individually, as men fall before rifle-fire, but collapsed in long, wind-rowed heaps against the locked wheels of the locomotives, clawing at their own throats as their lungs dissolved into hydrochloric acid, until the yellow fog covered the entire two-mile basin like a dirty sheep-fleece and nothing moved upon the snow except the flames of the burning hospital.

"Log the expenditure at seventy-two tons of chemical ordnance and four hundred gallons of Borneo benzine, Captain," Marcus Vance the third said, turning away from the glass pane and drawing his silk glove across his scarred cheek to wipe away the sweat. "And wire the Chancellery at Thalassia that the Baikal sector has balanced its labor-rolls for the winter at zero cost in rolling-stock."

***

When that telegram—accompanied by four photographic glass-plates taken at dawn from the reconnaissance-basket of the *Vengeance of Oahu* after the wind had blown the yellow vapor down the Angara—was laid upon the porphyry table of the Privy Cabinet at Thalassia on the morning of the twenty-fourth of October, the trade-wind outside the palace windows was blowing soft and warm through the blooming hibiscus, and the sixty-cycle transformers in the basement were humming their steady, sunlit chord.

Lady Kaiulani did not look at the glass plates through a stereoscope. Even through the milky white veil of her cataracts, when she held the four-by-five negative up against the blinding tropical glare of the veranda archway, she could make out the black, unmistakable geometry of the six-foot railway cut—and packed between the iron rails for two miles, frozen solid into a single grey pavement over which the pioneer-sleds were already laying new pine sleepers without bothering to dig graves, the twisted shapes of the women from the timber-sheds and the boys in the slate-gray coats of Berkeley.

Across the porphyry table, the twenty-eight-year-old Sacred Emperor Kalanimoku stood in his white linen Admiral’s undress, a silver pencil between his strong brown fingers as he initialed the promotion-warrant advancing Brigadier Marcus Vance the third to Marshal of the Northern Marches.

"With the Chita and Irkutsk pits cleared of the European strikers, we can bring eighty thousand fresh Cantonese and Javanese contract-coolies up the Amur line before the spring thaw," Kalanimoku said, his voice ringing with that hard, gravelly frontier cadence he had learned from the wax cylinders as he handed the wet sheet to Prefect-Chancellor Shen. "Tell Marshal Vance to leave the corpses frozen in the ballast along the sidings until April; when the new gangs step off the box-cars, the sight of forty thousand white debtors under the ties will save us two battalions of provost-guards."

Kaiulani slowly lowered the glass photographic plate to the table. She did not set it down gently; she let it drop from a height of six inches upon the polished stone, where it broke in two with a sharp, musical splintering of glass right across the Emperor’s signature.

Kalanimoku stopped his hand and looked down at his grandmother. For the first time in three years, she had refused her wheeled chair; supported on her left by old, lame Field-Marshal Marcus Vance—whose face was the color of wet salt-cod as he stared at the photograph of his grand-nephew’s handiwork—and on her right by her niece Malia, the eighty-five-year-old woman stood upright upon her two swollen, dropsical feet. She wore no silk of the Regency, nor the grey wool of the sick-room; she had put on a plain, coarse *holoku* of unbleached native tapa-bark, such as the fish-wives of Molokai wore when they went down into the salt-pans.

"Three hundred of those bodies in the ditch are your own cadets of the Seventy-First California Guard, Kalanimoku," Kaiulani whispered, her thin, rasping breath cutting through the quiet hum of the ceiling-fans. "Boys who passed the Monterey examination-sheds with your name stamped on their primers—gassed like wharf-rats in a grain-bin because young Vance was afraid to come down below five thousand feet and soil his gloves."

"They were an acceptable structural loss to save the Baikal tunnel-arches, Grandmother," Kalanimoku answered coldly, those pale gray eyes—the dead Protector's eyes—narrowing inside his smooth Polynesian face. "When my grandfather burned the cholera-ships at Panama, he did not ask whether the carpenters on the deck were from Kentucky or Canton. He counted the days to the opening of the locks."

"Your grandfather was a border-butcher who fought men with rifles in their hands so that this ocean might have a roof over its head!" Kaiulani’s voice rose suddenly from a whisper to a sharp, terrible cry that made the four Samoan guardsmen outside the veranda doors stiffen to attention. "I stood beside Elias Thorne for thirty years while we hammered the iron together, and I lied to my own dead brother’s ghost and told myself that the blood we spilled at Hankow and the Sacramento was the price of the peace! I cut the wire at Honolulu; I drowned Elias’s body in the deep water; I put the feathers of Kamehameha upon your shoulders and built you a house of glass so that you might rule like a father over living men!"

With a sudden, convulsive wrench of her shrunken brown hands, she reached up to her withered throat, seized the ancient braided hair-cord of the *lei niho palaoa*—the sacred curved hook of whale-tooth that had been the Regent’s seal of the Insular Chancery since the morning of the Sand Island truce—and tore the cord in two, flinging the heavy ivory pendant squarely across the broken glass negative at Kalanimoku’s knuckles.

"Take back your bone, grandson of the mainland!" she gasped, dark blood flecking her bluish lips as she leaned her feather-light weight against old Marcus Vance’s trembling arm. "You are no chief of Maui, and this is no city of peace! You have turned the Great Arena into an iron slaughter-house where children with numbers on their necks pour poison from the clouds upon women in their beds to save four cents on a ton of copper! Strike my name from the Regency rolls, Chancellor Shen! I will not die under a roof that is held up by frozen corpses—take me out to the leper-spit at Kalaupapa tonight, Malia, where the sea is clean and there isn't a telegraph-wire in the rocks!"

***

They carried the old Queen out of the palace at sunset aboard a coast-guard steam-launch, with retired Field-Marshal Marcus Vance sitting silent and uncovered upon a coil of tarred hemp at her feet, leaving the twenty-eight-year-old Emperor alone beneath the sixty-cycle lights of the Chart-Room; yet before her boat had even crossed the Molokai channel, the poison-cloud of Irkutsk had begun to rain back down in blood six thousand miles to the southwest.

To the Chronicler who was hurried southward from Vladivostok that November aboard the fast turbine-cruiser *Sendai*—transferred in mid-winter from the frozen birch-forests of the Baikal to the steaming, ninety-degree rubber-jungles of the One Hundred and Fourteenth Malayan Canton after the Singapore submarine cable went dead on the twelfth of the month—the speed with which the Siberian contagion leaped from the snow to the equator demonstrated that the machine had finally taught its slaves how to break the wheels.

For forty years, the great tropical plantation-belt of the Confederation—the tin-mines of Perak, the gutta-percha forests of Borneo, the petroleum-wells of Sumatra, and the endless, terraced rubber-estates of Mindanao and Cochin-China—had been the quietest, most profitable cellar of the Empire. There, beneath a perpetual green twilight of banyan and teak where no dreadnought could steam and no air-cruiser could see the ground through the hundred-foot canopy, three million indentured Tamil, Javanese, and Cantonese coolies—joined since nineteen-eighteen by eight hundred thousand deported French, Belgian, and Ukrainian labor-conscripts—bled the white latex from the trees and pumped the crude naphtha into the coastal pipe-lines.

When the news of the Innokentyevskaya gas-massacre reached the Singapore and Batavia docks—not through the censored Monterey bulletins, which spoke only of an accidental explosion in a chemical magazine, but carried word-for-word by the Ukrainian and Cantonese stokers of the returning ore-colliers who had smelled the burned flesh on the Vladivostok wind—the four hundred thousand European deportees in the Malayan jungle did not wait in their barracks to be strangled with chlorine in their sleep.

Unlike the quarry-men at Chita, they did not gather in an open railway-cut where a dirigible could find them.

On the afternoon of the twenty-eighth of November, 1920, I stood inside the sandbagged redoubt of Pumping-Station Six—forty miles up the muddy Pahang River in the interior of the Malay Peninsula, where the thirty-inch steel petroleum conduit from the central storage-tanks crossed the jungle gorge beside the narrow-gauge rubber-tramway.

The heat beneath the corrugated-iron roof of the blockhouse was a hundred and four degrees in the shade, saturated with the stench of rotting bamboo-leaves, stagnant river-slime, boiling crude petroleum, and the sharp, sweetish reek of the citronella-grease smeared over our faces to keep the malarial mosquitoes out of our eyes. Around the perimeter, the hundred-foot wall of the Pahang rain-forest stood thirty yards from the barbed wire—an impenetrable curtain of dripping green lianas, strangler-figs, and giant tree-ferns from which rose a continuous, deafening chorus of cicadas and the rhythmic, hollow *tok-tok-tok* of wooden slit-drums beaten miles away in the hills.

"Four days since the repair-train left Kuala Lipis, Citizen-Historian, and not a puff of smoke on the down-grade," said Captain Takahashi of the Nineteenth Satsuma Provosts, wiping the greenish sweat from the breech-block of his hot Maxim gun with an oily rag while his forty surviving cadets—half of them shaking with the tertian ague under their sodden slate-gray tunics—peered through the steel loop-holes into the green gloom. "Yesterday the air-cruiser *Kagoshima* came over the canopy at two thousand feet and dropped sixty tons of phosgene-cylinders along the river-trail where the telegraph-poles were cut. It didn't kill a single rebel! The triple-tier banyan leaves caught half the drums before they hit the mud, and the tropical updraft dissipated the gas in ten minutes—all it did was poison three miles of river-fish and blind our own Malay trackers in the launches!"

Down at the base of the timber trestle below the blockhouse, where the thirty-inch oil-pipe emerged from the dense brake of giant bamboo, a sudden, metallic ring of cold steel striking iron echoed through the afternoon stillness.

No bugle blew; no German major stepped out onto an anvil to shout a speech. Out of the dripping green fern-roots, smeared from head to foot with grey river-clay so that their naked skins vanished against the bark of the mangrove-trunks, wriggled two hundred men side by side: former French machine-fitters from the Creusot works with their brass debtor-tags filed off their wrists, bearded Cossack sappers from the Don, and sinewy Dyak and Moro wood-cutters carrying four-foot *parang* machetes between their teeth and heavy cast-iron pipe-wrenches stolen from our own tool-sheds.

"Depress the muzzle! Fire into the bamboo roots at thirty yards!" Takahashi yelled, his thumbs jamming the brass triggers of the Maxim forward as the gun began to hammer—sending a stream of .303 bullets ripping through the wet fern-fronds and splintering the green bamboo stems into white pulp.

The clay-smeared shadows did not charge the barbed wire of the blockhouse. While twenty Ukrainian riflemen lying flat in the mud behind the iron pipe-flanges returned a slow, deadly sniper-fire with captured Sacramento carbines—sending a heavy soft-nosed slug straight through the two-inch vision-slit beside my ear that took off the top of Takahashi’s skull and drenched my notebook in hot blood and brains—three French mechanics crawled underneath the curving belly of the thirty-inch petroleum main where our machine-gun bullets only ricocheted harmlessly off the half-inch steel.

Working with the calm, methodical precision of men who had built half the high-pressure boilers in Europe before the tariff-wars broke them, the Frenchmen fitted their four-foot iron spanners to the main expansion-collar of the pipeline, threw their weight together upon the levers until the twelve rusted Monterey bolts sheared open, and let a solid, roaring jet of black Sumatra crude oil—pumped at two hundred pounds of pressure to the square inch from the coastal tanks—fountain straight out across the muddy ditch and down the slope toward the trench surrounding our sandbags.

"Cut the main pump-valve inside the engine-house!" screamed young Lieutenant Miller—a nineteen-year-old boy from the Oakland sheds who had dragged Takahashi’s headless body away from the Maxim tripod and was frantically trying to clear a jammed canvas belt with his bayonet—as the black, stinking tide of raw naphtha and petroleum flooded knee-deep through the barbed-wire entanglements and began to soak into the dry palm-thatch of our ammunition-bunker. "If they drop a match into the ditch, the whole gorge will go up like a lamp-wick! Corporal, get the wireless key working—"

Out at the edge of the bamboo brake, a tall, bare-chested Belgian artilleryman with a six-digit debtor-scar burned across his forearm stood up for a single second in the open mud, whirling a homemade sling of braided rattan around his head in which blazed a ball of dry coconut-husk soaked in rubber-latex. As Lieutenant Miller wrenched the iron door of the pump-house open to reach the steam-cock, the flaming ball arched high over the barbed wire and struck the oil-slicked sandbags with a wet,闷-sounding *whump* that turned the entire Pahang gorge into a roaring funnel of orange flame, driving me and four scorched survivors headlong down the muddy river-bank toward our armored steam-launch while the ammunition-bunker behind us blew its corrugated iron roof straight through the banyan canopy.

***

Six hundred miles across the Gulf of Siam from that burning pipeline, Marshal Marcus Vance the third stood knee-deep in the warm, leech-infested bilge-water of the flat-bottomed river monitor *Tonkin*, his gold-rimmed pince-nez so crusted with dead gnats and yellow marsh-sweat that he could barely read the pressure-dials on the forward bulkhead.

There were no five-thousand-foot aluminum gondolas here above the Mekong Delta. When the rubber-estates of Cochin-China and the rice-canals of Mytho had risen in December behind a hundred thousand runaway Annamite canal-diggers and deported Belgian mechanics, Emperor Kalanimoku had ordered the victor of Irkutsk south to repeat his chemical miracle in the tropics. Marcus had brought six rigid airships down from Vladivostok; within three weeks, the ninety-percent equatorial humidity had rotted the doped silk of their gas-cells until the hydrogen leaked through the seams like water through a sieve, and the monsoon lightning over Cambodia had burned two of the silver giants out of the clouds before they could drop a single canister.

Now the Marshal of the Northern Marches was down in the mud he dreaded.

All around the shallow-draft iron hull of the *Tonkin*, for fifty square leagues between the Bassac and the Vaico branches of the great river, stretched a flat, steaming, emerald-green purgatory of twelve-foot elephant-grass, labyrinthine mangrove roots, and flooded rice-paddies that smelled of putrefying catfish, warm human ordure, and the sulfurous coal-smoke of his own stalled boilers.

"Why have the paddle-wheels stopped turning, Captain?" Marcus shouted, his high, reedy voice cracking as he slapped the blistered grey skin of his neck where a malaria-mosquito had bitten through his wet silk scarf. His left hand twitched continuously against the butt of his silver-plated pistol; the purple resin-scars from the Afghan pass itched intolerably in the hundred-degree steam of the delta. "If we do not clear the Vinh-Long canal-lock before dusk, the night-mists will blind the searchlights! Give the engines full steam and ram the barrier!"

Down in the open iron engine-pit amidships, Lieutenant-Commander Brooks—his uniform tunic stripped off to reveal ribs raw with prickly-heat sores—wiped his greasy forearm across his brow and pointed with amonkey-wrench toward the stern wheel-housing.

"There is no barrier to ram, Marshal," Brooks said, his voice flat with the dull, feverish exhaustion of a crew that had not slept onshore for forty days. "The Annamites and the French deportees didn't sink stone-junks in the channel this time. They floated three miles of twisted wire-rope and green water-hyacinth down the current while we were shelling the empty bamboo village on the left bank. The cables have wound themselves six inches thick around the main paddle-shaft, and the hyacinth-roots have choked the condenser intakes until the vacuum-gauge is at zero. If I open the throttle another notch, the cylinder-heads will blow out."

"Then send the Cantonese pioneer-squad over the side with axes and diving-helmets to hack the wire off the shaft!" Marcus screamed, stepping up onto the hot iron grating above the boilers while his scarred cheek jerked like a frog's leg. "We have twelve tons of chlorine-shells in the forward magazine! Clear the paddles and fire gas at zero elevation into the mangrove screen on both banks!"

"We put six boys over the side with axes at the noon bend, sir," Brooks answered, not moving a muscle as a sudden, hollow *plop* sounded from the green wall of nipa-palms forty yards away, and a four-foot bamboo blow-dart tipped with rotting buffalo-liver stuck quivering into the wooden chart-table between them. "The rebels have staked sharpened iron harrow-teeth and poisoned bamboo spikes across the mud-bottom under the hyacinths, and their frog-men swim underneath the hull with hand-augers to pull our diver-hoses loose. You can fire all twelve tons of chlorine into those mangroves if you please, Marshal—the afternoon sea-breeze will blow the gas straight back over our own deck in five minutes, and the rebels are already three miles away in the swamp-canals Poling their flat-punts where a ten-inch shell only throws up ten thalers' worth of warm mud."

Marcus stared wildly out through the armored gun-port at the motionless, shimmering wall of green reeds. Nothing moved; not a rifle-barrel glinted in the sun, yet from somewhere deep inside that miles-wide vegetable sponge came the mocking, rhythmic *clink-clink-clink* of an iron hammer striking a stolen railway-plate—the signal-telegraph of an invisible army that needed no coal, no brass collar-tags, and no Monterey logarithms to wait until the iron ships rusted to the bottom of the ditch.

"Fire the six-pounders into the reeds anyway!" Marcus shrieked, his trembling boots slipping on the wet slime of the deck as he dragged at the breech-lever of the nearest sponson-gun himself. "Fire by the clock every thirty seconds! I will not report another negative tally to the Palace!"

***

To the Chronicler who returned to Thalassia in the spring of 1921—limping ashore at the Waipahu quay with my left arm still bandaged from the Pahang oil-fire—the reports that Marshal Vance was firing sixty-thaler shells into empty mud-banks to manufacture casualty-lists for the telegraph caused no surprise whatever.

For by that April, the marble navel of the earth had ceased to believe in its own numbers, and the terror that had begun in the snows of Kabul and the swamps of the Mekong had crawled inside the crystal dome.

As my electric cab rolled along the *Via Triumphalis* toward the Chancellery, I looked out upon a capital where the sun still shone in Sunset Gold upon the twenty-ton blocks of red Agra sandstone, yet where the human life had frozen into a silent, sidelong crouch. The great geothermal fountains in the Piazza of the Pivot were dry; their high-tension power had been diverted to feed the six rings of electrified barbed wire and the forty searchlight-towers that now separated the Sacred Emperor’s artificial island from the municipal wards of Honolulu.

In the first generation of the Empire, when Elias Thorne had suspected a general or a silver-syndicate of treason, he had sent a company of cavalry in broad daylight to hang the offender from a telegraph-pole, and the streets had gone back to their business. Now, because the third generation had been taught from the cradle that the Polytechnic machine was mathematically infallible, the simultaneous collapse of the Siberian copper-output, the Malayan oil-lines, and the European tax-remittances could only be explained by a single, maddening hypothesis: that a vast, invisible conspiracy of saboteurs was falsifying the equations inside the Bureau of Integration itself.

The people in the street called it the *Audit of the Red Needle*; history will know it as the *Great Purge*.

When I entered the subterranean sorting-vaults beneath the Palace of the Double Horizon at ten o’clock that morning to deposit my Malayan field-diaries, the air did not smell of white ginger and clean transformer-ozone. It smelled of scorched paper, stale sweat, and the raw, vinegary reek of the photographic developing-acid that the new *Board of Internal Verification* was using to check the thumb-prints upon forty million civil-service dossiers.

Down the center of the main marble corridor—where five years earlier the young graduates of Berkeley and Kyoto had walked with the quiet arrogance of kings—stood a double file of Samoan and Choshu Household Provosts wearing the black-and-crimson brassards of the Palace Secret Police. Every twenty minutes, the heavy bronze elevator-doors at the end of the hall slid open with a greased sigh, and four guards marched out between them leading a Senior Prefect of the First or Second Class—men with grey hair at their temples who had spent thirty years calculating the grain-allocations of Canton or the customs-tariffs of Melbourne—with their silver identification-ciphers ripped from their collars and their thumbs locked together behind their backs in steel thumb-screws.

"Step aside to the wall, Citizen-Historian, and present your travel-warrant to the perforator," ordered a twenty-year-old Inspector of the Verification Board, barring my path before the archive-turnstile while his partner—a cold-eyed boy from the Nagasaki wards—held a magnifying-glass over the violet serial-stamp on my wrist.

Inside the glass-walled office of the Chief of the Chancellery, Prefect-Chancellor Shen the third was no longer sitting behind his steel podium.

The grandson of Elias Thorne’s auditor was kneeling upon the mosaic floor in his shirt-sleeves, his horn-rimmed spectacles broken across the bridge with a piece of adhesive tape, his hair hanging in damp grey strings over his forehead as he frantically fed bundles of old nineteen-eighteen European debt-ledgers into a portable brick incinerator that had been mortared directly into the base of the Great Gnomon.

"Shen!" I whispered, stepping past the unguarded inner glass door while the Samoan sentries in the corridor were dragging a screaming hydraulic-engineer from the Panama locks down the stairs toward the harbor-hulks. "What are you burning? Those are the Brussels master-schedules!"

Shen looked up at me over his shoulder; his face had shrunk to the yellow-gray parchment of a consumptive, and the fingers that held the brass poker were trembling so violently that the iron rattled against the brick.

"The Emperor signed Warrant Nine-Zero-Zero at midnight, Historian," Shen whispered, his eyes darting in terror toward the ceiling-ventilators where the Palace Secret Police had installed carbon listening-microphones in the bronze wind-gods. "The spring rice-fleet from Saigon arrived at Manila yesterday with sixty percent of its holds empty because the Mekong barges were burned at Mytho, and the Ruhr coal-syndics have suspended the April tribute. His Majesty refuses to hear that the peasants are in the jungle! He says that the fuel-oil and the rice are still in the warehouses, and that the Senior Assessors of the First Class have entered a treasonous league with the European debtors to shift the decimal-points on the clearing-sheets!"

With a wild, jerky movement of his arm, Shen shoved a three-hundred-page bound volume of the Siberian census into the white-hot coke of the furnace.

"They took Rector Norton’s successor out of the Berkeley mathematics hall on Tuesday and drowned him in the bay with an iron weight tied to his neck because the winter birth-rate in the Ohio cantons fell twelve percent below the curve!" Shen gasped, the orange glare of the burning paper reflecting in his cracked lenses as the heavy, rhythmic tramp of eight iron-shod boots sounded suddenly down the marble corridor outside my door. "And ten minutes ago, the Verification Board found a three-million-thaler discrepancy in my father’s nineteen-fourteen Rangoon opium-balance! If you have a single notebook in your satchel that says the Pahang pipeline is broken, throw it into the fire before the Samoan corporal reaches the glass, or by noon tomorrow you and I will be chained to an oar-bench in the Peruvian guano-pits!"

***

I did not wait for the Samoan corporal to reach the glass; slipping out through the pneumatic-tube service-tunnel behind the Molokai transformer-banks while Shen’s voice rose in a thin, mechanical scream of loyalty before his arresters, I boarded a returning mutton-collier for the southern hemisphere that same night—only to discover, when our rusty hull raised the heads of Port Phillip Bay three weeks later, that in the Eighty-Second Australian Canton the dying brain at Thalassia had found an even colder substitute for the human hands it could no longer trust.

For as the Great Purge emptied the examination-sheds of Berkeley and Kyoto, and the Hidden Wars in the Malayan jungles and the Siberian snow-drifts swallowed ten thousand young engineers a month, the remaining syndicate-lords who fed the fleet had reached the final, logical conclusion of Marcus Vance’s philosophy: if a man with a number on his collar could still catch the black grippe, or strike for four ounces of salt-fish, or throw a coconut-fireball into an oil-ditch, then the flesh itself was a structural defect in the iron.

Historians in the provinces have called this last convulsion the *Steel Revolution*.

When I walked up the long basalt wharf of Williamstown on the outskirts of Melbourne on a freezing, rain-lashed afternoon in June, 1921, I did not see a single stevedore, crane-man, or tally-clerk upon the two-mile curve of the docks. Instead, rising six stories above the oily gray swells of the bay, stood the newly completed *Automated Imperial Wool-and-Ordnance Complex Number Four*—a windowless, mile-long fortress of poured grey concrete and corrugated duralumin that hummed with a deafening, sixty-cycle roar like a hive of iron hornets.

Along the coping of the quay, forty giant gantry-cranes were unloading raw copper-ingots and bales of Riverina fleece from a line of crewless, gyro-steered steel barges; yet there were no glass cabins upon the crane-legs for a human operator. Guided by overhead copper trolley-wires and five-inch strips of perforated brass tape that unreeled continuously inside cast-iron control-pillars along the rail, the mechanical claws dropped straight down into the hatches with a rhythmic, unvarying *clank-whir-shunt*, gripped four-ton loads of greasy wool, and swung them directly into the open jaws of the electric scouring-vats at a speed no human wrist had ever matched.

Where, then, were the two hundred thousand Yorkshiremen, Irishmen, and Cantonese mechanics who had filled the Melbourne wards when old Senator MacArthur rose in the Crystal Palace five years before?
