Half a mile inland from the humming concrete wall of the automated foundry, across a waste of cold coal-slag and flooded clay-pits encircled by a double fence of ten-thousand-volt barbed wire and twin-turreted Maxim blockhouses, they stood in the freezing winter mud of the Yarra flats.

There were eighty thousand of them huddled beneath torn tarpaulins and rusted sheets of flattened kerosene-tins—men whose fathers had sheared the sheep of Victoria or puddled the steel of Ballarat, their grey canton-coats hanging in rags from their starved shoulders, their left wrists still bearing the riveted brass ration-shackles that no longer opened a single turnstile at the factory gates.

As I stood beside the armored gate-house of the foundry wire with Chief Mechanical Prefect Ozawa—a twenty-four-year-old graduate of the Osaka Cybernetic Institute whose left arm had been replaced at the elbow by a jointed steel prosthetic hook after the Chita explosion—a crowd of four hundred gaunt, barefoot foundry-smiths pressed up against the outer wooden palings in the sleet, holding up their cold iron hammers and their empty tin pannikins toward the twenty-foot-high intake-flues where the hot tallow-steam from the automated mutton-canneries vented into the sky.

"Open the third-shift wickets, Prefect!" shouted a grey-bearded giant in a leather apron—a master-boilermaker whose chest still bore the bronze medal of the nineteen-fourteen Panama Concrete Gang—his voice hoarse above the relentless *thump-thump-thump* of the crewless steam-hammers inside the windowless wall. "Our women haven't seen a pound of barley-meal since you locked the manual lathes in May! Put a hundred men back on the shell-presses at half-ration, or by God we’ll bring the timber-jacks down from the bush and pry the concrete off your dynamos with our bare hands!"

Prefect Ozawa did not even glance through the wire at the medal on the old man’s leather apron; with his steel hook, he calmly adjusted the brass rheostat upon the gate-post, increasing the current in the upper insulators until the rain-drops sizzling along the barbed wire gave off a sharp, blue smell of ozone.

"A human lathe-turner consumes three thousand calories of wheat and mutton per diem, requires eight hours of sleep in twenty-four, and introduces a four-percent variance in the driving-bands of a twenty-two-inch shell whenever his child dies of the winter grippe, Citizen-Historian," Ozawa said to me in his flat, metallic Osaka English, raising his voice slightly as down at the southern corner of the slag-heap a sudden, roaring crash of splintering pine-timber echoed through the rain, where two thousand desperate shearers and dock-men were swinging a forty-foot telegraph-pole like a battering-ram straight against the main power-conduit pylon.

"Whereas the Babbage-Nakajima tape-loom behind this wall," Ozawa continued, his hand dropping calmly toward the red brass trip-lever of the gate-house steam-mortars as the great iron pylon at the corner of the fence began to buckle and lean inward in a blinding, thirty-foot fountain of blue high-tension sparks and screaming men, "requires only two gallons of mineral oil a week, never petitions the Senate for salt, and cannot remember the name of its father."

He pulled the brass lever back against the stop.

With a hollow, coughing roar of compressed steam, the four short-barreled mortars on the blockhouse roof lobbed their canisters of liquid lime and shrapnel straight into the tangled mass of men around the fallen pylon. I did not stay to watch the gray mud of the Yarra turn red under the rain; I turned my back upon the humming concrete wall, realizing that the Empire had finally found the citizen it had been looking for since Elias Thorne rode into Sacramento: a wheel that spun in the dark without a mouth to feed.

***

Yet if the iron wheel in Melbourne needed no bread, it drank the blood of the islands like water.

Exiled by her own choice from the leper-spit of Molokai after Emperor Kalanimoku’s naval engineers seized the Kalaupapa cliffs in July to mount long-range acoustic hydrophones, eighty-six-year-old Lady Kaiulani had been carried sixty miles northwest across the channel to the last unfortified corner of the archipelago: the deep, red-walled canyon of Waimea on the island of Kauai.

Here, in her childhood, the world had smelled of wet mountain fern, crushed *maile* leaves, and the sweet, cold spray of the Waialeale cataracts tumbling four thousand feet from the clouds to feed the ancient stone-walled taro-patches of the valley floor. Now, on a stifling afternoon in August, 1921, as she sat propped upon a mat of woven pandanus beneath the thatched eaves of an old priest’s grass-house above the river-bend, the wind coming up from the coast tasted of blistered copper and dead fish.

She did not need her milky, cataract-clouded eyes to know what her grandson’s syndicates had done to the Garden Isle. Three miles down the gorge, where the sacred river met the sea at Koloa, the Bureau of Ordnance had erected the *Seventh Electrolytic Nitrate and Bauxite Works*—a sprawling, treeless scar of corrugated iron sheds and open-cut red-mud leaching vats that drew its power from a concrete dam thrown straight across the mouth of the high mountain waterfalls.

The river below her bamboo rail no longer sang over the boulders. Diverted through four-foot cast-iron penstocks to spin the Pelton wheels of the chemical vats, the ancient stream had shrunk to a stagnant, ankle-deep trickle of warm, rust-colored sludge that steamed with sulphuric acid and yellow picric run-off.

"Are the mullet-ponds at Lawai still breathing, Malia?" Kaiulani whispered, her tiny, shrunken head resting back against the rough cedar post while her niece knelt beside her, wiping the yellow chemical dust from the old Queen’s lips with a damp rag of native tapa-bark.

Malia looked down the valley toward the coast, where a solid, greasy bank of coal-black and saffron smoke from the bauxite roasting-kilns hung low over the dead palms like a bruised thunderhead, blotting out the sunset gold of the western water.

"The seawall at Lawai broke on Tuesday, Aunt," Malia said quietly, her voice tight with the grief she could no longer hide from a blind woman. "The dredging-barges were blasting the coral reef with dynamite to deepen the channel for the Osaka acid-tankers, and when the tide came in through the gap, it carried the yellow tailings from the copper-wash straight into the royal fish-ponds. Forty thousand silver mullet floated belly-up against the lava stones this morning, and the taro-terraces from here to Hanapepe are burned down to the gray clay. The roots turn to black slime in the women’s hands before they can pull them from the mud."

Down on the narrow gravel path below the grass-house, a file of thirty old Hawaiian fishermen and their wives—the last villagers who had not been drafted into the Koloa leaching-sheds—shuffled past in silence. They carried no throw-nets or carved wooden calabashes; they carried rusted five-gallon kerosene-tins balanced on shoulder-poles, walking four miles up into the high, dry rocks above the dam to dip muddy rainwater out of the goat-wallows because the wells in the valley burned the skin off a child’s throat.

Kaiulani’s withered brown hands—stripped now of the ivory rings she had left behind on the palace floor—closed slowly over the dry pandanus reeds of her mat.

"When Captain Cook’s iron nails first came to Kealakekua, my great-grandfather’s priests said the gods had sent us a harder stone for our adzes," she murmured, her breath whistling faintly in the sulfurous heat as the distant, rhythmic *boom-crump* of the reef-blasting charges shook a shower of dead, yellow fern-fronds down upon her white hair. "We thought we could take the white man’s steam-engine and the Chinaman’s abacus and wear them like a feather cloak over our own skin. Look at the mountain, Malia. We have eaten the reef to build the ships, and boiled the river to fill the shells, and now the island itself is dying of the iron before I can get into the ground."

***

To the Chronicler who crossed the turbulent autumn swells of the North Pacific six weeks later—fleeing northward from the burning wool-sheds of Melbourne aboard an automated grain-hulk whose gyro-compass brought us through the Golden Gate without a single sailor touching the wheel—the death of the earth that the old Queen mourned on Kauai had already produced its monstrous birth at the center of the web.

When I stepped ashore at the Market Street Ferry-Slips in San Francisco on the twelfth of October, 1921, I found the old brick metropolis where Elias Thorne had hammered his empire together lying half-abandoned under a perpetual, choking fog of unrefined Mexican bunker-oil and nitric-acid vapor.

No gentleman in broadcloth, no Senior Assessor, and no syndicate-director walked the cracked asphalt of Montgomery Street or climbed the steep cobbles of Rincon Hill anymore. Since the great bread-and-typhus riots of the previous winter—when sixty thousand unemployed foundry-hands from the automated Potrero works had tried to storm the Mint vaults with crowbars and been mowed down by the crewless Maxim-towers along the Embarcadero—the hereditary caste of the *Imperial Citizens* had severed their last gangplank to the soil.

Half a mile out in the deep, racing tide-way between Alcatraz Island and the Marin headlands, moored to the bedrock by sixteen-inch chains of vanadium steel, floated the three linked pontoons of *New Thalassia-in-the-Bay*—the first of the mobile, self-contained Sanctuary-Arks that the Osaka and Hunters Point slips had launched for the families of the First Class.

Viewed through my field-glasses from the rusted iron rail of the Telegraph Hill ruins, that floating island of three hundred acres rose out of the gray, oil-scummed water of the harbor like a wedding-cake of gleaming white porcelain, polished bronze, and triple-glazed crystal.

Encircled by a forty-foot outer breakwater of sloped Krupp armor-plate—upon whose coping automated torpedo-tubes and rapid-fire pom-pom guns tracked every fishing-skiff or drift-log that came within a thousand yards—the upper decks of the Ark knew neither the coal-soot of the shore nor the sweat of the cantons. Powered by its own submerged tidal-turbines and oil-reactors, the floating city carried forty-foot terraced gardens of imported Kyoto cherry-trees and Oahu hibiscus heated by artificial quartz-suns; its air was washed through water-curtains scented with sandalwood; and along its marble promenades strolled the three thousand surviving shareholders of the Great Arena.

They did not wear the plain dark wool of the old Polytechnic examination-sheds. Dressed in flowing, syncretic robes of imperial-blue Lyons silk and golden Vicuña fleece, the grandsons of Elias Thorne’s rough Missouri pioneers and Marquis Takashima’s samurai drank iced champagne from the mortgaged vineyards of Rheims while listening to the sixty-piece symphony orchestra of Vienna playing upon a bandstand of solid Burmese teak.

"They haven't set a boot on the California shore since the April quarantine, Citizen-Historian," said my guide, a one-legged former telegraph-clerk named Higgins who lived by boiling salt out of the bay-mud in a ruined tin-cannery beneath the cliff. He spat down into the greasy black water at the foot of the Meiggs Wharf, where the bloated carcass of a horse floated among the empty ration-tins. "Their meat comes straight up from the New Zealand freezer-ships by electric crane on the seaward side; their sons are examined for the peerage by wireless inside the glass dome; and when they want to move the price of copper in Chile or turn the steam-mortars onto a strike-camp in Seattle, they don't even have to look through a spy-glass at the smoke. They just press a pearl button on their dinner-tables, and the tape-machines down in the Hunters Point basement punch the warrant."

As the sun sank behind the Golden Gate, turning the toxic yellow smog over the Oakland mud-flats into a lurid canopy of blood and brass, the ten-thousand-candlepower pleasure-lanterns along the upper terraces of the Ark flashed on all at once—casting a shimmering, golden carpet across the oily tide toward the dark, silent wharves where half a million unnumbered men sat in the cold without a match to light a pipe.

***

Yet a fortress that floats upon chains can still be reached by a man who knows how to swim in the dark; and three thousand miles away from the lighted decks of the San Francisco Ark, the night-wind off the Kauai channel was bringing an unnumbered skiff through the dynamited gap in the Koloa reef.

It was two hours past midnight on the third of November when the mountain dogs in the mud lane below Lady Kaiulani’s grass-house began to bark—not the frantic, yapping alarm they gave when the Choshu tax-patrols marched up the valley in their iron-shod boots, but a low, uncertain growl at the smell of salt water and wet canvas.

Inside the dark hut, where the only light came from a single stone saucer of burning kukui-nut oil set upon the floor-mats, eighty-six-year-old Kaiulani was already awake. At her age, sleep came only in ten-minute shreds between the spasms of fluid in her lungs; she lay propped against her cedar post in her coarse bark-cloth wrapper, listening to the distant, unending *thump-hiss* of the bauxite-stampers down at the dam.

The woven reed screen at the doorway was pushed aside without a sound. Malia sprang up from her pallet with an iron fish-spear in her hand, then froze as two figures slipped out of the sulfurous mist under the eaves.

The first was old Kahuku, a seventy-year-old one-eyed canoe-steersman from Niihau whose grandsons had all died in the Bengal landing-craft seven years before. The second was a young man of no more than twenty-three, dripping wet to the waist from the surf, dressed in the greasy, unbadged blue denim trousers of an engine-room stoker and a torn Chinese quilted jacket.

Even through the milky veil of her cataracts, when the youth stepped into the red circle of the kukui-nut lamp and dropped upon one knee on the pandanus mat, Kaiulani could see that he belonged to no single race of the old earth. He had the high, broad cheekbones and copper skin of an Oahu boatman, the narrow, heavy-lidded eyes of a Cantonese furnace-man, and across his bare left forearm, where the sleeve had been ripped away by a machine-belt, the livid, unmistakable white scar where a six-digit Monterey brass ration-shackle had been pried off the bone with a cold chisel.

"Who brings the grease of a warship into a dying woman’s house?" Kaiulani whispered, her thin, claw-like hand resting motionless upon the reed mat.

"My name is nothing, Great Grandmother of the Islands," the young man said. He did not speak the clipped, mathematical English of the Berkeley primers, nor the old missionary Hawaiian; he spoke the rough, rhythmic *Creole of the Lower Decks*—that bastard tongue of Cantonese, English, Tagalog, and Polynesian which four generations of stokers and coolies had hammered out in the bilges of the Pacifica fleet. "In the Osaka rolling-mills they stamped me *Seven-Seven-Four-Zero-Two*. Down in the coal-bunkers of the flagship *Thalassia*, where the boys from the three shores pass the shovel in the dark, they call me *Keawe*."

"If you are off the *Thalassia*, you have swum from the Pearl Lochs roadstead with the provost-launches behind you," Malia said sharply, lowering her spear-point to his throat. "Why have you come to Waimea? The Queen has no gold left to buy you a passage to Mexico, and her name has been struck from the Chancery seals."

"We do not want gold, Lady, and we are not sailing to Mexico," young Keawe answered, not flinching from the iron barb at his windpipe, his dark eyes burning straight through the dimness into Kaiulani’s blind face. "The automated tape-ships have locked the grain-silos at Vallejo, and the Emperor on his floating pontoon in San Francisco has signed the winter order to clear the manual stokers out of the Battle Fleet and replace our watches with gyro-feeders from the Nagasaki yards. Forty thousand of us—Hawaiian gunners, Cantonese oil-tenders, Californian machinists, and the Russian debtor-gangs at the Waipahu dry-docks—have our fingers on the main Kingston sea-valves and the magazine-flooding cocks of every dreadnought between Diamond Head and the Golden Gate."

Kaiulani’s old heart gave a single, violent leap against her shrunken ribs, like a dying bird striking the bars of its cage.

"You are going to sink the fleet at its moorings," she breathed.

"Not sink it, Great Mother—turn the twenty-two-inch turrets inward upon the Crystal Palace and the San Francisco pontoons when the noon meridian-siren blows on the day of the Jubilee!" Keawe leaned forward across the mat, pulling from inside his oil-stained shirt not a pistol or a printed charter, but a six-inch strip of stiff crimson silk upon which someone had clumsily stenciled in white deck-paint the ancient, pre-Imperial emblem of the crossed Hawaiian canoe-paddles and the broken iron chain. "The Russian and German quarry-men in Siberia rose for their dead kings, and the airships strangled them with yellow fog. The hillmen in Kabul fought for their mullahs, and the steam-tanks burned their orchards. Our boys in the boiler-rooms have no kings and no mullahs—half of us don't know what island our mothers came from! The older petty-officers on the *Sakurajima* are afraid to turn the turret-keys unless there is a righteous law behind the gun. They remember that your hand signed the truce with the old Protector before the clerks took the sea. Put your thumb-mark in kukui-soot upon this silk, Queen Kaiulani—give the word of Kamehameha’s blood that the throne in the lagoon is forfeit—and before the sun goes down on the Exhibition we will blow the glass dome and the counting-machines into the coral!"

Outside in the dark gorge, the wind shifted suddenly from the sea, bringing the sharp, metallic screech of an armored railway-motorcar braking hard upon the narrow-gauge ore-track at the foot of the bluff, half a mile below the hut.

Kaiulani did not turn her head toward the window. With her trembling, blind right hand, she reached out through the red lamplight and touched the ragged white scar on the young stoker’s forearm where the brass collar of Elias Thorne’s machine had eaten into his flesh.

"And when you have blown the Crystal Palace into the lagoon, boy," the aged woman whispered, her fingers sliding down from his scarred wrist to dip the tip of her thumb into the black grease around the rim of the stone oil-lamp while down on the river-path the heavy, unmistakable *tramp-tramp* of twenty Choshu provost-boots began to mount the gravel grade through the dead taro-patches, "who will feed the four hundred million mouths when the ships stop running?"

"The earth will feed them, Mother, when the iron is off its chest!" Keawe hissed, snatching the crimson rag back into his bosom as the black print of her thumb touched the weave; and before Malia could blow out the saucer-flame, he and old Kahuku had dived headlong through the rear thatch into the sulfur-steaming cane-brake just as the rifle-butts of the patrol crashed against the cedar door-post.

***

Keawe’s conspiracy did not detonate that Friday. Betrayed at the eleventh hour by a terrified Cantonese turret-oiler aboard the *Golden Gate* whose brother was held hostage in the Nagasaki examination-wards, the mutiny of the manual stokers was drowned in the bilges before a single twenty-two-inch barrel could traverse toward the shore. For nine years thereafter—while the slow, gangrenous rot of the outer cantons ate steadily inward from the Vistula and the Indus toward the sea—the priesthood of the Pivot maintained its equilibrium by the simple expedient of replacing every mutinous human nerve with a strip of perforated brass tape.

Yet an empire that has lost the consent of the living must double the theater of its bronze; and to the Chronicler who returned to Thalassia in the October of 1930 to witness the opening of the *Centennial Exhibition of the Circumference*, the spectacle along the Pearl Lochs causeway resembled nothing so much as a paralytic giant painting his cheeks with vermilion to hide the mortification of his limbs.

Officially, the proclamation of the thirty-eight-year-old Sacred Emperor Kalanimoku invited the Hundred and Thirty Cantons to celebrate the completion of the first century since Elias Thorne’s birth—the final triumph of the Steel Revolution, wherein the machine had liberated humanity from the curse of Adam. In reality, half the chairs in the Pan-Pacific amphitheater stood empty because the trans-Siberian land-line ended now at a fortified trench outside Chita, the Suez canal-locks were choked with the scuttled hulks of Egyptian grain-rebels, and no steamer dared cross the Bay of Bengal without a convoy of four torpedo-destroyers to beat off the Tamil pirate-junks.

Yet within the six-mile electrified perimeter of the artificial lagoon, the grandeur of the display blinded the eye like the noon glare upon a sheet of tin.

Along the *Via Triumphalis*, where the twenty-ton blocks of red Agra sandstone were already cracking and spalling from the vibration of the subterranean bauxite-stampers, the Bureau of Public Harmony had erected the *Avenue of the Hundred Automaton-Tributes*. No living soldiers lined the marble curb; the remaining Choshu and Samoan flesh-and-blood regiments were all four miles inland, holding the barbed-wire stockades around the Waipahu coolie-compounds where two hundred thousand unemployed dock-hands were dying of the red beri-beri. In their stead stood eighty colossal, thirty-foot effigies of cast Pittsburgh aluminum and polished Osaka brass, representing the pacified races of the earth—the Hindoo, the Prussian, the Maori, the Californian—each wired to the high-tension Molokai conduits so that as the Emperor’s gilded electric barge glided down the central canal, the metal giants bowed in simultaneous, sixty-cycle unison from the waist, their internal steam-calliopes blasting out the syncopated chords of the Imperial Anthem in a cloud of synthetic Mysore sandalwood spray.

At the head of the lagoon, towering four hundred feet above the dwarfed dome of the old Senate House, rose the centerpiece of the Exhibition: the *Pylon of Perpetual Equilibrium*.

Built entirely from the melted-down bronze cannon of the European protectorates and the stripped copper roofing of the Westminster Parliament, it was no mere monument, but a working, ten-thousand-horsepower Babbage-Nakajima Difference Engine whose exterior faces were covered with forty-foot illuminated glass dials. Every ten seconds, as the master-pendulum swung across the gilded sun-and-anchor at the apex, the giant hands jumped forward with a thunderous, hydraulic *thwack* that shook the dead mullet-float in the harbor, registering for the awe of the spectators the exact, theoretical tonnage of coal, rice, copper, and human blood-tax existing at that moment between Antwerp and Valparaiso.

"Observe the third dial on the western face, Citizen-Historian," said Junior Minister Sato—the last surviving brother of that family of engineers, his left cheek twitching beneath the heavy white lead-powder that the court nobles now wore to mimic the porcelain masks of the Kyoto consort—as we stood upon the crimson-carpeted reviewing-barge beside the canal. "The Silesian coal-reserve registers four million tons above the autumn requirement, and the Bengal jute-index stands at par."

I did not take my field-glasses from my eyes; I was looking past the gilded shoulder of the thirty-foot aluminum Prussian automaton on the quay, straight out through the Honolulu Passage where two returning hospital-cruisers from the Mindanao rubber-war were limping inside the reef with their armored sides blackened by native naphtha-rafts and their scuppers running red into the peacock-blue swell.

Everyone upon that silk-awninged barge knew that the Silesian mines had been flooded by the Polish insurgents three winters ago, and that not a single bale of Bengal jute had cleared the Hooghly since March. The engineers in the basement of the Pylon had simply disconnected the broken submarine cables from the differential gears and coupled the four-hundred-foot brass hands directly to a closed-loop governor-wheel that spun in the dark, counting ghosts.

"It is a masterpiece of providence, Minister," I replied, bowing low as the Sacred Emperor Kalanimoku—grown corpulent and heavy-jowled at thirty-eight, his yellow feather mantle stiffer now with woven gold wire and bulletproof duralumin scales than with the plumage of dead mountain birds—stepped out onto the proscenium of his barge and raised his baton to salute the bowing iron statues that could not shoot back.

***

Across the Kauai channel, in the high red gorge of Waimea where the trade-wind could no longer clear the yellow sulphuric mist from the canyon walls, Lady Kaiulani did not hear the steam-calliopes of the Jubilee.

She was ninety-five years old—an age which the old island priests had called *ka wa maloo*, the season of the dry bone, when the spirit has already walked halfway down the cliff at Polihale to leap into the dark water, leaving only the husk upon the mat to wait for the tide. For five years she had been utterly blind and stone-deaf to the voice of a man; yet through the sole of the bare, withered foot that rested against the cedar center-post of her grass-house, she could still feel the unending, sixty-cycle tremor of the Koloa bauxite-stampers three miles down the dry river-bed, shaking the volcanic bedrock of her island day and night like a fever-pulse.

On the afternoon of the twentieth of October, Malia—herself an old, grey-haired woman of fifty now, with her linen skirt pinned up over her knees and her arms stained red to the elbows from digging wild fern-roots in the high goat-pastures—came into the hut and laid a strange, heavy piece of rusted iron across the pandanus mat between her aunt’s knees.

Kaiulani’s small, translucent hands, no heavier than two dried breadfruit leaves, crept slowly across the reeds until her fingertips touched the cold metal.

It was not a smooth duralumin casting from the automated Osaka presses. It was a four-foot bar of rough, hand-puddled California wrought-iron, pitted with seventy winters of mountain rust, with a square iron spike still wedged through the flange and the faint, chisel-stamped letters *S. P. & M. R. R. — 1861* raised like a scar along the web.

"Where did you dig this bone up, child?" Kaiulani whispered, her voice so thin and dry that Malia had to lay her ear down beside the old Queen’s cracked lips to catch the Hawaiian words.

"The washout above the Koloa dam broke the old missionary bridle-path this morning, Aunt," Malia shouted back, pressing her mouth against the hollow of Kaiulani’s temple so the vibration of her jaw might carry through the bone, "and uncovered the ballast of the first sugar-tramway that the Protector’s engineers sent over from Monterey in the year of your brother’s marriage! The Choshu scrap-patrols are coming up the gorge with sledges to break the old rails up for the electric furnace!"

Kaiulani did not let go of the rusted bar. Sitting there in the yellow chemical gloom, she drew her thumb slowly back and forth across those rough, uneven hammer-marks that a sweating Irish or Cantonese blacksmith had beaten into the red-hot iron at Sacramento seventy years ago, when Abraham Lincoln was still alive beyond the snows and Elias Thorne was a bearded forty-year-old wolf in a mud-splashed linen duster.

Suddenly, across the dark, milky gulf of her blindness, she did not see the fat, painted boy Kalanimoku sitting beneath his bulletproof feathers on the lagoon, nor the windowless concrete walls of the Melbourne tape-looms.

She saw Elias Thorne standing upon the windy bluff at Fort Point in the autumn of fifty-four, with the salt fog dripping from his square iron jaw and his short, thick fingers wrapped around a hickory walking-stick as he pointed out across the empty Golden Gate.

*"A man who builds a fence across his pasture isn't trying to own the stars, Princess,"* she heard that dead, gravelly voice growling inside her skull, clearer than the roar of the bauxite-mills. *"He’s just keeping the wolves out of the calves so his boys can eat their beef in the lamp-light without asking a banker in New York for the salt."* 

A dry, soundless laugh shook her tiny chest beneath the tapa-bark.

Elias had been a tyrant; he had burned the ballot-boxes, hung the strike-leaders from the snow-sheds, and drowned the Yangtze forts in naphtha. Yet every blow of his terrible hammer had been struck for the living flesh he could see with his eyes and smell with his nostrils. He had loved the roar of twenty thousand bearded track-layers drinking whiskey around a desert bonfire; he had known the name of every locomotive-driver on the Truckee grade; he had wanted an ocean of strong, fierce, meat-eating men who could hold a rifle and look their captain in the face.

If Elias Thorne could rise today out of the four-mile mud of the Marianas Trench and walk through the streets of Thalassia—if he could see his great-grandsons hiding behind forty-foot walls of floating Krupp steel on San Francisco Bay, painting their faces white and pressing pearl buttons to turn steam-mortars onto starving boilermakers while eighty-foot brass dolls bowed by electricity along a dead lagoon—he would not call for his crown.

He would call for Caleb Vance’s old twelve-pounder mountain-howitzers, and he would blow the Crystal Palace and his own bastard dynasty straight into the reef before he let a punch-card rule a man.

"Leave the iron on the mat, Malia," Kaiulani whispered, curling her shrunken fingers tight around the rusted 1861 flange as if it were the only warm thing left in the world. "Do not give it to the furnace. When the stokers come back through the reef, they will need a crowbar that was made by a man’s hand."

***

They were already forging that crowbar three thousand miles away—not in the sunlight of the mountain passes, where the airships could hunt them down, but eighty feet beneath the rotting wharves and vitrified brick cellars of San Francisco.

To the Chronicler who descended into the subterranean labyrinth of the old Potrero and Mission wards on the night of the nineteenth of November, 1930—guided by that same one-legged salt-boiler, Higgins, after I had bribed the automated turnstile-guards at the Ferry-Slips with three tins of stolen naval morphia—the underworld of the abandoned continental capital offered a spectacle more portentous than the gathering of the Christians in the catacombs of Nero.

Up above our heads, on the rain-swept surface of Market Street, nothing moved save the four-wheeled, gyro-balanced *Pacification Automaton-Patrols*—squat, crewless beetles of riveted nickel-steel that rolled endlessly up and down the six-foot tramway tracks on solid rubber tires, their selenium light-cells scanning the boarded-up shop-fronts and their twin Maxim muzzles traversing automatically toward any stray dog or starving child that broke the beam of their searchlights after curfew.

Down here, however, in the five miles of abandoned six-foot freight-tunnels, flooded storm-sewers, and old Comstock bullion-vaults that the elder Vance had honeycomb-blasted out of the Franciscan sandstone sixty years ago before the Court moved to the bay-pontoons, four hundred thousand human beings had learned to live like termites inside the foundations of the throne.

The air was stiflingly hot and thick, smelling of wet sandstone, fermenting rice-mash, human sweat, and the pungent, sweetish smoke of cheap joss-sticks mixed with the acrid tang of stolen nitric acid. Every fifty yards along the dripping brick arch of the old Southern Pacific freight-subway, where the rusted rails had been pried up to forge pike-heads and cold chisels, small iron dishes of rendered sewer-rat fat burned with a smoky yellow flame before shrines hacked straight into the rock.

Yet these were not the shrines of the state *Shinto-Christian* syncretism that the Polytechnic chaplains preached in the cantonments.

In the first generation of the Protectorate, when Elias Thorne had crushed the European internationals and burned the printing-presses of the eastern socialists, the Chancellery had congratulatingly assumed that the specter of *Communism* was buried forever beneath the prosperity of the Great Arena. They had forgotten that when you lock ten million Cantonese iron-puddlers, Russian deportees, Californian ditch-diggers, and Japanese stokers into the same dark cellar and strip the names off their collars, their ghosts will marry in the dark.

As Higgins and I limped round the bend of the flooded Howard Street siphon, the low, rhythmic drone of two thousand voices chanting in the *Creole of the Lower Decks* rolled down the tunnel like the hum of a giant dynamo, and we stepped out into the *Cathedral of the Unnumbered*—the vast, subterranean brick cavern of the old Mission Street Gasometer.

Around the circular iron catwalks and down upon the dry sludge-floor stood three thousand gaunt, rags-clad figures: white-bearded American machinists whose hands had been mangled by the Babbage-looms, runaway Polish and German debtor-youths with the livid white scars of the chiselled ration-rings upon their left wrists, and barefoot Cantonese women from the closed Potrero canneries carrying sleeping infants in slings of burlap.

In the center of the floor, raised upon an altar of stacked, unexploded twenty-two-inch naval shells that had been smuggled out of the Hunters Point magazines, stood the icon of the new faith.

It was a six-foot figure hammered out of scrap-copper and boiler-plate by some nameless foundry-sculptor: a three-faced, six-armed bodhisattva sitting cross-legged upon a broken gear-wheel. The center face was the bearded, ferocious visage of the old German prophet Karl Marx, cast like a wrathful Buddhist guardian-king with a third eye of red signal-glass blazing in his forehead; the left face was the compassionate, weeping countenance of Kwannon, Goddess of Mercy of the Chinese seas; and the right was the scarred, Polynesian mask of Maui-the-Snarer, holding in his six copper hands not a lotus or a scroll, but a pair of five-foot iron bolt-cutters, a coal-heaver’s shovel, and a stick of mining-dynamite.

Before this terrible trinity stood a man in the oil-stained blue denim of a fleet-stoker—forty years old now, his hair streaked with iron-gray, his left forearm bearing the deep, jagged trough of the Monterey shackle-scar, and pinned over his heart a six-inch strip of faded crimson silk stamped with a black thumb-print in kukui-soot.

It was Keawe.

"The Great Mother on Kauai is dead!" Keawe’s voice rang out across the gasometer vault, not amplified by any bronze horn, yet carrying to the highest iron gallery through the absolute, breathless silence of the three thousand outcasts. "They threw her bones into the salt-ditch at Koloa on Tuesday without a chant or a feather, because she spat upon the Emperor’s brass doll! And tonight, brothers of the shovel, the seven-digit lords out on the San Francisco pontoons are drinking wine under their quartz-lamps while the gyro-tenders load the winter phosgene-drums onto the *Thalassia* to gas the Melbourne camps!"

From three thousand throats rose a single, low, vibrating growl—neither English nor Chinese, but the deep, chest-rattling *Haka* of the ocean-floors:

*"Huli ka lima! Break the wheel! One blood, no number!"*

"For eighty years," Keawe cried, snatching a heavy iron spanner from the altar of shells and raising it toward the dripping brick vault overhead, through which could be heard the faint, rhythmic grind of the automated patrol-beetles rolling along Market Street directly above our skulls, "the bearded prophet of the West told our fathers that the iron belonged to the hands that hammered it! And for eighty years the Merciful Mother of the East promised that when the measure of the clerks’ wickedness was full, the Pure Land would rise out of the mud! They thought they could get away from us by cutting the gangplanks and floating out onto the bay on chains of vanadium steel! They forgot who forged the chains, and they forgot who walks along the bottom of the water!"

He leaped down from the shell-altar onto the top of a riveted iron air-lock that had been bolted directly over the mouth of the old municipal main-sewer outfall—the twelve-foot cast-iron pipe that ran straight out under the bay mud for three-quarters of a mile to discharge directly beneath the central buoyancy-pontoons of *New Thalassia-in-the-Bay*.

Around the base of the air-lock stood forty men in patched brass-and-canvas Siebe-Gorman diving-suits stolen from the Mare Island salvage-sheds, their heavy lead-soled boots already strapped to their feet, while upon their backs, in place of air-cylinders, Cantonese women were lashing waterproof gutta-percha knapsacks packed solid with four hundred pounds apiece of ninety-percent nitro-gelatine and clocked magnesium-fuses.

"Brother Ivan of the Baikal pits! Brother Chen of Hanyang! Brother Miller of the Sacramento shops!" Keawe shouted, his scarred hand grasping the brass rim of the first diver’s copper helmet as two mechanics stepped forward with iron wrenches to bolt the faceplate home. "You will not come back through this pipe! When you walk out through the silt onto the bedrock under the Emperor’s garden-pontoon, there will be no air-hose behind you—only twenty minutes of compressed oxygen in your dress, and the sixteen-inch anchor-chains of the Ark above your heads! Do you take the Pure Land tonight?"

Inside the open copper collar of the diving-suit, the gaunt, one-eyed Russian deportee smiled, leaned forward to kiss the red glass eye upon the forehead of the copper Marx-Bodhisattva, and spat once upon the iron floor.

"Screw the glass down, Comrade Keawe," the Russian said, raising his two lead-weighted hands in the sign of the broken chain as the Cantonese girls swung the heavy bronze helmet over his head and the wrenches began to squeal against the brass studs, while at the rear of the cavern a sudden, violent hammering of iron crowbars against the upper sewer-manhole announced that the surface patrol-beetles had detected the heat-plume from our tallow-lamps and were unbolting the street-grating.

***

It was not an unmanned patrol-beetle that dropped through the shattered brickwork of the Mission Street siphon three seconds later.

A thirty-pound breaching-charge of guncotton blew the rusted cast-iron manhole cover straight down into the sludge-floor with a deafening, yellow flash that extinguished half the rat-fat lamps in the vault; and out of the choking fog of pulverized mortar and nitric acid tumbled forty Choshu and Californian assault-provosts in gas-masks, their short-barreled automatic carbines already spitting orange flame into the packed tiers of the iron catwalks.

Behind their leveled bayonets, lowering himself gingerly down the iron ladder rungs with his silver-plated revolver drawn in his right hand and a silk handkerchief soaked in cologne pressed tight against his nostrils with his left, came Marshal Marcus Vance the third.

At thirty-eight, ten years of counter-insurgency in the jungles and the cellars had turned the victor of Irkutsk into a stooped, prematurely aged phantom. The purple pine-resin burn from the Hindu Kush still pulled the left corner of his mouth upward in a permanent, wet sneer; his hair beneath his peaked service-cap was as white as salted lard; and as his boots splashed into the warm, ankle-deep filth of the gasometer floor, he had to squint hard through his gold-rimmed pince-nez to see through the drifting cordite smoke.

"Seal the outfall sluice-gate before they flood the lock!" Marcus screamed, his high, reedy falsetto cracking against the brick vault as the three thousand unarmed machinists and cannery-women surged backward against the slime-coated walls, trampling one another in the dark while the provosts’ carbines hammered at point-blank range into the press. "Don't shoot the men in the diving-dresses—shoot the mechanics at the air-lock wheel! If a single four-hundred-pound sack of gelatine gets into the bay-pipe, the Emperor will have our skins nailed to the dry-dock!"

Up on the riveted iron lip of the sewer-lock, Keawe had already thrown his entire weight upon the four-spoked brass flooding-valve, straining to let the bay tide rush in and sweep the first six helmeted divers down the cast-iron tube; but before the rusted screw could turn a quarter-inch, three heavy .45-caliber slugs from the lead Choshu sergeant’s carbine tore through the calves of the stoker’s legs.

Keawe pitched sideways off the iron drum into the black silt, his fingers still clawing for a dropped wrench as two provosts leaped over his body and jammed an iron crowbar through the spokes of the air-lock wheel.

"Hold your fire on the center platform!" Marcus shouted, shoving his way past a bleeding Cantonese girl who was trying to drag a dead infant out from under the boots of the squad. He holstered his unfired pistol and stepped up onto the stacked twenty-two-inch naval shells at the base of the six-armed copper idol, his scarred cheek jerking rapidly as he looked down at the twelve men in Siebe-Gorman canvas suits who stood immobilized by their own eighty-pound lead boots around the sealed hatch.

"Unscrew their helmets!" Marcus ordered, pointing with his cologne-soaked handkerchief at the nearest diver, whose heavy bronze faceplate was already fogging from the inside with the rapid, desperate breath of a man whose oxygen-valve had not been turned on. "Don't cut the gelatine-sacks off their backs yet—I want the Verification Board photographers to take their faces while the fuses are still wired to their belts! Let us see what breed of wharf-rat thinks he can swim under the First Class!"

Two Californian corporals stepped forward, fitted their T-wrenches to the brass neck-studs of the lead diver—the one-eyed Russian from the Baikal pits—and wrenched the sixty-pound copper dome off his shoulders. The deportee did not blink at the electric torches; he spat a mouthful of bloody phlegm straight onto the shiny patent-leather toe of Marcus’s boot.

"Take the next three off!" Marcus snarled, stepping back half a pace and kicking the Russian in the groin with his heel as the wrenches squealed down the line of canvas figures.

The second helmet came off: a sixty-year-old Sacramento boilermaker with the bridge of his nose eaten away by the mercury-fumes.

The third helmet came off: a boy of seventeen from the Macao rope-walks, his eyes rolling white in terror.

Then the corporals lifted the bronze dome from the fourth diver in the file—the man who had been standing with his lead-weighted gauntlet resting directly upon the electric detonator-plunger of the air-lock chamber—and the high, triumphant sneer froze upon Marcus Vance’s scarred face.

The man inside the patched canvas collar was not a mutilated Russian quarry-slave, nor a starving Cantonese coolie with a chiseled wrist.

He was twenty-six years old, clean-shaven, with his hair cropped in the severe, unmistakable quarter-inch brush of the Monterey Staff Academy. Around his neck, tucked neatly inside the rubberized waterproof flange to keep the chafing off his skin, gleamed the high collar of an Imperial Naval Lieutenant’s service tunic; and pinned squarely above the breast-pocket—directly beneath the canvas harness of the four-hundred-pound nitro-gelatine pack—shone the golden winged-torpedo of the *New Thalassia* Submarine Guard.

"Lieutenant-Assessor... Hoshino?" Marcus stammered, his gold pince-nez slipping down his sweat-greased nose and dangling by its black silk ribbon against his chin as he stared into the calm, heavy-lidded Japanese eyes of his own third-tier ordnance-aide—the grandson of the old Hankow auditor, a youth who had stood behind Emperor Kalanimoku’s chair on the flagship barge not forty-eight hours before.

"Open the sixth and seventh helmets, Marshal," young Lieutenant Hoshino said quietly, speaking not in the bastard pidgin of the coal-bunkers, but in the crisp, faultless English of the First Class examination-halls, while down on the wet bricks at his feet the wounded Keawe raised his bloody head and laughed aloud through his broken teeth. "You will find Captain Miller of the Alcatraz Torpedo-Battery in the sixth suit, and Senior Navigator Kuroda—nephew of the late Fleet-General—in the seventh. And before you reach for your whistle to call the surface-launch, sir, you should know that the four Choshu corporals holding the carbines behind your shoulder took the red thumb-print on Tuesday night."

Marcus whirled around upon the stacked naval shells, his right hand diving blindly for his patent-leather holster—just as the lead Choshu sergeant calmly raised the butt of his automatic carbine and smashed the iron heel-plate squarely across the bridge of the Marshal’s nose, knocking him flat on his back among the tallow-lamps while the mutinous guards swung their muzzles around and cut down the two Californian wrench-men in a single, deafening burst that echoed down the dark sewer-pipe toward the bay.

***

To the Chronicler who learned of Marshal Vance’s narrow escape from that San Francisco sewer only three months later—after a loyal reinforcement company of automated flame-tanks had broken through the Howard Street brick-wall and burned the gasometer to black clinker, dragging the bleeding, half-strangled Marshal out from under a pile of dead divers—the discovery that the grandsons of the Polytechnic peerage were strapping nitro-gelatine to their own backs marked the true midnight of the Protectorate.

For an empire is like one of those giant hydraulic presses that I had watched in my youth at the Hanyang ironworks: so long as the cast-iron cylinder remains sound, it can crush ten thousand tons of cold stone into dust; yet let a single hairline flaw appear inside the metal of the piston itself, and the very pressure of its own steam will blow the machine through the roof.

During the winter of 1930 and the spring of 1931, that flaw ran crack by crack around the entire twenty-five-thousand-mile rim of the basin. In the First generation, a strike in the coal-pits of Nanaimo or the rolling-mills of Pittsburg had been a local ulcer, easily lanced by a regiment of cavalry while the rest of the ocean kept the forges hot. Now, however, the *Steel Revolution* had welded the Hundred and Thirty Cantons into a single, seamless, clockwork animal whose heart beat at Oahu, whose lungs breathed the oil of Sumatra, and whose stomach digested the iron-ore and fleece of Australia.

When the disciples of the three-faced Marx-Bodhisattva failed to blow the San Francisco pontoons into the Golden Gate from below, they did not waste another pound of gelatine upon eighteen-inch Krupp armor.

They went south to the place where the iron came out of the ground.

On the morning of the fourteenth of May, 1931, I stood upon the high basalt bluff overlooking the *Port Kembla and Newcastle Imperial Steel-Corridor*—that sixty-mile strip of blackened coast south of Sydney in the Eighty-Second Canton where twelve million tons of red Australian hematite and Southern Alps coking-coal were smelted every year in automated, tape-driven blast-furnaces to feed the shipyards of Yokosuka, Hunters Point, and the Pearl Lochs.

For twenty years, the sky above the Illawarra escarpment had never known the color of the sun. Day and night, fifty-two weeks in the year, the eighty colossal, four-hundred-foot Bessemer-Nakajima converter-chimneys had vomited a solid, roaring ceiling of blood-orange flame and greasy coal-black soot across the Tasman Sea, while the rhythmic, subterranean *thud-clank-hiss* of the crewless rolling-mills shook the eucalyptus forests ten miles inland.

This morning, the sky above Port Kembla was as blue, empty, and silent as on the day Captain Cook’s bark first raised the heads of Botany Bay.

Not a single ribbon of smoke rose from the eighty chimneys. Down on the three-mile concrete ore-wharf, six forty-thousand-ton gyro-steered colliers from the Osaka yards lay dead in the green swell, their automated unloading-claws hanging frozen in mid-air forty feet above the hatches like the legs of dead iron spiders.

There had been no riot at the outer wire; the eighty thousand starving, locked-out boilermakers and shearers in the Yarra and Newcastle mud-camps had not thrown their bodies against the Maxim towers a second time. Instead, at midnight on the tenth of May, the four hundred elite *Cybernetic Maintenance-Prefects* inside the windowless concrete walls—young graduates of the Kyoto and Melbourne polytechnics who wore the golden gear-wheel on their collars, and who had secretly swallowed the soot-stained rice-wafer of the *Cathedral of the Unnumbered* in the subterranean tram-tunnels—had simply walked down the central aisle of the tape-looms with pockets full of thermite-grenades and cold chisels.

They had not merely turned off the switches.

Wait until a four-hundred-ton blast-furnace is filled to the throat with molten white-hot pig-iron and slag at three thousand degrees Fahrenheit, and then cut the high-tension power-cables from the Snowy River hydro-dams and blow the auxiliary steam-blowers off their beds with thermite.

Within six hours, as the temperature inside the eighty giant brick-and-steel towers dropped below the melting-point, sixty thousand tons of liquid iron had congealed inside the hearths, the tuyeres, and the tapping-spouts into solid, immovable mountains of cold grey steel—what the foundry-men call a *frozen salamander*.

"You cannot drill it out with diamond-bits, Citizen-Historian, and if you put five hundred pounds of dynamite under the hearth, you will only blow the furnace-shell into the harbor," said Chief Assessor MacArthur—a distant, pale-faced nephew of the old senator, who stood beside me on the bluff with an unlighted pipe between his teeth, looking down through his field-glasses at the silent concrete fortress where ten thousand unarmed strikers from the bush-camps were now sitting quietly cross-legged upon the railway tracks, chanting the slow, three-note mantra of the *Kwannon-of-the-Shovel*. "To get a single pound of ship-plate out of Port Kembla again, the Chancellery will have to tear all eighty furnaces down to the bedrock with hand-picks and rebuild the fire-brick from the foundation. And there isn't a ton of spare structural steel between here and the Yangtze to build the scaffolding."

I lowered my glasses and looked out across the glittering, empty blue plains of the Pacific toward the north.

Already, before the iron in the Newcastle hearths had even grown cold to the touch, the paralysis was leaping across the submarine cables like mortification up a severed limb: at Yokosuka, the gantry-cranes had stopped riveting the hull of the new super-dreadnought *Kalanimoku II* for want of Australian nickel-plate; at Vallejo, the automated tin-canneries had shut down their stamping-presses, leaving forty thousand carcasses of Californian beef to rot on the sidings while the garrison-troops in Vienna and Warsaw went on quarter-rations; and down in the deep-water channel of Sydney Harbor, three leagues north of where we stood, the sixty-foot dark-blue turrets of the Pacific Battle Fleet were swinging their twenty-two-inch rifles toward the silent brick chimneys of the shore.

***

Marshal Marcus Vance the third stood upon the open flying-bridge of the armored cruiser *Monterey*, anchored four hundred yards off the Circular Quay in the heart of Sydney Cove, with a heavy steel splint strapped across his broken nose and his fur-lined greatcoat buttoned to the chin against the sharp May wind coming off the Southern Ocean.

Since the night in the San Francisco sewer when his own third-tier ordnance-lieutenant had tried to blow him into the bay mud, the Marshal had ceased to sleep in a cabin with a locked door; he had his camp-cot pitched directly inside the armored conning-tower between two mute, deaf-and-dumb Samoan bodyguards whose tongues had been cut out in childhood by the Palace surgeons so they could never repeat a password in the dark.

Now, leaning his gloved knuckles upon the wet teak rail of the bridge-wing, he stared through his new, heavy-framed spectacles at the semi-circular amphitheater of the Sydney docks.

There were no burning barricades along George Street; there were no red flags waving from the roofs of the wool-warehouses. From the water’s edge at Bennelong Point all the way back up the sandstone slope to the gates of the Botanical Gardens, a hundred and twenty thousand men, women, and children were sitting shoulder-to-shoulder upon the cold granite paving-stones in absolute, terrifying silence.

In the front ranks, dangling their bare feet over the timber string-pieces of the ferry-wharves not fifty yards from the *Monterey’s* bow-casemates, sat the four hundred young Cybernetic Maintenance-Prefects who had frozen the Port Kembla furnaces—still wearing their immaculate dark-blue Polytechnic tunics, but with the silver identification-numbers ripped from their collars and piled in a neat, glittering pyramid upon the capstan-head beside them. Behind them sat eighty thousand grizzled Australian sheep-shearers, Yorkshire foundry-hands, and Cantonese track-layers, their arms linked together through their ragged sleeves, their eyes fixed calmly upon the gaping black muzzles of the cruiser’s eight-inch secondary battery.

And lined up along the broad macadam roadway of the quay, standing at strict regulation parade-rest with a double belt of three-hundred-round Maxim cartridge-boxes at their feet and twenty rapid-fire pom-pom guns unlimbered on the cobbles, stood the three thousand flesh-and-blood infantrymen of the *Fourteenth Californian and Satsuma Pacification Regiment*—the last reliable mainland brigade that Marcus had brought south from the Golden Gate.

"The noon meridian-chronometer has ten seconds to run, Marshal," said Captain Noguchi at his elbow, holding a brass megaphone in one hand and a pocket-watch in the other, his voice dropping low so the Hawaiian quartermaster at the wheel could not hear the tremor in his throat. "They have not touched the coal-lighters, sir, and the furnace-engineers have made no move to return to the Port Kembla trains. If you fire the eight-inch ship-guns at four hundred yards into that granite slope, the ricochets will cut down our own regiment on the quay wall."

"I am not going to waste naval picric-acid on sheep-clippers when I have three thousand rifles on the pavement!" Marcus rasped through the steel nasal-splint, which gave his high, reedy voice a nasal, metallic whistle like a leaking steam-pipe. He stepped out to the tip of the starboard bridge-wing, snatched the brass megaphone from Noguchi’s fingers, and pointed it straight down across the narrow strip of green harbor water at the mounted figure of Colonel Kalakaua—brother to the officer who had died in the Khyber snows—sitting his bay charger behind the center company of the Californian line.

"Colonel Kalakaua!" Marcus’s amplified shriek echoed off the stone facades of the custom-house and rolled back across the silent bay. "The Emperor’s grace has expired! You will not fire blank cartridge, and you will not aim over their heads! Dress your front rank at thirty paces from the wharf-edge, load with flat-nosed riot-ball, and clear the stone to the warehouse doors! Give the word to the Maxim sections—*Fire!*"

Down on the granite quay, Colonel Kalakaua slowly drew his nickel-plated regulation saber from its scabbard and raised it straight toward the pale autumn sun.

"Fourteenth Regiment!" the Hawaiian colonel’s deep baritone rang out across the water, while among the hundred and twenty thousand sitting men and women on the stones not a single head ducked, and only a low, rhythmic murmur—that same three-note chant of the *Pure Land* that Marcus had heard in the black sewer under Market Street—began to rise from the wharves like the surf before a typhoon. "Load—*lock!* Present—*arms!*"

With the crisp, mechanical precision of boys who had drilled for four years on the Monterey asphalt, the fifteen hundred Californian and Satsuma riflemen of the standing rank brought their model-twenty-four magazine-rifles up to their shoulders; fifteen hundred steel bolts slid home with a single, oiled *snick*; and along the line of the twenty Maxim tripods, the gunners laid their thumbs against the brass firing-pieces.

"At the front rank of the mutineers—zero elevation—*Fire!*" Kalakaua shouted, slashing his saber downward toward the cobbles.

Nothing happened.

No crack of smokeless powder split the air; no grey smoke-puff jetted from the three thousand muzzles.

Instead, at the exact instant the colonel’s blade touched his stirrup-iron, the young Californian corporal at the right-flank guide of Company A—a tall, freckle-faced twenty-year-old boy from the Fresno irrigation-wards whose grandfather had ridden with Caleb Vance at the Truckee River—slowly lowered his rifle from his shoulder, opened the breech-bolt with a flick of his wrist so that the live brass cartridge spun out onto the stones, and drove his bayonet point-first into the crack between two granite paving-blocks until the steel stood upright by itself.

Then, reaching up with both hands to his throat, the boy tore the stitched linen strip bearing his six-digit Monterey birth-cipher off his tunic collar, tossed it onto the pile of silver badges on the ferry-capstan, and sat down cross-legged on the cold stone beside a one-armed Australian boilermaker.

*Tink—clink—tink—clatter.*

Like a line of dominoes falling down the three-quarter-mile curve of the Sydney waterfront, three thousand magazine-rifles came down from three thousand shoulders; three thousand steel bolts clicked open, showering the granite cobbles with a bright golden rain of unfired brass cartridges; and as Colonel Kalakaua wheeled his horse around in the trace, his dark Polynesian face grey with horror, and raised his revolver to shoot the Fresno corporal through the back of the head, four Choshu machine-gunners behind the nearest Maxim tripod stood up, caught their colonel by his gold-braided belt, and dragged him bodily out of the saddle onto the pavement—while up on the bridge of the *Monterey*, Marshal Marcus Vance dropped his brass megaphone over the rail and lunged backward into the armored conning-tower, his scarred hands clawing at the tunic of the quartermaster as he screamed, "Turn the main turrets on the regiment! Open the sea-valves of the magazine—Noguchi, why isn't the forward turret turning—"

***

It did not turn because the hydraulic return-pipes in the lower handling-room had been packed with shaved emery-stone at four o’clock that morning by the cruiser’s own warrant-machinists.

When the *Monterey* limped back into the Pearl Lochs roadstead nineteen days later—steered from the auxiliary hand-wheel on the after-deck by a skeleton watch of terrified Staff Academy instructors because the entire stoker-division had jumped overboard into the Sydney whale-boats—the Chronicler who stood upon the fortified mole at Waipahu knew that the Great Strike was merely the curtain-raiser. Now that the bayonets had turned to soft lead in the Emperor’s hand, the disciples of the three-faced idol no longer needed to sit upon railway tracks. They came inside the wire with the knife and the glass ampoule.

The Chancellery bulletins called that summer of 1931 the *Season of the Red Terror*; yet unlike the noisy bomb-throwings of the old Russian nihilists, this slaughter moved through the marble corridors of Thalassia with the silent, claustrophobic precision of a diving-bell sinking through dark water.

There was no longer a safe chamber between the Diamond Head batteries and the artificial reefs. Because the automated Babbage-Nakajima looms required human hands to oil their cams and replace their blown mercury-tubes, the assassin was already inside the fortress before the steel shutters were bolted down at sunset. He was the quiet Cantonese pantry-boy who had served the Senior Assessor’s papaya for twelve years; he was the Nagasaki torpedo-artificer who checked the pressure-gauges on the palace air-pumps; he was the third-class Californian cipher-clerk who carried the morning clearing-slips into the subterranean vault.

On the twelfth of July, Senior Minister Sato—the last surviving brother of that illustrious engineering house, who had stood beside me at the Exhibition barge only nine months before—was found sitting upright in his air-conditioned glass cubicle beneath the Great Gnomon, his white-leaded face turned the color of an eggplant and his tongue bitten through, because someone had poured two drams of anhydrous hydrocyanic acid into the sandalwood water-pan of his desk-ventilator.

Four nights later, when the Chief Justice of the Maritime Debt Court stepped into his private electric elevator at the top of the Coral Pavilion, the two-inch vanadium hoisting-cable—which had been neatly sawed nine-tenths through with a jeweler’s hack-saw above the grease-box—parted at the sixth floor, dropping the bronze cage two hundred feet down the shaft into the basement sump like a plumb-lead.

By the first week of August, the Imperial peerage had ceased to walk the mosaic floors above ground.

To the Chronicler who was summoned down into the *Third Sub-Basal Command Bunker* forty feet beneath the coral bedrock of the lagoon on the night of the fourteenth of August, the seat of oceanic providence resembled the flooded bilge of a sinking ironclad. The high, sunlit rotunda of the Crystal Palace above us stood completely deserted, its stained-glass maps dark and its ferns dead for want of water; down here in the low-ceilinged, steel-ribbed tunnel where the main submarine telegraph-trunks came up out of the ocean floor, the air was pumped down through triple-charcoal filters that hissed with a slow, suffocating wheeze at every stroke of the piston.

It smelled of wet Portland cement, sour carbolic, stale human terror, and the rank tallow of the emergency candles that burned beside the electric lamps lest the dynamo-tenders at Molokai cut the current. Every thirty yards along the dripping five-foot passage, heavily armed naval cadets of the First Class—boys whose fathers owned ten thousand acres of San Joaquin wheat—stood back-to-back behind sandbags of crushed coral, their fingers trembling on the triggers of short-barreled trench-shotguns, watching not the outer seaward hatches, but the brass food-lifts and the four-inch ventilation-pipes in the ceiling.

"Do not touch the tin water-dipper by the filter-butt, Citizen-Historian," whispered Junior Assessor MacArthur, meeting me at the third armored bulkhead with a drawn revolver in his hand and four days’ growth of red stubble on his hollow cheeks. "The relief-watch found two grains of soluble barium-salts in the ice-chest at noon, and the chief cook hung himself with his own apron-string in the scullery before the Verification Board could put the hot irons to his feet. Keep your hands outside your coat-pockets when you pass the Samoan—the Marshal has not slept since Tuesday."

***

Inside the innermost iron casemate—a windowless twelve-by-twelve box of two-inch Krupp plate that had originally been forged to house the master-gyroscope of the Pearl Lochs harbor-mines—Marshal Marcus Vance the third sat upon an upturned ammunition-crate with his back wedged tight into the ninety-degree angle of the steel walls.

He had chosen that corner because there was no ventilation-grating behind his head and no rivet-seam wide enough to pass a needle. The steel splint had been taken off his broken nose, leaving the bridge flattened and twisted sideways across his scarred left cheek like a lump of purple putty; his high-collared Marshal’s tunic was unbuttoned at the throat, stained down the front with spilled beef-tea that he had been afraid to drink, and across his knees lay a cocked, double-barreled ten-gauge riot-gun loaded with buckshot.

Two paces in front of his boots, standing motionless as twin statues of oiled bronze beneath the single naked carbon-bulb that swung from the sweating ceiling-plate, stood his two mute Samoan bodyguards, Tui and Mano.

Six feet four inches tall, bare-armed to the shoulder where the tattooed bands of the Pago-Pago guard encircled their biceps, they stood with their broad backs turned toward their master and their faces toward the bolted iron door, holding five-foot steel boarding-pikes slantwise across their chests. For four years, ever since the Palace surgeons had cut the tongues out of their mouths and punctured their eardrums with silver needles so that no rebel preacher could corrupt them with the Creole of the Lower Decks, those two mutilated giants had been the only living creatures within whose reach Marcus Vance dared close his eyes.

*Tick—tock—tick—tock—shunt.*

On the steel bulkhead beside the Marshal’s ear, the brass second-hand of the naval master-chronometer jerked around the dial toward two o’clock in the morning. Every sixty seconds, as the minute-hand touched the top of the circle, the pneumatic pressure-valve in the air-pipe overhead gave a long, wet sigh, followed by the dull, distant *thud-thud* of the harbor water slapping against the outer submarine caisson thirty feet away.

Marcus did not look at me when MacArthur slid the viewing-slot back and let me step over the high iron coaming; his bloodshot eyes behind his thick lenses were fixed with a terrible, unblinking stare upon the sweating, naked shoulder-blades of the two mutes.

*One minute past two.*

A drop of warm condensation formed on the rusted rivet directly above the carbon-bulb, hung trembling for five seconds in the yellow glare, and fell with a sharp *spat* onto the hot glass globe.

Marcus’s right thumb twitched against the hammer of the shotgun. His mouth was dry as boiler-scale; his tongue felt swollen behind his teeth. He had not eaten solid food for thirty-eight hours, ever since Captain Noguchi had dropped dead across the chart-table at Waipahu after licking the gummed edge of an official Monterey telegraph-envelope. Even the air coming out of the brass nozzle above the door smelled wrong to him tonight—not of charcoal and ozone, but faintly, sickeningly sweet, like the sewer-rat tallow that had burned before the copper idol in the Mission Street gasometer.

"Why is the left-hand Samoan shifting his weight onto his right heel, MacArthur?" Marcus’s voice was a cracked, nasal whistle through his ruined nose, loud and ragged in the twelve-foot iron box.

MacArthur stopped half a pace inside the door, his hand tightening on his pistol-butt as he looked at the broad, scarred back of the giant Tui. "The deck-plates are greasy from the bilge-seep, Marshal. They have been standing on watch since the six-o’clock bell."

"They stood fourteen hours on the *Monterey* without moving an ankle!" Marcus rasped, drawing his boots two inches tighter under the ammunition-box and raising the twin muzzles of the ten-gauge until they pointed squarely between the lower ribs of the two guardsmen. *Two minutes past two.* The chronometer escapement clicked like a beetle in a coffin. "Look at the sweat on the back of Tui’s neck! The air-pump is set at sixty-eight degrees—why is a boy from the islands sweating in a cold room unless his blood is up? Turn him around! Take the boarding-pike out of his hands and look inside his mouth!"

"Inside his mouth, sir?" MacArthur took a step sideways along the steel wall, keeping clear of the shotgun’s arc. "The surgeon cut his tongue out at the root in twenty-seven—I signed the hospital-voucher myself."

"They don't need a tongue to take the soot-mark!" Marcus shrieked, his scarred cheek jerking so violently that his heavy spectacles slipped crookedly across his broken nose, throwing the cramped steel cabin out of focus into a swimming double-blur of yellow light and bronze skin. "In the San Francisco pipe, Hoshino said they were passing the wafer in the water-ration! Pull his left wrist back—let me see if there is a kukui-oil smudge between his thumb and his forefinger!"

The two mutes could not hear a single word of that high, whistling scream through their ruptured eardrums; yet as MacArthur reached out tentatively with his left hand to tap the giant Tui upon the tattooed muscle of his shoulder, the vibration of the Marshal’s voice through the iron floor-plates—or the sudden shadow of the Assessor’s arm against the swinging bulb—gave them the signal.

Tui did not wait for the tap.

At four minutes and twelve seconds past two by the bulkhead clock, the two deaf-and-dumb giants moved as if their tendons were wired to the same sixty-cycle cam.

Mano—the right-hand guard—did not turn toward the Marshal; he drove the heavy iron butt-ferrule of his boarding-pike straight backward behind his hip, catching Junior Assessor MacArthur squarely in the pit of the stomach and doubling him voiceless into the corner by the door while the revolver spun from his fingers across the wet steel plates.

In the same half-second, Tui pivoted on the ball of his bare left foot.

Marcus Vance pulled both triggers of the ten-gauge shotgun at once.

The deafening, double-charged roar of smokeless powder inside the sealed twelve-foot iron box blew out the carbon-bulb in a blinding flash of orange fire and filled the casemate instantly with a solid, choking wall of white sulfur-smoke that split the eardrums of the living—yet because the Marshal’s crooked spectacles had thrown his sight three inches high in his panic, the double load of lead buckshot tore harmlessly through the fleshy top of Tui’s left shoulder, flattening against the two-inch Krupp armor-plate behind him in a hot shower of lead-spatter.

Before the deafened, half-blinded Marshal could drop the empty gun and claw at his holster, the six-foot-four Samoan stepped straight through the burning powder-smoke with his left arm hanging in red rags.

He did not use the steel point of his pike; the shaft was too long to swing in the cramped box. Dropping the wood, Tui reached down through the dark with his massive, uninjured right hand, caught the grandson of Caleb Vance’s brother by his windpipe and his broken nose, and lifted the hundred-and-thirty-pound Marshal clean off the ammunition-crate until his patent-leather boots kicked eighteen inches above the floor.

Through the acrid, ringing blackness, by the dim red glow of the emergency tallow-wick smoldering in the corner, I saw the mute giant open his mouth as he slammed the back of Marcus Vance’s skull once, twice, three times against the projecting two-inch iron corner-bolts of the gyroscope-mount—and pinned to the raw, scarred stump of the Samoan’s severed tongue, held fast by a brass safety-pin driven straight through the living gristle, gleamed a one-inch square of crimson silk.

***

When the last Vance had been carried feet-first out of the Pearl Lochs bunker with his skull crushed like a dropped seagull’s egg, the Chronicler did not remain in Thalassia to see whether Emperor Kalanimoku would replace his bodyguards with clockwork dolls. For a historian who wishes to record the death of an empire must follow the blood back to the heart; and in the autumn of 1931, the heart of the Great Arena was no longer beating in the coral lagoons of Oahu, nor upon the white porcelain decks of the floating Arks.

It had returned, in the delirium of its final fever, to the cold brick ruins of the shore where the first hammer had been lifted.

When our coal-starved mail-steamer crept through the fog of the Golden Gate on the afternoon of the third of November, I noticed first that the three hundred acres of *New Thalassia-in-the-Bay* were listing six degrees to larboard between Alcatraz and the Marin cliffs. Two of the sixteen-inch vanadium anchor-chains on the southern face had been cut through during the October tides—not by nitro-gelatine divers, but by the simple failure of the automated cathodic rust-preventers after the Snowy River power-strike—and the three thousand silk-robed shareholders atop the pontoons were now prisoners upon their own rotting raft, watching through their opera-glasses as a new, terrifying fire rose out of the abandoned streets of San Francisco.

For ten years, the mainland wards from the Embarcadero to the Twin Peaks had been left to the subterranean mole-people of Keawe’s cult and the rolling Maxim-beetles of the Chancellery. Now, however, as I walked up the steep, grass-grown cobbles of Montgomery Street toward the shell-pocked ruins of the old Mint, the crewless patrol-cars were gone—pushed over on their backs in the gutters like dead iron turtles, with their selenium eyes smashed out by sledgehammers.

Yet it was not the three-faced banner of the Marx-Bodhisattva that snapped from the rusted gas-standards along the avenue.

From every crumbling brick cornice and every burned-out window-frame hung thirty-foot vertical pennants of raw, unbleached Californian canvas, dyed a glaring, arterial crimson with red-lead ship’s paint, upon which was stenciled in coal-tar not the gentle Sun-and-Anchor of the Polynesian dynasty, nor the broken chain of the stokers, but a single, angular black emblem: the crossed *Broad-Gauge Spike and Cavalry Saber* of 1852.

And marching four abreast up the center of the torn-up tramway tracks—not shuffling in rags like the Melbourne strikers, nor stepping in the silent, oiled cadence of the Polytechnic cadets, but tramping with a heavy, flat-footed frontier swagger to the deafening crash of forty skin-drums and brass field-bugles—came a column of five thousand young men.

They wore no numbers upon their collars; they wore no collars at all. They were dressed in rough, sleeveless shirts of red Californian flannel, high-laced logger’s boots, and black leather gauntlets that reached to the elbow—the exact, theatrical costume of the *Vigilance Pioneers* who had burned the Sacramento legislature for Elias Thorne seventy-nine years before. They were the starving, unindexed sons of the middle wards: displaced third-tier tally-clerks whose fathers had been purged by Shen, unemployed locomotive-firemen from the closed Oakland roundhouses, and the feral, sun-browned grandsons of the San Joaquin wheat-foremen who had seen their harvests rot on the sidings while the court at Oahu painted its cheeks with white lead.

At the head of the column, riding not in an electric staff-car, but astride a massive, raw-boned sorrel stallion whose iron shoes struck sparks from the granite cobbles, rode a man of thirty-two with his head bare to the cold November mist.

"Take off your hat when the *Iron Blood* passes, grandfather, or the boys with the pick-handles will take it off along with your ears," muttered an old, toothless typesetter beside me on the cracked curb, pulling his own greasy cap to his chest as the horsemen drew level with the ruined façade of the Bank of California.

I looked up into the rider’s face, and for a single, cold instant my hand shook upon my notebook.

Whether he had any true drop of the Protector’s blood in his veins, no parish register in California could prove; the Verification Board swore before its dissolution that he was the bastard son of a Eureka sawmill-boss and a stage-actress from the Nevada silver-towns. Yet nature, in her most malicious mood, had given *Julian Thorne* the exact, unmistakable mask of the bronze statues that stood upon every breakwater from Valparaiso to Vladivostok: the same heavy, square-hewn jaw, the same short, iron-gray brush of beard trimmed close to the chin, and above the hawk-bridge of the nose, those pale, cold, unblinking eyes that looked through a crowd of men as if they were standing timber waiting for the saw.

Over his red flannel shirt he wore an old, mud-splashed linen duster—copied stitch for stitch from the glass reliquary in the Monterey Museum—and strapped across his pommel was no circular slide-rule, but a heavy, octagonal-barreled 1851 Colt dragoon revolver.

When the stallion reached the broad, broken granite steps of the Old Mint—where sixty thousand red-shirted men and women were packed shoulder-to-shoulder across the plaza beneath a forest of smoking pitch-pine torches—Julian Thorne did not dismount to walk up to a microphone.

He drove his iron spurs into the sorrel’s flanks and rode the horse straight up the twenty marble steps, scattering the broken glass of the doors beneath its hooves until the beast stood snorting and rearing between the Doric pillars above the crowd.

"Men of the First Shore!" Julian Thorne’s voice rolled out across the twilight plaza—not the smooth, nasal English of the Berkeley examination-sheds, nor the musical Hawaiian of the lagoon, but a harsh, gravelly, chest-rasping bark that he had practiced for ten years in the timber-camps until every syllable sounded like two mill-stones grinding dry corn. "This morning, out on that floating whore-house in the bay, the painted half-breed who calls himself the Sacred Emperor sent a wireless message to the Fort Point batteries! He ordered the coastal guns to turn their muzzles inward and shell the Mission wards unless we hand over the Vallejo flour-mills to his Cantonese clerks before sundown!"

A roar like the breaking of an ocean reef went up from the sixty thousand red shirts below the steps, while five thousand iron pick-handles and stolen magazine-rifles flashed upward into the red glare of the pitch-torches.

Thorne did not raise a baton; he leaned forward over the sorrel’s wet neck, his thick, bare forearm corded with muscle as he pointed a short hickory walking-stick straight out through the fog toward the listing white pontoons in the harbor.

"Seventy-nine winters ago," Thorne bellowed, the veins in his bull-neck swelling above his unbuttoned flannel collar, "my great-grandfather rode down from the Donner snow-sheds with four hundred white-handed pioneers and built an empire of iron and beef! He didn't build it for a pack of tea-drinking eunuchs on a coral reef to trade away by punch-card! And he didn't build it for a rabble of sewer-rats down in the gas-pipes to divide up with the Chinamen and the Russians before their four-armed brass monkey! The rotting body at Oahu is dead, brothers—and tonight the blood goes back into the iron! Colonel Miller, bring the three six-inch siege-howitzers up to the Telegraph Hill parapet and load with solid armor-piercing shot!"

***
