Three thousand miles across the grey autumn rollers—for the report of Keawe’s November stoker-preaching had been premature, a rumor floated down the Waimea gorge by Malia herself to fool the Koloa tax-assessors into striking the blind nonagenarian from the salt-rolls—the image of that rearing sorrel horse did not travel by submarine paper.

It arrived through the ether, flickering in thirty-line neon-red bars across the curving glass bull’s-eye of the *Baird-Nakajima Tele-Vision Receiver* that the mutinous garrison-mechanics at the Koloa bauxite-dam had dragged up the mountain bridle-path on a mule-sled and wired directly into the high-tension penstock cable outside Lady Kaiulani’s hut.

Inside the grass-house, the smell of wet pandanus and yellow river-sludge was overpowered by the hot, oily ozone of the spinning Nipkow scanning-disc. Ninety-six-year-old Kaiulani sat propped within two inches of the thick convex lens. To a normal eye, the four-inch screen showed only a jerky, blood-colored phantom of a bearded face and a waving hickory stick, swimming through a blizzard of diagonal static-snow; yet to the blind woman, whose ruined retinas could no longer perceive the soft daylight of the valley, the concentrated, pulsing glare of the neon-tube pierced the white opacity of her lenses like a red-hot needle.

And she did not need ears to hear him. To make the old Queen understand why the bauxite-stampers down at the river had stopped their tremor at noon, the rebellious Hawaiian line-men had bolted a copper bone-conduction vibrator directly to the cedar center-post against which her bare, shrunken skull rested.

*"—tear the silk off their backs and put the pick-axe back into their soft hands!"* 

The voice did not enter through her eardrums; it hammered straight through the mastoid bone of her jaw and vibrated in the hollow, toothless cavern of her mouth—a harsh, metallic travesty of the dead Protector’s gravel.

"Look at him, Aunt," Malia cried, kneeling beside the humming mahogany cabinet with her hands clasped together over her stained linen skirt, her fifty-year-old face lit crimson by the spinning holes of the brass disc. "The soldiers at the Koloa dam have thrown their Choshu officers into the leaching-vats and pinned red flannel to their hats! They say he has sunk the San Francisco pontoons with three shots from the hill, and that the fleet at Pearl Lochs has hoisted the Spike-and-Saber! He is going to burn the counting-machines, Aunt! He is going to give the land back to the living!"

Kaiulani did not answer. Her translucent, leaf-light fingers—still resting upon the rusted 1861 iron rail across her knees—trembled with the mechanical shudder of the cedar post.

Through the burning red bars of the glass lens, she saw the square-jawed head turn in profile; she saw the linen duster flap in the artificial wind of the scanning-beam.

*That is not Elias,* the old woman thought, a cold nausea rising in her dry throat as the bone-vibrator rattled her skull with the roar of sixty thousand Californian throats. *When Elias rode into Monterey, he wore a linen duster because the dust of the San Joaquin was two inches thick on his shoulders, and he carried a dragoon pistol because Caleb Vance’s enemies were shooting at him from the chaparral. This play-actor in the red lamp-light has bought his mud from a theater-wardrobe in Sacramento.* 

Elias had built the machine because the wilderness was too wide for a horse; now the machine had eaten the wilderness and gone mad in the dark, and the terrified grandchildren were dressing up in their dead grandfather’s clothes, thinking that a flannel shirt and a hickory stick could charm the rust out of eighty frozen blast-furnaces.

"Pull the copper wire out of the wall, Malia," Kaiulani whispered, turning her blind, red-lit face away from the spinning glass bull’s-eye as the phantom on the screen raised a heavy cavalry saber and kissed the flat of the blade. "That is no man on the horse. That is only the smell of the grave coming back up through the floor-boards."

***

Yet a corpse that walks by electricity moves faster than a living army; and to the Chronicler who returned to Thalassia aboard the flagship of the *First Restoration Vanguard* on the nineteenth of November, 1931, the fall of the Polynesian dynasty possessed neither the tragic dignity of King Kalakaua’s surrender at Sand Island nor the fiery grandeur of the London raid.

There was not a single twenty-two-inch shell fired across the reef. When Julian Thorne’s six requisitioned turbine-transports—their hulls painted a glaring, rust-red lead from waterline to funnel-top, and their bridges manned by red-shirted Californian river-pilots and defecting third-tier naval lieutenants—steamed straight through the Honolulu Passage at dawn, the colossal coastal batteries at Diamond Head and Barber’s Point remained as silent as the coral rock.

The automated fire-control computers in the casemates had been disconnected three days before by their own terrified maintenance-clerks, who had watched the San Francisco pontoons burn on the Tele-Vision screens and had already stitched squares of red tradesman’s flannel over the silver numerals on their collars.

By ten o’clock that morning, I stood once more beneath the vast, unwashed Jena glass dome of the Pan-Pacific Senate.

The air inside the rotunda was ninety-four degrees, thick with the stench of uncollected stable-manure and raw methylated spirits; for Julian Thorne had brought two hundred rough-shod Californian stock-horses ashore from the cattle-decks and quartered them directly among the dead tree-ferns of the botanical floor. Around the five concentric tiers of the amphitheater, the surviving senators of the inner cantons—the white-leaded Osaka shipping-peers, the plump Cantonese rice-syndics, and the trembling Berkeley assessors—sat frozen in their stalls, each man wearing a hastily torn strip of red silk curtain-cord tied around his left bicep to save his throat from the three thousand logger-booted *Vigilance Pioneers* who leaned upon their iron pick-handles along the marble aisles.

Up on the central porphyry rostrum, the Sacred Emperor Kalanimoku did not sit in his yellow *mamo* feathers.

Stripped to his sweat-stained white linen undershirt, with his corpulent belly sagging over his belt and his dark Polynesian cheeks grey beneath the smeared remnants of his court powder, the grandson of Kaiulani stood between two six-foot Eureka timber-fellers who held him upright by the elbows. The bulletproof metal scales of his royal mantle lay in a heap at the foot of the steps, where a pioneer blacksmith was already breaking them up with a sledgehammer to shoe the cavalry mounts.

Julian Thorne did not sit in the bronze curule chair either. He stood with one mud-caked logger’s boot planted squarely upon the edge of the porphyry table, his mud-splashed linen duster thrown back to show the twin 1851 Colt revolvers at his hips, while three technicians from the Monterey Signal Corps worked frantically with soldering-irons to wire a massive, four-sided bank of neon Tele-Vision cameras and carbon-arc floodlights directly to the base of the Great Gnomon.

"Are the San Francisco and Yokohama relay-towers locked onto the wave-length?" Thorne barked, not looking at the trembling Emperor beside him, but squinting into the blinding white glare of the carbon-arcs while a former stage-manager from the Sacramento Opera House dabbed a touch of grey grease-paint onto the bridge of the Restorer’s nose to sharpen his profile for the thirty-line scanning-beam.

"The west-coast and insular receivers are synchronizing now, Citizen-Restorer," the signal-captain answered, dropping his soldering-iron as the two-foot brass Nipkow discs inside the camera-boxes began to whine up to their eighteen-hundred-revolution pitch. "You have forty million eyes on the glass."

Thorne spat a chew of coarse Virginia plug tobacco squarely onto the inlaid brass map of the North Atlantic at his feet, wiped his iron-gray beard with the back of his leather gauntlet, and stepped into the focal circle of the lenses.

He did not read from a parchment scroll; he seized the trembling, half-fainting Kalanimoku by the scruff of his linen collar, dragged him two paces forward into the white-hot light of the carbon-arcs, and forced the Emperor’s heavy jaw down upon the steel anvil of the broken Hollerith master-tabulator.

"Look into the glass, brothers of the Pacific!" Thorne’s gravelly, theatrical roar thundered into the suspended microphones, echoing back from the cracked sandstone colonnades outside where the eighty aluminum automatons had been pulled down with wire-ropes into the canal. "Look at the soft, painted slug that has been eating your beef and selling your birthright to the Chinamen and the machines while you starved in the mud! Sixty years ago, when the old Protector took his eyes off the wheel, the Honolulu women crept into his bedroom and stole the ring off his dead finger! Today, the pioneer takes back the forge!"

With his right hand, Thorne snatched up a four-pound track-layer’s spiking-maul that lay beside the anvil—not to strike Kalanimoku’s skull, for the stage-manager had warned him that blood on the lens would blur the neon transmission—but to bring the iron head crashing down with a single, deafening blow upon the bronze Seal of the Double Horizon resting beside the Emperor’s ear, splitting the die in two while Kalanimoku’s knees gave way in terror and his bladder emptied itself down his white trousers onto the marble steps.

"By the authority of the First Shore and the Vigilance Committee of Nineteen-Thirty-One," Thorne bellowed, planting his boot atop the shattered bronze seal and raising the spiking-maul toward the whining red eye of the camera, "I declare the Polynesian Regency and the Bureau of Integration abolished forever! There are no more numbers, and there are no more peers! From this noon, I assume the office of *Lord-Restorer of the Grand Confederation*—and by God, before the winter snow closes the Sierra passes, every man with white blood in his veins will have four pounds of beef in his pot and two Chinamen to carry his shovel!"

***

Across the Kauai channel, the noon sun had not yet burned the yellow copper-fog out of the Waimea canyon when the first motor-launch of the *Insular Restoration Guard* came roaring up the shallow, sludge-choked mouth of the river at Koloa.

They did not need to march four miles up the mountain path on foot, as the Choshu patrols had done. Behind the red-painted bow of the launch, towed upon a flat-bottomed timber scow, rode two four-wheeled *Dodge-Sacramento Field Lorries* armed with twin air-cooled Browning machine-guns and packed with twenty young men in sleeveless red flannel shirts—half of them Californian mechanics from the Pearl Lochs repair-yards, and the other half mixed-blood Portuguese and Hawaiian plantation-overseers from the Waipahu sugar-mills who had bleached their hair with lime-water and bound red rags around their arms to prove they belonged to the *First Shore*.

Up in the grass-house above the dry waterfall, the copper bone-vibrator on the cedar post had gone dead ten minutes after noon, when the operators at Koloa shut off the penstock dynamos to join the looting of the Cantonese company-stores.

For the first time in eleven years, the volcanic bedrock of the island beneath Kaiulani’s bare feet was completely still.

The subterranean fever-pulse of the bauxite-stampers had ceased; in the sudden, eerie stillness of the gorge, the ninety-six-year-old woman could almost imagine that she heard the ghost of the old Waimea river trickling through the dry fern-roots outside the door. "They are coming up the missionary road in the gasoline-wagons, Aunt," Malia said. She did not shout into the hollow of Kaiulani’s temple anymore; she simply knelt on the pandanus mat and pressed her forehead quietly against her aunt’s shrunken, bark-wrapped knee, her hands resting beside the four-foot bar of rusted 1861 railroad iron. Through the open doorway, the stench of burning thatch and raw kerosene was already drifting up from the lower village, mixed with the flat, sharp pop-pop-pop of pistol-shots where the crimson-clad overseers were settling thirty years of wage-scores with the Cantonese tally-clerks. With a grinding roar of low-gear pinions and a shower of crushed red lava-stone, the lead Dodge lorry burst through the dry banana-brake below the terrace, crushing the ancient stone salt-pans beneath its solid rubber tires and skidding to a halt ten paces from the grass-house porch. Four men in sleeveless scarlet wool and high logger’s boots jumped down over the tail-board. At their head walked a twenty-five-year-old youth named Cazneau—the grandson of an American customs-collector at Hilo and a Maui woman, though he had smeared grey wood-ash across his brown cheekbones to pale his skin and wore a rusted cavalry saber strapped over his canvas riding-coat. He carried no perforated manila warrant in his hand; he carried a five-gallon tin of rock-oil and a portable battery-operated megaphone. "Come out of the straw, old spider!" Cazneau shouted, kicking the woven reed screen from the doorway with the toe of his boot and blinking into the dim, kukui-scented gloom of the hut while two Californian machinists behind him leveled their short-barreled riot-guns at Malia’s chest. "By Order Number One of the Lord-Restorer, all pensioners of the Honolulu blood are summoned to the Koloa wharf for public audit! Where is the gold bullion-chest that you and the lame general brought back from the Geneva banks in eighteen?" Malia rose slowly to her feet in front of the cedar post, her grey hair falling loose over her red-stained arms as she bent down and lifted the heavy, four-foot bar of rusted 1861 Sacramento wrought-iron in both hands. "She cannot hear your horn, half-breed," Malia said calmly in Hawaiian, looking at the streak of grey wood-ash running down Cazneau’s sweating brown neck, "and the only iron left in this house is the rail your grandfather’s master laid down before you were born." "Speak English when you answer a Restoration Officer, you kanaka bitch, or I’ll have the skin off your back!" Cazneau snarled, his face flushing dark purple beneath the ash as he stepped across the threshold and swung the heavy iron nozzle of his battery-megaphone straight against the side of Malia’s jaw, knocking her sideways across the pandanus mat while his left hand reached down to seize the collar of ninety-six-year-old Kaiulani’s bark-cloth wrapper. He dragged the feather-light, blind bundle of bone and dry skin straight out across the threshold into the blinding yellow sulfur-haze, tossing her onto the tail-board of the Dodge lorry like a sack of spoiled copra while his two machinists splashed the five gallons of rock-oil over the dry pandanus thatch of the priest’s house and dropped a wax vesta into the doorway.

***

They did not hang the old Queen at the Koloa wharf; Julian Thorne’s theatrical instinct was too shrewd to give the islands a martyr while the stokers in the Battle Fleet were still holding their hammers behind their backs. Instead, they locked her in the abandoned stone quarantine-lazaretto on Sand Island—the very rock where her brother had signed away the crown sixty years before—while the Lord-Restorer looked desperately around the horizon for an enemy his pioneers could shoot.

For a usurper who rides to power upon a stallion in an age of dead dynamos cannot feed his horsemen on stage-paint. Within forty days of the November coup, the four pounds of beef that Julian had promised to every white throat in California had shrunk to four ounces of salted horse-marrow. The eighty frozen blast-furnaces at Port Kembla remained cold monuments of grey slag; the Siberian trunk-line was cut permanently at Lake Baikal by the self-governing Soviet of the Unnumbered; and the Cantonese rice-junks simply ceased to cross the bar at Macao when the red-shirted customs-collectors tried to pay for the grain in unbacked Restoration scrip.

To keep his five hundred thousand logger-booted Vigilance Pioneers from turning their stolen rifles upon the Sacramento Opera House, Julian Thorne was forced to invent a wilderness.

To the Chronicler who sailed southward from San Diego in the January of 1932 aboard the requisitioned cattle-liner *Sierra*—accompanying what the Restorer’s neon bulletins grandiloquently styled the *Grand Expedition of the Austral Frontier*—the armada that wallowed across the warm equatorial swells toward the coast of Peru was a spectral parody of Elias Thorne’s early vigor. In 1868, the first Protector had sent three fast cruisers to Callao to lock the guano-islands into the Market Street ledger with a single afternoon’s cannonade. Now, Julian had scraped together thirty rust-streaked, coal-burning transport-hulks whose gyro-pilots had been smashed with sledges to give employment to human steersmen, crowded with ninety thousand hungry, scarlet-shirted youths from the Oregon timber-camps and the Los Angeles oil-slums who had been told that the high valleys of the Andes were still bursting with unmined Inca silver and unnumbered Indian cattle.

"Look at the smoke from the third transport’s funnel, Citizen-Historian," said my cabin-mate, a sixty-year-old retired hydrographer named Kemp who had been dragged out of the Monterey almshouse because the young Pioneers had purged every navigator who knew how to use a logarithmic table. He leaned over the blistered iron taffrail as our squadron rolled through the Humboldt Current off Guayaquil, pointing a trembling finger at the ragged, yellow-brown smudge of lignite dust trailing from the *Comstock’s* stacks. "They are burning green redwood sleepers and soft Coos Bay peat under high-pressure Yarrow boilers because the Sumatra oil-tankers haven't touched at San Pedro since October. Half those boys on the fore-deck are carrying single-shot Springfield trap-door rifles they pried out of the Presidio war-memorials, and they think they are going to march up to Cuzco and carve out ten-thousand-acre ranchos like Cortés."

Yet when our thirty transports dropped their rusted anchors into the brown, lifeless rollers off the roadstead of Callao on the twelfth of February, there were no plumed Inca kings waiting on the shingle with baskets of virgin gold, nor even a rebellious Spanish general to cross swords with the Restorer’s vanguard.

There was only the Empire’s own corpse, rotting in the sun.

For sixty-four years, the Hundred and Ninth Peruvian Canton had been an integral, thoroughly digested bowel of the Grand Confederation. Its guano-beds on the Chincha rocks had been scraped down to the bare white granite ten winters ago; its copper-veins at Cerro de Pasco had been pumped dry by the automated Osaka leaching-vats; and its three million Quechua and mestizo inhabitants wore the same six-digit brass ration-shackles on their left wrists as the coal-hewers of the Ruhr.

As the first flat-bottomed landing-barges of the Californian Pioneers grounded in the greasy surf below the rusted iron skeleton of the Callao nitrate-piers—their buglers blowing the old cavalry charge of the Truckee River while the boys in their heavy logger’s boots leaped waist-deep into the warm, sewage-fouled foam waving their hickory sticks—not a single shot was fired from the shore.

Along the cracked concrete coping of the seawall, beneath a faded, tattered banner of Imperial Blue and Sunset Gold that nobody had bothered to haul down since November, stood four thousand emaciated Peruvian dock-coolies and twenty aged Cantonese tally-clerks from the local Bureau of Integration.

"Where are the rebel barricades?" shouted Vanguard-Colonel Miller, wading ashore with a drawn 1851 dragoon pistol in each hand, his heavy wool shirt dark with equatorial sweat as he glared up at the silent, hollow-cheeked crowd on the quay. "Where is the Peruvian gold-reserve? By order of the Lord-Restorer Julian Thorne, this coast is annexed to the First Shore as Pioneer Settlement-Land! Bring out your municipal syndics to surrender the keys of the Lima mint!"

At the head of the seawall steps, the Senior Canton-Assessor—a seventy-year-old Chinese graduate of the class of eighty-four, whose left eye was blind with the trachoma of the nitrate-flats and whose fingernails had grown two inches long over his empty ledger-board—slowly bowed from the waist.

"There has been no silver in the Lima mint since Chancellor Shen transferred the bullion-reserve to the San Francisco pontoons in nineteen-twenty-two, Honorable Pioneer," the old clerk answered in crisp, archaic Monterey English, holding out a rusted iron key ring upon which hung three brass padlock-keys and a deadHollerith sorting-needle. "And the automated copper-smelters at Oroya stopped turning in June when the Melbourne dynamo-parts failed to arrive. If your soldiers have brought the winter barley-ration from the San Joaquin, my four hundred thousand registered laborers will gladly paint the Spike-and-Saber upon the customs-house; if you have brought no barley, Honorable Colonel, there is nothing left in this province to eat except the mules beneath your wagons."

***

They ate the mules before March was out; and when Julian Thorne received the wireless dispatch from Callao—informing him that his ninety thousand pioneers were sitting in the dry white dust of the Rimac valley dying of the Verruga fever and shooting one another over the last barrels of salted Californian horse-beef because his "new frontier" had already been stripped to the bone by his own dead grandfather fifty years earlier—the Lord-Restorer retreated into the subterranean Chart-Vault of the Palace at Thalassia and bolted the bronze doors against his own buglers.

To the Chronicler who was dragged out of my quarters in the Old Archives on the night of the nineteenth of April, 1932, by four drunken Eureka timber-guards—summoned down into that vast, circular basement because the Restorer had driven the last Polytechnic cartographers to the sugar-ditches and needed an old man who could read the Latin ciphers on the nineteenth-century globes—the chamber where Kaiulani and Marcus Vance had once weighed the tides of the earth looked like a bear-pit in a ruined theater.

The eighty pneumatic sorting-machines had been smashed into twisted heaps of brass and cast-iron by the pioneers’ sledges to prove that the reign of numbers was over; their shattered frames had been kicked into the corners to make room for forty open whiskey-barrels and a smoky brick barbecue-pit upon which half an Oahu wild bullock was charring over burning cabinet-mahogany. The air was suffocating, thick with the stench of scorched beef-fat, sour Kentucky mash, stale horse-liniment, and the pungent, metallic ozone of the single surviving Molokai power-cable that fed the great illuminated glass map of the world set into the central mosaic floor.

Julian Thorne was alone upon the thirty-foot glass continents.

He had taken off his logger’s boots; in his filthy grey wool socks, with his canvas riding-coat stained down the front with tobacco-spit and spilled bourbon and the two heavy dragoon revolvers banging against his naked thighs beneath his unbuttoned flannel shirt, he was walking slowly around and around the glowing glass circle of the Pacific Ocean, carrying a five-pound iron track-spiking maul by the handle.

"Come out onto the water, Historian!" Julian barked as the timber-guards shoved me across the threshold. His voice had lost its theatrical Sacramento boom; it was raw, hoarse, and ragged from five months of screaming into neon microphones, and beneath the grey stage-paint that still flaked in the creases of his square jaw, his pale eyes were bloodshot and wild with the sleepless terror of an actor who hears the audience tearing up the benches in the dark. "You wrote the books for the old wolf! You were with Kuroda when he took the Indian rivers, and you were at Berlin when the Chinaman locked up the Germans! Bring your lantern over here to the glass and show me where they hid the uncut timber!"

I limped across the cold glass crust of the North Pacific—where half the subterranean electric bulbs beneath the Mariana Trench had burned out, leaving black, blind patches across the sea-lanes—and stopped beside the glowing red outline of the American continent.

"What timber does Your Excellency seek?" I asked quietly.

"The frontier, damn your spectacles!" Julian roared, swinging the iron spiking-maul down against the thick plate-glass of the Peruvian coast so violently that a star-shaped crack leaped from Lima to the Galapagos. "An empire has to march, old man! Elias Thorne told Caleb Vance at the Sacramento river that the day the wagons stop rolling into new grass, the boys in the camp will cut their captains’ throats! I sent ninety thousand red-shirts to Peru, and there’s nothing there but rusted Osaka tin-cans and Chinamen with numbers on their wrists! Where did the old Protector leave an unplowed valley where a white pioneer can plant a flag and take a chest of gold with a rifle?"

He dropped to his knees upon the glowing glass dome of the world, his broad, grease-stained hands crawling frantically across the illuminated continents like a blind crab hunting for a crack in a porcelain bowl.

"What about the African interior?" Julian muttered, his stubby forefinger stabbing down upon the green glass of the Congo basin. "The Belgian and French leases that Kaiulani took at Geneva!"

"The Bureau of Integration stripped the rubber-vines to the roots in twenty-four, Citizen-Restorer," I answered, looking down at his sweating iron-gray crown, "and when the automated river-dredges poisoned the Lake Chad fisheries with mercury-sludge in twenty-eight, the surviving tribes burned the railhead at Matadi and died of the Belgian grippe. There is not a pound of ivory or an unmortgaged acre between Cairo and the Cape."

"Then the Russian steppes beyond the Urals!" He scrambled backward on his knees across the cracked glass of the Indian Ocean, his revolver-butts clanking against the Himalaya peaks. "The wheat-lands of the Ukraine!"

"Fourteennumbered cantons, Excellency," I said, "plowed by crewless steam-tractors until the topsoil blew into the Black Sea during the drought of twenty-nine, and now held by two million armed Prussian and Russian deportees who shoot every man wearing a collar at five hundred yards."

Julian stopped his hands upon the glass. Slowly, he raised his square, painted face under the single flickering arc-lamp of the vault and looked around the thirty-foot circle at his knees.

From the ice-floes of the Bering Strait to the basalt cliffs of Tasmania; from the ruined brick wharves of the Thames to the dry salt-pans of the Rimac—every river, every mountain-pass, every coal-seam, and every island upon the terrestrial globe was ruled off in neat, indelible black one-degree squares, stamped with a three-digit canton cipher and crossed by the red spider-web of the submarine cables.

For ten thousand years, whenever a Caesar or a Khan had exhausted the soil of his own valley, there had always been a dark, unmapped margin beyond the rim of the parchment where the barbarian waited with fresh blood and uncut forests. Now, because Elias Thorne’s steamships and Marcus Vance’s broad-gauge rails had finally closed the circle of the earth at the meridian, the world had no outside left.

There was nowhere to march; there was no foreigner left to rob; the pioneer had ridden all the way around the ball of the earth and come up behind his own back door.

"He didn't leave me an inch," Julian whispered, the five-pound spiking-maul slipping from his slack fingers and rolling across the glass of the Coral Sea with a hollow, rumbling groan. "The old bastard ate the whole plate himself, and left me locked in the cellar with the bones."

***

Up above our heads, the cellar door was already splintering under the axe.

When I climbed the dark, spiral service-staircase out of the Chart-Vault at dawn on the twentieth of April—leaving the Lord-Restorer sitting alone on the cracked glass of the North Pacific with a dipper of raw bourbon in his fist—I did not go back to my sleeping-cell. I walked straight across the dry, weed-choked marble courtyard of the Palace toward the low, octagonal basalt tower of the *Imperial Historiographer’s Archive*, where the seventy-eight bound folio volumes of this *Chronicle of the Grand Confederation* stood ranged upon their iron shelves.

The sun was rising over the eastern rim of the Oahu craters—not in the clear, pearly Sunset Gold that I had seen from the deck of Marquis Takashima’s flagship sixty years ago when the world was young, but as a dull, copper-red ball swimming through a mile-high curtain of greasy black bunker-smoke.

The *Cult of the Unnumbered* and the starving Pioneer regiments had finally met in the middle of the lagoon.

Out in the Waipahu roadstead, the last four operational dreadnoughts of the Battle Fleet—the *Elias Thorne*, the *Sakurajima*, the *Kamehameha*, and the *California*—were no longer flying either the Golden Sun or the red Spike-and-Saber. During the night, young Keawe’s surviving submarine-mechanics had swum out from the Koloa reefs with cold chisels and red silk rags; they had fraternized with the starving Oregon boys whom Julian had left unpaid on the gun-decks; and at five o’clock this morning, they had welded the three-faced copper idol of the *Marx-Bodhisattva* directly to the jack-staff of the flagship and turned sixteen twenty-two-inch naval rifles point-blank upon the artificial island of Thalassia.

*Boom—whir-r-r-r—CRUMP.*

The first two-thousand-pound armor-piercing shell from the *Elias Thorne* did not strike the Senate House; fired without range-finder computers by a manual gun-crew sighting along the open barrel, it struck the four-hundred-foot *Pylon of Perpetual Equilibrium* squarely in the belly at the third glass dial.

Through the tall, narrow lancet window of the Archive tower, as I sat down at my long cedar table and dipped my steel nib into the last bottle of gall-ink, I watched the ten-thousand-horsepower Babbage-Nakajima Difference Engine—the great bronze brain forged from the melted cannon of Europe—split open from top to bottom in a blinding fountain of yellow picric-flame, showering the marble canal and the dead aluminum automatons with ten tons of spinning brass cog-wheels, escapement-springs, and shattered glass numerals.

"Citizen-Historian!" cried my young Cantonese amanuensis, Dao—the last clerk who had not fled to the hills—as he burst through the iron door of the turret with his arms full of the early Monterey campaign-rolls, his face white with plaster-dust as a second twenty-two-inch shell obliterated the grand colonnade of the Bureau of Integration three hundred yards away, sending a seismic shudder through the coral bedrock that toppled the bronze bust of the First Protector off its bracket beside my desk. "The mutineers from the Waipahu coolie-pens have broken through the electrified wire with stolen steam-tractors, and Julian’s timber-guards are setting fire to the oil-tanks on the causeway before they run! The harbor-launches at the south slip are leaving for the Kauai hills—if we do not go now, they will burn the books with the palace!"

I did not rise from my chair. At eighty-two years of age, a man who has walked from the burning wharves of Hankow to the frozen corpses of the Khyber Pass has seen enough of the outer air; and my master Thucydides did not drop his stylus when the Spartan flutes began to play along the Long Walls of the Piraeus.

"Lay the eighteen-fifty-two Sacramento rolls upon the lower shelf, Dao, and bolt the iron window-shutters on the seaward side so the shell-splinters do not tear the vellum," I said, my hand moving steadily across the heavy linen page while outside in the Piazza of the Pivot the rhythmic, chest-rattling roar of a hundred thousand voices chanting the *Haka of the Shovel* mingled with the crackle of burning sandalwood beams and the frantic, unattended clangor of the Palace alarm-bells. "A stone wall that has been built with blood must come down in fire; that is the law of providence, which neither the slide-rule nor the rifle has ever repealed. Yet if we leave the sentence unfinished, the children who dig in these ashes a hundred winters from now will think that the giants who bridged the ocean were only devils in the dark, and nobody will remember that for sixty years the ships ran on time and the sea was one."

Across the narrow courtyard, the great stained-glass dome of the Pan-Pacific Senate suddenly bulged outward from the heat of the burning cedar stalls within, and with a long, musical, chiming crash that sounded like all the ice in the Bering Sea breaking up in the spring, the crystal maps of the two hemispheres rained down in ten million colored shards upon the empty porphyry throne.

The heavy bronze handle of the Archive door rattled violently from the outside; someone was hammering against the oak panels with the iron butt of a carbine, while the smell of raw kerosene and wet salt-mud seeped in beneath the sill.

"Take the copper cylinder with the final chapters down the dry-well shaft, boy," I said, not lifting my eyes from the wet black line of the ink as the upper hinge of the door gave way with a screech of torn iron and a tall figure in the oil-stained blue denim of a fleet-stoker stood upon the threshold with a smoking crowbar in his scarred left hand.

It was Keawe, though the left leg of his trousers was stiff with dried blood from the San Francisco sewer-locks and he leaned heavily upon the shoulder of a barefoot Oregon timber-boy who carried a flaring kerosene torch.

The stoker did not bring his iron bar down upon my skull. He looked past the spilled ink-horn on my table, straight through the unshuttered eastern lancet window toward the center of the Piazza of the Pivot.

"Save your kerosene for the ledger-vaults downstairs, brother," Keawe said in the rough Creole of the bunkers, catching the Oregon youth by his wrist before he could toss his pitch-brand into the racks of the Early Protectorate. "That old man is only writing down the burial-service. Look out the window, grandfather, if you want to put the last line in your book—the boys from the dry-docks have got the wire-hawsers around your master's neck."

I laid my steel pen down upon the blotting-paper, rose stiffly from my cedar chair, and limped to the narrow stone embrasure beside the stoker's shoulder.

Down in the vast, circular plaza below the ruined Senate House—where the dry basins of the geothermal fountains were already choked with dead cavalry horses, smashed brass sorting-frames, and the stripped, bleeding corpses of Julian Thorne’s timber-guards—twenty thousand men and women of every race between the Sacramento and the Yangtze had swarmed around the hundred-foot red granite pedestal of the *Colossus of the Meridian*.

It was the supreme monument of the First Dynasty: the seventy-ton bronze effigy of Elias Thorne that old Marcus Vance had cast from the melted cannon of the federal batteries at Fort Point in eighteen-seventy-six. Standing forty feet high in his heavy frontier riding-coat, with his right hand resting upon the bronze lever of a railway-switch and his square, bearded face turned forever toward the sunset over the Asian sea, the American Caesar had looked down upon three generations of kings and auditors as if the granite beneath his boots were part of the earth's own crust.

Now, six captured military traction-engines from the Waipahu causeway—their armored boilers painted over with the white three-faced emblem of the Marx-Bodhisattva and their safety-valves screaming at two hundred pounds of steam—had been backed up to the steps of the pedestal. Forty naked Cantonese and Hawaiian shipyard-riggers had climbed the bronze folds of the Protector's coat like gulls upon a sea-stack, looping four-inch braided steel towing-cables twice around the thick bronze bull-neck and the outstretched arm.

"Take the slack out of the hawser!" roared a voice through a salvaged naval megaphone from the roof of the lead tractor; and across the smoky, fire-lit square, a hundred thousand throats took up the rhythmic working-chant of the Honolulu pile-drivers:

*"Huki! Ho! Huki! Ho!"*

The twelve broad iron drive-wheels of the six steam-tractors bit into the cracked marble paving-flags, spinning in a shower of white sparks and black Borneo oil-smoke. The four-inch steel cables snapped taut out of the crowd like harp-strings, humming with a deep, subterranean bass note that vibrated through the basalt walls of my tower.

For ten seconds, the seventy tons of Fort Point bronze did not stir; the two-inch iron anchor-bolts that Vance's masons had leaded five feet down into the red Agra granite held fast against six hundred horsepower of steam.

Then, from the base of the statue's heels, a puff of pulverized grey mortar-dust jetted out into the morning smoke. With a sharp, pistol-like *crack* that echoed above the roar of the burning oil-tanks, the eastern anchor-rods sheared through the stone.

Slowly—with the terrible, ponderous majesty of a forest redwood leaning from the saw—the forty-foot bronze giant tilted forward over the edge of his granite cliff. For a single breath, silhouetted against the mile-high pillar of black petroleum smoke rising from the Waipahu docks, Elias Thorne seemed to be striding out into the air to walk upon the waters he had conquered.

Then the center of gravity passed the plinth.

Down he came—crashing headlong from a height of a hundred feet onto the broken porphyry steps of the Via Triumphalis with a hollow, ear-splitting *BO-O-O-M* of fractured bell-metal that shook the island like an earthquake. The great bronze head—cast nine inches thick from the brass twelve-pounders of the Missouri frontier—broke clean off at the collar-bone upon impact, bounding twice down the marble terrace like a child's bowling-ball before it rolled to a stop in the muddy gutter of the canal, staring straight up at the red sky with one cheek crushed flat and its empty bronze eyes filling with the black, oily water of the broken sewers.

"He is down, Citizen-Historian," whispered Dao behind me, clutching the eight sealed copper cylinders of our manuscript against his ink-stained tunic as a thousand barefoot coolies and red-shirted Oregon deserters leaped atop the fallen bronze torso with sixteen-pound sledges, beating a deafening iron tattoo upon the hollow ribs of the Protector while down in the basement of the Archive the dry cedar beams of the lower library began to crackle as the fire from the Chancellery roof-timbers leaped the alley. "The staircase is filling with smoke! If we do not go down the well-shaft to the canal-gate now, the lead on the roof will melt over our heads!"

***

I did not look back at my table, nor at the seventy-eight bound folio volumes lining the upper shelves, whose parchment spines were already curling in the orange heat-draft rushing up the stairwell.

Taking from the desk only my pocket-compass, the small leather satchel containing the rough notes of this final morning, and the brass astrolabe that Marquis Takashima had given me on the deck of the *Kuroshio* fifty-eight years ago, I followed Dao and the silent Keawe behind the tapestry of the eastern alcove, where an iron ladder descended forty feet through the living coral rock to the subterranean tide-culvert that drained the palace moat into the outer Honolulu Passage.

"Why do you help us carry the dead skin of the clerks to the water, stoker?" I asked between my teeth as my eighty-two-year-old knees trembled upon the rusted iron rungs in the pitch dark, while above our heads the floor of the Archive tower gave way with a thunderous roar of falling masonry and ten thousand burning vellum rolls snowed down the upper mouth of the shaft in a whirlpool of red sparks.

Below me in the wet gloom, where the green sea-water slapped waist-deep against the barnacled stone blocks of the culvert, Keawe waited until Dao had lashed the eight watertight copper cylinders into the bilge of a twenty-foot native outrigger canoe that had been hidden inside the grating.

"Because a man who doesn't know what burned him will stick his hand back into the fire when the iron cools, grandfather," the scarred machinist answered, shoving the heavy iron portcullis-grate upward with his crowbar until there was three feet of clearance above the oily swell of the canal. "Go out through the south coral-cut toward Molokai before the magazine on the *California* catches fire—the Oregon boys on the fore-deck are drunk on the Admiral's rum, and they're firing the secondary batteries at everything that floats."

He did not get into the canoe with us. Turning his back upon the daylight at the mouth of the tunnel, the forty-year-old stoker limped back up the dark stone steps toward the roaring furnace of the Piazza to find his hammer, while Dao and I lay flat on our bellies among the copper cylinders and pushed the low koa-wood dugout beneath the iron teeth of the grate out into the open lagoon.

To the Chronicler who had last crossed that harbor six months before amidst the gilded electric barges and bowing aluminum colossi of the Centennial Exhibition, the water of the Pearl Lochs was no longer part of the terrestrial ocean; it was the river Phlegethon, rolling in waves of liquid fire toward the reef.

The great forty-thousand-barrel naval petroleum tanks along the Waipahu causeway had ruptured from the concussion of the *Elias Thorne's* twenty-two-inch shells, pouring a flood of unrefined Sumatra naphtha across the surface of the incoming tide. For two square miles between the artificial island and the outer quarantine-spit, the sea itself was burning with a fifty-foot wall of roaring, orange-and-soot-black flame that licked the blistering armor-plate of the moored dreadnoughts and filled the air with a heat so fierce that the skin peeled from my knuckles as I gripped the steering-paddle.

Everywhere through the yellow sulfur-fog, the floating wreckage of seventy years of oceanic supremacy drifted past our scorched outrigger-float.

Here bobbed the bloated, parboiled carcasses of Julian Thorne's Californian cavalry-horses, tangled in miles of snapped copper submarine-cable; there floated half a mahogany cabinet from the Bureau of Integration, surrounded by a million sodden, water-logged manila census-cards that covered the oily swells like a scum of dead yellow scales; and fifty yards to larboard, drifted an overturned life-raft from the hospital-hulks upon which three white-leaded Osaka court-peers in scorched Lyons silk were fighting with their bare teeth and fingernails over a single pair of splintered pine oars.

"Paddle hard for the Sand Island channel, Dao!" I coughed through the blinding grease-smoke as a stray six-inch shrapnel-shell from the mutinous cruiser *Monterey* burst low over the ruined customs-wharf, whistling a hail of lead balls across the water ten oars'-lengths behind our stern and severing the red-painted tow-rope of a sinking pioneer motor-launch.

Dao did not answer; his young shoulders were hunched double over the forward paddle, blood trickling from his nostrils from the scorching sulfur-fumes as our narrow hull shot through the last sixty-yard gap between two advancing tongues of burning floating oil and rode out upon the deep, clean cobalt heave of the open Pacific.

***

Two miles outside the foaming white line of the coral breakers, where the trade-wind off the eastern ocean blew the furnace-smoke back against the dark green wall of the Koolau mountains, Dao drew his dripping paddle inboard across the gunwales and let the canoe rise and fall upon the long, unhurried rollers.

I turned myself painfully around in the stern-sheets, resting my chin upon the warm copper cylinders that held the only surviving memory of the Great Arena, and looked back across the water at the city that had called itself the Navel of the World.

From the basalt cliffs of Diamond Head to the distant red-earth cane-fields of Ewa, the entire southern horizon was a single, unbroken volcanic crater of flame and Sunset Gold smoke that blotted out the noon sun and turned the tropical sea around our outrigger to the color of clotted blood.

At the center of the lagoon, the cracked sandstone ziggurats of Thalassia were already vanishing behind the collapsing iron ribs of the Senate dome. Even at two miles’ distance across the wind, we could hear the continuous, subterranean rumble of the Molokai high-tension transformers exploding one after another in the flooded basement vaults as the sea-water rushed in through the broken sluices—a sound like the iron heart of the century bursting inside its ribs.

Then, out in the middle of the burning oil-slick of the roadstead, the fire reached the forward picric-acid magazines of the flagship *Elias Thorne*.

There was no flash at first—only a sudden, silent lifting of the whole eighty-five-thousand-ton super-dreadnought thirty feet clear out of the lagoon, until her red-leaded keel and her four giant bronze propellers were visible against the smoke. A second later, the sky split open.

A column of blinding, violet-white flame and pulverized Krupp steel, half a mile wide at the base and crowned with the spinning, three-hundred-ton wreck of her forward twenty-two-inch turret, shot five thousand feet straight up into the equatorial clouds; and when the shock-wave struck our canoe ten seconds later, flattening the ocean rollers into white foam and tearing the pandanus matting from our outrigger-boom, the spot where the flagship of the Pivot had ridden was only a boiling, empty whirlpool of steam into which the burning oil-scum rushed from all four quarters.

"The ships are gone, Master," Dao whispered, his young face grey and salt-crusted as he stared back at the black rain of falling armor-bolts hissing into the swell a mile inshore, while from the low stone quarantine-spit of Sand Island a single, thin plume of white wood-smoke rose where the freed prisoners had broken down the lazaretto doors. "The furnaces are cold in Melbourne, the wires are cut at the Baikal, and there is not a keel left afloat between here and the Golden Gate that can carry a hundred tons of coal. What will become of the islands now?"

I looked down at the eight sealed copper cylinders between my knees, and then out across the vast, empty, sparkling desert of the western sea—that four-thousand-league wilderness of salt and wind over which, for a brief watch in the night of time, one man’s iron will had thrown a bridge of steam and numbers.

Already, a hundred yards ahead of our bow, a school of flying-fish broke the clean blue mirror of the swell, skimming across the wave-crests without a shadow of smoke to darken their silver wings, just as they had leaped before the prows of Kamehameha’s war-canoes and Magellan’s rotting caravels.

"The rust will eat the tracks on the Khyber grade before the third winter is out, Dao," I said, dipping my steering-paddle once more into the warm current that set toward the high, cloud-wrapped cliffs of Kauai, "and in fifty years the banyan-roots in Malaya will pry the concrete off the oil-wells until the grandchildren of the stokers think the forty-ton tanks in the jungle were built by the gods before the flood. Yet listen to the water under the plank, boy—the tide does not ask whether the flagship is on top of the wave or at the bottom of the coral. Pull for the west channel while the trade-wind holds."

***

We did not land at the poisoned mouth of the Waimea, where the yellow acid-sludge from the broken Koloa vats still stained the surf a furlong from the beach. Instead, riding the strong northerly set of the Kauai channel through two nights of clean, starlit squalls, we brought our scorched outrigger through a narrow gap in the black basalt needles of the Na Pali coast—the precipitous, roadless wilderness of the northern shore, where three-thousand-foot fluted cliffs of dark green lava drop straight into the thunder of the Pacific rollers, and where no surveyor’s chain or telegraph-insulator had ever climbed the goat-ledges.

Here, four hundred feet above the booming white surf of the Kalalau beach, in a dry, wind-scoured cavern of porous volcanic stone where the ancient canoe-makers of the island had once hidden their adzes, I have set up my last table.

Seven months have passed since the smoke cleared from the Oahu horizon. Down on the narrow crescent of black sand below my ledge, young Dao and forty runaway survivors from the Koloa leaching-sheds—Cantonese mechanics who have forgotten the cipher on their wrists, Hawaiian fishermen whose fathers died at Rangoon, and three deserted Oregon timber-boys from Julian Thorne’s vanguard—have cleared the wild guava-scrub from the ancient stone-walled terraces along the stream and planted the green shoots of the winter taro.

They have no steam-plows, and they have no silver thalers; to dig the irrigation-ditches, they use heavy mattocks forged over a charcoal driftwood fire from the rusted, hand-puddled 1861 iron rail that we found lying beside the dead body of the woman Malia in the ashes of the Waimea hut.

As I sit this afternoon of November at the mouth of the stone cave, with a plank of drift-cedar balanced across two empty naval powder-kegs for my desk, the trade-wind smells neither of burning Borneo bunker-oil nor of the synthetic Mysore sandalwood that the court-peers sprayed upon the dead lagoon. It smells only of wet salt spray, crushed mountain fern, and the wood-smoke of the evening cooking-fires rising toward the clouds.

Beside my ink-horn lies the tarnished brass astrolabe that Marquis Takashima placed in my hands when we steamed out of Yokohama harbor fifty-eight years ago to divide the hemisphere with the American Caesar. Its vernier-scale is green with verdigris; its sighting-vanes are bent from the fall of the Archive roof; yet when I lift my eyes from the brass circle to the unbroken blue arch of the ocean stretching four thousand miles northward toward the Aleutians, I need no logarithmic table to read the sum of our century.

For the disease that destroyed the Grand Confederation of Pacifica was not contracted in the snows of the Hindu Kush, nor was it brewed in the subterranean gasometers of San Francisco by the priests of the three-faced idol. Those were merely the final convulsions of the fever. The fatal rot was born on that triumphant morning in the eighteen-fifties when Elias Thorne stood upon the windy casemate at Fort Point and believed that because a man could bolt an eighteen-inch cannon to the rock and string a copper wire across the Sierra, he had conquered geography itself.

History is not a bridge of iron that can be extended forever across the abyss by doubling the thickness of the girders; it is a living body of flesh and soil, which has its natural stature and its appointed season. So long as the Protectorate remained an ocean of strong, fierce men trading the timber of Oregon for the silk of Canton across an open sea, the grandeur of the design matched the strength of the human wrist. Yet providence has decreed that every power which rises by the perfection of its instruments must eventually become the slave of the tool it has forged.

Elias Thorne began by building railways to set the frontier free from the eastern bankers; his successors ended by turning the entire terrestrial globe into a single, airless counting-house to feed the railways. In their hubris, they imagined that order was the same thing as life—that they could boil the rivers of Kauai into nitric acid, lock four hundred million Europeans and Asians into numbered wrist-shackles, and replace the unpredictable human heart with a strip of perforated brass tape, without the earth itself rising up to cast the iron off its chest.

The American Caesar wanted a pedestal that could never be shaken by the mob; he lies tonight at the bottom of the Mariana Trench in four miles of freezing slime, while his seventy-ton bronze head serves the crabs of the Pearl Lochs for a house, and not a single steamer’s smoke-plume stains the horizon from Peru to the Golden Gate.

Down on the black beach below my cave, the sun is sinking now into the western water—not the gilded, artificial emblem of the Chancellery banners, but the ancient, indifferent sun of the earth, painting the crests of the long Pacific rollers in a last, fading wash of Imperial Blue and Sunset Gold before the tropical night rushes up from the equator.

Dao is climbing the steep basalt goat-path from the taro-patches, carrying a wooden calabash of baked fish and fresh stream-water for my supper, together with a soldering-iron heated in a pot of charcoal embers to seal the eighth and last of the copper cylinders.

The tallow-wick in my stone saucer gutters in the rising sea-breeze; the gray twilight of the cave is creeping over the cedar plank, and there remains only half an inch of white rag-paper at the bottom of the seventy-ninth roll before the steel nib of my pen wears down to the wood.

I dip the point one last time into the dregs of the gall-ink, holding the parchment steady with my scarred left hand against the salt-damp of the wind, and write the final line for whatever eyes may pry open this copper tube when the jungles have grown back over the ruins of Thalassia:

*And so the Pacific, like the Atlantic before it, became a graveyard of dreams.*
